10087-old-lady-number-31:
Louise Forsslund's 1909 novel, dedicated to her mother, opens at the tea-table and moves through good-by, a candidate, one of them, and the head of the corner. Indian summer, old letters and new, and an anniversary follow, in a story of later life and family ties.

Later chapters bring a winter butterfly, the turn of the tide, mental treatment, a passel of meddlers, a prodigal's departure, and cutting the apron-strings. Forsslund, author of The Story of Sarah, writes warmly about older women. Readers get a gentle domestic novel, where age brings both comedy and quiet courage.
15262-christianity-and-islam-in-spain-a-:
C. R. Haines's 1889 history traces Christianity and Islam in Spain from 756 to 1031, from barbarian invasion to Saracen rule. Early chapters follow Vandals, Visigoths, and Suevi, the planting of Christianity, councils at Elvira and Nicea, and the rise and fall of Arianism. Priscillian's heresy and burning mark a dark turn.

Later chapters weigh Muslim conquest, Christian survival, and the slow clash of faiths that shaped medieval Spain. Haines writes as a careful Victorian historian, with a full table of contents to guide readers. The book remains a solid, if dated, survey of a complex frontier of faiths.
15631-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly for boys and girls, for June 10, 1897, number 31 of volume one, cost five cents, at two dollars fifty a year. William Beverley Harison published it from West 18th Street, New York. The front announces a premium catalogue: readers who fall short of the bicycle's hundred subscriptions may choose smaller prizes from a selected list, mailed for five cents.

The bicycle offer itself repeats: any wheel in the market for one hundred regular subscriptions, sent in as fast as received. The atlas inducement repeats too: a Rand McNally 1897 Atlas of the World for a new yearly subscription of two dollars fifty. The atlas holds 160 pages of colored maps from new plates, on special paper with a marginal index. The number shows the paper layering its prizes: a bicycle for the ambitious, a catalogue for the rest, and an atlas for every new subscriber.
19780-report-of-the-national-library-ser:
New Zealand's National Library Service reported yearly on its work. This report covers the Service as a whole and its four divisions. They were the Country Library Service and the School Library Service. The Library School and the National Library Centre complete the four. The writer submits it formally, with the honour due official reports. Country service took books to rural districts by van and post.

Library reports sound dry until their reach becomes clear. A small nation was building reading access for every town. School services put books into children's hands nationwide. The divisions show a complete system, planned as one. Historians of libraries use reports like this as benchmarks. They record staff, stock, and ambition in plain figures.
22725-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, offers its issue of March 31, 1920, from volume 158. The catalog record names no editor. Parliamentary reporting gives this number its sample joke, from Question Time in the House of Commons, where Welsh place names tripped English tongues.

Trouble arose, Punch reports, over how to pronounce Bryngwran and Gwalchmai. One Welsh member present joked that he could have played those names, had he brought his harp. The gibe is gentle, and very Punch: politics softened into music-hall wit. Around the joke sit cartoons and verses of postwar life. The number catches the magazine in 1920, its war service done, settling back into the ancient trade of teasing the House.
28012-the-american-quarterly-review-no-1:
The American Quarterly Review, Number XVII, for March 1831, was published in Philadelphia by Carey and Lea, sold also in New York, London, and Paris. The first article reviews Lady Morgan's France in 1829-30, opening on a Dublin night when the streets lie silent save a watchman announcing the hour.

Lady Morgan and her husband are packing, trunks scattered with novels, travels, and volumes on Salvator Rosa, while the reviewer considers her account of France on the eve of revolution. The quarterly preserves early American periodical criticism, with reviews, essays, and notices across literature, politics, and history.
2822-london-in-1731:
Don Manoel Gonzales, the pen name used for a travel account of Great Britain, describes London as it stood in 1731. The writer compares the city's churches and squares with St. Peter's in Rome and the Vatican, judging buildings by how they can be seen from every side. Chapels rich in furniture spoil the prospect of a fabric, he argues, even when their contents draw admiration.

The account moves through streets, public buildings, and daily life, giving a foreign visitor's view of Georgian London. Its value lies in the detail of what a newcomer noticed, from the siting of churches to the manners of the town. Historians still use it as a snapshot of the capital before its great later rebuilding.
29309-the-death-traps-of-fx-31:
Sewell Peaslee Wright published this Commander John Hanson adventure in Astounding Stories in March 1933. Hanson recalls a harrowing trip among the giant spiders of FX-31. Hanson opens by defending himself against prejudice toward scientists, saying he has observed the scientific mind in action on many occasions and finds it rather incomprehensible.

Some scientifically minded men, Hanson admits, can be trusted side by side in an emergency. Young Hendricks, his junior officer on the Ertak in the early days of the Special Patrol Service, was one of these. Readers get a pulp space adventure of giant spiders and scientific courage, told by a commander who distrusts theory but trusts a good officer.
30124-astounding-stories-february-1931:
Astounding Stories for February 1931, volume 5, number 2, gives a full pulp issue under editor Harry Bates, priced at twenty cents. D. W. Hall opens with werewolves of war, the torpedo plan, and Captain Lance in America's last mighty battle with the United Slavs. Anthony Gilmore follows with a complete novelette, as Commander Keith Wells duels blind with marauding machine-fish in tremendous ocean depths.

Captain S. P. Meek adds a scientific mystery for Dr. Bird and Carnes, while F. V. W. Mason begins a two-part novel on Atlantis and Victor Nelson's Arctic adventure. Charles W. Diffin concludes The Pirate Planet, as Earth and Sub-Venus strike at the man-things of Torg. Wesso painted the cover from the Gilmore tale, and a readers' corner closes the issue.
30166-astounding-stories-march-1931:
Astounding Stories for March 1931, volume 5, number 3, gives a full pulp issue under editor Harry Bates, priced at twenty cents. Charles W. Diffin opens with a man who bluffs for his life against a prehistoric savage in Sentinel Mountain, using magic against magic. Ray Cummings follows with a complete novelette on a golden atom and an adventure in size, while Harl Vincent looses invisible robots on a gangster chief.

F. V. W. Mason closes a two-part novel as an aviator rides a strange sky steed to a great ziggurat, and Jack Williamson sends Charlie King through the fourth dimension to rescue the Meteor Girl. Wesso painted the cover from the Cummings tale, and a readers' corner closes the issue. For fans of early science fiction, the number is a compact sample of the Clayton era.
30177-astounding-stories-of-super-scienc:
Astounding Stories for January 1931, volume 5, number 1, opens the year under editor Harry Bates, priced at twenty cents. Sewell Peaslee Wright leads with the dark side of Antri, as Commander John Hanson tells an interplanetary adventure of the Special Patrol. H. Thompson Rich follows with a sunken empire, as Professor Stevens meets the Antillians on the floor of the Sargasso Sea, and Hal K. Wells brings a strange man of metal to Earth.

C. D. Willard adds the eye of Allah, with a secret service man in the president's chair on a fatal seventh of September. Murray Leinster supplies a complete novelette, as Tommy Reames rescues Professor Denham and his daughter, marooned in the fifth dimension. Charles W. Diffin carries The Pirate Planet into part three, with two Yankees on Venus. Wesso painted the cover from the Wells tale.
30452-astounding-stories-april-1931:
Astounding Stories for April 1931, volume six, number one, priced at twenty cents, repeats the Clayton standard for pulp science fiction. Publisher W. M. Clayton, editor Harry Bates, and consulting editor Douglas M. Dold promise clean, interesting, vivid stories by leading writers, bought under terms approved by the Authors' League.

Union shop manufacture, fair profit for dealers, and guarded advertising also feature in the pledge. Sister magazines range from Ace-High and Ranch Romances to Clues, Five-Novels Monthly, and Western Love Stories. Cover design by H. W. Wesso opens the issue, which served a monthly demand of more than two million Clayton copies.
30532-astounding-stories-may-1931:
Astounding Stories for May 1931, priced at twenty cents and sold on the first Thursday of each month, presents pulp science fiction under publisher W. M. Clayton and editor Harry Bates, with Douglas M. Dold as consulting editor. The Clayton standard promises clean, interesting, vivid stories by leading writers of the day, bought under terms approved by the Authors' League.

It also pledges union shop manufacture by American workmen, a fair profit for newsdealers and agents, and guarded advertising pages. Sister Clayton magazines listed include Ace-High, Ranch Romances, Cowboy Stories, Clues, and Western Adventures. More than two million copies were needed each month to meet demand, a sign of the pulps' vast readership.
31168-astounding-stories-july-1931:
Volume seven, number one of Astounding Stories, dated July 1931 and published by W. M. Clayton with Harry Bates as editor, shows pulp science fiction in its early magazine form, priced at twenty cents. The cover, painted by H. W. Wesso from a scene in Jack Williamson's The Doom from Planet 4, leads a contents page of adventure tales.

Other stories include H. G. Winter's The Hands of Aten, in which Craig hews three frozen Egyptians from solid ice, H. Thompson Rich's The Diamond Thunderbolt, A. R. Holmes's The Slave Ship from Space, Schachner and Zagat's The Revolt of the Machines, and the conclusion of Ray Cummings's The Exile of Time. The issue is a time capsule of the genre's wonder years.
31893-astounding-stories-june-1931:
This June 1931 issue of Astounding Stories, edited by Harry Bates and published by W. M. Clayton, carries the Clayton standard: stories clean, interesting, and vivid, by leading writers of the day, manufactured in union shops by American workmen. The issue opens with a castaway tale whose sidenote promises a young man, Bentley, swinging high in jungle treetops with a human brain imprisoned in a mighty ape.

Bentley survives the sinking of the Bengal Queen, which struck a hidden reef and went to pieces so fast that lifeboats were smashed in their davits. He swims away from the suction as women and children screamed. Readers get a full pulp issue from the early years of American science fiction, when wonder and horror shared the same pages.
33016-astounding-stories-august-1931:
Astounding Stories for August 1931, volume seven, number two, edited by Harry Bates and priced at twenty cents, offers a full issue of early science fiction pulp. Its contents open with Ralph Milne Farley's Danger from the Deep. In it, young Abbot, marooned on the sea floor with his hoisting cable cut, faces man-sharks. The contents also include Charles Willard Diffin's Brood of the Dark Moon.

Other stories include Starzl's If the Sun Died, Winter's Midget from the Island, Vincent's Moon Weed, and Meek's Port of Missing Planes, plus a readers' corner. The Clayton standard on the cover promises clean, vivid stories by leading writers of the day. The issue is a rich sample of the magazine that helped shape American science fiction.
5934-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Sancho's government begins in chapters forty-four and forty-five of this Don Quixote portion. Chapter forty-four tells how Sancho was conducted to his government. It also tells of the strange adventure that befell Quixote in the castle. The history's true original, Cide Hamete, supposedly left a passage untranslated by his interpreter. Chapter forty-five shows the great Sancho taking possession of his island, to govern in earnest.

Readers watch a squire become a governor, with ceremony, advice, and islanders ready to test him. The chapters favor comic administration, as Sancho's proverbs meet real disputes. This part suits readers following volume two's ducal episodes, since Sancho's rule becomes the novel's great experiment in wisdom from below.
alkhwarizmi-algebra-rosen-1831:
Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote the founding text of algebra in ninth century Baghdad. Frederic Rosen translated the Arabic work into English in 1831 for the Oriental Translation Fund. The edition prints the English alongside the Arabic. Algebra takes its very name from the book's Arabic title word, al-jabr.

Al-Khwarizmi teaches how to solve equations by restoring and balancing both sides. He sorts problems into types and works each one with clear rules. Trade, inheritance, and land measure supply his practice cases. The book carried Hindu-Arabic methods toward Europe through later copies. Readers meet a science at its birth. The voice is calm and practical.
an-accursed-race-pg2531:
Elizabeth Gaskell opens by listing England's own prejudices — Jews tortured, Catholics and Protestants burnt, witches hanged — before turning to a worse case abroad. In the valleys of the Pyrenees and up the west of France into Brittany live the Cagots, a people shunned for centuries. No one can say what their ancestors did, or even who they were.

Gaskell recounts the rules that fenced the Cagots off: separate church doors, forbidden trades, marriages refused. She writes as an advocate, angry at cruelty that needs no reason but habit. The short piece, part essay and part history, shows the novelist's conscience at work on real suffering.
arxiv-2412-00231:
Gupta and co-authors show how gust bursts, not smooth winds, lift glide eagles. Rough air grounds craft and costs force to fight in flight. Wild fliers still ride rough days with seeming ease. How glide birds meet short gust bursts had stayed dim. Past work dwelt on big, smooth flows in heat or slope glide. Tags on gold eagles showed short up-push bursts in flight.

Those bursts hint the birds seek strong, rare up gusts by choice. Lift shifts in them hit 25 spreads past the mean mark. That tops three times the pull of the world in size. Such force breaks a tale of gust dodge or soft cure. Burst shapes mimic swirl moves in rough air flow. At short spans, bursts skew up more than stock rough flow.
arxiv-2412-01031:
Razi Mahmood and a team of co-authors present a way to grade reports written by artificial intelligence for chest X-rays, in two thousand twenty-four. Older grading tools read only the words of a report. They can miss whether a finding is placed in the right part of the chest.

The new method first pulls out fine details for each finding, such as its site, side, and severity. It then locates the matching region on the image itself. Word and image scores join into one grade for the report. Tests against a gold standard set drawn from a large hospital collection showed the grade was robust and quick to catch factual errors.
arxiv-2412-03331:
Philippy and co-authors build a sentence embedding model for Luxembourgish, in this 2024 paper. Such models turn sentences into number codes that computers can compare, powering search and grouping tools. They need matched pairs across languages, which small languages largely lack.

The team hand-built a small but high-quality set of matched pairs and trained their model, LuxEmbedder, on it. The model codes sentences in the language well and links them across tongues. Tests also suggest that adding small languages to training helps other small languages more than big-language pairs do. They add a new test set for spotting reworded sentences.
arxiv-2412-04331:
Kriewald, Pinsard, and Teixeira compute, in a 2024 preprint, what a proposed muon collider could see of forbidden flavor changes. The processes would turn a muon and an electron into other charged leptons, breaking a near-sacred rule of the Standard Model. Heavy neutral leptons, hypothetical partners of the known neutrinos, could allow them. The authors work out the rates and angular shapes of the signals in that model family. They then judge the reach of the future μTRISTAN collider for spotting them.

Low-energy experiments still lead for muon-electron flavor violation. But for channels involving tau leptons, the collider searches win by wide margins. They beat related low-energy probes and planned Z-pole studies by several orders of magnitude in some cases. The authors say a high-energy muon machine would sharpen limits on heavy neutral lepton models. It would cover flavor corners that tabletop experiments cannot touch.
arxiv-2412-05431:
Pieter van Staden, Peter Forsyth, and Yuying Li rethink leveraged funds in long-term investing in a 2024 paper. Leveraged exchange traded funds promise a multiple of an index's daily move. Critics call them poor long-term holds, yet investors keep buying them. The authors argue past studies used naive strategies that undersold what these funds can do.

They study strategies that aim to beat a benchmark by the information ratio, a reward-to-risk score. A leveraged fund's payoff bends like a call option, so it can add cheap leverage with some downside shelter. Under simple assumptions they derive best strategies in closed form. For realistic settings, a neural network trained on resampled past data finds the strategies. Leveraged versions beat the benchmark more often than plain-fund versions, and sometimes dominated them in final wealth.
arxiv-2412-06031:
Amrutam, Gao, Kunnawalkam Elayavalli, and Patchell prove a comparison property for group C star algebras in twenty twenty-four. These algebras encode the symmetries of a group into operator mathematics. Strict comparison lets one compare projections by trace size. It is a key regularity property in the classification program for such algebras.

They prove it first for free groups on any number of generators. The method extends to a large family of non amenable groups. That family includes hyperbolic groups, free products, and mapping class groups. Applications resolve a standing problem about selflessness of these algebras. Embeddings of the Jiang Su algebra become unique in a suitable sense. The full Cuntz semigroup is also computed.
arxiv-2412-06331:
Qianqian Liu, Yaxian Zhang, and Heping Zhang wrote a 2024 mathematics paper on a count tied to how chemists judge the stability of ring structures. The count starts with a graph whose points pair off completely, a perfect matching, with none left out. For each matching, ask how few pairs must be named to pin it down as the only matching containing them. The largest such count, over all matchings, is the mark of the graph, its maximum forcing number.

For a square-grid torus of set even size, an earlier worker found the mark years ago. This team takes a fresh path beyond that route. They find the maximum forcing number for all square-grid tori with four links per point, except one class left out. The work neatly extends a line of counting that chemists use to grade how fixed a ring bond pattern is.
arxiv-2412-06531:
Egor Cherepanov and four co-authors bring order to the fuzzy word memory in reinforcement learning. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-four. Agents need memory to act on the past, yet the field uses the term loosely and tests it inconsistently, so claims about smart agents often mislead.

Borrowing categories from cognitive science, the team splits memory into long-term and short-term, and into knowing-that versus knowing-how kinds. Each published agent design is sorted into the scheme. A standard test protocol follows, so different memories face the same honest exam. Experiments with several agents show what goes wrong when the protocol is skipped: scores inflate and comparisons collapse. The authors offer the scheme as common ground.
arxiv-2412-07231:
Lubin Meng and co-authors present 2024 attacks on brain-computer links that read brain waves to control a device. Such links are cheap and handy, and most work aims at reading the waves with care. Their safety has had far less study, though models in these links can be fooled by crafted inputs.

The team builds two attacks on a filter step: one that slips past a trained model and one that plants a hidden back door. Both are simple to carry out and need no deep access to the target. Tests on three data sets from unlike link tasks showed both attacks work well. The authors say this is the first study of filter attacks on such links, and they call for more care on link safety.
arxiv-2412-08431: Zdeb, Warda, Robledo, and Giuliani study the role of pairing when an atomic nucleus splits in two, a change called fission. Their short paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Pairing links pairs of parts inside the nucleus. Fine models give three facts tied to it: the pairing gap, shifts in the count of parts, and a factor that damps the effect. The authors test how each of these three facts shapes a still, step-by-step picture of the split.
arxiv-2412-08831:
Kazuki Tomioka, Thomas T. Yang, and Xibin Zhang present a new way to estimate cost models for panels of firms, in a paper from 2024. These models split a firm's costs into noise and waste. Firms in a panel may also fall into hidden groups that share traits. Older methods often miss that hidden group structure.

The authors build a general method that lets the data reveal the groups. Their approach mixes firm-level steps with joint steps that use the full panel. They show the method works for a model where waste acts as a random effect. It can also extend to fixed effect forms used in past work. Tests on made-up data show strong results. The team then applies the method to cost waste in United States banks.
arxiv-2412-10231:
Liang and co-authors teach computers to cut 3D scenes into named parts using plain language in this 2024 paper. A popular rendering method builds scenes from millions of soft blobs, but attaching word meanings to each blob eats memory. Their system, SuperGSeg, separates the jobs.

First, neural blobs learn shape, object identity, and grouping from photos plus ready-made masks. A sparse set of super-blobs then carries language features lifted from flat images into the scene. This keeps memory moderate while supporting layered understanding. Tests showed strong results on picking objects by description and on labeling scene regions. The design suits interactive tools that must answer open-ended language queries about 3D spaces.
arxiv-2412-10931:
Haoran Sun, Upendra Harbola, Shaul Mukamel, and Michael Galperin wrote a 2024 paper on a method for probing tiny quantum devices. Two-dimensional spectroscopy spreads a signal across two axes, revealing how parts of a system talk to each other. The team extend the method to open systems where several flows can be watched at once.

Their test case is a nanoscale junction. Light signals and electric current through the junction are recorded together, giving a two-axis map in both channels. They build the theory with a standard tool for systems out of balance, then run sample calculations on a simple model junction. Combined maps like these could expose links between light and charge flow that single measures miss.
arxiv-2412-11231:
Tingfeng Hui and five co-authors argue that small models write better training instructions than big ones in a 2024 paper. Instruction tuning teaches models to follow commands, and rich, varied instructions matter. The field has assumed giant models should generate them, so most pipelines use the biggest available.

Across three evolution scenarios, the authors found the opposite: smaller models produced more effective instructions. Their outputs ranged more widely, yielding more complex and varied training data. Existing quality scores missed this, so the authors propose a complexity-aware metric that judged the data better. The result questions a costly default in model training, and the team releases its code for others to check.
arxiv-2412-11731:
Christoph Laaber, Shaukat Ali, Thomas Schwitalla, and Jan Nygård test a cancer registry's rule engine with auto-generated test suites, in work from 2024. Norway's registry checks cancer data with a web of medical rules. Hand testing alone cannot keep pace as rules evolve.

Three tools were compared: a general tester in two modes, and a registry-tuned variant. Ten versions of the engine faced the suites. Code coverage and plain errors found came out even across tools. The tuned tool and the general black-box mode covered the most rules with clear pass, fail, and warning outcomes. Injected faults were caught best by the tuned tool and two white-box runs. The registry is advised to adopt the tuned tool.
arxiv-2412-12731:
Dave and five co-authors present a paper from twenty twenty-four on judging mood in text with a mixed smart system. Mood reading of posts helps track public views and user feedback. Older methods can miss the right group count, handle noise poorly, and slow down on big data. The team mixes quantum computing steps with a fuzzy neural network, a system that copes with vague cases. They test it on two sets of tweets.

Their system beat classical, quantum, and mixed rivals on both tweet sets. It reached full marks on one set and nine in ten right on the other. It also held up under six kinds of added noise. The authors say the mix could speed mood reading at large scale.
arxiv-2412-13631:
Eitan Wagner, Nitay Alon, Joseph Barnby, and Omri Abend wrote this position paper in two thousand twenty-four. It argues that theory of mind in language models runs deeper than the reasoning step most tests grade.

Mind study splits the skill in two: first, judge if mind reading is called for, and how deep the nesting runs; then, draw the right call at that depth. The authors sort work from four camps, on benchmarks, add-ons, probes, and formal models. Most of it grades the second step alone, as a fixed logic task. They urge tests grown from the shifting scenes used in mind labs, so the first step is graded too.
arxiv-2412-14731:
Tian-Tian Li, Ze-Hong Guo, Xiao-Ning Wang, and Qizhong Zhu map the ground states of a spin-one Bose-Einstein cloud in a twisted grid. The work came out in 2024. The cloud sits in a light grid with three layers. Twisted grids make moire marks that cold atom tests can now build and tune.

In this three-layer setup, the moire marks come from links among the atom types. They do not come from hops between layers. The team weighs both pull types for the spins. One type draws spins to line up. One type draws them to point in flipped ways. They find the ground state forms a mark of split phases. On top sit swirls and flaws kept safe by the shape of the setup. Cold atom rigs probe moire laws past what hard stuff allows.
arxiv-2412-16131:
Beck, Eitler, and Gmeineder prove new smoothness facts for minimizers in a class of strain-based models, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. These models use the symmetric part of the strain, not the full strain. Minimizers can be rough, so even a weak slope may fail to exist. Past results covered the full-strain case, but the symmetric case lagged.

The team shows that bounded minimizers do have weak slopes that can be summed locally. Their proof works for the full sharp range where the full-strain case is known to work. As a direct gain, they get the first such results for an area-type model in this setting. The work closes a clear gap between the two cases.
arxiv-2412-16331:
Anas Mifrani writes a math paper from two thousand and twenty-four on efficient choices when sets of options are added together. In hard decisions, some options cannot be ranked against each other. The efficient options are the ones that nothing else beats. Adding two sets of options point by point gives a new and larger set. Mifrani asks when the best options of the sum match the best options of one part alone.

The paper proves exact conditions for that match to hold. Some conditions work for endless sets as well as finite ones. Others hold only for finite sets. Worked examples show each result in action. Such results help economists and planners who merge choice sets from several sources.
arxiv-2412-16531:
Atticus Sims examines, in a 2024 paper, how generative AI is forcing arts universities to rethink what they teach. Tools that produce original images from text have broken the old assumption that image-making is a purely human classroom act. Sims centers on Stable Diffusion, the open image model, and draws on workshops run in July 2023 that ended in an exhibition of AI-made work.

The paper maps the open-source art ecosystem, where artists, developers, and researchers build on each other in public. It then turns to the institutions: what breaks, what must change, and what cannot wait. The argument is for fast adoption rather than cautious delay. Graduates will work in an AI-augmented art world, and schools owe them fluency in its tools, its ethics, and its new divisions of labor. The workshops serve as the proof of concept.
arxiv-2412-17131:
Rushendra Sidibomma, Pransh Patwa, Parth Patwa, Aman Chadha, Vinija Jain, and Amitava Das wrote a 2024 paper on spotting hate speech in Devanagari-script languages. These languages, such as Hindi and Nepali, have few labeled data sets, so detection tools lag behind those for English. Full fine-tuning of large language models is also costly.

Their method tunes only a small slice of the model's parameters, a cheaper approach that still adapts it well. They tested several models on a shared data set with posts labeled for hate and for its target. The results show the light tuning works for these scripts. Better tools in local languages matter as online abuse crosses every language border.
arxiv-2412-17431:
Meunier and Gallet challenge a standard prediction about how swirling two-dimensional flows spread particles. Classic theory ties the spreading rate to the energy flow and friction alone, based on a smooth, scale-free cascade of energy toward larger swirls. Their computer solutions of the governing equations break that prediction.

Instead, strong isolated vortices form, and friction acts mostly inside their small cores. New scaling laws built on that picture match the simulations closely. The authors argue the vortex pattern is a universal feature of flat turbulence. Their result links textbook turbulence to the grand swirls seen in oceans and atmospheres.
arxiv-2412-18031:
Chiyu Wei, Sean Noh, and Ho-Chun Herbert Chang compare what faces and words each reveal in election posts on Instagram. Text sentiment tools are standard for social media, but images carry feeling too, and faces show it most directly. The team analysed posts about the 2024 United States presidential election from April to August 2024, scoring the sentiment of captions alongside the emotions on faces in the images.

Faces broadly agreed with text, with happy faces matching positive words, though neutral and negative faces added information that negative words alone missed. Around major events, including Trump's conviction and the attempt on his life, posts showing him grew 12 percent more negative. The parties also used faces differently: Democrats framed the opponent's fear as weakness, while Republicans framed their candidate's anger as strength. The authors argue for reading faces and text together.
arxiv-2412-18531:
Umut Cihan and co-authors wrote this industry study in 2024 on AI code review. Review by peers lifts code quality but eats time. Tools that let a language model comment on each change promise relief, yet their real effects at work were untested. The team tracked one firm that adopted such a tool, built on an open-source agent, across ten projects.

They zoomed in on three projects with 4,335 pull requests, of which 1,568 got machine reviews. About three-quarters of the machine's comments led to fixes. Yet the average time to close a request rose from under six hours to over eight. Most coders felt quality rose a bit, and bug catching improved. Faulty or off-point comments were the chief gripe. The authors weigh the trade-off for teams eyeing such tools.
arxiv-2412-19031:
Ma and four co-authors drill small tongue tools on code bank forms to fix faults in this twenty twenty-four paper. Big tools fix bank faults well but cost much and raise hush fears. Small tools lag on such tasks for want of bank form sense.

Inside, past faults and their fix pulls build two drill file kinds. One kind drills step-wise fault place finds in the bank. One kind drills patch writes from the found fault's near code. Tests on two known benches show small tools gain hard from the drill. Long bank reads also rose in the same test rounds.
arxiv-2412-19631:
Xiaoding Wang, Xiao-Han Ma, and Yi-Fu Cai study how primordial black holes could form in the early universe, in a 2024 paper. These black holes may have been born from dense lumps just after the Big Bang. Their model of cosmic expansion has an upward step, which warps the statistics of those lumps away from the usual bell curve.

Because of that warp, the standard way of counting black holes fails, and the authors rebuild the count. The expected number first rises with a key setting, then drops sharply past a threshold, then rises again. They also show a case where a positive skew does not boost formation, against common belief. Their care resolves a clash with recent gravity-wave data.
arxiv-2501-00531:
Frédéric Robert, writing alone, studies how solutions of high-order equations can spike in a 2024 mathematics paper. The equations are critical nonlinear ones on curved spaces, where solution families may concentrate at a point into a sharp peak, called a bubble. Robert analyzes the pointwise behavior of such families as they near that limit.

He proves a sharp bound that controls the solution everywhere by its peak shape and height. The key step is tight control of the Green's function for operators with a Hardy potential. From the bound flow obstructions: rules that can forbid concentration from happening at all. Which rule applies depends on the dimension. One involves the mass of the Green's function. Another involves how far the operator sits from a conformally invariant one. The paper gives a precise picture of when bubbling can and cannot occur.
arxiv-2501-02631:
Aleksei Dorkin, Taido Purason, and Kairit Sirts wrote this research paper in two thousand twenty-five. It asks how well a language model built for many tongues can be tuned to one tongue, Estonian. The team tests two ways to reshape the model's word list. One way trains a fresh tokenizer. The other way cuts tokens the model never uses.

The authors judge both ways on a named entity task, where the model must spot names in text. Training a fresh tokenizer made the scores worse, and they say the word vectors may need more time to settle. Cutting unused tokens did no harm, even after more training. The work helps builders shrink models for small languages at lower cost.
arxiv-2501-02931:
Charles O'Neill rebuilds the self-attention mechanism of transformer networks in the language of category theory, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Self-attention powers modern deep learning, yet its core mathematical structure is still not fully understood.

O'Neill focuses on the linear parts of the mechanism: the query, key, and value maps. He shows these maps form a parametric morphism inside a two-level category built from vector spaces. Stacking attention layers then corresponds to iterating a functor, and the whole stack becomes the free monad on that functor. He also treats position encodings, the signals that tell the model where each token sits. Plain additive encodings act like monoid actions, while the standard wavy sinusoidal ones obey a universal property of their own. The framework gives attention a precise algebraic home.
arxiv-2501-03031:
Fedoseev and co-authors wrote this 2025 laboratory astrophysics paper on cooking saturated hydrocarbons the way dark clouds might. Telescopes keep finding long unsaturated carbon chains in space, while comet and asteroid samples carry fully saturated ones, propane up to heptane. A surface route linking the two families was plausible but unproven in the lab.

Working under ultra-high vacuum at ten kelvin, the team first blasted a thin acetylene ice with ultraviolet light to grow longer chain molecules called polyynes. Then they exposed those chains to hydrogen atoms, mimicking cloud chemistry step by step. The two-step recipe tests whether hydrogenation on icy dust can saturate the chains into the alkanes the missions found. Their setup frames the hunt for the products.
arxiv-2501-03731:
Lorenzo Del Moro and five co-authors use a digital twin of the radio environment to estimate wireless channels, in a 2025 paper. A channel estimate tells a receiver how the signal was bent in transit, and good estimates mean faster links. Their twin is an electromagnetic model of the surroundings that predicts what the channel should look like before any measurement.

The Bayesian method folds that prior knowledge into the estimate and updates it as pilots arrive. Simulations show error dropping by more than ten decibels against standard methods, with data rates near the perfect-knowledge ideal. At low signal strength the method also slashes the number of pilot signals needed. Site-aware twins may thus pay for themselves in saved airtime.
arxiv-2501-05731:
Ding Ning and co-authors published this overview paper in 2025. It reports the results of a forecasting competition on sea surface temperatures, run at a major machine learning conference in 2024. Ocean surface temperature steers weather, fisheries, and climate monitoring, so predicting it months ahead is valuable.

Competitors had to forecast temperature anomalies, departures from the seasonal norm, three months ahead worldwide, using a standard climate data set. A side task pushed the horizon to nine months for the Baltic Sea alone. Teams brought varied machine learning approaches, from tree ensembles to deep networks, and the paper compares what worked and what failed. Lessons include how predictability varies by region and season. The authors draw guidance for future climate prediction challenges and for operational forecasting. They stress that careful validation matters as much as model choice in this field.
arxiv-2501-07831:
Juhi Jang and co-authors build a family of waiting time solutions for gas flow, in a 2025 paper. The setting is a half line of gas that meets empty space at a fixed edge. For a while the edge stays still, as if the gas waits, and then it starts to move.

The authors show that smooth solutions can hold that waiting form for a set time. At the switch, the flow turns rougher near one point and a weak break spreads along a sound curve. Away from the edge and the curve, the flow stays smooth. The work adds exact cases that test how gas and vacuum meet.
arxiv-2501-07931:
Waqar Hussain and John Grundy wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tests how well ChatGPT, in its three point five and four versions, guides people who manage their own diabetes day to day.

The pair put patient-style queries to both models and judged the depth and fit of the replies. They found gaps in accuracy and slant in the text, and note the models give firm advice without asking key facts first, which can be unsafe. Good replies mostly came only with skilled prompts. To fix this, they propose a sense-check layer for prompts and a memory store built for the disease, drawn on by search at run time. The aim is safer health use of such models.
arxiv-2501-09531:
Van Thien Nguyen, William Guicquero, and Gilles Sicard present a study from twenty twenty-five on a compact neural network for tight hardware, named MOGNET. Its core block stacks two point wise convolutions with a group wise one in the middle. That split keeps the model small. The second block's weights are not stored at all.

A cellular automaton crafts those weights on the fly, which trims chip memory. Low precision weights and signals are used with the aid of a multiplexer trick. That trick folds in skip paths with a bit shift rescale and no extra hardware fuss. A new three level weight scheme aids training. On a sub two megabyte budget, scores beat top rivals.
arxiv-2501-09731:
Wenlong Ji, Lihua Lei, and Tijana Zrnic link, in a 2025 paper, an old idea from biostatistics and economics to a new one from the AI age. When a true outcome is costly to measure, past work used a cheaper surrogate outcome that tracks it. Now, predictions from pretrained AI models can play that surrogate role for large datasets, in a method called prediction-powered inference.

The team build a recalibrated form of the new method. A step they call recalibration learns the best imputed loss from the cases where the true outcome is known. Their version always improves on an estimator that uses only the true cases, even when the imputed loss is learned imperfectly. When it is learned well, it gives the smallest variance among such estimators. Tests on three real tasks with top models show large gains in effective sample size.
arxiv-2501-10731:
Hope McGovern and co-authors study what translation does to echoes between texts, in a 2025 paper. Writers often quote or hint at older works; such links are called intertextuality. The device is hard to carry across languages, yet it shapes how readers read.

The team uses multilingual embedding spaces, which place texts from many languages in one map of meaning, to track the links. Bible texts serve as the test bed, since they brim with inner quotes and exist in countless tongues. Human and machine versions are compared. The study shows how much of the echo web survives the crossing, and where it frays.
arxiv-2501-11431:
Soares and five co-authors review what shapes the daily experience of blockchain developers. Their 2025 multivocal review spans papers and industry writing. Smart contracts opened blockchain to app builders, with fresh headaches attached. Tools must tame distributed designs and permanent data.

Sixty-two sources were mapped for themes and reach. Blogs and company posts dwarf journal coverage of the topic. Efficiency, multi-network support, and usability lead the tool agenda. Five lenses organize the field: hiding complexity, easing adoption, boosting output, teaching, and more. Academic work trails practice here, the review finds. Toolmakers are writing the field's real literature.
arxiv-2501-13131:
Vladimir Iglovikov benchmarks Python libraries that decode JPEG images, in work from 2025. Loading images is a bottleneck in machine learning pipelines, and JPEG remains the dominant photo format. The study compares nine popular decoding tools across two computer architectures.

The tools range from classic image libraries and big learning frameworks to specialised fast decoders. Tests ran on an ARM-based high-end chip and on a many-core desktop processor. Modern builds based on an optimised decoding engine ran up to one and a half times faster than traditional options. The author gives evidence-based advice for choosing a decoder by scenario, from high-throughput training to real-time serving. The results can help teams cut training time by fixing an overlooked step.
arxiv-2501-14531:
Xiao Wang, Hendrik Borras, Bernhard Klein, and Holger Fröning ask how to keep neural networks accurate when the hardware that runs them is noisy, in a 2025 paper. Analog computing could run the heavy math of these networks with far less energy than digital chips. Its weakness is noise, which drags accuracy down. The team compares two training-time defenses across several network designs.

One defense trains the network with quantized weights, using fixed scaling factors. The other mixes noise into training so the network learns to expect it. Both raised the networks' tolerance for noisy hardware. Noise training won, above all on the more complex networks. The authors present the comparison as guidance for teams designing analog accelerators for neural networks.
arxiv-2501-14631:
Robert Szafarczyk, Syed Nabi, and Wim Vanderbauwhede let sibling loops run at once in chip design tools in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. High-level synthesis turns code into circuits. Irregular code with many sibling loops is common, but tools run those loops one after another.

Their dynamic loop fusion is a joint compiler and hardware design. It needs only that memory addresses never decrease inside inner loops. A fresh schedule, borrowed from polyhedral compiler ideas, checks addresses on the fly without searching past history. Tests showed average speedups of fourteen-fold over static synthesis and four-fold over dynamic synthesis. The authors present it as a fix for a long-standing bottleneck.
arxiv-2501-15331:
Zexin Pan, Peter Kritzer, and Takashi Goda approximate many-variable functions with a median-based lattice method, in a 2025 mathematics paper. The setting is a weighted space where some variable mixes matter more than others. Their method estimates Fourier weights, the building blocks of the target function. Each weight is guessed many times with shifted lattice rules, and the median guess is kept.

Taking the median guards the estimate against unlucky shifts. The authors prove the error falls at nearly the best possible rate as more samples are used. The cost grows only mildly with the number of variables, or not at all, when weights fade fast enough. Computer tests back the theory. The work extends a median trick known from integration into full function building.
arxiv-2501-16931:
Christoph Lehmann and Yahor Paromau argue that single scores hide too much about model quality. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Accuracy or error is often reported as one fixed number. Yet training involves chance at many steps. Data splits, starting values, and tuning searches all vary. The same recipe can yield a spread of results.

The authors treat each metric as a random quantity with its own spread. They study quantiles of that spread and the confidence ranges around them. Real cases in classification and regression anchor the work. Simulations check the methods under known truth. Small samples get special care, since practice often allows few runs. The paper gives teams a more honest way to report performance.
arxiv-2501-17131:
Self-driving systems learn from huge piles of street scenes, and sorting those scenes by type would help, but labeling them by hand is slow and costly. Esteban Rivera, Jannik Lübberstedt, Nico Uhlemann, and Markus Lienkamp test whether large visual language models can do the sorting. They try models such as GPT-4 and LLaVA on their own dataset and on a public driving dataset.

The models read each traffic scene and answer context questions, sorting scenes without retraining for new types. Numbers and close reading both showed the models grasp urban traffic scenes well. The team packages the approach as a captioning pipeline that can be pointed at fresh datasets. They present it as a cheap way to organize the data that driverless research runs on.
arxiv-2501-17731:
Alberto Carlevaro, Teodoro Alamo, Fabrizio Dabbene, and Maurizio Mongelli pin down safe decision zones for classifiers, where a safe class call is backed by a chance bound. Trust in machine learning rests on a clear line between safe and unsafe calls. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

They define such a zone in formal terms, set by the chance of the target class and the faith put in the call. When data come from a broad family of distributions, the zone's shape is fixed by math and can be tuned by design. Since real data may break that family, they add a support vector method that mimics the zone and handles lopsided data. Tests and shared code back the claims.
arxiv-2501-18031:
Mateus Souza and co-authors present a 2025 cosmology paper that maps a sign-switching dark energy idea into a twisted gravity frame. The source idea lets the cosmic constant flip sign late in the universe's life, a mirror jump that eases two big tensions in cosmic measures. Inside classic gravity, the flip changes only the backdrop, not how clumps grow. The map into f(T) gravity keeps the backdrop but adds a growth effect.

In the new frame, an effective gravity strength steers how matter clumps grow. The team derive growth rate forms and fit them to galaxy drift data. They also refit the source idea with the newest supernova and sound-wave data. Growth tests could one day split the two frames apart.
arxiv-2501-18231:
Wesley Fussner, Simon Santschi, and Borja Sierra Miranda give, in a 2025 logic paper, one uniform method to build clean proof systems for a family of action algebras. These algebras extend classic Kleene algebras with meets and residuals, and they model programs and actions. The proof systems avoid the cut rule, which makes proofs easier to check and search.

The method covers any class of such algebras picked out by a broad family of mild conditions, given as analytic quasi-equations. Those conditions mirror most known structural rules of logic. Both well-founded and looping proof styles are covered. The work joins older results on looping proofs with tools from algebraic proof theory.
arxiv-2501-18531:
Hurtado and Marculescu applied graph learning to contact tracing on real human mobility data in twenty twenty-five. For fast-spreading diseases with many silent cases, tracing must be swift and automated. Exposure apps warn individuals, but reconstructing the actual routes of transmission needs the contact network itself.

The authors define a new network measure, Infectious Path Centrality, which scores contacts by their role on likely transmission paths. A graph learning classifier using that measure identified important transmission events with an F1 score of ninety-four percent. They also tested bidirectional tracing, quarantining contacts both backward and forward in time. When only thirty percent of symptomatic people were tested, bidirectional tracing cut the effective reproduction rate by seventy-one percent, far outperforming forward-only tracing.
arxiv-2501-19231:
Zihao Chen and Federico Botta map how unevenly bus travel times vary across England, and what that means for reaching health care, in a 2025 paper. Access studies often use one fixed travel time, but real trips change with the hour of departure. Using national bus timetable data, the team computed hourly trips from each small area to the nearest hospital and doctor's office, then built a score for how much those times swing.

The maps show a sharp urban-rural divide, clusters of steady and swingy areas, and some odd outliers. Linking the score with deprivation data split areas into four types, each calling for a different fix. The authors note that timetables give only a planned picture, and real-time data would sharpen the measure. They offer the score as a tool for fairer transport planning.
arxiv-2502-00331:
Ayyar, Matsumoto, Meyer, and Park, for a large lattice group, study the heat shift of a dark matter theory where the dark stuff is a bound state. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The theory's first-order shift, when its force first binds, could send out gravity waves in the young cosmos. The dark stuff here is a bound boson of low mass. The team fakes the theory on a grid, with a form of quarks that keeps fine traits. They watch three marks as heat and mass shift: a loop gauge, a mass gauge, and a twist count. The aim is to map where the shift is first-order, so its wave mark can be sought.
arxiv-2502-01131:
Daniel Munoz rethinks how the units of a network learn, by work in function space in place of parameter space. A past boosting method climbs by what each unit does, not by its weights. His 2025 work shrinks that climb to a steered gradient descent, where the input of each unit is first whitened, set to even spread with no cross-talk. The whitening sits outside the inference path, so run cost stays flat.

A live estimator tracks the whitening with no matrix store, and step sizes tune on their own. The method works where automatic gradients work: fold networks and transformer networks both take it, at home or spread across machines. Fast convergence shows in both rounds and wall time on a spread of tasks.
arxiv-2502-02531:
Blake Bordelon and Cengiz Pehlevan present a study from twenty twenty-five on how deep linear networks learn from a random start. Such stripped networks are a test bed for the math of deep learning. The pair track gradient descent at large width and on large random data sets. Their theory catches the sense that wider nets learn more well under one scaling rule.

It also shows how best dials can stay put as width grows, unlike under a rival scaling. Forms with skip links get a limit of endless depth when branches shrink at a set rate. One pass training is matched with training that reuses data. Power law data yields fast power law learning curves in the rich mode.
arxiv-2502-04631:
Henryk Laqua, Linus Dittmer, and Martin Head-Gordon explain a paradox of quantum chemistry: the basis sets that sharpen accuracy also destroy the sparsity that makes big calculations fast. Their paper appeared in 2025. Diffuse basis functions, spread wide in space, are essential for weak interactions between molecules. Yet with them, the electron density matrix fills in far from its diagonal, defying the expected exponential fade, and the effect worsens as basis sets grow.

Using an endless chain of helium atoms as a clean test bed, the team pins the blame on the flipped overlap matrix, whose entries are far less local than the basis itself. The authors say the artifact is now understood, which points the way to cures.
arxiv-2502-06031:
Safaa Menssouri and El Mehdi Amhoud build a guard for smart-device networks that can catch rare attacks. Such networks now run in homes, farms, and plants, yet rare attack types hide in a flood of normal traffic. A guard trained on skewed data learns the flood and misses the rare hits. Their 2025 system works in two stages to fix the skew.

First, a generative network forges fresh rows for the rare attack classes. Next, a cleanup pass lifts data quality by blending and pruning near the class edge. Tests ran on a known guard dataset with many attack kinds. The full system hit 99.9 percent overall accuracy and 80 percent on the rare classes. The team frames the gain as proof that forged data, used with care, can teach guards to see what they once missed.
arxiv-2502-06231:
Rickard Karlsson and Jesse Krijthe propose a test in two thousand twenty-five for a key assumption in causal inference. Estimating treatment effects from observational data usually assumes no unmeasured confounding, an assumption that cannot be tested directly. Their method tries to falsify that assumption using data from several settings.

The idea is that hidden confounding makes separate causal mechanisms look dependent when they should not. Their two-stage algorithm hunts for such dependence with high power while keeping false alarms in check. It needs no randomized data and works even when settings affect the outcome directly. Tests on simulated and semi-synthetic data showed it detects confounding efficiently. The work gives observational studies a sharper self-check.
arxiv-2502-08831:
Gandotra and co-authors work out the best way to send quantum signals through channels limited in both bandwidth and time. Classic systems describe channels by their spectra, which support frequency multiplexing. Quantum signals, though, decay fast and face delays, so they cannot stretch in time. The team derived channel capacities for these bandwidth-and-time-limited links. For pure-loss bosonic channels, they solved the best encoding and decoding shapes in closed form for two spectra.

Other spectra got numeric solutions. A general pattern emerged: channels switch on in sequence as the signal lasts longer. With only a few channels in play, some middle signal length works best. The results map realistic limits for quantum links.
arxiv-2502-09031:
Tomoyuki Tsuyama and a large team smooth the tiny bumps on metal films with a plasma process, and show why heavier gas wins. Bumps a few atoms wide mar disk films, and a glow of inert gas can shave them. Their 2025 study fires four inert gases at a bumpy cobalt slab in atom simulations, from light neon to heavy xenon. Then real disk films got the same treatment, for checks by fine probe and X-ray counts.

In simulations, the heavier the gas, the more the bumps shrank per pass, while the etch rate of the film slowed. Mass exchange between gas and slab atoms set the split. On real films, bump counts fell the same way, with less film lost for heavy gas. Fine surface shape can thus be tuned with small cost in depth.
arxiv-2502-09231:
Mohimenul Kabir studies how to count the answers a logic program can give, and what that counting is good for, in a 2025 paper. The setting is answer set programming, a way of stating problems so that each valid answer forms a stable model. Counting those models sounds simple but is hard to do fast, and older counters often waste effort on bulky encodings.

Kabir built an exact counter, sharpASP, that uses a compact encoding and beat current counters on several test sets. A second tool, ApproxASP, gives fast estimates by mixing hashing with equation solving inside a standard solver. As a real use case, the estimate tool was put to work judging how reliable a network is. There it beat both classic reliability methods and counters built for a related counting task, showing the approach pays off beyond its home field.
arxiv-2502-09331:
Mondshine, Paz-Argaman, and Tsarfaty ask when translating a prompt into English helps a multilingual language model. Many users pre-translate prompts because models still favor English. Others translate only parts of the prompt, with little evidence to guide the choice.

The team split prompts into four parts: instruction, context, examples, and output format. They tested every mix across 35 languages and four tasks, from question answering to summarization. Results turned on how close each language sits to English, how good the translation was, and how much training data the language had. The authors close with practical rules for picking a strategy in each setting.
arxiv-2502-09831:
Zhuangzhuang Jia, Hyuk Park, Gökçe Dayanıklı, and Grani Hanasusanto present a 2025 paper on fair policies for fighting infectious disease. Vaccination and lockdown plans can protect some groups more than others. The authors build a decision framework that treats fairness as a goal alongside saving lives and money.

Their test bed is a stochastic disease model with several population groups. The learning method, based on path integral control, searches for action plans under uncertainty. Different measures of unfairness can be plugged into the goal. In a case study, the method produced vaccination and lockdown plans that were more even-handed than conventional ones. The authors offer the framework as a source of insight for policy makers.
arxiv-2502-10131:
Lorenzo Pastori, Arthur Grundner, Veronika Eyring, and Mierk Schwabe tested quantum neural networks as cloud schemes for climate models in a 2025 paper. Global climate models run too coarsely to resolve clouds, so cloud cover enters through semi-empirical parameterizations, a leading source of projection doubt. Machine learning trained on short, fine-grained mock runs is a promising replacement. Quantum networks, with their maybe high expressivity, are options for the job.

The team trained several quantum network designs and old-style networks side by side on high-resolution mock runs from the ICON weather and climate model. Comparing accuracy under matched conditions. The extensive check maps where quantum models currently stand against strong old-style usual tests for a real geophysical task. Grounding quantum machine learning claims in a demanding application.
arxiv-2502-10431:
Janaka Chathuranga Brahmanage, Jiajing Ling, and Akshat Kumar present a 2025 method for teaching software agents to act within safety limits. In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by trial and error, but many tasks forbid certain actions. Older methods fix bad actions after the fact with a correction step, which is slow and can stall learning. Newer methods train a generator on examples of allowed actions, which are themselves hard to gather.

The new method instead builds a target pattern for allowed actions from signals that report how badly each action breaks the rules. A flow model then learns to produce only allowed actions, with no need for gathered examples. In control tests, the method broke the rules far less often than leading rivals, while matching or beating their task scores.
arxiv-2502-10931:
Capture-the-flag contests are the training ground of computer security, and language model agents are learning to play them. Meet Udeshi and co-authors build D-CIPHER, a team of agents modeled on how human squads divide the work. One planner agent holds the overall strategy while specialist executor agents tackle single tasks.

An extra agent writes a strong opening prompt for each challenge. Feedback loops let the team revise as results come in. On three public benchmarks the system set new marks: about 22 percent on one, 22.5 on another, and 44 percent on HackTheBox. It also covered 65 percent more standard attack techniques than earlier systems. The authors map the solved challenges to a public attack catalog for a fuller picture of offensive skill.
arxiv-2502-11231:
Kohei Yamamoto, Jan Niklas Reinhardt, and Olaf Hartwig recast a noise-cancelling recipe for space gravity detectors so it runs straight off the instruments' own readings. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Time-delay interferometry blends delayed signals to cut laser noise by a huge factor. Classic versions treat the craft as points and bolt on delay corrections from calibration.

In the new scheme, every delay in the blend is written in terms of onboard measures. Ranging signals that ride along with the science data supply those measures. Only the ranging chain's own digital delays still need fixing, and those are set by commands. The method also skips any prior syncing of the craft clocks. It even corrects drift between the clocks that time the phase readings. The authors expect a cleaner, more complete processing chain.
arxiv-2502-11431:
Ze Liu and co-authors propose in 2025 that all information, text, tables, charts, and images alike, be searched as pictures. Their idea, visualized information retrieval, renders everything as screenshots in one common format. Search then works on the pictures themselves, whatever the source was.

The team built a large dataset of screenshots in captioned and question-answer forms. On it they trained a family of retrieval models that let screenshots search, or be searched by, any kind of content. A broad benchmark test showed existing multimodal retrievers struggle with this format, while their models improved results substantially. Code and data are shared to seed the new field.
arxiv-2502-12231:
Shuai and eleven colleagues estimate objects' physical properties from three dimensional scenes in twenty twenty-five. Robots know object categories and poses but not mass, friction, or hardness. Their method, PUGS, rebuilds objects with Gaussian splatting, a fast scene representation. It then predicts physical properties with no task specific training.

Two added losses improve the rebuild: one sharpens geometry, the other groups regions. At inference, features spread properties across similar regions. A volume integration step suits the Gaussian format. The system set a new best score on a standard mass prediction benchmark. Ablation tests confirmed each design choice. The authors show the method helps with hard real world grasping tasks.
arxiv-2502-13531:
Lobillo, Santonastaso, and Sheekey wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on skew polynomial rings, a twist on ordinary polynomials where the order of multiplication matters. Quotients of these rings are a factory for building division algebras, structures where division works like it does for numbers. Those structures in turn yield strong error-correcting codes called MRD codes.

The authors prove new results about these rings and their quotients. Among them is the first clear example where a certain degree ratio for a skew polynomial is not at an extreme value. Their methods produce new division algebras, including ones that do not obey the usual rule that multiplication order can be swapped in grouping. Over finite fields, they obtain new semifields and new MRD codes for endlessly many parameter choices. The new families contain and extend many of the best constructions known before.
arxiv-2502-14131:
Enoch Kang and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on learning what drives choices from past behavior data. In one frame, agents pick acts over time to gain reward; in the twin frame, buyers pick goods under future gains. Both frames ask the scholar to recover the hidden reward from records alone.

Their method treats the task as risk reduction, a classic learning frame, and solves it with gradient steps. It skips the hard step of guessing move odds inside the core equation. It also drops the need for rewards of a fixed linear form. That frees the method to use neural networks and large state spaces. A math fact about the error surface gives fast global settling. Tests on fake data beat rival methods.
arxiv-2502-14431:
Buddha Nath Sharma and four co-authors dissect the COVID-19 market crash with tools from topology, in a 2025 paper. Topology reads the shape of data clouds, which can change abruptly in a panic. The team applied it to United States stock and commodity prices across the crash.

A distance measure between shape summaries spiked sharply for both markets at the crash, and the gap between the two markets' shapes spiked as well. Sector pairs inside the stock market showed the same pattern. Because spikes can mean either different crash sizes or a time lag, the authors ran causality tests too. Influence ran both ways between stocks and commodities during the crash. The work shows markets coupling more tightly exactly when calm analysis is hardest.
arxiv-2502-15931:
Akhil Jalan and Marios Papachristou model opinion change with many adversaries in two thousand twenty-five. In their model, users shift views based on peers and their own core views. Past work let one actor rig the network to spread strife. Real cases, like election meddling, hint at more than one hand.

Here any subset of users can act with a fake core view. Actors may push rival stories at once. The pair find the Nash balance of the game among actors. Tests on real data from social sites show actors can raise strife a lot. They also give bounds on the cost and ways for platforms to spot and name the actors.
arxiv-2502-16131:
Weichao Chen and co-authors present a training ground where fire engines and traffic lights learn to work as a team. In a city emergency, a fire crew's worst enemy is gridlock, and saving minutes takes coordination across departments. Their framework plugs multi-agent learning methods into the Unity game engine, so the teamwork can be rehearsed in lifelike streets.

Users can set how many and what kind of agents take part, how they learn, what they are rewarded for, and what limits they face. The demonstration scenario is urban fire rescue, where engines race while signals adapt to clear their way. The authors offer the framework as a simulation tool for city emergency departments, a place to test dispatch ideas safely before trusting them with real streets and real fires.
arxiv-2502-16331:
Akash Kumar, Rahul Parhi, and Mikhail Belkin wrote a 2025 mathematics paper on a gap between two learning worlds: Gaussian kernel tools and single-layer neural networks. A wide single-layer network, held to a fixed size cap, can represent a wide class of functions. That class takes in many classical smooth function sets, and some rough ones that vary in few directions. On a bounded domain, the kernel set sits strictly inside that class.

On an unbounded domain, with no box, the story flips, the team shows. Some functions in the kernel set have no finite size at all in the network class: the cap is burst by them. That is a real gap, not a trick of terminology. Kernel tools can represent functions that networks cannot, on the whole of space.
arxiv-2502-16631:
Radostin Stoyanov and seven co-authors present a 2025 paper on saving and restoring AI training jobs that run on graphics processors. Training at scale can span thousands of chips for weeks. In shared centers, jobs get paused or moved often, so clean checkpoints matter.

Saving a graphics job in a transparent way is hard, since its memory and thread systems differ sharply from the main processor's. Past tools trap and replay each device call, which costs speed and needs custom work per chip. Their tool, CRIUgpu, takes a different route and plugs into standard container systems. The paper reports how it handles live workloads.
arxiv-2502-16931:
Matthijs Douze reflects on why machine learning, for all its reach, has barely changed the craft of vector search, in an opinion paper from 2025. The two fields grew side by side in neighboring research towns. Big data fields around them were remade by learning, yet search over high-dimensional vectors kept its classic tools.

The essay walks the many bridges between the fields: learned indexes, compressed codes, and graph methods among them. It asks what kept those bridges lightly used, from speed demands to exactness needs. Douze writes from inside a major search library's team. The piece is short and pointed, meant to stir both camps. It closes by scanning where learning might still land.
arxiv-2502-17531:
Hongyu Zhou and Zorah Lähner published this paper in 2025. It brings a classic geometry tool to a new way of storing 3D scenes. In Gaussian splatting, a scene is a cloud of soft blobs rather than a mesh, and many uses, from editing to quality checks, need surface math done directly on those blobs.

The tool in question, the Laplace-Beltrami operator, reads how a surface curves and how heat or waves would spread on it. The authors build it straight from the blobs, using a distance measure that respects each blob's stretch and tilt. Stray blobs, common in these scenes, are kept from spoiling the result. Tests beat methods that first flatten the blobs into points. The operator can also grade a scene while it is still being trained.
arxiv-2502-18431:
Frederikus Hudi and colleagues built a benchmark of text-based puzzle games to test how well language models reason. The games, described in a twenty twenty-five paper, demand pattern spotting, spatial sense, arithmetic, and step-by-step logic. Models were tested on single answers and on longer exchanges where they could use feedback to fix earlier answers. The team compared general models with models tuned for reasoning, and they compared model scores with what people can do given enough time.

Models handled most easy and medium puzzles but failed often on hard ones, while people could solve all of them. Extra turns with self-correction helped, yet models still slipped on ordering, counting, and strict rule following. Models tuned for reasoning did better than models tuned mainly to follow instructions, which the authors take as a sign that hard puzzles reward real reasoning practice.
arxiv-2502-18631:
Milan Brož and Vladimír Sedláček revisit the encryption mode that guards most disk drives. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. XTS mode encrypts data sector by sector on storage devices. It is the standard behind full-disk encryption tools. A proposed change to the IEEE standard would alter its key scope. Confusion about what XTS can and cannot do clouds the debate.

The authors summarize how the mode works in plain terms. Its limits are drawn sharply, especially for sector-based use. They aim to give the standards discussion a shared factual base. Wider encryption modes that might one day replace XTS are weighed. Storage security policy gains a clear reference point.
arxiv-2502-18831:
Volker Perlick characterizes the light rays that circle endlessly inside a plasma surrounding a rotating or static compact object. The plasma is unmagnetized, pressure-free, and made of electrons and ions, sharing the spacetime's axial symmetry and stationarity. Circular rays matter because they mark where light can orbit, shaping shadows and lensing.

His main tool is a pair of potentials, one for forward and one for backward rays, whose critical points are exactly the circular light rays. With no plasma, their level surfaces reduce to the classic relativistic von Zeipel cylinders. The potentials' gradients split the effective force into centrifugal and Coriolis parts, with plasma affecting only the first. Examples on four spacetimes illustrate the theory.
arxiv-2502-19631:
Wen-Han Zhou and co-authors explain why so many asteroids spin slowly, in a research paper from 2025. Surveys from the Gaia mission found a surplus of slow spinners, split by a gap from faster ones. Past ideas did not explain the gap. Spin rates by size can reveal what asteroids are made of and how they change.

The team built a model of spin change over time. It pits hits from other bodies against inner friction that calms wobbly spin. In the model, the slow group is made mostly of tumbling bodies. The fit hints that many asteroids are loose rubble piles with thick dust layers, not solid rock.
arxiv-2502-20331:
Arunima Bhattacharya, Chinmoy Dey, and Vaibhav Pandey, with a colleague named Kumar, sharpen predictions for Higgs production in this two thousand twenty-five particle physics paper. The process pairs a Higgs boson with a massive W or Z boson at the Large Hadron Collider. It is a crucial channel for measuring how the Higgs couples to those bosons and for testing electroweak symmetry breaking. Near the production threshold, large logarithms spoil fixed-order calculations and must be resummed.

Using the universality of threshold logarithms, the authors apply soft-virtual and next-to-soft virtual resummation to next-to-next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy. Matched to fixed-order results, they present the invariant mass distribution and total cross sections for current collider energies at high combined accuracy. Such precision matters because small deviations from the standard model prediction could signal new physics hiding in the Higgs sector.
arxiv-2503-01631:
Joongi Shin, Anna Polyanskaya, Andrés Lucero, and Antti Oulasvirta tested in twenty twenty-five whether language models help designers reframe problems. Reframing recasts what a design problem is about, a creative step that demands fresh yet fitting perspectives. The team compared three ways of working with these models across two hundred eighty participants: free-form use, direct generation, and a structured method based on reframing theory.

None of the conditions improved the quality of the frames produced. Worse, model use widened the gap between experienced and novice designers, and novices felt less agency when working with a model. The authors conclude there is no evidence of benefit in this setting and discuss why the tools may fall flat at this particular creative task.
arxiv-2503-02031:
Richard Samuel, Charles Chimedza, and Caston Sigauke present a 2025 study of stock market volatility. Volatility clusters, drifts back to a mean, and reacts unevenly to bad news. Tails are fat, and shocks echo at two speeds. Risk managers need models that capture all six of these traits. The team runs five time-varying models against the trait list. Both simulated data and a real index, the Indian S&P index, serve as tests.

Market returns in the tests show all six traits. Long-memory analysis splits volatility into long and short parts. Shocks hit the short part harder but fade fast there. The long part persists strongly yet moves slowly. Traders and regulators get a trait-by-trait grading of common models. Picking a model by one trait alone can leave a risk desk blind to the others.
arxiv-2503-02131:
Arya Akhavan and Alexandre Tsybakov study gradient-free optimisation for additive objective functions. Their twenty twenty-five mathematics paper works from noisy observations only. No gradient information is available to guide the search. The target function splits into a sum of simpler parts.

Additive structure greatly improves accuracy in function estimation problems. Whether it helps optimisation was the open question here. The authors build a randomised gradient estimator for descent methods. Their method reaches the best possible error rate for this setting. Surprisingly, additive structure brings no large accuracy gain for optimisation. That negative result separates optimisation theory from estimation theory in a useful way.
arxiv-2503-02931:
Yago Bea simulates the radial flow of quark-gluon plasma with a well-behaved form of the relativistic flow laws, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The standard soup model works well yet strains on cause and sense at its edges. A newer flow theory drops those faults.

Runs under the new theory are matched to hadron push data from lead-lead crashes at the LHC. The fit tests whether the cleaner math still reads the real fireball. Readers in heavy-ion physics get a safer engine for the hottest fluid known, checked against collider fact.
arxiv-2503-03931:
Schmidt and nine colleagues describe an instrument for reading exoplanet atmospheres quickly in twenty twenty-five. When a planet crosses its star, its air filters the starlight. The ETSI camera captures that signal in fifteen colour bands at once. It works on moderate telescopes of about two metres.

A prism spectrometer and custom filters span visible to near infrared light. One transit can be enough to characterise an atmosphere. That speed helps pick the best targets for larger observatories. The system reaches near photon limited precision on bright stars. The paper details the optics, detectors, controls, and data pipeline. Early science results and other uses for variable objects are summarised.
arxiv-2503-04231:
Maciej Zuziak, Roberto Pellungrini, and Salvatore Rinzivillo present a one-shot way to group clients in federated learning in a 2025 paper. Federated learning trains a shared model across many data owners without moving their data. When clients differ sharply, splitting them into cohorts with personal models helps, but knowing when and how to split is tricky.

Their algorithm watches the angle between clients' training gradients and a temperature measure of convergence. Together these signal the earliest good moment to cluster, and the split then happens once, with no hand-tuned settings. Tests across more than thirty tasks on three benchmarks showed the automated approach performs well. The authors aim to make clustered federated learning turnkey.
arxiv-2503-04631:
