Dhanpal Bairwa and co-authors test whether a rare-earth compound hosts a quantum spin liquid, in a research paper from 2025. The compound, SmTa7O19, places its magnetic atoms on a triangle grid, a layout that blocks simple magnetic order. Such blocked systems may settle into a spin liquid, a state where the spins keep moving even near absolute zero.

The team made a powder sample and probed it with X-rays, heat measures, and muon beams down to very low temperatures. The tests found no sign of frozen magnetic order, even at 30 thousandths of a degree above zero. The muon signal changed in the pattern expected for a spin liquid, and it stayed dynamic under an applied field. Heat data also fit a gapless state, with no energy gap for spin motions.
arxiv-2503-05131:
Jia-Liang Lu and co-authors hunt in 2025 for new particles made of two heavy mesons bound together. Mesons are particles built from a quark and an antiquark. When two of them stick together loosely, they form a short-lived state that labs can try to spot.

The team used a model where the mesons swap light particles to bind, plus a math trick that can find both bound and fleeting states. They found several bound states and one fleeting state in these pair systems. One bound state matches the known Tcc particle, which supports the model. The other predicted states give experiment teams fresh targets to search for in their data.
arxiv-2503-05331:
Pikovnik and Zaplotnik use balloon soundings to check a huge wind loop in the north sky, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The loop drives rain for close to four billion people. Models say the loop has grown weak over past decades. Past wind data sets said the reverse, so the true trend was in doubt.

The team rebuilds the three-part wind field from sparse balloon reads with a neural network. They run the same rebuild on five modern data sets for a fair test. All five data sets understate how strong the loop is. The balloon-based rebuild shows a clear weakening since nineteen eighty. That result matches what models predict for the years ahead.
arxiv-2503-05831:
Tanner Mengel and co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on measuring how jets of particles lean in heavy-ion collisions. When nuclei smash, they briefly form a quark-gluon plasma, and particle output is lopsided at both low and high momentum. Jets, the sprays from hard scatters, carry clues about the plasma's flow and shape.

The team built simulated events by mixing a fluid-like background generator with a standard jet generator, then clustered the sprays. Multi-particle correlation methods, called cumulants, extracted the jet lean, and a Bayesian unfolding cleaned the signal. The method recovered the true pattern well, offering a firmer handle on high-momentum behaviour in the plasma.
arxiv-2503-06231:
Shankar, Chen, van Deursen, and Hai stitched generated time series in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Many tasks need synthetic sequences that honor both background metadata and a partial observed signal. Older methods condition on one source or the other, rarely both. They also force a choice between slow coherent generation and fast disjointed output.

WaveStitch, a diffusion method, conditions on both sources at once. Metadata enters during training, while observed values steer generation through gradient guidance. Windows are produced in parallel, then stitched with a coherence loss. Mean squared error ran nearly half the best rival's. Output came up to about one hundred sixty-six times faster than step-by-step generation.
arxiv-2503-08231:
Antoine Picard-Weibel and co-authors ask how well a PAC-Bayes bound can explain generalization in a 2025 paper. Such bounds promise guarantees that a learned model will do well on new data. The authors derive conditions a bound must meet to give a meaningful guarantee. Their analysis shows the best possible guarantee hinges only on how the starting distribution spreads risk.

In short, reaching a target level needs the starting choice to place enough weight on strong predictors. That finding bears on the common practice of building the starting choice from data in deep learning. It also questions claims that the framework by itself explains why models generalize. Readers get a clear limit on what these bounds can say.
arxiv-2503-08731:
Seyyed Moosavi Khorzooghi and co-authors grade face-blurring tools for both toughness and fairness. Blurring faces protects privacy in photos shared or stored at scale. Each tool had been tested on its own turf with its own yardsticks. Their FairDeFace platform lines up data sets, detectors, attacks, and fairness scores in one place.

Six attacks and several privacy, utility, and fairness metrics ship with the frame. Over five hundred runs compared seven blurring methods head to head. Some tools cracked more easily under attack than their claims suggested. Others guarded some gender or racial groups less well than the rest. Heat maps show which facial zones each method changes and misses.
arxiv-2503-09031:
Jisu Park and a large collaboration of co-authors calibrate the light sensors of a far detector hunting sterile neutrinos. Their paper from twenty twenty-five reports on JSNS2-II at the J-PARC neutron source. Two liquid scintillator detectors sit near and far from the beam. The far unit is built and now in calibration. An embedded LED system does the tuning.

Two ultraviolet LEDs flash the whole tank at once. Wavelength shifters in the liquid turn that light visible, spread near evenly. Gain, high-voltage curves, and peak-to-valley ratios were read for each working tube. Gain trims of a set size will even out the set for sharp energy reads. Timing precision was gauged as well. The values match the maker's specs, which clears the tubes for physics runs.
arxiv-2503-10731:
Mamunur Rahaman, Ewan Millar, and Erik Meijering wrote a paper from 2025 on sorting tissue images with no labeled examples of the target class. Doctors read such slides to find cancer, but labeled sets are costly to build. A new kind of model learns from both images and text, so it can match a slide to a written class name it never trained on. Tissue images are hard for it, though, since the cues are fine and layered.

Their method copies how a doctor works, by reading the slide at more than one zoom. It blends a whole-image read with reads of small patches, weighted by how much each patch fits the class. Rich written prompts, filled with like terms and clinical traits, guide the match. In tests, the method beat past zero-shot tools clearly. At times it beat models trained on labeled data too.
arxiv-2503-12431:
Abhinav Sharma and co-authors present a 2025 mathematics paper on Le Roy type functions. These special functions generalize several classics of analysis. Analysts judge such functions by shape properties. The question is whether they bend like a star or a convex lens when mapped into the complex plane. The authors seek clean conditions on the parameters that guarantee those shapes.

They derive sufficient conditions for the functions to sit inside an exponential mapping. That placement is the test for exponential starlikeness and convexity, in one variable and several. Close-to-convexity is treated too. Worked examples, consequences, and pictures illustrate where the conditions bite, giving users a checklist instead of guesswork.
arxiv-2503-12631:
Dana Fisman and Elina Sudit define omega-regular robustness in two thousand twenty-five. A robust system resists disturbance and still acts right. For range specs, tighter ranges plainly mean more robust. Omega-regular specs lack numbers, yet a like ranking feels natural.

A reply in two ticks beats a reply in ninety ticks, for instance. Their ranking rests on Wagner's hierarchy and a natural rank of infinite words. It is semantic, free of how the language is written. It fits intuition on common cases and meets set math criteria. A past five valued semantics is refined to an infinite one.
arxiv-2503-13131:
Yaxi Chen and seven co-authors present a 2025 method for reading knee MR images with simple, explainable features instead of a black-box model. Radiomic features describe image patterns in numbers that doctors can inspect, but plain models using them often trail deep learning in accuracy. The team lets a simple regression model pick a different feature set for each patient, drawn from a larger pool.

The pool grows through a second idea: a diffusion model rebuilds what the same knee would look like if it were healthy. Features from that healthy version give the model a personal baseline for spotting damage. The method matched or beat deep learning on tasks such as finding ligament and meniscus tears. It also shows which features drove each call, which doctors can check.
arxiv-2503-13431:
Vincent Herrmann, Róbert Csordás, and Jürgen Schmidhuber propose a way to tell when a neural network is doing interesting computation, in a 2025 paper. The usual score, next-token loss, misleads: low loss may mean a trivial sequence, and high loss may mean irrelevant noise. Their alternative measures how well a model can predict its own future hidden states. Empirically, that score tracks how interesting a task feels far better than token loss.

A small add-on layer, fitting any architecture, bottlenecks the model's main stream to make the measurement possible. A learned prior then prices the new information gained at each step. A honest gauge of internal computation could guide architecture search and help researchers spot where models genuinely reason.
arxiv-2503-13731:
Hongchao Li, Cheng Shang, Tomotaka Kuwahara, and Tan Van Vu wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It sets hard speed limits on how fast particles can be moved across leaky quantum systems of bosons, particles that can crowd into the same state.

Real devices lose particles, so transport theory must handle open systems. The authors build a version of optimal transport theory for such systems and prove how the shortest travel time grows with distance. The physics splits sharply by loss type: losing one particle at a time behaves differently from losing several together. With even a trickle of gain added, dilute gases can still travel far. Protected pockets where coherence survives turn out to enable perfect long-range transport. The paper also caps the chance of delivering a fixed number of particles under loss, and sketches experiments to test the bounds.
arxiv-2503-14531:
Boyang Ma and Michael Krüger build, in twenty twenty-five, a stronger theory model for ultrafast electron flow through tiny metal-insulator-metal junctions. Laser pulses can drive currents in these junctions at petahertz speeds, which could enable ultra-fast electronics and new microscopes. Their earlier strong-field model for tunneling microscopy is extended here to such junctions. The update adds several refinements. It accounts for the image potential inside the gap, an attraction from induced charge, and for boundary effects.

They also find that the Keldysh parameter, a standard gauge of tunneling regime, is not enough for thin junctions. A new parameter captures the effect of the junction's small size. Above a threshold of that parameter, photon-assisted tunneling dominates the flow, whatever the Keldysh value. In that mode, electrons absorb photons and then tunnel.
arxiv-2503-14731:
Ben Chiaro and Yaxing Zhang found a way to cut leakage in single qubit gates. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a core need for quantum machines. A qubit must spin fast and true between its two base states. Real qubits hold more than two levels, so fast gates leak state out of the working pair. That leak harms the gate's truth.

The pair added a second drive tone near the leak path. It cancels the leak the main drive makes. They also set out a test run to tune the new drive. Used on a known type of circuit qubit, the leak fell to a very low level. Readers who build quantum gates get a path to fast, clean control.
arxiv-2503-15331:
The Euclid Collaboration shares an early data release from a space telescope in a 2025 paper. The Euclid mission maps the sky to study dark matter and dark energy. This quick release joins Euclid galaxy counts with older Spitzer telescope data for very distant galaxies. The team hunts for dense clumps of quiet, old galaxies at early cosmic times.

Such clumps mark the seeds of today's galaxy clusters. The combined catalogs flag strong over-density in regions Spitzer had already marked as crowded. Finding old, dead galaxies packed together so early strains simple growth stories. Early releases like this one let the wider field test the data and sharpen the main survey's tools.
arxiv-2503-16431:
Lama Ahmad, Sandhini Agarwal, Michael Lampe, and Pamela Mishkin set out how one large AI firm uses outside red teams to probe its models for risk. Their white paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Red teaming — set attacks by testers — has grown into a key way to bare new risks and stress the guards in place. It can feed risk scores, build new safety marks, and shore up public trust. The paper sets out the design calls: who is on the team, how much access they get, and what guide they are given. It shows what the work can yield, such as input to risk calls and to auto tests. It also marks the method's limits.
arxiv-2503-16731:
Richie Li and Sicheng Chen built a hardware accelerator for the matrix math at the heart of transformer language models, in a 2025 paper. The attention step in these models leans on heavy matrix products, which form a key bottleneck. Their chip design runs on a small, resource-tight FPGA board.

The design keeps data on chip, reuses it through two levels of tiling, and unrolls its compute engine like a systolic array. Paired with a compact transformer model for its key projections, it ran seven times faster than a phone-class processor baseline. Against a naive software version the gain was about two hundredfold. The authors pitch it for efficient inference at the edge.
arxiv-2503-18731:
Pedersen and co-authors keep neural forecasts of chaotic flows from blowing up over long runs, in this 2025 paper. Fast surrogate models roll their own outputs forward, and small errors snowball until the forecast leaves reality. The fix they propose borrows from diffusion models.

For steady systems, a diffusion model can estimate the score of the long-run distribution. During a rollout, that estimate guides gentle denoising nudges, a step they call thermalization. In turbulent test systems, stable forecast horizons grew about tenfold. The work opens a new job for diffusion models: babysitting other models' predictions.
arxiv-2503-19031:
Arshi Ali and a team of colleagues wrote a 2025 astronomy paper on the galaxy NGC 5972. This galaxy holds a glowing spiral cloud of gas that stretches more than 10 kiloparsecs. A bent radio structure spans about 470 kiloparsecs across it.

The team joined data from three tools: the MUSE instrument on the Very Large Telescope, plus the GMRT and VLA radio arrays. Their sharp radio views caught the southern jet for the first time. The jet lines up with the southern glowing cloud, which backs a jet origin for the radio glow. Maps of gas and star motion show how the jet stirs the galaxy. Such feedback shapes how galaxies grow.
arxiv-2503-19131:
Muhammed Irshad and three co-authors study how magnetic fields grow in a collapsing gas cloud, in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Star and galaxy birth needs magnetism, and churning turbulence is the main amplifier. Past work on collapse leaned on a few computer runs. The team build a math frame, in coordinates that shrink with the cloud, and back it with simulations of both small-scale and large-scale dynamos.

In a collapsing cloud the field grows faster than the usual exponential curve, since eddies spin faster as the cloud shrinks. The final field also ends stronger than plain squeezing of field lines would give. The frame works for growing clouds and expanding regions too. The authors say fields may start to matter in star birth far earlier than long assumed.
arxiv-2503-19231:
Mane gives a general way to solve stepped equations with an added source term, in work from 2025. The equations are linear difference equations, where each step builds on past steps, and their rates may vary by step. The answer is written as a weighted sum of base solutions of the matching source-free equation.

The note frames the method through Green's functions, a standard tool for such tasks. Both forward and backward forms of the function are needed for a full answer. The setup fits an initial value task, as with smooth change equations. Mane also confirms past work for the simpler case where the rates stay fixed.
arxiv-2503-19731:
Junhyuk So, Jiwoong Shin, Chaeyeon Jang, and Eunhyeok Park present a 2025 method that speeds up diffusion models by guessing their end point. Such models build images step by step, which is slow. A past trick ran steps in parallel with an old fixed-point loop, but the loop could still crawl. The new model is trained to jump straight to the loop's final answer from any mid-way state.

A switching move patches the jump's weak spots and keeps the output exact. Tests across image making and robot control showed gains up to near threefold over step-by-step runs. Parallel hardware sits idle in the old flow; this design feeds it. Faster sampling cuts the cost of every generated image and move.
arxiv-2503-21031:
Malcolm Jones gives higher-rank graphs a local treatment of finite alignment, a property that many such graphs lack globally. He identifies the finitely aligned part inside any higher-rank graph. That part turns out to be a constellation in its own right and forms a relative category of paths with the original graph.

The elements of the aligned part are exactly those whose cylinder sets are compact. That fact yields fresh definitions of locally compact path spaces and boundary-path spaces for graphs that are not finitely aligned. Jones then extends a semigroup action and its semidirect product groupoid to build path and boundary-path groupoids for this wider class. The groupoids are amenable, and in the classic aligned case they match known constructions. The work hands operator algebraists tools for a class of graphs that older theory could not reach.
arxiv-2503-21431:
David Hofmeyr introduces a new clustering method in a 2025 paper. Clustering groups data points so that similar points sit together, and many methods need the user to guess settings first. His method defines a cluster by an equilibrium condition that balances the size of the group against how tightly its points hold together. Each point also gets a score for how strongly it aligns with its cluster.

Those alignment scores lead to a natural rule for choosing among candidate groupings, so the method can run with little user input. The algorithm is simple to code and fast, and it produced very strong results against known benchmarks. Code in R is shared freely for others to use and test.
arxiv-2503-21531:
Carlo Flore, Cynthia Hadjidakis, Daniel Kikoła, Aleksander Kusina, and Anton Safronov forecast what fixed-target measurements at LHCb will do for nuclear parton distributions, in a two thousand twenty-five particle physics paper. Those distributions describe how quarks and gluons share momentum inside nuclei.

The SMOG2 program will collide the LHC beam with gas targets of helium, neon, argon, krypton, and xenon, plus hydrogen as a baseline. Using the PDF reweighting method, the authors show D-meson and B-meson data would sharply cut uncertainties on the nuclear gluon distribution. Sea-quark uncertainties would also shrink, and the assumed dependence on atomic mass could finally be tested systematically.
arxiv-2503-22231:
Yishen Ji and nine co-authors introduce CoGen, a system that makes driving videos that stay true in three dimensions. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Fake driving footage can give self-driving cars cheap, varied training data. But clips guided only by flat maps and boxes often warp the scene from view to view.

CoGen first builds rich 3D guides that capture the shape of the street scene. These guides replace the coarse flat ones that older tools rely on. A special adapter then helps the model obey several guides at once without breaking down. The team reports strong gains in how well the scenes hold their shape. The clips also keep a real look, which makes them fit for training and testing car software.
arxiv-2503-22631:
Nicolas L Guidotti, Per-Gunnar Martinsson, Juan A Acebrón, and José Monteiro speed up a restarted Krylov method for matrix functions using randomization. Their 2025 paper serves applications that need a matrix function applied to a vector. Krylov methods excel here, but their memory and arithmetic costs force restarts that slow convergence.

The authors add random sketching to the restarted cycle. Experiments show the randomized version beating the classical one at equal accuracy. In some cases randomization even improves the convergence rate itself, not just the cost per step. The paper also benchmarks several randomized schemes on very large, ill-conditioned problems, comparing speed and stability. The work complements earlier theory with practical guidance for huge systems.
arxiv-2503-23231:
Hangzhan Jin and Mohammad Hamdaqa introduced CCCI in twenty twenty-five, a method that helps language models complete code inside large existing systems. Completing code is harder than writing it fresh: the model must respect variable scope, object models, and database links around the gap. For data transfer code, which leans heavily on such links, acceptance of suggestions can fall well below a third.

CCCI feeds the model the missing context: table relations, object models, and library details. The team tested it on nearly three hundred Java snippets drawn from over eight hundred working industrial scripts. It reached build pass rates near forty-nine percent and code match scores on par with leading methods. The study shows context, not just model size, drives useful completions for enterprise code.
arxiv-2503-23331:
Hongwei Zheng and six co-authors present a 2025 paper on estimating 3D human pose when body parts are hidden. Lifting a flat skeleton sketch into three dimensions fails under occlusion, because the sparse input simply lacks the missing joints. Their method, HiPART, first fattens the sparse pose into a richer, layered one. A token module compresses dense poses into graded tokens with an alignment step that keeps the layers consistent.

A generative model then rebuilds the layered pose step by step, filling occluded joints from context. The enriched pose feeds standard lifting to produce the 3D result. On single-frame tests the method set state-of-the-art scores and proved sturdy under heavy occlusion. It even beat many multi-frame rivals while using fewer parameters. The authors offer it as a complement that can boost existing video methods too.
arxiv-2503-23931:
Ryan Sweke, Seongwook Shin, and Elies Gil-Fuster simplify a method for showing that a quantum learning model can be matched by a classical one, in a short paper from 2025. Dequantization results mark the true limits of quantum advantage. A recent route uses kernel methods, estimating the kernels with random Fourier features.

The note shows that, for a wide range of cases, those kernels can be computed exactly and cheaply on a classical machine. The random approximation step can then be dropped. The setting is variational quantum models for regression, where tuned circuits do the learning. The authors say the simplification strengthens the kernel toolkit for judging when quantum models add anything at all.
arxiv-2504-00131:
Quim Llorens studies gravity in enhanced brane-world models, in a research paper from 2025. In such models, our universe is a brane inside a higher-dimensional bulk. Gravity must stay localized on the brane for the model to work. Past results cover branes with positive, negative, or zero cosmological constant.

Llorens extends those results through bulk perturbation analysis and through a holographic reading of the brane theory. An added Einstein-Hilbert term on the brane is then studied. Bounds on its coupling emerge, past which the theory turns pathological. The limit where the brane reaches the boundary is also treated. Added higher-derivative terms are discussed at the end.
arxiv-2504-00231:
Jeffrey L Linsky and co-authors make a 2025 case for a future space instrument that reads ultraviolet light at very high detail. A top survey of astronomy named the cycle of matter in and out of galaxies a priority theme. Tracing the thin warm and cold gas in that cycle needs sharp ultraviolet spectra from space, above the atmosphere.

The current Hubble instrument that pioneered such work is aging, and the telescope's life is limited. The authors argue for large new optics covering the near ultraviolet band at a resolving power near one hundred thousand. Targets range from interstellar gas and young stars to the outflows that leave galaxies.
arxiv-2504-00631:
Rob den Teuling and colleagues worked out in 2025 how spin waves travel through a pair of thin magnetic layers stacked together. Spin waves are ripples in magnetization that can carry signals without moving charge. In a bilayer, the waves feel exchange coupling between the layers and dipolar interactions within and between them. The layers' relative magnetization direction changes the resulting spectrum.

Working in the continuum approximation, the authors analyze how the magnetic stray fields emitted by the waves propagate nonreciprocally, favoring one direction over the other. They connect the theory to measurements on synthetic antiferromagnets and weakly coupled van der Waals antiferromagnetic bilayers, where an applied field flips the alignment. Such systems are candidates for low-power magnonic devices. Predicting their spectra tells experimentalists which signals to expect from magnetometry.
arxiv-2504-01031:
Shuntuo Xu, Zhou Yu, and Jian Huang present a 2025 statistics paper on estimating density ratios when they roam without bounds. A density ratio compares how likely data are under two distributions. It underpins many methods in statistics and machine learning. Older theory demanded tidy conditions, with ratios confined to bounded ranges. Real problems often break those limits, especially when data shift between domains.

The authors study estimators built from least squares and logistic losses. They prove error bounds that reach the best possible rates, up to small factors, even for unbounded ratios. Applying the theory, they show when a model trained on source data can transfer cleanly to a new domain without correction. The tail behavior of the ratio turns out to be the key factor. Simulations back the theory's predictions.
arxiv-2504-01231:
Camacho-Sánchez and co-authors test air blowing to cut drag on a blunt model vehicle in a 2025 study. The model is a squareback Ahmed body, a boxy shape used to stand in for vans and SUVs. Air blown out of the flat back can reshape the swirling wake and lower drag. The team asked whether the shape of the blowing slot matters, holding its total area fixed.

Four slot shapes were tried: square, vertical, cross, and horizontal, across the same range of blowing rates. The centered square slot cut drag the most. It stretched the swirl zone behind the body, calmed backflow, and reduced a lopsided wake pattern. Vertical and cross slots barely helped and kept or worsened the lopsided wake. The horizontal slot sat in between. The authors say slot shape is a key design choice.
arxiv-2504-01431:
Hao Zhu, Shengchao Yan, Jasper Hoffmann, and Joschka Boedecker present a shared toolkit for fitting discrete latent factor models in two thousand twenty-five. Such models sort data by hidden yes-or-no factors and serve fields from machine learning to psychology. Each model once needed its own custom solver, a slow and narrow path.

Their frame builds on CVXPY, a Python library for optimization. A user states the fitting problem in a short script, for regression or sorting tasks alike. Extra terms for shrinkage and limits on factors slot in with ease. The open-source code ships with worked examples. The goal is fast prototyping: try a model shape in minutes, not weeks of solver work.
arxiv-2504-01631: Baêta studies functional John ellipsoids and how to build a decomposition of the identity for them, in a mathematics paper from 2025. Functional ellipsoids, in the sense set out by Ivanov and Naszódi, extend the classic ellipsoid tools of convex geometry to functions. Fritz John's famous theorem gives such a decomposition for ordinary ellipsoids, with weights and contact points that sum to the identity. Baêta asks how to construct the same kind of decomposition in the functional setting, step by step rather than by a pure existence claim.
arxiv-2504-01831:
Noémie C Combe and Hanna Nencka propose a new way to rebuild hidden shapes from broken or noisy data, in a 2025 math paper. Rebuilding from partial evidence is a core problem across science, from imaging to physics. Old methods often blur or fail when noise grows.

Their approach draws on a geometric framework named for Atiyah and Molino, recasting the rebuild task in a form computers can handle. At its heart sits a new quantity, which they call the Hantjies tensor, that tracks how noise spreads through the rebuild. That tracking allows results with stated error bounds, a rare promise in this area. The authors claim the method stays robust under heavy noise and could serve many fields, though the paper is a theory statement rather than a field test.
arxiv-2504-02031: Vitek and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on a new job for a classic optics sensor: measuring how coherent a light signal is. The Hartmann sensor normally maps wavefronts through an array of small apertures. The team draws a formal parallel between the coherence matrix of light and the density matrix of a quantum state. That parallel recasts the sensor's reading as a quantum estimation problem. In lab tests, the sensor extracted coherence information even where aperture signals overlap strongly, where standard wavefront sensing gives up.
arxiv-2504-03031:
Arno Granier, Katharina Wilmes, Mihai Petrovici, and Walter Senn lay out a framework for modeling how the cerebral cortex computes. Their paper appeared in 2025. The cortex repeats the same basic parts and wiring patterns across areas and species. That repetition hints at one shared algorithm behind many skills. The authors distill current knowledge of cortical structure into two principles for model builders.

First, each cell type in the cortex plays its own computational role. Second, the wiring between cell types follows a few standard blueprints. Starting there, the authors sketch how to build models that are both functional, doing the task, and mechanistic, doing it the brain's way. They offer the framework as common ground for neuroscience and machine intelligence.
arxiv-2504-03131:
Edet, Inyang, Abah, and Ali model tiny heat machines, in a 2025 preprint, that use a two-atom molecule as the working substance. Quantum heat machines run cycles like steam engines but at the scale of single particles. The molecule here is described by a deformed potential, a math curve with a knob that changes its shape. The authors ask how that knob and other settings affect work output and efficiency.

They work through two classic cycles, the Otto cycle and the Carnot cycle. For each, they derive formulas for work and efficiency in terms of the model's settings. Across all settings tried, the system runs as a heat engine rather than a fridge or pump. The Otto cycle's efficiency can be tuned by turning the deformation knob. The authors say the results help show how uneven molecular shapes affect the design of quantum thermal machines.
arxiv-2504-04831:
Sanjeev Muralikrishnan, Niladri Shekhar Dutt, and Niloy Mitra present SMF, in a 2025 preprint, a way to transfer motion onto new characters without templates or rigs. Animation retargeting turns sparse keypoint motion into a full moving mesh. Older methods need a template shape or an artist-built rig. They also jitter or fail on unseen bodies and moves. SMF learns from sparse motion alone, with no dataset-specific labels. Its core is Kinetic Codes, an autoencoder that packs motion into a rich latent code. Separate predictors handle spatial and temporal gradients of the deformation.

Tests span several public motion sets plus raw video from one camera. Characters varied widely in shape and mesh structure. On a leading benchmark, SMF set a new best for handling motion it never trained on. The latent code is credited for the calm, coherent output. Code and weights are public on the project page.
arxiv-2504-05831:
Mingye Zhu and co-authors tackle a flaw in training language models on machine made preference data, in a 2025 paper. Cheap synthetic data can drift away from real human taste. A model tuned on drifted data may learn the wrong lessons about what people value.

Their method first scores each training case by how well it matches the target taste, using trained classifiers. It then optimizes for the worst case within the regions that matter most to human preference. That focus blunts the harm of drift. Tests show replies that track intended values more closely. The work speaks to teams who align models with limited human data.
arxiv-2504-06831:
Lucila Kraiselburd and co-authors explore whether small clumps in the universe can ease the Hubble tension in this 2025 paper. That tension is a firm gap between two ways of measuring how fast the universe expands. Early-universe data give one value, and local star ladders give a higher one. The standard math assumes light travels through smooth space. The team relaxes that assumption using an older approximation. It lets some light paths pass through emptier regions than average.

Two forms of that approximation were tested against the data. If clumpiness bends distance estimates, the local value could shift toward the early one. The authors frame this as an alternative path to closing the gap. No new particles or forces are needed under this idea. The paper is a theory test within standard cosmology tools. Its verdict rests on how well the forms fit observations.
arxiv-2504-07031:
Pawel Pukowski and Venet Osmani wrote a study from 2025 on bias in how computer models learn from data. A model may do well on one class of items and poorly on another. This gap is often blamed on having more items in one class than in the rest. The pair show that the gap can stay large even when all classes have the same count.

They argue that some classes are just harder to learn than others. Their fix picks training items based on how hard each one is, not on how often its class shows up. In tests on two image sets, the fix cut the gap in recall scores by a wide margin. It beat the usual way of picking items by class count.
arxiv-2504-07231:
David Akhihiero and Jason Gross build a relocalization pipeline that lets a lost robot in a mine or tunnel find itself again by registering its laser scan against a prior map. Underground, GPS is absent, lights are poor, surfaces repeat, and dust corrupts the data. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the framework picks distinctive feature points with a shape-signature method in both the live and map clouds. Histogram descriptors computed at those points are matched to propose correspondences. A first transform follows, refined in two stages by distribution-based and closest-point registration.

Experiments in simulated subterranean settings validated the chain, the authors report. The staged design tolerates dust and large initial misalignment better than a single registration pass. The target users are autonomous machines in mines and tunnels, where getting lost is a mission-ending event.
arxiv-2504-08231:
Tianyu Cao and four co-authors present a 2025 study of how the wording of a question affects search-aided AI systems. These systems, called RAG systems, look up documents and then write an answer. The team rewrote questions along four dimensions: formality, reading level, politeness, and grammar. They then ran two search models and nine language models, of many sizes, on four question-answering data sets.

Rewording alone caused large drops in quality. Less formal questions cut search recall by up to about 40 percent, and grammar errors cut answer scores by up to about 39 percent. The full search-aided systems suffered more than models answering alone, because errors in search fed errors in writing. The authors call for design work that makes these systems steadier under real-world wording.
arxiv-2504-08731:
Jingxin Zhang, Christian Hill, Jonathan Tennyson, and Sergei Yurchenko launch a database that computes highly accurate molecular spectra for hot gases, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Astronomers reading exoplanet air need spectral lines they can trust. The parent ExoMol project supplies vast line lists, sharpened by experimentally derived energy levels.

Their calculator filters those lists using the stated uncertainties, keeping only the most accurate lines. Users pick a wavelength range and temperature, then plot the spectrum online or download it as a spreadsheet file. A companion Python tool computes cross sections. The database opens with over twenty-four million lines covering thirty-three molecules and fifty-eight variants, and grows as ExoMol updates.
arxiv-2504-09131:
Kazashi Nakano, Katsuma Inoue, Yasuo Kuniyoshi, and Kohei Nakajima build a robot neck that feels by its sway, on the plan of the neck of a bird. Fully soft robots break and lag; bone-and-muscle builds bend yet hold. Birds peck with fine feel through just such necks. Their 2025 study sets a flexible neck on a robot and runs body-as-computer sums on its sway.

With the right spring-and-damping mix, the sway of the neck splits goods by softness grade. The sway also holds that call through the act, a form of in-body memory. Simulation runs back the bench story. Shape does part of the computing here, so feel can be fast and learned in few shots. Flexible builds may thus gain acts past their first plan, they hold.
arxiv-2504-09231:
Chijing Zang, Luke Omodt, Moumita Dasgupta, and Xiang Cheng spin pairs of microscopic helices in thick fluid to learn how bacteria swim and how tiny pumps might work. A lone rotating helix is a classic model of a flagellum; two helices, bundled as in real bacteria, interact through the fluid. Experiments meet hydrodynamic modeling head-on. Spacing and phase difference between the pair are the control knobs.

Rotating in phase at fixed speed, the pair needs less torque than two loners; out of phase, more. At one critical phase difference the coupling vanishes despite the tight spacing. A simple model built from a single helix's flow predicts the pair's torque in both open and confined geometries. Axial flux and pumping efficiency follow the same knobs. The results speak to flagellar bundle function and to low-Reynolds pump design alike.
arxiv-2504-09331:
Andrej Bogdanov, Alon Rosen, Neekon Vafa, and Vinod Vaikuntanathan study a classic dimension-cutting tool and where it can be attacked. Their 2025 paper concerns a random projection that shrinks high-dimensional data while keeping distances roughly intact. That guarantee holds for moderate point sets, but a huge grid of points is expected to contain one that collapses badly.

The question is how hard such a collapsing point is to find. Their online algorithm reaches a threshold they identify, borrowing ideas from discrepancy theory. Hardness evidence comes from two directions: a gap property that covers online methods, and a reduction from lattice problems. As an application, the rounded projection serves as a hash that preserves closeness in exactly the hard regime, a useful trait for cryptography.
arxiv-2504-09731:
Uri Bader and Alex Furman build a new framework for the Lyapunov spectrum, a set of numbers that measure how systems stretch and fold over time. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. The setting is random-like dynamics valued in Lie groups, the smooth groups of symmetry in geometry.

They prove the spectrum is simple, meaning its values do not collide, for a wide class of systems. They also prove it changes smoothly under small tweaks. The class covers many familiar examples. The proofs borrow ideas from boundary theory, a tool first built for rigidity results about groups. That borrowing gives a fresh view even of random matrix products, the most studied case. A follow-up paper will treat more examples.
arxiv-2504-10831:
Hyojun Ahn and five co-authors pair language models with a safety pilot for delivery drones. Their 2025 paper presents SafeGPT for last-mile aerial deliveries. One model assigns sectors from above; a second plans routes on each drone. Language models can hallucinate, though, and drones cannot afford invented moves.

A reinforcement learning filter watches every model decision. It overrides moves that would drain batteries or repeat visits. Dual replay buffers let the models and the filter improve together. Simulations beat a model-only baseline on delivery success. Battery use and travel distance also fell sharply. Formal guardrails make generative control fit for real airspace.
arxiv-2504-11131:
Mert Ozates and three co-authors design a random access scheme for many devices that transmit without any coordination or timing sync. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. In unsourced access, the receiver must sort out who sent what from a jumble of overlapping signals.

Users scatter their data across a time block in sparse patterns, starting whenever they like. The receiver decodes through two nested sliding windows. Inside the smaller window it detects start times and patterns, decodes single users, and cancels their signals in rounds. No preamble header is needed, since the patterns themselves reveal the start. Simulations show the fully asynchronous scheme beats existing rivals. The result suits swarms of simple sensors that cannot sync clocks.
arxiv-2504-11531:
Pengjun Lu, Mingyu Li, Dalya Baron, Minghao Yue, Song Huang, and Zheng Cai published this astronomy paper in 2025. It reports a giant glowing nebula, nicknamed Oxyster, found beside a starburst galaxy seen as it was when the universe was half its present age. Such glowing clouds trace the gas that surrounds galaxies.

Narrow-band images from a large ground telescope revealed oxygen light stretching some thirty thousand parsecs. The cloud outshines similar regions around nearby active galaxies, yet its color balance looks wrong for a lit-up echo of a black hole. The host galaxy is a disturbed red disk with one blue spiral arm and barely any active nucleus. Standard models of gas lit by stars or shocks cannot explain all the clues at once. The authors float a recent starburst plus a faint hidden nucleus, and flag the cloud for follow-up.
arxiv-2504-12431:
Arroyo-Ureña and co-authors search for a forbidden interaction that would let photons turn an electron into a muon at future colliders, in a physics paper from 2025. Such lepton flavor violation never occurs in the Standard Model, so seeing it would prove new physics. Photon fusion in electron-positron collisions offers a clean place to look.

Working in an effective theory framework, the team maps where the signal could rise above background at two planned circular colliders. Two momentum patterns, of the scattered electron and of the central muon, separate signal from noise best. A neural network classifier sharpened the reach beyond simple cuts. The authors conclude these machines have real discovery potential for this rare process.
arxiv-2504-13731:
Yixin Wang, Fanhui Meng, and Xiao Ma strengthen the theory of a random code family in a 2025 paper. Bernoulli generator matrix codes build codewords from random coin flips and were already known to reach channel capacity when errors are counted bit by bit. The harder question was whether they also reach it when whole frames count as failures.

The authors prove they do, with a new proof strategy that works directly on systematic codes, where the message sits visibly inside the codeword, instead of inflating the code family first. A side result shows a common independence assumption in older proofs is not needed. The proof reveals a division of labor: clean message bits bound the candidate list, while check bits pick the winner. Error floor bounds follow.
arxiv-2504-19231:
Alexander Dubbs works out the best split of data into training and test parts for ridge regression, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Ridge regression shrinks weights to curb overfit, and its tuning strength might sway the best split. The math is done in the large-data limit with the feature count held fixed.

The tuning strength turns out to matter only weakly and can be dropped in the limit. The best split then rests on row count and feature count alone. It matches the known plain regression split to the first two terms. The aim is honest error reads, as close as can be to true skill. Readers get a first exact split rule of its kind.
arxiv-2504-19331:
Mikhail Ermakov extends a classic measure of test quality to a middle zone of error chances, in a paper from 2025. Statisticians use Bahadur efficiency to grade how fast a test's error odds shrink as data grow. The classic bound was proven for extreme cases. Many real tests live in the moderate zone between normal and extreme.

He proves a matching lower bound for that zone. The conditions match those used for a famed minimax bound in local testing theory. His bound turns out to be a special case of that broader result. The link ties two lines of theory that grew up apart. It gives a firm floor for how well any test can do in the moderate zone. That floor can grade new tests proposed for such settings.
arxiv-2504-20431:
Hwiyoung Lee and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on handling dependence in omics association studies. Omics data hold thousands of linked measures, and those links can warp standard tests. Genes switch on in co-expression groups, so the dependence has a known shape that few methods use head on.

Their method folds the co-expression network into a joint regression of many outcomes at once. That lets the model credit the links between measures while it tests each one. Fake data runs showed sharper test accuracy and results that repeat better across studies. The authors liken the gain to what mixed models give for repeat measures in small data. They pitch the method as a fresh route for omics work.
arxiv-2504-20731:
Michael Zacharias and co-authors model how blazar light curves in different bands will correlate in the coming CTAO era, in this 2025 paper. The giant gamma-ray observatory will record faint states in detail for the first time. Blazar correlations appear and vanish unpredictably, so theory must say what to expect.

Long X-ray and optical records for two famous blazars drove a one-zone particle code. Adding relativistic protons changed the correlation pattern, stretching the brightest gamma states through pair cascades. Neither pure electron nor mixed models fully matched existing data. The study sets benchmarks for the observatory's first correlation hunts.
arxiv-2504-20931:
Rolando Ramos and David Whiting wrote this 2025 algebra paper settling, in modified form, a conjecture about two families of algebras. Cluster algebras grow from seeds by mutation rules and appear across geometry and physics; generalized cluster algebras loosen the exchange relations to higher order. Chekhov and Shapiro conjectured every generalized example hides inside an ordinary one.

Embedding, strictly, was too strong. Ramos and Whiting instead construct an ordinary cluster algebra for any generalized one, of which the generalized algebra is a subquotient. The construction runs over the original ground ring, via restriction of scalars. It confirms the spirit of the conjecture: nothing truly new escapes the ordinary theory. The result tidies the border between the two frameworks for future users.
arxiv-2505-00431:
Julián López-Gómez, Eduardo Muñoz-Hernández, and Fabio Zanolin charted solution families for a nonlinear equation in a 2025 paper. Their Moore-Nehari type problem has a coefficient that jumps between values in steps, and a spectral parameter tunes the equation's strength. Positive solutions can multiply or vanish as the step position shifts the problem between its autonomous and linear extremes, behavior earlier numerics had only suggested.

The authors prove several of those multiplicity patterns rigorously. They also analyze the delicate limit as the step approaches the endpoint, where solutions blow up pointwise and numerics go blind. That singular limit, handled here for the first time, shows analysis succeeding exactly where computation fails.
arxiv-2505-00531:
Mikhail Rybakov, a solo author, presents a study from twenty twenty-five on a long open ask in logic. The logic in play is a superintuitionistic predicate logic set by linear Kripke frames. Its two variable fragment was not known to be decidable or not. The same ask maps to a modal logic through a known translation. Rybakov proves the fragment cannot be decided.

The proof holds even for the positive fragment with thin language: one two place sign and many one place signs. A logic set by the frame of whole numbers is worse still, not even listable. Tools in the proof come from tiling tasks rephrased with single numbers. A double label trick keeps the count at two variables.
arxiv-2505-00831:
Big language models plan robot routes well but are too heavy to run on small devices at the edge. Quang Pham led a team that built SmallPlan, a way to shrink that skill into small language models. A big model acts as teacher: the small models learn from its guidance through rounds of training mixed with practice in simulation, where feedback rewards shorter, smarter routes.

The small models learn to output step-by-step actions across a simple graph that stands in for a full 3D scene. In tests they matched a top-tier big model on route planning, without its wild guesses or overfit answers. The result is planning that fits on modest hardware in real robots.
arxiv-2505-01631:
Sergio Mendoza and Sarahí Silva settle a long-running choice in the theory of fluids and gravity, in a 2025 paper. Models of an ideal fluid in Einstein's theory need a quantity called the matter Lagrangian. Textbooks have used either the fluid's pressure or its total energy density, treating the two as interchangeable. The authors show the pressure choice leads to physical inconsistencies.

Once the fluid is coupled to the gravitational field, only the energy density choice stays consistent. The conclusion is firm: for an ideal fluid, the matter Lagrangian must be the total energy density. The result cleans up a quiet ambiguity that sits inside models of stars and of the early universe.
arxiv-2505-02031:
Xiao-Gang He, Xiao-Dong Ma, Jusak Tandean, and German Valencia test a light dark matter idea with kaon decay data, in a research paper from 2025. A recent lab result saw more of a rare B-meson decay than the standard model predicts. A light scalar particle might explain the excess, if it acts as dark matter.

The authors check that idea against a new kaon decay result from the NA62 lab work. They find a narrow mass range where the particle could fit both results and past dark matter bounds. Future data from both labs could test the idea more sharply. The paper links two rare decays into one check.
arxiv-2505-02531:
Ramon Codina, Hauke Gravenkamp, and Sheraz Khan turn a stabilization trick into an error gauge for flow simulations. The convection-diffusion-reaction equation models transport with spread and source terms. Finite element answers need honest error bars, above all when flow dominates. Their multiscale method splits the problem into solved coarse scales and modeled fine scales.

The fine-scale model, tied to the leftover residual, doubles as the error estimate. Contributions count both inside elements and along their edges. A scaled norm of those fine scales prices the error in a stabilized measure. That measure keeps grip on the flow term itself. Tests show the gauge tracks true error reliably against rival estimators.
arxiv-2505-03531:
Haoqi Yang and co-authors study how to run very large mixture-of-experts language models faster in a 2025 computing paper. Such models split work among many expert subnetworks, firing only a few per query. Newer designs slice the experts finer, and serving them well is poorly understood. The team measured speed and quality while varying how many experts stay active and how many exist in total.

Cutting the active expert count bought large speed gains in some load conditions, with only small quality loss. Cutting the total count saved little speed yet hurt quality badly. The asymmetry gives operators a clear tuning rule: trim what fires per query, not what the model owns. Their method raised throughput on top of that insight.
arxiv-2505-03631:
Linhan Cao and a team of co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on judging video quality with no human grades. Quality scores guide how video is made and sent. Hand graded sets are the norm, but models trained on them fail on new kinds of clips. Their route, weak-to-strong learning, has a weak teacher grade clips for a strong student.

A plain form of this route let the student match its teacher on home tests and beat it on new ones. Their frame blends grades from many teachers, both off the shelf models and fake warp tools, in a learn to rank form. Each strong student then teaches the next round. Scores top the field, most of all on new clips.
arxiv-2505-04031:
Richard Wang and Natalia Berloff study how networks of light oscillators fall into step in a 2025 paper. Such networks settle into synchronized states, but they can get stuck with phase windings, defects that spoil the true ground state. The authors work on rings and toroidal lattices modeled by standard laser equations.

They find two reliable escapes. Running just above threshold lets the amplitude dip to zero in spots. Those holes let the phase slip and unwind. In two dimensions the holes pair into pulses that sweep defects away. Seeding the start with uneven amplitude or phase also triggers the collapses. Slow pumping favors the process. The lesson: amplitude freedom is the key to defect-free sync.
arxiv-2505-04231:
Taoyuan Yu, Kui Wang, Zongdian Li, Tao Yu, and Kei Sakaguchi design a roadside-unit brain for cooperative self-driving through unsignalized intersections, in a two thousand twenty-five transportation paper. Intersections without lights are among the hardest, most dangerous traffic scenes.

The roadside unit perceives globally and commands connected vehicles over vehicle-to-infrastructure links. Its policy is trained in two stages: offline pretraining with conservative Q-learning plus conduct cloning, then multi-agent fine-tuning with a self-attention mechanism for inter-agent dependencies. In the CARLA simulator, failure rates stay below 0.03 percent coordinating three vehicles, far better than the long-used Autoware starting. Robustness holds as agent counts and maps change.
arxiv-2505-04331:
Yu Zhu and co-authors show that brains with very different wiring still hold matching activity codes, using a probabilistic alignment method across animals, in work from twenty twenty-five. Brains differ in structure and firing detail, yet behavior codes look alike across individuals. Proof without hand alignment was missing.

Their framework aligns neural and behavior representations while modeling variation across trials, sessions, and subjects. Safeguards keep the shared code from collapsing. Zero shot checks found preserved codes in monkey motor and premotor cortex. Mouse visual cortex showed the same preservation. The results support behavior decoding straight onto new brains, and point to a general coding principle across regions and species.
arxiv-2505-04531:
Josh McGiff and Nikola Nikolov review ways to build text generating models for languages with little data, in a 2025 paper. Flagship chat tools serve big languages well and most others poorly, a gap that feeds linguistic inequality. Their review is the first to focus on this fix alone.

Fifty-four studies were sorted by trick: padding data, translating back and forth, training across languages, and prompt craft. Transformer designs dominate, work clusters on a few languages, and scoring habits vary too much to compare cleanly. The authors urge wider language coverage and shared yardsticks. The stakes include keeping small languages alive in a model shaped age.
arxiv-2505-05631:
Jiachen Tu, Yaokun Shi, and Fan Lam clean noise from MRI scans without clean training labels in this 2025 paper. MRI gives superb soft-tissue views, but fast or low-field scans come out grainy. Supervised cleaners need pristine example scans, which clinics rarely have.

Their method learns from noisy scans alone. A score-based trick compares each scan with even noisier copies of itself, teaching the model what clean structure should look like across many noise levels. A detail-refining step guards the fine features that older self-taught cleaners blur away. The same frame can borrow strength across scan types. On two public datasets, it led self-supervised rivals and rivaled supervised ones.
arxiv-2505-07331:
Fa-Xin Yang and five co-authors study a rare Higgs boson decay at a future muon collider in a 2025 paper. Their theory adds a new scalar particle and a heavy neutral lepton to the standard model. Mixing between scalars lets Higgs bosons decay in a way that violates lepton number, a clue to how the heavy lepton gets its mass.

At a high energy muon collider, Higgs bosons are made mainly by vector boson fusion. The authors trace a signal where the Higgs decays to two heavy leptons, each giving a muon and jets. With enough data, a three or ten trillion volt collider could discover the signal across a wide range of model settings.
arxiv-2505-07431:
Jianan Li and a team of co-authors built a system to advise which medical exams a patient needs. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with AI in health care advice. Past work aims at the care phase: drugs or diseases to pick. The exam phase, which sets what to test to judge the state, had no such aid. The team states this task in formal terms for the first time.

Their model joins a diffusion step with a graph and sequence frame that tracks space and time. Exam choice holds more complex links than shop advice, since each test shapes the next call. Readers in health AI get a first frame and tool for the diagnostic front end.
arxiv-2505-07731:
Neeraj Agrawal and Sriram Ganapathy teach speech-understanding models to handle tasks they have never seen, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Spoken language tasks range from pulling facts out of speech to sorting intent, and training data for each new one is often missing. Speech-text language models promise a way out, yet their out-of-the-box scores on such tasks disappoint.

The authors fine-tune with scrambled class labels, forcing the model to learn the shape of a task from a few examples in the prompt rather than memorize fixed answers. On unseen tasks, the trick lifted performance well past standard fine-tuning and plain prompting. No fresh annotation was needed to switch the model to a new task.
arxiv-2505-07831:
Michael Pichat and co-authors propose a new view of polysemy in artificial neurons in a 2025 paper. Single neurons in language models often respond to many unrelated features. The standard account blames superposition: too many features packed into too few dimensions of the latent space.

The authors instead define a neuron geometrically as a categorical vector space. Its basis directions come from sub dimensions extracted from neurons in the previous layer. An attention process inside the neuron then selects a critical zone where those categories overlap. That zone, they argue, is more homogeneous and explains how the model uses the neuron efficiently.
arxiv-2505-08531:
Chenru Duan and seven co-authors present a 2025 generative model that designs metal-organic frameworks, porous crystals built from metal nodes joined by organic links. The design space is far too large to search by making each candidate in a lab. Older models either reused known building blocks or handled only small crystal cells. The new model learns the three-dimensional shapes of the blocks themselves and builds crystals block by block.

The model produced crystals with cells of up to 1,000 atoms that looked valid, new, and varied. It invented metal nodes and links not seen in its training data. One high-scoring design was then made in a real lab. Tests confirmed that the made crystal matched the design, showing the tool can guide real synthesis.
arxiv-2505-09031:
Adarsh Kumar, Hwiyoon Kim, Jawahar Sai Nathani, and Neil Roy test ways to stop language models from making things up, in a 2025 paper. Models often state falsehoods with full confidence, a failure called hallucination. Step-by-step prompting helps reasoning but does not cure the problem. The team combines that prompting with outside fact lookup and self-checking tricks.

In their setup, the model reasons in steps while pulling facts from external sources. Self-consistency samples several answers and takes the consensus. Self-verification asks the model to check and revise its own output. The authors compare plain models against each add-on and their blends. They report which mixes cut falsehoods most while keeping answers fluent and reasoning deep, giving builders a practical ranking of defenses.
arxiv-2505-09131:
Kunwoong Kim, Jihu Lee, Sangchul Park, and Yongdai Kim make clustering fair without wrecking it in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Fair clustering asks each group to hold balanced shares of protected groups. Past methods paid for fairness with poor clusters or shaky math. The authors split the fair clustering goal into two simpler parts. Their method alternates between two steps.

First it aligns the data of different groups through a shared distribution. Then it places cluster centers in that aligned space. The loop carries a guarantee: near-best cluster quality for any fairness level chosen. Stability in practice is a further claim. The work serves machine learning researchers who must audit group outcomes. It suits hiring, lending, and policy data.
arxiv-2505-09231:
Erika Nishio, Kengo Tomida, Yuki Kudoh, and Shigeo Kimura wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It models how planet-forming disks are born when cosmic rays, the main source of ionization in star-forming clouds, fall unevenly through the gas.

Magnetic pull moves angular momentum in disks, but weak ionization dulls that pull through non-ideal effects. The team built a full cosmic ray transport module into a known code and ran three-dimensional collapse models. Dense disk gas blocks the rays, so fields inside the disk stay less twisted than in even-rate models. Pull at disk scale drops hard, and the disks grow less stable, with bold spiral arms.
arxiv-2505-09731:
William Xie, Max Conway, Yutong Zhang, and Nikolaus Correll show how vision-language models can teach robots forceful skills by reasoning about forces rather than paths. The models hold broad knowledge of the physical world, and with fine-tuning they can output robot motion. The team instead asks the model for wrenches, the pushes and twists a task needs, and overlays matching coordinate frames on camera images.

Across four tasks, opening and closing a lid and pushing a cup or a chair, the method worked on two robot platforms over two hundred twenty trials, with about half succeeding. The setup also let the model react to feedback and recover from failures, with or without a human watching. The authors also note that such prompting can slip past model safeguards, and they weigh what that means.
arxiv-2505-10031:
Awasthi and four co-authors rebuilt nuclear interaction potentials from scattering data in twenty twenty-five. When alpha particles bounce off carbon-12 nuclei, the scattering pattern encodes resonances. These are short-lived excited states of the combined system. Working backward from data to the underlying potential is an inverse problem.

Their method uses the variable phase approach. It tracks how the scattering phase builds up with distance. A flexible reference potential supplies the shape. It is built from three smoothly joined Morse functions. A genetic algorithm evolves its parameters, generation by generation. The aim is to minimize the mismatch with expected phase shifts. The resulting potentials reproduced the measured resonance energies and widths very well, for four spin-parity states. The authors present the approach as a computational complement to conventional direct methods in nuclear scattering studies.
arxiv-2505-10131:
Chatterjee and Ghosh map phase marks in a chain model with long hops. The base model, called SSH, is a chain with paired hop strengths. New terms add hops past the next site, at more than one reach. Stock chains take one wrap count to mark their phase type. Driven chains take two counts in the Floquet read used here. More reach brings phases with higher wrap counts in both reads. Still chains and driven chains alike show the high marks.

Phase charts cover four reach spans for still chains first. One broad rule then spans all reach spans at once. Like charts cover four driven chain forms as well. Each form sets its hop terms in its own way. Edge states at zero and pi showed in each case. Those states fit the bulk-edge rule for this chain class.
arxiv-2505-10531:
Hossein Hosseinabadi, Yaroslav Tserkovnyak, Eugene Demler, and Jamir Marino report a new kind of instability in driven magnets, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Magnets can be pushed out of balance by an outside drive. The small waves that travel through a magnet are called magnons, and their pattern can shift in surprising ways.

A first amplification step piles magnons into a tuned pattern across momenta. That pattern then seeds a second shift, in which order of the opposite type grows stronger, even though the base couplings favor the first type. The authors stress that this effect exists only out of balance. It cannot appear in a settled, thermal magnet, which sets it apart from classic driven effects.
arxiv-2505-11331:
Arindam Mitra, Sumit Mukherjee, and Changhyoup Lee build, in a 2025 paper, ways to count the worth of quantum measurements as a resource. In quantum work, a measurement can itself be the scarce good, not just the state it reads. When a state or a set of measurements is known only in part, plain worth counts can miss what is there. A looser count, built on a small slack term, may catch it.

The team set up distance-based counts for measurement resources. They then work through the properties of the slack counts, called epsilon-measures. Links tie those counts to core quantities used when resources are worked or swapped. Their framework fits one measurement and whole sets alike, though sets allow richer moves, such as switches guided by a control bit. The authors aim it at all measurement resource theories, built or yet to come.
arxiv-2505-11431:
David Lin, Siddhartha Banerjee, Giannis Fikioris, and Éva Tardos design a sharing rule for a single item given out round by round. Agents value the item anew each round, drawn from a fixed spread. Past rules gave each agent either a fair play outcome that needs full knowledge of spreads, or a safe outcome alone that is weaker. The two seemed hard to join in one rule.

Their rule gives each agent a plain strategy that does both at once. It is a best reply when others play fair, and it guards each agent even against collusion. The build leans on a classic theorem about fair lotteries, which they strengthen. A convexity argument shows the needed lottery set is never empty. The stronger theorem may aid other design problems too.
arxiv-2505-12631:
Li Lin presents a network that forecasts how a person will move next, in a paper from 2025. Guessing future poses from past motion matters for graphics and vision work. Human motion shifts along both time and body axes at once, and methods that mine one axis at a time miss that blend.

The network uses a wave-style transform that lifts joint paths into a finer grid. There, time and space facts can be read together at several scales. A part-removal study found the multi-scale block does most of the work. Full tests beat prior top methods, with the clearest gains on hard cases such as free posing and greeting moves. The author frames the gain as coming from a wider view of each motion.
arxiv-2505-14431:
Gölgeleyen, Imanuvilov, and Yamamoto prove that a map that meets a bound on its curve, and fades fast far out, must be zero in all its domain. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The bound ties the map's second slope to its own size and its first slope, each with weights that fade by set powers. The domain is all space past a bounded hole. The map fades at a fast rate in one set of paths, and at a slow rate in the rest. If those fade rates meet set terms tied to the weights, the sole such map is the zero map. The key tool is a weighted gauge with cut-off steps.
arxiv-2505-14631:
Lingjie Jiang and co-authors teach language models to think only when a question deserves it. Recent reasoning models write long chains of thought before answering, which boosts hard problems but wastes time and tokens on easy ones. The team's hybrid models decide for themselves whether a query needs deep thought or a quick reply.

Training runs in two stages. First, a cold-start phase teaches the model both modes and when each fits. Then online reinforcement learning sharpens the choice, using a new method that rewards picking the right mode for each question's difficulty. The authors also define a score, hybrid accuracy, to grade this judgment. In wide tests, the hybrid models beat both plain and always-thinking rivals on reasoning and general tasks, while cutting cost sharply. A model that matches its effort to the question is cheaper to run and, on their evidence, better overall.
arxiv-2505-17031:
Dylan Magill and co-authors released Super-SNID in 2025, a bigger template bank for SNID, a tool that names exploding stars from their light spectra. Wide-field sky surveys now catch far more blasts than the old bank could sort. Rare classes had too few sample spectra, and some new classes were missing in full.

The new bank holds 841 spectra for 161 objects. It fattens thin classes, such as a faint kind of Type Ia blast, and adds fresh ones, from super-bright blasts to stars torn apart by black holes. Most spectra come from a public European survey of passing sky events. The team also ships files that make it easy to fold this bank, and others, into the base tool. The library sits on GitHub with plain install steps.
arxiv-2505-17131:
Arbabi and Kerschbaum propose a way to measure bias in large language models by comparing models against each other. Bias is hard to pin down in the abstract, and new models appear faster than audits can track. Their framework, Relative Bias, scores how one model's behavior departs from its peers in a chosen domain.

Two methods do the scoring: one compares sentence embeddings, the other uses a language model as judge. Case studies on bias and alignment scenarios show the two methods agree well, backed by statistical tests. The authors offer the framework as a scalable routine check. It gives deployers a grounded sense of where a model stands.
arxiv-2505-18231:
Donghyun Son, Euntae Choi, and Sungjoo Yoo shrink the memory cache of large language models without any calibration data, in a paper from 2025. The cache of past keys and values swells with long chats and big batches. Squeezing it into few bits helps, but older squeezers lean on sample data and break when real inputs drift.

Their trick reshapes the numbers before squeezing: normalize each token, shift each channel to center, then normalize again, with a mixing transform on top. The result looks like a standard bell curve, so one shared codebook fits all inputs. Tests at one and two bits beat prior methods and ran up to three times faster than full precision.
arxiv-2505-18931:
Ryan Saklad, Aman Chadha, Oleg Pavlov, and Raha Moraffah test whether language models can pull cause-and-effect links out of real-world writing, in a paper from 2025. Past tests used short, made-up passages where causes were spelled out. Real texts bury causes in long, messy prose. The team built a benchmark from real academic papers to close that gap.

Their set varies in length, in how plainly causes are stated, and in field. Models were graded on how well their drawn links matched the marked ones. Even the best model scored only about half on the shared measure. The team breaks down where models fail: hidden causes, many linked events, and long texts all hurt. They share the data and code in public. The work gives the field a harder, fairer test of causal reading.
arxiv-2505-19631:
Splitting text into words is a first step for language software, and for languages written without spaces it is a hard one. Zihong Zhang and five co-authors flip the usual order in a 2025 paper: instead of segmenting before understanding, they let large language models understand first and segment later. They test how well the models cut raw text in many languages using simple prompts.

Bigger models generally cut better. The team also builds a hybrid method pairing the models' insight with a classic fast pattern-matching machine, forming a word model that adapts to context. It beats traditional approaches, and the authors use the tests to probe what the big models truly grasp.
arxiv-2505-19731:
Daniil Tiapkin and co-authors speed a way to train AI from human likes without a score card for each answer. The older route builds a reward model from likes, but real likes can loop and clash. The Nash route skips the score card and seeks a tie point of a game built from the likes. Their 2025 paper works in a real frame where the model is a set of knobs, not a free table.

A plain self-play rule ties to a known method and comes with strong odds that its last step lands near the tie. Yet its path can wobble. The team wraps the rule in a steady frame that pulls each step back toward the last good point. That blend, called Nash Prox, keeps the proof and calms the path. Tests on large language models back the claim.
arxiv-2505-20131:
Yuanxin Zhuang, Dazhong Shen, and Ying Sun (2025) build a molecular editor that changes a molecule's properties without wrecking its structure. Editing is hard because molecules are graphs, while many editors work on strings or smooth spaces and lose the shape. Their framework, MolEditRL, works in two stages. First, a discrete graph diffusion model learns to rebuild a target molecule from a source one, following instructions. Then reinforcement learning fine-tunes the editor, rewarding property gains and structural fidelity together.

To train and test it, the team built the largest editing dataset yet: three million examples across ten chemical attributes, for single and combined property tasks. MolEditRL beat leading methods on both accuracy and fidelity. Its success rate rose by 74 percent while using 98 percent fewer parameters. The authors credit the pairing of diffusion with reinforcement learning, under graph constraints, for controllability that keeps up with editing power.
arxiv-2505-21631:
Jahmall Bersini, Simeon Hellerman, Domenico Orlando, and Susanne Reffert study a classic fermionic field theory in a limit where both its conserved charge. Its number of fermion flavors grow large together at a fixed ratio. Large-charge methods turn hard questions about strongly coupled theories into tractable calculations of operator dimensions. A similar program had been carried out for a bosonic model, but fermions bring new difficulties. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team maps the theory spectrum in both small and large ratio limits, pushing expansions well beyond the first few orders.

A resurgence analysis then links the two regimes: the well-behaved small-ratio series secretly encodes the exponential corrections that govern the large-ratio side. The authors read the pattern geometrically, as particles traveling along shortest paths on a cylinder. The work extends large-charge methods to a fermionic setting.
arxiv-2505-22031:
Hasan Yucedag and Adam Jatowt present a 2025 paper on a web game that asks people to guess the age of old photographs. Players work in two modes: naming the year of a single photo, or picking the older of two photos side by side. Scores and leaderboards keep players engaged.

The platform draws on 10,150 images from a public dataset of photos dated 1930 to 1999. In trials, 113 users played 15,473 games and rated the site 4.25 out of 5. People were far better at picking the older photo, at 65.9 percent accuracy, than at naming an exact year, at 25.6 percent. Older decades were easier to spot. The game doubles as a teaching tool and a source of labeled data.
arxiv-2505-22431:
Mina Akhyani, Luca Zanini, and Henrik Rønnow introduce, in 2025, an open-source tool that computes brightness in neutron sources. Brightness is a key measure for designing sources and beamlines, yet standard simulation packages cannot compute it directly. Their tool, Brightify, reads particle list files produced by several Monte Carlo codes.

Brightify scans both position and direction to map brightness in fine detail, exposing hotspots that guide better source design. The authors check it against standard tally methods and report good agreement, especially in high-resolution cases. The tool promises faster redesign cycles and less computation for source developers.
arxiv-2505-22931:
Andreu Ballús Santacana studies what remains of a diagram when only its connection pattern counts. The starting system is built from a single copying operation in a formal diagram language. An ancestry map sends each diagram to a corelation, recording which ports end up connected. Its image keeps only patterns where each class holds exactly one input.

Dividing by the map's kernel yields a quotient system. That quotient turns out to match the known system for commutative copying without a delete operation. The paper then slots the construction into the standard cospan and corelation landscape. Known collapses and a presheaf envelope are laid out, each reduced to cited classic results. The author is explicit that only the quotient identification is claimed as new. The rest is careful organization of the surrounding theory.
arxiv-2505-23031:
Jinyi Chang and co-authors tackle fine-grained image sorting under privacy limits in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Sorting look-alike classes, such as bird species, usually needs a label for every image. In fields like medicine, such labels may be too private to share.

Their method trains from bags of images where only the share of each class in the bag is known. It uses the natural hierarchy of fine-grained classes, refining features step by step from broad to narrow groups. A new loss function adds guidance at each level. Tests on three standard data sets beat earlier bag-based methods. The authors plan to release code and data.
arxiv-2505-23131:
