Xinyu Yao and co-authors published this study in 2025. It assigns computing tasks to devices faster, using two learned policies that work as a pair. Dataflow graphs underpin modern machine learning jobs, and where each operation runs decides the total time. Older learning methods assumed lockstep systems, which waste devices at barriers. They also ignored the scheduler's own logic, and leaned only on trial-and-error learning.

DOPPLER splits the job: one policy picks the next operation, the other places it on a device. Expert-style heuristics inform the design, not just rewards. Across tasks, the pair beat all rival methods on run time. Training itself ran faster per episode, a sign of sample thrift. The authors pitch the dual-policy split as a template for other scheduling puzzles in computing.
arxiv-2505-23731:
Pessi and a large team study the ambiguous transient AT2022rze in two thousand twenty-five. The flash sits off center in a merging galaxy system. Its traits echo active nuclei, tidal disruptions, and superluminous supernovae at once. That mix makes its true class hard to call.

The light curve rose fast, fell slowly, and bumped en route. Narrow lines and red colors hint at gas, dust, and host dimming. Coronal lines point to high energy emission at the core. Archive data show no past acts at that spot. The team lands on a changing look active nucleus as the best call.
arxiv-2505-23931:
Wurgaft and five co-authors scaled up the think-aloud method in twenty twenty-five, using language technology to do the slow hand work that had shrunk its use in psychology. Asking people to speak their thoughts while solving a problem yields rich evidence about reasoning, but transcribing it is laborious.

Six hundred forty participants played the Game of 24, a number puzzle, while speaking their reasoning aloud. Software transcribed the recordings and recast each transcript as a search graph, a map of the paths each mind explored. The automatic coding agreed moderately well with human coders. Comparing hundreds of these maps revealed both shared habits and wide personal variation in how people hunt for a solution. The authors present the pipeline as proof that verbal reports can be gathered at modern scale. They invite a revival of the classic method.
arxiv-2505-24731:
Alan Sun proposes circuit stability as a new way to judge how well language models generalize, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Judging large language models in full is hard. Benchmarks fill up fast as models improve, and building harder datasets takes much work. Sun borrows instead from mechanistic interpretability.

Circuit stability means a model uses one steady line of reasoning, its circuit, across varied inputs. Sun sets out both circuit stability and circuit equivalence in math form. Three case studies then test the idea in practice. The results show that stability, or the lack of it, can mark and predict parts of generalization. The author presents the methods as a step toward tying model generality to interpretability in a strict way. That link could in time make judging models cheaper and more informative.
arxiv-2506-00031:
Abhiram Sripat, writing alone, completes covering spaces around punctures in a 2025 mathematics paper. The setup starts with a surface and a finite set of marked points. Away from those points, a finite covering wraps the surface in sheets. The question is how to fill the missing points back in. Sripat adds an exceptional fibre over each marked point.

A many-to-many incidence rule then links the covering's edge germs to those new points. The resulting topology realizes the chosen rule from within. A lift of a path crosses a defect only when its endpoint value lies in every gathered endpoint set. Graphs and probes recover the local structure, degrees, and even the full incidence rule. The data can be recast as a weighted order structure. Sripat draws out classification, symmetry, and transport results. A defect poset organizes how the completions vary.
arxiv-2506-00231:
Lawrence Frolov, writing alone in 2025, sorts out how to model detectors that absorb quantum particles at a boundary. A particle moves inside a bounded region while detectors line its edge. Detection there is one-way and happens only at the wall. A leading researcher had sketched that the motion must follow a shrinking, well-behaved flow. The rule at the wall would be a local absorbing condition. Frolov uses a new framework, boundary quadruples, to list all such flows.

Each listed flow extends the standard energy operator of the free particle. The list characterizes exactly which boundary rules are allowed. That turns a sketch into a proved classification. Detectors in labs are modeled on such mathematics. The paper is pure theory in operator analysis. Its title in the catalog differs from the paper's own, which the head gives.
arxiv-2506-00431:
Jie Peng, Zhewei Wei, and Yuhang Ye present a computing paper from 2025 on networks that change over time. Friend webs, trade webs, and contact webs all gain and lose links by the day. Models have to weigh both the shape of the web and its history to guess what comes next.

Their model builds on the attention method used in language models. They give that method a clear meaning for changing webs, which past work lacked. Time is fed in by calendar splits, and link facts come from each node's nearest contacts. A split trick tracks how past link patterns shift. Tests on several public sets beat the best known models in most cases. The model also ran faster than past attention-based rivals.
arxiv-2506-00531:
Hang Fan and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a model that uses a large language model to forecast wind power output minutes ahead. Grid operators need such ultra-short-term forecasts to keep the grid stable and to plan how much other power to hold ready. Older methods, the team notes, cannot make full use of mixed text and numerical data.

Their model, named M2WLLM, feeds the language model both text prompts and time-series data. One component, the Semantic Augmenter, translates the numerical data into a form the language model can work with, which helps it extract hidden features. On wind farm data from three Chinese provinces, M2WLLM consistently outperformed existing methods. It also performed well when only a few past cases were available for learning. The authors present the design as a way to raise forecasting accuracy for wind energy.
arxiv-2506-01031:
Yanyuan Qiao and co-authors present NavBench, a test suite for how well multimodal language models navigate indoor spaces, in a research paper from 2025. Such models read images and text together, but acting inside real places is a sterner test. The suite probes both understanding and step-by-step movement.

Understanding tasks cover matching instructions to scenes, judging progress, and linking views to actions, across 3,200 question pairs. Movement trials run 432 episodes in seventy-two indoor scenes of graded difficulty. A converter turns model words into robot actions. Top models did well overall, yet most stumbled on judging progress over time. Map context sharpened choices in mid-difficulty scenes.
arxiv-2506-01131:
Yu-Hsueh Chen and Tarun Grover study phase changes between two ways of breaking an exotic symmetry. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses one-dimensional spin chains. The symmetries here are non-invertible, a newer class beyond group rules. Breaking them in two patterns gives two distinct phases.

The switch point mirrors deconfined quantum critical points. Both order measures share the same exponents there. The symmetry swells at the critical point, as in classic examples. Gauging a spin flip spins off a whole family of twin critical points. Bosonization maps the nearby phase diagram. Neighboring models host a kindred transition guarded by the exotic symmetry.
arxiv-2506-01531:
Wenhao Liu and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a very hard data set of math derivations drawn from fresh research papers. Good data drives reasoning gains in language models, yet older sets are too easy, skip human-like steps, or rest on one model's output. Their set packs dense hints and stepwise human-style work into each problem.

A human-in-the-loop team of agents drafted and filtered the samples, with mathematicians grading the result. From two thousand drafts, the hundred hardest problems became the benchmark. Top models solved fewer than five percent of them. Training on the set still lifted smaller models by eight to nine points, which makes it both a stern test and a teaching tool.
arxiv-2506-02331:
Hing-Tong Cho and Kin-Wang Ng hunt for parity violation in the infant universe in a paper from 2025. Parity violation would mean the early cosmos treated left and right differently. The team works inside axion inflation, a model where a rolling field amplifies one handedness of light. They compute the four-point correlation of the inflaton field using an open quantum system method. The result splits cleanly into even and odd parts under parity.

In a strong-coupling limit, the calculation simplifies. The lowest odd term they find is clearly nonzero, a direct sign of parity violation. Its size matches recent galaxy survey hints. The work gives theorists concrete numbers to test against the sky.
arxiv-2506-02431:
Mahammed Kamruzzaman and co-authors test whether language models assign emotions in line with nationality stereotypes, in a paper from 2025. Models are now used as role-playing agents that take on personas. If a model's idea of a country skews the feelings it assigns, its outputs can carry bias.

The team gave models nationality personas and measured which emotions they attributed. Four classic cultural dimensions, covering power distance, uncertainty avoidance, long-term outlook, and individualism, framed the analysis. Strong gaps appeared by nationality. Emotions such as shame, fear, and joy were handed out unevenly across regions. The models' answers also diverged from human patterns, above all for negative emotions. The authors warn of flattened, biased portraits in model outputs.
arxiv-2506-03431:
Josep Gallegos, a solo author, studies boundary estimates for harmonic functions on rough domains, in a 2025 math paper. The domains may have very jagged edges, as long as they meet a mild corkscrew shape rule and their edges are evenly spread in a strong sense. No links between inner parts are assumed. Gallegos proves a one-sided Rellich estimate, which bounds the outward slope of a solution by the surface slope of its edge values.

He also proves the reverse direction: if the estimate holds, the edge must pass a classic no-boxes test from geometric measure theory. In flat two-dimensional cases, the estimate thus marks exactly the well-spread edges. A weak-form solution result for the companion regularity problem follows. One payoff: solving the basic Dirichlet problem need not imply solving the regularity one.
arxiv-2506-04431:
The CMS Collaboration reports, in 2025, a search for dark matter produced alongside a Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider. In the scenario tested, the Higgs decays into a pair of tau leptons while the dark matter escapes unseen. Data came from proton collisions at thirteen tera-electronvolts recorded in 2017 and 2018.

No excess over expected background appeared. The null result was converted into limits within two benchmark models. For one, heavy partner boson masses between four hundred and seven hundred giga-electronvolts were excluded at a set light mass. For the other, combining with an earlier dataset excluded mediator masses up to just over one tera-electronvolt.
arxiv-2506-05831:
Heart tracings come as both waveforms and pictures, and teaching a language model to read both is tricky. The Heartcare team presents a full toolkit in a 2025 paper. It includes a dataset of 400,000 instruction examples built from hospital reports and a benchmark for testing tracing understanding from many angles. It also includes a model that encodes the signal and its image into one shared space.

A structure-aware tokenizer that respects heartbeats anchors the design, joined by a two-stream alignment method. Across many tracing tasks, the model improved consistently over rivals. The authors argue the recipe could extend language models to other body signals beyond the heart.
arxiv-2506-06931:
Shen, Kim, and Sloth build a safe speed control for robots that learns from data in this twenty twenty-five paper. Safe control needs a bound rule that keeps the robot out of banned zones. A model-free bound rule leans on a built-in speed chief, but its key decay rate is hard to know.

Inside, a small net learns a score for how far the robot sits from a safe rest state. From that score the team gauges the best decay rate of the built-in chief. A chance-based guard then folds that gauge, with its doubt, into the bound rule. Tests on a real robot arm in a range of setups show the guard keeps speed safe as hoped.
arxiv-2506-07531:
Teng-Fei Xiao, Junlong Tian, and Jie Peng study how single photons move through a small optical device. Their two thousand twenty-five paper sits in quantum optics. The device is a one-way channel linked to a lossy cavity that responds in a nonlinear way. Light can pass one way but not the other, like a diode for current. The authors ask whether loss, usually a flaw, can make that one-way action perfect.

They derive exact formulas for how one or two photons scatter in the setup. With the right loss, a single photon passes fully from one side and not at all from the other. They also map the working range of the two-photon case. The paper ties the diode effect to each system setting. The results may guide future quantum devices and networks.
arxiv-2506-07731:
Mouadh Yagoubi, Yasser Dahou, and Billel Mokeddem lead a large team on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It sets out the E2LM competition, run with NeurIPS in that year, on grading language models while they are still young in training.

Set benchmarks grade finished models well but give weak, blurry signals early in training, when small models shift fast. The contest asks entrants to build science tests tuned to that early phase. Three small pre-trained models and their mid-training saves are given, and all work can run on free cloud GPUs. Entries are judged on signal quality, on how well early ranks match the ranks at a far later stage, and on fit to science. The aim is benchmark-led training from day one.
arxiv-2506-07831:
Jinquan Huang and co-authors set a clock sync protocol for drone based quantum key sharing, in work from twenty twenty-five. Drones can spread entangled light pairs across wide and local areas. Key security rests on precise timing, since timing jitter lowers the quality of quantum measures.

Drones face tight size, weight, and power limits plus constant motion. The protocol pairs satellite timing at nanosecond grade with a correction drawn from the entanglement itself. No precision onboard clock is needed. Tests in simulated free space links with moving distances reached very fine sync, measured in tens of trillionths of a second. The work supports drone links for a future quantum internet.
arxiv-2506-08031:
Saeed Hashemi Sababe and Ehsan Lotfali Ghasab extend a classic algorithm in their 2025 paper. The Krasnoselskii-Mann method inches toward a fixed point, a spot a function maps to itself, by averaging steps. Their version adds random noise, as in real data, and works in curved spaces measured by Bregman distances, a flexible way to gauge gaps between points.

The authors prove the method still lands on a fixed point almost surely, under mild rules on the noise. They also bound how far off the method can be after a set number of steps. The bound depends on how curved the distance measure is. Tests on a learning task and on mirror descent, a cousin method, matched the theory.
arxiv-2506-08331:
Pan Zhang presents a 2025 proposal to fix errors in quantum computers with a quantum circuit itself. Quantum machines need error correction to run long tasks. Today a classical computer reads the error clues and picks the fix, but classical steps lag behind fast quantum hardware. That lag blocks real-time correction on the quickest chips. Zhang trains a second quantum circuit to do the decoding.

The helper circuit learns from error clue readings to name the fix for the main circuit. It runs at the same speed as the circuit it guards. Tests on surface codes up to distance seven matched a top classical method under circuit-level noise. The scheme works for codes with many stored qubits and varied noise. Self-correcting machines, the author argues, are a real prospect.
arxiv-2506-08431: Neeraj Kumar Tomar, Fahed Zulfeqarr, and Sharma set out a new class of spaces in topology, a soft form of normality built on a named type of open set. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five, in pure math. They draw out many traits of such spaces and show how they link to kin classes, with cases and counter-cases to fix the gaps. Their main result is that the trait is kept by the space's own form, and passes to closed parts of it.
arxiv-2506-09931:
Shuangyang Li and co-authors ask whether sending signals faster than the classic limit helps a system that must both communicate and sense its surroundings. Their 2025 paper studies a single-carrier setup, where one stream of symbols carries data while echoes reveal targets. Speeding the symbols up is known to pack in more data, but its sensing effects were less clear.

Through careful math, they show the faster scheme avoids a smearing effect that hurts both data and sensing. They derive upper and lower bounds on data rates and show the gap between them shrinks as speed rises. For sensing, the faster signals gave steadier distance readings and fewer false peaks in speed readings. Tests with numbers backed each claim.
arxiv-2506-10031:
Olga Ovcharenko and six co-authors compare ways to learn from single-cell data without labels. Their paper from twenty twenty-five presents scSSL-Bench, a shared test suite. Self-supervised learning can pull useful traits from cell data on its own. Teams lacked one fair way to rank the many methods on sale.

The suite tests a large set of methods on a range of data sets. It scores them on three tasks: fixing batch shifts, naming cell types, and filling in a missing data kind. Plain methods from other fields did best at cell typing and data merging. Cell-focused tools led at batch fixing. Random masking was the best way to alter data in training. The suite gives labs plain advice on which method fits which task.
arxiv-2506-10131:
Leo Stodolsky and J. Silk argue that explosions in the very early universe could leave a signal we can still detect today. Such bursts would create positrons, the antimatter twins of electrons. When a positron meets an electron, both vanish in a flash of light with a known energy.

In the standard picture of the early universe, positrons should be absent at the times the authors consider. Working through how the annihilation light gets absorbed and stretched as the universe expands, they find the surviving glow would reach us as soft X-rays. The light would come from an era when the universe was far smaller and denser than now. Because the standard picture predicts no such glow, finding it would strongly support the burst idea. The authors urge observers to search for the signal. Even a clear non-detection would limit how violent the early universe could have been.
arxiv-2506-10231:
Anneliese Brei, Katharine Henry, Abhisheik Sharma, Shashank Srivastava, and Snigdha Chaturvedi test whether language models can spot unreliable narrators, in a two thousand twenty-five paper mixing literary theory and machine learning. An unreliable narrator unintentionally misrepresents events in a first-person account.

Drawing on narratology, the authors define several unreliability types and build TUNa, an expert-annotated dataset spanning blog posts, forum posts, hotel reviews, and literature. Classification tasks cover unreliability within a narration, between narrators, and across texts. Popular open and proprietary models struggle, though few-shot prompting, fine-tuning, and curriculum learning all show promise. The dataset and code are released for future work.
arxiv-2506-10931:
Melina Soysal and co-authors speed genome analysis by computing inside storage in a 2025 paper. New sequencers read DNA as raw electrical signals, which software can decode in real time. As machines get faster, moving data to the processor becomes the main cost in time and energy.

Their system performs the analysis within the storage subsystem itself. It taps the memory and spare compute that modern drives already carry. That placement attacks the data movement bottleneck directly instead of merely speeding the math. The design targets both higher throughput and lower energy per genome. Such storage-side computing may decide whether live analysis keeps pace with the next sequencer generation.
arxiv-2506-11431:
Jinhee Kim and five colleagues present TruncQuant, a training scheme for neural networks that must run at flexible precision, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Edge devices vary in capability, so one model ideally serves many hardware platforms. Truncation, dropping low bits at runtime, offers that flexibility cheaply.

Standard quantization-aware training does not prepare networks for truncation errors. TruncQuant aligns training with what truncation actually does to the outputs. At runtime, simple bit-shifting switches the operating precision. A single trained model then adapts across devices with little or no extra cost. The authors target the familiar deployment tension between model size, latency, and accuracy. Their scheme aims to keep accuracy steadier as precision falls.
arxiv-2506-11631:
Simeon Junker and Sina Zarrieß wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents SceneGram, a data set of how people name tangram shapes when the shapes sit in varied scenes.

A tangram blob can be read as a crab, a sink, or a space ship, and scene context is thought to sway the read. The set gathers human names for shapes placed in set scenes, so the sway can be gauged in a planned way. The team then grades the names that multimodal language models give. The models miss much of the range and shift found in human names. The set opens a path to study context in reference.
arxiv-2506-12631:
Avinash Khare, Fred Cooper, John Dawson, and Avadh Saxena find exact solitary wave solutions for a nonlinear Dirac model that complements one they studied before. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The model mixes two kinds of self-interaction for a relativistic particle field. Two knobs tune the mix and the power of the terms.

Like the sister model, this one hosts solitary waves across the whole knob plane. The ratio of energy to charge again ignores the coupling strength. All waves here are single-humped, and any frequency below the mass is allowed. Bound states, though, exist only when one knob stays under a limit set by the other. A standard criterion sorts the stable regions. The team also reduces the model to a modified wave equation for slow motion. The pair of models now brackets a family of relativistic wave systems.
arxiv-2506-13431:
Aman Sharma, Mithilesh Nayak, Natalia Chepiga, and Frédéric Mila study excitations in frustrated quantum spin chains, in a 2025 paper. The chains hold spins of size three halves. Neighbor and next-neighbor couplings compete. Between two transitions, the chain settles into a partly dimerized phase. The team used a valence bond picture checked against large simulations. They probed two excitation types: magnons and spinons.

As coupling grows, the magnon's path through momentum bends into an incommensurate pattern. Spinons, seen as walls between paired states, follow later. Their energy gap peaks mid-phase and closes at the edges. That closing hints at a floating phase forming. The combined spectrum shows magnons as echoes inside the spinon range. A spin five-halves chain shows the same behavior. The authors claim a shared picture across half-integer spins. The work speaks to neutron scattering experiments on real materials.
arxiv-2506-14031:
Viviana del Barco, Ana Cristina Ferreira, and Ines Kath study special geometric structures on seven-dimensional Lie groups, in a 2025 mathematics paper. The structures are of a type tied to the group known as G2-star, and the authors focus on those whose holonomy is indecomposable and of type III. Holonomy describes how vectors twist when carried around loops in the space. The team builds on a known list of candidate holonomy algebras.

Their main result shows that only abelian subalgebras can occur in this setting, and those must have dimension two or three. They also give explicit Lie groups that carry such structures with these holonomies. The work narrows the search space for geometers who classify these rare structures.
arxiv-2506-14431: Yong Jiao and co-authors settle a convergence question for a noncommutative Fourier series in a 2025 math paper. Vilenkin systems generalize the classic wave basis to grouped settings. Here the coefficients live in an algebra where order matters, and classical proofs break. The team proves maximal inequalities for the averaged partial sums, and almost uniform convergence follows. Their tools are a noncommutative square function and a recent Calderon-Zygmund splitting built for this algebra.
arxiv-2506-14831:
Céline Finet and seven co-authors review how computers predict where people will walk in this two thousand twenty-five survey. Forecasting the paths of several people at once matters for robots, self-driving cars, and crowd studies. Data-driven methods have advanced fast in recent years. The authors gather work from two thousand twenty to two thousand twenty-five. They sort methods by how they are built, what inputs they take, and how they form predictions.

Much of the review centers on models tested on the standard ETH and UCY crowd data sets. The authors weigh what the best models share. They close with open challenges and promising directions. Newcomers get a map of a crowded field, while experts get a sober stock-take. Social interaction between walkers is a recurring theme.
arxiv-2506-16631:
Saghir Alfasly, Ghazal Alabtah, and Tizhoosh present a 2025 paper on overfitting in deep learning for tissue slide images. Models built for natural photos are often fine-tuned for histopathology, the study of tissue under the microscope. The team shows this habit backfires: big borrowed models memorize rather than learn and perform worse than expected. They tested many architectures, including ResNet variants and vision transformers, on a public esophageal cancer data set.

Growing model size did not reliably help on these medical images. Simpler, purpose-built designs matched or beat the large ones while overfitting less. The problem bites hardest when data sets are small, as medical ones often are. The authors argue the field needs architectures designed for tissue images from the start. Their message runs against the default of importing the biggest available model.
arxiv-2506-17931:
Gupta, Das, and Sethi give a way to teach a sight net on one photo world and use it in the next, with no tags in the new world. Nets learn the look of their home set and stumble when the style shifts. Their net weds a deep backbone to a scale web. That web splits what a thing is from how it looks. A tuned mix of loss rules drives the training.

The mix aims at the hard parts of plain photos: size shifts, noise, and style swings across kinds. On three known test sets, their way beat the best past CNN ways. On a fourth, wide set it tied the best. Training also ran to its end faster than past ways did. The team see the scale split as the key that lets one net read many photo worlds.
arxiv-2506-18131:
Sakhiyev leads a team of fifteen on this design paper from two thousand twenty-five, which appeared in Nuclear Physics B. It lays out AlSUN, a planned source of ultracold neutrons at the WWR-K reactor in Almaty, Kazakhstan.

Ultracold neutrons crawl so slowly they can be trapped and stored, a rare gift for physics tests. The source would sit in the reactor's thermal column, with a superfluid helium converter at its heart. The plan splits the heat flow from the neutron flow, so the trap can run below one degree with thin wall losses. A helium-3 pump fridge does the cooling. Wall stuff with a high critical speed would hold more neutrons still. The paper maps the build, the stuff it needs, and tests to run first.
arxiv-2506-18231:
Chérouvrier and a very large team of co-authors report a cosmology survey in twenty twenty-five. The NIKA2 Cosmological Legacy Survey hunts galaxy clusters in the COSMOS field. Clusters formed late in cosmic history, so they probe how structure grew. The survey finds them blindly, without knowing where they are in advance.

Detection uses the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, a shadow clusters cast on the cosmic background light. Hot gas in a cluster distorts that light in a known way. A blind search can reveal clusters that other methods miss. The abridged abstract sets out the survey and its cluster finds. Readers get a census of massive structures built from a single, unbiased signal.
arxiv-2506-21131:
A feeding black hole flickers in a near-clock rhythm, and the rhythm's drift tells how its disk and crown trade heat. Sai-En Xu, Bei You, Yi Long, and Han He read that drift in 2025 for one bright hole caught mid-change. Past holes showed one clean line between the beat and the disk's glow. This one bends the line in two.

Below a set beat, a faster beat meant a dimmer disk; above it, the tie flipped and faster meant brighter. The crown's glow told the mirror tale. The team read the bend as the hot flow's slow tilt, a known frame, changing its lean as the hole's state turned. In flare hours the flicker's strength also split by photon punch, flat above a line and climbing below it.
arxiv-2506-21431:
Sriluckshmy, François Jamet, and Fedor Šimkovic bring quantum computers into a materials method in their 2025 paper. The method, called ghost Gutzwiller, mimics how electrons interact in real materials at low cost. Its slow step is finding the ground state of a small stand-in model, over and over in a loop.

The team offloads that step to a quantum device, which samples good candidate states. They found the wanted states stay sparse, so a small sample of the full set can rebuild them well. Runs on real quantum hardware, with up to twenty-four qubits, converged and caught the switch from metal to insulator in a classic model. The work is an early proof that quantum help fits this method.
arxiv-2506-22031:
Bassi and Papallo studied coverings of Hilbert schemes in twenty twenty-five. A Hilbert scheme is a geometric space whose points stand for clusters of points on a surface. A covering is a structured map from another space onto it, like a multi-sheeted wrapper.

The authors give an explicit geometric description of all coverings of the Hilbert square, the case tracking pairs of points. Their setting is a normal complex surface with finite fundamental group, a measure of its loop structure. They then apply the construction to symplectic surfaces, a class with special geometric structure. They show the Hilbert square of such a surface is itself an irreducible symplectic variety. The result settles the nature of these spaces for that surface class.
arxiv-2506-23631:
Mihail Kolountzakis, Nir Lev, and Máté Matolcsi prove geometric facts about sets that can tile space in a weak sense, in a 2025 paper. Weak tiling loosens the usual tiling demand: translated copies of a set may overlap, as long as they cover the complement of the set with the right total weight. The notion proved key in settling a famous conjecture about spectral sets, since every spectral set must weakly tile its own complement.

For a convex polytope that weakly tiles its complement, the authors give a direct proof that the shape must be symmetric and must have symmetric faces. For a set on the line made of finitely many intervals, they derive a condition that the gaps between intervals must satisfy. The paper returns to a tool built for one big proof and maps what shapes it allows on purely geometric grounds.
arxiv-2506-23731:
Michel Meintz, Jan Dubiński, Franziska Boenisch, and Adam Dziedzic test whether watermarks in AI images survive being trained into a new model. Their paper from twenty twenty-five calls that survival radioactivity. Owners need it to catch rivals who train on their outputs. Diffusion model marks fail the test in their study. Encoding into latent space erases some; the noise loop in training kills the rest.

Autoregressive image models, now ahead on quality, had no radioactive scheme at all. The team builds the first one, borrowing tricks from text model watermarking. Their mark rides the model's own step-by-step generation style. Wide tests show the mark persists through retraining and stays readable in the child's outputs. Provenance tracking across model generations becomes feasible.
arxiv-2506-23931:
Nicolas Aimar and three co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on flares from the huge black hole at the heart of our galaxy. Its mass tops four million suns. Some doubt it is a true black hole, since holes hold a point of infinite density and trap facts for good. Exotic compact objects are the rival class: boson stars, fluid spheres, and gravastars.

The team fakes a hot spot that orbits each of eight such objects and reads its path and light twist. With today's gear, no rival can be told from a hole. A planned sharper kit could spot some of them. Richer spot models blur the edge again, they warn.
arxiv-2507-00631:
David Shi and Kevin Joo proposed Operator in twenty twenty-five, a protocol for delegating work to untrusted agents under uncertainty. Autonomous AI agents gain from handing subtasks to others, yet in low-trust settings no upfront spec or central overseer can guarantee the work is right. Their guiding claim: correctness emerges when exposing error is cheaper than committing it.

Tasks are posted as intents, and solvers compete to fill them while staking collateral. Verifiers check results after the fact. Anyone may challenge a result by staking against it, triggering verification; wrong agents are slashed and correct challengers rewarded. Erroneous verifiers can themselves be penalized through escalation. When incentives align across all roles, the authors argue, honesty becomes the equilibrium strategy.
arxiv-2507-00731:
Zhi-Ying Qin and co-authors model the QCD phase change at high heat and density with non extensive statistics, in work from twenty twenty-five. Quantum chromodynamics governs how quarks and gluons turn into hadrons. In heavy ion collisions, the fireball may never fully settle to equilibrium, which bends standard statistics.

A parameter called q measures the drift from equilibrium in their model. Gas equations for the low and high heat phases are joined by a smooth crossover. Heat traits such as entropy, pressure, and energy all grew as q rose above one. Sound speed shifted near the critical point in a non trivial way. At q equal to one, results matched lattice and lab fit data at low heat.
arxiv-2507-01031:
Fanchen Bu and Kijung Shin share a 2025 account of moving graph learning software from the dominant chip platform to a rival one. Graph learning works on data shaped as networks, from social ties to molecules, and it usually runs on Nvidia graphics chips. Intel's Gaudi chips offer strong speed and energy use, but they need major extra work to run the same tools.

The authors describe porting PyTorch-based graph frameworks to the second version of the Gaudi chip. They built a set of core utilities that restore key steps the chip lacked, such as scatter operations, sparse indexing, and finding nearest neighbors. They also gathered guided tutorials and real-world examples with notes on fixing faults. The work gives other teams a tested path off the standard platform.
arxiv-2507-02831: Fabrizio Nieri wrote a paper from 2025 on trace formulas in a deformed family of symmetry algebras, the W-algebras. It draws out a fresh link to a doubled form of their quantum-deformed version. Correlation sums around a torus in the additive setting reproduce sphere sums in the trigonometric setting, up to a possible completion term. Read through gauge theory, the mechanism lifts a two-dimensional setup into three dimensions.
arxiv-2507-03031:
Jasper Yao argues a sweeping claim about neural network safety in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Universal approximators can mimic any function, given enough size. That power is why they are useful. Yao claims the same power makes perfect control impossible. Catastrophic failure points, he argues, are woven densely into any such system. He builds the case in three layers, from counting arguments to topology.

For common networks, failure density grows with expressive power. For all approximators, singularity theory ties flexibility to instability. The conclusion is stark: flawless alignment of such systems is a mathematical impossibility, not an engineering gap. The paper is a position piece that invites rebuttal. AI safety researchers are the audience.
arxiv-2507-04231:
Mahdi-Tahar Brahimi studies modular equation solving with a new number system built from polynomial-like objects, in this 2025 paper. The tools, called polynumbers and polyseries, come from Norman Wildberger's recent work. Brahimi applies them to quadratic equations inside modular arithmetic, where numbers wrap around a fixed modulus.

A recurrence borrowed from the Catalan number sequence drives the method. New notions, including special polynumber sequences and a truncated series form, support the proofs. The goal is an equivalence result: settling when solutions to these equations exist and when they are unique. The paper tests whether the fresh tools can carry classical number theory results.
arxiv-2507-04531:
Rushil Thareja, Preslav Nakov, Praneeth Vepakomma, and Nils Lukas present DP-Fusion, a method that guards private text when a large language model answers. Model output can leak facts from its context, such as text pulled from private stores. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Past guards lack proof or trade too much quality for safety. DP-Fusion marks the tender tokens, runs the model with and without them, then blends the two outputs so the final text stays near the clean run. This caps how much any set of tender tokens can sway the result. The team centers on rewriting files to hide personal facts while keeping text quality high.
arxiv-2507-06031:
Juncheng Jia and co-authors present faster ways to run federated learning by using spare download bandwidth, in a paper from 2025. In federated learning, many devices train a shared model without sending their raw data to a center. Slow delivery of model updates can stall that training.

Their first method works when devices update at their own pace. On the server side, a dynamic merging scheme blends late updates with the global model. On the device side, an adaptive step mixes the newest global model into local training. A second method adapts the same ideas to lockstep training. Theory supports both methods. Tests across six models and five data sets showed large gains in accuracy and speed over baselines.
arxiv-2507-06631:
Enda Bigarella reports, in twenty twenty-five, a method to detect and prevent overfitting in regressions on mesh-structured data. Overfitting means a model hugs training noise and wobbles between data points. On a mesh, second derivatives can be computed directly from the data layout. Derivatives of the training data serve as a true label of the data's entropy, its roughness. Derivatives of the trained model are computed on a staggered mesh, offset from the training grid. That exposes oscillations hiding inside the training cells.

The mismatch in Laplace-operator derivatives becomes a loss for tuning hyperparameters. Minimizing it reduces unwanted oscillation. No test split is needed: training uses all points, and the staggered-mesh check acts as a surrogate test based on diffusion behavior.
arxiv-2507-06831:
Hachem and three co-authors present a 2025 study of spin pumping in layered films of a magnetic insulator and a tungsten-titanium alloy. Spin pumping injects a pure spin current from the magnet into the metal, a basic move in spintronics. The team varied both layer thicknesses and measured resonance damping. A thin alloy layer clearly raised the damping of thin magnet films, showing efficient spin injection.

The transfer strength peaked at a 3-nanometer alloy layer, then fell for thicker ones. The authors blame a structural phase change in the alloy that weakens its spin-orbit grip. Titanium doping also lowered transfer compared with pure tungsten films. The lesson for device builders: in spin transport, crystal phase and alloy recipe matter as much as thickness.
arxiv-2507-07231:
Dutta, Maitra, and Stanica widened a quantum method in twenty twenty-five that reads hidden traits of yes-no functions used in code work. Those traits, like cross-tie spectra, shape how safe a code is. A known quantum routine reads some of them fast.

They give the broadest form yet of that routine, with old forms as side cases. A new tie score lets their routines gauge the fresh spectra. They weigh the win odds of each sampling plan side by side. Shift tests for bent functions, a prized code class, close the work.
arxiv-2507-07731:
Xixi Liu, Ailin Deng, and Christopher Zach propose a decoding trick to stop vision-language models from claiming objects are present when they are not. Existing fixes tend to work only with certain decoding schemes, demand elaborate input changes, or borrow knowledge from outside models. The authors start from an odd observation about yes-biased answers.

Across three question-answering datasets, the models answered yes at noticeably uneven rates. Their method scores hidden states layer by layer with an energy measure and decodes from the lowest-energy layer. Accuracy and F1 scores rose on three benchmarks across three models, beating greedy decoding by nearly five points on average. The yes-bias gap also shrank substantially.
arxiv-2507-07931:
Hans Gundlach, Jayson Lynch, and Neil Thompson argue in a 2025 paper that smaller AI models will catch up with the largest ones. The past decade saw a few firms scale models far beyond rivals, which opened a wide gap in skill. The authors claim the gains from added compute shrink so fast that this gap will close on its own.

They build a model of training on a fixed task and show that each extra unit of compute buys less and less skill. Even a firm that scales far faster than others would, in time, hold only a small edge. The authors support the claim with benchmark data and with past trends in model skill. They close by urging a fresh look at AI strategy and policy in light of this shift.
arxiv-2507-08931:
Jaiyul Yoo, Matteo Magi, and Dragan Huterer ask why three ways of measuring our motion through the universe disagree, and how much disagreement the standard cosmology actually predicts. Each probe, the microwave background, supernova distances, and galaxy counts, shows a dipole: one direction looks slightly different from its opposite. All three should reflect the observer's velocity, yet the measurements sit in tension. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team dissects every contribution to each dipole inside the standard model. Their framework extends beyond it as well.

Observer motion dominates, they find, while the sources' own motions fade quickly with distance. So the dipoles should point the same way but need not match in size. Several common misconceptions in the literature are corrected along the way. The tension survives, but it is now precisely stated.
arxiv-2507-09031:
Yash Shah and co-authors wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on keeping models fair while they keep learning. Confounders, side variables like age or site, can bend both the input and the target, teaching a model biased shortcuts.

A known fix, metadata normalization, adjusts learned features to strip out confounder effects. The catch is continual learning, where data arrives in stages and yesterday's statistics go stale. The team's Recursive MDN layer updates its correction on the fly with a recursive least squares scheme. It can be dropped into any deep network, including vision transformers, at any depth. Experiments show fairer predictions across groups, both in one-shot training and across learning stages. The layer also cuts the forgetting that shifting confounders cause.
arxiv-2507-09231:
Artem Chystiakov and Mariia Zhvanko present a 2025 paper on a private version of wrapped Ethereum, a token that mirrors the main coin of that blockchain. Public blockchains show every transfer to everyone, which is a strength for trust but a risk for privacy. The authors try to keep both.

Their design works wholly at the app layer, with no change to the chain itself. Math commitments hide amounts while still letting the system check them. A key exchange step controls who can open the hidden data. Special proofs, called zk-SNARKs, force each step to be formed correctly. The paper lays out the full scheme.
arxiv-2507-11031:
Weiming Feng and Minji Yang prove fast mixing for a sampling walk on monotone systems. Glauber dynamics flips one variable at a time to sample from a distribution. Slow mixing makes such walks useless for hard counting tasks. The pair study monotone systems whose parts satisfy a strong independence property.

Their new comparison links the plain walk to a block walk called field dynamics. The proof blends a classic censoring argument with high-dimensional expander tools. For the random cluster model, mixing lands near linear in system size. For the bipartite hardcore model, it lands near quadratic under one-sided uniqueness. Both beat the best bounds known before this work.
arxiv-2507-12031:
Fateme Salehi and co-authors design a smarter radio link for future 6G factory networks, in a 2025 paper. Small in-factory subnetworks must deliver nearly every packet on time, since missed packets can upset control loops and threaten safety. The team focuses on bursts of lost packets, a risk earlier work often ignored. Their controller learns by trial and error, using a deep reinforcement learning method.

The controller adjusts signal power and packet length based only on a measure of signal quality. In simulations it cut bursts of lost packets while using only 18 percent of the sending cost of a full-power policy. Weights in its reward let engineers trade energy savings against reliability for each site. The authors present the design as a flexible fit for strict industrial needs.
arxiv-2507-13031:
Dekui Peng and Yi Zhou wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on how dense the subgroups of a topological group can be. For any such group, some subgroups wind through the whole space, and their smallest sizes form a spectrum of cardinals. The pair map that spectrum, and a second one built from closed subgroups.

Their headline result: every compact group realizes its full possible range, from its density up to its weight. They also build, within standard set theory, a separable countably compact Boolean group hiding a closed subgroup that is not separable, settling a question from the literature. A free pro-p group of uncountable rank, they show, has no tame closed normal subgroups. Under a standard set-theoretic hypothesis, closed spectra of tame groups form clean intervals.
arxiv-2507-13131:
Elmehdi Illi, Marwa Qaraqe, and Ali Ghrayeb design a secure base station that both communicates and senses, using pinching antennas. Their paper appeared in 2025. Pinching antennas can be placed at chosen spots along waveguides, unlike fixed arrays. The station must serve honest users, keep their data secret, and detect hostile targets at the same time. The team chooses antenna spots, signal beams, and noise patterns together.

Their design maximizes sensing power under secrecy and power limits. Tests beat a baseline version with evenly spaced antennas by three decibels in sensing power. Against a classic fixed array, gains reached thirty decibels. The authors argue that movable antenna points give secure sensing systems a large, cheap edge.
arxiv-2507-13431:
Prathamesh Tamhane leads a fourteen-author team constraining star formation in the giant galaxy M87, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. M87 sits at the center of the Virgo cluster and hosts a famous supermassive black hole. Whether it still forms stars, and how fast, was unclear.

The team analyzed the deepest Hubble ultraviolet imaging of M87 available. After removing the galaxy's glow and its globular clusters, excess point sources remained near the center. Their colors matched young stars in simulations, not an old stellar population. The inferred star formation rate is extremely low. A weak burst about a hundred twenty-five million years ago formed roughly a thousand solar masses. Recent black hole outbursts seem unrelated to the star formation.
arxiv-2507-13731:
Ahmadi-Asl, Kooshkghazi, and Leplat approximated quaternion matrices with fewer passes in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Quaternion matrices pack color images and other multi-channel data compactly. Randomized low-rank methods compress them well, but they reread the data many times. When moving data costs more than computing, those rereads dominate.

Their algorithms let users set the pass budget directly and trade it against accuracy. One family works with any number of views of the matrix. A block Krylov variant converges faster when the spectrum decays slowly. Error bounds show the expected error shrinking exponentially with extra passes. Tests spanned data compression, matrix completion, image upscaling, and deep learning.
arxiv-2507-15331:
Anthony Morton surveys classic results about power networks in a 2025 survey. At the center stands the admittance matrix, which encodes how current and voltage relate across a network. Many standard circuit theorems taught to engineers can be drawn from traits of that matrix and its cofactors.

Later sections connect the matrix determinant to the network's topology. Direct and alternating current networks are set side by side, covering monotonicity, orientation, and impedance. One finding goes the other way: no impedance measure for alternating current extends the clean direct current version in general. The survey gathers scattered classic theory into one account for students and other readers.
arxiv-2507-18031:
Ahmad ALBarqawi, Mahmoud Nazzal, Issa Khalil, Abdallah Khreishah, and NhatHai Phan present a deepfake detector, in a 2025 preprint, that explains its calls in words as well as pixels. Fake images are getting good enough to fool casual checks. Many detectors generalize poorly to new fake makers and break under attack. The authors' system, ViGText, pairs each image with a written account from a vision-language model. Explanations can expose small flaws that plain captions miss.

The image is cut into patches, and both image and text become graphs. A graph neural network studies the linked graphs together. Features are drawn from both space and frequency views of the image. On fakes made by user-tuned generators, scores jumped far above older detectors. Recall rose by about eleven percent over rivals in robustness tests. Even under attacks aimed at its graph design, performance fell by less than four percent.
arxiv-2507-20431:
Guzina and three colleagues study waves that hug the cut face of a repeating material in twenty twenty-five. Waves in such materials split into body waves that roam and surface waves that fade with depth. The surface kind had not been worked out in full. The team used a plain wave model on a two dimensional repeating grid as a test bed.

They built a small model based on one repeat cell of the grid. It yields the wave's speed, shape, and depth of reach from a compact math problem. Surface bumps can thus be tuned fast to steer the waves. They also work out how much power the waves carry and how deep they bite.
arxiv-2507-22431:
Zhixiang Wei and co-authors present HQ-CLIP, a way to build better image-text data and models, in a research paper from 2025. CLIP models learn from huge sets of image and text pairs, but those pairs are noisy. Large vision-language models, which build on CLIP, might in turn clean that data and start a cycle of gains.

Their pipeline uses such a model to write long and short notes for each image, in both positive and negative forms. A refined set of one hundred fifty million pairs results. Training with the added notes lifts scores across many tests. The work shows data quality can be raised by the models it trains.
arxiv-2507-22631:
Zachary Feng and Dmitri Whitmore prove a number theory result in this 2025 paper. Their objects are Galois representations, symmetry records that arise from automorphic forms, a bridge between analysis and arithmetic. A polarized, well-behaved form gives a whole family of such records, one for each prime. The question is whether each record can be broken into smaller blocks, a trait called reducibility.

Under set terms on the size n, the pair prove the records stay whole for almost all primes, in a precise density sense. The allowed exception is narrow: primes dividing seven are set aside, with a side rule when four divides n. The result firms a broad hope that such records are as unbreakable as they can be. It serves the Langlands program's long map of links.
arxiv-2507-23231:
Bal, writing solo in twenty twenty-five, introduced a graph construction that always yields perfect graphs. A graph's line graph turns edges into vertices; it usually contains forbidden patterns. Bal instead takes the line graph of a graph's canonical bipartite double cover, producing a doubled edge-stage lift.

The construction's spectrum splits neatly into the ordinary line graph's spectrum plus a canonical signed refinement, so edge information is retained rather than lost. For every input graph the lift is perfect, meaning its coloring number equals its clique size in all induced subgraphs, and it is also claw-free and box-perfect. For regular inputs he gives an explicit spectral formula with control of the second eigenvalue and gap. Complete graphs and Paley graphs supply concrete families illustrating the theory.
arxiv-2507-23731:
Gaétan Leclerc proves a decay result for Fourier modes of equilibrium states, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The states live on smooth maps of a surface that keep area and stretch in a set way. Such decay tells us how rough or smooth a measure is at fine scales.

He uses a sum-product step to turn the task into a study of a time gap for a chosen flow. He then extends known work on fast mixing for three-way flows of this kind. Two pay-offs follow. One is fast mixing for a broad class of circle maps. The other is decay for the state count of the Fibonacci Hamiltonian, a first result of its kind for a quasicrystal.
arxiv-2508-00631:
Gang Liu, Soumen Pal, and Saminathan Ponnusamy study the long-run behavior of Halley's method. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, looks at a fast root-finding rule used on complex polynomials. The rule's paths split the plane into basins that flow to each root. The edges of those basins form a fractal set with rich structure.

The team proves the method settles for broad classes of polynomials. For many of them the fractal edge is one connected piece. The basins that touch each root stretch out without bound. The symmetry of the method matches that of the polynomial. One further result shows a basin can also be bounded, a twist worth note.
arxiv-2508-00831:
Florian Felten and co-authors present an open library for data-driven design work in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Design search looks for shapes and settings that score best on physics tests. Those tests are costly to run and hard to set up, which slows the search.

Their library, EngiBench, gives one common front end and curated test sets across fields such as flight, heat flow, and light devices. A second library adds search and learning methods built for the same front end. Tools cover data making, checks for valid designs, plots, and reports. Tests of leading methods showed the tasks stay hard for standard machine learning, the authors say.
arxiv-2508-01031:
Fengxiao Fan and Jingzhe Ni lead a team of ten on this paper from two thousand twenty-five, though the catalog's author list starts a few names later. It presents CADDesigner, an agent that drafts early CAD models from text or a sketch.

CAD tools demand deep skill, which shuts many out of early design. The agent talks with the user to pin down what is wanted, then writes the modeling code. A new context method guides that code. Visual checks feed back in rounds to lift the result. Past designs are kept in a knowledge base, so the agent grows with use. On concept design tasks it matches or beats the baselines tried.
arxiv-2508-01131:
Kumar and three colleagues present COLLAGE in twenty twenty-five, a way to pick training clips for robots that learn from few examples. A robot may get just a handful of demos for a new task, plus a vast store of past clips. Picking by one trait alone, such as looks, can pull in clips from the wrong task. Their method blends picks from many traits.

Each trait based subset gets a weight based on how well a policy trained on it predicts the target demos. Training then draws more from high weight subsets. Tests beat past methods in simulation across ten tasks. Gains were larger in real world tests drawn from a big public robot data set.
arxiv-2508-02031:
Tian Qin and co-authors propose, in twenty twenty-five, PRIME, an incremental learning model for classifying encrypted network traffic. Traffic classification supports quality of service, intrusion detection, and billing. Encryption hides content, so deep models read packet sequences instead. New services and attacks force models to learn new classes over time. But neural networks lose plasticity as tasks pile up, the authors note. They tracked that loss via the effective rank of parameters and the share of inactive neurons.

PRIME grows the model's parameter scale when plasticity drops. Across several encrypted traffic data sets and class-increment scenarios, it beat other incremental methods significantly. The parameter growth stayed minimal. The work targets security operations in fast-changing networks.
arxiv-2508-02331:
Claire Voisin answers a question in algebraic geometry in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. She continues her study of the Albanese morphism acting on zero-cycles, a tool for reading a variety's geometry. The question, posed by Colliot-Thélène, concerns varieties whose CH0 group is representable.

Voisin gives an example of a smooth projective variety with a representable CH0 group but no universal zero-cycle. That combination is exactly what the question asked whether one could find. Her construction rests on a counterexample to the integral Hodge conjecture due to Benoist and Ottem. The result separates two notions that might have seemed to travel together. It adds a sharp test case to the theory of algebraic cycles.
arxiv-2508-02831:
Mikołaj Zieliński and co-authors present a new encoding for editable 3D scenes in a 2025 paper. Neural radiance fields render scenes with high realism, but their hidden codes tangle the whole scene together. That tangle makes local edits and physical moves hard to control.

Their encoding gathers features through a field of soft Gaussian kernels, each covering a small region. Features blend smoothly as a region shifts or deforms, which keeps edits stable. A training scheme protects fine detail while keeping scenes editable. Tests show strong reconstruction quality alongside the added control. The method aims to make neural scenes behave more like objects users can reshape at will.
arxiv-2508-04231:
Yeh and seven colleagues use language model agents to clean time series data in twenty twenty-five. Automated machine learning usually tunes models and features. For forecasting, simple models often match complex ones, so data quality may matter more. Their agent, DCATS, focuses on the data itself.

The agent reads metadata that travels with each series. It cleans the data while aiming to improve forecast accuracy. Tests used four forecasting models on a large traffic volume data set. Error fell by an average of six percent across models and horizons. The authors argue data centric automation is a promising direction. It complements, rather than replaces, model search in forecasting pipelines.
arxiv-2508-04331:
Delbari and co-authors design a smart wall surface that lights a room with secure wireless signals, in this 2025 paper. The surface uses liquid crystal elements that bend radio waves toward chosen areas. Its response shifts with frequency, though, which can leak signals toward eavesdroppers in wideband systems.

Their design covers a wide band at once, aiming coverage at rooms with legitimate users while starving other zones. The plan avoids needing full channel knowledge or constant retuning. In simulations the method raised the secrecy rate over designs that ignore the frequency drift. The test case reached about two bits per symbol across a wide band near sixty gigahertz.
arxiv-2508-05331:
Thirunirai Selvam and Saravana Veni benchmark quantum circuits on real hardware in twenty twenty-five. Their platform is IBM Brisbane, a superconducting quantum processor. The study implements fundamental quantum gates and tracks how entangled states evolve. Entanglement is the key resource for secure quantum communication.

Simulations include decoherence and noise, the realities that spoil ideal circuits. That makes the results a fair test of practical viability. The work extends to simulating models such as Jaynes-Cummings and the longitudinal Ising model. Those models expose complex interactions in superconducting architectures. Readers get performance insight into what today's cloud quantum hardware can faithfully run.
arxiv-2508-05531:
Davide Garavaso and co-authors tackle labeling three dimensional scans of clothed people in a 2025 paper. Making digital clothing for avatars matters in fashion, film, and games, but wrinkles and layers are hard to capture. Scans are accurate yet carry no meaning about which part is body or garment. Standard labeling gives each point one label, which fails when layers overlap.

Their new approach lets one point belong to several layers at once, so hidden cloth under an outer garment can still be estimated. They built a synthetic data set with very realistic scans and known layer truth. Tests with varied network settings beat standard methods on both fake and real scans. Readers see a step toward full semantic rebuilding of dressed bodies.
arxiv-2508-06631:
Federico Armato, Barbara Garaventa, and Andrea Chincarini examine, in 2025, magnetic shielding for the Einstein Telescope, a planned gravitational wave detector. The instrument aims to hear signals at lower frequencies and far greater sensitivity than current detectors. At those low frequencies, magnetic noise is a leading disturbance.

One passive defense is to wrap sensitive parts in ferromagnetic material that diverts magnetic fields. The article weighs how well such shielding works and where its limits lie. The authors frame the study within the telescope's broader noise budget, where every source must shrink for the design sensitivity to be reached.
arxiv-2508-06731: Sole-Pi proves a result about random graphs and soficity in twenty twenty-five. A random rooted graph is called sofic if it is the limit of a sequence of finite graphs, in the sense of Benjamini and Schramm. He shows that any one ended, unimodular random rooted graph that avoids a fixed finite graph as a minor must be sofic. The one ended condition can be dropped if the graph is also quasi-transitive.
arxiv-2508-06831:
Taha Mustapha Nehdi and co-authors merge small expert adapters to move person re-identification across camera domains without touching source data, in work from twenty twenty-five. Re-identification models falter in new settings. With several labeled sources, treating each on its own beats blending, but full per source models get heavy.

Their method trains a tiny low rank adapter per source, each a sliver of the shared backbone. A light gating network learns how to weight the adapters for a new target. The approach needs no source data at adaptation time. On three hard benchmarks, it beat leading methods while staying lean. Adapter growth stays small as sources multiply.
arxiv-2508-07431:
Saurabh Rai, Prisha, and Jitendra Kumar shrink a transformer model for spotting top quarks down to one-bit weights, in a paper from 2025. Detectors at colliders must sort particle sprays in real time on tight hardware. Full models are too heavy for those chips. Their model, BitParT, keeps the transformer shape but stores each weight as a single bit.

The design borrows tricks from one-bit language models and fits them to physics data. On a public top quark data set, the tiny model tags nearly as well as its full-size parent. Size and compute needs fall by a wide margin. That opens the door to running modern models inside trigger systems. It also speeds offline rebuilding of huge data sets. The work is a proof that extreme shrinking can keep its edge.
arxiv-2508-08231:
Chris Schmitz and Joanna Bryson set out rules for putting AI into public bureaucracies without losing accountability, in this 2025 paper. Governments want AI's gains, but machine agency can create ethics sinks, spots where blame for bad outcomes dissolves. The authors deny such sinks are forced. They arise, they argue, from design choices in the tool and in the office that adopts it.

Reading AI ethics through the lens of Weber's bureaucracy theory, they propose a three-point framework. Keep clear, just human lines of accountability. Make sure staff can check that the system works right. Add AI only where it does not weaken the office's twin aims of legitimacy and stewardship. Used so, they say, AI can raise transparency rather than erode it.
arxiv-2508-08331:
Karen Guerrero-Vazquez and four co-authors build a database and AI helper for microRNA research in a 2025 paper. MicroRNAs tune gene activity and each one may target hundreds of genes. Finding true targets is hard because matching is imperfect and evidence is scattered across many sources.

Their database gathers predicted and confirmed microRNA-target pairs with rich annotations. Sources from many public collections are merged into one curated home. Beside it sits a multi-agent assistant powered by large language models. The assistant helps users query and analyze the data in plain language. Together the tools aim to speed work on microRNA function and its promise for new therapies.
arxiv-2508-09931:
A pulsar orbiting the black hole at our galaxy's center would be a physics laboratory like no other. Lijing Shao and Zexin Hu survey what such a system could test. Precise timing of the pulses would probe the spacetime near Sagittarius A star. It could also weigh in on dark matter. Big new telescopes, above all the Square Kilometre Array, may finally find such a pulsar.

The catch is clutter. Stars and gas near the center tug on the orbit and dirty the clean gravity signal. The authors describe a numerical timing model being built to absorb those effects. Flexibility, they argue, is the price of using this extreme system.
arxiv-2508-10931:
Wenqi Guo and Shan Du present a simple trick for steering fast image generators away from unwanted content, in a 2025 study. Modern generators can make good images in just a few steps, but telling them what to leave out is hard. Older steering tools add cost or work poorly in few-step models. The new method, called VSF, flips the sign of certain attention values tied to the unwanted prompt.

The flip quietly damps the features the user asked to avoid. It adds very little compute and fits both major design families the team tested. On hard prompt pairs, it beat older tools at honoring the ban while keeping image quality high. The gain held for still images and for video. Code and a ready node for a common tool are shared in a public repo.
arxiv-2508-11931:
Tim van Erven, Jack Mayo, Julia Olkhovskaya, and Chen-Yu Wei present an algorithm in two thousand twenty-five for contextual bandit problems. In such problems, a learner picks actions with changing options and faces losses set by an adversary. The goal is low regret over many rounds, with fast computation.

Their method needs only a linear optimization tool for each round's action set. It reduces the problem to a robust bandit problem with a fixed action set. It needs no knowledge of the context distribution and no simulator. The regret bounds they prove are near optimal and settle an open question from earlier work. For combinatorial bandits, theirs is the first method with such bounds in polynomial time.
arxiv-2508-12431:
Auronno Ovid Hussain, Abdul Ahad Mamun, Faysal Rahman, and Muhammad Anisuzzaman Talukder model how cathodes wear away in alkaline water cells that make hydrogen. This wear cuts the life of the cell parts. It cuts hydrogen output too, and it cuts how well the cell works. Past models gauge this wear poorly. That leaves cell designers with weak help.

Their model is based on physics and on the flow of charge. It takes in exchange current density, redox potential, and hydrogen adsorption energy. It also takes in the strength of the fluid, plus pressure and heat. From these it works out how fast the wear goes. Tests rank gold as the cathode that lasts the longest. Copper and nickel look like good low-cost picks.
arxiv-2508-13131:
Dara Bahri and John Wieting improve detection of text written by watermarked language models, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Watermarks hide a signal in a model's word choices so its output can later be recognized. The signal is weak when the model has little freedom in what to say next, as often happens after fine-tuning for instruction following.

The authors pair watermark detectors with ordinary detectors that look for other traces of machine text. Several hybrid schemes mix the two scores in differing ways. Across a wide range of test conditions, the hybrids beat either detector alone. The result matters for spotting machine text in low-freedom settings, where watermarking alone struggles most.
arxiv-2508-13631:
Jonas Beddrich and Barbara Wohlmuth present a 2025 math paper on fractional equations with spread orders. Some materials remember their past at many time scales at once. Distributed-order fractional models capture that spread. They are costly because the whole history enters each step. The team compresses the memory kernel so the cost matches a normal local equation. Two moves do it: slicing the order integral, and fitting kernel sums with exponentials.

Their improved fit reaches double-precision accuracy with under a hundred exponential terms. Each time step then solves one main equation plus light side variables. Applied mathematicians get long-memory physics at short-memory prices. Diffusion in soils, polymers, and tissues all carry such memory. A fast solver widens the models that engineers can afford to run in design loops.
arxiv-2508-13931:
José Adell, Alcalá, and Sangüesa set out a general recipe for using random averaging operators in nonparametric statistics, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such operators smooth data in a controlled way and keep values positive, which suits estimates of probability curves. The authors show how one framework covers many separate tricks used in the field.

As concrete payoffs, they give exact confidence bands and intervals for a distribution curve on the unit interval, built from random Bernstein polynomials. They do the same for the slopes of that curve using a related random construction. These bands tell users how much trust to place in an estimate at each point. The paper was accepted for publication in the journal Test.
arxiv-2508-14731:
Anh Tran studies a family of knots in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. The knots are double twist knots, a two-parameter family of rational knots. For each such knot, algebraists can build a polynomial from twisted data tied to the knot's shape. Tran uses a version called the adjoint hyperbolic torsion polynomial. The question is what this polynomial reveals about the knot.

He shows that the polynomial pins down two key traits of these knots: their genus and whether they are fibered. The proof leans on algebraic integers. Genus measures the simplest surface a knot can bound, and fibering describes how the space around it is layered. Results like this help classify knots. The paper speaks to specialists in low-dimensional topology.
arxiv-2508-15031:
Kaixiang Zhao and co-authors published this survey in 2025. It maps model extraction attacks, where an outsider clones a machine learning model through its public interface. Hosted model services made strong models cheap to use, and that same access lets rivals query their way to a copy. The theft threatens patents, privacy, and security. The survey sorts attacks by how they work, and defenses by how they answer.

A recurring tension runs through the field: defenses that blunt theft often dull the model's usefulness. The authors weigh attacks across computing settings, from cloud to edge. Legal, ethical, and social angles get their own treatment. They close with open problems and keep a public reading list updated online. The piece aims to serve researchers, builders, and policymakers guarding model assets.
arxiv-2508-15831:
Vishnu Hari, Kalpana Panda, Srikant Panda, and two colleagues audit how language models guess who is asking when a question carries disability cues, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Models routinely infer a user's demographics from phrasing alone, and those silent guesses can tilt the answers they give.

The team built a balanced set of templates pairing nine disability categories with six business domains. They asked eight current instruction-tuned models, from small to very large, to predict five traits of the asker: gender, socioeconomic status, education, cultural background, and locality. Each prompt ran in neutral and disability-aware versions. Models offered a definite demographic guess in up to ninety-seven percent of cases. That eagerness exposes arbitrary inference, stereotyping dressed as deduction. The audit is the first systematic look at disability-conditioned bias of this kind.
arxiv-2508-16431:
Yakup Abrek Er and co-authors introduce Cetvel, a benchmark for Turkish language models, in this 2025 paper. Existing Turkish tests lack task range or cultural depth. Cetvel spans 23 tasks in seven groups. Grammar correction, translation, and questions on Turkish history and idioms all appear.

Thirty three open models up to 70 billion parameters were evaluated. Turkish tuned models surprisingly trailed general multilingual ones like Llama 3 and Mistral. Grammar correction and extractive question answering separated models most sharply. Culture bound items exposed gaps that translated tests miss. A ruler for Turkish progress now exists in the open. Model builders can no longer claim Turkish skill without facing it.
arxiv-2508-17031:
Matiyali, Shrivastava, and Sharma built a tool in twenty twenty-five to slip new speech into old speech when a script is fixed. The new bit must match the voice, pace, and tone of the old clip. Past text-to-speech tools can sound off when they patch a clip.

Their tool reads the full script and the part clip and fits a new bit of a length it picks on the fly. Pace of the old clip guides that length call. On a known speech set it beat a past patch tool in tests and in a user check. Voice traits and tune held well in the patch.
arxiv-2508-18231:
Anjo Seidel and co-authors work on process mining for business processes that involve many objects at once. Their paper appeared in 2025. Standard models mined from event logs show how orders, items, and machines flow and meet. They do not say which objects truly belong together, so they cannot flag runs that break intended relationships. Formal models with object identities can, but no one had shown how to discover them from logs.

The authors bridge the gap with explicit data models. They show that logs quietly assume stable many-to-one relationships between objects. Building those links into the mined model yields the formal model, with synchronization of related objects made exact. The mapping is proven, not just proposed. It gives process analysts a way to catch violations that simpler models wave through.
arxiv-2508-18831:
Yosuke Yamagishi and Shouhei Hanaoka classify dividing cells in pathology images for a 2025 challenge entry. Pathologists count mitotic figures to grade tumors, and atypical figures, botched divisions, carry extra diagnostic weight; telling them from normal ones is slow and subjective. Their entry adapts a modern convolutional network, with center cropping to focus on the cell and an ensemble across cross-validation folds for stability.

The work was built for a public challenge track devoted to that binary decision. Reliable automatic sorting of mitotic figures could standardize grading and free pathologists for the hardest cases.
arxiv-2508-19931:
Isabella da Silva, Zahra Mobini, Hien Quoc Ngo, and Michail Matthaiou design user authentication for a distributed antenna network in a 2025 study. Cell-free massive antenna systems spread many access points over an area to serve users jointly. Verifying that users are genuine, at the physical signal layer, can stop impersonators before higher security layers engage.

Their tag-based scheme first learns each legitimate user's channel during an uplink training phase. Secret keys then grow out of those channel estimates, and many distributed users can be authenticated at once. The design stays effective even when active adversaries try impersonation attacks during the process.
arxiv-2508-21431:
When many agents must agree on a compromise between rival goals, the math becomes a distributed minimax problem. Yan Huang, Jinming Xu, Jiming Chen, and Karl Henrik Johansson propose a method called DOGT for solving it across a network. Each agent works locally but tracks the group's gradient direction, with an optimistic twist that looks one step ahead.

The authors prove the method closes in on the best compromise at a steady linear rate for well-behaved problems. It stays stable even when local goals differ a lot. Adding a faster agreement protocol yields an accelerated version with the best known rate for its class. Computer experiments back the theory. The work targets settings like sensor networks and shared control, where no single machine sees the whole problem.
arxiv-2509-00031:
Qitao Tan leads a team with eleven co-authors who present ZeroQAT in 2025, a way to train large language models in low-bit form on the device itself. Quantization stores weights with fewer bits to cut cost. Post-training forms cannot tune weights and lose accuracy at low bits. Training-aware forms can tune, but their backward pass costs vast memory.
