ZeroQAT uses zeroth-order methods, which gauge slopes from forward passes alone, so no backward pass is needed. It quantizes both weights and activations, which are the live signals inside the net. A light variant freezes and pre-quantizes most weights for cheap fine-tuning. The aim is end-to-end gains at a cost close to plain use.
arxiv-2509-00131:
Ivan Slootweg, Natalia P. García-De-La-Puente, Geert Litjens, and Salma Dammak present a self-supervised model in 2025 that flags kidney harm in drug safety studies. Every preclinical drug program must check kidneys for toxic change. Experts scan hundreds to thousands of slide images per study, most of them normal, to catch subtle harm, which is slow and costly.

Their model is the first large-scale self-supervised one for kidney pathology, built across studies of one hundred fifty-eight compounds. Features from a foundation model alone, paired with a simple neighbor classifier, score at chance level. A self-supervised method on those same features does better than chance. The gap shows that task-tuned learning, not raw features, unlocks detection at scale.
arxiv-2509-00431:
Arghyadeb Roy leads a team of seven authors who compute how strongly molecules stick to interstellar ice in 2025. The binding energy of a molecule sets how long it stays on a dust grain in space. That sticking time drives the chemistry that plays out on grain surfaces. Most models use one binding value per species, as if all sites on the ice were alike.

Quantum chemistry calculations show that picture is too simple. For monohydric alcohols, thiols, and their likely precursors, the team finds a spread of binding values across distinct ice sites. The species set also covers aldehydes and thioaldehydes, close kin of the main pair. Trends across like species hint at which reaction paths dominate and which precursors matter most. A spread of values, not a single one, gives a truer account of diffusion and growth on grains in cold clouds.
arxiv-2509-00631:
Giacomo Acciarini leads a team of ten authors who forecast the ionosphere. The ionosphere is a charged layer high in the atmosphere. It affects satellite navigation and radio communication. Its swings are hard to predict from sparse data. The team targets total electron content, a key measure of that layer.

They use Temporal Fusion Transformers for the forecast task. That model is built to handle varied inputs at once. Inputs include solar output, magnetic indices, and navigation satellite data. Tests across many years give firm forecasts up to a day ahead. Solar ultraviolet input proves the most predictive of all inputs. Attention analysis helps explain what the model uses. The team also releases its code as the open ionopy toolkit.
arxiv-2509-00731:
Houji Jin leads a team of eight authors on detecting AI-written Chinese text. Subtle features of the Chinese language make this task hard. Detectors must also survive shifts in the data they face. The team compares encoder models with decoder models head to head. A simple FastText baseline is included as well.

Encoders such as BERT and RoBERTa are fine-tuned with prompt-based masked modeling. A decoder model, Qwen, is adapted with LoRA instead. LoRA is a low-rank method that tunes few weights. Tests use the NLPCC 2025 task dataset. Encoders nearly memorize their training data but degrade under shift. FastText stays robust on word-level cues. The LoRA-adapted decoder reaches the highest test accuracy. Its precision and recall are also well balanced.
arxiv-2509-01631:
Jailbreak attacks coax language models into harmful output, from dangerous instructions to disinformation, and defenses have often worked without a clear account of why they help. Chongwen Zhao, Yutong Ke, and Kaizhu Huang present a neuron-level method that focuses on safety-related knowledge neurons inside the model. Their method projects internal representations into a more consistent, readable vocabulary space.

Adjusting the activation of those safety neurons controlled the model's behavior with a very high success rate in their tests. Building on that finding, they propose SafeTuning, a fine-tuning strategy that reinforces safety-critical neurons to harden the model against jailbreaks. Zhao and the co-authors argue that locating safety inside the network turns defense from surface filtering into a targeted, explainable intervention on the model's own machinery.
arxiv-2509-01731:
Tran Duc Le, Phuc Hao Do, Truong Duy Dinh, and Van Dai Pham assess whether firms are ready for quantum safe security. Future quantum computers could break codes that guard most online data today. The authors view readiness through three lenses: the tech expert, the firm leader, and the attacker. They draw on fresh standards, surveys, and threat reports, then map strengths and gaps.

Few firms have a formal switch plan, and many play down the risk of data stolen now and read later. Banks, phone firms, and government bodies have started to move, while most fields lag. Experts place code breaking quantum machines in the next decade or later, but delay still risks old data. The authors urge road maps, flexible code systems, and staff training now.
arxiv-2509-02831:
Erika L. Mehring, Amparo Figueroa, Matias Berdakin, and Hernán L. Calvo wrote a 2025 condensed matter paper on using topological insulators as platforms that break molecules apart under electric current. Topological materials host protected surface states, and a young field called topocatalysis hopes to exploit them for chemistry.

Using non-equilibrium Green's function methods, the authors place a two-atom molecule on either graphene or a Kane-Mele topological substrate and drive current through it. They compare how bonding and antibonding levels fill, plus the forces acting on the molecule. The topological substrate dissociates the molecule more strongly, mainly because its edge states are localised. Adding vacancy disorder widens the gap further. The results tie molecular breaking under current to topological protection itself.
arxiv-2509-03631:
A 2025 research paper from Anders Kjelsrud and four co-authors examines lightweight image segmentation for echocardiography, ultrasound imaging of the heart. Outlining the left ventricle automatically would let clinics extract volumes and ejection fraction, the share of blood pumped out, without manual tracing. Leading models configured by nnU-Net work well but are large and slow.

Through a step-by-step ablation study, the team tests which ingredients actually matter: data augmentation, architecture changes, loss functions, and post-processing. Simple affine augmentations, which rotate or scale images, plus deep supervision drive most of the performance. Complex augmentations and sheer model size add little. Their slim U-Net uses two million parameters instead of thirty-three million, matches nnU-Net scores on the CAMUS dataset of 500 cases, and runs about four times faster. A separate internal dataset confirms the model generalises comparably.
arxiv-2509-04031:
Mohammad Nourbakhsh and one co-author's 2025 research paper is about probing the Chern-Simons portal at the High-Luminosity LHC through displaced vertices. The portal adds a massive neutral boson, call it X, tied to a new gauge symmetry. Heavy chiral fermions, needed to cancel gauge anomalies, are felt through topological Chern-Simons interactions although they sit beyond collider reach.

The signal pairs X with a W boson plus jets, and X decays at a displaced vertex, a decay point away from the collision. The study targets fourteen tera-electronvolt running. Boosted decision trees perform the multivariate separation of signal from background. Simulation, tuned to the high-luminosity environment, models detector effects, including pile-up averaging two hundred interactions per bunch crossing. Exclusion limits at ninety-five percent confidence are derived across two-dimensional parameter spaces. Sensitivity reaches small couplings, showing the collider can constrain anomaly-induced interactions.
arxiv-2509-04331:
Andrés Megías and eight co-authors train a neural network to read the recipe of interstellar ice from its infrared fingerprint in under a second in a 2025 research paper. Dust grains between the stars wear icy coats made mostly of water, carbon monoxide, and carbon dioxide, with traces of methanol, ammonia, and methane. The James Webb Space Telescope records their absorption spectra superbly, but decoding the mix by hand is slow and complex.

Their tool, AICE, learned from hundreds of laboratory ice mixtures that were cleaned and normalized uniformly. Typical errors run near three percent per ingredient. Two real telescope targets matched earlier painstaking estimates well. Hundreds of spectra can now be surveyed systematically.
arxiv-2509-04531:
Simone R Hagey and one co-author, Aaron Boley, release a Python package for tracking how exoplanet orbits evolve over long times in a 2025 research paper. Orbital periods can shrink through tides or shift through precession, the slow swivel of an orbit's orientation. Their package, OrbDot, fits evolutionary models to mixtures of observations: radial velocities, transit durations, and transit and eclipse mid-times. Nested sampling, a method that explores parameter space in layers, drives the fitting.

Interpretation tools accompany the fits. Reports compare models, give precession rate forecasts, derive tidal decay values, and discuss what the numbers imply about unseen planetary companions. Observers studying orbital decay gain a shared, ready-made analysis toolkit.
arxiv-2509-04731:
Robotic soccer exposes why purely end-to-end learning struggles with long tasks. Brennen Hill argues in a solo-authored 2025 paper that agents need a world model of task meaning, not just physics. His review of 2024 research on low-resource multi-agent soccer finds a trend toward symbolic and hierarchical methods.

Methods such as hierarchical task networks break large goals into manageable subgoals, creating a built-in curriculum. Hill formalises that trend as Hierarchical Task Environments. Large language models act as generative world models of tasks, producing the scaffolding dynamically. He argues the framework improves exploration, learning signals, and sample efficiency for embodied agents.
arxiv-2509-04831:
Dark matter inside a compact star could change whether quark matter forms at its centre. H. C. Das investigates that influence in a solo-authored 2025 astrophysics paper on hybrid and twin stars. The model treats dark matter and normal matter as two fluids interacting only through gravity.

Das uses a self-interacting fermionic dark matter model with relativistic descriptions of nuclear and quark matter. Solving the two-fluid stellar structure equations across a wide parameter space, he classifies hybrid stars and four twin star categories. Dark matter can form a halo or a compact core, enhancing or suppressing quark matter formation depending on the regime.
arxiv-2509-05031:
Pointing at an object is a natural way to tell a robot what you mean. Luca Müller, lead author with four co-authors, build a system that reads such gestures in a 2025 human-robot interaction paper. Their architecture predicts which tabletop object a person intends, in experiments with the NICOL robot.

Using inter-modality attention, the model maps two-dimensional pointing gestures to object locations and scores each candidate. It identifies the most likely target accurately from monocular colour images in their tests. A patch confusion matrix gives extra insight into predictions across locations. The authors release their code publicly.
arxiv-2509-05231:
Family trees inside growing populations are the topic of a 2025 probability paper by Mathilde André and two co-authors. In their model, each individual reproduces on its own, but the rate depends on how crowded the population already is, which breaks a handy standard property.

The authors build a way to compute shared moments, averages of products that reveal how sampled individuals are related. From those formulas, the family tree can be read off by studying population density with tools from stochastic calculus. Near a stable balance point, and as capacity grows without bound, the genealogy settles into Kingman's coalescent, a classic random tree model.
arxiv-2509-05331:
Digital forensic investigators need realistic practice data that privacy rules rarely allow, and Youssef Chakir with Iyad Lahsen-Cherif answer with a dataset in a 2025 paper. ForensicsData is built from actual malware analysis reports and organised as question, context, and answer triples.

The set holds more than five thousand such triples. A workflow extracts structured facts from reports, uses large language models to reshape them into the triple format, then checks quality with a dedicated evaluation step. Among models tested, one commercial system aligned best with forensic wording. The authors aim to support reproducible experiments with language models on forensic tasks and to widen collaboration in a field short on shared data.
arxiv-2509-05531:
Dusty stars in the Magellanic Clouds are sorted more honestly by spectroscopy than by brightness alone, Sepideh Ghaziasgar and six co-authors show in a 2025 astronomy paper. Young stellar objects and several kinds of ageing, dust-shrouded stars enrich galaxies with new elements, but their brightness patterns overlap.

The team trained machine learning models on stars with spectroscopic labels from the SAGE survey, then applied them to the larger photometric catalogues. The spectroscopic model reached accuracy near ninety percent. Nearly all oxygen-rich ageing stars and most young objects kept their labels, while carbon-rich and red supergiant labels often changed. Rare or overlapping classes, they conclude, still need spectra.
arxiv-2509-05731:
Cholera spreads harder where food is insecure, Jean-Marc Mandeng models in a solo 2025 disease paper. The model divides people across patches, linked by travel, and splits them by food security status to capture weak nutrition.

Spread runs through human contact, germs in the surroundings, and tainted food. Mandeng derives the basic reproduction number, the threshold for whether an outbreak grows. He also studies the disease-free state and finds a forward bifurcation. Model runs show food insecurity worsens outbreaks and deaths. Place, social life, and surroundings shape the pattern jointly. The work argues outbreak control cannot ignore hunger.
arxiv-2509-05931:
Quantizing a particle whose momentum space is a compact Lie group is the program of a 2025 paper by Alexey A. Sharapov. His domains pair a bounded region in the dual of the group's algebra with the group itself, sitting inside its cotangent bundle. Bounded symplectic volume then allows something rare: a finite-dimensional quantum theory.

Sharapov delivers that scheme in full, with observables as Hermitian matrices on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, given by a concrete construction. The boundary forces changes to the usual von Neumann and Dirac conditions behind the correspondence principle. Physically, the group plays momentum space while its dual becomes a noncommutative position space. Consequences include supertunneling and a maximum possible fermion density, both foreign to standard quantum mechanics.
arxiv-2509-06031:
Telling a robot to reshape its path in plain words is the interaction GELATO enables, in a 2025 paper led by Junhui Huang with four co-authors. Earlier learning-based editors struggle with several instructions at once and ignore scene geometry. GELATO instead registers objects as six-dimensional geometric primitives through a vision-model pipeline over multiple views.

A language model then translates free-form instructions into explicit, checkable geometric constraints. Those constraints feed a vector field optimization that bends the original trajectory while keeping it smooth, feasible, and clear of obstacles. A multi-agent layer with observer feedback untangles interacting goals without retraining. Simulations and real-world trials show smoother, safer, and more interpretable path edits than strong baselines.
arxiv-2509-06331:
Reading banknotes for people who cannot see them, including spotting worn and fake notes, is the system built in a 2025 paper led by Md Sultanul Islam Ovi with two co-authors. Existing recognizers mostly classify denominations and ignore damage and forgery, which matter most in low-resource, offline settings. The authors' framework unifies three modules on a dataset of over eighty-two thousand annotated note images.

A lightweight custom neural network classifies denominations with few parameters. A new damage index scores each note's usability from mask loss, color distortion, and structural loss. Template matching catches counterfeits across varied imaging conditions. The whole system runs in real time on-device, aiming at inclusive, practical currency checking.
arxiv-2509-06631:
Forcing language models to answer in a set format, inside search-augmented systems, is examined by Özgür Uğur and six co-authors in a 2025 paper. Retrieval-augmented generation pairs a model with fetched documents, but outputs must match expected formats and avoid invented facts. Guided decoding steers the model's word choices to obey a format.

Three tools are compared: Outlines, XGrammar, and LM Format Enforcer. Each is tested under plain prompting and under one or two rounds of follow-up conversation. The authors measure success rates, hallucination rates, and output quality. Multi-turn interaction changes performance in unexpected ways, so the best tool depends on how the system will actually be used. The study gives builders of retrieval systems practical guidance on picking a decoding method, alongside a clearer picture of how structured generation behaves.
arxiv-2509-06731:
A hoped-for shortcut in convex geometry is shown not to exist by Sutanoya Chakraborty and one co-author in a 2025 mathematics paper. Infinite versions of the (p,q)-theorem promise that if every large subfamily of sets has some members pierced by one line, then finitely many lines pierce everything. Such results power many covering arguments.

The authors construct a family of compact convex sets in three-dimensional space with no finite set of piercing lines. Yet every infinite subfamily still contains arbitrarily many sets that a single line can pierce. That combination kills any infinite (p,q)-theorem for piercing compact convex sets with lines in three dimensions. Counterexamples of this kind matter because they mark the exact border where a tempting generalization stops being true, saving others from searching for proofs that cannot exist.
arxiv-2509-07331:
Hitesh Poddar and 1 co-author derive path loss models for indoor wireless signals in 2025 from measurements at five frequencies. Path loss describes how a radio signal weakens as it travels, and indoor hotspot models guide the design of Wi-Fi and cellular coverage inside buildings. The measurements come from NYU WIRELESS, using a wideband channel sounder in both line-of-sight and blocked conditions.

Seven model families, including close-in, floating-intercept, and alpha-beta-gamma forms, are fitted for single frequencies and for wide combined ranges up to 150 gigahertz. Some parameter sets were submitted to the 3GPP standards body to check its indoor models for the 7 to 24 gigahertz band. Reliable loss models help engineers predict coverage before a single access point is installed. The work also sharpens the channel models that future wireless standards will assume.
arxiv-2509-07431:
Moving data between servers usually forces a choice between fast but rigid hardware tricks and flexible but slower software. Md Ashfaqur Rahaman and 6 co-authors present NAAM in a 2025 research paper. NAAM stands for network-accelerated active messages. Each message carries a small portable program, written in eBPF, that says what to do with its data.

Because eBPF programs run almost anywhere, the system can steer each message to a client, a server, or a smart network card. It can shift that choice within tens of milliseconds when a server gets busy. Tests with a hash table and a B-tree show NAAM offloading millions of operations per second from server processors. It also supports hundreds of application offloads where an earlier framework managed only eight, with little added delay.
arxiv-2509-07531:
Zheng Dou and 4 co-authors present FLeW in 2025, a method for representing scientific documents as embeddings that respect their facets. An embedding is a numeric summary used for search and recommendation. Existing methods either underuse citation signals and give one flat vector, split documents finely at high integration cost, or need hand-made task categories to adapt.

FLeW unifies the three approaches. A new triplet sampling method uses citation intent, whether a citation gives background, method, or results, plus citation frequency to strengthen training signals. Those intents partition each document into facet-level embeddings aligned with how scientific writing is structured. A simple weight search then blends the facet embeddings into a task-specific summary without extra task modules. The design targets better scholarly search and recommendation across fields.
arxiv-2509-08031:
Audio language models finally get a shared measuring stick in a 2025 toolkit paper by Hoang Nguyen and 11 co-authors. Large audio models are advancing quickly, but evaluation tools are slow, non-standard, and hard to compare across studies. Long multi-turn conversations, where context must carry across exchanges, are especially poorly supported by existing frameworks.

AU-Harness is open-source and built for holistic evaluation, aiming at faster pipelines and unified, scalable assessment that keeps pace with model growth. Fair comparison is not bureaucratic tidiness: without it, claims about listening, reasoning, and dialogue ability cannot be checked. A common harness lets researchers see which audio models genuinely improve and which merely test well on friendly setups.
arxiv-2509-08131:
Luke K. Davis and 1 co-author extend a classic space-counting idea to self-driven particles in a 2025 physics paper. For plain hard spheres at rest, the free space left for one more sphere fixes the pressure law exactly. Active particles are not at rest. Each one pushes itself along. The old link may break, and the pair test how.

They study one- and two-dimensional systems, on grids and off them. In one dimension, neat formulas give the mean hole size, the number of holes, and the total free volume. Simulations agree well. Self-driving makes the total free volume grow. It also keeps the holes linked up. Such counts may one day give pressure laws for swarms and bacteria.
arxiv-2509-08231:
In Chicago, a learning-based decision support system kept buses evenly spaced during 2022 and 2023 pilots described by Joseph Rodriguez and 2 co-authors in a 2025 transport paper. Headway control holds buses briefly so gaps stay regular, fighting the bunching that ruins reliability. Reinforcement learning chose the holding actions, and supervisors used an interface to monitor service and record what was applied.

One pilot held buses at the terminal on a route hurt by absenteeism and missed trips, and reliability improved beyond what extra service days achieved. A second pilot applied control en route. Rider impacts, human factors, and scalability recommendations round out the report, since a system supervisors distrust will not survive deployment.
arxiv-2509-08531:
Cutting a random regular graph's edges as evenly as possible gets sharper bounds from Endre Csóka and 3 co-authors in a 2025 combinatorics paper. Their engine is a factor of IID process, a local random algorithm, based on a method of Díaz, Serna, and Wormald, with a new recolouring phase appended after the original algorithm finishes.

The improvement raises known bounds on minimum and maximum bisection width and on the maximum cut of random regular graphs of degree above four. As an application, random five-regular graphs almost surely admit internal partitions, splits where every vertex keeps at least half its neighbours on its own side. Local algorithms that provably beat global bounds are prized: they run in parallel on enormous networks.
arxiv-2509-08831:
Language models mimic human language, but do their internal states resemble brain activity doing something non-linguistic? Doai Ngo and 5 co-authors test that deeper similarity in a 2025 research paper. They use a sensory-motor task built on anticipation and spatial behavior. Human volunteers performed the task while intracranial electrodes recorded their brain signals.

The task was translated into natural language so the models could attempt it too. Hidden states from pre-trained models were extracted at key moments. Those states mapped linearly onto the human neural activity surprisingly well. The authors draw two conclusions. Model-brain similarity extends beyond language tasks. And models might help neuroscientists study brain questions that are otherwise hard to reach. The work treats the model less as a chatbot and more as a rough, testable stand-in for neural processing.
arxiv-2509-09031:
Tung Nguyen and 2 co-authors prove a result on path-width and additive quasi-isometry in a 2025 paper. Quasi-isometry compares graphs at large scale, usually allowing multiplicative and additive error. Path-width measures how tree-like a graph's structure is.

Suppose a graph is quasi-isometric to a graph of bounded path-width. The authors assign a nonnegative integer length to each edge of the target graph. The same map then becomes a quasi-isometry to that weighted graph with error only an additive constant. Multiplicative error is thus removed by reweighting edges. The work is part two of an asymptotic structure series on coarse graph theory.
arxiv-2509-09231:
Rejeb Hadiji and 1 co-author prove convergence results for the Ginzburg-Landau equation in a 2025 paper. This equation models superconductors and phase change. A family of solutions is fixed to one boundary value, with degree zero.

If the energy of these solutions stays at or below the energy of the limit harmonic map, then it must equal it, and the solutions converge to that map. If energy stays strictly above, the solution size does not settle uniformly to one on the whole domain. Like results hold for two component systems, both symmetric and not. The work pins down when rough solutions calm to the expected limit.
arxiv-2509-09331:
SSH keys guard the internet's back doors, yet client keys, unlike servers, cannot be surveyed by scanning. Fabian Bäumer and 4 co-authors measure them anyway in a 2025 research paper. Owners publish their public keys on platforms like GitHub and GitLab. The team extracted tens of millions of such keys from public sources, twice, and ran security tests on them over time.

Most keys were sound, and use is shifting from RSA toward modern EdDSA signatures. Still, the scans found short broken keys, keys born from weak randomness, and keys sharing factors. A second part tested twenty-four SSH client programs in the lab. One popular client's deterministic signing scheme let its private key be recovered from a few dozen signatures. The vendor acknowledged the flaw as a formal vulnerability and replaced the algorithm. The study is a rare census of a security layer everyone assumes and nobody sees.
arxiv-2509-09831:
Asaf Ferber and 3 co-authors study how well connected the skeleton of a random zero-one polytope is in a 2025 combinatorics paper. Such a polytope is the solid hull of chosen corners of a high-dimensional cube, and its graph joins corners linked by edges of the solid. A famous conjecture claims every such graph expands by at least a factor of one, meaning small corner sets always have many edges leaving them.

Rather than attack all polytopes at once, the team picks each cube corner independently with a fixed chance and studies the typical outcome. Sharpening earlier findings, they show that for any such chance the random polytope's graph expands by at least some fixed positive amount with high probability. Random cases, at least, behave far better than the worst case feared.
arxiv-2509-10131:
Daniel Martínez-Gil and 2 co-authors turn the motion of an open quantum system into classical equations in a 2025 theory paper. Their start is a five-step recipe. It rewrites an N-level quantum system in classical terms, with no loss. The stage for that rewrite is complex projective space. Onto that stage they add a classical bath. The bath is a set of harmonic oscillators. It stands in for an environment that drains energy and scrambles phases.

A Langevin treatment then gives a compact set of Hamilton's equations. The set carries both the system and its bath. The picture extends the Caldeira-Leggett model into curved quantum geometry. Two test cases follow. One is a two-qubit system with entangling links. The method tracks its state counts and its entanglement well. The other is a seven-state complex from photosynthesis. Its state counts are tracked over picosecond scales.
arxiv-2509-10231:
Ayan Kumar Nai and 4 co-authors demonstrate a simpler route to quantum key distribution in this 2025 paper. Quantum key distribution uses entangled photons to share secret keys, and most setups pick measurement settings with beam splitters. Those parts waste photons, split unevenly, and react to polarization, all of which cap the key rate and add errors.

Their scheme uses the natural spread of photon pairs from a down-conversion source instead. The emission ring is split into four zones, forming two sources, and the measurement basis is assigned after detection using detector timing jitter. In tests the sifted key rate rose several-fold, errors fell, and the two bases stayed evenly balanced, pointing to a scalable design for quantum networks.
arxiv-2509-10331:
Who holds the pen when a person and an AI make music together? Zhejing Hu and five co-authors argue in this 2025 paper that popular creative tools concentrate interpretive authority in the machine, flattening expression and sidelining marginal voices. The old saying that knowing is easy and doing is hard gets a new twist: the real difficulty is who governs the step from knowing to doing.

The authors offer a framework for redistributing that authority, built on contestability, agency, and plurality. In interactive studies with one hundred eighty music practitioners, backed by deep interviews, the principles reshaped how authority moved between human and AI and reawakened participants' own creative drive. They present the work as a step from critiquing creative AI toward redesigning it in practice.
arxiv-2509-10931:
Seongho Joo, Hyukhun Koh, and Kyomin Jung present a jailbreak technique in this 2025 AI safety paper, written to expose weaknesses so defenses can improve. Their method, Harmful Prompt Laundering, needs only black-box access to a target model. It combines two disguises for a harmful request.

First, abductive framing asks the model to infer plausible intermediate steps toward a harmful activity rather than answer a blunt harmful question. Second, symbolic encoding obfuscates the dangerous content, exploiting the fact that models still key on explicit harmful keywords. The combination succeeded against over ninety-five percent of attempts on GPT-series models and about seventy percent across all targets, and varying the encoding rules did not rescue the defenses. The authors' deeper point: tuning models safe without gutting their helpfulness on benign requests remains unsolved.
arxiv-2509-11231:
Mashroor S. Nitol and four co-authors built a machine-learned model of two promising alloys in this 2025 materials science paper. The medium-entropy alloys CoCrFeNi and CoCrNi owe their strength to chemical disorder, but accurate quantum simulations are too slow for large samples, and simpler classical models miss key effects.

The team trained a moment tensor potential on a broad database of quantum calculations covering one- to four-element compositions. The potential reproduced energies, forces, and stresses with near-quantum accuracy and matched predicted elastic properties. Large hybrid simulations then captured chemical short-range ordering, including which atom pairs attract or repel, and the model pinned down stacking fault energies and how local chemistry shifts them. The result is a tool for studying these alloys at realistic scales.
arxiv-2509-11631:
Ruo-Yu Guan, Fei-Fei Wang, and Yuan-Chuan Zou measure the memory inside gamma-ray burst light curves. This 2025 astrophysics paper treats the most powerful events known. The flicker of a burst's prompt emission records its central engine at work.

The team applied detrended fluctuation analysis to past burst data. More than one hundred sixty long bursts from BATSE were used. A Hurst index was drawn from each curve. The index gauges how strongly flickers link across time. Set against twelve other traits, it anti-correlated with burst length. It correlated in a moderate way with peak photon flux. Standard spectral traits showed no tidy linear tie. The index gives a new handle on burst time structure.
arxiv-2509-11731:
Yudong Shen and five co-authors draw road maps from the trails drivers leave behind, in this 2025 geographic information science paper. Trajectory data are cheap and constantly updated, but their uneven density breaks map inference: sparse regions yield fragmented roads, while dense regions sprout redundant false segments.

Their framework, DGMap, decodes the map twice with global context in view. Multi-scale grid encoding and mask-enhanced keypoint extraction sharpen the detection of road keypoints, fighting fragmentation where trajectories are thin. A global context-aware relation predictor then decides which keypoints truly connect, modeling long-range trajectory patterns to suppress the false links that plague crowded areas. On three real-world datasets, including ride-hailing trajectories from Didi Chuxing, DGMap beat the state of the art on the standard path-similarity metric.
arxiv-2509-12031:
Sampling from lumpy probability distributions whose gradients grow faster than linearly defeats ordinary Langevin algorithms, and Iosif Lytras with one co-author tame the problem in 2025. Their setting is kinetic, or underdamped, Langevin dynamics for log-concave targets.

A carefully built taming scheme reins in the superlinear growth, yielding two new discretizations of the kinetic Langevin equation. Both turn out to be contractive, meaning two copies of the sampler pull toward each other, and both satisfy a log-Sobolev inequality, a strong mixing guarantee. From those properties the authors derive non-asymptotic bounds, in the 2-Wasserstein distance, between what each algorithm actually produces and the target distribution it aims for.
arxiv-2509-12531:
Scott Jones, Liyou Zhou, and Sebastian W. Pattinson examine pre-trained vision in model-based reinforcement learning in a 2025 paper. In visuomotor learning, a robot's policy derives directly from visual inputs. Training a policy and vision encoder together from scratch often generalizes poorly when scenes change visually.

Pre-trained vision models help in model-free reinforcement learning, yet earlier work found them ineffective in the model-based setting, a surprising result. The authors investigate generalization under visual domain shifts. Under severe shifts, pre-trained models performed much better than a from-scratch baseline. Varying how much the vision model was fine-tuned showed that partial fine-tuning kept the highest average performance under the most extreme shifts. The results argue that pre-trained representations do matter where generalization is hardest.
arxiv-2509-13331:
Reza Pirayeshshirazinezhad fuses AI with supervisory control in 2025 for precise spacecraft pairing in the VTXO virtual telescope. Two craft form a kilometer-focus X-ray telescope: one holds the lens, one the camera. Precision needs rival the finest angular marks.

Timed automata supervise control, Monte Carlo runs test stability, and deep nets estimate mission parameters. A constrained optimizer predicts best settings. The AI layer forecasts energy use and mission error per setting set. Clear trade-offs run in real time, unlike classic adaptive control. Energy falls and accuracy rises under dynamic disturbance in tests.
arxiv-2509-13431:
Zhonghao Zhang and 7 co-authors give a fast way to design passive resonators for MRI in a 2025 paper. Such parts are used to shape the radio wave field inside a scanner. Full wave sims of each new design are far too slow, all the more so for large arrays with many free choices.

Their trick is to run one full wave sim with the part's small parts swapped for ports. Fast circuit math can then try huge numbers of part values at low cost. A search that borrows from evolution, a genetic algorithm, hunts for the best values to boost the field in a chosen spot. The team checked the method in three cases, from a single loop on a ball phantom to a two-loop array on a human head model, with close matches each time.
arxiv-2509-13531:
Guidance and control of systems hit by strong disturbances is the subject of a 2025 paper by Piotr Łaszkiewicz, Maria Carvalho, Cláudia Soares, and Pedro Lourenço. The team studies how the choice of system model changes the tracking error of an LQR controller, a standard optimal controller, when the system keeps changing over time.

Three models were compared on perturbed spring-mass-damper systems: a fixed linear model, an identified time-varying model, and a smooth time-varying model learned directly from data. The data-driven model propagated the state best, beat the fixed model on tracking error, and matched a linearized time-varying model. The results make the case for learning models from data in safety-critical control.
arxiv-2509-14031:
Paweł Mąka and three co-authors test the you are what you train idea for context-aware translation in a 2025 paper. Good translation needs surrounding context to resolve pronouns and keep coherence, and a leading suspicion blames sparse context-rich examples in standard training data for models' weak context use. Nobody had verified that suspicion systematically.

The team built training sets with controlled proportions of contextually relevant examples, in single-language-pair and multilingual settings. Data sparsity tracked performance strongly, confirming it as a key bottleneck. But gains on one contextual phenomenon did not transfer to others, and cross-lingual transfer was no stronger within language families than across them. Two training strategies they propose squeeze more from the available data, adding several points of accuracy on a context test suite.
arxiv-2509-14331:
Yakov Solomons and five co-authors show in 2025 how trapped ion quantum computers can stay fully programmable with shared control fields. Trapped ions can entangle many qubits at once using shared motion modes. Driving each ion alone gives full control but is hard to scale.

Individual driving with many tones creates a multi qubit gate whose pair couplings are all adjustable. That cuts gate counts while keeping accuracy high. The snag is delivering light and signals to long ion chains. Solomons and colleagues show global and semi global drives, paired with single qubit flips, can reproduce the full gate set. Shared control could make large ion systems far easier to build and run.
arxiv-2509-14731:
Petar Popovski and ten co-authors bring in 1Q in 2025, a plan for a first wireless wave that joins classic and quantum comms. Quantum base stations would share entanglement over free space optical links, next to plain radio service. New parts take in quantum cells and quantum user gear.

Hybrid resource plans must span classic time and frequency slots plus quantum entanglement stocks. Use cases take in quantum key sharing, blind quantum computing and spread out quantum sensing, each with design needs the authors spell out. Odd quantum caps, above all decoherence time, bind each design choice. Naming a wave frames the hunt: standards, hardware and rules can now be planned against one shared 1Q picture.
arxiv-2509-14831:
R. Sasireka, S. Sabari, A. Uthayakumar, and Lauro Tomio study pattern-forming instability in ultracold atomic gases in a 2025 physics paper. Their system is a two-component Bose-Einstein condensate with spin-orbit coupling, held inside a deep optical lattice. Modulational instability, where small ripples grow into patterns, is their focus.

Discrete Gross-Pitaevskii equations model the gas, and linear stability analysis gives exact conditions for instability to start. Spin-orbit coupling and the nonlinear interactions within and between the two components each play distinct roles. The authors compare unstaggered and staggered modes and find very different instability landscapes for the two. Detailed simulations of the full nonlinear system confirm the analysis, showing how wave patterns, phase coherence, and energy localization evolve once instability sets in.
arxiv-2509-15231:
Kaustav Giri and V. Sreedhar study classic mechanics on finite spaces in a 2025 paper. Shape and topology rule quantum physics, from the Aharonov-Bohm effect to anyons and the quantum Hall effect. Classic mechanics is a limit case of quantum theory. So the authors ask what topology does on the classic side, where its marks show in fluid vortices and air flows.

They work in a frame built by Bering. In that frame they pick out the fixes that finite-space mechanics makes to the Klein-Gordon problem. Finite spaces, with just a finite set of places, force a fresh look at motion, momentum, and waves. The paper seeks a deeper account of how much of the famed shape-quantum link holds in the classic limit.
arxiv-2509-15331:
Edgar Vidal and ten co-authors refresh a fake infrared sky to match what the Webb telescope counts in real skies, in a 2025 paper. Webb's mid-infrared tool has found many dust-hidden active nuclei. That haul strains models of how galaxies and their core black holes grow as one. The SIDES frame builds a mock sky beyond our galaxy to test those models.

The refresh reworks spectral templates for star-forming, starburst, quiet, and active galaxies. Each fake galaxy also gets a chance-based share of infrared light from an active core. The new fake sky now matches the seen source counts, redshift spreads, and active shares from the surveys. Active cores rule the bright end of the counts, a claim the checked model now backs with numbers.
arxiv-2509-15531:
Xinran Ma leads a team that speeds up nearest neighbor search on huge vector sets. Graph based search is fast and accurate at billion scale. One popular graph trims links by a rule set by a parameter that is costly to tune. The team wanted theory to replace that trial and error.

They model the trimming as a fair game process that evolves by chance. With that model they bound the graph's largest link count and its expected search path length. From the bounds they derive a closed form rule for the best trim value. On real data sets, their tuned graph builds far faster on average, with peaks well above that. Search quality holds or improves.
arxiv-2509-15631:
Tomoya Yamashita leads a team that erases knowledge from inside a language model. Many past methods train the model to mute bad outputs. Muting is not forgetting: the knowledge can stay live in the model's inner signals. Such methods can also break the model. The team wanted to change the inner signals themselves.

They define forgetting as a state where a target's inner signal looks like that of an unknown item. A sparse autoencoder gives a clear inner space to work in. Their training goal pushes the target's signal away from known items and toward unknown ones. This shifts how the model itself treats the target. The aim is true removal, not just silence.
arxiv-2509-15731:
Kazuya Mameda and Naoki Yamamoto add a missing trait to the theory of near particles. Quasiparticles can carry a twist in momentum space called Berry curvature. They can also carry a quantum metric, a measure of how states change shape. The pair build a clean formal frame for particles with both traits.

Their frame rests on a special bracket for constrained systems. It shows the metric changes the count of states in phase space at a small order. That change flows into the rules for how particles move and how energy spreads. In uneven electric fields, the metric shifts energy density and flow. Applied to chiral particles, the frame extends their kinetic theory in line with field theory.
arxiv-2509-15831:
Leonardo Cavenaghi, Ludmil Katzarkov, and Maxim Kontsevich join two young theories to build new invariants in geometry. One theory, atoms, grows from recent work by Katzarkov and others. The other, modular symbols, comes from Kontsevich and co-authors. Their union targets birational geometry with group actions, where shapes are compared up to controlled cuts.

They launch a theory of Chen-Ruan atoms for orbifolds, shapes with mild singularities from group quotients. The launch assumes a blowup formula for a quantum cohomology theory. Striking applications are outlined. They also build purely geometric invariants for small group actions on surfaces and threefolds. Many examples show actions that cannot be linearized, handled by the new tools.
arxiv-2509-16131:
Text-to-image models rely on a guidance scale that steers how closely the picture follows the prompt, but one fixed scale fits all prompts poorly. Pinelopi Papalampidi and seven co-authors let the scale change at each step, guided by live checks of the work in progress. Small scoring tools rate match to text, image quality, and human taste as the picture forms.

A greedy search picks the best scale step by step, giving each prompt its own schedule. On small models and a leading large model, results gain in text match, quality, and text rendering. Human raters preferred the new outputs in about half of head-to-head tests.
arxiv-2509-16331:
Pulsating stars whose brightness follows a strict rule serve as mileposts for measuring cosmic distances. Bastian Lengen and three co-authors jointly calibrate those rules for two star families, RR Lyrae stars and type-II Cepheids, in one global fit. More than a thousand such stars in star clusters anchor the fit, tied to precise parallax measures from the Gaia mission.

The shared fit pins distances to ninety-three clusters with accuracy near one percent and no sign of bias. Checks with many variant fits support the result. The work also flags that light-based metal estimates for these stars need more work, a caveat for future distance studies.
arxiv-2509-16431:
Factory quality checks usually sound the alarm only after a bad reading has already happened. Mohammad Iqbal Rasul Seeam flips that order for chip making: a forecasting tool predicts the next process value, and classic control rules then grade the forecast as safe, warning, or critical. The forecaster, a time-series tool built for trends and seasons, learns from past plant data.

On real data from a chip maker, with readings taken at uneven times, the system forecast well and graded future risk correctly. Early warning gives technicians time to act before parts are wasted. The blend makes quality control proactive rather than reactive.
arxiv-2509-16531:
Junghwan Kim, Haotian Zhang, and David Jurgens ask whether training in many languages helps identify authors, in a 2025 paper. A model can learn the style of a writer from their texts. Past work leaned mostly on English alone. The team test whether mixed-language training makes style models stronger and more flexible.

Their model, trained across languages, beats a model trained only on English. It holds up better when it moves to new languages. It also holds up better in new domains. Tests confirm that both of their added methods play a part. The findings matter for cases where texts cross borders and genres, such as abuse and fraud reports.
arxiv-2509-17131:
Filip Bajraktari, Luke Bhan, Miroslav Krstic, and Yuanyuan Shi study control systems where each input acts only after its own delay. Their 2025 arXiv paper gives the first stability results for systems that use rough predictors with several inputs and distinct delays. Such delays make control hard, because the system must act now on the basis of what will happen later.

The team shows that a uniform bound on the predictor's error is enough to secure a practical form of stability. How tight that bound must be depends on the region the system starts in and on the count of inputs. The proof turns the delay into a transport equation and studies the linked system. Tests with neural operators, in theory and on a mobile robot, show the bound can be met.
arxiv-2509-17231:
Johanna K. Teske leads a team of twelve co-authors on a 2025 arXiv paper about a scorching super-Earth called TOI-561 b. The planet circles its star in under a day and sits close enough to be blasted by starlight. Such planets are expected to lose any air early on and show bare rock faces. This one, though, is oddly light for its size.

The team took the first spectrum of the planet's day side with the JWST space telescope. The day side glows too coolly for bare rock at high confidence, which points to a thick blanket of gas moving heat around. That result rejects the view that such planets must dry out fully. It also backs the idea that deep magma oceans can hold on to large stores of gas, which future studies can probe through the air above them.
arxiv-2509-17431:
Keyu Du and six co-authors match parts across three-dimensional shapes by meaning. Their 2025 arXiv paper targets semantic correspondence: finding, say, the wing tip on every bird shape, even when the shapes differ a lot. Good matches unlock tasks such as shared segmentation, keypoint matching, and moving textures from one shape to another.

Their representation stacks a global semantic feature, which captures the whole structure, over local geometric features at several resolutions, which keep fine detail. The features draw on priors from pretrained 3D generative models. Matching runs from coarse to fine: the global feature sets a first map, and local features refine it step by step. The frame needs no training and accepts many generative backbones. Tests, both qualitative and quantitative, show accurate, consistent maps that hold up even across shape categories.
arxiv-2509-17831:
What makes the faint star glow that fills a galaxy cluster? A Contreras-Santos leads a large team that traces that glow in a suite of cluster sims. Their 2025 paper uses The Three Hundred set, with hundreds of re-run clusters. The glow comes from stars not bound to any one galaxy.

Half the glow was in place fairly late in cosmic time. Most of it was torn from galaxies, groups, and clusters that fell into the host. Big mergers brought a fair share, with small mergers and smooth inflow adding the rest. Code variants gave the same broad tale.
arxiv-2509-18131:
Jean-Michel Tucny and 3 co-authors ask why trained physics nets end up with weights that look random. Their 2025 paper works on physics-informed neural networks, which bake an equation into training. Tests use a classic flow equation, with and without friction.

Trained weights sit in a high-entropy zone, as random matrix theory would predict. The team then views signal flow inside the net as a neural partial equation. Each weight style maps to a known step scheme for that equation. Steady schemes gave clean signal flow, while shaky ones spoiled it. Net shape and scheme steadiness thus steer what passes through.
arxiv-2509-18231:
Sein Minn and Roger Nkambou make student skill trackers that teachers can read and trust. Their 2025 paper deals with knowledge tracing, which guesses what a student has mastered and how they will do next. Deep models score well at that task, but their inner weights mean little in mind terms.

The pair add plain features drawn from student click data to a clear model. Key added traits reflect how a student learns, not just what they clicked. Scores rose while the model stayed tied to mind theory. That balance aims to make smart tutoring tools more useful and more trusted.
arxiv-2509-18431:
Massive stars rarely live alone; most have companions that shape how they age and die. F. Tramper, H. Sana, A. de Koter, and T. Pauwels convert survey views of southern massive stars into physical terms in this 2025 paper. The smash+ survey used sharp imaging methods to find companions at mid-range separations. That range had stayed largely unexplored.

The team built a calibration that links a star's type and brightness class to its mass. With it, they estimated distances and the masses of main stars and companions. Within its limits, the survey is near complete for pairs over a wide span of separations. Separations spread evenly on a log scale. Mass ratios follow a power law whose slope drops at wider separations. Beyond a wide threshold, near-equal-mass pairs grow scarce. The results refine how massive pairs are born and spread.
arxiv-2509-18931:
Austin Eide and two co-authors study paths through a cube whose edges carry random time stamps. The graph is the n-dimensional hypercube, where each corner is a string of bits. A vertex counts as reachable from another when some path between them has steadily increasing time stamps. The authors focus on direct paths that run from one corner to the exact opposite corner.

They show that as the dimension grows, the number of such direct paths settles into a mixed Poisson distribution. The mixing factor is the product of two independent exponential random variables. The proof mixes a method for rare events with pairing arguments. A key step shows that typical pairs of reachable paths overlap only a little, which keeps the counting honest.
arxiv-2509-19131:
Half of the elements heavier than iron were forged in the rapid neutron capture process, where nuclei swallow neutrons faster than they can decay. Jan Kuske and three co-authors test how fresh nuclear mass calculations change predictions of that process. Many nuclei on the path are too exotic to weigh in a lab, so theory must supply their masses. The team uses masses from an ab initio method, one built from basic nuclear forces rather than fitted patterns.

They focus on the region near the shell closure at 82 neutrons, a natural waiting point in the flow. With the ab initio masses that waiting point grows stronger. The flow slows, fewer nuclei form beyond the second peak, and the third peak shifts more strongly. The authors show, for the first time, that such first-principles masses can sharpen r-process predictions beyond global fitted models.
arxiv-2509-19331:
Signals like radar returns and wireless channels carry both strength and phase, but most neural networks attend only to real-valued similarity. Enhao Huang and eight co-authors build a Holographic Transformer that bakes wave interference into the attention mechanism itself. In their design, interactions between signal parts are modulated by relative phase, and values combine coherently, the way light waves add. A two-headed decoder rebuilds the input while predicting the task output, which stops the model from letting phase collapse.

The authors show their attention acts as a discrete interference operator and stays phase-consistent when signals mix. Experiments cover polarimetric radar image classification and wireless channel prediction. Scores were strong on both, with low regression error and extra robustness when phases were perturbed. The work offers a physics-based framework for learning from complex-valued signals as coherent wholes.
arxiv-2509-19431:
Collider physicists sort jets of particles with classifiers, and Rikab Gambhir and two co-authors warn that chasing a single score can mislead. A network tuned only for accuracy or background rejection may lean hard on the details of one simulation model. Such a tagger scores beautifully and then wobbles when the data or the model shifts. The authors explore this trade-off between peak performance and resilience directly.

They demonstrate what happens when high-scoring but brittle networks are used in an analysis. The consequences include hidden uncertainty and bias in the physics results. Competitive alternatives sacrifice a little headline performance for much steadier behavior. The paper's title names the frontier between the two virtues, the set of choices where neither can improve without the other worsening. It is a caution about what optimization targets quietly choose for us.
arxiv-2509-19531:
In Parkinson's disease, large groups of brain cells can fall into lockstep, and breaking that sync may ease symptoms. Jeff Moehlis, Michael Zimet, and Faranak Rajabi study stimuli designed to push paired oscillators out of sync as fast as theory allows. Their approach rests on how each oscillator's phase shifts in response to a pulse. Unlike older methods, it needs no heavy boundary-value solving.

Two shortcut designs both reach near-best breakup of sync in tests. They also work inside an event-based control scheme, where pulses fire only when needed. Tests use noisy, linked neuron models that mimic real brain tissue. The results support a path toward smarter deep brain stimulation. Gentler, well-timed pulses could replace steady stimulation that drains batteries and causes side effects.
arxiv-2509-19631:
Long recordings pile up faster than anyone can listen, so speech summaries are in demand. Shaoshi Ling and three co-authors teach multimodal language models to summarize speech directly, with no transcript step in between. Open models of this kind trail text-only leaders. Their fix is a multi-stage reinforcement learning scheme that rewards better summaries in steps.

The trained model beat strong baselines and even larger rival models. It also closed much of the gap with top text-based systems that read perfect transcripts. Direct speech input keeps tone and emphasis that transcripts drop. Style control and zero-shot use come along from the base model. The gains matter for meetings, lectures, and media archives where audio is the source of truth.
arxiv-2509-19831:
Text-to-audio models often make clips that sound fine but miss the prompt, or match the prompt yet sound poor. Jaemin Jung and three co-authors improve generation at inference time, with no retraining. Their method, SCORE, guides sampling with several reward signals at once. Each reward is rescaled to a shared range before they are combined, keeping any one from dominating.

Balanced guidance lets users steer toward quality or faithfulness explicitly. The team also proposes a new alignment metric judged by an audio language model. Tests show gains in both semantic match and perceptual quality. Inference-time scaling is attractive because it upgrades deployed models directly. Standardized rewards make that upgrade steadier and easier to control.
arxiv-2509-20031:
Venkatkrishna Karumanchi, Gabriel Rioux, and Ziv Goldfeld wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on optimization. Quadratic assignment problems show up in many fields but are too hard to solve exactly. A common fix adds an entropic penalty, a smoothing term that makes the problem tractable. The paper asks how close the smoothed answer stays to the true one.

For concave problems, the authors prove the gap between the two answers shrinks exponentially fast as the smoothing fades. For general convex or indefinite problems, the gap can shrink only linearly. Their proof links concave programs to families of linear programs with changing costs. They also give an algorithm that takes a smoothed solution and certifies a candidate answer for the original problem. The results extend to Gromov-Wasserstein problems, a tool for comparing shapes and data. There they obtain the first exponentially small error bound of this kind.
arxiv-2509-20131:
J. Holder and Qiqi Jiang report a search for high-energy light from an old supernova in this 2025 arXiv conference paper. Only five supernovae in our galaxy were recorded by astronomers in the last thousand years. The remnant of the 1181 event was identified only in 2021, so it had never been checked at tera-electronvolt energies.

The remnant, called Pa 30, likely came from a rare Type Iax explosion that left a merged zombie star behind. Four sibling remnants have all been detected at these energies after long exposures. The authors used the VERITAS telescope array to look for similar gamma-ray emission from Pa 30. Their paper presents what that search found. It closes a gap in the study of historically recorded supernova remnants.
arxiv-2509-20531:
Blue stragglers look younger than their neighbors because a companion star fed them. Robert Mathieu and Onno Pols catalog the observational record of such binary products in a 2025 literature review. It supplements their Annual Review article on close low-mass binaries. The scope is the first stage of evolution for pairs whose stars weigh under twice the Sun's mass.

The review sorts products into a taxonomy: blue straggler dwarfs, yellow straggler giants, subdwarf B stars, and giant-like oddballs such as red stragglers. Each family is traced through three homes: open clusters, globular clusters, and the general galactic field. Key figures from the main article are referenced throughout. The closing date for coverage was January 2025, with some citations updated afterward. The supplement gives researchers the full evidence base behind the review's integrated picture.
arxiv-2509-20731:
Designers are meeting a new kind of AI tool, one that acts on tasks by itself rather than waiting for prompts. Samangi Wadinambiarachchi and three co-authors explored how designers feel about that shift in a 2025 paper for the Australian OZCHI conference. They used design fiction, asking professionals to imagine working with an agent.

Ten professional designers pictured collaborating with an AI agent that organizes inspiration sources and helps with early ideas. Their stories surfaced the roles agents might play in a studio. They also raised hard questions about who holds authority, human or agent. A further theme was how designers could explain their intent to an agent beyond plain prompts.
arxiv-2509-20831:
How long a machine lasts, or a patient lives, is often fit with a flexible lifetime model. Lazhar Benkhelifa offers a new one in a solo-authored 2025 paper on statistics. The model is called the Modi linear failure rate distribution.

Its hazard rate, the risk of failure at each age, can take many shapes. It can fall, rise, dip like a bathtub, peak like an upside-down bathtub, or mix those forms. Two older Modi models, the exponential and the Rayleigh, sit inside it as special cases. Benkhelifa works out its moments, quantile function, and entropy, among other traits. He fits the parameters by maximum likelihood. A final test applies the model to real survival time data.
arxiv-2509-20931:
Automatic differentiation powers modern machine learning, and category theory can axiomatize how it works. Aaron Biggin and Jean-Simon Pacaud Lemay prove a reverse-mode version of a classical formula in a paper from the ACT 2024 proceedings. The formula is a reverse Faa di Bruno formula.

Cartesian reverse differential categories capture reverse differentiation abstractly. One axiom is the reverse chain rule for a single composition. The Faa di Bruno formula generalizes the chain rule to higher derivatives. The authors define partial and higher-order reverse derivatives inside the categorical framework. They then prove the corresponding higher-order reverse chain rule. The result gives implementers and theorists a compositional account of derivatives that deep learning frameworks compute every day.
arxiv-2509-21231:
Keeping a humanoid robot hand steady while its legs walk is a stubborn control problem. Its authors are Jaehwi Jang and 4 co-authors. A humanoid robot walks on two legs and uses its arms to handle objects. Walking shakes the body, so the hand tends to drift. Past model based controls need exact models and fail with friction or play in joints. Learned controls can cope, but often need full retraining.

The team proposes SEEC, a control framework with model enhanced residual learning. A model guides reinforcement learning, and a disturbance maker mimics shakes from the lower body. The upper body policy learns to cancel those shakes. The aim is a hand that stays precise and steady. Tests aim to show gains over past methods in new scenes.
arxiv-2509-21331:
Mahedi Hasan wrote a 2025 paper on seismic velocity inversion with deep learning. The task rebuilds underground structure from seismic wave data. It is key for clear seismic imaging in exploration. Classic methods are costly, sensitive to starting points, and limited by data bandwidth. Deep learning treats the task as dense prediction from shot data.

Hasan benchmarks three encoder decoder networks: U-Net, U-Net plus plus, and DeepLabV3 plus. He also tests SeismoLabV3 plus, a tuned variant with a stronger backbone. The data set pairs five channel shot gathers with high resolution velocity maps. Results show the tuned variant achieved the best scores in the study. The work gives a guide for choosing networks for this task.
arxiv-2509-21431:
First light for a major upgrade to the Very Large Telescope Interferometer is reported by the GRAVITY+ Collaboration in a 2025 paper. The upgrade improves sensitivity, sky coverage, and contrast by orders of magnitude. Its adaptive optics system, GPAO, corrects wavefronts for all four large unit telescopes. It works with natural guide stars and laser guide stars, in visible and infrared light.

The paper presents the design, operations, and performance of GPAO. Commissioning observations from late 2024 show the gains. They include the first optical interferometry of a quasar at redshift near four. A very faint cool brown dwarf was also observed spectroscopically. The results open faint targets to interferometric study.
arxiv-2509-21531:
MRI scans take long to acquire, which raises cost and invites motion artifacts. Rohan Sanda and 5 co-authors extend a patch based diffusion method for MRI reconstruction in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models learn data driven priors that can fill in undersampled scans. Whole image models need large, expensive training sets. Patch based models learn priors from small data sets instead.

Their solver, PaDIS-MRI, handles complex valued, multi coil data. It was compared with a whole image diffusion baseline on sevenfold undersampled brain data. Models trained on as few as a few dozen k-space images beat the baseline on image quality metrics. Radiologist preference was also assessed. The work shows data efficient diffusion priors can carry clinical value.
arxiv-2509-21631:
Language models are black boxes, and high stakes users need reasons behind their outputs. Avash Palikhe and 6 co-authors survey explainable language models in a 2025 paper. Explainable AI methods were built for simpler models and strain against large architectures. Huge training corpora and broad generalization add further limits. Existing surveys miss challenges from architectural diversity and evolving capabilities, they argue.

The survey maps methods for interpreting internal mechanisms and decision processes. Stakeholder accountability in high stakes domains motivates the review. Architectural families are treated separately where their explanation needs differ. Gaps between explanation research and deployed language models are identified. The authors aim to bridge that gap toward transparent AI that users can audit.
arxiv-2509-21831:
Hesam Sarkhosh, Uzma Maroof, and Diogo Barradas survey how criminals wash money through Web3 in this 2025 paper, accepted at the APWG eCrime conference. Web3 finance runs on blockchains and smart contracts, with no central overseer. That open design gives users freedom, but it also gives launderers room to hide the source of stolen or illegal funds.

The survey sorts laundering schemes into a taxonomy, from high-level strategies down to the tricks beneath them. It shows how fake names, weak rules, and complex tools help move dirty money in secret. The authors also map what makes these schemes hard to detect and stop. They close with research directions meant to make Web3 finance more open to scrutiny, for scholars, lawmakers, and firms alike.
arxiv-2509-22631:
Debargha Ganguly and 8 co-authors built an AI agent that curates vision data sets on its own. Curating domain data is a bottleneck for robust vision systems, with trade-offs among quality, diversity, and cost. Their Labeling Copilot centers on a multimodal model that reasons in steps and calls specialized tools. Calibrated Discovery pulls relevant data from large repositories. Controllable Synthesis makes new data for rare cases, with filtering.

Consensus Annotation labels data by orchestrating several foundation models with voting and suppression rules. On the dense COCO data set, it proposed far more candidate objects per image than the ground truth holds. On Open Images, it found hundreds of new box categories despite heavy class imbalance.
arxiv-2509-22831:
Sean Trott asks when a mechanism found inside one language model can be claimed for others. Mechanistic interpretability names the parts behind a model's behavior, but the field lacks rules for generalizing its claims. Trott proposes five axes along which a claim might carry over. A mechanism might match in function, in when it develops, in position, in how it relates to other parts, or in weight-space structure.

He tests the frame on attention heads that look one token back, tracked through training in Pythia models of several sizes and seeds. Development paths were strikingly consistent, while positional consistency was weaker. Larger models showed earlier onsets and higher peaks. The paper closes with objections and replies.
arxiv-2509-22931:
Compact codes that keep key facts apart are prized for search and edge devices. Shreyas Gokhale presents MonoCon, a framework that earns such codes through function rules. A small monotonic network head sits on top of any pre-trained encoder. Monotonic means the head never reverses the order of its inputs. Contrastive training shapes both parts at once.

On CIFAR-100 image tests, MonoCon codes were about nine times smaller than the baseline codes. They were also about half again as robust, with near full accuracy kept. A sentence task showed the same trade at smaller scale. Gokhale frames MonoCon as a domain-free route to tiny, sturdy codes.
arxiv-2509-23131:
Comparing graphs by their structure is a basic need from chemistry to social networks. Matthias Dehmer and 3 co-authors build similarity measures from vectors of topological indices. Edit distance and kernel methods can be slow or miss fine detail. Index-based scores compute in polynomial time. Using several indices at once captures more structure than any single one.

Standard distance rules on those vectors give graph-level scores. Comparisons show the measures track subtle structural change well. Two demos apply the method in practice. One studies random graph models, and one scores molecular similarity among isomers. Early results look promising across fields.
arxiv-2509-23431:
Physical networks like brains and blood vessels cost material, yet their branching breaks the classic cost rules. Xiangyi Meng and 4 co-authors test local branching geometry across many such networks. Length and volume minimization forecasts fail in systematic ways. Their hypothesis: true cost needs the full 3D geometry, an intractable sum in general. A surprise mapping rescues the problem.

Surface minimization maps exactly onto Feynman diagrams in string theory. As links thicken, surface rules predict trifurcations and branching angles that match real networks. Stable orthogonal sprouts also emerge from the theory. Those sprouts help synapse formation and nutrient access in real systems.
arxiv-2509-23931:
Vision-language models read hundreds of image tokens when a handful might carry the answer. Hanshi Wang and 7 co-authors prune those tokens adaptively with AutoPrune, a training-free framework. Human vision explores broadly first, then narrows; their experiments show models do something similar. A fixed pruning schedule cannot fit inputs of differing complexity, so AutoPrune measures mutual information between visual and text tokens.

That signal is projected onto a budget-bound logistic retention curve shaped per task. Applied to LLaVA-1.5-7B, the method cut most visual tokens and three quarters of the compute while keeping nearly all accuracy. It also transferred to driving-oriented vision-language-action models.
arxiv-2509-24131:
Jian Huang and 2 co-authors report a link between magnetism and electric response in assemblies of magnetite nanoparticles. The link, called magnetoelectric coupling, held up at temperatures hundreds of times lower than in past studies. At the lowest temperatures the response stopped falling and leveled off into a plateau.

That plateau points to a quantum effect, the authors argue, not a size or surface artifact. The response also shifted form with magnetic field, from a squared curve to a straight one. The size of the squared part followed a power law in temperature that hints at a nearby quantum critical regime. The team presents these assemblies as a new platform for quantum magnetoelectric study.
arxiv-2509-24431:
Embeddings that fuse text, image, and sound are powerful but bulky to store and process. Eleonora Grassucci and 3 co-authors prove a strong link between shrinking the modality gap and the chance to compress such embeddings after training. The gap is the leftover separation between embeddings of different modalities that mean the same thing.

When the gap is small enough, same-meaning embeddings share a common region, and their centroid can stand in for all of them. Their method works direct on pre-trained encoders and replaces groups of embeddings with single centroids. On large multimodal tasks, it saved much memory without sacrificing performance.
arxiv-2509-25531:
Huu Nguyen and co-authors release a web scale training data set for language models built from low legal risk sources, in work from twenty twenty-five. Many top data sets lean on broad web scrapes with murky rights. Their corpus, called MixtureVitae, puts permissive sources first.

Sources span public domain and open license text, plus low risk government and regional text. Each source is tiered by risk, with shard level origin records for safe use. The mix is rich in instruction and reasoning text, usually scarce in open corpora. Models trained on it beat other permissive sets at set budgets. At the largest test size, scores neared a top closed recipe. Math and code scores stood out as strong.
arxiv-2509-25731:
Zhenghao Zhang and a team of co-authors present a face editing system guided by facial landmarks in a 2025 paper. Instruction based editors can change a face's expression or pose, but they often lose the person's identity or miss the requested detail. Landmarks, the key points of a face, help steer edits, yet treating them as rigid constraints hurts when the target pose differs a lot.

Their system turns landmark coordinates into discrete tokens the model can reason with flexibly. A vision language predictor guesses target landmarks from the instruction and photo, thinking step by step for accuracy. To train it, the team built a dataset of over one hundred fifty thousand real face pairs with detailed instructions. Tests showed clear gains in identity preservation and instruction following.
arxiv-2510-00131:
Laura Escobar and Cesar Meza wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on matrix Schubert varieties. Fulton introduced these sets of matrices in 1992, defined by rank limits on their submatrices. A torus action lets each variety split into a core piece times a simple flat factor. The authors measure the core's complexity, meaning how far it sits from the nicest torus actions.

Building on earlier work, the authors pin down every complexity value the core can take. For an n by n setting, any whole number in the range can occur, with one small exception. The value one never occurs, no matter the choice of permutation. The result completes a classification question for this family of varieties. It also gives geometers a clean test case for how wild torus actions can become.
arxiv-2510-00231:
Alex Chen and four colleagues published this 2025 paper warning about a popular trick for speeding up language models. Compressing the KV cache shrinks stored attention data and raises throughput. Papers report almost no quality loss, but mostly on single-instruction tests. The team probed what happens when one prompt carries several instructions at once.

They found that cache eviction hits some instructions far harder than others, an effect they call eviction bias. A squeezed instruction can end up ignored by the model entirely. As a case study, they show system prompts leaking more often under compression. Instruction order and the compression method both change how bad the leakage gets. Two simple tweaks to eviction policy cut the damage greatly in their tests. Practitioners, they argue, should audit multi-instruction behavior before deploying compressed models.
arxiv-2510-00331:
Grzegorz Gutowski and three colleagues wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on drawing bipartite graphs with fewer crossings. Place the two vertex sets on two parallel lines, and crossings depend only on vertex order. In the one-sided version, one line's order is fixed in advance. A local variant asks not for fewest total crossings, but for the fewest crossings on any single edge.

Earlier work proved the weighted one-sided local problem hard and conjectured the unweighted case hard too. The authors confirm that conjecture: the unweighted problem is NP-hard as well. They also revisit the classic median heuristic of Eades and Wormald for this setting. With a specific tie-breaking rule, they prove the heuristic guarantees an approximation ratio of three. Results like these guide the layered drawing methods used in software such as the Sugiyama framework.
arxiv-2510-00631:
Zhang and a large team of co-authors report optical monitoring of the blazar OP313 during its strong 2024 flare, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Blazars are active galaxies whose jets point almost straight at Earth, so their light varies fast and brightly. The Fermi space telescope saw OP313's gamma-ray flux jump to about sixty times its average level at the peak.

The team followed the event with optical telescopes for about one hundred days. They found the source grew active roughly fifty days before the flare and stayed active afterward. During the flare its spectrum shifted from quasar-like to BL Lac-like, and its broad emission lines faded from view. The authors link the long active phase to changes in the accretion rate feeding the jet.
arxiv-2510-00731:
Gozzi and Perra model how to stop deception-based cyber-threats spreading through online social networks, in this 2025 arXiv paper on network science. Phishing-style attacks spread person to person, and defenders with a budget must choose whom to make aware and protect. The authors simulate activity-driven temporal networks where users differ in gullibility and interact with their own kind. Threats spread under a susceptible-infected-susceptible dynamic, much like a recurring epidemic.
