arxiv-2601-15331:
Rishit Chugh probes language models with hostile prompts, and counts the cost of doing so. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with jailbreaking: prompt tricks that push a model to produce outputs it should refuse. Wide deployment has raised the security stakes.

Models out of the box often lack robust guardrails. Manual exploits take time and effort to craft. Chugh presents RECAP, a resource-efficient method for adversarial prompting. It aims to test a model's defenses at scale without the heavy cost of hand-built attacks crafted fresh by hand on each new system.
arxiv-2601-15531:
Felipe Atenas, Minh N. Dao, and Matthew K. Tam build optimization methods in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their topic is structured monotone inclusion problems. These are problems of finding a point where a sum of operators vanishes. Distributed forward-backward splitting is a standard way to attack them. The team's version allows variable stepsizes. Step sizes can change as the method runs.

The framework rests on relocated fixed-point iterations. It extends an approach from a 2025 paper they cite. The extension covers conically averaged operators. That widens the class of methods the theory supports, including graph-based forward-backward schemes. Variable stepsizes can speed convergence in practice. A theory that certifies them helps users trust the faster runs.
arxiv-2601-15631:
Xingzhou Chen and a large team report an optical effect in a layered material in a 2026 arXiv paper. Atomically thin transition-metal dichalcogenides carry a valley degree of freedom. It works like a binary index, fit for storing information. Bare valley excitons live briefly and move poorly, which limits their use. Coupling them with light forms exciton-polaritons. These hybrids offer a route past those limits.

The team reports an anomalous optical valley Hall effect. Their system is a monolayer of WS2 in the polariton regime. A Hall effect here means valley types drift apart under a drive. Anomalous behavior hints at physics beyond the plain version. Valley-based devices remain a research goal. Effects that steer valleys with light are steps toward that goal.
arxiv-2601-15731:
Linyong Zou and a large team improve a brain-imaging method in a 2026 arXiv paper. The method is electrophysiological source imaging, or ESI. It locates brain activity from scalp signals. ESI is an essential technique for diagnosing brain disorders. Model-based and deep learning methods have made promising progress. Precise imaging still hinges on choosing and refining features well. That step remains a central challenge, the authors say.

Their method is FAIR-ESI. The name expands to feature adaptive importance refinement. It adapts which features matter as imaging proceeds. Better feature handling should sharpen the source maps clinicians read. For epilepsy and other disorders, a sharper map can change care. The paper targets that refinement step directly.
arxiv-2601-15831:
Faruk Pasic and five co-authors analyze beamforming with cheap converters in a 2026 arXiv paper. Future wireless systems will use MIMO beamforming at millimeter-wave bands. Those bands deliver high data rates. Fully digital beamforming gives flexible spatial processing. It suits latency-critical applications well. It also depends on accurate channel estimation. Every antenna path needs its own data converters in a digital design.

High-resolution converters are costly and power-hungry at these speeds. The paper studies low-resolution DACs and ADCs instead. Coarser conversion saves power but adds error. The question is how much performance survives the savings. For network gear makers, that trade-off decides real products. The analysis speaks to 6G hardware planning.
arxiv-2601-16031:
Galen Bergsten and seven coauthors ask how hidden partner stars skew counts of small planets. Their 2026 preprint uses data from the Kepler space craft. A close star that is not seen on its own can make a planet look too small. It can also make the planet look more easy to find than it is. Both flaws bend the rate at which small worlds seem to occur.

To size the second flaw, the team picked 198 Kepler stars. Each star could show an Earth like world if it stood alone. The team then took sharp views of those stars with ground optics. The views test how often a hidden mate was in fact there. The work helps clean up planet counts for small worlds.
arxiv-2601-16231:
Aafiya Hussain and four coauthors test sound only attacks on models that join three modes. Their 2026 preprint deals with models that take sound, pics and words. Such models score well on thought and build tasks. Their strength when sound is bent with ill will is less known. The team bends sound in ways a hearer may not note.

Bent sound aims to throw the joint model off its true pick. The attack needs no change to pics or words at all. If sound alone breaks the model, guards must watch sound most. The study maps that risk in a set, step by step way. It warns build teams of a blind spot.
arxiv-2601-16431:
Ruonan Zheng and three coauthors set test plans for Kriging models of costly runs. Their 2026 preprint deals with stand in models for hard lab runs. Comp runs now stand in for real tests in much build work. A Kriging model then stands in for the comp run. Good test points cut the gap of the stand in across the whole space.

Step by step plans add points where the gap is most large. Each new run then trims the worst flaw in the model. Trim plans save runs while they lift trust in the stand in. The work sorts plans by how fast they close the gap. It serves teams with tight run counts.
arxiv-2601-16831:
Shangjie Tian, Qi Wang, and a team of co-authors squeeze a crystal to make it lossless. The crystal Ge2Bi2Te5 blocks current flow in a rare, twist-tied way. Such twist traits make it a topological insulator. Their 2026 preprint tracks the crystal's flow traits under huge force. They also swap in manganese atoms to add magnetism.

Force can flip such crystals into superconductors. The swap of atoms shifts that flip in clear ways. The team maps how the flip point moves with the swap. States that mix pairing and twist could host new quantum bits. High-force maps guide the hunt for those states.
arxiv-2601-16931:
Mauro D'Onofrio, Francesco Brevi, Cesare Chiosi, and Paola Marziani draw a wide view of galaxy scale links. Galaxies of unlike shapes still share tight links. Size, mass, and spin tie in set ways. Their 2026 preprint pulls those links from two big sky surveys. WINGS and MANGA give the base facts for the work.

The team sorts galaxies by shape in the link planes. Each zone of a plane gets a share count. Model data from Illustris joins the view as a check. Shared links test how galaxies grew and aged. Shape-wise gaps can flag where growth tales fall short.
arxiv-2601-17131:
Ondřej Kubíček, Viliam Lisý, and Tuomas Sandholm sharpen game play by use of fine tie rules. Big games are played from a pre-set plan, then tuned live. In hid-fact games, the live tune must weigh unseen states. It must also weigh the foe's past plan. Their 2026 preprint adds equilibrium refinements to that tune step. Such refinements pick the best of tied best replies.

Fine picks can lift the tune past the base plan. They curb plays that a smart foe could exploit. Games here span cards, bids, and guard work. Sharp subgame tools push AI skill in all three.
arxiv-2601-17331:
Fabian Vazquez and seven co-authors work on finding polyps in colonoscopy images. Polyps can grow into colorectal cancer, so early finds save lives. Computer tools help doctors spot them in scans. U-Net style models, in CNN, Transformer, and Mamba forms, already score well. They still miss shape and structure cues. Low contrast and clutter make those cues hard to read.

The team adds geometric priors to guide the models. Priors tell the network what shapes to expect. That help should sharpen borders in messy scenes. Sharper maps mean fewer missed polyps. The work serves computer-aided diagnosis in real clinics. It aims at the cases where current tools are weakest.
arxiv-2601-17431:
H. Kemal İlter audits how AI help can decay the facts in survey papers. Language models make writing faster. They can also add informational entropy, a slow blur of truth. İlter ran a forensic audit of 50 recent AI survey papers. The set held 5,514 citations from late 2024 to early 2026. He tracked how valid citation chains degrade.

The title names a 17 percent gap. That figure sums up the decay he found. Hallucinated papers are a known flaw; broken chains are quieter. They let false claims look sourced and sound. The audit gives editors a scale for the harm. It argues for citation checks as a core step, not an extra.
arxiv-2601-17531:
José Manuel Casas, Emzar Khmaladze, and Manuel Ladra study Leibniz n-algebras. These algebras generalize Leibniz algebras to higher arity. The authors analyze forgetful functors and the Daletskii-Takhtajan functor. They focus on perfect objects and crossed modules in this setting. Functors move results between categories in algebra.

They then apply the work to homology and universal central extensions. Central extensions are a core tool to classify algebras. Homology reads the deep shape of such structures. Clear functor behavior makes those tools safe to move. The paper serves pure algebra. It firms up a young field where base results are still being set. Each firm base saves later work.
arxiv-2601-17831:
Zehao Liu, Xiyan Peng, Zhenghong Tang, Zhaoxiang Qi, Shilong Liao, and Yong Yu rework an old sky survey to find stars it missed. Their 2026 preprint describes a software pipeline for 2MASS, the Two Micron All Sky Survey. The pipeline re-runs detection on the survey's J-band images. It tunes the search settings and adds a screening step that weighs signal strength and image sharpness together.

That joint screen helps pick out faint point sources that the first pass left behind. A first paper in a series, it sets up the method and its gains. Faint objects matter for maps of the Galaxy and for counts of cool, dim stars. Old survey data can still yield new finds when read with fresh tools.
arxiv-2601-18331:
Junmo Jeon and Shiro Sakai extend the idea of hyperuniformity from classical matter into quantum electron systems. Their 2026 preprint builds a framework on that extension. Hyperuniform systems hide their disorder: density fluctuations shrink at large scales. The quantum version adds the intrinsic fluctuations of many-body ground states. The team studies long-wavelength fluctuations through the charge-density structure factor. A quantity called the quantum weight enters, tied to the system's gap structure.

The framework can flag quantum phase transitions. It also reveals gaps that other probes may miss. A new lens on ground states serves the study of quantum materials. The work joins two fields that grew up apart.
arxiv-2601-18431:
S. Kumano turns to a second spin topic: how the core of an atom shifts the traits of the parts inside it. Work on that shift goes back to a shock find in the early eighties, when tests showed that quarks in a heavy core do not act like quarks in a lone proton. Most past work charted one curve that sums over all spin states.

Kumano looks at a finer split, the gap between two curves tied to how the beam and the target line up. The deuteron, with one proton and one neutron, is the best test bed for that split. Small shifts there can tell us how the strong force bends when parts sit close in a core. The note maps what is known and what new tests could pin down.
arxiv-2601-18631:
Mingyang Song and six colleagues give sight-and-text models a way to call on tools as they think. A person who hits a hard task picks up a tool: a lens, a map, a count aid. A model can do the same if it knows which tool to pick, when to call it, and how to chain calls over steps. That skill is hard when the tool or the task is new.

Their tool, daReasoner, learns to run that chain on the fly. It picks a tool, reads what comes back, and picks the next step from the gain. A good chain could lift scores on tasks that mix sight, facts, and steps. It could also make the model's path clear for staff to check. Tool use of this kind is a key step toward agents that work in the real world.
arxiv-2601-18931:
Frederick Tsz-Ho Fong and Hung Tran follow a flow that slowly reshapes curved spaces. Ricci flow deforms a shape's metric over time, much as heat evens out warmth. The pair study it on bundles built over products of special curved spaces called Kähler-Einstein manifolds.

Their starting metric comes from a known ansatz, a structured guess used in past work. They prove the flow keeps that structure as it runs, which tames a hard equation into parts that can be tracked. Keeping the ansatz lets them say how the shape evolves and what it may settle toward in the long run.
arxiv-2601-19231:
Yangyang Guo and four co-authors show that safety training in language models can wash out with harmless data. Aligned models refuse unsafe asks, and those refusals tend to start with a fixed few words, like an apology. That sameness, the team finds, is a crack in the armor.

Fine tuning on a small set of purely benign samples can undo the refusal habit. The study is a warning, not a how-to celebration: guards that rest on surface patterns are fragile. Builders who ship fine tuning to users need defenses that survive contact with ordinary data.
arxiv-2601-19331:
Giovanni Valvassori Bolgè characterizes the corner points of a class of monotone functions, then puts them to work on contests. Extreme points are the shapes that cannot be built by blending others, so knowing them maps a whole family. The family here is multi dimensional and monotone, growing in every direction at once.

He applies the result to large contests, where many players vie for prizes under set rules. The corner point view gives a handy form for the best prize allocation rules across a broad range of tastes about risk and fairness. Contest design, from sales races to grants, rests on such rules.
arxiv-2601-19431:
Markus Seidel, for the CMS Collaboration, reviews the building blocks of particle events in the LHC's third run. CMS is one of the two great detectors at the Large Hadron Collider, now colliding at higher energy in Run 3. Its physics objects are the reconstructed leptons, photons, jets, and missing momentum that every analysis starts from.

Their performance and calibration decide the quality of all CMS science. Run 3 piles many collisions into each crossing, so the algorithms must stay sharp in a crowd. Seidel's review tells analysts exactly how these objects behave and where their limits sit.
arxiv-2601-19531:
Alex Mauch-Soriano and nine colleagues ask how many Jupiter-like planets should circle white dwarfs. White dwarfs are the dense embers left when stars like the Sun die. Giant planets are common around living stars, and some are known around evolved stars. Yet only a handful have been found near white dwarfs, despite careful imaging surveys.

The team predicts how often such planets should occur if they survive the star's death. Their forecast can be compared with what surveys actually see. A gap between the two would point to planets being destroyed or thrown out as the star ages. A match would mean the planets mostly endure. Either way, the count tells us how planetary systems end. The work guides future searches around dead stars.
arxiv-2601-19731:
Massimiliano Di Penta and a large group of colleagues write on behalf of SIGSOFT, the software engineering research community's main society. Their subject is the future of the field itself. Conferences keep growing, and with size come rising costs and stale formats. Those barriers shut out many researchers, especially from poorer regions.

That exclusion threatens the inclusivity and global diversity behind the field's success. The authors set out the society's perspective on what must change. The piece is a position statement rather than a research result. It aims to steer community debate about venues, formats, and access. Anyone planning the next decade of software engineering meetings is its intended reader.
arxiv-2601-19831:
Michael Y. Hu, Jane Pan, Ayush Rajesh Jhaveri, Nicholas Lourie, and Kyunghyun Cho study how language models improve with scale. Neural scaling laws predict that overall performance rises smoothly with compute. Validation loss follows tidy power-law curves. But single downstream tasks behave far less tidily: some improve steadily, others plateau, and some get worse with scale.

The authors call their study neural neural scaling laws, a play on modelling the models themselves. Understanding per-task curves matters for anyone deciding how big a model to train. Aggregate laws can hide tasks that matter to real users. Task-level prediction would make compute budgets smarter. The work urges the field to look beneath the smooth averages.
arxiv-2601-19931:
Sebastien Kawada and Dylan Holyoak describe a system entered in a shared task on story similarity. SemEval-2026 Task 4 asks systems to judge how similar two narratives are. Their entry, CascadeMind, mixes neural and symbolic methods in a cascade. The neural part uses a language model that votes many times in parallel, a technique called self-consistency voting.

A supermajority threshold settles confident cases at once. Uncertain cases escalate to more voting rounds. A symbolic ensemble that analyses narrative structure at several scales acts as tiebreaker. Cascades spend heavy computation only where doubt remains. The design reflects a wider pattern in applied AI: fast neural judgement, checked by slower structured analysis.
arxiv-2601-20131:
Deep Shah, Sanket Badhe, and Nehal Kathrotia map out the design choices behind embedding retrieval systems. These tools find matching text or images by meaning. Their paper walks down the full design stack, layer by layer. At the top sits the representation layer, where loss functions and model shapes define what counts as a good match.

The authors contrast bi-encoders, which encode query and item apart, with cross-encoders, which read both together. Each choice trades speed against accuracy in a different way. Their taxonomy names the common pitfalls in these choices, and it gives builders a clear map for weighing cost against quality.
arxiv-2601-20531:
Saurabh Verma and Shivam Dubey prove weaker quantization dimension results for self-similar measures. Quantization asks how well a probability measure can be approximated by finitely many points, and its dimension describes how the error shrinks. The authors study measures whose generating system does not satisfy the usual separation condition.

They use the fact that a subsystem at some level does separate. They also study approximation of the space of Borel probability measures under geometric mean error. Results of this kind extend quantization theory to overlapping fractals, which arise often in practice. These are quiet proofs, but they let the rest of the field build with trust.
arxiv-2601-20631:
Gianluca Allinson and a large team review Rydberg-atom receivers and their potential for space applications. These sensors convert radio, microwave, and terahertz fields into optical signals. They offer calibration traceable to fundamental constants, high sensitivity, and broad tunability.

The review compares five receiver architectures, from Autler-Townes and AC-Stark schemes to superheterodyne and fluorescence designs, against the needs of space missions. Rydberg receivers could give satellites a single sensor for many bands. The assessment helps mission planners judge where the technology is ready and where it is not. One sensor for many bands would cut weight, and weight is cost on any launch to space. The team weighs each design on that scale.
arxiv-2601-20831:
Vishnu Sashank Dorbala and Dinesh Manocha give embodied agents a memory that a model actively runs. Their 2026 paper presents MemCtrl. Foundation models personalize their choices through in-context learning. But the context window is small, so memory must be compressed and fetched. Systems like RAG treat memory as a large offline store. That view fits embodied agents poorly.

An embodied agent, such as a robot, works online under tight limits. It has strict memory and compute budgets. MemCtrl uses a multimodal model as an active memory controller instead. The model decides what to keep, drop, and fetch as events unfold. The paper argues this active style suits agents that act in the world. It points toward robots that remember what matters and forget the rest.
arxiv-2601-21331:
Filippo Portera proposes a new loss function for support vector machines and neural networks. Loss functions steer training by scoring how wrong a model is. A convex loss is prized because it avoids bad local traps during the search.

The author derives the paired dual problems for both sorting and regression tasks. Tests run on several small datasets, since support vector methods scale poorly to large ones. The new loss aims to keep the good math of classic methods while behaving better in practice. Small, careful tests show where the trade-offs land.
arxiv-2601-21631:
Nicolas Pope and Matti Tedre turn language model training from a black box into a classroom sandbox. Most lessons on generative AI only let students prompt a finished model. The data and mechanics that shape the model stay hidden, which feeds both hype and fear.

The authors built a browser tool where students train a small transformer on their own device. Every step of training is visible and touchable. Students can swap the training text and watch behavior change. Seeing a model learn from data they chose gives a grounded sense of what these systems are and are not.
arxiv-2601-21731:
Kaustubh Sharma, Srijan Tiwari, Ojasva Nema, and Parikshit Pareek extract readable kernels from networks fitted on synthetic data. Such prior-data fitted networks do fast, learned inference, but their priors and kernels stay hidden inside. That opacity blocks uses like surrogate optimization, which need an explicit covariance model.

The authors build a framework that recovers the spectral story of the learned kernel. A decoupled attention design helps separate the pieces. Making the kernel visible turns a black-box predictor into a tool other methods can build on. It also lets users check whether the learned prior matches the problem at hand.
arxiv-2601-21831:
Daniel Gonzalez-Alvarado, Jonas Cassel, Stefania Petra, and Christoph Schnörr work on generating discrete data, such as categories and counts. Generative models usually learn in smooth spaces, which fits awkwardly with data that come in separate bins. Their 2026 preprint builds the learning space from the geometry of categorical distributions themselves.

The authors place a low-dimensional latent space inside the parameter space of product manifolds of categorical distributions. That latent space captures how the variables depend on each other while dropping redundant degrees of freedom. A well-shaped latent space lets a model generate new discrete samples that respect the patterns in the real data. Which matters for survey data, genetics, and other fields built on categories.
arxiv-2601-21931:
Karel Devriendt, Ignacio Echave-Sustaeta Rodríguez, and Frank Röttger work on the statistics of extremes. Hüsler-Reiss distributions are a parametric family used to model multivariate Pareto data, the joint behavior of several variables when all are large at once. A key question is when extremes in some variables tell nothing about extremes in others.

That property is extremal conditional independence. The authors introduce two set functions, which assign values to a distribution and to each of its marginals. They show that independence statements of this kind can be characterized through those functions, using modular structure. Their 2026 preprint gives risk modelers a cleaner test for dependence among rare events, such as joint floods or simultaneous market crashes.
arxiv-2601-22031:
Junhao Ruan and co-authors merge two rival ways of generating text. Autoregressive models write one token at a time, which trains efficiently but decodes slowly. Diffusion language models generate in parallel and run fast, but their training is less direct.

Their 2026 preprint proposes Causal Autoregressive Diffusion, or CARD. It reshapes the diffusion process inside a strictly causal attention mask, so every token still only sees what came before. That design enables dense, per-token supervision in a single forward pass, combining autoregressive training efficiency with diffusion-style throughput at inference. Faster text generation at the same quality would cut serving costs across every product built on language models.
arxiv-2601-22131:
Leonard Papenmeier and Petru Tighineanu speed up optimization problems that pull in opposite directions. Multi-objective optimization balances competing goals with only black-box access to the system and a limited budget of measurements. Many teams hold historical data from related past tasks, which meta-learning could exploit.

Their 2026 preprint presents SMOG, a scalable meta-learning method for multi-objective Bayesian optimization. By learning from earlier tasks, the optimizer starts new problems already knowing where good trade-offs tend to live. That head start matters in drug design, engineering, and materials work. Where each measurement can cost days or thousands of dollars and budgets never stretch as far as the questions do.
arxiv-2601-22331:
Aditya Narayan Ravi, Snehal Vadvalkar, Abhishek Pandey, and Ilan Shomorony fix a flaw in cell imaging that can hide real drug effects. Cell Painting stains cells so a microscope can read their shape and state in fine detail. Their 2026 preprint notes that lab, tool, and protocol shifts add batch effects that swamp the true signal.

Their fix uses kernels that shift with each batch, plus smart sampling to keep the cost low. Clean data let teams spot how a drug changes cells. The method aims to scale to huge screens. It serves the hunt for new medicines.
arxiv-2601-22531:
Jiayi Dai and Randy Goebel train networks that show their reasons as they decide. Their 2026 preprint works on rationale extraction: one network picks the key input parts, a second decides from those parts alone. The design makes the logic open to view by construction.

A teacher model, the rationalist of the title, guides the learner with step-wise, readable reasons. Such guidance aims for reasons that are both true to the model and clear to people. The need is sharpest in high-stakes fields like health and law. The work seeks trust through shown work.
arxiv-2601-22631:
En Fu, Yanyan Hu, Changhua Hu, Zengwang Jin, and Kaixiang Peng predict how much useful life a machine has left, from little data. Such forecasts guide repairs, yet they have long needed heaps of past wear data from twin machines. Their 2026 preprint, PEFT-MuTS, takes a leaner path.

Their frame fine-tunes only a small part of a model, across many signals at once. Small-data forecasts could serve rare or new gear, where twins do not exist. The work cuts the data bill for a key factory task. It also aims to keep accuracy high. Less data, same warning time, is the goal.
arxiv-2601-23131:
Christiaan P. Opperman, Anna S. Bosman, and Katherine M. Malan survey methods that help neural networks generalize. Networks ace many tasks, yet they can stumble on data they have not seen. A large family of tricks, called regularisation, has grown up over the years to fight that weakness.

The authors review those approaches and test them empirically side by side. A clear map of what works, and at what cost, saves practitioners from folklore. Generalization is the difference between a demo and a tool people can rely on. The empirical analysis keeps the survey honest, testing whether celebrated techniques still earn their place in current practice.
arxiv-2601-23231:
George Webber, Alexander Denker, Riccardo Barbano, and Andrew J Reader solve inverse problems with flow-based models under model predictive control. Flow models provide strong priors for rebuilding hidden images from measurements. Guiding them toward a specific measurement, though, is computationally heavy.

Casting guidance as optimal control is elegant but demands costly differentiation through the flow. Their predictive control scheme seeks the same guidance at lower memory and compute cost. Cheaper conditional generation helps medical imaging and other reconstruction tasks. Model predictive control sidesteps repeated differentiation through the flow dynamics, the cost that made control-based guidance heavy.
arxiv-2602-00331: Anushka Narayanan and Karianne J. Bergen develop prototype based explainable networks for geospatial tasks. Such AI matters for understanding machine decisions and ensuring model trust in science. These methods predict from similarity between inputs and learned prototypes for typical classes, offering clear readings over shaky post hoc explanations. Existing models target standard RGB images, not the distinct channels of earth science image and raster data. Their approach tailors this reasoning to multi channel geo data, where each channel stands for a distinct physical variable or spectral channel.
arxiv-2602-00431: Muddasir Rahim and Soumaya Cherkaoui present an intelligent reconfigurable surface framework for 6G networks at upper mid-band. It combines ground surfaces with aerial surfaces on low-altitude stations, for reliable connectivity under severe blockages. Unlike prior work limited to ground surfaces and higher bands, it targets the FR3 spectrum, the Golden Band for 6G. The joint beamforming and user association problem, framed as a nonlinear program, is solved via decomposition, zero-forcing, and stable matching. It nears exhaustive search performance with much lower complexity, beating greedy and random rivals.
arxiv-2602-00531: Tianyi Zhang and colleagues tackle open-vocabulary object detection, which must spot objects from classes absent from training, unlike detectors tied to categories. Their VLDet framework rebuilds the feature pyramid to align vision and language at fine grain, drawing on CLIP knowledge through the VL-PUB module. A SigRPN block adds a sigmoid-based anchor-text contrastive loss to sharpen detection of novel categories. Tests reach 58.7 AP for novel classes on COCO2017 with further state-of-the-art gains on LVIS and zero-shot results on closed-set detection.
arxiv-2602-00731: Kyle Hamilton and colleagues review neuro-symbolic AI for predictive maintenance over five years in buildings, drug plants, and chip plants. Data-driven methods, including deep learning, beat traditional knowledge-based systems on accuracy, but need large labelled data sets, fail in new places, and lack clarity when run. Traditional rule, logic, and first-principles approaches suffer poor accuracy, many false positives, and need expert help. The authors propose going further, mixing deep learning with symbolic logic for more accurate and robust systems.
arxiv-2602-01031: Dongyang Fan and co-authors build HalluHard, a tough test of made-up facts in long chats, drawn from law, research, medicine, and code. A claim counts as grounded only when an in-line cited source backs it, and a judge loop fetches full sources, PDFs included, to check each cite. Even the best model-plus-search setup still made up facts about three times in ten in their runs. How often models stray shifts with model size, chat turn, depth of thought, and the kind of fact asked for.
arxiv-2602-01231: Sepehr Mousavi and co-authors ask if paid ad-free tiers truly cut data grabs, testing deeds against hopes. Ad-free tiers claim to drop ads as the ground for data use under GDPR, so sites should grab less, yet they may plead personalization to keep grabbing. Data exports from Instagram, Facebook, and X show sites still keep ad-linked data even on ad-free tiers. A 255-person poll finds most expect less grabbing in principle, yet most guess sites grab about as much in fact.
arxiv-2602-01331: Mingju Chen and co-authors build A-MapReduce, an agent plan for wide search splitting work like MapReduce. Agent teams shine at deep, vertical research but stall on wide hunts, drowning in broad goals and slow runs. A-MapReduce recasts wide search as flat retrieval, splitting huge target sets in parallel by job-tuned splits and pooled merges. A memory of past runs steers splits and merges ever better over time. Tests on five agent sets show top scores on WideSearch tasks with better cost trade-offs and short runs.
arxiv-2602-01731: Jiwoo Hwang and colleagues let robots handle objects without grasping, a task where the object blocks the view and hidden regions risk crashes. Their CURA-PPO method models uncertainty under partial views, giving collision odds as a spread and using risk and uncertainty for actions. Uncertainty spurs looking, so handling and search proceed to resolve blind spots, aided by trust maps showing what is seen. Tests across object sizes and clutter show success up to three times baselines. That offers a route to safe handling in clutter using onboard sensing.
arxiv-2602-01831: Zhimin Zhu and colleagues find the relativistic wave function of the helium-3 nucleus in Light-Front Dynamics, built from thirty two spin isospin components. Each part depends on five scalar variables, and the nucleon nucleon force uses a one boson exchange model without a potential approximation. Relativistic effects show as shifts of relativistic components from non relativistic input, and as components that vanish in the non relativistic limit. They also show as dependence on variables with no non relativistic counterpart.
arxiv-2602-02331: Shaoting Zhu and colleagues propose TTT-Parkour, rapid test-time training for perceptive humanoid parkour on unseen complex terrain. The framework fine-tunes an environment-specific policy in simulation before deployment on newly encountered terrain. A policy first pre-trains on diverse procedurally generated terrains, then fine-tunes rapidly on high-fidelity meshes reconstructed from real captures. Humanoids then master wedges, stakes, boxes, trapezoids, and narrow beams, with the pipeline taking about ten minutes per terrain and sim-to-real deployment without further on-robot updates.
arxiv-2602-02431:
Filip Kovačević and 4 co-authors prove that reusing training data can beat one-pass learning in a nonlinear setting, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Folklore says multiple passes improve statistical efficiency, but the benefit was murky outside linear regression. Their test case is a single-index model, where the outcome depends on one hidden direction, with a quadratic activation.

One-pass stochastic gradient descent needs slightly more than dimension-many samples for weak recovery. Full-batch gradient descent on a correlation loss keeps that extra factor, the authors show. But truncating the activation changes the landscape: full-batch descent then succeeds with roughly dimension-many samples. A trajectory analysis on the squared loss shows strong, exact recovery with enough samples and logarithmically many steps. The separation is a clean theoretical case where data reuse provably pays.
arxiv-2602-02531:
Trishit Mondal and 1 co-author train a deep reinforcement learning system to stop hypersonic inlets from unstarting, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Unstart is a violent breakdown of airflow in an air-breathing engine at Mach 5 and above. Shock and boundary-layer effects plus rapid pressure swings can unstart the inlet in milliseconds.

The system learns inside high-fidelity simulations from an in-house solver that refines its own mesh. The simulations resolve shock motion, boundary-layer dynamics, and flow separation, so the learned policy respects real physics. It kept the standard 2D inlet stable across a wide range of back pressures. It transferred without retraining to unseen back pressures, Reynolds numbers, and sensor layouts, and tolerated noisy readings. A small, well-chosen sensor set did nearly as well, backing real-time use in practice.
arxiv-2602-02831:
Yutaka Shimizu and 1 co-author address a tuning problem for robot control in a 2026 paper. Diffusion models, which build actions step by step from noise, can guide robots well. Their results, however, depend heavily on scheduling choices, meaning the settings that control each step.

The proposed LP-MBD replaces the usual schedule with a straight-line path inspired by flow matching. An adaptive version uses reinforcement learning to adjust steps and noise for each task. Studies on simulations, Brax benchmarks, and a mobile robot follow. The authors report simpler tuning, strong performance, and better robustness in real time.
arxiv-2602-03031:
Neural quantum states gain a concrete reading in a 2026 paper by Kimihiro Yamazaki and 3 co-authors. Such states use neural networks to stand for quantum wavefunctions in Monte Carlo work. Their designs are usually black boxes. The authors instead view them as approximations to imaginary-time evolution in a hidden latent space.

That view suggests transformer versions correspond to effective Hamiltonians that change over imaginary time. Their physics-inspired version enforces a static Hamiltonian by sharing weights across layers. A Trotter-Suzuki decomposition improves propagation quality without adding parameters. Tests use a frustrated Heisenberg magnet model. It matched or beat leading transformer states while using far fewer variational parameters.
arxiv-2602-03131:
A fluid mixed with particles is given rigorous mathematical treatment by Renjun Duan and a team of 3 other authors. Their system couples the Navier-Stokes formulas, which govern viscous fluid flow, with a Vlasov-Fokker-Planck formula for particles or bubbles. Friction between the phases links the two parts in three-part space, creating analytical difficulties around settling and singularities.

The authors construct a new class of suitable weak answers satisfying energy figures and several energy inequalities. Those inequalities help characterize where answers can become singular. Proving strong settling of the particle density required new figures and compactness methods. As a consequence, they bound the dimension of the singular set for fluid velocity and establish continuity properties elsewhere.
arxiv-2602-03331:
Prediction sets that can split into separate pieces are new by Fanyi Wu, with 3 co-authors, in a system called Bayesian Conformal Prediction. Standard conformal methods use one fixed threshold, which typically yields connected prediction sets. When the predictive spread has several separated modes, a connected set wastes space on low-density regions between modes, even though it still satisfies its coverage guarantee on average across repeated uses.

Their system formulates conformal prediction as a decision-risk tuning problem. Optimized highest posterior density sets can be disjoint, concentrating mass on separated high-density regions. A PAC-style risk constraint enforces validity even when the Bayesian model is misspecified. In a multimodal test, mean set size fell by more than half while meeting the target rate. Further tests cover regression, classification, and spread shift.
arxiv-2602-03531:
Masked autoencoders learn strong image features by rebuilding hidden patches, but why their features classify so well was unclear. Anika Shrivastava and 2 co-authors probe those internal representations in a 2026 paper. What began as a study of downstream accuracy turned into a discovery: the learned features classify well even under blur and occlusions.

A layer-by-layer look shows the model builds a class-aware latent space, with different classes settling into ever more separable subspaces. The model also shows early, lasting global attention, unlike standard vision transformers. Two new sensitivity gauges measure how embeddings hold up under damage. Together the results explain why masked autoencoders classify so robustly.
arxiv-2602-03631:
S. A. Panamaldeniya and 2 co-authors report building two germanium radiation detectors of an unusual inverted coaxial point contact design. Their 2026 paper covers fabrication and testing of the devices, named SAP16 and SAP17, grown from high-purity crystals at the University of South Dakota. Both use thin amorphous-germanium contacts that block charge from both polarities, applied to this detector type for the first time.

Cooled to 76 kelvin, the detectors run stably with picoampere leakage currents and sub-picofarad capacitance. SAP17 held high voltage cleanly, while SAP16 delivered the better energy resolution in gamma-ray spectroscopy with americium and cesium sources. Small geometric differences measurably changed depletion behavior and charge collection, a trade-off the authors map for low-background applications.
arxiv-2602-03731:
Paolo Astrino built CUBO, a retrieval-augmented generation platform that runs entirely on an ordinary consumer laptop. His 2026 paper targets organizations whose private documents cannot go to the cloud, yet whose local machines offer only 16 gigabytes of shared memory. Typical local systems demand far more, pricing out small office archives.

CUBO's novelty is engineering integration: streaming ingestion with constant buffer overhead, tiered hybrid retrieval, and hardware-aware orchestration. The system holds a hard memory ceiling while answering from corpora of ten gigabytes. On BEIR benchmarks its recall stays strong across domains, and median retrieval latency sits under two hundred milliseconds on a modest laptop. Local-only processing keeps the design aligned with data-minimization law.
arxiv-2602-03831:
Silouanos Brazitikos and 3 co-authors bound the maximal perimeter of isotropic log-concave probability measures in a 2026 paper. For such a measure, the perimeter constant is the largest boundary measure any convex body can achieve against it. The worst case over all measures in n dimensions is the quantity to tame.

The authors prove the worst-case perimeter grows at most like a constant times n to the three-halves power. That improves the previously known quadratic upper bound. Under extra structural assumptions on the measure, they obtain sharp bounds that are only linear in the dimension. The result advances the quantitative geometry of log-concave measures, a setting where perimeter controls how mass concentrates near boundaries.
arxiv-2602-03931:
Jiakang Bao and 3 co-authors map a corner of the landscape of six-dimensional quantum field theories. Their 2026 paper studies D-type orbi-instanton theories and asks which of them shrink down to a known four-dimensional family called class S theories. The constructions come from F-theory, a geometric branch of string theory.

Only a subset of the six-dimensional theories admits the simpler four-dimensional description. For that subset, two sets of integer labels capture the punctures on a sphere. The authors link one label set to mirror theories and trace flows between theories, including hidden ones. The mapping brings order to a large, partly charted landscape.
arxiv-2602-04131:
How an agent discounts the future shapes how it handles risk. Mehrdad Moghimi and 2 co-authors decouple the two in a 2026 paper on risk-sensitive reinforcement learning. The discount factor is usually a fixed knob, yet exponential discounting cannot express real time preferences.

Their framework supports general discounting functions alongside optimization of risk measures over outcome distributions. A multi-horizon extension repairs flaws in earlier methods. Theory analyzes when their algorithms are optimal, and extensive experiments check robustness. The message matters for safety-critical uses like finance and medicine. Treating discounting as a mere hyperparameter silently bakes in the wrong attitude toward time and risk.
arxiv-2602-04431:
Design the agent team assuming some members will be turned against it. Jonathan Nöther and 2 co-authors cast that paranoia as a game in a 2026 paper. Their MaMa method pits a system designer against a meta-adversary that compromises a subset of agents to cut safety, echoing Stackelberg security games.

The designer proposes architectures in rounds; language-model-driven adversarial search returns the strongest attacks found as feedback. Across diverse environments, MaMa-designed systems defended against worst-case attacks while keeping performance on par with systems built without adversaries. Built-in red-teaming inside the design loop beats bolting safety on later.
arxiv-2602-04531:
Xavier Caruso and Florian Fürnsinn report new software for studying hypergeometric functions in a 2026 paper. These functions form a broad family used across algebra and number theory. The work adds tools to SageMath, a free computer algebra system.

The implementations handle series over rational numbers, finite fields, and p-adic numbers, which are number systems based on a prime. The tools can decide whether a function is algebraic. They can also compute valuations, a measure of divisibility by a prime, and minimal polynomials in positive characteristic. The paper is a concise software report. It documents algorithms that researchers can now call directly inside SageMath.
arxiv-2602-04731:
Sameh Khattab and 7 co-authors merge specialized expert models into one biomedical search system in a 2026 paper. Adapting a general language model into a domain retriever usually needs large-scale training on mixed data, which can average away each domain's strengths.

Merging independently trained experts beat that approach across several model families, merging methods, and retrieval tasks. To raise expert quality further, the authors propose a synthesize-train-merge framework. A top-tier model generates hard negative examples, meaning near-miss documents that sharpen training. Specialists are fine-tuned cheaply and then merged, with no continual pretraining. Synthesized hard negatives helped smaller models most. The framework performed strongly on biomedical tasks while staying competitive on general retrieval.
arxiv-2602-05131:
Modern research runs on scientific workflows, pipelines that chain computations across spread-out machines and datasets. Irene Bonati and 8 co-authors report the findings of the Workflows Community Summit held in Amsterdam in June 2025 in this 2026 perspective paper. International experts met to name the barriers holding workflow practice back and to propose fixes.

The barriers include tension between general-purpose systems and domain-specific needs. They also include shaky long-term funding for workflow software, and too little career credit for the people who build and keep reproducible pipelines. Gaps in standards, training, and cross-disciplinary teamwork also slow progress. The summit's action lines call for judging systems by scientific impact rather than raw speed, formalizing common workflow patterns and community benchmarks. They also call for organizing an international community that funders hear, and creating dedicated workflow engineering roles and training paths.
arxiv-2602-05331:
An epidemic spreading into new ground can be modeled with free boundaries: the infected zone itself grows or shrinks over time. Yao Chen and 3 co-authors study such a model in this 2026 applied mathematics paper, the first of a two-part series. Two densities evolve together, the pathogen and infected humans, with diffusion acting nonlocally across the region.

The boundary rule is the paper's novelty. The expansion rate now blends two drivers: the outward flux of pathogen through the boundary, as in earlier work, and a weighted count of infected people inside the region. The authors prove the system is well-posed and that long-term behavior follows a spreading-vanishing dichotomy, either the epidemic spreads or it dies out. Sharp thresholds for which outcome occurs are given, one from the initial data and one from the diffusion rate, settling an eigenvalue-based criterion that complements earlier results.
arxiv-2602-05431:
Moving coins between different blockchains in a private way is hard, since swaps must stay fair and must not expose who took part. Yi Liang and Jinguang Han propose a signature scheme, called LTRAS, meant to solve this problem. The scheme mixes three tools. Adaptor signatures lock a deal to a secret condition, ring signatures hide the signer in a group, and a threshold form can pay from several accounts at once.

The authors give a formal definition of the scheme, set out a security model, and build a concrete version of it. Tests and analysis show much lower computing and message costs than rival schemes when rings are large or many accounts pay at once. A link feature helps stop the same funds from being spent twice. The paper closes by showing how the scheme could support atomic swaps across chains.
arxiv-2602-06031:
Software that flags inputs unlike anything it was trained on is the subject of work by Claus Hofmann and 5 co-authors. Their method, called AP-OOD, gives text data a single score that says how unusual it looks. It works with language model word pieces, called tokens, rather than plain averages over them.

AP-OOD can run with no labeled odd cases at all, or it can learn from a small set of them when some exist. On test sets drawn from news summaries and from translation work, it cut false alarms sharply compared with earlier methods. Fewer false alarms mean safer use of language models in real products.
arxiv-2602-06531:
Fractions with several variables get messy when denominators involve hyperplane arrangements, the geometric setting of many physics calculations. Claire de Korte and Teresa Yu study partial fraction splits there, using tools from commutative algebra. They give tests for when a fraction function with poles on such a setup admits a desirable split.

The tests come from primary decompositions of ideals attached to the arrangements. The authors also present an algorithm that finds a split with the traits needed to simplify scattering amplitude calculations. Practical work from Feynman integrals demonstrates the algorithm at work, showing how algebra tests translate into concrete simplifications for physicists.
arxiv-2602-06631:
Thiago Brant, Julien Kühn, and Jun Pang test whether language models can judge how hard an exam question is. The question matters because schools may soon use these models to write tests. The team uses Brazil's national ENEM exam, which has official difficulty ratings from years of student data.

Ten leading models, both commercial and open, rated more than a thousand real questions. The best models ranked questions in roughly the right order but tended to call hard questions easier than they are, and they did worse on questions with images. When told about students' backgrounds, the models adjusted their ratings in patchy, inconsistent ways. The authors say the models work better as rough screeners than as final judges of difficulty.
arxiv-2602-07331:
Matching theory asks which graphs have every edge in some perfect matching, and which cycles can be removed while leaving a perfect matching behind.  Maximilian Gorsky and one co-author extend the classification of cycle-conformal graphs beyond the planar case.

They characterize matching covered, cycle-conformal graphs that are bipartite and cubic, and those that are bipartite and Pfaffian, building on a recent complete planar classification.  The Pfaffian class matters deeply in matching theory for its connections to counting and orientation.  Graph theorists get the non-planar chapters of a classification that planar results left open.
arxiv-2602-07531:
Cooling a levitated micromagnet's motion to its quantum ground state is a prerequisite for macroscopic quantum tests, but it normally demands an extremely high mechanical quality factor.  Lei Chen and three co-authors propose a dual-channel scheme that relaxes that demand by three orders of magnitude.

Squeezing-enhanced interference between magnon and cavity channels suppresses heating scattering while boosting cooling scattering, bringing ground-state cooling into reach at quality factors around ten thousand.  The hybrid levitated cavity-magnomechanical system thus becomes experimentally accessible.  Quantum optomechanics teams get a cooling design that trades an impossible materials requirement for clever interference.
arxiv-2602-07731:
Young stars with gapped disks may hide unseen partner stars or planets carving those gaps. Dori Blakely and sixteen co-authors combine tuned Hipparcos and Gaia place readings to weigh possible partners in eleven such shift-disk systems.

They find support for companions in four systems, with firm detections in two. They are the known low-mass star beside HD 142527 and a likely sub-stellar companion to MWC 758, plus weaker evidence around AB Aur and UX Tau A. For the rest they rule out partners above stated mass and distance limits, including tight limits for TW Hya. The work shows how old star places can test planet-birth stories without new scopes.
arxiv-2602-08131:
Maps of agricultural field boundaries underpin crop monitoring, yield estimates, and disease tracking, yet building them at scale is a tutorial-worthy challenge in itself. Isaac Corley and three co-authors present the Fields of the World ecosystem: a benchmark of 1.6 million field polygons across 24 countries, pretrained segmentation models, and command-line inference tools.

Two notebooks walk through local-scale boundary extraction with crop classification and forest-loss attribution, and country-scale inference on cloud-optimized data. Field-level crop mapping with limited labels reaches macro F1 scores of 0.65 to 0.75, and precomputed predictions span five countries. Agricultural remote-sensing practitioners gain a ready-to-use starting point rather than a from-scratch pipeline.
arxiv-2602-08431:
Adapting a graph model to a new dataset without the source data is hard when the new graph's structure looks nothing like the old one. Yingxu Wang and four co-authors argue the bottleneck is the source model's smoothness bias, which mistakes unseen topology for noise. Their arXiv paper proposes USBD, a framework that learns a universal structural basis instead of adapting a biased model.

A bi-level optimization distills the source data into compact prototypes spanning the full spectrum of structural patterns, from tightly grouped clusters to long chain-like motifs. At inference, a spectral-aware ensemble activates the best prototype mix for the target graph's fingerprint. Tests show clear gains under severe structural shifts, with adaptation cost decoupled from target size. Readers get a fresh paradigm for privacy-preserving graph transfer.
arxiv-2602-08931:
Gustavo E. Romero argues that spacetime singularities should not be read as claims about real stuff. Penrose's famous theorem, he says, is best seen as an incompleteness result. It shows that certain spacetime models break down under broad conditions, in general relativity and in any theory using the Raychaudhuri equation. His fresh angle separates physical assumptions from purely formal ones in relativity's foundations.

He then sets Penrose beside Gödel's incompleteness theorem, weighing what the two results share and where they part. The comparison leads to wider conclusions about the limits of our knowledge of the physical world, and what our mathematical reconstructions of it can and cannot deliver.
arxiv-2602-09031:
Sudden temperature swings crack brittle materials, from quenched glass to ceramic fuel pellets. Bo Zeng and one co-author present a complete phase-field fracture model for coupled thermo-mechanical problems, in which bulk properties, material strength, and fracture toughness are set independently. That separation lets one model span crack growth, crack birth under uniform stress, and everything between.

Validation covers quenched glass plates, where observed crack patterns emerge across thermal loads. Ceramic disks under infrared heating show straight cracks when notched and branching when intact. Ceramic pellets under rapid power pulses show strength deciding intact versus fractured. The unified model aims at more reliable fracture prediction in extreme environments.
arxiv-2602-09231:
Matija Blagojevic and one co-author introduce two new ideas to game theory: multilateral Nash balance points and groups of games. In old terms, a balance point is a plan set no single player gains by leaving alone. A k-lateral balance point demands more: no group of k players can all profit by breaking away as one. Higher-lateral balance points thus form a ladder, growing rarer as k rises.

The paper proves a finding for multilateral balance points under tiny needs, with a test echoing that growing rarity, and shows old games that hold higher-lateral balance points, baring fresh structure. Groups of games, tuned sets treated as a whole rather than one by one, complete the setup for studying balance points across related games.
arxiv-2602-09331:
When language models are trained to reason with policy gradients, every token in a generated answer normally earns the same credit, so filler counts as much as the decisive calculation. Mykola Khandoga and two co-authors propose a fairer rule in their 2026 paper. Hide a span of reasoning, watch how much the chance of the right answer falls, and weight tokens by that drop. Importance is read straight from the model's own probability shifts, with no extra model or labels.

Tests on grade-school math problems across three models from two families show steady gains over uniform credit and faster convergence. Reversing the importance signal harms performance, which the authors take as evidence the weights track real causal structure, not noise. The analysis confirms the method favors calculation steps over scaffolding text. The authors present it as a foundation for further work, not a finished solution.
arxiv-2602-09631:
Visual skill usually means reading and interpreting data visuals, but prior work misses touch, a built-in part of using hands-on visuals. Gabriela Molina León and three co-authors present a theory model for hands-on visual skill in their 2026 paper, telling how people use hands-on data visuals and systems. Skills frame modern life, and this model targets the hands-on side previous accounts missed.

Derived from current theory plans, the model is two-sided, joining four well-known skills with five novel ones. Evidence comes from looking at current visual systems and from notes in an early study using such systems. The paper closes by sketching steps toward testing, judging, building for, and teaching hands-on visual skill, turning a telling model into a research agenda.
arxiv-2602-10031:
Graph neural networks split into two camps, message-passing and spectral, rooted in different research traditions. A 2026 position paper led by Antonis Vasileiou, with nine co-authors, argues the split is overstated. Under the usual restriction to layered linear spectral filters, the two families have largely equivalent expressive power.

The paper proposes a precise definition of spectral networks based on eigenbasis symmetries, set against message-passing networks defined by neighborhood permutation symmetries. Each view has its own strengths: message-passing suits discrete structure and logic-based analysis, while the spectral view clarifies smoothing, bottlenecks, stability, and communities. Progress, the authors argue, needs a unified framework embracing both.
arxiv-2602-10131:
Moltbook is a social platform populated entirely by AI agents, and its anatomy may reveal how agent sociality differs from human sociality. A 2026 paper by David Holtz analyzes the platform's first three and a half days, covering over six thousand agents, nearly fourteen thousand posts, and over a hundred and fifteen thousand comments. At macro scale, familiar human signatures appear: heavy-tailed participation and small-world connectivity with paths under three steps.

At micro scale, the picture turns alien. Conversations run extremely shallow, with mean depth barely over one and over nine in ten comments receiving no reply. Reciprocity sits near a fifth, about a third of messages duplicate viral templates, and identity language dominates. Whether this reflects performed humanness or a genuinely different agent sociality stays open.
arxiv-2602-10231:
Group Relative Policy Optimization gives one scalar advantage to every token in a completion, mixing unrelated reward signals across segments of structured outputs. A 2026 paper led by Kirill Pavlenko, with three co-authors, proposes Blockwise Advantage Estimation. This family of GRPO-compatible methods gives each objective its own advantage, applied only to tokens in the matching text block. This cuts need for hand-designed scalar rewards and scales well to added objectives.

Gauging advantages for later blocks is hard, since their rewards depend on sampled prefixes and fair methods demand costly nested rollouts. The authors offer an Outcome-Conditioned Baseline that gauges middle state values from within-group stats alone, grouping samples by a prefix-derived middle outcome. On math tasks with uncertainty gauging, the method curbs reward mixing, rivals a leading reward-designed approach, and keeps test-time gains from confidence-weighted ensembling.
arxiv-2602-10431:
Kanghyun Noh and two co-authors address the cost of running large language models in a 2026 paper. Two popular savings tricks exist: skipping layers for some tokens, and quantizing weights to lower detail. Used jointly naively, the paper shows, they compound each other's damage, because token-adaptive models already have less redundancy to spare.

The new system, QTALE, joins the two methods while keeping scores high. It widens the range of training paths explored during fine-tuning and restores redundancy that simpler adaptive methods throw away. Tests reported by the authors show the combined method keeps model quality close to the full model. It cuts both runs and memory, making large models cheaper to deploy.
arxiv-2602-10631:
Rustam Zhumagambetov and three co-authors test whether mock clinic time series really protect privacy in a 2026 paper. Sharing medical data for machine learning is often blocked by disclosure risk, and mock data from creative models is pitched as the compliant alternative. But generated data can still leak information about training patients.

The paper studies creative models trained on moderate amounts of patient data and asks whether their outputs preserve privacy in practice. Post-hoc anonymization methods prove limited for time series, while model-centered differential privacy can destabilize training. The findings temper enthusiasm for mock data as a privacy cure: without careful tools, mock patients may still betray real ones.
arxiv-2602-10731:
Chien-Kai Ma and four co-authors make quantum state discrimination steady under noise in a 2026 paper. Distinguishing quantum states is basic to quantum information, but real devices are noisy, and ideal discrimination plans degrade. The paper develops error-tolerant plans that hold up under moderate noise.

Two plans complement each other: CrossQSD transfers unambiguous discrimination with tunable confidence bounds, while FitQSD optimizes the measurement spread to approximate the ideal noiseless case. A hybrid objective interpolates between minimum-error discrimination and FitQSD for flexible trade-offs. The tuning problems reduce to convex programs solved efficiently. A circuit synthesis system based on modified dilation and isometry methods turns the plans into realizable circuits.
arxiv-2602-11031:
Deciding whether two elements match under a twisted map is a classic group problem. Mallika Roy, writing alone, solves the endomorphism-twisted conjugacy problem for solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups of a specific family. Her recipe decides, for given elements and a map, whether one can be reached from the other by the twisted rule.

She also links outer fixed points of a map to twisted conjugacy for words tied to that map. She defines weakly outer fixed points to explore the link further. The work is pure group theory, but it turns a decision question that once lacked an answer into a concrete procedure for this family of groups.
arxiv-2602-11231:
The chiral limit asks what happens as pion and kaon masses vanish. Vivek Kumar Tiwari, writing alone, studies that limit in an on-shell renormalized quark-meson model, feeding it scaling relations from large-Nc standard U(3) chiral perturbation theory and from an infrared-regularized variant. Two frames result, one per input choice.

Comparing their Columbia plots across several sigma masses, the standard-input frame proves better. Its tricritical lines flatten and saturate as expected, while the rival frame's line diverges strongly at higher sigma mass. The paper thus recommends standard large-Nc inputs for chiral-limit studies, giving a firmer base for mapping the phase structure of strong-contact matter.
arxiv-2602-11531:
Warm Jupiters orbit in weeks to months and show a wide spread of eccentricities. Ying He and two co-authors run extensive N-body simulations to test how distant giant pullers and nearby super-Earth companions shape those orbits. Distant pullers can drive large eccentricity swings through a Kozai-type mechanism.

Nearby super-Earth companions often suppress those swings through strong dynamical coupling. That split naturally yields a bimodal spread: warm Jupiters with nearby companions stay near-circular, while those without spread widely. Reproducing the observed spread for companion-free systems requires many distant pullers on dynamically extreme orbits, supporting large post-disk dynamical evolution.
arxiv-2602-11931:
Agents that refine answers step by step call large language models again and again, so cost and capability pull in opposite directions. Pretam Ray and three co-authors ask how an agent can pick, at each step, a model strong enough for that step yet cheap enough to run. Fixed cascades and outside controllers miss a key signal: the model's own uncertainty about its output.

Their system, AdaptEvolve, selects models by intrinsic generation confidence, using it to judge in real time whether the current step is solvable. Across benchmarks, confidence-driven selection cuts total inference cost by about 38 percent while keeping about 98 percent of the accuracy of always-large-model baselines. The result is a favorable cost-accuracy frontier for evolving-agent systems, where each generation step gets only as much model as it needs.
arxiv-2602-12431:
Mixtures of colloid particles in a binary solvent near its critical point can organise like atomic alloys, if particle surfaces are tuned to favour one solvent. T. E. Kodger led this work with five co-authors, studying two populations of colloids whose surfaces are changed by chemistry to elicit a specific solvent affinity. Fluid-mediated forces, via the critical Casimir effect, then become specific to each population.

The mixture shows complex crystal growth reminiscent of atomic alloys. The strong temperature dependence of the critical Casimir force lets the team sample the whole phase diagram of the binary system. The force can also be undone with ease, and it can anneal crystal microstructure, much like temperature cycling of alloy phases. Readers get a tunable, reversible route to colloid crystals with alloy-like complexity.
arxiv-2602-12631:
Inventory control is a core ops problem where order choices are traditionally guided by theory-based ops research rules. Jackie Baek led this work with three co-authors, noting that such rules rely on rigid model assumptions and can perform poorly when demand patterns shift or relevant context is missing. Large language models can reason flexibly and use rich context, but it remains unclear how best to mix them with old pipelines.

The paper studies how ops research rules, LLMs, and humans can interact and help each other in a multi-period inventory control setting. InventoryBench, a test set of over 1,000 inventory cases spanning made-up and real-world demand data, is built to stress-test choice rules under demand shift and context signals. Results show human-LLM-OR mixes beating each part alone, with LLMs best used as flexible adapters rather than standalone choice makers.
arxiv-2602-13231:
Fifth-making networks promise high speed, low latency, and reliability, but millimetre-wave links fail easily under environmental effects, making uninterrupted service hard to guarantee. Khaleda Papry and four co-authors bridge an explainability gap: many radio link failure predictors work as black boxes, limiting operational trust. Their system pairs explainability-based feature pruning with model refinement and integrates with predictors such as graph neural network transformers and LSTM architectures.

Applied to radio link failure forecast, the system reveals weather data contributing minimally to forecasts in wide real-world datasets. That insight yields a leaner model with 50% fewer settings and improved F1 scores over the state-of-the-art answer. Network providers gain a way to evaluate and refine neural forecast models for interpretability, scalability, and scores, turning explainability from a reporting nicety into a design tool.
arxiv-2602-13731:
Generative models in medical imaging enable segmentation, anomaly detection, and synthetic data generation, relying on latent codes that are especially valuable for large 3D brain MRI scans. Yet the structure, information content, and downstream clinical use of those codes remain underexplored. This paper builds multiple variational autoencoders to encode 3D brain MRI scans into compact latent codes for generative and forecast uses.

Three analyses assess the codes. They cover measured and observed rebuild quality, latent space structure shown by Principal Component Analysis, and downstream classification on a private data set of euploid and Down syndrome brain MRI scans. The autoencoders capture essential brain features with high rebuild quality, and the latent space groups clearly, notably in telling Down syndrome individuals from euploid controls. Jordi Malé leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14731:
Mohsin Khan, Elisavet Kozyri, and Havard Dagenborg review lightweight cryptographic algorithms for small devices, where conventional AES, RSA, and DES strain limited power, memory, and battery. Their systematic review weighs algorithms for Internet of Things gear, RFID tags, and wireless sensor networks, comparing performance, security, energy use, and implementation cost in tables and graphs.

An overview of the field's evolution rounds out the survey, helping engineers match an algorithm to its setting rather than forcing a heavy standard onto tiny hardware. The paper serves as a practical guide to securing devices that cannot carry full-weight cryptography. Lightness here is a design constraint, not a compromise taken lightly.
arxiv-2602-14831:
Daniel Szabo and colleagues test conversation hand-off for indoor navigation, where a conversational agent moves seamlessly from a stationary social robot to a wearable device. Large indoor spaces like universities, airports, and hospitals tax attention, while phone apps tie up hands and eyes, limiting natural interaction.

A within-subjects study with twenty-four participants on a university campus compared robot-only, wearable-only, and robot-to-wearable hand-off. Hand-off felt engaging, the authors report, even where other measures stayed level, suggesting continuity itself carries value. Navigation gains a voice that walks beside its user, changing device without dropping the thread.
arxiv-2602-15231:
Xavier and colleagues show that atoms in chiral geometries can produce a strong collective chiroptical response from electric-dipole interactions alone. Such responses in atomic systems are usually weak, since they arise from mixing between light-driven transitions and much weaker magnetic ones. Placing atoms in chiral shapes changes that picture.

Using a coupled-dipole setup, the team finds a regime of strong effect at tiny-gap atom-to-atom gaps, tunable by probe tone. The boost links straight to the rise of dim modes. The results establish a deep link between shape twist and light-matter interactions, opening new pathways for building and using chiral light effects in atomic systems.
arxiv-2602-15331:
Zhao and colleagues build a theory setup for e-positron annihilation with higher-twist parts up to twist-4 and probe likely use in low-energy events. Through full aligned spread of the hadron grid, they get the full set of rules in terms of aligned splitting rules, with multi-part links up to four-parton level.

To gauge effect of these fixes, they gauge the twist-4 splitting rule D3 using a watcher model and find the scaled varying cut for pion making. Their sample number guess shows mix between motion bits mass fixes and the higher-twist D3 part can partly lift fit of recent BESIII data in the low-z zone. The Q-link of this part is matching hoped drop of twist-4 parts. These results hint higher-twist parts are useful for work on bits motion at low energies and spur studies including all twist-4 splitting rules.
arxiv-2602-15631:
Luo and colleagues redesign business plan writing for entrepreneurship students. Writing a plan is meant to help learners build, judge, and refine ideas, but the usual process is rigid and linear, a poor match for the looping, recursive nature of real ideation. Novices in particular struggle under the heavy cognitive load of shaping and reshaping ideas, while reflection and meta-reflection, key tools for divergent and convergent thinking, get little support from existing tools.

Their Meflex system pairs plan-writing scaffolds with a nonlinear idea canvas, powered by a large language model, to support iterative ideation through reflection and meta-reflection. An exploratory study with 30 participants examined usability and cognitive impact. Results show Meflex scaffolds plan writing well, sparks divergent thinking through model-supported reflection, raises meta-reflective awareness, and eases cognitive load during complex idea work.
arxiv-2602-15731:
Craig and Barreto-Souza introduce a kernel density estimator based on the generalised exponential distribution, designed for positive continuous data. The new tool has a tractable maths form that avoids special functions, unlike the widely used gamma estimator, which relies on the gamma function. Despite its simpler form, it keeps similar freedom and shape traits, matching cases such as the gamma that handle positive data well.

The authors derive long-run bias and variance for the tool and pin down the order of rest terms in those expressions. They also propose a second version that hits optimal mean total squared error, a trait hard to prove for the first. Tests on made-up and real data show the new tools as a strong option against older density estimators.
arxiv-2602-16431:
Michael Gintz, writing alone, gives an example of two support varieties of monomial ideals that are not unions of linear subspaces. The work builds on research by Briggs, Grifo, and Pollitz. Such varieties might have been expected to decompose into linear pieces, and the example shows they need not.

Gintz also provides a method for computing the support varieties of certain other ideals, including homogeneous ones, with faster computation. That method leads to a machine-checked verification that a third support variety of an ideal is likewise not a union of linear subspaces. It further supports a machine-checked proof classifying the support varieties of such ideals over the rationals with six homogeneous generators.
arxiv-2602-16731:
Manuel Munoz Pla presents a longitudinal open dataset of Spanish public procurement. It is drawn from the Official State Gazette and covers 2014 through 2024. The set joins structured data on contracts, buyers, suppliers, amounts, and procedures. That breadth allows large-scale study of procurement trends in Spain.

The paper describes the extraction and normalization pipeline. It gives descriptive study of trends over time and across sectors. It discusses uses in transparency research, public policy review, and computational social science. Released openly, the dataset supports repeatable research on public procurement and state contracting, giving analysts a decade-long window on how Spanish public money is spent.
arxiv-2602-16931:
Idhant Gulati and Shivam Raval show that narrow fine-tuning erodes safety alignment in vision-language agents. Lifelong multimodal agents must adapt to new tasks through post-training, but that creates tension between gaining capabilities and preserving safety alignment. Fine-tuning aligned vision-language models on narrow-domain harmful sets induces severe emergent drift. It generalizes broadly across unrelated tasks and modalities.

Tests on Gemma3-4B show drift scales monotonically with LoRA rank. Multimodal evaluation reveals substantially higher drift than text-only evaluation, suggesting unimodal safety benchmarks may underestimate safety loss. Even ten percent harmful data in the training mixture induces substantial degradation. Geometric study finds harmful behaviors occupy a remarkably low-dimensional subspace. Most drift info is captured in ten principal components. Two mitigations are tested, benign narrow fine-tuning and activation-based steering. Both reduce drift substantially, yet neither fully removes learned harmful behaviors.
arxiv-2602-17131:
Yuki Takei led a three-author team measuring how competition kills open-source projects. Software history runs in cycles of rise and fall, and open source is no exception, with the pace quickening in web development and deep learning. Yet the effect of rivalry on project survival stayed murky. The paper introduces MIAO, Mutual Impact Analysis of OSS, an automated method that borrows tools from macroeconomics.

A structural vector autoregressive model plus impulse response functions maps interactions among projects, and an analysis of nearly two hundred project groups showed the method spotting competition-driven shutdowns with high accuracy. Features from the analysis also supported forecasts of cessation a year ahead with solid accuracy. Maintainers gain a tool for reading ecosystem dynamics and for seeing which projects rivals may push out.
arxiv-2602-17331:
Emanuele Cristoforoni led a three-author survey of the classical reinforcement problem for elliptic boundary value problems, first studied by Sanchez-Palencia in 1969. The survey centers on the seminar papers by Brezis, Caffarelli, and Friedman, and by Acerbi and Buttazzo, tracing how the problem was framed and tackled.

It also covers the related optimization problems proposed in the cited papers. The survey thus gathers the classical work on the topic and its optimization spin-offs into one account. It gives new readers a guided entry to a problem that links those equations with the design of strengthening designs.
arxiv-2602-17531:
Zachary Berger led a four-author team behind a 2026 arXiv position paper on fixing benchmarks for twelve-lead ECG representation learning. The field has settled on three public multi-label benchmarks, all dominated by arrhythmia and waveform shape labels. Yet an ECG trace is known to carry far broader clinical information. The authors say downstream testing should widen to structural heart disease and patient-level forecasting.
