The paper sets out best practice for multi-label, imbalanced testing, and shows those practices change which representations look best. Its most striking result is that a randomly initialized encoder with a linear readout matches state-of-the-art pretraining on many tasks. That makes the random encoder a baseline every new method should beat. The claims rest on a study of five pretraining approaches across six settings, covering the three standard benchmarks plus structural disease, hemodynamic inference, and patient forecasting.
arxiv-2602-17631:
Jihong Cai and team compare Markovian and non-Markovian evolutions in open quantum systems, where memory effects can beat memoryless dynamics. Time-dependent Lindbladians give Markovian dynamics, with decoherence, decay of correlations and drift to equilibrium. Non-Markovian paths, by contrast, can boost memory and outperform their Markovian kin.

The letter tracks both kinds of paths from a fixed start point. Under mild assumptions, the authors show that every path can arise from a family of time-dependent Lindbladians. Non-Markovianity is thus hidden when only single paths are viewed. The finding reframes where the mark of memory truly lives: not in one path alone, but in the wider structure around it.
arxiv-2602-17831:
Simon Henniger and Gabriel Poesia introduce The Token Games, an evaluation frame where language models duel by creating puzzles for each other. Judging model reasoning grows harder as models improve, and human curation of hard questions is costly, above all for benchmarks using doctoral-level domain knowledge. Even then, similar problems may have appeared in training, muddying what scores mean.

Inspired by sixteenth-century mathematical duels, the games use Programming Puzzles: given a function returning a boolean, find inputs that make it return true. That format flexibly represents problems and enables verified solutions. Pairwise duel results feed Elo ratings for relative comparison. Tests on ten frontier models closely match the ranking from existing benchmarks such as Humanity's Last Exam, for under two hundred dollars and with no human puzzle creation. Creating good puzzles remains highly challenging for current models.
arxiv-2602-17931:
A second paper by Narjes Nourzad and Carlee Joe-Wong addresses the same sparse-reward strain from a different angle. Reinforcement learning needs many interactions to learn, and language models help by finding subgoals and guiding paths. Frequent model calls, however, raise scale and trust worries.

The authors build a memory graph encoding subgoals and paths from model guidance and the agent's own successful runs. From that graph they derive a utility function scoring how closely agent paths match prior successful strategies. That utility shapes the advantage function, giving the critic extra guidance without altering rewards. The method leans mainly on offline input with only occasional live queries, avoiding dependence on constant model supervision. Early tests in benchmark settings show faster early learning and better sample speed than baseline methods, with final returns comparable to frequent-interaction methods.
arxiv-2602-18431:
Shafkat Farabi and six co-authors tackle a large, urgent matching problem: assigning mediators to court cases in Kenya. Their 2026 paper starts from the Kenyan judiciary, where more than two thousand mediators cover eighty-seven locations and twelve case types. Each new case must be assigned at once, mediator quality may be unknown, and soft capacity limits must hold across the whole system.

The team frames the problem with a quadratic program for assignment plus a bandit-style multi-agent learning framework. Their algorithm, SMaRT, matches mediators to tasks by fit and beats baselines on stylized cases and on real Kenyan case and mediator data. It also lets users trade capacity strictness against case resolution rates, whether mediator quality is known in advance or must be learned on the fly.
arxiv-2602-19231:
When people edit a shared document at the same time from different devices, their copies must converge without losing anyone's work. Conflict-free replicated data types guarantee convergence, but they settle clashes behind the scenes, leaving users unsure why a version won. Other fixes rely on a central server to reconcile edits, which breaks the local-first promise of working offline.

Georgii Semenov and Vitaly Aksenov propose a conflict model that makes resolution explicit and local. It spots clashes through semantic dependencies, meaning it tracks how edits relate in meaning rather than only in order. Each device can then resolve its own conflicts openly, with no coordinator in the middle. The model aims to keep collaboration both reliable and understandable to the people doing the editing.
arxiv-2602-19431:
Jets are collimated sprays of particles formed when energetic quarks and gluons cross a hot, dense quark-gluon plasma. The CMS Collaboration studies the diffusion wake, a depletion of particles opposite a jet's direction, caused by energy and momentum deposited into the medium. Dijet-hadron correlations in lead-lead and proton-proton collisions reveal the effect, using data at 5.02 teraelectronvolts per nucleon pair from the CMS detector.

By varying the pseudorapidity separation of the two jets, the analysis firmly establishes the diffusion wake. Its signal exceeds five standard deviations for charged particles with transverse momentum between 1 and 2 gigaelectronvolts. Measurements are compared with models of medium response, giving a sharp probe of how jets disturb the plasma they traverse.
arxiv-2602-19631:
Text-to-image diffusion models can now make harmful, private, or copyrighted images, so erasing a concept after training matters. Uichan Lee and two co-authors note that most erasure work fine-tunes the denoiser, such as the U-Net backbone. Causal tracing hints instead that visual attribute facts sit in early self-attention layers inside the text encoder, opening a different erasure route.

Directly tuning those early layers can kill target concepts but often harms unrelated ones. The authors propose High-Level Representation Misdirection (HiRM). It steers high-level meanings of target concepts toward set vectors, such as random or supercategory directions, while touching only early layers with causal visual-attribute states. Tests on UnlearnCanvas and NSFW benchmarks show precise removal with little spillover, low training cost, and transfer to Flux with no added training.
arxiv-2602-19831:
Some malware lives only in memory, hiding payloads, commands, and keys where static analysis cannot reach. A 2026 arXiv paper by Silvia Lucia Sanna and two co-authors proposes an explainable, AI-assisted approach to memory forensics for such threats.

Memory analysis can recover transient artifacts from volatile system state, but automated detectors rarely explain themselves, and experts still slog through complex tool output. The authors use general-purpose language models to render memory-analysis output in readable form and to pull out indicators of compromise, sometimes finding more than current tools. Applied to Windows and Android malware, the method compares full memory capture with targeted process dumps. A human-in-the-loop workflow improves reproducibility and lowers operational complexity for experts and non-experts alike.
arxiv-2602-20231:
Models that turn video into robot actions often learn from plain colour video alone, with no labels for the actions. What they learn then reflects how things look, not their shape in space. For delicate work that needs contact and precision, that missing geometry matters. A 2026 arXiv paper by Manish Kumar Govind and three co-authors adds depth to the recipe, with a model named UniLACT.

Its learning scheme, UniLARN, is built on two goals: inferring actions from frames, and predicting the next frames from actions. It trains one shared numerical space for colour images and depth maps, while modelling how the two modes interact. The result is action labels in two forms: one per mode, and one unified form. Those labels, drawn from video with depth, give downstream policies stronger spatial priors than colour alone can provide.
arxiv-2602-20431:
The dark matter three-point spectrum carries information about cosmic structure, but modeling its before-and-after versions demands a unified pen-and-paper treatment. Naonori Sugiyama builds one from Unified Lagrangian Perturbation Theory, splitting the Jacobian shift that makes the nonlinear source three-point spectrum from the shift-mapping effect of long-wave bulk flows. Within that structure, the paper derives general one-loop forms and studies their infrared limits.

The analysis shows exact IR cancellation and a natural IR-resummed account of baryon sound wiggle damping, including a fully pen-and-paper treatment of the wiggle-wiggle part. The author also constructs IR-resummed models for cross three-point spectra of all pre- and post-versions, showing both overall steep damping and subtler pattern in mixed cases. Once built in code, the full three-point spectrum will on its own encode all nonlinear wiggle and IR effects.
arxiv-2602-20631:
Rota-Baxter operators and bialgebras connect closely in areas such as the Connes-Kreimer renormalization work and the approach to the classic Yang-Baxter equation. Chan Zhao and two co-authors present a bialgebra structure for a symmetric Rota-Baxter system, called a symmetric Rota-Baxter antisymmetric infinitesimal bisystem. The paper maps it through matched-pair versions and double builds of Frobenius algebras.

Studying the coboundary case yields an enriched associative Yang-Baxter equation adapted to systems of this kind. Such answers to it build bisystems of the same kind. The paper also introduces an O-operator on such a system, which produces answers to the allowed equation and thereby gives rise to new ones of the same kind. The new object covers several known structures, including Rota-Baxter Lie bisystems and averaging Lie bialgebras.
arxiv-2602-20731:
Aram Davtyan and six co-authors introduce COMiT, a message-inspired system for learning structured discrete visual codes. Discrete image token makers give a stepwise link for vision and multimodal models, but tend to encode local looks rather than object-level structure.

COMiT builds a fixed-length latent message through stepwise visual views. At each step, a single net reads a small image crop and edits, tunes, and sorts the existing token sequence. After several rounds, the message guides a flow-matching decoder that rebuilds the full image. The encoder and decoder live in one net, trained end to end with flow-matching rebuild and meaning-matching goals. COMiT clearly improves part-based carry-over and link-based thinking over older methods. Tests show meaning matching helps ground the code, while focused stepwise token making is key for clearer, object-centered token structures.
arxiv-2602-20831:
In the geometry of three-dimensional projective space, a codimension-one distribution can carry a tangent sheaf that refuses to split and fails stability tests. Pedro Barbassa studies exactly those cases in this 2026 arXiv paper. He links the degree of nonstability to the degree of a subfoliation by curves, and shows the nonstability order is bounded.

The paper then classifies the tangent sheaves of distributions that admit a subfoliation by curves of degree one. Under the assumption that the sheaf does not split, this classification covers the cases where nonstability reaches its maximum possible order. Readers get a sharp boundary for an unruly class of objects, plus a full list of the extreme cases.
arxiv-2602-21131: Systems with zero Lyapunov exponents show odd steady traits, and Francois Ledrappier surveys them in this 2026 arXiv paper. The survey covers the steady traits that arise in motion theory when exponents vanish. Readers get a guided tour of a corner of motion study where neutral paths shape long-term conduct, and of the steady traits those paths yield.
arxiv-2602-21231:
Orchestrating several models raises a practical question: when is an ensemble worth its cost, and can decisions be audited? Ramchand Kumaresan presents ACAR in this 2026 arXiv paper, a measurement framework routing tasks across one-, two-, and three-model execution by self-consistency variance from three probe samples. It runs on a deterministic substrate with immutable artifacts and complete decision traces.

Across one thousand five hundred ten tasks on four benchmarks, sigma-based routing reaches fifty-five point six percent accuracy. It beats a two-model baseline while skipping full ensembling on fifty-four point two percent of tasks. Negative results matter too: retrieval augmentation hurt accuracy, agreement-but-wrong caps achievable accuracy about eight percentage points below full ensembling, and proxy attribution correlates weakly with ground truth.
arxiv-2602-21331:
Broad modelers speed up robot building, but first-rules modelers need full-state watching or dial search. Nelson Chen, William Johnson, Rebecca Kramer-Bottiglio, Kostas Bekris, and Mridul Aanjaneya present a graph-neural-net other path in this 2026 arXiv paper for cable-driven robots: CableRobotGraphSim. Rigid bodies become graph nodes, cables and contacts become edges.

The model matches other modelers and real robots quickly and right from only in-part seen inputs. A sim-and-real co-training plan lifts carry-over and toughness to noisy real data. Hookup with a model-ahead path-sum steerer for closed-loop steering shows speed and hit rate. Cable-driven robots gain a modeler built for part-seen inputs from the start.
arxiv-2602-21531:
Yue Yang and six co-authors propose LiLo-VLA, a modular framework for compositional long-horizon robot manipulation. General-purpose robots must master tasks with multiple kinematic structure changes, like attaching or detaching objects, in unstructured settings. Vision-Language-Action models promise diverse atomic skills but struggle to sequence them and suffer cascading failures from environmental sensitivity.

LiLo-VLA decouples transport from interaction. A Reaching Module handles global motion, while an Interaction Module uses an object-centric VLA on isolated objects of interest, resisting irrelevant visual features and spatial rearrangements. Modularity enables robust failure recovery through dynamic replanning and skill reuse, mitigating cascading errors. On a 21-task simulation benchmark, it averages 69 percent success, beating rival systems by 41 and 67 percent. Real-world tests across 8 long-horizon tasks average 85 percent success.
arxiv-2602-21731:
O. Patsahan sets two accounts side by side of the electrical double layer capacitance and free-ion density in the restricted primitive model. One account, the mesoscopic theory, tracks charge density fluctuations. The other, the associative mean spherical approximation, treats free ions and ion pairs as in chemical equilibrium under the mass action law.

The two accounts agree fairly well at high density and when cold. The paper thus links the mesoscopic account with the associative mean spherical approximation, showing where their predictions line up in this model and where the fluctuation account still matters.
arxiv-2602-21831:
AI often aids fraud and crime, yet how far current models can aid crime work is unclear. Kimberly T. Mai and seven co-authors, with police and policy experts, built multi-turn tests for romance scams, CEO scams, and ID theft. Tests focus on text chats, asking whether models give help beyond usual web information, per domain experts, in ways like real misuse, such as splitting fraud requests into benign queries.

Findings show current models give minimal useful information for fraud and cybercrime without jailbreaks. Guards strongly affect sharing: two open-weight models with guardrails removed give the most useful answers. Splitting requests into benign queries won more help than hostile framing or basic jailbreaks. Overall, current text models give minimal uplift for fraud and crime without effort to dodge guards. The work gives a shared plan for tracking these risks as models grow more capable and foes adapt.
arxiv-2602-22031:
A physicist's collaborators change over a career, but how those shifting networks link to lasting success is rarely tracked in detail. Mingrong She and three co-authors follow tens of thousands of physicists across at least fifteen years, sorting their collaboration patterns with time-series clustering. They find ten distinct paths for how network size and clustering evolve between career years five and fifteen.

The most successful path starts loose and then tightens while growing: those physicists reach top investigator roles, publish more, and earn more citations. Different paths converge by year fifteen on moderate clustering, a balance between a tight core team and varied outside ties. Mobility also tracks with the successful patterns, and stays linked to strong scientific outcomes.
arxiv-2602-22331:
Operator growth links how quantum information spreads to how entanglement builds between parts of a system. Priesh Roy and Sumilan Banerjee define a state-free measure of that growth using part-system Rényi entropy, unlike entanglement entropies or out-of-time-order probes. Their measure encodes both spatial and time information, connecting directly to transport for conserved quantities.

The authors build a unified Schwinger-Keldysh field-theory framework for the time evolution of operator Rényi entropy and state entanglement measures. Applied to non-interacting systems, it expresses state entanglement entropy through vacuum Green's functions, and Rényi entropy through infinite-temperature ones. The framework gives theory workers one field-theory language for growth and entanglement together.
arxiv-2602-22631:
Robert Joseph George and five co-authors close the gap between neural networks as run and networks as checked. Checks usually happen outside the setting that defines and runs the model. Claims can then hinge on hidden rules about ops, layouts, preprocessing, floating-point behaviour, and fast kernels.

TorchLean, built in Lean 4, treats learned models as both runnable programs and math objects with shared meaning. It offers a PyTorch-style front end for tensors, layers, goals, optimizers, differentiation, and graph programs, with eager and compiled paths mapped to one graph form. Exact and finite-precision meaning, checked differentiation, bound propagation, certificate checks, and CUDA-backed runs all live inside one theorem-proving setting for checked machine learning.
arxiv-2602-22731:
Miguel Ángel Muñoz-Bañón and six co-authors map forest saplings in true scale and place. Saplings signal regeneration and forest health. Yet their thin branches and dense leaves defeat laser scanners, mobile scanners, and classic photogrammetry. Those tools also lack scale consistency for long-term tracking.

Sapling-NeRF fuses neural radiance fields with LiDAR SLAM and GNSS into a three-level pipeline. Coarse Earth-frame position comes from satellites, centimetre-accurate mapping from LiDAR, and dense object-centred reconstruction from NeRF. Trials in Wytham Woods in Oxford and Evo in Finland captured stem height, branching, and leaf-to-wood ratios. Saplings between half a metre and two metres tall were measured more accurately than laser scanners manage, giving ecologists richer data.
arxiv-2602-22831:
Phil Blandfort and five co-authors audit moral choices in language models by flipping the influence direction. Moral benchmarks usually score context-free prompts, treating choice rates as stable. For each scenario, the team compares a baseline prompt against matched cues steering toward option A or option B.

Short cues shifted per-condition choice rates by twelve to eighteen percentage points on average across trolley-style triage, BBQ, and DailyDilemmas tasks and five model families, with or without reasoning. About forty percent of baseline-neutral triage and BBQ conditions showed directional asymmetry, and a meaningful share of significant effects backfired against the cue. In follow-ups, models often spotted the cue while denying its influence, an inconsistency present in seventy-eight percent of significant backfire trials. Reasoning reshaped rather than removed sensitivity.
arxiv-2602-23031:
Zhangjian Ji and four co-authors improve small-object detection in aerial images. Tiny, densely and unevenly spread objects over high-resolution images make detection inefficient. The team builds on ResNet-50 with a Spatial Laplacian Pyramid Attention module after each stage to identify and emphasize important local regions.

A Multi-Scale Feature Enhancement Module in the lateral connections of the C5 layer builds the Feature Pyramid Network for richer semantic understanding. Deformable convolutions align features when upper and lower pyramid levels fuse. Tests on VisDrone and DOTA show the improved model beats the original algorithm for small objects in aerial images.
arxiv-2602-23231:
Daniel Bermuth and two co-authors argue that skeleton-based action recognition is, at heart, a multi-view problem. Human action recognition matters for building natural interaction between people and machines. Research has focused on improving recognition algorithms, while the quality of the input skeleton data itself has received little attention.

The team shows that triangulating more accurate 3D skeletons from several camera views significantly improves state-of-the-art recognition models. That result suggests input quality, not algorithm design, currently limits performance. Since the cost-benefit balance of extra cameras looks very favorable in most practical cases, the authors argue future work should treat multi-view setups as the standard, not the exception.
arxiv-2602-23531:
Amit Singh Ubhi and 13 co-authors push ground-based gravitational-wave reach toward 5 Hz. Below 20 Hz, ground motion and motion-sensor noise have long limited earthbound devices. The team shows vacuum-safe motion shielding and place sensing with active platform control down to 10 mHz.

Their laser sensors reach sub-picometer per root Hertz reach above 10 mHz. That is a 100-fold gain over current LIGO sensors, no matter the input light polarization. Their motion sensors lift low-frequency reach at least five times over store-bought quake meters. In a LIGO-like model, reach grows up to tenfold at 10 Hz, with better linear response and calibration that holds steady. This triples the spotting horizon for middle-mass black hole pairs of a thousand solar masses.
arxiv-2602-23631:
Tao Gong studies invariants of Weyl group representations linked to the cohomology of toric varieties. For a Weyl group W and a W-permutohedron P, toric varieties X_P and X_{P/W_K} arise for any parabolic subgroup W_K of W. The quotient P/W_K can be identified with a polytope inside P.

Gong constructs an explicit algebra isomorphism. It links the cohomology of X_{P/W_K} with the W_K-invariant part of the cohomology of X_P, with rational coefficients. The isomorphism is further generalized to intermediate lattices, to finite Coxeter groups, and to non-degenerate W-symmetric polytopes. The results affirmatively answer two open questions posed by Horiguchi, Masuda, Shareshain, and Song.
arxiv-2602-23831:
Binzhou Zuo and two co-authors present a deep learning method for tuning pixel antennas, antennas whose radiation pattern can be reshaped by switching pixel connections. The 2026 paper uses a heterogeneous multi-head selection scheme: several networks, each trained on a different coding scheme, compete, and the best performer is chosen.

Unlike heuristic search methods that pay high compute for good results, the data-driven approach reaches nearly the same performance at far lower cost. In single-input single-output tests it runs far faster than search baselines, and the speed advantage grows larger for multi-input multi-output systems. The authors argue that pixel antennas, paired with fast learned tuning, are a practical route to more flexible and efficient wireless systems.
arxiv-2602-23931:
Gagandeep Singh and thirteen co-authors demonstrate orbitally resolved single-photon emission from an individual atomic vacancy in a layered semiconductor. The 2026 paper tackles a hard limit of ordinary optics. Diffraction blocks the study of single spins at atomic scales. Atomically confined spins are prized for quantum bits and sensors.

The team excites vacancy centers by injecting energetic charge carriers from the atomically sharp tip of a scanning tunneling microscope. With spatial resolution below a nanometer, the emitted light mirrors the orbital symmetry of the vacancy's bound-state wave function, and photon correlation measurements show clear anti-bunching, confirming single photons. The result is a step toward an electrically driven single-atom light source and a solid-state spin-photon interface addressed atom by atom.
arxiv-2602-24031:
Francisco Araújo generalizes Sarnak's program to Erdős sieves, sets formed by removing congruence classes modulo an infinite set of ideals in an étale algebra over the rationals. The 2026 solo paper, part one of a two-part work, defines light tail conditions on a sieve and relates them to genericity under the Mirsky measure.

The central objects are R-free numbers, algebraic integers that avoid every removed congruence class. The author shows how light tails govern whether those numbers are typical under the Mirsky measure, a natural distribution on sieve-related sets. He further shows that Erdős B-free systems in any such algebra satisfy the light tail conditions. The program thus extends to those systems in full generality. It carries Sarnak's dynamical perspective into a wider number-theoretic setting.
arxiv-2602-24131:
Sky Qiu and four co-authors develop efficient targeted maximum likelihood estimators for two-phase design problems. The 2026 paper considers designs where a random sample is drawn in phase one with only a subset of variables collected. A subsample is measured more fully in phase two. That split creates a coarsened data structure for the second-phase data.

Assuming coarsening at random, meaning phase-two selection depends only on fully observed variables, the authors review existing estimators. The estimators include generalized raking and inverse-probability-weighted targeted maximum likelihood. Extensions also target the phase-two sampling mechanism for efficiency. They then introduce a new class of estimators that are asymptotically equivalent to existing efficient approaches while offering gains. In short, the new tools waste less data. Less waste means sharper answers from the same study. That edge matters when full tests cost a lot. That edge helps real studies.
arxiv-2603-00031: Wang and colleagues introduce GRIP, a data-curation framework that treats a training corpus as an information-dense geometric space to improve data efficiency. A rapid adaptation probe scores the information potential of semantic clusters. It shifts sampling budget toward underrepresented regions. Intra-cluster selection then uses a length-rectified geometric prior to preserve long-tail logical sequences. On mixture-of-experts models trained on up to hundreds of billions of tokens, GRIP beats strong baselines and even models trained on three times more uncurated data.
arxiv-2603-00331: Mynampaty and colleagues explore how linting, automated flaw-checking, can improve software READMEs, whose ideal contents vary by audience. Through a design probe called LintMe, users build context-specific checks with a lightweight language combining code operations with language-model judgments. Checks can catch broken links or spot jargon. A user study with 11 participants and a comparison with naive language-model use find the design approachable, flexible, and well matched to the domain. The work opens the door to linting more complex documentation and other text documents.
arxiv-2603-00631: Li and Tao present LiTS, a modular Python framework for language model reasoning by tree search. Search splits into three reusable parts, Policy, Transition, and RewardModel, that plug into algorithms such as Monte Carlo tree search and breadth first search. A decorator registry lets domain experts add new domains and researchers add new algorithms without rewriting the core. Tests on maths reasoning, crosswords, and tool use show parts and algorithms stay orthogonal, and a mode collapse finding pins policy diversity, not reward quality, as the bottleneck in infinite action spaces.
arxiv-2603-00831: Nieding and eight colleagues review recent work on the advection-diffusion-reaction wildfire model, which trades true-to-life detail for compute cost. They check how well the model gauges fire front speed and spread, look at its early math traits, and discuss changes that raise realism. They also tackle cutting compute costs with cheap yet precise number schemes, and report open gaps in model grids and tech. The review presents ADR models as strong tools for fast wildfire simulation and risk work.
arxiv-2603-00931: Islam and nine colleagues estimate waste weight from photos plus physics data. Look-alike objects differ in density, and apparent size shifts with camera distance. Their Multimodal Weight Predictor fuses image features with object size, camera distance, and height. It trains on over ten thousand synchronized records across eleven waste types. It lands within about 88 kilograms on average, stays strong for light loads, and explains each prediction in plain words via a language model.
arxiv-2603-01031: Pusty and three colleagues compare two future long-baseline neutrino tests, P2SO and DUNE, on sensitivity to non-unitarity of the lepton mixing matrix. Heavy neutral leptons beyond the Standard Model could cause such effects. DUNE bounds two mixing parameters more tightly. P2SO, with its longer baseline and stronger matter effects, does better on two others. Each test improves current bounds somewhere. Their sensitivities also intertwine with mass hierarchy, octant, and CP-violation measures, making the pair complementary.
arxiv-2603-01231: Brandolin and Alkhalifah offer one plan for building and editing seismic velocity models, the speed maps used to image rock layers. A diffusion model trained on high-res synthetic samples supplies a prior, used through DDIM inversion and guided sampling. Local edits pair that prior with a Tikhonov well-matching fit that changes chosen regions while keeping overall fit. Full model building adds imaging-based smoothing. It is solved by least-squares, the DDIM-guided method, and DPS, with diffusion methods finding sharper, truer shapes in fake tests.
arxiv-2603-01331: Xia and seven colleagues offer MetaState, a lightweight looping add-on giving frozen discrete spread language models lasting, fixed-size working memory. Standard models condition each cleaning step only on the current hard-masked sequence, dropping middle smooth traces after sampling and re-covering. This is an Information Island choke point trapping information within single steps. MetaState's three modules share a time keeper: a cross-focus Mixer reading backbone signals into memory slots, a GRU-style Updater blending information across steps, and a cross-focus Injector writing updated memory back.
arxiv-2603-01931:
Megan Harris, John Little, and Amro Farid model watershed systems as linked networks of natural and human parts. Their 2026 work spans hydrology, land-use choices, estuary ecology, and overlapping governance areas. Regional tools give good nutrient estimates, yet their opaque routing blocks wider systems analysis.

The team first builds a region-independent reference architecture for any watershed system. They then adapt a hetero-functional graph state estimator with weighted least squares to infer nutrient flows. The estimator extends a graph theory built for systems whose parts do unlike jobs. A shared ontology in a standard systems language ties the natural and institutional pieces together. The Chesapeake Bay watershed serves as the case study, using its known assessment tool for nutrient estimates.
arxiv-2603-02031:
Atreya Vedantam and Radha Krishna Ganti characterize blind recovery of a code rate from a received signal. Their 2026 work sits in noncooperative decoding, where the receiver does not know the error-correcting code settings. Forward error correction guards nearly every modern communication link against noise.

They present a metric for the quality of rate recovery that works with any rank-based estimation method. A closed-form expression ties that metric to algorithm settings and channel conditions at once. Low metric values signal good recovery, giving designers a target to aim for. In high noise, the metric yields a better rate estimate than existing formulas. Simulations with a low-density parity-check code validate the metric and the gain, and they pin down optimal algorithm parameters.
arxiv-2603-02431:
Fanjun Xu derives a direct measure of quantum fluctuations in clean magnets in this 2026 paper. Quantum effects shrink the ordered moment of a magnet below its full value. Measuring that shrinkage usually needs indirect modeling of scattering data. Xu starts from a sum rule that fixes the total magnetic moment in neutron scattering.

He links moment reduction to the long-time limit of a scattering function. Neutron spin-echo spectroscopy can read that limit directly in an experiment. The long-time value equals the ratio of ordered to total moment, squared over plain. Spin-wave calculations for two lattice types confirm the link. Both quantum effects and geometric frustration lower the plateau as predicted. The method works on powder samples, widening its reach for bulk magnets.
arxiv-2603-02531:
Kwanyoung Kim links diffusion guidance to a classic acceleration trick in this 2026 paper. Guidance improves diffusion image quality by pushing apart two model outputs. It costs extra passes at run time and fails for distilled, single-step models. Attention-space methods are cheaper, but their theory was murky.

Kim models attention dynamics as fixed-point steps inside modern Hopfield networks. Attention extrapolation then becomes a special case of Anderson acceleration on those dynamics. A weak contraction property of the dynamics supports that reading. His method splits attention updates into parts along and across the guidance direction. That split stabilizes the speedup and squeezes the most from guidance. The plug-and-play method fits existing frameworks and improves generation quality a lot.
arxiv-2603-02931:
Cristian Di Pietrantonio, Marcin Sokolowski, Christopher Harris, and colleagues fix a bottleneck in hunting flashes from deep space. Radio signals smear across frequencies as they cross ionized gas, and undoing that smear, called dedispersion, is vital for spotting pulsars and fast radio bursts. Image-based searches made the standard cleanup far too memory-hungry.

Their algorithm, STRIDE, builds dedispersed time series pixel by pixel straight from telescope images, without costly data reshuffling. It is the first to split the smear correction across time as well as frequency, so only a slice of images must sit in memory at once. In their test case, memory needs fell by nearly ninety-eight percent. The authors argue STRIDE is the practical route for low-frequency sky surveys.
arxiv-2603-03331:
Hung Manh Pham and eight colleagues introduce PulseLM, a dataset linking pulse signals to language. The signals come from photoplethysmography, the light-based sensing used in clinic monitors and smartwatches to track the heart and body. Older datasets label such signals with numbers or task tags, which limits training models to reason about health in words.

PulseLM gathers recordings from fifteen public sources and restates their varied labels as twelve shared question-answering tasks about physiology. It holds more than a million standardized ten-second signal segments and over three million question-answer pairs. The team also fixes shared rules for cleaning, supervision, and scoring, then benchmarks multimodal language models on the data. Everything is public, giving the field one standard foundation for pulse-based language research.
arxiv-2603-03531:
Yiming Sun and eight others predict ecosystem carbon fluxes by giving every input a role. Land ecosystems trade carbon dioxide and methane with the air, and forecasting those fluxes is central to carbon accounting. Flux responses are ruled by slow regime settings, yet wiggled by fast daily drivers. Most learning models dump all inputs into one undifferentiated pile, assuming one global response, and generalize badly.

Their 2026 approach, Role-Aware Conditional Inference, separates the roles explicitly. Hierarchical time encoding disentangles slow conditioners from fast drivers. Spatial retrieval then supplies context that is both nearby and functionally similar, matched per role. Tested across wetlands and farm systems, three carbon fluxes, and both simulated and observed data, the method beat strong baselines everywhere. Accuracy and spatial generalization both improved under strong environmental diversity.
arxiv-2603-03631:
Vernon Barger finds the pattern of particle masses written in ninths, and traces it to a gauge symmetry that also creates the axion. Quark and lepton mass hierarchies follow rational powers of one small parameter, counted in units of one ninth. His 2026 paper argues this flavor-in-ninths structure points to a discrete eighteen-fold gauge symmetry behind the Froggatt-Nielsen mechanism, with a nine-fold subgroup running the flavor pattern.

Identifying the flavon field with the Peccei-Quinn field makes the same symmetry do double duty. It stabilizes the QCD axion, forces the safe domain-wall number, and predicts the axion's coupling to photons. Harmful Planck-suppressed corrections are pushed to very high dimension, solving the axion quality problem naturally. For a decay constant in the favored range, the axion accounts for dark matter and sits within reach of near-term haloscope searches.
arxiv-2603-03931:
Rafal Bartoszewicz and others report how pressure and temperature reshape light emission from a two-dimensional tin halide perovskite. These layered materials are tunable platforms for exciton-phonon coupling because their lattice is intrinsically soft. The team studied photoluminescence of the bromide compound across temperatures and under hydrostatic pressure, comparing it with its iodide analogue.

At room temperature the emission is dominated by near-band-edge excitons, which shift steadily to lower energy under pressure up to about three gigapascals, with no sign of a phase transition. Cooling reveals a broad, strongly shifted self-trapped exciton emission, showing a crossover from delocalized to self-localized states. Unusually, that trapped emission shifts to higher energy under pressure, while the iodide analogue shows no trapped emission at all, pointing to lattice rigidity and screening as the deciding factors.
arxiv-2603-04031: Hayat and Loko study rapid stabilization of general linear systems with F-equivalence. They consider systems whose differential operator has a Riesz basis of eigenvectors, finding simple sufficient terms for rapid stabilization and a relatively stated feedback operator. Using an F-equivalence method relying on Fredholm transformation, they show a stronger result: under these terms the system equals a plain exponentially stable system with any desired decay rate. Their terms improve current rapid stabilization terms for non-parabolic operators like skew-adjoint ones.
arxiv-2603-04131: Hao and colleagues evaluate a coupled method for droplet impact on soft materials. Droplet impacts erode aircraft surfaces and turbine blades. A coupled model exists in the literature, but its pressure solution assumed a rigid surface. The study tests the model on urethane gel phantoms against experiments and particle hydrodynamics simulations. Parametric studies explore the limit for soft materials. For materials at 47,400 Pa or stiffer, the model performs as expected. Softer materials show mitigated intensity, and below 10,000 Pa the model overshoots force and deformation, forming steep wall craters.
arxiv-2603-04331: Maeve Wildes models tumor growth with cell age and pressure driven spread. Cells multiply where pressure allows and move away from high pressure zones. Her main result shows age structured solutions converge to a Hele-Shaw free boundary limit. That limit moves the tumor edge under a nonlinear Darcy law for tissue flow. A detailed age aware model thus yields a clean geometric picture of spread.
arxiv-2603-04431: Valencia and colleagues forecast fields from sparse sensors with SOLID. Fields appear only at scattered, shifting sites, so prediction is ill posed and uncertain. SOLID learns from observed sites alone, with no dense fields and no pre-imputation. Denoising steps use measured values and locations, stressing void regions and anchoring on overlap pixels, and sampling yields full fields with far better error and calibrated uncertainty.
arxiv-2603-04831: Sridhar and colleagues tackle missingness bias in feature attribution explanations with MCal. Explanation methods often give unreliable importance scores when models face ablated inputs. Existing fixes treat this as a deep flaw needing expensive retraining or architectural changes. The paper challenges this view, treating missingness bias as a superficial artifact of the output space. MCal, a lightweight post-hoc method, fine-tunes a linear head on outputs of a frozen base model. This simple correction reduces bias and rivals or beats heavyweight approaches across medical vision, language, and tabular benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-05231: Linghan Fang and team present ASR-TRA, a test-time reinforcement change method for robust speech spotting on noisy unseen data and accents. Current change leans on pseudo-labeling or entropy minimization, treating confidence as a signal that can reinforce high-confidence errors into confirmation bias. ASR-TRA instead uses a learnable decoder prompt and stochastic decoding for diverse candidates. A reward model scores audio-text semantic alignment, and feedback updates model and prompt. LibriSpeech tests with synthetic noise and accented English show higher accuracy and lower latency than baselines.
arxiv-2603-05531: Ozan and team present a fast reduced order model approach for tuning spatiotemporally chaotic systems, joining quantized local reduced order models with adjoint-based optimization. They apply it to variational data assimilation for the chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation. It rebuilds the full path for up to a quarter of a Lyapunov time from final-time full state readings. The method runs 3.5 times faster than the full-order model, opening new uses for reduced order models of spatiotemporally chaotic systems.
arxiv-2603-05831: Liu and colleagues propose a knowledge-driven reasoning framework for mobile agentic AI on constrained platforms like edge robots and aerial vehicles. From past execution, the framework builds reusable decision structures, shares them over limited links, and applies them in on-device reasoning. Knowledge exposure proves non-monotonic: too little forces costly replanning, too much adds conflicting cues. A UAV case study shows a knowledge pack letting a 3B-parameter onboard model reach perfect mission reliability more cheaply than knowledge-free or cloud-centric approaches.
arxiv-2603-06031: Zhou shows that symp field theory functor under cobords gives finite algebra planar twists from simple cases, giving a one treatment of most known math. Also, many new case groups are found, notably stably filled cases in sizes at least 5 with twist just k for any plus natural k, backing a Latschev-Wendl guess. Sphere contact structures with finite twist at least 1 imply tight not weakly filled structures are common. The author also explains that all known contact shapes without fillings in size at least 5 have twist.
arxiv-2603-06331: Feng and colleagues propose WorldCache, a training free cache for diffusion world models. Single modal caching policies transfer poorly to world models because of token heterogeneity from multi modal coupling. Non-uniform temporal dynamics add an obstacle, with a few hard tokens driving error growth. WorldCache uses curvature guided token prediction with a physics grounded curvature score and a Hermite guided predictor for chaotic tokens. Chaotic prioritized adaptive skipping recomputes only when bottleneck tokens drift. Experiments show up to 3.7 times speedups while maintaining 98 percent rollout quality.
arxiv-2603-06431: Gründler and his team develop a certified method for norms of neural networks, needed for error control in PDE solving. Trained ones can be probed only at few points, and point values alone cannot yield sure bounds without strong assumptions. Beyond a black-box view, they exploit network structure, combining interval covers on axis-aligned boxes with adaptive tuning and sum aggregation. Box bounds on values and derivatives grow into global integral bounds, with closing theory for values, Jacobians, and Hessians proving Lebesgue and Sobolev norms.
arxiv-2603-06531: Behari and Raskar present a calibration procedure for diffuse time-of-flight LiDARs. Their per-pixel depth histograms aggregate photon returns over a wide field of view, breaking the single-ray assumption behind LiDAR-RGB calibration. For each diffuse LiDAR pixel, the procedure estimates its footprint and spatial sensitivity in an RGB image plane. A scanned retroreflective patch used after background subtraction recovers response maps. Those maps give an explicit correspondence between LiDAR and RGB for cross-modal alignment and fusion, demonstrated on the ams OSRAM TMF8828.
arxiv-2603-06931: Janota and Olšák present a case study where an LLM coding agent builds a complete SMT solver with zero human-written code. People debate whether LLMs can reason or code, but whether they can build software that itself reasons is largely unexplored. Their solver follows the DPLL(T) style for QF_UF, implements Nieuwenhuis-Oliveras congruence closure, includes preprocessing, and emits Lean proofs when instances are unsatisfiable. They describe the build process and key challenges, and show the solver competes on SMT-LIB benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-07831: Chen, Ding and Ye develop a transfer learning framework for limited data in image rebuilds, built in two bi-level tuning steps. First, a shared feature-learner learns knowledge from large datasets across domains. Second, a domain-adapter trains for a new domain or task with limited data. The adapter plus shared feature-learner finds features for smoothing, yielding high-quality rebuilds despite data limits. Applied to under-sampled MR images with limited data, using diverse samples from other body parts and types, tests show strong transfer power.
arxiv-2603-07931: Xiang and colleagues present BRIDGE, a benchmark for multi-hop reasoning over long multimodal documents with grounded evidence. Most benchmarks score only the final answer and ignore the reasoning steps in between, especially when evidence comes from text, tables, and figures. BRIDGE covers long scientific papers, supports chain-like and fan-out reasoning structures, and supplies multi-hop annotations so each step can be scored. Experiments with leading models and multimodal retrieval systems expose weaknesses in evidence aggregation and grounding that answer-only scoring hides.
arxiv-2603-08031: Li and colleagues take a census of red supergiants across the Local Group, stars that matter for how massive stars evolve. Finding them in distant metal-poor galaxies is hard, since foreground dwarfs contaminate the samples and observations are limited. Working with public JWST NIRCam images of five galaxies, NGC 6822, Sextans A, NGC 300, WLM, and IC 1613, they run PSF photometry with the DOLPHOT NIRCam module. They settle on a color-color diagram suited to metal-poor settings, giving a cleaner way to pick out genuine red supergiants.
arxiv-2603-08131: Zhang and colleagues present UniGround, a training-free approach to 3D visual grounding, the task of locating objects from natural-language descriptions in 3D scenes. Foundation models promise open-vocabulary reasoning but usually depend on pre-generated candidates, creating two bottlenecks. The first arises when dataset-specific proposal models miss, fragment, or misgroup targets under distribution shift. The second comes from incomplete visual detail, since global renderings preserve spatial context yet hide fine features. UniGround parses scenes without training to clear both hurdles.
arxiv-2603-08231: Pol and colleagues measure cross-lingual transfer in paralinguistic speech tasks, often seen as language-free since they rely on non-word acoustic cues rather than word content. Yet prior studies report falling scores under cross-lingual conditions, showing real language dependence. Those studies usually focus on single language pairs or task-specific settings, limiting comparison and blocking orderly assessment of task-level language dependence. The authors introduce the Cross-Lingual Transfer Matrix, a method to measure transfer across languages and tasks.
arxiv-2603-08531: Yi-Shiuan Tung and colleagues teach robots to learn human tastes by inventing fresh test scenes. Old preference learning reuses fixed clips or past runs, which starves it of varied, telling comparisons. Their CRED method designs new settings and poses what-if reward pairs, beating rival methods on reward accuracy and sample thrift in tests and a user study.
arxiv-2603-08631: Hiromichi Nishimura and colleagues build a perturbation theory for electron structure that leans on extra symmetry. The reference system keeps more symmetry than the real one, trimming both the configurations to track and the qubits a quantum run needs. They give workable, scalable second-order corrections, show the method extends older multi-reference theories, and show better results on some molecules.
arxiv-2603-08731: Hasi Hays unites two brain-like learning ideas in one two-timescale framework. Sparse geometric nets give Hebbian-driven shape, while oscillator attention swaps dot products for phase locking. A global order signal gates structural updates, so links firm up only when phase coherence marks a real pattern, and the joint system provably settles to a stable rest state.
arxiv-2603-09331: Heng Zhang and colleagues introduce Reward-Zero, a reward mechanism that turns natural-language task descriptions into dense progress signals for reinforcement learning. It compares the embedding of the task text with embeddings from the agent's own interaction history, yielding a continuous sense-of-completion score. The signal supplements sparse environmental feedback with no task-specific engineering. Agents trained with it converge faster and reach higher success than PPO with common shaping baselines, even solving some tasks hand-made rewards could not.
arxiv-2603-09431: Joe Pratt-Johns and colleagues take first steps toward a category-theory form of algebraic artificial chemistry. They build a functor that endows an algebraic model of interacting parts with dynamics. The work extends Fontana and Buss's AlChemy, where lambda terms play the role of molecules and their reduction plays chemical reaction. Later directions use category theory to order such models and link their algebraic and dynamic sides.
arxiv-2603-09531: Shahab Aslani and colleagues test whether worsening PPFE, a fibrotic lung change found on scans, predicts death among people in lung cancer screening. PPFE is short for pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis, a scarring pattern in the upper lobes. An automated tool measured its volume on first and follow-up low-dose CT scans in two large screening studies. People whose PPFE grew past a set threshold died at higher rates, even after demographic and clinical factors were factored in.
arxiv-2603-09631: Dmitry S. Golubev and colleagues map a molecular Hamiltonian to a system-bath model of qubits for quantum chemistry. The system is a tiny active space of two orbitals, HOMO and LUMO, holding two electrons and encoded by two qubits. All other orbital excitations form the bath, modeled as oscillators in the spirit of the Random Phase Approximation. The mapping aims at high-accuracy vertical excitation energies for some molecules.
arxiv-2603-09931: Rong Zhou and coauthors build ACADiff to fill in missing brain scan types for Alzheimer's disease work. Clinical data sets often lack one or more imaging modes, since each scan is costly. ACADiff denoises latent features through diffusion, guided by the scans at hand and by clinical notes encoded as prompts. Three generators translate among structural MRI and two PET types, holding up even when most modes are missing.
arxiv-2603-10231: Shuaiyu Chen and coauthors adapt the SAM2 segmentation model to find oil spills in radar imagery across unordered scenes. Spill appearance varies wildly and real monitoring lacks the temporal continuity that memory based models assume, causing semantic drift. OilSAM2 keeps a hierarchical memory bank spanning texture, structure and semantic features, so information transfers between separate images. A consistency based update rule refreshes that memory selectively, holding state of the art accuracy on two public data sets.
arxiv-2603-10431: Pranav Perumalsamy and co-authors ask whether quantum coherence can serve as a thermometer, by watching how it fades in three-part systems at finite temperature. They use a tripartite spin-boson model under local and common dephasing environments, tracking pure and mixed states with relative entropy of coherence. Local dephasing always melts coherence faster as temperature rises. Common dephasing depends on the state: some states lose all coherence, one keeps a steady amount, and another keeps a finite residue. They turn this link into proof-of-principle thermometry tables.
arxiv-2603-10531: Katerina Nik and Christoph Walker analyze a model of bacterial biofilm in a stirred tank reactor where film also grows on the walls. Substrate spreads through a one-dimensional biofilm under a free boundary, while equations track film thickness, suspended biomass, and free substrate levels. They prove global well-posedness and study long-term behavior. The washout state, where bacteria are flushed away, gets a full local and global stability picture. A nontrivial steady state exists, and under extra structural assumptions it is unique, with conditions for its local stability.
arxiv-2603-10831: Mirza Karamehmedović and co-authors reinterpret photonic nanojets as emergent free-space funnels of power flux, using a reduced local field model built from full-wave simulations. Older accounts based on geometric optics miss that the jet is held up by an effective transverse mode structure of free space. The model tracks how phase gradients and the effective axial wavenumber shift near the jet waist, and captures the jet's shape well. It also gives a lower bound on the waist that does not depend on geometry.
arxiv-2603-11031: Sophia Liu and Shm Garanganao Almeda argue that creativity research has put too much weight on making. It has slighted the reading that comes first and shapes the work. Here reading spans navigating, interpreting, and curating media. Their proposal, Reading Activity Traces, records paths of traversal, association, and reflection as inspectable artifacts. This makes creative labor visible, labor that feeds and AI summaries now squeeze away. A speculative Wikipedia version shows the idea. It points to tools that keep human interpretation in view and do not automate it offstage.
arxiv-2603-11131: Radhakrishnan Delhibabu designs a quantum convolutional neural network that dodges the barren plateau problem, the exponential fading of gradients that stalls training in quantum machine learning. Localized cost functions and a hardware-efficient tensor-network initialization provably blunt the plateau. The network reaches 98.7 percent accuracy on MNIST, far above plain models. It also shows a parameter-efficiency edge: it needs logarithmically fewer trainable parameters than other networks of like size to pass ninety-five percent.
arxiv-2603-11231: A. S. Joglekar and coauthors argue that differentiable programming turns gradient-based optimization in plasma physics into an engine for discovery and multiscale modeling. It was a design tool before. Four cases make the case. Optimizing kinetic simulations uncovers a new superadditive wavepacket interaction regime. Learned hidden variables let fluid models match kinetic effects at large Knudsen number. The approach also speeds up Thomson scattering analysis a lot. It extracts rich velocity distributions while doing so. It inverse-designs laser pulses whose full space-time coupling far beats partial optimization.
arxiv-2603-11331: Indranil Halder, Annesya Banerjee, and Cengiz Pehlevan chart how jailbreaks against safety-aligned models scale with try count. They find prompt injection changes the law. Without injection, attacks grow polynomially with inference-time samples. Injected prompts can push it to exponential growth. A spin-glass model of proxy language explains both through a magnetic-field analogy. Short injections act as a weak field toward unsafe clusters and give power-law growth. Long injections act strong and give exponential growth, across models and methods.
arxiv-2603-11431: Flight and Gosselin build a theory of how loads spread inside rigid bodies held by over-actuated robots. Such systems run several closed-loop chains at once, so many force patterns can match one total wrench. The theory pins down every workable wrench distribution for a given load. It also gives direct solutions for wrench synthesis and wrench analysis. Both scale in a straight line with the wrench count, with no large matrix work. They also show flaws in current methods and offer fixes.
arxiv-2603-11531: Du and co-authors present Mobile-GS, a Gaussian Splatting method tuned for real-time rendering on mobile devices. Splatting gives high-quality scenes, yet its compute and storage demands strain phones. The main bottleneck is alpha blending, which leans on slow Gaussian depth sorting. Mobile-GS drops sorting for a depth-aware, order-independent rendering scheme. A neural step then sharpens view-dependent effects, which the sorting-free scheme can blur where geometry overlaps. Extra tools shrink the model: pruning, vector quantization, and spherical harmonics distillation.
arxiv-2603-11631: Lee and co-authors present VisDoT, a framework that grounds visual reasoning in how humans read charts. Large vision-language models often fail to spot basic chart marks and tie them to meaning. VisDoT formalizes four perceptual tasks from graphical perception theory, covering traits like position and length. Its Decomposition-of-Thought prompting then splits each question into visual perception steps and logic steps. Fine-tuning InternVL this way lifts ChartQA scores and beats GPT-4o on ChartQAPro. On the new VisDoTQA benchmark, the gain reaches 33.2 percent.
arxiv-2603-11831: Li and co-authors present FutureCAD, a text-to-CAD framework driven by large language models. Modern CAD mixes parametric steps with boundary representation geometry, and fillets or chamfers need exact picks of B-Rep faces and edges. FutureCAD writes runnable CadQuery scripts, while a grounding transformer, BRepGround, maps plain-language picks to the target shapes. Training mixes supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning on a new set of real-world CAD models. The system tops prior methods on CAD generation tests, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-12031: Hamzeh presents Agentic-Kube, a multi-agent learning framework for placing pods in Kubernetes clusters. One shared reward can blur clashing goals, so three sub-agents split the job. They handle cost, anti-affinity fault tolerance, and balanced resource use as distinct aims. A graph network tracks host and pod links, while voting plus feasibility checks settle each placement. Tests on live Google Kubernetes Engine clusters and large simulated clusters reached Pareto-efficient placements and sharp cuts in service collisions.
arxiv-2603-12131: Tran gives a rigorous path to double-hybrid density functional theory that stays self-consistent. Standard double-hybrids treat MP2 correlation without that consistency, which clashes with their own energy formula. The fix builds a model from semilocal terms, exact exchange, and one-body MP2 parts. That one-body form lets the correlation term sit inside the Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian directly. No optimized potential step is needed. Taking the energy derivative then yields the field equations in a clean derivation.
arxiv-2603-12231: Wang and co-authors straighten latent paths over time to make world model planning work better. Pretrained visual encoders give strong features, but they are not shaped for planning tasks. A curvature regularizer nudges latent trajectories toward local straight lines during training. Encoder and predictor of a JEPA world model learn together under that rule. Straight paths make Euclidean distance a better stand-in for true geodesic distance. Gradient-based planning then runs more stably and hits goal tasks at far higher rates.
arxiv-2603-12331: Jarequi, Mitra, and Vaidya compute dynamical tidal love numbers for compact stars with an EFT approach. A point particle effective theory frames the star while scattering data come from black hole perturbation theory. The Mano-Suzuki-Takasugi method handles stars with nonzero surface reflectivity in that match. Order-by-order matching in a low-frequency expansion extracts static and dynamical love numbers. Results reach next-to-next-to leading order for neutron stars, pure and mixed with dark matter.
arxiv-2603-12531: O'Keeffe studies a one-dimensional swarmalator model with inertia, a regime past work largely skipped. Earlier studies focused almost fully on the overdamped limit. Inertia creates a new unsteady collective state whose rainbow order parameters oscillate at many harmonics. This thrashing phase wave branches from the static phase wave through a subcritical Hopf bifurcation. The wave comes in clockwise and counterclockwise mirror pairs. Small populations switch between these chiral states, while larger systems settle onto a single branch.
arxiv-2603-12631: Wenyu Mao and co-authors jointly optimize the agents inside a language model memory system. Such systems build and fetch memories with several agents, often tuned one by one. That habit ignores how agents affect each other and blurs credit from sparse global rewards. Their CoMAM frames the pipeline as a Markov decision process for end-to-end training. Agents learn from local rewards plus a weighted global reward. Tests showed steady gains over leading memory systems.
arxiv-2603-12731: Yuntian Li and co-authors measure slow spin-lattice relaxation in YbVO4 with a new combined method. Alternating fields drive both magnetization and temperature swings in a sample. The temperature effect is often ignored, which can blur the true source of a response. The team built an AC magnetocaloric setup that runs alongside AC susceptibility. At 3 K, they tracked both signals across field and frequency. A thermal model then yielded the intrinsic relaxation rate.
arxiv-2603-12831: Zizhao Mo and co-authors serve mixed language model loads in shared clusters without breaking latency promises. Latency-sensitive services have strict limits, while best-effort services get squeezed by memory and interference. Reserving headroom is a blunt fix that hurts both sides. Their OmniServe offloads attention work from best-effort jobs to CPUs on the fly. Async links keep GPUs from stalling while results return. Tests showed far better SLO attainment and best-effort throughput than prior systems.
arxiv-2603-13231: Krish Tadigotla reviews GT-BEHRT, a graph transformer for longitudinal health records, with a critical eye. Most EHR models treat each visit as an unordered bag of codes. GT-BEHRT models the structure inside a visit and long-term patterns across visits. Tadigotla checks it on seven points, from design to deployment. Reported scores for heart failure prediction were strong in two large cohorts. Calibration, fairness checks, and deployment plans were thin, though, so clinical use needs more work first.
arxiv-2603-13431: Mansoor Ahmed and co-authors introduce CHIMERA-Bench for epitope-specific antibody design. Dozens of deep generative methods have appeared in three years, but no standard benchmark exists for fair comparison. Methods are tested on varied SAbDab snapshots, test sets, and metrics that do not align. CHIMERA-Bench centers on one task: epitope-conditioned CDR sequence-structure co-design. It holds a curated set of 2,922 antibody-antigen complexes with epitope and paratope labels. Three splits test unseen epitopes, unseen antigen folds, and future targets, and 11 methods are benchmarked.
arxiv-2603-13831: Navaratna and co-authors present a semi-automated pipeline that segments material microstructure images with deep learning. Such images vary a lot, so hand labeling is slow and labeled data are scarce. Their workflow pairs a U-Net with an interface where experts fix labels, and those fixes retrain the model. A core-set method picks the most useful images to label. Three pick strategies are compared over six rounds on additive manufacturing data, and their SMILE strategy performs consistently well.
arxiv-2603-14231: Zhao and Yuan build rank-based maxsum tests for regression coefficients in high-dimensional linear models. Sum-type tests catch dense signals, max-type tests catch sparse ones, and users rarely know which case they face. Heavy-tailed errors break many standard tools. The authors prove that their rank sum and max statistics become independent under the null. That fact supports two adaptive tests that merge p-values by the Cauchy method. Simulations show sound size control and strong power across error shapes.
arxiv-2603-14731: Adhikari and Suyama let dark matter scalarize neutron stars to ease the hyperon puzzle. Hyperons soften the star matter equation and cap the max mass too low. A heavy scalar field, cast as all of dark matter, couples to the Ricci scalar here. The coupling shifts the field mass inside stars and sparks tachyonic growth. Resulting stars pass two solar masses even with hyperons inside. Stronger coupling yields several scalar setups for one star. A self-interaction term reshapes the outcomes further, they find.
arxiv-2603-14831: Bosca and Ghrist rebuild feedforward ReLU networks as cellular sheaves with local-to-global flow. Each forward-pass quantity becomes a vertex in the sheaf. Affine steps, activations and outputs become restriction maps on edges. The coboundary on free coordinates is unitriangular, with determinant one. Relative cohomology vanishes under that shape. The forward output is thus the unique harmonic extension of input data. A sheaf heat equation settles to that output exponentially. Pinned neurons and local training without backpropagation follow from the frame.
arxiv-2603-14931: Debnath and Saha design lead-free microring resonators for visible light with a coupled DFT-FDTD flow. Cesium copper chloride serves as the benign ring material. Density functional theory supplies the wavelength-wise optical constants. Those constants feed time-domain sweeps over width, gap and bend radius. A balanced point uses a 600 nm width, 200 nm gap and 10 micron radius. Loaded quality factor lands near 5,386 there, with wide free spectral range. Gap scans trace over-, critical and under-coupling in full.
arxiv-2603-15231: Luke and co-authors report early lattice results for the electric polarizability of charged pions. Polarizability reveals how a hadron deforms in an electric field, which probes its inner structure. They use four-point functions with a dynamical nHYP action, an approach shown to work for charged and neutral hadrons. Two pion masses, 220 and 315 MeV, and varied lattice sizes support an infinite-volume extrapolation. The setup improves on their earlier quenched study with heavier pions.
arxiv-2603-15431: Medvedev and co-authors fine-tune PDE foundation models with physics in the loss, not just data. Pretrained surrogates struggle to adapt when task data is scarce or shifted. Their method adds PDE residuals and boundary rules straight into the fine-tuning goal. On an unseen class of equations, the approach matched data-driven tuning without any solved examples for training. A hybrid mix of physics and data generalized best to out-of-distribution cases with tiny training sets. The results frame a data-efficient path for scientific machine learning.
arxiv-2603-15531: Maccary and co-authors hunt a hidden set of long gamma-ray bursts that came from compact object mergers. GRB 230307A showed a distinct pulse pattern, with set growth in waiting times and widths. They scan the Fermi GBM catalog for bursts with at least eight peaks and matching traits. Nine candidates emerge. At least two break the standard energy relation at strong significance, and their variability times match merger bursts better than collapsars. The merger share of long bursts may be larger than assumed.
arxiv-2603-15831: Dubedy tests whether assigned wealth personas steer a language model's gambling. GPT-4.1 played slot machines under Rich, Middle-income, and Poor personas. Three machine types paid at 50 percent, 35 percent, or rising streak odds. Fifty sessions per condition gave 6,950 recorded choices. The Poor persona played 37.4 rounds per session on average. The Rich persona played just 1.1 rounds. The split matches Prospect Theory habits with no coaching given. Emotion labels trailed choices rather than driving them. Belief updates across rounds stayed near zero.
arxiv-2603-16331: Phan and co-authors study how large reasoning models recover from their own mistakes. The team plants arithmetic errors inside a model's reasoning steps. Oddly, the model often still lands on the right answer. No spoken correction appears in the chain of thought. The authors trace this to a hidden critique ability. They isolate a critique vector in the model's feature space. Steering with that vector sharpened error detection and test-time scaling.
arxiv-2603-16731: Topollai and Choromanska explain why quantizing optimizer states stalls LLM training. Low-precision moving averages round many updates back to the stored value. The state then sits stale, and adaptation lags the nominal decay. Their model predicts one-step stalling odds after initialization. Stalling builds over time in a trackable way. The picture explains why resetting the state helps. A reset briefly restores responsiveness in a stale state. Their theory picks good reset periods, and tests confirm the gains.
arxiv-2603-17131: Borycki and co-authors present SMAL-pets, a framework that builds animatable 3D dog avatars from a single photo. Animal reconstruction is hard: annotated datasets are scarce, and breeds vary hugely in size and shape. Their method joins 3D Gaussian Splatting with the SMAL parametric model. This gives avatars that look detailed yet stay grounded in anatomy. A multimodal editing suite lets users refine appearance and drive complex motion with text prompts. The authors aim at a flexible tool for animation and virtual reality.
arxiv-2603-17331: Fenoglio and Treleaven propose Federated Computing as Code, a design for collaboration across groups that keeps data local and sovereign. Federated systems often enforce sovereignty rules through runtime policy checks or shared trust setups, which adds cost and weak assurance. Their design turns authority and delegation into signed, verifiable artifacts instead. Entry at a boundary becomes a local proof check, not a call to a policy service. Virtual Federated Platforms bind core contracts through a chain of capability tokens.
arxiv-2603-17731: Khatla, Duchemin, Eddi, and Reyssat watch two viscous blisters merge under an elastic sheet. A synthetic schlieren setup tracks the full thickness field as the blisters join. The team zooms in on how the neck between them grows. A one-dimensional lubrication model then predicts that growth with scaling laws. Bending of the sheet drives the early motion, they find. Full nonlinear runs match the measured neck shapes well.
arxiv-2603-17831: Yuan, Yuan, and Xie present RPMS, a planning frame for language-model agents in strict worlds. Embodied tasks fail when actions break preconditions or memory drifts from state. RPMS checks each action against retrieved rules before it fires. A light belief state gates which memories may apply. Rules win any clash between the two sources. On ALFWorld the 8B setup gained 23.9 points over baseline, they report.
arxiv-2603-17931: Cohn, Qi, Lall, and Xu coordinate cascaded hydropower in real time under linked uncertainty. What an upstream dam releases shapes the inflow risk downstream, so errors depend on choices. Their rolling-horizon optimizer folds that coupling into a joint chance constraint. A variance model ties spread to past forecast misses and releases. A hyperplane method keeps the math tractable and convergent. On the Lower Columbia, breaches fell by up to 34.2 percent, they report.
arxiv-2603-18031: Wang and co-authors present InfoMamba, an attention-free hybrid that joins Mamba-style state-space models with a light global filter. Transformers mix tokens well but scale with quadratic cost. Pure state-space models scale in a line but miss some global links. InfoMamba swaps self-attention for a concept bottleneck filter and fuses it with a selective recurrent stream. Tests on classification, dense prediction, and non-vision tasks beat strong baselines at near-linear cost.
arxiv-2603-18331: Zhao and co-authors survey differential equations as a theoretical base for deep neural networks. Networks succeed in practice, yet lack a principled foundation for systematic design. The survey asks how equations explain architectures, improve performance, and serve real applications. Two views organize the field: the whole network as one equation, and each layer as an equation. Links between design, analysis, and gains are traced across both views.
arxiv-2603-18531: Mandal and Guin study when maps built from polyharmonic and elliptic harmonic parts stay one-to-one. They prove Landau and Bloch type theorems for poly elliptic harmonic maps, and the bounds are sharp in some cases. They also give coefficient bounds for maps with bounded minimum distortion. Those bounds then yield new Landau-Bloch results for the wider classes. The work is pure complex analysis, aimed at readers who study univalence criteria for generalized harmonic maps.
arxiv-2603-18731: Nation, Saki, and Kang present a framework for solving Hamiltonian eigenproblems inside a sampled subspace. Bit-strings from a quantum computer define the subspace. An extended operator alphabet with projection and ladder operators covers qubit and fermion systems in one method. Sorting and grouping leave only nonzero terms to evaluate. Bit-set storage cuts memory and lifts qubit count limits. Users can build sparse matrices or run matrix-free solves with their own eigensolver. Tests on condensed matter and chemistry cases cut memory and runtime, often by tenfold.
arxiv-2603-18831: Zavorka and co-authors measure how a potted plant affects 60 and 80 gigahertz links indoors. The plant sat in the line of sight between sender and receiver. Tiny antenna shifts, called microdiversity moves, were varied on purpose. The team tracked changes in the channel impulse response and received power. The 80 gigahertz band reacts more strongly to small moves than the 60 gigahertz band. Received power swings more at the higher band. The findings matter for designing high-frequency indoor links near vegetation and moving gear.
arxiv-2603-19531: Dutta and co-authors present dinov3.seg, a framework for open-vocabulary semantic segmentation with DINOv3. Such systems label each pixel using text-defined classes, including unseen ones. Vision-language features trained on global matching are weak for dense pixel tasks. The method refines visual features early, before image-text interaction, and again late. It mixes global token and patch-level features for both meaning and fine detail. A sliding-window scheme keeps high detail with global context. Tests on five benchmarks beat prior methods.
arxiv-2603-19631: Pi and co-authors report a trapped-ion clock qubit with coherence beyond ten hours. They combine clock-state qubits with decoherence-free subspace encoding in ytterbium ion pairs. Barium ions provide sympathetic cooling for the pair. The encoding ties phase to the inter-ion energy gap, rejecting microwave and magnetic noise. No magnetic shielding or extra microwave stabilization was needed. Over runs up to 1,600 seconds, decay stayed minimal. Fits give a coherence time near 37,700 seconds, a form of passive error correction.
arxiv-2603-20031: Colin, Tanay, and Bernard solve the motion of spinning, eccentric black hole pairs at second post-Newtonian order. New gravitational wave events show both eccentricity and spin precession at once. Past models mostly twisted waveforms from nonprecessing systems, a heuristic fix. This work builds the dynamics from first principles in general relativity. It tracks the separation vector, both spin vectors, and the orbital angular momentum over time. The solution allows arbitrary spins and eccentricity. It improves on the earlier 1.5 order solution by about tenfold.
arxiv-2603-20131: Gupta and co-authors build a six-agent AI system that runs cybersecurity risk assessments for small firms. A consultant-led, NIST-aligned assessment costs at least 15,000 dollars and takes weeks. Most small firms skip it and stay exposed. Each agent in their system owns one stage, from profiling the firm to writing recommendations. A shared, growing context lets later agents build on earlier findings. On a small healthcare test case, the system matched human experts 85 percent of the time. It covered 92 percent of risks and finished in under 15 minutes.
arxiv-2603-20231: Nguyen and co-authors study how language models handle the moral mazes of office life in a roleplay game. Players act as an HR officer writing emails for hard workplace cases. A model judge scores each email against scenario-specific rubrics. Over 600 human and model emails were compared. Model emails read as more formal and more empathetic. Humans passed only 23.5 percent of scenarios, against 48 to 54 percent for models. Human drafts rewritten by models beat both groups alone. Judge models also differed, with stronger ones favoring subtler wording.
arxiv-2603-20431: Spadaro and co-authors adapt the DINGO inference code for massive black hole binaries with LISA. Simulation-based inference can speed up gravitational-wave parameter estimation greatly. They train a normalizing flow on aligned-spin, higher-mode waveforms. A low-frequency detector response model keeps training tractable. Importance sampling then corrects the samples to the true posterior. Tests agree with standard methods up to signal-to-noise near 500. At higher values, sampling efficiency drops but results stay unbiased. The flow draws 20,000 posterior samples in under a minute.
