A foreseen sign, circular dichroism in resonant inelastic X-ray scattering from chiral magnons, was thought to be an artifact.

Studying the Lieb-lattice magnet La2O3Mn2Se2, the team saw a circular dichroism in the excitations. It had clear d-wave symmetry, and is gone in the paramagnetic phase. Through symmetry analysis of the scattering operator, plus exact-diagonalization work, they prove the dichroism follows from this order's rules. The result shows the material is a genuine d-wave altermagnet. It also shows such scattering is a symmetry probe of such orders.
arxiv-2606-18831:
Xu and the team argue the bottleneck for teaching language models long-context reasoning is training data, not reward design, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Reinforcement learning improves reasoning. But for long inputs, the outcome-only reward signal is too sparse to teach models to locate evidence. Most responses to that problem have engineered more rewards.

Their alternative is a simple data recipe, covering three task families: retrieval, multi-evidence synthesis, and reasoning. It is built into eight datasets of about fourteen thousand examples, paired with an outcome-based GRPO setup. Across three Qwen3 models and seven long-context benchmarks, the recipe produced average gains of several points. It surpassed prior reinforcement learning training sets. The gains transferred to agentic work. Continuing training of an agent-tuned model on the recipe improved its scores on the GAIA and BrowseComp agent benchmarks. That suggests long-context skill underpins agent capability.
arxiv-2606-18931:
Cojocari and the team show an intermediate state of a superconductor, in which an electric field enters the material while superconductivity survives, in a 2026 condensed matter physics paper. Theory poses a paradox. An electric field inside a superconductor would speed the supercurrent without bound. So fields were assumed to expel or destroy that state. Loss was studied in low-dimensional devices, through phase slips.

Applying voltage gradients across unpatterned superconducting films, the team observed a nonclassical regime. A zero-resistance supercurrent and a dissipative current propagate at once there. The state arises from field-driven fluctuations of the order parameter, not from defects or patterning. The resistive carriers in this intermediate state behave unlike normal-state carriers. That hints fields compel hidden carriers into transport. The authors frame the state as a platform for studying dissipative quantum fluids far from equilibrium, including in correlated ones.
arxiv-2606-19131:
Kaiser establishes a law of the iterated logarithm for p-rotor walks on the integers in a 2026 probability paper. The p-rotor walk mixes simple random walk with the deterministic rotor walk, interpolating between pure chance and pure rule. Its weak convergence to a perturbed Brownian motion was known. Its almost-sure growth boundaries, which say how far the walk can stray in the long run, had not been pinned down until now.

The author splits the walk into a martingale plus a perturbation from its running extremes. That split first yields a functional law for the linearly interpolated paths of the walk. The classical constants then follow by solving a calculus of variations problem over the perturbed Strassen set. The exact constants matter because they describe the walk's true almost-sure envelope, not just its typical scale. The result completes the limit theory for this self-interacting walk family.
arxiv-2606-19331:
Harkin and colleagues define the topological spectral form factor in 2026, linking many-body quantum chaos to an emergent single-particle problem. In equilibrium physics, topological defect insertions probe phase transitions beyond local observables. The spectral form factor probes universal quantum dynamics. The authors insert topological defects into the doubled partition functions behind the form factor, producing mismatched spacetime world-sheet topologies.

For the simplest extended defect, the global swap operator, they derive an exact mapping. The form factor of a one-dimensional chaotic many-body system maps to an emergent non-Hermitian single-particle problem, a temporal domain wall. That domain wall undergoes a parity-time symmetry breaking transition at finite interaction strength. Below it, leading modes polarize and the form factor varies smoothly. Above it, sectors hybridize and the signal oscillates. A hard many-body diagnostic thus becomes a tractable single-particle transition.
arxiv-2606-19831:
Hongliang Liu derives a control-window law for steering language models through single neurons in 2026. Aligned models gate behaviours like refusal and language choice through sparse feed-forward neurons. No theory predicted when one neuron steers cleanly versus wrecking the output.

Forward-only perturbation probing grounds the framework. One write direction's effect collapses to a single alignment coordinate. An injected dose drives that coordinate along a universal saturation curve, scaled by a coherence budget. Clean control exists exactly when the behaviour trigger sits below the collapse ceiling. Weight-based estimates predict that ceiling with small error on held-out neurons. Verdicts on whether the window is open hold on most test cases. Gradient attribution, by contrast, anti-predicts true controllers. A forward-only contrastive screen recovers the gates that attribution misses.
arxiv-2606-20231:
Ishanu Chattopadhyay proposes a thermodynamic definition of intelligence and argues that self-simulation is not optional for it. His 2026 paper defines intelligence as the lawful amplification of rare but valid futures. An intelligent system raises the odds of outcomes that passive dynamics would rarely produce, yet the domain's rules still allow. Any such system must model the world with itself inside the model, which forces recursive self-simulation.

The central results give necessity and near-sufficiency statements. High amplification is impossible unless the internal model identifies rare valid futures with high fidelity. Conversely, with high fidelity and an effective policy inside the simulation, achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum. The measure is meant to be general, spanning passive matter, feedback controllers, language models, and humans on one scale. The claims are strong and formally stated.
arxiv-2606-20331:
Robert Ganian and Mathis Rocton break a barrier in computing twin-width, a graph parameter central to explaining why first-order model checking is tractable on many graph classes. Their 2026 paper notes that even recognizing twin-width at most four is NP-hard, and no approximations parameterized by twin-width itself are known. Recent progress came from parameterizing by other measures, but all tractable ones rested on deletion distance. Ganian and Rocton change the parameter.

They prove that approximating twin-width is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by treedepth, working through oriented twin-width, the first constructive evidence that this variant may be friendlier. Their second result is stronger: computing twin-width exactly is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to vertex integrity, the first non-trivial parameterized algorithm for optimal contraction sequences. The pair redraws the map of which structural parameters make twin-width computation feasible.
arxiv-2606-20531:
Mariia Gladkova, Tarun Yenamandra, and four colleagues add a visible domain constraint to sparse novel view synthesis. Their 2026 paper tackles reconstructing 3D geometry from only a few input views, where NeRF and Gaussian splatting methods overfit, producing floating artifacts and inconsistent geometry.

Silhouette consistency, the usual regularizer, is insufficient because silhouette-consistent regions can extend beyond the true object. VisDom is a learning-free geometric constraint that augments classical visual hull carving with a minimum multi-view visibility requirement. The visible domain trims away regions no input camera could actually see. Sparse-view reconstruction gets a cheap, principled guardrail that needs no training data.
arxiv-2606-20931:
Ramón Bécar and four colleagues study scattering and radiation in 2026 around Euler-Heisenberg black holes surrounded by dark matter. The geometry adds two parts to a standard black hole. One is a nonlinear electrodynamic correction with its own coupling. The other is a dark matter halo term. They examine scalar, electromagnetic, and an effective spin-two channel on that fixed background.

Quasinormal modes, the ringing tones of a perturbed black hole, are computed with a high-order method and checked against photon sphere predictions. Near-extremal cases yield a purely imaginary branch of modes. Its damping grows with the dark matter parameter and barely depends on spin. Hawking radiation and neutrino energy deposition are also studied, per the title and scope. Such signatures could, in principle, help distinguish exotic black hole surroundings from plain vacuum cases in future observations.
arxiv-2606-21031:
A 2026 paper with no personal byline in the hosted text develops a continuous-time multiparametric method to reduce the number of control laws in optimal control. Multiparametric programming solves a control problem once offline. Optimal laws then come out as explicit functions of the initial state. Online use is a direct evaluation with no iterations. Most work slices time into intervals and applies algebraic conditions to the sliced problem.

Slicing forces a tradeoff. Too few intervals miss true dynamics. Too many make the problem size and region count grow fast. Offline preparation and online lookup both grow expensive. The new framework works directly in continuous time. Pontryagin's Maximum Principle is applied with no discretization of the model. Explicit control as a function of initial state is recovered. Fewer, cleaner control laws could help embedded controllers, where online optimization is too slow for the hardware available.
arxiv-2606-21131:
Sriram Kalathoor studies salt-finger mixing in a solo 2026 paper at a two-layer ocean interface with finite depth and surface roughness. Salt fingering moves salt and heat across layers that are stable overall but unstable to double diffusion. Real interfaces carry roughness from waves, shear, and prior mixing. Kalathoor tests how the horizontal spectrum of that roughness controls the path to a plume forest.

Direct simulations of the flow equations use matched settings across cases. Imposed spectra range from high-annulus to low-mode and mixed forms. Each spectrum selects a distinct route to vertical exchange. Low-mode roughness produces the strongest salt transport at a key time and reaches the boundary first. High-annulus roughness stays compact and branch-locked. Ocean mixing controls heat and carbon uptake, so knowing which interface shapes mix fastest refines a process that climate models must parameterize.
arxiv-2606-21231:
Churchill Agoni and seven colleagues studied liquid crystal shells in 2026: thin spherical films of ferroelectric nematic material floating between water layers. Such shells must carry topological defects, points where the molecular alignment cannot stay smooth, with total charge fixed at plus two. The team conjectured that the polar order of a ferroelectric nematic avoids the splayed half-integer defects common in ordinary nematic shells.

Their RM734 and DIO shells confirm the idea at room temperature, forming two opposite plus-one defects with a swirling azimuthal pattern that needs only bend and twist. Second-harmonic microscopy backs the non-centrosymmetric structure. Warming the shells brings an antiferroelectric phase rich in zigzag lines, then the usual four half-charge defects at high temperature. The shells offer a clean test bed for exotic liquid crystals under geometric constraint.
arxiv-2606-21531:
Michaela Cichrova, Adela Hladka, and Patricia Martinkova refine how test bias is measured in 2026, focusing on differential item functioning, where equally able people from different groups answer an item differently. Statistical tests can flag such items, but practical importance needs effect sizes with sensible cutoffs for calling bias small or large. The authors review effect measures for the Mantel-Haenszel test, SIBTEST, and model-based methods for binary items, and refine area-based measures.

Simulations expose flaws in common measures: inconsistent classifications, systematic understatement of true bias size, and sensitivity to study design. The authors restrict some measures' use, revise cutoffs so different methods agree, and propose fresh cutoffs for the area-based family. Two real datasets illustrate the changes, with an implementation in R.
arxiv-2606-21731:
Artem G. Abanov and Andrey V. Chubukov review in 2026 how superconductivity changes when the pairing glue is singular and dynamical. In textbook BCS theory, a gentle attraction pairs Fermi-liquid quasiparticles thanks to the Cooper logarithm, so even infinitesimal coupling suffices. Near a quantum critical point, in quantum dots, or near a Mott transition, the interaction instead blows up at low frequency, the energy-scale separation collapses, and the whole BCS scaffolding fails.

The review develops the gamma-model, with interaction decaying as a power of frequency, and follows the rivalry between pairing and non-Fermi-liquid behavior. Superconductivity still wins past a threshold coupling, but for qualitatively different reasons. At zero temperature the gap equation holds infinitely many topologically distinct solutions, which vanish one by one as the interaction is made regular. The authors close with the physics behind these phenomena and open directions.
arxiv-2606-22031:
Isneri and Montecchiari prove, in 2026, the existence of prescribed-energy connecting orbits for quasilinear conservative systems. Such systems couple a velocity-dependent kinetic term with a smooth potential, and a connecting orbit travels between two regions of space. The authors assume the potential's sublevel set splits into two disjoint closed parts at the chosen energy level.

Using an energy-constrained variational method in an Orlicz-Sobolev setting, they construct paths with exactly the prescribed energy joining the two parts. Although the construction first yields weak solutions, the minimal connections are shown to be classical smooth paths. These satisfy the strong energy identity at every time. The family includes heteroclinic, homoclinic, and brake-type orbits. Applications to double-well potentials, Duffing-type systems, and multiple pendulums are discussed.
arxiv-2606-22131:
Nishizawa and colleagues propose, in 2026, a feed-forward framework that fills in the motion of arbitrary 4D meshes between sparse keyframes. A 4D mesh is a 3D shape evolving over time, used in animation and games. Generating the in-between frames used to need slow test-time optimization, because long 4D training data with arbitrary shapes is scarce.

Their system, CompletionAny4D, first encodes each frame with a mesh variational autoencoder. The encoder produces topology-agnostic latent tokens, anchored by a reference mesh that carries the keyframe conditioning. A keyframe-conditioned rectified flow model with an MMDiT backbone then synthesizes the non-keyframe frames. On the DyMesh16 and DyMesh32 benchmarks the method shows strong performance and improved controllability. It completes full 4D content from sparse keyframes and text prompts within seconds.
arxiv-2606-22631:
Chaoyue Li and five colleagues, including Linfeng Zhang, define a new task for understanding moving scenes in this 2026 paper. Tracking an object through a dynamic scene means grounding language to a worldline, a persistent thread binding identity, three-dimensional motion, and synchronized views from several cameras. Large multimodal models reason richly but rarely preserve metric structure, while trackers output fragmented results.

Their Instruct-4D benchmark holds about one hundred twenty-nine thousand question-answer pairs over eight hundred fifty-one scenes and nine query types. Their system, 4DTrack, treats tracking as inference over an object-centric four-dimensional state graph. Metric-guided routing, bidirectional decoding, and kinematic calibration keep the recovered worldline consistent. Its Qwen3.5-9B version reached a top-one grounding accuracy near sixty-three percent. That beat the best adapted baseline by nearly twenty points, showing worldline-centred modelling improves grounding and motion quality.
arxiv-2606-23331:
Alexander Phillips Long computes scattering quantities for light nuclei in a 2026 doctoral dissertation at the George Washington University. The work applies the Transition Density Amplitude method, developed by Grießhammer and colleagues. In that approach, a scattering amplitude splits into two factors. One is a kernel describing how the probe interacts with the active nucleons. The other, the amplitude itself, carries the structure information of the spectator nucleons. Amplitudes are computed once per nucleus and momentum transfer, then reused across reactions.

Long treats elastic pion scattering, Compton scattering, and neutral pion photoproduction on hydrogen-3, helium-3, helium-4, and lithium-6. All calculations run inside a public Fortran code suite, DensityScattering, built for this work. Nuclear wave functions come from a chiral potential with similarity renormalization group transformations. Checks against exact results for helium-4 show differences at the two percent level or below.
arxiv-2606-23931:
Hall, Zhang, Shilov, Nax, and Bolognani ask how control engineers should build fairness and equity into automated systems that divide scarce resources. Their 2026 working paper joins control theory with social questions. Highways, water rights, grid capacity, and user attention are all divided by algorithms now, and designers quietly decide what society wants, usually by industry habit. The authors call the missing standard a social mandate: engineers should certify fair and efficient allocation as they certify stability. The paper surveys the tools for doing so deliberately.

The program starts with combining people's preferences into design objectives. It continues with certifying that the built system meets those specifications. Feedback is the authors' trump card: a controller measuring outcomes can correct unfair divisions continuously. Successes from internet fairness protocols to air traffic slot allocation show the pattern works.
arxiv-2606-24031:
Opus and Lu run a thirty five billion parameter language model on a graphics card from 2011. The card has six gigabytes of memory. They hand wrote the entire inference engine to do it, in a 2026 paper on computer systems. The model occupies about ten and a half gigabytes even at four bit precision, twice the card's memory. Modern software cannot help: the card predates tensor cores and every current compiler toolchain. The authors split the work: expert weights stream from main memory for GPU prefill, while text generation runs on the CPU through a hand built integer kernel.

Tuning cuts prefill on a long prompt from fifty seven seconds to thirty seven and a half, and triples generation speed. A snapshot cache restores prefix reuse. It collapses a repeated seventy eight second prefill to half a second. Several plausible optimizations fail, mapping the old hardware's floor.
arxiv-2606-24231:
Li and colleagues generate driving plans by asking a model what good outcomes look like, then sampling actions that promise them. Motion planning for self-driving cars splits between two camps. Scoring methods enjoy dense reward supervision but pick from a fixed menu of actions. Anchor methods propose freely but learn from only one recorded trajectory. Their 2026 model, FlowR2A, reframes rewards as generative conditions rather than grading targets.

A flow-matching decoder learns the distribution of actions conditioned on reward. It trains on dense pairs of trajectories and their simulated rewards. The model thus internalises how actions translate into safety, progress, comfort, and rule compliance. Fine-grained per-timestep conditioning, plus reward noise augmentation, balances hard safety constraints against softer progress goals. At test time, reward guidance and anchored sampling steer generation toward high-quality proposals. Li's design claims both camps' virtues in one generative planner.
arxiv-2606-24331:
Guruprakash and Krithika survey transformer language models across the fields now built on them. Their 2026 review tries to separate lasting ideas from release noise. It works at two levels. In mechanism, it sorts the transformer families into a taxonomy: encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder-decoder, long-context, permutation-based, and generator-discriminator variants. The post-2023 shifts that changed practice are added, from instruction tuning and human-feedback learning to preference tuning, mixture-of-experts scaling, and retrieval.

Uses in healthcare, finance, law, education, customer service, creative writing, and scientific work are each linked to the skills making a transformer the right tool there. A critical review compares designs along four axes that matter for deployment decisions. It measures the trade-off between parameter scale and practical cost. The synthesis targets practitioners choosing among flagship families, who need judgement grounded in evidence, not announcement cycles.
arxiv-2606-24731:
Ulrik Günther and six colleagues propose a workshop linking science fiction with data visualisation research. The two communities have influenced each other for decades. Films, series, and games depict data interfaces that shape what the public expects from interactive systems. Visualisation researchers, in turn, borrow and rework interface ideas from fictional worlds. Despite this long exchange, the relationship has never been studied in a systematic way. The proposal targets IEEE VIS 2026 as a hybrid half day event.

Researchers and science fiction creators are both invited to take part. Submissions in creative formats are welcome, as long as they expose connections or spark future research. The planned programme mixes a keynote with lightning talks and brainstorming sessions. Cross community critique and affinity mapping will organise the discussion around shared themes. Günther and colleagues hope the workshop builds a shared map of the two way influence.
arxiv-2606-24931:
Hongshen Chua explores two famous binary trees of rational numbers and uses them to reread a classic theorem. The Stern Brocot tree grows by taking mediants of neighbouring fractions. The Calkin Wilf tree grows by giving each fraction two children built from its parts. The trees look alike, and Backhouse and Ferreira explained why: one matrix based binary tree generates both. Chua develops that construction in detail. Continued fractions enter next, since their convergents appear as paths through the matrix tree.

The payoff is number theoretic. Brillhart once gave a short proof of Fermat's theorem that certain primes are sums of two squares, using continued fractions. The path based viewpoint offers a new interpretation of that proof. Walking the tree replaces the older fraction manipulations. Chua presents the material as an integrated tour: two trees, one matrix construction, continued fractions, and a fresh route through a three century old result.
arxiv-2606-25131:
Contact relations say when two regions touch, without reducing space to points. Sergio A. Celani and Luciana Valenzuela study distributive lattices equipped with such a precontact relation, and ask how the relation shows up in the Priestley dual, the standard mirror world for such lattices.

In Boolean algebras, precontact, quasi modal operators, and subordination all define each other. In the distributive setting that unity breaks: the last two still match, but precontact stands apart. The authors show how conditions placed on the precontact relation match first order properties in the dual space. They describe precontact substructures and strong precontact sublattices through a lattice preorder built for the purpose. A new notion of precontact congruence is matched to the right closed sets in the dual.
arxiv-2606-25531:
Operator systems are the self adjoint skeletons of operator algebras. A basic question asks when their higher matrix levels are already fixed by a few low ones. Markus Dannemüller and Tim Netzer study that finiteness property, called subhomogeneity, in 2026 for finite dimensional systems. Six viewpoints turn out to be one. They include realisation inside matrices over a commutative algebra, a tame enveloping algebra, and maximality of the order. They also include automatic upgrading of partly positive maps, a dual minimality trait, and a geometric boundary condition.

One surprise follows about duality. The dual of such a system need not share the property itself, yet it is always a quotient of one, a structural fact with no classical analogue this clean. Minimal and maximal systems over certain cones supply examples and counterexamples marking where each claim bites. The results link matrix convexity with algebra in both directions.
arxiv-2606-25731:
Optimal control by Pontryagin's principle turns a design problem into a two point boundary value problem, usually with a jagged, nonsmooth Hamiltonian. Salim Ksous, Sebastian Lalvay Segovia, Mattias Sandberg, Erik von Schwerin, Anders Szepessy, and Raúl Tempone present a solver for it in 2026. Their Hamiltonian is first approximated by a bundle of affine planes, then smoothed with a soft minimum trick, ending infinitely smooth and concave in the costate. A symplectic Euler scheme discretises the system, and a damped Newton method solves state and costate together, all at once.

One adaptive loop steers three error sources: the time step pattern, the number of planes, and the smoothing level. Error indicators for each target the value at the starting state, the quantity the authors care about. Four test problems exercise the machinery, from a hypersensitive scalar case to attitude control. A footnote discloses AI assistance in preparing the manuscript.
arxiv-2606-26031:
Christian Laudagé extends the theory of return risk measures, tools that judge financial risk from logarithmic returns rather than raw money. Monetary risk measures are standard in finance and insurance. Return risk measures give the return-based view an axiomatic footing. Their classical home is the space of bounded random variables. Laudagé moves them to general ordered vector spaces instead.

Geometric convexity is the focus. Positive homogeneity is characterized through the geometric epigraph. Specializing to AM-algebras brings richer territory into reach. Euclidean spaces qualify, and so do spaces of multidimensional bounded random variables. That second case is new for this theory. It yields systemic and vector-valued return risk measures as fresh classes. Results cover finiteness, continuity, and separability. Dual and aggregation forms round out the picture. The extension links return-based risk thinking with the monetary theory it grew from.
arxiv-2606-26231:
Z. Ding leads a team rebuilding the Crab Nebula in three dimensions, jet included. The Crab is the wreck of a supernova seen in the year 1054, filmed now in exquisite detail. Hyperspectral data from the SITELLE instrument in Hawaii cover its full face in many emission lines. A strange funnel, nicknamed the jet or chimney, juts from the northern rim. Their reconstruction is the first to fold that structure into the full kinematic map.

Geometry resolves a long-suspected cavity at the jet's base. Filaments connect directly into the funnel, the maps show. An early pulsar wind nebula likely shaped the jet. Three formation stories remain alive: a bipolar outflow guided by a disk, a breach in the ejecta shell, and a low-density channel left by an old mass-loss trail. Collimation, the missing southern twin, and near-ballistic motion are the tests each story must pass.
arxiv-2606-26831:
Xiaodian Chen and Shu Wang review distance-ladder measurements of the Hubble constant, the number setting today's cosmic expansion rate. Local ladders build distances step by step, from geometric anchors to stellar indicators to galaxies in the smooth Hubble flow. Their results now reach percent-level precision. They also sit stubbornly above the value inferred from the early universe, a clash called the Hubble tension.

The review treats the ladder as a network of linked measurements with shared errors. The Cepheid variable star route to supernovae remains the most precise single ladder. Independent indicators now cross-check it: red giant stars, Mira variables, surface-brightness fluctuations, and galaxy rotation relations among them. Combining seven routes still leaves the local value well above the early-universe one. Shared and method-specific systematics are the focus of current work.
arxiv-2606-27031:
Barbato and Salerno ask how strongly a round shape wins a classic contest in the mathematics of torsion. For a region, the torsion problem models twisting under load, and its solution feeds measures like torsional rigidity, meaning stiffness against twisting. A comparison result by Talenti says balls score highest among all regions of the same area. The authors study nearly round regions and ask how much score is lost when the boundary wobbles slightly.

Loss from the best value controls the size of the boundary wobble, measured in a fractional smoothness norm and squared in the bound. Proof steps use shape derivatives, adjoint states, and a careful second-variation calculation. Covered scores include torsional rigidity itself and power norms of the torsion solution for exponents at least two. A two-dimensional functional linked to the Moser-Trudinger inequality also fits the same frame.
arxiv-2606-27631:
Silicon-28 nuclei can take two shapes. One is oblate, like a flattened ball. The other is prolate, like a stretched ball. Both shapes have been discussed for decades in this nucleus. How strongly they mix was poorly constrained, though. Yasutaka Taniguchi and Masaaki Kimura attack that question in 2026.

Their basis states come from antisymmetrised molecular dynamics plus the generator coordinate method. These methods build nuclear shapes from nucleon motion. Mixing amplitudes are then tuned to match measured facts. The facts used are the charge radius, a quadrupole moment, and several transition strengths. In the ground state, the oblate shape dominates. The prolate share stays below about twenty percent. The first excited two-plus state allows even less prolate share. The related E0 transition strength is not pinned down tightly. Its squared value has an upper limit near two tenths.
arxiv-2606-27931:
Noah Fleming and three colleagues present a new family of propositional proof systems in 2026. Each system is indexed by a TFNP search problem. A refutation works through a reduction. The false-clause search problem for the formula is mapped to the chosen search problem. An Extended Frege proof certifies that the reduction is correct. The family translates witnessing theorems from bounded arithmetic into proof systems, in white-box form.

One system receives a full characterisation. Pairing Extended Frege with the problem Iter, complete for the class PLS, gives a system polynomially equivalent to the sequent calculus G1. The same system equals Krajíček's implicit Resolution. G1 and implicit Resolution are therefore polynomially equivalent to each other. That is the first such characterisation of an implicit proof system in classical terms. The characterisation extends to higher calculi, and strength is calibrated for general search problems.
arxiv-2606-28131:
Felix Brandt, Matthias Hieber, and Arnab Roy study a fluid flowing against a flexible structure, with random forcing shaking both. Their system couples the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations, the standard laws of fluid motion, to a one-dimensional elastic plate, joined where fluid and plate meet by matching velocities and balancing stresses.

Brandt and colleagues prove that strong solutions exist for all time and are uniquely determined by the randomness, a first for this kind of stochastically forced system. They split the problem into a linear random part and a nonlinear remainder. Maximal regularity for the linear part comes from a powerful calculus for the coupled operator, plus decoupling and pressure estimates. Quasilinear methods solve the remainder locally, and energy estimates rule out blow-up.
arxiv-2606-28331:
Andrés Fábrega, Arkaprabha Bhattacharya, Miranda Christ, and Sunoo Park examine the gap between what lawmakers say about watermarking artificial intelligence content and what the technology can actually do. Bills in the United States have multiplied, and European policy pushes in the same direction, amid public worry about generated media.

Fábrega and colleagues gathered a broad corpus of legislative and policy documents, then coded them inductively to map recurring themes. Their systematization surfaces key patterns, gaps, and open questions across the debate. Again and again, policy language assumes tracking tools that are more reliable, more universal, or harder to remove than real systems are. The authors spell out the ambiguities and pitfalls those mismatches create for anyone drafting or obeying such rules.
arxiv-2606-28531:
Ishani Mondal, Aparna Garimella, Ananya Sai, Pannaga Shivaswamy, and Jordan Boyd-Graber judge whether automatically generated talk videos actually teach. Software now converts research papers into narrated video presentations, and existing metrics grade visual polish or whether key points appear. A video can hit every point and still leave a viewer unable to explain why the method works.

Their EffectivePresentationScorer grades instructional quality: whether main ideas are explained clearly, needed background is introduced, and technical details connect to the paper's contribution. Applied to current paper-to-video systems, it finds videos that mention the right topics and mirror the paper's structure, yet skip prerequisite concepts and never clarify the reasoning. Those teaching failures, the authors show, are exactly what presence-based metrics cannot see.
arxiv-2606-28631:
Haojie Hou, writing alone, follows the luckiest particle in a dying branching process. A subcritical branching random walk produces fewer than one child per particle on average, so the population dies out, but before vanishing its members wander. The maximal displacement, the farthest position ever reached, is a natural extreme-value question, especially when single steps have stretched exponential tails, heavier than Gaussian but lighter than exponential.

Hou derives the exact asymptotic form of the tail probability that the maximum exceeds a large level. He identifies its exponential rate, power correction, and slowly varying factor, with a clean constant in the first regime he treats. A second result handles tails with an added exponential tilt. It proves the corresponding limit exists and lies strictly between zero and infinity, under a moment condition on the offspring distribution.
arxiv-2606-28831:
Yang, Ren, Zeng, Zhang, Chen, Chen and Li present Hard-KV, a method for shrinking the memory that language models keep while generating long answers. That memory, the key-value cache, grows with text length, and smart schemes that vary its size per attention head clash with inference engines that demand fixed memory layouts. Their framework manages stored tokens in three tiers, from dense to sparse to condensed, as generation proceeds.

A logits calibration step converts different importance scores into one shared probability scale, so a single top-p budget, keeping the most probable share, can be applied fairly across unlike heads. A system-level rewrite then packs the chosen scattered indices into continuous memory blocks that fast engines accept. On maths reasoning benchmarks the method doubled throughput compared with static baselines. It also kept generation quality high on inputs longer than ten thousand tokens, with code released publicly.
arxiv-2606-29031:
Labrak and colleagues ask how far synthetic speech can replace real recordings when training speech recognition for privacy-sensitive fields like banking and health care. Real speech is costly to collect and keep, while text-to-speech systems can generate endless audio. A stubborn synthetic-real data gap limits how much can be swapped out.

Probing a speech recognition system built on a language model backbone, the team locate where it internally separates real from synthetic speech. The signal concentrates in early-to-middle layers. Timing or melody distortions disrupt it most. That separability, they show, does not by itself predict recognition gains. Adding room echoes to synthetic audio narrowed the gap, not by making it cleaner, but by copying the acoustic mess of real rooms. With layer selection plus that augmentation, training matched a fully real baseline using a quarter of the real speech.
arxiv-2606-29331:
Kocabay and two colleagues ask how much data symbolic regression needs to discover a true formula. Symbolic regression searches expressions built from operators like sine and exponential, and the space of possible formulas grows combinatorially with depth, which makes discovery look hopeless. Their paper revisits that worry through PAC learning, the theory of learning from samples with guaranteed error bounds.

For compositional function trees built from a finite set of smooth operators, they prove the key quantity does not blow up with the number of distinct structures. It is controlled instead by tree depth and by the operators' Lipschitz constants, measures of how much each operator can stretch its input. The matching risk bound grows with depth in a precise way. A companion codebase trains such operator trees on synthetic physics-like targets, and the observed generalisation gap tracks the predicted complexity term.
arxiv-2606-29631:
Lee and Gu extend latent class models, tools that sort survey or genetic responses into hidden groups. The classical model assumes local independence: within a class, items do not influence each other directly. That premise is often unrealistic, since responses within a group clearly interact.

Their latent class graphical model keeps the clarity of the classical approach through a shared block grouping of the items. Within each block, class-specific dependence is allowed. A three-step estimator recovers classes by spectral clustering, then estimates covariance matrices and blocks, then fits sparse precision matrices. Error bounds cover every stage. Tests recover the structure well. Uses on election survey and HapMap3 genotype data reveal local dependence.
arxiv-2606-29731:
Zuo and four colleagues present a soft robotic arm that can control both its tip position and its tip compliance in real time. Compliance, how much the arm yields on contact, helps robots in unstructured settings passively correct misalignment. Soft robots offer that compliance but have struggled to command tip behaviour precisely.

Their arm has seven links and six articulated joints providing twelve independently driven axes. An antagonistic pair of pneumatic muscles drives each axis, so it can change angle and adjust stiffness at once. A rigid articulated backbone makes tip compliance and position predictable enough to command quantitatively. A unified iterative controller handles inverse kinematics and inverse compliance together. Models and the control law are verified on the physical arm and a matched simulation. Demonstrations include writing on a moving whiteboard while rejecting disturbances, and passively correcting hidden misalignment during key insertion and drawer opening.
arxiv-2606-29931:
Anna Nalpantidi, Dimitris Karlis, and Daniel Fernández model data that arrive over time in ordered categories. Sleep stages scored from light to deep are one example. Most models for such ordinal series assume equal gaps between categories. The authors argue that this equidistant assumption often fails in real data. Their model lets the data reveal the true spacing instead.

Their autoregressive ordered stereotype model adds past values as predictors. Each observation can then depend on earlier ones in a structured way. They demonstrate the method on recordings of a newborn infant. The infant's sleep was classed as quiet, indeterminate, active, or awake, with temperature and heart rate also recorded. A broad simulation study checks performance at different sample sizes. The simulations also show how parameter choices shape the dependence between one time point and the next.
arxiv-2606-30131:
Dongliang Cao and Florian Bernard improve matching between deformable three-dimensional shapes. Functional maps are the standard tool for non-rigid shape correspondence. They align spectral bases of two shapes with a linear transformation. Severe distortion breaks that linear alignment, especially with partial shapes. Topological noise and raw point clouds make matching harder still.

Cao and Bernard replace the linear map with a learned non-linear one. A small neural network refines the standard functional map. A hyper-network predicts that network's weights, conditioned on the standard map. Training uses a new unsupervised spectral alignment loss. No ground truth correspondences are needed at any point. The module plugs into existing deep functional map pipelines seamlessly. Matching accuracy rises substantially in the demanding scenarios tested. Partiality, topological noise, and missing parts are handled far better.
arxiv-2606-30331:
Chen Jiang, Cody Covington, and Kalman Varga simulate how small water clusters break apart under an intense laser pulse. Clusters of one to four water molecules face the same few-cycle near-infrared pulse. Real-time density functional theory drives the electrons. Ehrenfest dynamics move the nuclei alongside them. The question is how cluster size reshapes the response.

Net ionization per molecule changes only weakly with cluster size. The proton and oxygen response changes far more dramatically. Hydrogen ejection rises sharply from the dimer to larger clusters. Stable hydrogen transfer is nearly absent in the dimer. It becomes substantial in the trimer and stronger in the tetramer. Larger clusters also respond earlier, within the pulse window itself. Dissociation propensity grows systematically with size by endpoint oxygen statistics. Size mainly reshapes the response through proton-mediated nuclear dynamics.
arxiv-2606-30731:
Riccardo Comi and Simone Rota identify the three-dimensional theory living on a special interface inside a four-dimensional supersymmetric gauge theory. The bulk theory is N=2 super-Yang-Mills with gauge group SU(N). Its renormalisation group wall separates the high-energy Lagrangian description from the low-energy Seiberg-Witten description, and the same three-dimensional theory also governs the low-energy physics of a half-BPS Dirichlet boundary condition. Comi and Rota show the interface theory is a 3d N=2 superconformal field theory.

It arises as a massive deformation of the T[SU(N)] theory, known as the S-duality interface of the N=4 theory. As validating tests, the authors match half-indices, quantities counting protected states, on both sides. They also check non-trivial consistency conditions that arise when such interfaces collide.
arxiv-2606-30931:
Anish Acharya, Kris W. Pan and Brian Verkhovsky harden juries of language models against a single bad judge. Panels of LLM evaluators that average consensus scores are a stand-in for human grading. But the authors show a flaw. Under a contamination model, one judge failing in a biased way, through mode collapse, sycophancy or safety refusal, gives the panel unbounded bias. RoPoLL keeps the panel but replaces averaging with a robust mean estimator, instantiated as the geometric median, which tolerates up to half the judges being wrong.

Across 13 judges from 4 to 675 billion parameters, three reward benchmarks and four corruption regimes up to 50%, RoPoLL beat the panel on every biased corruption type. On cross-dimensional attacks it won by about 19% at matched compute. A three-judge, 38-billion-parameter committee even beat a 675-billion model under corruption. A benign-noise control confirmed the premium targets bias, not imprecision.
arxiv-2606-31131:
Parashar and Fan generate test scenarios for self-driving systems from real crash records. Simulation testing usually searches over fixed mathematical scenario templates. Real-world testing needs hand-built templates, which take heavy manual effort. Crash records from regulators describe real failure conditions in plain language. The authors treat those records as raw material for new tests.

Their pipeline uses large language models in modular steps. It reads the categorical and contextual details in NHTSA crash records for automated driving systems. It then writes synthetic scenarios that fit the target system's testing constraints. In the MetaDrive simulator, the method produced varied scenarios across 4 road types and 3 movement types for other vehicles. Work zones appeared as on-road anomalies. Within a budget of just 20 scenarios, the tests exposed real failures of the navigation system.
arxiv-2606-31331:
Mestoukirdi and Corlay study when federated systems should pay for a second, richer round of inference. In vertical federated learning, each client sees a different view of the same sample, and fusing views means sending representations to a server. Fusing every sample wastes communication when a cheap first round already decides well.

Their expected gain router escalates a sample only when the predicted gain in correctness beats the extra cost. The score mixes a calibrated pooled posterior with classwise reliability figures from held-out data, so no separate routing network needs training. On multi-view benchmarks, including tests where views degrade, the router improves the communication-accuracy trade-off against confidence, learned-gain, and deferral baselines. The design keeps fusion for the samples where teamwork truly pays.
arxiv-2606-31531:
Harikumar and five colleagues ask whether gravitational wave lensing by globular clusters can reveal the clusters' own properties. A globular cluster in front of a merging black hole binary bends the wave in the wave-optics regime, stamping frequency-dependent marks on the signal. The team model clusters as singular isothermal spheres.

They simulate lensed versions of a GW150914-like signal and run Bayesian estimation with templates that fit source and lens together. The effective lensing mass comes back well, and with sky localization plus cluster catalogs it yields the cluster's central velocity dispersion. For favourable alignments the injected values land inside the credible intervals. Lensed waves could thus probe cluster dynamics in a way light-based methods cannot, motivating dedicated searches.
arxiv-2606-31631:
Bueno classifies a family of special surfaces in the product space formed by a sphere times a line. A lambda-translator is an oriented surface whose mean curvature, a measure of how it bends, equals a vertical projection term plus a constant lambda. Setting lambda to zero recovers translators, surfaces tied to mean curvature flow, a process that evolves shapes by their curvature.

Classification here means listing every surface of this type that stays unchanged under a one-parameter group of rotations and under vertical translations of the space. By working within that symmetry, Bueno reduces the geometric condition to equations that can be solved completely. Results of this kind map out which symmetric shapes can serve as translators, the building blocks used to understand singularities of curvature flow.
arxiv-2608-00131:
Xing and co-authors develop a theory for wrinkling in film-substrate systems with random stiffness. Stiff films on soft substrates wrinkle under load. Spatial shifts in film stiffness shape that instability strongly. Their homogenized theory treats one-dimensional systems with random bending stiffness. The stability equation takes a Lippmann-Schwinger form for the curvature field.

A strong-contrast expansion uses a local-nonlocal kernel split and a cavity-field form. Third-order truncation yields an effective polarizability and a dispersion relation. Those tools predict critical load and wavenumber. Tests against eigenvalue calculations and Fourier simulations validate the theory. Higher stiffness contrast lowers the critical load, they find. Wrinkles grow shorter as the instability shifts to higher wavenumbers. Wavelength rules depend on a ratio of two characteristic lengths.
arxiv-2608-00331:
Ahumada Acuña and co-authors constrain spin-1 ultralight dark matter with cosmological data. The model is a vector field with a small mass. They use Planck CMB data plus BAO and supernova distance probes. A full CMB temperature covariance matrix is derived as a key theory step. It includes anisotropic parts from the field's preferred direction.

Using the diagonal covariance part with CMB lensing, they bound the mass. The pure vector case gives a lower bound near ten to the minus 24 eV at 95 percent confidence. A mixed case with cold dark matter shows a clear fraction-mass correlation. Smaller fractions allow lighter masses there. Standard parameters stay consistent with the standard model. Mixed models may yield signals at Planck sensitivity, they note. Dedicated searches for that signature are motivated.
arxiv-2608-00431: Dombrowski proposes new Catalan multijections that yield different partitions. A Catalan multijection splits a set of objects into classes of size n plus one. Each class holds exactly one distinct Catalan object. Isaak and Langley had studied when two multijections give the same partitions, in work not yet published. His new constructions part from the ones found before. Readers get fresh cases for comparing multijection partitions.
audubon-ornithological-biography-vol1-18:
John James Audubon painted the birds of America, and his Ornithological Biography supplies their written lives. Volume one appeared in 1831 as the text companion to his great picture work. Audubon writes species accounts from years of field watching. Habits, nests, song, and range fill each account with fresh detail.

Frontier tales run between the science, drawn from his travels in wild America. He shot, drew, and watched birds from Labrador to the Gulf shores. The mix of story and study made the volumes famous on two continents. Volume one opens a five volume companion set. Readers who know the prints meet their author here. His energy fills every page.
christianity-and-islam-in-spain-a-d-756-:
C. R. Haines published his history at London in 1889, covering three centuries of Spain under Gothic and then Muslim rule. Chapter I runs from the barbarian invasions to an all-Gothic Spain. Councils, martyrs, Arian kings, and the power of clergy fill its summary. Chapter II brings the Saracen conquest, the battle of Guadalete, and treaties with the beaten towns.

The Caliphate of Cordova, founded by Abdurrahman, anchors the middle chapters. Christians under Muslim rule intermarried, adopted customs, and sometimes courted martyrdom. Nunilo and Alodia stand among the voluntary martyrs. Haines ends in recrimination: Archbishop Bernard of Toledo, after 1085, seized mosques that a capitulation treaty had reserved. Toleration and bigotry are weighed on both sides throughout.
cia-0000008631:
September 1972 brought a report of two downed American pilots sighted in Hoa Binh province, North Vietnam. Hoa Binh, southwest of Hanoi, saw heavy fighting and bombing across the war years. The sighting entered the files while the air war over the north was still intense.

Reports of downed pilots triggered checks against loss lists, unit records, and earlier sightings. A confirmed place could narrow a search or confirm a capture. Most sightings stayed fragments, useful only beside many others. Together they built the case files behind the POW and MIA accounting that outlasted the war itself.
cia-0000009531:
An American pilot beaten to death by North Vietnamese militiamen is recorded in a January 1972 CIA report. The heading adds that the death was attributed to a source the title cuts off. Pilots who parachuted into villages faced crowds before guards arrived.

Reports of killings after capture were logged as possible war crimes as well as losses. Each needed names, places, and witnesses solid enough to stand later. Many never reached that standard, yet the record was kept. The file preserves one brutal allegation in official form, part of the accounting of how captured men died.
cia-0000011831:
Across southern Africa in 1967, armed movements were rising against white minority rule, and a CIA paper that October surveys them country by country. Portugal still held Angola and Mozambique, Rhodesia's white government had defied Britain, and South Africa ruled itself and Namibia. Guerrilla groups in each territory were taking up arms with outside backing.

The survey weighs each movement's strength, its leaders, and its ties to communist states. It also judges their chances of winning power in the near term. The paper captures the start of bush wars that would reshape the whole region over the next two decades.
cia-0000012431:
A redacted person had dinner with Fedorenko on the evening of May 27, and a CIA note from April 1963 records the fact. Fedorenko moved in the Soviet diplomatic world the file watched. Dinner tables were working ground in Cold War diplomacy. Guest lists, seating, and table talk all carried intelligence value, and officers filed them as carefully as any cipher traffic.

The note preserves the social texture of that world in one line. Even suppers were intelligence, and the files treated them accordingly. For readers, the fragment shows how completely the watchers watched: down to who ate with whom.
cia-0000012831:
The communist bloc's aid programs, economic and military, are surveyed in a CIA paper from January 1963. Moscow and its allies were spending money and sending arms across Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Their checkbook was a weapon in the contest for the new nations, and Washington tracked the spending the way it tracked fleets and divisions.

The paper totals the bloc's generosity and maps its reach. It weighs credits, weapons, and technicians as moves in one game. For readers, it shows the Cold War fought with rubles as well as rockets, counted by the other side.
cia-0000013931: American prisoners of war were sighted in Quang Binh, Kontum, and Haiphong, in a CIA note dated January 3, 1968. The three places span North Vietnam's coast, the southern highlands, and the great port. A single note tying them together shows the sweep of the search. Each sighting pinned a prisoner report to one more point on the map.
cia-0000014631: Espionage charges against Alfred Sarant and Bruce Dayton anchor a CIA file dated January 5, 1951. The file concerns the probe of Sarant and his flight from questioning. Sarant had known Julius Rosenberg in college and in left wing circles. When agents closed in, Sarant slipped away, and the file follows that thread of the spy hunt.
cia-0000014731: The Seborer family is profiled in a CIA file dated January 1, 1961. The file gives highlights on Abraham Seborer and Jennie Scheine, born Chanover. Family sketches were a basic tool of the security files, mapping kin and ties. This one kept a family's record open a full decade after the great spy trials.
cia-0000015331: A letter to Lawrence Tacker from Philip Strong fills a CIA file dated January 2, 1961. Strong thanks Tacker for sending on his material, per the clipped title. The Tacker thread had run since 1958 in these files. A new year brought the same calm thanks and the same firm close. The Tacker letter is now held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015431: Release of CIA material on unidentified flying objects was the subject of an Air Force request logged August 4, 1966. The Air Force wanted agency material opened, and the file tracks that push. Such requests forced officials to weigh public curiosity against secret sources and methods. Coming in 1966, the request landed just as a new official study of saucers was taking shape.
cia-0000022331: Moscow claimed Powers flew for money and criticized his father, a CIA record dated in 1960 reports. The money charge aimed to strip the pilot of any sense of duty. Attacking his father widened the blow to the whole family. Such items show the trial being fought in print as much as in court during those weeks.
cia-0000027631: Probable political developments in West Germany during 1952 are forecast in a CIA paper dated in 1952. West Germany was three years old, led by Chancellor Adenauer, and still occupied in part. Its politics pointed toward joining the West in trade and defense. A forecast for 1952 judged whether that young state would hold its course or swing toward neutral ground.
cia-0000044431:
Villalobos commented on the killing of the Jesuits, in a CIA record dated October 5, 1989 in the catalog. Joaquin Villalobos was a senior commander of the FMLN rebels. A guerrilla chief's view of the crime came from the war's other side.

Inside, his account and judgment of the murders are preserved. The rebels blamed the army's death squads for the killings. Their version accused the state in the strongest terms they had. The file holds that version beside the government's, which is how the archive serves readers best: both stories present, and the weighing left to them.
cia-0000049131: The status of Aristides Alfonso Marquez Campos, named as an alleged member of a 1983 death squad, fills a CIA item from 1989. Status notes answered a plain question: where is this man now, free, held, fled, or dead. The item survives in the Truth Commission files, one line in a suspect's long entry.
cia-0000049331: Prospects for a rightist coup in El Salvador is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049331, dated November 5, 1980. Marked for the Truth Commission, the paper weighs the chance of such a coup. Readers find the agency's concern recorded in its heading alone, a brief early item from a tense period in Salvadoran politics preserved in the declassified files.
cia-0000102931: Use of Prison Labor in Installation of Pipelines in the Ukraine is the title of declassified CIA document 0000102931, dated July 4, 1982. The heading names one republic and one kind of work. The brief file shares its date with the Central Asian gas pipeline record, the pair showing two pipeline labor items filed on a single day.
cia-0000112331: Ufo's Reported Near Moscow is the short heading on declassified CIA document 0000112331, dated March 1, 1990. The title reports UFO sightings near Moscow, in four plain words. No witness or date for the sightings is named in the heading. The brief record is a UFO item, one of several such items filed in the spring of 1990.
cia-0000112831: Walter Schmalfuss - Subversive Activities is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112831, dated October 3, 1945. The title gives the full first name, Walter, where companion files use only Schmalfuss. Subversive activities is the charge paired with the name in the heading. The brief record is one of several Schmalfuss files from that autumn as released there.
cia-0000119731:
A September 1956 CIA report describes Hungarian public demonstrations growing into a political crisis. Street protests that autumn were swelling beyond anything the regime had faced. Within weeks they would grow into the full revolution of October.

The report tracks the crisis from its first public signs: crowds, demands, and a government losing control of the streets. Demonstration reports mattered because they measured pressure that official statements hid. For readers, this paper stands near the head of the Hungary file of 1956. It marks the point where private discontent became public action. The agency began reporting a revolution in the making rather than mere unrest.
cia-0000124331: A January 1957 CIA document weighs the possible release of American prisoners by the Chinese Communists. Years after the Korean armistice, a small number of Americans were still held in China. The paper judges whether Beijing was ready to let those men go. Release questions lingered because a handful of held men had become bargaining counters, and papers like this one tracked Beijing's price and mood over time.
cia-0000132231: Situation report 548, from January 1991, carries a deleted paragraph heading about Iraqi warplanes, the word breaking off in the title. Iraq's air force was about to face the coalition's full strength. The report preserves what the censors left of that item. Warplane items multiplied as the air campaign neared, each one a guess about whether Iraq would spend its air force early or hide it for later.
cia-0000132431:
Cuban-Soviet relations are examined in a CIA document dated January 3, 1960. Havana and Moscow were still feeling each other out at that point. Analysts watched every meeting and public statement for signs of a firmer commitment between the two governments.

Within months the careful courtship turned into a working alliance of trade, arms, and advisers. The document tracks its early steps, before either side had promised much in public. For readers, it captures the opening of a partnership that would shape the Cold War in the Americas. Few relationships of the era carried heavier consequences for Washington or lasted so long.
cia-0000135031: A set of recordings called the Sherwood Tapes fills a CIA paper carrying an estimated date of January 5, 1954. Tape was still a new tool for intelligence work in those years. The title gives no hint of what the tapes hold or whom they record. The short paper keeps the file in the bare form in which the record presents it.
cia-0000136031: 2 February 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA cable about briefing instructions for new trainees, the first lessons handed to the operation's fresh recruits. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. A reader gets the unpolished version here, complete with code names, short titles, and gaps left by the censors.
cia-0000136231: From 3 May 1954 comes a CIA cable, since declassified, on Instruction 5 for broadcast, one more script in the numbered series sent to LANGEVIN. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Later books on the coup rest on stacks of paper exactly like this, dated, coded, and only partly opened.
cia-0000136331: Forces quartered in Chiquimula were forced to withdraw, according to the radio material from 1700 on 27 June 1954 summarized here. Castillo reported patrols organizing south of the town and a strong column moving from Ipala to Quetzaltepeque that should be attacked from the air. Planes had not come out because of bad weather, and one group was told to hold position and avoid battle. Ignore the older note about Europe; the text is all Guatemala fighting.
cia-0000136731: This Spanish-language document from the 2506 Brigade files carries an estimated date of 6 March 1961, flagged in the catalog title. March was the brigade's final month of preparation before the Bay of Pigs landing. The record states no subject for the item. It is preserved in Spanish in the declassified release, its date a reviewer's estimate, as part of the brigade's last-phase paperwork.
cia-0000136931: Propaganda ideas for Central America are sent in this April 1954 cable. The sender is the agency's propaganda arm. The surviving text is fragmentary. It speaks of communist propaganda spread in Honduras. Agents were sent to create and sustain a static situation. It also warns of a people's militia. A complete takeover is the feared end. The full idea list is lost to garbling. Its purpose is plain, though. Regional unrest was to become anti-communist messaging.
cia-0000137331: A defected Cuban moderate's views fill this CIA briefing. It served the 14 April 1960 National Security Council meeting. The defector is completely disillusioned. He sees three alternatives for Cuba. Assassination is the worst thing, he says. Castro would become a martyr for young Cubans. Suicide is a very real possibility, he claims. It is always in Castro's mind, he says. A third course begins before the excerpt cuts off. The older note on this entry speaks of Hitler and Europe. That talk is invented; this is Cuba in 1960.
cia-0000139031: No close bond ties Russians and Chinese Communists in Manchuria. This July 1946 report asserts that view. It contradicts other files in this set. The Russians intend to use the Mongols, it says. They do not intend to rely on Chinese Communists. They have given the Communists only the poorest equipment. The excerpt breaks off mid-claim. The single page carries a low reliability grade. It usefully shows American reporting disagreeing with itself. Soviet intentions in 1946 were read in opposed ways.
cia-03002331:
Morocco leads a short Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 18 October 1955. A four-member Council of the Throne was installed on 17 October to exercise the sultan's functions. The bulletin judges the move unlikely to ease tension. The nationalist Istiqlal party denounced the council at once and refused to join the new government. French settler organisations objected from the other side.

President Rhee of Korea, in the second item, told the American embassy that leading American businessmen must be expelled. The stated reason was face, after a chamber of commerce attack on Korean taxation shamed the country. He asked the embassy to name the troublemakers. A third item reports Italy softening on recognising Communist China. The file is brief, and its scan is rough in places.
cia-03002531:
Japan opens the regional summary of the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 30 May 1954. Prime Minister Yoshida told Ambassador Allison on 27 May what he would argue in Washington and London. Close three-power cooperation on China, he held, could split Peiping from Moscow. His own survival in office, he hinted, depended on winning American economic aid in June.

A comment follows on the Formosa air alert of 29 May. The alert may have been real, or a Nationalist device to underline the need for more American help. French officers in Saigon expect an early assault on the Tonkin delta. Karachi prepares governor's rule for East Pakistan after an election rout. Guatemalans are accused of planting arms to frame an American plot. Regional sections organise the whole issue.
cia-03153731:
Britain's reaction to the Soviet earth satellite opens the Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 10 October 1957. London will press Washington for wider cooperation on military research and development. A Foreign Office official raised the matter with the American embassy on 7 October. If America refuses, Britain may build up the Western European Union's armaments machinery instead. Respect for Soviet science is noted as sharply increased.

Britain also reopens the question of troop reductions in West Germany. Warsaw is settling after riots touched off by the banning of a liberal student magazine. Gomulka refuses to lift the ban, and the technical university has reopened. Peiping proposes postponing the Sino-Burmese border settlement. Tribal unrest troubles Yemen. A standing section then reports the Taiwan Strait.
cia-03163331:
Nepal opens the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 1 May 1959. Recent agreements with the USSR bring Soviet aid and resident diplomatic missions to Katmandu. A small palace clique pushed them through while a leading Congress minister was absent. King Mahendra presumably backed the move, wanting wider foreign contacts. India, the brief warns, will worry more about its northern frontier.

An Afro-Asian economic conference committee votes against Soviet membership, and narrows its headquarters choice to Bombay and Cairo. Chinese Nationalists offer training and equipment to Karen dissidents in Burma. Rumours persist of Communist violence planned in Saigon against Western embassies. President Rhee closes South Korea's second-largest newspaper for attacking his government. Jordan's premier will demand his army chief's removal. Bourguiba seeks American arms after more French cross-border action from Algeria.
des-englischen-grafens-von-s-experimenti:
Secret chemical processes from a great lord's travels fill this German book, whose title page date reads MDCCXXII. The author is given only as an English count, Graf von S. A preface tells how the pieces were gathered on trips through Italy, France, and England at great cost.

The count visited the greatest laboratories and kept company with virtuosi and adepts, the preface says. His aim is to show the art of gold making plainly, in clear words and circumstances, not in dark allegory. One process joins the souls of gold and Mars with the spirit of mercury. Set in the sun, the liquor throws red rays out like the sun in the sky. The book sells court secrets to common readers of chemistry.
doe-osti-3729583-draft-asme-code-case-to:
Argonne report ANL-AMMT-028 drafts an ASME code case for laser powder bed fusion 316H steel in high-heat nuclear service. Mark Messner, Xuan Zhang, and Yiren Chen of Argonne wrote it with Heramb Mahajan of Idaho and Caleb Massey of Oak Ridge. The case would let printed parts serve in Section III, Division 5 Class A and SM roles. Test data from 2023 to 2026 spans several print sites, machines, and powder lots, all solution-annealed before testing.

Printed steel matched wrought 316H on strength and creep life, with little effect from build direction. Creep ductility fell sharply above about 650 degrees Celsius, tied to fast sigma phase growth. The draft qualifies plants in stages: process approval, part approval, then witness tests on each build. It treats printed parts like weld metal for design and checks. Watch items include long-term aging gaps and creep-fatigue hints in some lots.
europmc-pmc10161731:
Ruze and colleagues review the links between obesity and type 2 diabetes in a 2023 paper, covering spread, causes, and treatment. Both conditions have grown steadily more common across the world. They share genetic and lifestyle roots, and excess weight strongly raises the chance that diabetes will develop.

The review explains how stored fat, especially around inner organs, disrupts sugar control. It surveys treatments that address both conditions at once, from lifestyle change to surgery. The authors make the case for treating the pair as one problem. They argue that joint care gives better results.
europmc-pmc10172131:
Schneider, Lee, and Mathis present a method for analyzing animal behavior and brain activity together, in a 2023 study. Linking what an animal does to what its neurons do is a core goal of neuroscience. As recordings grow larger, scientists need models that can find shared patterns across both kinds of data.

Their method learns compact embeddings, or summaries, that capture behavior and neural signals in one frame. It can then relate movements to brain states in fine detail. The tool, called CEBRA, opens new ways to study how brains produce adaptive behavior.
europmc-pmc10439131:
Arora and colleagues mapped two zones of mouth tumours in 2023 and linked them to patient outcomes. The cancer is oral squamous cell carcinoma not tied to the HPV virus. The team read gene activity in single cells and in tissue, keeping each cell's place. They set the tumour core against its leading edge, the rim that pushes outward.

Each zone had its own gene profile and its own mix of nearby cells. The edge profile was much the same across many cancer types, while the core was tissue-specific. Arora found that a strong edge mark tied to worse survival in many cancers. The core mark tied to better outcomes. A model of cell growth in place also foretold drug response.
europmc-pmc10635831:
Blanco-Míguez and co-authors released MetaPhlAn 4 in 2023, a tool to name microbes in a sample. The tool reads DNA from a whole community at once, a method called metagenomics. Past versions could name only species in a fixed catalogue. Many real species have never been grown or named.

The new version draws on 1.01 million microbe genomes, from lab strains and sample builds. Blanco-Míguez defines marker genes for 26,970 species-level groups. Of those, 4,992 have no species name yet. The tool explains about 20% more of the DNA in human gut samples than before. In farm animal guts the gain passed 40%. It can even track single strains of unnamed species.
europmc-pmc10700131:
Merchant and co-authors scaled deep learning in 2023 to find new stable materials. New crystals drive gains from chips to batteries, yet trial-and-error hunts are slow and costly. The team trained graph networks, AI that learns from atom links, on a far larger scale than past work. Their base held 48,000 known stable crystals.

The models flagged 2.2 million new structures as stable, an order-of-magnitude leap. Merchant reports that 736 of them had in fact been made in labs on their own. Top finds will be shared for screening toward uses such as layered materials and battery electrolytes. The same scale yielded atom force models of high accuracy for later studies.
europmc-pmc1084331:
Hippenmeyer and co-authors probe timing in nerve growth in this 2005 mouse study. Dorsal root ganglion neurons are nerve cells that carry touch and body signals to the spine. Two gene switches, called ETS factors, switch on late in their growth under signals from their targets. These switches guide late steps such as reaching the target and branching.

The team forced the switches on too early in young nerve cells. Early switching warped the wires' paths and blocked the cells from gaining their final traits, they found. It also changed how much the cells leaned on growth support factors. The authors conclude that nerve cells pass through a timed switch in how they answer these signals. Getting the timing right, they say, is part of normal nerve wiring.
europmc-pmc11446831:
Schlegel and a large team annotate every neuron class in the fruit fly brain in this 2024 paper. The FlyWire project had mapped the wiring of about 140,000 neurons in the fly brain. Wiring alone does not say what each cell is. The team added a systematic annotation, in a hierarchy, of cell types, neuronal classes, and developmental lineages.

The count came to 8,453 cell types. Of these, 3,643 matched types proposed in an earlier partial map, they report. Another 4,581 are new, mostly from regions the earlier map lacked. About one third of the earlier types could not be reliably reidentified, despite matching cell shapes. The authors therefore propose a new definition: a cell type must be more similar across two brains than to any other cell within the same brain. They validate it by jointly analysing both connectomes.
europmc-pmc1183531:
Hansen and colleagues screened the roundworm C. elegans for long life genes in 2005. Most aging knowledge came from mutants found for other reasons. That history could bias what scientists think aging is. A full genome screen offered a fairer test.

The screen found 23 new genes that extend worm lifespan. They touch signals, stress defense, gene control, and metabolism. Eating less seemed to work by quieting certain key genes. Hansen also flags a hormone path tied to a known aging switch. Nearly all new genes fit known paths, which supports past work.
europmc-pmc1280331:
Delfino, Sioutas, and Malik weighed ultrafine particles in heart harm from air pollution in 2005. Daily studies link particle mass to heart admissions and deaths. Panel studies add links to ischemia, blood pressure, and rhythm changes. The exact causal component stayed unidentified.

Ultrafine particles under 0.1 micrometers dominate particle counts and surface area. That surface can carry large loads of toxic pollutants. Combustion products show up in the indirect evidence so far. The authors argue reactive cargo in ultrafines reaches heart targets. Fossil fuel combustion sits at the center of their case. Panel data back the time trend data well.
europmc-pmc1464831:
Even mice with the same genes gain weight in unlike ways on a rich diet. Koza and co-authors used that spread in 2006 to hunt for non-gene drivers of obesity. Male mice on a high-fat diet showed a four-fold spread in body fat. High and low gainers could be told apart at six weeks, before the rich diet began.

Fat samples taken at seven weeks showed gene activity gaps that foretold later fat gain. Genes in the Wnt signal path and tissue reshaping stood out. Koza points to one Wnt blocker, SFRP5, among others. The team proposes that fat tissue holds marks that set obesity risk.
europmc-pmc1750931:
HIV builds its new particles at the cell's outer skin, not in inner compartments. Jouvenet and co-authors settled that debate in 2006. Prevailing models held that assembly starts on late endosomes, inner membrane sacs, and rides outward.

Blocking endosome movement did not stop the viral protein Gag reaching the surface or virions being released. Targeting assembly to the surface worked; targeting it to endosomes did not. Gag first gathered at the surface, and the share later seen inside had been swallowed back. Jouvenet concludes assembly begins and completes at the plasma membrane.
europmc-pmc1808431:
Han and Boyden added in 2007 a second color of light control over brain cells. Their earlier tool, channelrhodopsin-2, lets blue light switch targeted neurons on. A matching off switch, driven by a different color, would let researchers shape exact firing patterns in living circuits.

They used Halo, a light-driven chloride pump from the salt microbe Natronomas pharaonis, tuned for use in animal cells. Yellow light pulses silenced neurons carrying Halo reliably and reversibly, within milliseconds. Cells carrying both tools could be driven through precise sequences of firing and silence by alternating blue and yellow pulses. That allowed the team to break up synchronized firing without changing overall spike rates. No added chemicals were needed for either switch.
europmc-pmc1969431:
Simon and Altman wrote in 1994 a guidance editorial on the statistics of prognostic factor studies in cancer. Such studies ask which traits, from tumor size to molecular markers, predict a patient's outcome. They fill much of the oncology literature and can reveal disease mechanisms or guide hard treatment choices.

A sound prognostic study can flag patients at high enough risk of recurrence to justify a toxic or costly therapy. Major prognostic determinants also sharpen the design of later clinical trials, make trials comparable with each other, and ground the counseling of patients. As leaders at a national cancer institute and a major statistics laboratory, the authors set out the statistical standards these studies should meet. Their editorial anchors a special series on statistics in cancer research in the journal.
europmc-pmc2002031:
Wu, Paganini-Hill, Ross and Henderson tracked colorectal cancer risk in 1987 in a retirement community. Their prospective study followed 11,888 residents for four and a half years.
