During that time 58 men and 68 women developed colorectal cancer. The team examined alcohol, body weight, activity and several nutrients as possible causes.

Daily alcohol drinkers had nearly twice the risk of others. Higher body mass, measured by Quetelet index, also raised risk. Leisure physical activity lowered it. These patterns held for both sexes but reached significance only in men. Most nutrients showed no link. People with three or more children had a markedly lower risk, with a relative risk of 0.45, and confidence limits excluding no effect.
europmc-pmc2048531:
Morschhäuser and colleagues found in 2007 the switch behind drug resistance in the yeast Candida albicans. This fungus often resists fluconazole, a common antifungal drug, by overproducing a pump called MDR1. The pump ejects toxic compounds from the cell. Why the pump gene stays switched on in resistant clinical strains was unknown. The team compared gene activity across resistant and sensitive isolates.

A regulator gene, MRR1, rose together with MDR1 in resistant strains. Deleting MRR1 in two resistant isolates abolished both pump production and resistance. Resistant strains carried single-letter changes in MRR1, at positions 683 and 997. Adding those changed versions to a sensitive strain switched the pump on permanently. Many MRR1 target genes make oxidoreductases, enzymes that may limit drug damage.
europmc-pmc2125231:
Moyer S. Fleisher and Leo Loeb of the Barnard Free Skin and Cancer Hospital in St. Louis produced liver necrosis at will in guinea pigs in 1914. Injections into the veins of substances of very different character (leech extract among them) all left multiple dead patches in the liver. In the mouse the same substances did little or nothing.

The patches sit between the portal and central zones of the liver lobules. Control animals rarely show the lesion, and then mostly after some injury. One mercy: the dead areas organize into connective tissue and quietly vanish within weeks, without scarring the surface or ending in cirrhosis. Readers get a liver injury that many poisons share, compared by the authors to the stomach ulcers toxins raise in the same animal.
europmc-pmc2125331:
J. Bronfenbrenner of the Western Pennsylvania Hospital in Pittsburgh pursued the nature of anaphylatoxin in 1915, the poison Friedberger had shown arising when antigen, antibody, and complement unite. His experiments mix fresh serum from pregnant or immunized animals with the matching boiled protein and watch poison form.

The poison's origin is the surprise: it comes from the serum, not from the protein partner. Serum left to digest itself, once its antitrypsin guard is removed (specifically or not), yields the toxin. Such poisons harm only animals of the same species as the serum. Let the self-digestion run long enough and it passes beyond the toxic stage entirely. One experiment sets rabbit and guinea pig sera against boiled human placenta, male serum standing as control. Readers get anaphylaxis's poison reclassified as the blood digesting itself.
europmc-pmc2130931:
Peter K. Olitsky reported growing the agent of mosaic disease of tobacco and tomato plants in laboratory culture. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1925. The agent in plant tissue causes disease at strong dilution but only rarely beyond it, which gave him a yardstick for true growth in his tubes.

Carried from tube to tube of his special medium, the agent was diluted far past any effective limit. Yet the remote subplants still induced mosaic as fast and as strongly as undiluted material. Plants sickened by the culture fluid passed the disease to further plants, and the agent could be propagated again from those. One odd fact stood out: the agent in the remote subplants was not readily filterable, unlike its state in plant juice. Something changes in its condition during culture. The increase across dilutions, Olitsky argues, is good reason to call this true cultivation.
europmc-pmc2131231:
Bronfenbrenner and Muckenfuss published part eight of their bacteriophage studies in The Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1927. Twort and Gratia had reported that dead staphylococci can still dissolve when living ones and a fitting phage are present. The pair set out to learn how that odd event works, and what controls it.

Dead bacteria dissolved only alongside living bacteria of the same kind, and the balance of numbers mattered. Too many dead cells soaked up the phage before it could start changes in the living ones, and then nothing dissolved at all. A membrane between the two groups blocked the effect. The agent that acts on dead cells does not pass through. The agent that starts lysis in living cells crosses freely.
europmc-pmc2131431:
Annie Luverne Harris, John Sugg, and James Neill, at Vanderbilt University Medical School, compared antibody responses in mice and rabbits in a 1928 paper. Both animal kinds were immunized with typical Type III pneumococci or with a strain close to Type III but not the same. Part two of their series asks whether one germ is simply stronger than the other as an antigen.

The answer depended on the animal. In rabbits, the related strain drew the better antibody response. In mice, the typical Type III strain worked more effectively. The same pair of near-identical germs thus ranked in opposite order in the two hosts. The authors present the case as a clear instance of host species shaping the value of a bacterial antigen.
europmc-pmc2140631:
Samuel Brody, at the University of Missouri in Columbia, wrote on the kinetics of senescence in a 1924 paper. Senescence is the decline of vitality with age. Brody defines vitality as the reciprocal of senescence and asks what curve the decline follows once growth no longer masks it.

Untangled from growth, the decline follows a simple exponential law, the same shape as a monomolecular chemical change. At any moment, vitality stands at a constant percentage of its value the moment before, whatever the age. During the growing years the vitality index rises instead. The full life curve, rising then falling, can often be matched by an equation with two exponential terms, like two chemical reactions running in sequence.
europmc-pmc2360431:
Frattini and colleagues looked for markers that predict who benefits from cetuximab in spread colon cancer in 2007. Cetuximab blocks EGFR, a growth receptor on tumor cells. The team checked three parts of that signal path in 27 treated patients: EGFR itself, the K-Ras gene, and a brake protein called PTEN.

Ten patients had their tumors shrink on the drug. Every patient whose tumor had lost PTEN gained nothing, a pattern the statistics flagged as strong. All 16 patients with normal PTEN included the 10 responders. Extra copies of the EGFR gene also marked likely responders, with six of eight such patients shrinking. A mutated K-Ras gene pointed the other way, with only one responder among 10 cases. The authors presented PTEN loss as a new warning sign of non-response.
europmc-pmc2483731:
Novaes and colleagues produced the first broad gene survey of the eucalyptus tree Eucalyptus grandis in 2008. This species is the world's most planted hardwood, yet its genome was uncharacterised. The team sequenced expressed genes, the stretches of DNA actually read in cells, using fast 454 pyrosequencing.

They generated 148 million bases of sequence from mixed tissues and tree varieties, finding matches to almost half of all known genes in the model plant Arabidopsis. Comparing reads across varieties exposed 23,742 single-letter variants, called SNPs, and lab checks confirmed 83% of a tested sample as real. Diversity in protein-changing positions ran about four times lower than in silent positions, the fingerprint of purifying selection weeding out harmful changes. The catalogue fed the United States Department of Energy's effort to sequence the full eucalyptus genome.
europmc-pmc2567431:
Ku and colleagues mapped in 2008 how two silencing machines, the Polycomb complexes PRC1 and PRC2, sit on DNA in embryonic stem cells. Stem cell genes for development are often held in a poised state called bivalent, carrying both activating and repressing chemical marks. The team charted these marks and both complexes across the genomes of human and mouse stem cells.

Bivalent regions split into two classes: those bound by both complexes and those bound by PRC2 alone. The doubly bound class kept its repressive mark more stubbornly when cells specialised, and it covered nearly all the key developmental regulator genes. Computer analysis showed the complexes' landing spots could largely be predicted from CpG islands, stretches of DNA rich in particular letters. Large islands lacking activating signals seemed to recruit the full silencing set.
europmc-pmc2605931:
Teixeira, Ferreira, and Ashburner reported in 2008 that a common insect bacterium, Wolbachia, protects fruit flies against RNA viruses. Wolbachia live inside cells, pass from mother to offspring, and are famous for manipulating host reproduction. In the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster no strong effect had been found, so discovering protection was unexpected.

Flies carrying Wolbachia resisted Drosophila C virus and carried lower virus loads than uninfected flies. The protection extended to two other RNA viruses, Nora virus and Flock House virus. It did not extend to a DNA virus tested. This is the first strong beneficial effect of Wolbachia reported in this fly. The authors argue that shielding hosts from natural viruses may explain why Wolbachia is so widespread in wild insect populations.
europmc-pmc2630331:
Meyer, Lafitte, and Bontempi released a software package called minet in 2008 for reconstructing gene networks from microarray data. The package works in R and Bioconductor and builds networks where genes are nodes and edges represent statistical dependence between their activity levels. Dependence is measured by mutual information, a quantity capturing how much knowing one gene's activity tells you about another's.

Minet offers four ways to estimate that information from data, from a simple empirical estimator to a shrinkage estimator. On top of these it implements four network inference methods: relevance networks, ARACNE, CLR, and MRNET, which differ in how they prune indirect links. The package also integrates accuracy tools. These include F-scores and ROC and precision-recall curves. They compare an inferred network against a trusted reference. It is freely available.
europmc-pmc2671031:
Garrido and colleagues reviewed in 2009 the mismatch negativity, a brain wave that fires when a sound breaks an expected pattern. Play a stream of identical tones with one odd note slipped in, and the brain produces this wave even if the listener pays no attention. It measures how well the brain learns sound rules and notices change.

Two explanations had long competed. One says nerve cells simply tire of the repeated tone, and fresh cells answer the odd one. The other says the brain builds a model of the pattern and flags a mismatch against it. The review weighs the proof for each and offers a unifying frame called predictive coding. In that view, the brain constantly predicts incoming sound and passes surprises upward. Tiring and model updating then become two sides of one process, not rivals.
europmc-pmc2687931:
Samuels and Szabadi reviewed in 2008 the locus coeruleus, a tiny blue-tinted cluster of brain cells that supplies most of the brain's noradrenaline, a wakefulness chemical. Despite its size, this nucleus sends fibers almost everywhere. It sits at the crossing of two jobs. One is keeping us aroused. The other is steering the body's automatic systems, such as heart and gut.

Part two of their review covers what pushes the nucleus up or down in living people. Pain, threat, and temperature extremes fire it up, as do stimulant drugs and medicines that block noradrenaline recycling. Sedatives and drugs that press its own brake receptors quiet it, bringing drowsiness and a shift toward the rest-and-digest mode. The nucleus also fails early in aging, Parkinson disease, and Alzheimer disease, which may explain some of those illnesses' sleep and mood symptoms.
europmc-pmc2697331:
Reimann and colleagues studied single gut L cells in 2008. These cells release GLP-1. That hormone boosts insulin and helps control blood sugar in type 2 diabetes. Drugs mimicking GLP-1 already treat diabetes, but coaxing the body to release more of its own supply needs basic knowledge of how these scattered cells sense glucose.

The team bred mice whose L cells glow, fished them out pure, and probed them with electrodes and calcium imaging. Single L cells fired electrically and answered glucose directly. Their behavior pointed to two sensors: a sodium-glucose transporter that hauls sugar in, and potassium channels that close when energy is plentiful, the same design the pancreas uses. Gene readings confirmed both parts run high in these cells. Each identified pathway, the authors note, is a possible handle for future diabetes drugs.
europmc-pmc2697631:
Banks reviewed in 2009 what lets a compound cross the blood-brain barrier, the sealed vessel lining that guards the brain. Most brain drugs are small, fat-loving molecules that slip through cell membranes by diffusion, a route that never fills up. But that is only one of several doors, and the others decide the fate of modern large-molecule drugs.

Transport systems ferry chosen cargo across and boost uptake roughly tenfold, but they can be saturated, and illness changes their settings. Pumps also push many compounds back out, an exit system that silently defeats drugs. Blood flow, protein binding in plasma, and enzymes at the barrier further trim what arrives. Banks details two newer delivery hopes: short DNA-like drugs and replacement enzymes, both with newly found transporters. The review doubles as a design brief for getting medicines into the brain.
europmc-pmc2698831:
Verstraelen and co-authors followed 100 pregnant women in 2009 to learn which vaginal bacteria keep the vaginal community stable. A healthy vagina is dominated by lactobacilli, friendly bacteria that hold rivals down. In some women the balance flips mid-pregnancy toward abnormal flora, a state tied to early birth risk. Swabs were taken three times across pregnancy.

Seventy-seven women started with normal flora. Thirteen of them flipped to abnormal by the second or third visit. The starting species mix predicted the flip strikingly. Women whose flora lacked the species Lactobacillus crispatus were about ten times more likely to flip. Flora built on L. gasseri or L. iners carried the same raised risk, while crispatus-based flora was fivefold protected. Not all lactobacilli guard equally, the authors conclude; identity matters, not just presence.
europmc-pmc2702831:
Cani and colleagues tested in 2009 whether changing gut microbes, the tiny living things in the bowel, can calm swelling in obese mice. Obese mice often have a leaky gut wall, so bits of bacteria pass into blood and drive low-level swelling. The team focused on a gut hormone called GLP-2 that helps keep the gut wall strong.

Mice fed prebiotics, foods that feed good gut microbes, had lower blood markers of swelling and a tighter gut wall. Blocking GLP-2 wiped out most of that gain, while giving GLP-2 alone copied it. The work ties microbe shifts to better gut barrier health through GLP-2 in these mice.
europmc-pmc2736831:
Loupakis and co-authors tested in 2009 whether extra mutations in KRAS and BRAF genes predict resistance to two drugs in metastatic colorectal cancer. Those drugs are cetuximab plus irinotecan. The cancer is of the large bowel and has spread. Mutations in KRAS codons twelve and thirteen, gene positions, were already known to block benefit from anti-EGFR antibody drugs. Other KRAS positions and BRAF were less certain.

Among eighty-seven patients lacking the known mutations, eight carried KRAS changes at codons sixty-one or one hundred forty-six, and none of them responded. None of thirteen patients with the BRAF mutation responded either, while about a third of mutation-free patients did. Mutation carriers also progressed sooner, which supports wider gene testing before treatment.
europmc-pmc2746531:
Antoniou and co-authors built in 2002 a comprehensive model of familial breast cancer that includes BRCA1, BRCA2, and other genes, for use in genetic counselling. Carrier probability calculations must allow that other susceptibility genes may exist beyond the two known ones. They fitted models to a population series of cases and to high-risk families in the United Kingdom with known mutation status.

BRCA1 and BRCA2 alone could not explain all family clustering seen. A polygenic effect, many small-effect genes acting together, fit the remaining familial risk best, though a single recessive gene fit almost as well. Other genes also significantly modified risk in BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers. Estimated breast cancer risk by age seventy averaged about one third for BRCA1 carriers and about one half for BRCA2 carriers.
europmc-pmc2793031:
Li and co-authors showed in 2010 how a tiny RNA called miR-30 helps control when cells die. MicroRNAs are short RNA pieces that dial down gene activity. The team focused on fission, the splitting of mitochondria, the cell's energy units, which helps trigger apoptosis, a form of planned cell death.

Members of the miR-30 family blocked fission and slowed cell death in the experiments. They did so by holding down p53, a protein that switches on a splitting protein named Drp1. When death signals arrived, miR-30 levels fell and p53 rose, freeing Drp1 to split mitochondria. The chain gives a clear new route by which small RNAs steer cell death.
europmc-pmc2829031:
Mercer and colleagues tracked long noncoding RNAs during brain cell development in 2010. These long RNA strands never become proteins, yet they help steer which genes switch on. The team followed mouse neural stem cells as they split into neurons and oligodendrocytes, the cells that wrap nerve fibers in insulation.

Many noncoding RNAs rose and fell at set stages of each fate path, including the insulation-building stages. They clustered near key development genes and matched those genes' timing, and some sat in known control regions or nuclear landmarks. A drug that blocks insulation-cell maturation by reshaping chromatin, the DNA packaging, also shifted the RNA patterns. The work links these RNAs directly to fate decisions and rewiring in stem cells.
europmc-pmc2831931:
Clark and colleagues asked in 2010 whether breathing polluted air before birth and in the first year of life helps cause asthma, rather than just triggering attacks. Their study followed every child born in 1999 and 2000 across southwestern British Columbia, over thirty-seven thousand children, checking health records for asthma diagnoses by age three or four.

About nine percent of the children developed asthma. Risk climbed with early exposure to carbon monoxide, nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide, coarse particles, sulfur dioxide, and black carbon, and with living near pollution sources. Traffic-related pollutants carried the highest risks of all. The authors read the pattern as support for a role of early-life air pollution in causing the disease.
europmc-pmc2865531:
Eckerle and co-authors disabled the proofreading tool of the SARS coronavirus in 2010 and watched its copying accuracy collapse. Most RNA viruses copy with many errors, but coronaviruses carry an enzyme, in a protein called nsp14, that can snip out mistakes. The team engineered viruses lacking that snipping activity and read their full genomes after growth in culture.

The mutant viruses grew with stable defects and made about twenty-one times as many copying errors as the normal virus. Mutations piled up across the genome during passage, far beyond what the intact virus allows. The result proves the enzyme guards the large coronavirus genome. It also shows how much error the virus can bear before fitness fades. Drug designers hope to push the virus past that limit.
europmc-pmc2913331:
Cassano and co-authors built in 2010 computer models that predict whether a chemical can harm a developing baby, for Europe's REACH chemical safety law. REACH demands assessment of thousands of market chemicals, and developmental toxicity testing is among the slowest, costliest, and most animal-heavy. Their CAESAR project trained quantitative structure-activity models, which infer toxicity from molecular structure, on curated experimental data.

Two models using different mathematics, a random forest and a fuzzy partitioning method, both classified chemicals well. The designers deliberately tuned them to minimize false negatives, the dangerous error of clearing a harmful chemical, even at the price of extra false alarms. The random forest model was placed in a free online application, so industry chemists and regulators can screen a structure in seconds before any animal test.
europmc-pmc2948931:
Rakhshandehroo and co-authors reviewed the target genes of PPAR-alpha, a fat-sensing switch protein, in a 2010 article. The switch responds to fatty acids and to fibrate drugs used to lower blood fats, and it reshapes gene activity across many pathways.

Because the switch works by turning target genes up or down, its roles in burning fat, handling energy, and calming inflammation all trace back to those genes. The review organises the known and likely targets gene by gene, with emphasis on the liver where the switch is busiest. Readers get a map for judging new drugs and diet effects.
europmc-pmc2953531:
Collins and colleagues hunted signalling peptides in the flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea in a 2010 genome and peptide study. Planarians can switch between sexual and non-sexual reproduction and rebuild reproductive organs, hinting at flexible chemical control.

Combining genome scans with direct peptide measures, they logged more than two hundred candidate nerve peptides. One conserved peptide proved necessary for the reproductive system to mature and stay functional. Because related parasites also reshape breeding in response to conditions, the worm's peptide set offers leads. It may help explain flatworm breeding control. It could even help break parasite life cycles.
europmc-pmc2987831:
Katzourakis and Gifford screened animal genomes for viral fossils, DNA copied from viruses into the germ line and inherited like ordinary genes, in a 2010 study. Retroviruses were famous for this trick, while other virus families were thought to rarely leave such traces.

Computer screening turned up elements from ten non-retroviral families, including first examples for several major virus kinds and the first DNA virus fossils in mammal genomes. Family trees of the fossils revealed fresh detail on virus origins. Some elements still hold intact genes or are switched on, and one primate element shows strong signs of being put to host use.
europmc-pmc2998531:
Wang and colleagues built prediction tools for how strongly small protein pieces bind the immune display molecules HLA DR, DP, and DQ in a 2010 study. Such predictions shortlist candidate targets from germs, allergens, and tumours, but DP and DQ had been neglected.

They measured binding for tens of thousands of peptide and molecule pairs, more than doubling the data for the neglected types. Learning methods trained on the enlarged set predicted binding for all three families about equally well, with accuracy up over earlier reports thanks to the bigger training pool. They warn that near-duplicate peptides in tests inflate scores.
europmc-pmc3048531:
Greaves and the IMAGE study group reviewed in 2011 what makes diet and activity programs work for people at risk of type 2 diabetes. Rather than reviewing single trials, they reviewed thirty existing reviews covering a decade of work, and extracted well over a hundred analyses that tied program features to results. Programs on average produced modest weight loss and a real rise in weekly activity.

Features tied to better results included enlisting social support and targeting food and movement together. Programs worked better with more frequent contact and with a cluster of self control techniques such as setting goals and tracking one's own behavior. Setting, delivery style, and who delivered the program showed no clear effect. The authors note that keeping new habits going needs more attention, and they advise program funders to require the proven ingredients.
europmc-pmc3130631:
Teresa Hart and colleagues worked out how many days of activity tracking older adults need in a 2011 paper. Studies link daily movement and sitting time to health, but guessing habits from a single day misleads. Fifty-two adults around age seventy wore two motion devices and kept activity logs for three straight weeks.

Three days of one motion sensor and four days of a step counter or written log captured usual activity levels well. Judging sitting time took longer, needing five days of sensor data. Differences between weekdays were small but not zero, so very short tracking windows still carry risk. The paper gives designers of aging studies a clear, tested minimum for believable activity estimates.
europmc-pmc3131731:
Stefano Ferrari and colleagues reviewed an inherited eye disease group in a 2011 paper in Current Genomics. The condition slowly destroys the light-sensing cells of the retina, starting with night vision and side vision, and often ends in blindness by middle age. It strikes roughly one person in several thousand and can pass through families in three different patterns.

More than forty genes have been tied to the disease, most of them working in the light sensors or their supporting layer. Different faults in the same gene can cause different diseases, which tangles efforts to match a patient's genes to their outlook. The review maps the known genes and fault mechanisms, arguing that better gene-to-symptom matching will guide future treatment choices.
europmc-pmc3148231:
Dwi Karolina and colleagues fingered a tiny RNA as a driver of insulin failure in type two diabetes in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Small RNAs that tune gene activity drift out of balance in many diseases. The team profiled them across tissues and blood in diabetic rats, then checked blood from men with early and full diabetes.

Eight small RNAs formed a signature separating healthy, pre-diabetic, and diabetic samples. One stood out as sharply raised in blood, and its level matched falling levels of a key insulin-signalling protein in target tissues. Direct tests confirmed the small RNA switches that protein off. The work suggests blood small RNAs can flag metabolic trouble early and points to one culprit worth blocking.
europmc-pmc3150331:
Kira Makarova and colleagues unified the protein families of a bacterial immune system in a 2011 paper in Biology Direct. Most archaea and many bacteria carry this system, which stores snippets of invader DNA and uses RNA copies of them to destroy matching viruses. Its proteins are numerous, diverse, and fast-changing, which had tangled classification.

Comparing sequences and shapes across species revealed hidden kinships. A major protein clan split neatly into three large groups. The big subunits of most systems proved related to one family, with an active copying domain in some types and a silenced one in others. Since many parts share a common RNA-gripping core, the authors propose the system began in heat-loving archaea and spread sideways between microbes.
europmc-pmc3230631:
Giuseppe Esposito and colleagues tested how cannabidiol, a cannabis compound without mind-altering effects, protects rat brains from amyloid damage, in this 2011 study in PLoS ONE. The compound had shown promise in Alzheimer's models, but its mechanism was unclear. The team focused on a receptor called PPAR-gamma, recently suggested as cannabidiol's binding partner.

In rats given beta-amyloid, cannabidiol reduced the inflammatory reaction in brain support cells and the neuronal damage that followed. When the researchers blocked PPAR-gamma with antagonists, those protective effects were largely blunted, showing the receptor is required. Through the same receptor, cannabidiol also stimulated the birth of new neurons in the hippocampus, the brain's memory center. The findings pin the compound's benefits to this pathway.
europmc-pmc3257631:
James Lattimer and Mark Haub reviewed dietary fiber and metabolic health in this 2010 article in Nutrients. Fiber and whole grains carry a distinctive mix of resistant starches, vitamins, minerals, and plant chemicals. Population and clinical studies consistently tie higher fiber intake to lower rates of obesity, type 2 diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease, and the authors examine the evidence component by component.

Even defining fiber turns out to depend on whether the lens is nutritional or analytical. The review separates fiber into fractions such as arabinoxylan, inulin, pectin, bran, cellulose, beta-glucan, and resistant starch, and asks what each contributes. Proposed mechanisms include thicker gut contents, slower nutrient absorption, faster transit, and the short-chain fatty acids and gut hormones fiber produces. The authors note where studies disagree and where the case is firmest.
europmc-pmc3291531:
Liu and a large team studied a gene tied to inherited Parkinson disease, publishing their findings in 2012. Changes in the gene, called PINK1, cause some early onset cases, and earlier work linked it to the health of mitochondria, the cell's power plants. What remained unclear was how its roles fit together, so the team tested it in fruit flies and in human cells grown in the lab.

They found that PINK1 also controls how mitochondria move along nerve fibers. In flies, lowering a transport protein called Miro rescued many defects caused by faulty PINK1, while extra Miro alone killed dopamine producing nerve cells. In human cells, PINK1 worked with a second disease gene to tag Miro for removal, linking movement control to the cleanup of damaged mitochondria.
europmc-pmc3406031:
Gauffin Cano, Santacruz, Moya, and Sanz tested in 2012 whether a gut bacterium could undo the damage of a fatty diet in mice. Obesity is tied to shrunken numbers of Bacteroidetes bacteria in the gut, but cause and effect were unproven. Obese mice on a high-fat diet received the strain Bacteroides uniformis CECT 7771 daily for seven weeks.

Treated mice gained less weight, stored less fat and cholesterol in the liver, and showed smaller fat cells. Blood sugar, insulin, and cholesterol readings all improved, and the mice absorbed less dietary fat. Immune defenses dulled by obesity recovered as well. The strain also partly restored the gut community the diet had disturbed.
europmc-pmc3470931:
Jackson, Riley, and White weighed the promise of multivariate meta-analysis in Statistics in Medicine in 2011. Standard meta-analysis pools one outcome at a time, but medical studies often measure several linked outcomes, such as survival with and without disease return. Pooling them jointly can sharpen estimates, at the cost of more assumptions about how the outcomes relate.

The paper grew out of a one-day meeting where statisticians aired hopes and doubts about the approach. Four examples show where joint pooling helps and where it can mislead. Jackson's team concludes the methods hold real potential and can give estimates with better properties. Still, they urge even more care than with ordinary meta-analysis, since wrong assumptions undo the gains.
europmc-pmc3472231:
Williamson and colleagues laid out the issues in building core outcome sets for clinical trials, in Trials in 2012. Trials in the same field often measure different outcomes, which blocks fair comparison and lets authors report only flattering results. A core outcome set is an agreed minimum list that every trial in an area should measure and report.

The authors cover how to set the scope of such a set and whose voices must be heard, including patients and the public. They also discuss how to run the agreement process and judge when agreement is real. Williamson's team stresses that core sets add a floor, not a ceiling, and that trials remain free to measure more. Wider use would raise the value of each trial.
europmc-pmc3492331:
Overweight patients say doctors treat them worse, and Janice A. Sabin, Maddalena Marini, Brian A. Nosek, and Richard Fielding measure doctors' own weight attitudes in 2012. Their data come from the Project Implicit website, where volunteers take the Weight Implicit Association Test; 2,284 of the test-takers identified as medical doctors.

Doctors show strong implicit anti-fat bias, with an effect size of 0.93, nearly matching the general public's 1.0. Stated attitudes agree: a strong preference for thin over fat people. Results hold across doctors' own body mass, race, and gender groupings. Bias as deep in medicine as outside it, the authors conclude, deserves attention as a driver of unequal care.
europmc-pmc3558331:
Geoff Wong, Trish Greenhalgh, and colleagues published publication standards for realist syntheses in BMC Medicine in 2013, from the RAMESES project. Realist synthesis is a review method that tries to explain why complex programs succeed, fail, or do mixed work in real settings. No agreed reporting standard existed for this kind of review, so weak reporting could hide weak methods.

Building the standard took several steps. The group read the existing guidance, checked how thirty-five published syntheses had followed it, gave live help to nine ongoing reviews, and ran a three-round Delphi survey, a structured vote among experts. The result is a set of steps and reporting rules for authors of realist reviews. Journals, reviewers, and research teams get a shared checklist for judging whether such a review was done and described well.
europmc-pmc3650931:
Homebound poor adults sit on the far side of the digital divide, Choi and DiNitto show in a 2013 study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Their group was 980 people in central Texas who got meals brought to the home, most aged 60 or more, many with disability. Surveys asked about internet use, skill at finding health facts online, and views on computers.

Only 17 percent of the older group used the internet at the time, against 34 percent of the under-60 group. Cost and disability had pushed many past users offline. Never-users were more often black or Hispanic and had lower incomes than users. Skill at online health facts fell with age and rose with how often a person went online. Steps to close the gap close the study.
europmc-pmc3710231:
Kim Bouillon and seven co-authors published a review in BMC Geriatrics in 2013 on how frailty is measured in large population studies. Frailty means the loss of strength and reserve that comes with aging. The authors searched the medical literature from 1948 to May 2011 and checked the reference lists of the papers they found.

Their search found 27 separate frailty scales, and the scales differed a lot in what they counted. Some used one item, others used as many as 38, covering movement, illness, mood, memory, food intake, and social support. Only seven of the 27 scales had been tested for how reliable and valid they were. The Phenotype of Frailty was the most used and most tested scale, ahead of the Frailty Index.
europmc-pmc3739931:
Caroline Apovian and co-authors, with the COR-II Study Group, reported a phase 3 trial in Obesity in 2013 on a combined weight-loss drug. The drug pairs naltrexone and bupropion, two medicines that act on brain paths controlling food intake. The trial enrolled 1,496 overweight or obese adults, assigned two to one to the drug or a placebo for up to 56 weeks.

At week 28 the drug group had lost about 6.5 percent of body weight, against about 1.9 percent on placebo, and the gap held at week 56. About 56 percent of drug patients lost at least 5 percent of their weight, against about 18 percent on placebo. Heart and metabolic risk markers, quality of life, and control of eating also improved more on the drug. Nausea was the most common side effect.
europmc-pmc3744431:
Everett Smith and co-authors reported a study in PLoS Pathogens in 2013 on proofreading in coronaviruses. No vaccines or treatments existed for human coronaviruses, and the SARS virus resisted the drug ribavirin. Coronaviruses carry an unusual enzyme, an exoribonuclease in protein nsp14, thought to proofread their genome copying.

Viruses with that enzyme working resisted ribavirin and another mutagen, 5-fluorouracil. Viruses lacking it were up to 300 times more sensitive. With the mutagen, the crippled viruses picked up 16 times more mutations, most of them the kind expected from the drug. The authors present this as direct proof of the proofreading role. They propose that blocking the enzyme could anchor future treatments that pair it with mutagen drugs.
europmc-pmc3780531:
Martin Pall wrote a review in the Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine in 2013 arguing that electromagnetic fields act on the body through calcium channels. How low-energy fields produce non-heating effects on tissue was unsettled. Pall gathers studies he reads as pointing to one direct target: voltage-gated calcium channels, the gates that let calcium into cells.

He cites 23 studies in which channel blockers stopped or greatly reduced field effects. Downstream, he proposes, calcium drives nitric oxide production along two paths. One is tied to healing effects, such as field-stimulated bone growth. The other is tied to harm through oxidative stress, as in field-induced DNA strand breaks measured in cells. He also allows roles for calcium effects that bypass nitric oxide. The paper presents this channel-first account as substantially supported.
europmc-pmc3798631:
Seiji Yasumura and co-authors, with the Fukushima Health Management Survey Group, published a study protocol in the Journal of Epidemiology in 2012. After the March 2011 earthquake and tsunami wrecked the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, residents faced long-term anxiety about low-dose radiation. Fukushima Prefecture launched a long-term survey, led by Fukushima Medical University.

The survey enrolled everyone living in the prefecture, about 2.05 million people. A basic survey estimates each resident's external radiation dose. Four detailed surveys cover thyroid ultrasound for all children aged 18 or younger. They also cover full health checks and mental health and lifestyle checks for evacuation zone residents, and records of all pregnancies and births. Early results showed a low basic-survey response rate, under 30 percent, and no cancers among the first 38,114 children scanned.
europmc-pmc3840331:
Daniël Lakens wrote a solo primer on effect sizes in Frontiers in Psychology in 2013. An effect size states how big a study result is, not just whether it differs from zero. Lakens argues that such sizes are the most useful part of a study, since they let science build up over time.

The primer shows how to work out and report sizes for two common tests, the t-test and analysis of variance. It gives close care to studies that test the same people twice, where linked measures change the right formula. Sizes feed plans for new study sizes and pooled reviews of many studies. A free spreadsheet comes with the paper so readers can run the math in their own work.
europmc-pmc3893531:
Travis J. Wheeler, Jody Clements, and Robert D. Finn present a logo tool in BMC Bioinformatics, with the record dated 2014. Sequence logos are stacked-letter charts that show how conserved each spot in a gene or protein family is. Biologists use them to read alignments and model profiles at a glance.

Their tool, Skylign, builds logos for both alignments and profile models in one frame. Beyond still images, it makes web logos that scroll, zoom, and reveal the numbers under each letter. It can down-weight near-duplicate sequences to cut bias and blend in prior counts. Gap settings are shown in a simpler way, and letter heights can scale by alternate conservation math. Skylign runs as a website, a web service, and a download.
europmc-pmc3894431:
Janusz Marcinkiewicz and Ewa Kontny review taurine in inflammation in Amino Acids, with the record dated 2014. Taurine is the most plentiful free amino acid in the human body. It steadies calcium, cell water, and membranes, calms cell death, and fights oxidants. It piles up in tissues that face heavy oxidant loads, such as inflamed sites.

At those sites, taurine traps a harsh acid made by neutrophil enzymes and turns it into milder compounds. Those products kill germs and calm inflammation in short bursts. What taurine does in long inflammatory diseases is far less clear. The review sums the solid ground on acute control and marks the open ground on chronic disease, where taurine's role may help or hinder healing.
europmc-pmc3905731:
Bing Xiao leads a large team in a protein structure study in Nature Communications in 2013. AMPK is a cell enzyme that senses low energy and rebalances fuel use. It draws drug interest for diabetes and cancer. Several small molecules switch it on, yet no one knew where they bind.

The team froze human AMPK with one activator bound and read its crystal structure. The drug sits in a pocket between the enzyme's working head and its sugar-binding part, gluing the two together. The pocket's shape hints that a natural body molecule may also bind there to tune the enzyme. The structure hands drug designers a map for building better activators for metabolic disease.
europmc-pmc3931231:
Eleftherios Garyfallidis and colleagues present Dipy, a free software library for diffusion MRI, in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics in 2014. Diffusion MRI tracks how water moves in tissue, which reveals the layout of the brain's white matter wiring. Many analysis methods exist for each step, but they were scattered across separate tools with different styles of use.

Dipy gathers them in one Python project with a uniform interface. It covers cleaning the raw signal, rebuilding the diffusion pattern in each tiny volume, tracing fiber bundles between brain areas, and processing and visualizing the results. Both classic methods, such as the diffusion tensor model, and newer ones, such as constrained spherical deconvolution, are included with transparent code that other researchers can inspect and extend.
europmc-pmc3965031:
Vincent Lombard, Hemalatha Golaconda Ramulu, Elodie Drula, Pedro M. Coutinho, and Bernard Henrissat report the 2013 state of CAZy in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. CAZy classifies the enzymes that build, modify, and break down sugars and their chains, a group called carbohydrate-active enzymes. Its sequence-based families link each enzyme to what it attacks and to its three-dimensional shape, with facts curated from new literature as it appears.

The update covers five years of growth: new families added, several families split into subfamilies for finer resolution, and heavy use of the scheme to annotate whole genomes and metagenomes. A new display shows the sugar molecules captured in crystal structures of these enzymes. The authors note that CAZy's stable naming system may be its largest service to the field.
europmc-pmc3966331:
Jaspinder Kaur reviews metabolic syndrome in Cardiology Research and Practice in 2014. She writes as the sole author. The syndrome is a cluster of linked problems. Belly fat is one. Insulin resistance is another. Unhealthy blood fats, raised blood pressure, and weak vessel linings join the list. So does a tendency to clot. Together they raise the risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes. They also raise the risk of early death.

Chronic low-grade inflammation helps bind the cluster. Odd fat-tissue signals feed that inflammation. The review covers how the syndrome is defined. It covers its causes and disease process. It then turns to care. Lifestyle change is the first treatment. Diet and exercise plans pair with behavior strategies there. Drugs are added when lifestyle steps fall short. They aim at the single parts of the cluster.
europmc-pmc3971631:
René L. Warren and colleagues sequence the microbes that live in bowel tumors. Their paper appeared in Microbiome in 2013. Earlier work had tied Fusobacterium bacteria to colorectal cancer. Bowel cancer is a leading cancer killer. The colon swims in microbes, so the link deserved a deeper look. The team sequenced tumor tissue from 130 patients. Matched healthy tissue served as the control. They built networks of microbes that appear together. They also noted which host genes switch on beside them.

Fusobacterium was again over-represented in tumors. It rarely came alone, though. Leptotrichia and Campylobacter species co-occurred with it. The trio formed a multi-species signature inside single tumors. All three are oxygen-shunning bacteria known from the mouth. Tumors with the trio over-expressed host genes for inflammation. Interleukin-8 was one such gene. The pattern hints at a joint microbial role in the tumor setting.
europmc-pmc4051631:
Mathieu Jacomy and four colleagues document ForceAtlas2, the layout engine inside the Gephi network software, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Network maps turn tangled link data into pictures a person can read. Gephi aims that power at users from many fields, and its default layout runs while the user watches and drags.

ForceAtlas2 treats nodes as charged particles that repel and links as springs that pull. Several tricks keep it handy at the sizes users actually bring, roughly ten to ten thousand nodes. A gravity shortcut borrowed from physics speeds the repulsion maths. Repulsion scales with node degree so hubs do not crush the map. Speed adapts locally and globally to settle the picture without wild swings. The paper gives the full formulas and each setting's meaning. The authors claim craft, not theory.
europmc-pmc4061531:
Amelia L. Parker, Maria Kavallaris, and Joshua A. McCarroll reviewed microtubules, the cell's internal rails, and their part in how cancer cells survive stress. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Oncology in 2014. Microtubules drive cell movement, internal transport, and division, and several chemotherapy drugs attack them.

Changes in microtubule stability, tubulin types, and chemical tags on tubulin appear in many solid and blood cancers. Those changes track with poor outlook and drug resistance, though the reasons were unclear. The authors gather evidence that tubulins and their partner proteins help cells answer metabolic, protein, oxygen, and oxidative stress. Understanding that network, they suggest, could open new treatment routes.
europmc-pmc4108331:
Charles K. Fisher and Pankaj Mehta introduced LIMITS, a method for inferring which gut microbes affect each other from abundance data collected over time. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Sequencing now lets researchers follow human microbial communities as they change, but turning counts into an interaction map is fraught.

Three obstacles stand out: linked abundances need not mean interaction, the shares in a sample must sum to a whole, and measurement errors bias the estimates. LIMITS answers with sparse linear regression over many resampled data sets, fitting a classic predator-prey style model of community dynamics. The authors test the method on synthetic communities where the truth is known. Finding keystone species this way could steer microbiome medicine.
europmc-pmc4123031:
Jackye Peretz, Jodi A. Flaws, and a team of peers brought the proof on bisphenol A and the power to have children up to date. BPA is a chemical used in plastics. Their review came out in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2014. A panel of experts had last weighed the topic in 2007, and much new work had since come out.

The team read human and animal work from 2007 to 2013. They class BPA as a toxin for the ovary. It upsets egg cell growth, the ripening of egg sacs, hormone output, and egg grade. This holds even in women in the midst of fertility care. They class it as a toxin for the womb too, since it harms the growth of the womb lining. Proof of harm to male fertility is also on the rise. Their joint verdict is that BPA is a toxin for the act of breeding in both sexes.
europmc-pmc4134331:
Chris Feudtner, James A. Feinstein, Wenjun Zhong, Matt Hall, and Dingwei Dai updated a classification system for children's complex chronic conditions. Their paper appeared in BMC Pediatrics in 2014. The original system, built in 2000, needed revision for the ICD-10 coding era.

The team fixed omitted and wrong codes in the old system, then translated between the two code sets using official mappings. They reviewed every code again to catch signs of technology dependence and organ transplantation. The draft system was applied to death certificates and two care-use databases, and errors were corrected by hand. Checks showed the new version stays stable across code sets and over years. It gives researchers a shared, current way to identify seriously ill children.
europmc-pmc4209231:
Tingting Du, Xuefeng Yu, and four co-authors compared simple blood markers of insulin resistance in Cardiovascular Diabetology in 2014. Insulin resistance is an early step toward diabetes, but the direct clamp test is too costly for routine care. Doctors instead use ratios built from standard lab values, and the team asked which works best.

Using survey data from 7,629 Chinese adults, they pitted lipid ratios, a belly-fat index, and the triglycerides and glucose index, called TyG, against a standard resistance score. TyG tracked resistance most strongly and separated resistant from non-resistant people best. Two cheaper markers, the triglyceride to HDL ratio and the visceral adiposity index, also did well, while the apoB to apoA-I ratio beat no simpler measure. The authors favour TyG for early screening.
europmc-pmc4219031:
Bowen Lin, Shokei Kim-Mitsuyama, and eight co-authors tested a diabetes drug in obese mice in Cardiovascular Diabetology in 2014. Empagliflozin blocks the kidney transporter SGLT2, so excess sugar leaves in urine instead of returning to the blood. The team asked whether it also protects the heart, vessels, kidneys, and brain that diabetes damages.

In db/db mice, a model of obesity and type 2 diabetes, a week of treatment raised urine sugar and volume while blood sugar fell steadily. Over ten weeks the drug held blood sugar down and eased cardiovascular injury, vessel dysfunction, kidney damage, and measurable cognitive decline. The results support the idea that this drug class shields organs beyond its sugar-lowering job, at least in this mouse model.
europmc-pmc4290631:
Jodi Woan-Fei Law, Nurul-Syakima Ab Mutalib, Kok-Gan Chan, and Learn-Han Lee review fast tests for bacteria that cause food poisoning. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2014. Old culture methods take days and much labor, while food moves fast and outbreaks demand quick answers.

The rapid methods fall into three families: DNA based tests such as PCR and its variants, biosensors, and antibody based tests. For each, the review explains the principle, where it is used, and its strengths and limits in speed, cost, and accuracy. The survey helps food safety labs weigh which quick test fits which food and which pathogen.
europmc-pmc4331431:
Wenjing Zhao and eleven co-authors mapped pig gut microbes across ages and gut segments. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. Most microbe surveys sample dung, but the communities living along the gut itself may differ, and pigs are both a farm animal and a stand-in for human gut studies.

Dung was sampled at four growth stages and gut contents from four intestinal segments in adults. The balance of the two dominant bacterial groups shifted tenfold as pigs grew past one month, and profiles steadied with age. In adults, small and large intestine held clearly different communities, so dung only partly represents the tract. The results guide how pig studies should sample and how far dung data can be trusted.
europmc-pmc4439031:
Nahid Darvishi, Mehran Farhadi, Tahereh Haghtalab, Jalal Poorolajal, and Martin Voracek pooled studies on alcohol use disorder and suicide in PLoS ONE in 2015. Single studies disagreed about how strongly troubled drinking raises suicidal thoughts and acts, so a combined estimate was needed. The team searched major databases and journals up to February 2015 for observational studies on the link.

Thirty-one studies, with a large combined pool of participants, met their rules. Alcohol use disorder was tied to clearly higher odds of thinking about suicide, of attempting suicide, and of dying by suicide, with the strongest link for attempts. The authors checked for uneven results across studies and for publication bias. Their synthesis supports treating alcohol problems as a real, measurable part of suicide risk in prevention and care.
europmc-pmc4443731:
Jochen Schmid, Volker Sieber, and Bernd Rehm reviewed bacterial exopolysaccharides in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2015. Bacteria release these long sugar chains outside the cell, where they form slime and protective layers. The genes for making each kind usually sit together in the genome, and the chains are built by a few distinct routes.

Because these natural polymers are renewable and can be tuned, they attract interest for medicine and industry. Sorting out how each route works, and how the cell controls it, is the key step before engineers can redesign production. The review gathers the main building routes and the latest genetic, metabolic, and protein engineering used to make tailor-made versions. Such designer polymers could serve as high-grade materials, from wound care to food and coatings.
europmc-pmc4517131:
Nagayasu Egawa leads a five-author review of human papillomaviruses in Viruses in 2015. These viruses have evolved over millions of years to live in skin and lining tissues of many host species. With that long history comes a wide spread of types and survival plans.

Many types keep a low profile: quiet, long-lasting infections with limited gene activity, so the immune system leaves them alone. Others make raised, persistent warts even in healthy people, using stronger tricks to dodge immune attack. The review ties these plans to how each type's genes are switched on at its chosen site. It also covers why site and cell setting change harm, and how DNA testing and vaccines against cervical cancer grew from this knowledge.
europmc-pmc4521131:
Emily Herrett and six co-authors profile a British health database in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 2015. The Clinical Practice Research Datalink holds anonymized records from family doctors across the UK. Since those doctors gatekeep most care, their files capture symptoms, tests, diagnoses, drugs, habits, and referrals in one place.

The database covers over 11.3 million patients from 674 practices, with 4.4 million active patients meeting quality checks, about 6.9% of the UK population. Its patients broadly match the country in age, sex, and ethnic mix. For more than half, links to hospital, disease, and death records widen the data. Over 1,000 studies have used it. The profile also warns that routine records take skill to handle well.
europmc-pmc4598831:
In 2015, William Menegas and colleagues' mouse brain study mapping inputs to dopamine neurons appeared. Different dopamine cell groups send signals to different targets, such as parts of the striatum. The team traced single-step connections using a modified rabies virus, tissue clearing, and whole-brain imaging. The work appeared in eLife.

Most dopamine groups received a broadly similar set of inputs, including dense clusters from the ventral striatum. One group stood apart: neurons projecting to the posterior striatum got few ventral striatum inputs. Instead they received more from the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, and zona incerta. That odd wiring marks them as a distinct class, and the maps give later studies a base for linking circuit wiring to behaviour.
europmc-pmc4658431:
Thiago T. Braga, Juan S.H. Agudelo, and Niels O.S. Camara published a 2015 review of macrophages during fibrosis, the scarring process. Macrophages shift their behaviour with local signals, forming inflammatory and regulatory populations. The review focuses on the regulatory M2 type during tissue repair. It appeared in Frontiers in Immunology.

Inflammatory macrophages dominate early damage control and burn sugar quickly. Regulatory macrophages arrive as scarring develops, burn oxygen more efficiently, and produce fewer damaging byproducts. They can both promote fibrosis and restrain scar formation, acting as friend and foe at once. The authors discuss innate immune receptors, metabolic switches, and where these cells come from. Understanding the balance may help therapies steer repair toward healing rather than scar.
europmc-pmc4668831:
Martyn D. Kirk and colleagues brought out a 2015 World Health Organization data synthesis estimating the 2010 burden of twenty-two foodborne diseases caused by bacteria, protozoa, and viruses. No global estimate existed for this group. Sources ranged from systematic reviews to surveillance data published between 1990 and 2012. The work appeared in PLOS Medicine.

The twenty-two diseases caused an estimated two billion cases, over one million deaths, and 78.7 million disability adjusted life years in 2010. Applying expert estimates of the foodborne share, about twenty-nine percent of cases, or 582 million, came through food. Study counts per pathogen ranged from five to nearly five hundred. The figures give governments a first regional and global yardstick for food safety priorities.
europmc-pmc4728131:
Min Zhang, Samuel J. Kenny, Liang Ge, Ke Xu, and Randy Schekman traced how the inflammatory signal IL-1 beta leaves cells, in eLife in 2015. Most secreted proteins exit through the cell's standard shipping route, but IL-1 beta has no shipping label and takes an unconventional path tied to autophagy, the cell's recycling system. Working in engineered non-immune cells, the team rebuilt the secretion process step by step. They found the mature signal first docks onto autophagy membranes.

Then, surprisingly, it crosses into the space between a vesicle's two membranes rather than its center, a move that likely needs the protein unfolded. Two short motifs, working with a chaperone protein, are required for the crossing. Completing the exit also needs Golgi stacking proteins and a second vesicle system. The study gives unconventional secretion a concrete route map, relevant to inflammation diseases where IL-1 beta drives damage.
europmc-pmc4728631:
Yoona Kim, Jennifer B. Keogh, and Peter M. Clifton reviewed dietary polyphenols and blood sugar control in Nutrients in 2016. Polyphenols are plant chemicals found in tea, coffee, cocoa, grapes, berries, and olive oil, among many foods. Animal studies suggest some of them fight diabetes. The review asks how they might work and what human trials actually show. Proposed mechanisms are plentiful: slowing starch digestion, blocking sugar uptake in the gut, prompting insulin release, and cutting the liver's sugar output.

Other candidate routes include better insulin-driven sugar uptake, switching on a key energy sensor, calming inflammation, and reshaping gut microbes. Human evidence, though, is inconsistent, with trials pointing in different directions. The authors close by calling for stronger intervention studies before dietary polyphenols can be prescribed for type 2 diabetes. The review is useful precisely for its restraint, separating plausible chemistry from proven benefit.
europmc-pmc4772531:
Jonathan F. Wendel, Scott A. Jackson, Blake C. Meyers, and Rod A. Wing review how plant genomes took their present shape, in Genome Biology in 2016. Cheap sequencing has laid bare the genome of crop after crop, and three big lessons stand out from the flood of data.

First, every plant line carries a history of whole-genome doubling, again and again, followed by slow loss of the spare copies. Second, most of the size gap between plant genomes comes from jumping DNA pieces that copy themselves in and later get trimmed away, at rates that differ by line. Third, small RNA pieces help police that jumping DNA and shape gene use. The authors tie each lesson to breeding, since genome history sets the raw material crops can draw on.
europmc-pmc4812631:
Morten Nielsen and Massimo Andreatta present an upgraded prediction tool in Genome Medicine in 2016. For a virus or tumor fragment to wake killer T cells, it must first bind an MHC class I molecule, the cell's display stand. Predicting that binding by computer lets vaccine and therapy teams screen fragments fast, without lab work for each one.

Their model, NetMHCpan-3.0, learns from many display types and fragment lengths at once. A new alignment step lets fragments of different lengths share one model, filling gaps where one display type has little data. The upgrade beat the best rival tools and caught how each display type favors its own length range. The authors also show that ranking fragments against a percentile scale picks true display cargo better than fixed strength cutoffs.
europmc-pmc4820631:
Helen Bolton and seven co-authors build a mouse model of mosaic embryos in Nature Communications in 2016. Most human early embryos are mosaics, mixing normal cells with cells carrying the wrong chromosome count. Their fate decides many early pregnancy losses, and clinic staff must judge which embryos to transfer. The team forced the error in mouse embryos with a drug that jams cell division checks.

Pure mosaic embryos died around implantation. In mixed embryos filmed cell by cell, wrong-count cells met different ends by lineage: those in the fetal line killed themselves, while those in the placental line grew poorly. Either way the wrong cells thinned out as development ran. Embryos with enough normal cells developed fully, a finding the authors say should inform embryo grading in fertility clinics.
europmc-pmc4824831:
Kazuhiro Yoshida and four co-authors propose a new sorting for advanced stomach cancer in Gastric Cancer in 2016. Some stage IV cancers, spread beyond the stomach, can still be cut out after chemotherapy shrinks them, a strategy called conversion therapy. Which patients qualify has been guesswork, so the authors sort stage IV disease by its biology into four categories.

The split turns on spread into the belly lining, which behaves differently from spread through the blood. Categories range from spread that is removable at once to spread across belly and organs that no surgery can cure. Conversion surgery, they propose, fits mainly the second category, some of the third, and almost none of the fourth, where care should lead. Expected survival follows the same order.
europmc-pmc4894931:
Sandra U. Schmitz, Phillip Grote, and Bernhard G. Herrmann reviewed how long noncoding RNAs work in development and disease in 2016. Deep sequencing recently uncovered thousands of these long RNA strips, which build no protein. They touch nearly every step of gene control, from gene reading to protein output and stability.

Fresh work casts them as key players in cell fate choice, organ building, and tissue upkeep. Faults in their ranks feed cancer and heart and vessel disease, which makes them candidate markers and drug targets. The review works through clear cases that show their range: guiding gene marks, shaping genome folds, and tuning messages. A once-dismissed RNA class now sits near the center of gene control.
europmc-pmc4931331:
Jianhui Wang and five co-authors design a superconcentrated electrolyte for a high voltage lithium ion battery. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. A 5 volt class battery stores more energy, but no fluid inside one yet holds up well. The standard salt breaks down and speeds metal loss from electrodes. Swapping in a stable salt, though, lets the aluminum collector corrode instead. The team mixed a stable salt, LiN(SO2F)2, with dimethyl carbonate at very high concentration.

The dense mix forms a network where anions and solvent grip lithium ions tightly. That network blocked both aluminum corrosion and metal loss at about 5 volts. A test battery built with it cycled well, charged fast, and ran more safely. The authors present concentration itself, not a new chemical, as the fix for the voltage dilemma.
europmc-pmc4937031:
Jens P. Andersen and five co-authors review P4-ATPases, pump proteins that flip fats across cell membranes. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Physiology in 2016. Cell membranes have two layers, and their fat mix differs by side. That asymmetry supports vesicle traffic, signaling, blood clotting, and cell death routines. P4-ATPases burn energy to move specific fats from the outer layer to the inner one, keeping the balance in place.

Some family members move phosphatidylserine and phosphatidylethanolamine, while others handle phosphatidylcholine. Defects in two members, ATP8A2 and ATP8B1, cause severe human disease. The review explains the pump cycle by analogy with the better known sodium potassium pump. It also airs open puzzles, such as how a bulky fat head fits through the pump. The authors call the transport path the field's central unsolved problem.
europmc-pmc4987531:
Fucai Liu leads a large team reporting room temperature ferroelectricity in ultrathin flakes of a layered crystal. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Ferroelectrics hold an electric polarization that a field can flip, a trait prized for memory and sensors. Whether the effect survives in two dimensional materials was open. The team studied CuInP2S6, a layered compound, and found switchable polarization at room temperature, with a transition near three hundred and twenty kelvin.

The effect held in flakes only about four nanometers thick. As a proof of use, they built a diode by stacking the flakes on silicon. The device showed memory behavior with an on to off current ratio near one hundred. The authors say adding ferroelectricity to the two dimensional family opens routes to sensors, actuators, and non-volatile memory that keeps data without power.
europmc-pmc5007331:
Hao Du, Ya Zhao, Jinqiu He, and five co-authors explain in Nature Communications in 2016 how a common RNA mark leads to RNA breakdown. The mark, called m6A, is the most frequent change found on messenger and long noncoding RNAs. Reader proteins spot the mark, and one reader, YTHDF2, was known to shorten the life of marked RNAs by an unclear route.

The team shows that marked RNAs lose their protective tail faster, and that the CCR4-NOT complex does this tail trimming. YTHDF2 grabs that complex directly, through a contact between its front region and the CNOT1 part of the complex. Without that contact, the trimming stalls and marked RNAs last longer. The study fills in the step-by-step route by which a single RNA mark speeds up RNA disposal in mammal cells.
europmc-pmc5007431:
Daniel McDonald and eleven co-authors report in mSphere in 2016 on the gut microbes of people in intensive care. Severe illness is thought to kill off helpful gut bacteria and let harmful ones take over, a shift called dysbiosis. That shift may open the door to hospital infections, sepsis, and organ failure. The team sampled the microbes of 115 critically ill subjects.

The samples showed fast, extreme change after admission to intensive care. Helpful gut species fell away, disease-linked bacteria grew, and some of the new microbes traced back to the hospital setting itself rather than the patient's own body. The authors argue that tracking the ICU microbiome is a needed first step. Later care might fix the shift with probiotics or with lab-built microbe mixes that restore a healthy gut community.
europmc-pmc5040731:
Sarah Bargiela, Robyn Steward, and William Mandy study late-diagnosed autistic women in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders in 2016. Autism in girls and women is often missed or mislabeled, partly because the female pattern of the condition is poorly described. The team interviewed fourteen women, aged twenty-two to thirty, who learned their diagnosis only in late adolescence or adulthood, and analyzed their accounts with a framework method.

The women described working hard at pretending to be normal, copying social behavior to fit in. Many said their gender led teachers and doctors to overlook autism, and they felt torn between their condition and expected feminine roles. Experiences of sexual abuse were widespread in this group, tied in part to the risks of growing up undiagnosed. The authors call for training so professionals spot autism in females sooner, and for measures that can capture camouflaging itself.
europmc-pmc5055731:
Ruth Pidsley and nine co-authors test a DNA methylation chip in Genome Biology in 2016. Methylation chips profile chemical marks on DNA in many samples at once. The older chip missed most control regions far from genes, so the maker released the MethylationEPIC chip with far wider reach. The team benchmarked it against the old chip and against full genome sequencing of the marks.

The new chip covers over 850,000 sites, keeping more than ninety percent of the old chip's sites and adding 413,743 more, including over half of a major enhancer catalog. Still, only a small share of distant control elements is covered, and one probe cannot always speak for a whole variable region. Readings were highly repeatable and matched other methods well, and the team lists probes that cross-react or sit on variable DNA. They judge it a real advance that keeps arrays central to the field.
europmc-pmc5089131:
Karoline Faust and Jeroen Raes presented a software paper in F1000Research in 2016. They describe an app version of CoNet, their tool for finding links between living things in repeated measurements, now built to run inside the Cytoscape network program. The tool began with microbe data from sequencing studies in mind.

CoNet can spot pairs that tend to appear together or avoid each other, and it offers several ways to build such networks that users can combine. Faust and Raes show the app at work on microbe counts from arctic soil, gathered by sequencing a marker gene. The app runs on two Cytoscape versions and is free to download, so labs can test links in genes, metabolites, or species with the same method.
europmc-pmc5120331:
Giuseppe Suaria and eight co-authors surveyed plastic litter in Mediterranean surface waters, reporting in Scientific Reports in 2016. The sea had been called one of the world's worst regions for microplastics, but what the floating pieces are made of was largely unknown. The team chemically identified every collected particle larger than 700 micrometers.

All 4,050 particles fell into 16 classes of synthetic material. Light plastics used in packaging, polyethylene and polypropylene, dominated, followed by polyamides, paint flakes, and other common polymers. One biodegradable polyester turned up floating offshore for the first time. Mixes differed between sub-basins, a pattern the authors link to where pollution enters, where it gathers, and how long each plastic type lasts at sea.
europmc-pmc5121131:
Andrew Pickles and a large team of co-authors reported long-term results of a parent-led autism therapy in The Lancet in 2016. The PACT approach trains parents of preschool children with autism to communicate in ways that draw the child into interaction. Whether such early help still shows years later was unknown.

The follow-up traced 121 of the original 152 children, now about ten and a half years old, roughly six years after treatment ended. Children whose parents had the training still showed milder autism symptoms on blinded ratings, and they started more exchanges with their parents, though language scores did not differ from the control group. The authors present this as the first trial proof that early autism help can ease symptoms over the long run.
europmc-pmc5182031:
David A. Raffelt and six co-authors introduced a finer way to analyze brain wiring in NeuroImage, with the hosted text dated 2017. Diffusion MRI can probe white matter, but most voxels mix several fiber populations crossing each other, so ordinary voxel measures blur which fibers changed.

Their fixel-based analysis treats each fiber population within a voxel as its own unit, a fixel. It adds morphometry. That means not just the microscopic density of fibers, but the macroscopic size of the whole bundle. A combined measure multiplies the two, tracking the total number of axons more directly. Simulations on a phantom bundle and a patient-control comparison show the three measures give distinct, complementary information, with the combined one likely most sensitive to some diseases.
europmc-pmc5209531:
André M. Comeau, Gavin M. Douglas, and Morgan G. I. Langille presented Microbiome Helper in mSystems in 2017, a free workflow meant to make microbiome research easier to run well. Studying the microbes of a place or a body now relies on DNA sequencing, and both the lab steps and the computer analysis are hard for newcomers. Their package pulls the whole path into one documented set of standard procedures.

Microbiome Helper covers detailed steps for building sequencing libraries, then step-by-step guides for the bioinformatic analysis that follows. The protocols, tutorials, and bundled software are openly available, and the team commits to updating them as methods change. The aim is fast, reliable, and repeatable analysis, so researchers can spend more effort on study design and on reading their results than on rebuilding basic pipelines.
europmc-pmc5216131:
Corey Rogers, Teresa Fernandes-Alnemri, Lindsey Mayes, Diana Alnemri, Gino Cingolani, and Emad S. Alnemri traced how dying cells move from apoptosis to secondary necrosis in Nature Communications in 2017. Apoptosis is a quiet, controlled form of cell suicide run by enzymes called caspases. When dead cells are not cleared away, they swell, burst, and spill inflammatory contents, but the switch behind that change was unknown.

The group found that caspase-3 cuts a protein called DFNA5, freeing a fragment that moves to the cell surface membrane and damages it. Cells carrying DFNA5 burst in this way after death triggers such as a chemotherapy drug or virus infection, while cells lacking DFNA5 instead broke apart into small, tidy bodies. Because both this route and the related pyroptosis route depend on caspases, the authors class them together as programmed necrosis.
europmc-pmc5240031:
Di Chen, Jie Shen, Weiwei Zhao, Tingyu Wang, Lin Han, John L. Hamilton, and Hee-Jeong Im reviewed the mechanisms of osteoarthritis in Bone Research in 2017. Osteoarthritis is the most common degenerative joint disease and a leading cause of pain and disability in adults. Joint injury, obesity, aging, and heredity all feed into it, yet the molecular chain that starts and drives it stays poorly mapped, and no treatment can rebuild lost cartilage.

The review treats the joint as a whole organ, since the disease strikes cartilage, the bone beneath it, the lining tissue, and the meniscus together. It walks through the hallmark changes: cartilage breakdown, bone spurs, bone thickening, and lining overgrowth. It links them to signals found in mouse models, including TGF-beta, Wnt, and Indian hedgehog pathways and the factor Runx2. The aim is a joined picture that could point to ways of slowing the disease.
europmc-pmc5251331:
Wu Zhang and Jie Xu reviewed DNA methyltransferases and their part in cancer formation in Biomarker Research in 2017. Methylation, a mark placed on DNA, helps control gene activity, chromosome stability, and imprinting, the parent-specific silencing of certain genes. Three enzymes write and keep the marks in mammals: DNMT1, which copies the pattern onto new DNA during cell division, and DNMT3A and DNMT3B, which lay down fresh patterns in the embryo.

Faults in these enzymes scramble the marks and help turn cells cancerous. The review gathers recent findings on how changed methyltransferases drive the abnormal traits of cancer cells. Mutations in DNMT3A carry special weight in blood cancers, where they reprogram the cell's marking system early in the disease. Small-molecule drugs aimed at these epigenetic faults were first developed for leukemia and now guide targeted treatment work in solid tumours as well.
europmc-pmc5267531:
Matthew R. Brier and fifteen colleagues compared tau and amyloid imaging with spinal fluid measures and thinking tests in Alzheimer's disease, in Science Translational Medicine in 2016. Alzheimer's carries two signature deposits: amyloid plaques and tau tangles. Until new tracers arrived, scans could show only amyloid in living people, while autopsy work tied tau more closely to symptoms.

Scanning cognitively normal elders and patients with mild Alzheimer's, the team found tau and amyloid settle in distinct but related patterns that shift with disease stage. Spinal fluid tau matched tau deposits in the temporal lobe. Temporal lobe tau tracked dementia status and predicted test performance better than amyloid anywhere in the brain. The results back models in which tau spread, more than amyloid load, follows the loss of brain function that brings on early symptoms.
europmc-pmc5296331:
Vivek Kumar, Neha Chaudhary, Mohit Garg, Charalampos S. Floudas, Parita Soni, and Abhinav B. Chandra reviewed the side effects of immune checkpoint inhibitors in Frontiers in Pharmacology in 2017. These cancer drugs release the brakes on T cells by blocking CTLA-4 or the PD-1 pathway, and their approved uses keep growing. Unleashed immunity, though, attacks healthy tissue too, producing immune-related adverse events.

The common sites are skin, gut, and hormone glands, but rarer attacks on nerves, blood, and kidneys are now documented, and safety data are accumulating for patients who already have autoimmune disease. Caught early, most events reverse fully; only the severest grades need treatment paused and immune suppression with steroids or infliximab. The review lays out recognition and management algorithms for the main drug families and notes the research frontier: preventing these toxicities and finding markers that predict who will suffer them.
europmc-pmc5303831:
Michela Palmieri, Rituraj Pal, Hemanth R. Nelvagal, Parisa Lotfi, and a large team of colleagues found a new switch for cellular clearance in Nature Communications in 2017. It is aimed at neurodegenerative storage diseases such as Batten disease, where cells choke on undigested waste. The master regulator of the lysosome system is a protein called TFEB, and the known brake on it was the mTORC1 complex. The team found a second brake.

The signaling protein Akt tags TFEB at a specific site, Ser467, holding it out of the nucleus, independently of mTORC1. The sugar trehalose lifts this brake by damping Akt, switching TFEB on. Given to mice with Batten disease, trehalose cleared stored aggregates, eased brain pathology, and prolonged survival. Blocking Akt pharmacologically likewise boosted clearance in cells from patients with several different lysosomal diseases. The authors argue the Akt-TFEB route is a broadly usable drug target for storage disorders.
europmc-pmc5307731:
Andrew E. Teschendorff, Charles E. Breeze, Shijie C. Zheng, and Stephan Beck compared computer methods for blood and tissue studies in BMC Bioinformatics in 2017.
