Large studies of chemical marks on DNA face a snag. Each sample mixes many cell types, and the mix can hide or fake a signal. Software must split the mix before the marks can be read.

The team built a sharper reference set from open DNA sites in known cell types. They then tested three ways to split samples. A method based on robust partial links beat the standard forced-fit method in most tissues and noise levels. Their combined tool, called EpiDISH, improved cell counts in blood and skin-type mixes. A smoking study showed its added value, and the tool is free as an R package.
europmc-pmc5312531:
Lisa M. Pfadenhauer led a team that built a framework for health programs in Implementation Science in 2017. Complex health programs often work in one place and fail in another. Their success turns on local context and on how they are put in place. Older frameworks treated those two forces apart, or stuck to one field or one type of setting.

The team drafted a model from a scan of past work, then tested it on quick reviews and found gaps. A closer study of the core terms reshaped the model. They tried the new version on reviews, a health technology review, and fit checks for varied programs. The final CICI framework has three parts: context, the work of putting a program in place, and the setting. It gives planners a shared map for judging why a program lands or fails.
europmc-pmc5321731:
Yun Teng and co-authors studied how colon cancer cells shed a useful molecule, in Nature Communications in 2017. Cancer cells send out tiny bubbles called exosomes that carry small RNAs. Some of those RNAs hold tumors back. The team asked what happens to the sender cells when such RNAs leave in bubbles, using mouse colon tumors and their liver spread.

In later stage disease, more tumor-holding RNAs were packed into the bubbles. One of them, miR-193a, binds a protein called MVP. When MVP was knocked out, the RNA stayed inside the sender cells, and tumor growth slowed. Inside cells, miR-193a halts the cell cycle by hitting a gene that lifts growth signals. Blood tests in patients matched the pattern: later stage cases carried more of the RNA in blood bubbles. Shedding a brake, it seems, helps the tumor grow.
europmc-pmc5323831:
J. L. Milton described a rare skin swelling he called giant urticaria in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1876. Years before, he had shown the disorder to a London medical society. Most members had never seen its like. One recalled a sailor treated as gout, and Sir Benjamin Brodie had seen a mild case or two but had no name or cure to offer.

Milton builds the paper from cases seen since then, with the debate they stirred. The swellings rise on the skin in huge patches and can linger for years. One patient, a musician, fretted over the long course of the illness and his lost power to work, and grew weak and low in spirit. Diet seemed to make no difference to him. Salts, then iron and colchicum pills, brought relief in that case. Milton argues the disorder deserves study as a thing of its own.
europmc-pmc5329931:
Li Yang and Yi Zhang reviewed macrophages that live inside tumors in the Journal of Hematology & Oncology in 2017. Macrophages are immune cells that can take two broad stances: attack mode or repair mode. Inside tumors, the repair stance rules. These tumor-linked macrophages, called TAMs, act as friends of the tumor rather than foes.

The review traces where TAMs come from and how the tumor bends them to its side. They help tumors start, spread to new sites, and grow their own blood supply. They also blunt the T cell attack that could clear the cancer. Because TAM levels track how a cancer behaves, they may serve as signs for diagnosis and outlook. Drugs that cut, reprogram, or block TAMs are a growing hope for therapy.
europmc-pmc5331431:
Tessa Gryp, Raymond Vanholder, Mario Vaneechoutte, and Griet Glorieux reviewed a gut-made toxin in Toxins in 2017. When kidneys fail, waste builds up in the blood. One such waste, p-cresyl sulfate, clings to blood proteins and harms the body. High levels track worse outcomes for kidney patients. Standard dialysis removes it poorly, since it rides on proteins.

The toxin starts in the gut. Bacteria there break down two building blocks of protein and release the raw form, which the body then tags with sulfate. The review lists the bacterial families that do this work, drawn from lab studies. It also sums up the harm the toxin does to cells and vessels. Since the source sits in the gut, the authors see gut microbes as a future target: curb them early and toxin levels may fall, slowing kidney decline.
europmc-pmc539331:
Derrick E. Fouts leads a large author group in a 2005 PLoS Biology study that reads and compares the genomes of several Campylobacter species. These spiral germs are a top cause of human gut illness worldwide. The team sequenced strains of three less-studied species and set them beside the best-known one to find what sets each apart and what might make each harmful.

Big genome gaps traced to chunks of DNA picked up from viruses and plasmids. The outer coat parts of the germs varied a lot, while many genes for settling in a host were shared by all. Strains also differed in fuel use and drug resistance. The authors say the many still-unknown genes may hold the keys to host choice and harm.
europmc-pmc5417431:
Luyten and co-authors build a short questionnaire on how parents read their baby's mind. Their research article appeared in PLoS ONE. The skill is called parental reflective functioning. It means treating an infant as a person with thoughts and feelings. Past tools for measuring it used long interviews. Those are hard to run in large studies. A brief self-report form could fill the gap.

The team ran three studies to test the new form. The first used 299 mothers of children aged up to three. The second used 153 first-time parents, mothers and fathers. The third paired 136 mothers with infant attachment tests. The answers split into three factors. One caught pre-mentalizing modes. One caught certainty about the infant's mental states. One caught interest and curiosity in those states. Scores linked in expected ways to attachment, stress, and distress. The authors say more work must confirm the tool.
europmc-pmc5420131:
Pai and co-authors review a cell signaling path that links cancer growth with immune defense. Their review appeared in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. The path is called Wnt/beta-catenin signaling. It guides cell growth, movement, and stem cell renewal. Faults in the path show up in many cancers. Drug makers have long chased it as a target. New work adds an immune angle.

Tumors with this path switched on tend to keep immune cells out. That cold setting may blunt immunotherapy drugs. The review explains how beta-catenin builds up and enters the nucleus. There it switches on growth genes. The authors survey trials that block the path at several points. They also weigh how such drugs might pair with immune treatments. Readers get both the basic biology and the treatment outlook in one place.
europmc-pmc5423631:
Balsells and co-authors map which pneumococcal types still cause grave illness in children after vaccination. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in PLoS ONE. Conjugate vaccines cut disease from the types they cover. Other types then filled part of the gap. This shift is called serotype replacement. Knowing which types now lead is key for vaccine design.

The team found 68 studies and reports on childhood invasive disease. They split the data by vaccine era. Under the first seven-type vaccine, type 19A led. It caused about 22 percent of cases. Where broader vaccines had arrived, 19A's share fell to about 14 percent. Types outside the broadest vaccine caused about 42 percent of cases overall. Shares varied widely by region. Europe and North America ran highest. The authors urge steady surveillance, above all in poorer countries.
europmc-pmc5443231:
Holman and co-authors pool twenty studies to define the core gut microbes of pigs. Their meta-analysis appeared in mSystems. Pig gut microbes aid digestion and immunity. Farms hope to steer them for health gains. Each study used its own methods, though. That makes results hard to compare. The team reanalyzed public 16S gene data in one frame. The pool held 939 gut samples. It held over 25 million quality-filtered sequences.

Two factors shaped the microbe mix most. One was the study itself. The other was the gut site sampled. Technical gaps between studies can hide real biology. Still, a core set of bacteria emerged. These taxa appeared in at least 90 percent of samples. They persisted across countries, diets, ages, and breeds. The sequences spanned 35 phyla and 887 genera before trimming. The authors offer the core list as a base. Future work can aim feeds or drugs at it.
europmc-pmc5452131:
Almeida and co-authors review how plants juggle sodium and potassium to survive salty soil. Their review appeared in Genetics and Molecular Biology. Salinity cuts crop yields across the world. Over six percent of land is salt-affected. A fifth of irrigated land suffers too. Salt harms plants in two phases. First it blocks water uptake. Later sodium builds to toxic levels in leaves.

Tolerant plants keep a high potassium-to-sodium ratio inside cells. That balance rests on transport proteins and proton pumps. The review profiles the key players. SOS1 expels sodium from cells. HKT transporters guard the shoot. NHX exchangers lock sodium in storage sacs. Proton pumps supply the driving force for all of them. Each player works in set tissues. Each answers salt stress in its own way. The authors aim the knowledge at crop breeding.
europmc-pmc5463031:
Elovainio and co-authors ask why people who are socially cut off or lonely tend to die earlier. Their analysis appeared in The Lancet Public Health. They used data from the UK Biobank study. The group held 466,901 men and women. Their mean age at the start was about 57 years. Follow-up ran for about six and a half years on average.

Isolation carried a stark link to death. At first pass, isolated people faced about 73 percent higher risk. Full adjustment for other factors cut that excess to about 26 percent. Loneliness behaved in a different way. Its excess risk began near 38 percent. Full adjustment erased it almost completely. Four factor groups did most of the explaining. Money and social position led, along with health habits. Low mood and body measures followed. The authors say policy aimed at those factors could cut the excess deaths.
europmc-pmc5471831:
Madsen and co-authors, with the IPD-Work Consortium, present a systematic review and meta-analysis in Psychological Medicine. They ask whether job strain raises the risk of clinical depression. Job strain means high demands paired with low control at work. Past work mostly tracked symptoms, not diagnosed illness. That gap left the clinical link unclear.

The team pooled six published cohort studies with about 27,000 people. They added unpublished data on about 120,000 more workers. Job strain was linked to higher risk in both sets, they report. The link held across social groups and after some checks. The authors say trials should test if easing job strain prevents depression.
europmc-pmc5482931:
Zhang and co-authors present a review in Biomarker Research on engineering CAR-T cells. These are T cells fitted with a lab-built receptor that targets cancer. Such cells have shown strong results in B cell blood cancers. Trials now test them in other blood cancers and solid tumors. Wide use still faces many hurdles.

The review explains the receptor's three parts and how designs evolved. Four generations of CAR design are traced in turn. Tools for making the cells come next, from gene transfer to cell growth. A closing section faces the main challenges, such as safety and solid tumor barriers. Readers get a compact map of a fast-moving therapy field.
europmc-pmc5535831:
Adamska and co-authors present a review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences on pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. This cancer makes up 90 percent of pancreatic cases. It ranks fourth among cancer killers worldwide. Five-year survival sits near 5 to 7 percent. A dense scar-like stroma shields the tumor from drugs.

Standard care spans surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, they report. Most treatment only eases symptoms and buys time. Targeted drugs have disappointed so far, since backup pathways switch on fast. Four tumor subtypes may support more personal choices ahead. The review surveys current trials hunting for better options.
europmc-pmc5539431:
Spitzer and Haegens offer a review article in eNeuro. Their subject is beta oscillations, brain rhythms near 13 to 30 hertz. Such rhythms were long tied to sensing and movement. New work links them to working memory and decision making as well.

The authors argue that beta activity can carry specific content. Short bursts of sync may wake up cell groups that hold task-relevant information. That view goes past the older idea that beta only keeps the current brain state. Readers get a clear account that joins monkey and human findings with current models.
europmc-pmc5597631:
Mattsson and co-authors report an ecology study in Scientific Reports. Plastic breaks down in water into particles too small to see. The team followed such nanoparticles through a three-step food chain. Algae came first, then water fleas, then crucian carp.

The particles cut survival of the water fleas. They also moved up the chain into the fish. Microscopy found plastic inside the fish brains. The particles had crossed the blood-brain barrier. Exposed fish showed clear behavior disorders. Effects depended on particle size and charge. The authors warn that harm at the top of a food chain can unsettle whole ecosystems. Readers get the first direct chain from plastic uptake to brain effects.
europmc-pmc5615331:
Nieberler and co-authors review a family of cell-surface receptors in Cancers. Integrins link cells to their surroundings and pass signals both ways. Eight of them recognize a tiny three-part motif, RGD, in matrix proteins. Those eight help cancers grow and spread.

Because the receptors sit on the cell surface, drugs can reach them. Chemists have built small peptide-like blockers for single subtypes. Others carry glowing or radioactive tags for imaging tumors. Still others coat nanoparticles so poisons ride straight to cancer cells. Trials are testing whether blocking these receptors slows adhesion and invasion. Knowing each subtype's own job is the key to clean intervention. The review sorts the subtypes and their ligands. Readers get a target map for personalized cancer work.
europmc-pmc5617631:
Kanow and co-authors map energy flow in the vertebrate eye in eLife. The retina burns glucose at a furious rate. How fuel moves between its layers was murky. The pigment layer beneath it, the RPE, controls the supply route.

Measurements of flux and enzyme placement support a new model. Glucose passes through the RPE into the retina. Photoreceptors grab most of it and convert it to lactate. They then export that lactate as fuel. The RPE and Müller glial cells burn the lactate instead. Human RPE cells in culture confirmed the trade. Given lactate, they consumed less glucose themselves. More glucose then reached the retina beyond them. Readers get an ecosystem view of eye metabolism, with clues for retinal disease.
europmc-pmc5647431:
Kobayashi and co-authors report a mouse study in Scientific Reports. It tests a probiotic strain against Alzheimer's-type decline. The strain is Bifidobacterium breve A1. Mice got amyloid-beta injections to model the disease. Daily oral doses of the bacterium followed. Behavior tests checked memory and learning.

Treated mice kept normal alternation behavior in a Y maze. Their passive avoidance performance also held up. The authors report that this means cognitive dysfunction was prevented. Dead bacterial parts and acetate each helped in part. Gene profiling showed lower inflammation gene activity in the hippocampus. Amyloid-beta normally raises those genes. The findings suggest value in gut-brain approaches to prevention.
europmc-pmc5664031:
Hewlings and Kalman present a review in Foods. It covers curcumin and its effects on human health. Curcumin is the main polyphenol in turmeric spice. People use it for oxidative and inflammatory conditions. Listed uses include metabolic syndrome, arthritis, and anxiety. It may also ease exercise soreness and speed recovery.

Most benefits trace to antioxidant and anti-inflammatory action. A key problem is poor bioavailability. The body absorbs little curcumin and clears it fast. Adding piperine from black pepper changes that picture. One study found a rise of about twentyfold in availability. The review also covers use in healthy people. Safety data from trials look favorable at high doses.
europmc-pmc5708531:
Sorrenti and co-authors review polymerization that runs outside equilibrium. Their tutorial review appeared in Chemical Society Reviews. Supramolecular polymers can sit in four states. How they are prepared decides the state. The authors explain how to tell states apart. Kinetics matter in every state, they stress, not just in one.

Different pathways can yield different structures. The same conditions can hold distinct assemblies, side by side. The preparation protocol selects between them. Kinetic models help untangle this complexity. Living systems use such assembly for key tasks, such as cell membranes and ribosomes. The authors call non-equilibrium work an exciting direction for the field. It may in time yield materials with life-like traits, much like the stuff of life itself.
europmc-pmc5713331:
Begicevic and Falasca review ABC transporters in cancer stem cells. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. These membrane proteins pump drugs out of cells. That pumping drives much chemotherapy resistance. Cancer stem cells carry especially high levels. They also cycle slowly and seed relapse.

The authors argue the proteins do more than pump. They release bioactive molecules outside the cell. That release may shape the tumour niche. The review covers how their expression is regulated. It also covers their metabolic support roles. Targeting these transporters could hit stem cells. Specific inhibitors may spare other cells. The authors present that as a treatment opportunity.
europmc-pmc5750231:
Linde and co-authors study how breast cancer spreads at a very early stage. Spread was long thought to start only in advanced tumors. In a mouse model of HER2+ breast cancer, early cells leave before lesions turn malignant. Macrophages prove to be required for that early exit.

Removing macrophages in the pre-malignant phase cut later spread. Cancer and myeloid cells make CCL2, which draws in a set of macrophages. Those cells raise Wnt-1, which weakens E-cadherin links between cancer cells. Macrophage rich spots act as gates into blood vessels. Human tissue samples show like signs, the authors note.
europmc-pmc5817731:
Peng and co-authors survey long noncoding RNAs in glioma. Gliomas are brain tumors with grades from slow to deadly. Glioblastoma, the worst grade, resists standard care and returns fast. Long RNAs that code no protein may drive part of that behavior.

These RNAs run over 200 letters long and abound in tumor samples. Many sit at odd levels in glioma tissue and cell lines. They steer gene activity nearby and at a distance. Some mark tumor grade or likely outcome. Others could serve as drug targets. Readers get a guide to a young field with clear clinical hopes.
europmc-pmc5827731:
Mitrea and co-authors show one protein switching between two droplet modes. Nucleophosmin, or NPM1, helps build ribosomes in the nucleolus. It forms liquid droplets with RNA and partner proteins. The team finds it can also droplet with itself.

NPM1 carries floppy, charged regions that attract each other. That self-grip drives a second kind of phase separation. The two modes push against each other. Shape changes inside the protein flip which mode wins. The authors tie the switch to ribosome assembly flow. Readers get a neat case of one molecule holding two routes to the same droplet state.
europmc-pmc5840831:
Jellinger and Korczyn ask whether two Lewy body dementias are really one disease. Their review appeared in BMC Medicine. Dementia with Lewy bodies and Parkinson's disease dementia share symptoms, chemistry, and brain pathology. Clinicians split them only by which trouble comes first.

If thinking fails before or within a year of movement signs, the label is Lewy body dementia. Later decline in known Parkinson's earns the other label. The review finds heavier cortical amyloid and tau in the first group. Yet the two blend across a spectrum of synuclein disease. The authors lean toward one continuum with two extreme ends.
europmc-pmc5867031:
Sánchez and co-authors engineer wheat with far less gluten using CRISPR/Cas9. Their article appeared in Plant Biotechnology Journal. Gluten proteins in wheat trigger coeliac disease in susceptible people. The alpha-gliadin gene family holds the most potent triggers. One peptide, the 33-mer, drives most of the immune response. The team designed guide RNAs to cut near that peptide's code.

They produced twenty-one mutant wheat lines in bread and durum types. Some lines had up to 35 gliadin genes altered. Immune reactivity fell by 85 percent in the best results. Lines free of foreign DNA were also identified. No off-target cuts were found at checked sites. The lines could supply low-gluten foods in the future.
europmc-pmc5927631:
Mitchell and co-authors time the landmark events in clear cell kidney cancer. Their article appeared in Cell. They analysed whole genomes from 95 biopsies. Samples came from 33 patients with this cancer type. Loss of chromosome 3's short arm marks nearly every case. That loss removes several tumour suppressor genes at once.

The key event often strikes in childhood or teens, they report. It can precede the tumour's common ancestor by decades. A shattering event often causes both the loss and a gain elsewhere. Inherited cases follow the same early pattern. Very few cells with the loss can start sporadic tumours. Early trajectories may offer chances for early action.
europmc-pmc5978931:
Prada and co-authors show that brain support cells pass small gene bits to nerve cells in tiny sacs, changing nerve links when tissue is inflamed. Their study was published in Acta Neuropathologica. Link failure is an early step in such brain disease. How stirred clean-up cells cause those flaws was not fully known. Inflamed clean-up cells shed sacs rich in picked gene bits. One bit is found just in these clean-up cells. It aims at two key link proteins.

A test proved the sacs hand this cargo to nerve cells, they report. The handover cut two link proteins in the cells that got them. Long contact thinned link spines and dulled the links. Blocking sac contact stopped the effect.
europmc-pmc5986831:
Mouton and co-authors map macrophage polarisation across the first week after myocardial infarction in mice. Their study appeared in Basic Research in Cardiology. Heart macrophages steer inflammation and scar building after a heart attack. The team guessed their states shift over that week. They isolated macrophages from the infarct zone at days 1, 3, and 7. RNA sequencing profiled each time point against day 0 controls.

Day 1 cells were pro-inflammatory matrix degraders, they report. Day 3 cells grew, ate debris, and rewired their metabolism. Day 7 cells turned pro-repair and made matrix genes. The cells even supplied collagen and periostin directly.
europmc-pmc5993831:
Song and co-authors pair immunogenic chemotherapy with a locally expressed PD-L1 trap for cancer immunotherapy. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Checkpoint inhibitors face low response rates and immune side effects. Oxaliplatin chemotherapy can boost antibody therapy in mouse colon cancer. The team designed a PD-L1 trap protein instead of an antibody. Its gene rides into tumours inside a lipid-protamine-DNA nanoparticle. The trap is then made briefly, right at the tumour.

The pairing shrank tumours together better than either part alone, they report. Unlike antibody pairing, it did not pile up Th17 cells in the spleen. That hints at better tolerance for patients.
europmc-pmc6018631:
Cahill and co-authors present an updated method for gene studies. Their article appeared in Scientific Reports in 2018. The method compares ranked lists of gene activity. It looks for genes that change in the same direction. It also finds genes that change in opposite directions.

Most tools rely on strict significance cutoffs. Those cutoffs can miss real but subtle shared patterns. The updated approach, called RRHO2, avoids a single cutoff. It scans overlap across a full gradient of ranks. Tests used simulated data and real brain data. Data came from postmortem brains in psychiatric disorders. The package also offers clearer plots. Readers get a practical guide to finding shared expression signatures.
europmc-pmc6038331:
Crucian and co-authors review immune problems during spaceflight. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Studies show immune control slips during six-month orbital flights. Sleeping herpes viruses can wake up again. Some crew members develop lasting sensitivity reactions.

Deep space trips will add radiation and longer durations. Which crew members will be affected cannot be predicted. Broad countermeasures are therefore needed, the authors argue. Options include nutrition and functional foods. Exercise, vaccines, and drug options are also weighed. Bone health links closely with immune health. Personal immune profiles could guide tailored plans. Readers get a planning guide for Moon and Mars missions. It stresses effects on other body systems too.
europmc-pmc6068531:
Ward and co-authors update the evidence on nitrate in drinking water and health. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Fertilizer and manure have raised nitrate in water worldwide. Legal limits were set to protect infants from one blood condition. Other health effects went unweighed at the time.

Over 30 studies have appeared since the group's last review. Colorectal cancer drew the most attention. Thyroid disease and neural tube defects also stood out. The strongest links sat with those three outcomes. Many studies found raised risk below legal limits. Risk grows when the body forms N-nitroso compounds from nitrate. Readers get a call for better exposure tracking in future work.
europmc-pmc6100431:
Lambert and co-authors review ways to drug transcription factors in cancer. Their review appeared in Molecules. Transcription factors switch genes on and off. They account for about a fifth of known oncogenes. For years they were classed as undruggable.

New structural knowledge changed that verdict. Drugs can lower a factor's production or speed its destruction. Others block its partner proteins. Some stop it binding DNA at all. A few such drugs are already in use or in trials. Modern chemistry designs molecules for these awkward targets. The review sorts the approaches by attack point. Readers get a field guide to a newly open drug frontier.
europmc-pmc6127031:
Dunphy and co-authors present a research article in Molecular Cell on how DNA damage triggers an immune alarm. A protein called STING helps cells sense stray DNA. It was thought to need a partner sensor, cGAS. The team found a second route after damage to nuclear DNA.

They treated human cells with a drug that harms DNA. Within hours, an immune response switched on. This route used the proteins IFI16, ATM, and PARP-1 instead of cGAS. They built an alternate complex around STING. It turned on NF-kappaB, a master immune switch. The work casts STING as a hub with more than one mode.
europmc-pmc6238331:
Breitwieser and co-authors present KrakenUniq, a tool to classify microbes from DNA reads. Metagenomics sorts millions of short reads by species. False positive hits are a major problem. Contamination can create spurious species calls. The paper appeared in Genome Biology.

The tool builds on the fast Kraken classifier. It adds counts of unique short words per species. Those counts show how well a genome is covered. That helps split true low-level pathogens from false hits. Tests showed better recall and precision than rivals. A smart counting method keeps the tool fast. It needs little extra memory over Kraken. The software is freely shared online. It suits infectious disease samples well.
europmc-pmc6272531:
Jenkins, West, and Koulman review odd-chain fatty acids, a small family of fats once thought trivial. Their review appeared in Molecules. Two members draw most attention, pentadecanoic and heptadecanoic acid. Labs once used them only as measurement standards. They were assumed too scarce in people to matter. New data changed that view.

Higher blood levels of these fats track with lower heart and metabolic risk. Dairy eating may raise them, but direct proof is still thin. The body may also make them itself. One route trims a longer fat by one carbon at a time. Blood ratios hint at that inner making. Dairy fat holds the two fats in a two to one ratio, while blood shows the reverse. The review weighs diet against inner production. It names tests that could settle the question.
europmc-pmc6288131:
The International League Against Epilepsy Consortium on Complex Epilepsies ran a genome wide mega-analysis of the common epilepsies. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Epilepsy affects about 65 million people worldwide. Much of its inheritance was still missing before this work. The team joined data from over 15,000 people with epilepsy. Nearly 30,000 controls completed the sample.

Sixteen genome regions reached firm significance. Eleven of them were new. The team named twenty-one likely epilepsy genes at those spots. Many sit in generalized epilepsies, the most heritable forms. The genes cover ion channels, transcription factors, and a vitamin B6 enzyme. Known drug targets and single gene epilepsy genes were enriched in the results. Seven epilepsy subtypes were also pulled apart genetically. The findings offer fresh leads for therapy design.
europmc-pmc6297231:
Tron and co-authors describe AZD5991, a drug built to block the protein Mcl-1. Their report appeared in Nature Communications. Mcl-1 helps cancer cells avoid a built-in death program. High levels of it drive tumors and drug resistance. The team designed a ring-shaped molecule that binds Mcl-1 tightly.

AZD5991 bound Mcl-1 directly in lab tests. It set off fast cell death in blood cancer cells. Myeloma and acute myeloid leukemia cells were hit hardest. The drug worked through Bak, a partner protein in the death path. In mice, one tolerated dose shrank tumors fully in several models. It also worked with two standard drugs. A first human trial in blood cancers followed from these results.
europmc-pmc6303331:
Chen and co-authors build a catalyst from single iron atoms for oxygen reduction. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Fuel cells and zinc-air batteries need this reaction at the cathode. It runs slowly and often relies on costly platinum. The team sought a cheap, durable stand-in.

They set lone iron atoms in a hollow carbon shell. The shell was doped with nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur. This structure sped the reaction in both acid and alkaline media. Tests in a zinc-air battery and a hydrogen-air fuel cell worked well. The authors say the design could replace platinum in such devices.
europmc-pmc6325731:
Schurz and co-authors review the X chromosome in infection risk. Their review appeared in Human Genomics. The X chromosome holds many immune-related genes. Yet studies often skip it, as its analysis is tricky. Many infections strike one sex harder than the other. Hormones and behavior explain only part of that gap.

Women carry two X chromosomes, men carry one. One X is largely switched off in each female cell. That silencing varies, and some genes escape it. Skewed patterns of silencing also occur. The result is a mosaic immune system in females. The authors argue this can bring an edge against infection. They use tuberculosis, with its clear male bias, as their main example.
europmc-pmc6329831:
Loo and co-authors chart cell types in the developing mouse cortex. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The cortex forms through waves of birth, movement, and maturing. Many neuron and glia types arise in strict order. The team read gene activity in single cells. Samples came from mid-development and from birth.

They found many classes of neurons, progenitors, and glia. Each class showed its own state of growth or travel. Relatedness maps linked cells within and across the two ages. Disease genes were then placed onto the cell map. Genes tied to brain and mental disorders clustered by type. Some patterns matched known clinical features of diseases. The atlas gives a template for how the cortex is built.
europmc-pmc6368831:
Cobos and co-authors present a software article in PeerJ. They introduce kuenm, an R package for building ecological niche models with Maxent. Such models predict where species can live, but careful calibration is slow and often skipped.

The package automates candidate model creation across many parameter settings. It selects the best models by statistical significance, predictive power, and simplicity. It then builds final models, transfers them to new scenarios, and evaluates the results. A mobility-oriented parity metric flags risky extrapolations in those transfers. The authors aim to make niche modeling more rigorous and reproducible while saving researchers about a week of manual work.
europmc-pmc6381631:
Du and co-authors present a software article in BMC Bioinformatics. They introduce ElemCor, a tool that corrects data from stable isotope labeling studies measured by high-resolution mass spectrometry. Natural isotopes and tracer impurities distort the raw signals, so the true labeling pattern must be recovered before metabolic rates can be judged.

ElemCor offers two correction methods. One uses mass difference theory and needs only chemical formulas. The other learns from unlabeled samples run beside the experiment. Tests on simulated data and yeast samples showed better accuracy than older tools. The authors suggest the theory method for small compounds and the sample-based method for large ones.
europmc-pmc6602931:
Smith and co-authors train a neural network potential for molecular simulation. Their research article appears in Nature Communications. Quantum methods give accurate energies but cost too much for large systems. Classical force fields run fast but transfer poorly. The team sought one model with both speed and accuracy.

They first trained the ANI network on density functional theory data. Transfer learning then retrained it on coupled cluster results. Those gold-standard calculations spanned chemical space with care. The final potential, ANI-1ccx, nears coupled cluster accuracy on key benchmarks. Tests covered reaction energies, isomerization, and drug-like torsions. The authors report it runs billions of times faster than the gold standard. They expect wide use in chemistry, biology, and materials science.
europmc-pmc6625431:
Sharma reviews cholinesterase inhibitors as treatments for Alzheimer disease. His article appears in Molecular Medicine Reports. Alzheimer disease slowly erodes memory, language, and judgment. A shortage of the messenger acetylcholine helps drive that decline. Blocking the enzymes that break it down can raise its levels.

The review covers natural inhibitors, synthetic copies, and hybrid drugs. Four drugs now on the market are mostly of this class. Their gains are modest, and side effects grow with dose. None can halt the disease outright. Dual-target drugs add action against amyloid clumping or tau tangles. Multi-target designs aim at the disease's many drivers at once. The author maps current use, limits, and paths to safer drugs.
europmc-pmc6680731:
Surai and co-authors update the science of antioxidant defence in poultry. Their review appears in Antioxidants. Farmed birds face many stressors each day. Excess reactive species and oxidative stress follow. Birds evolved layered defences against that threat. Inner enzymes and glutathione form one layer. Dietary antioxidants like vitamin E form another. All parts work together as a team. Their balance steers gene activity in the cell.

The update centres on vitagenes and Nrf2. Switching these genes on boosts inner protection on demand. Standard premixes already supply base antioxidants. Hard conditions may demand more support. Feed mixes that switch vitagenes on are the proposed answer. Firms are chasing that direction. Keeping redox balance is the shared goal.
europmc-pmc6736231:
Brydges examines effect sizes and statistical power in gerontology research. Researchers often judge effects by Cohen's fixed cutoffs for small, medium, and large. Those cutoffs were never based on field data. Brydges asked what effects aging research actually produces, pulling values from meta-analyses in ten top gerontology journals.

For individual differences, a correlation of 0.12 counts as a small effect in this field. A value of 0.20 counts as medium, and 0.32 counts as large. For group differences, the matching guideposts are 0.16 for small effects, 0.38 for medium ones, and 0.76 for large ones. Cohen's rules seem to overstate typical effects here. Real field values should give better sample size plans.
europmc-pmc6813331:
Wagg and co-authors report a research article in Nature Communications on soil microbes and grassland function. They worked with fungi and bacteria in soil. Soil microbes hold a large share of life on Earth. Still, their joint effect on how land works was unclear.

The team altered the soil microbiome in grassland microcosms. Richer and more linked networks gave higher scores across many functions. Those functions centred on nutrient cycling. Poor networks had less backup for each task. They also had fewer distinct roles. The authors report that loss of such links can weaken the whole system.
europmc-pmc6938631:
Brnich and co-authors set rules for using lab test evidence when judging gene variants. Their recommendations appeared in Genome Medicine. Clinical guidelines sort variants with evidence codes. Two codes, PS3 and BS3, cover functional assays that show a variant harms or spares gene function. The guidelines never said how to weigh such assays, so laboratories often disagree.

A working group of the Clinical Genome Resource built a structured approach. Evaluators first define how the disease works. They then judge which assay types fit, and whether a given assay was properly validated. A four-step framework assigns the right strength of evidence. Shared rules, the group argues, should cut discordant calls between laboratories.
europmc-pmc6952431:
Bian and co-authors show that a faster lab setup can measure proteins reliably at huge scale. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Protein studies usually use nano-flow liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry. It is sensitive, but often fragile and slow. Large studies need a setup that stays steady for thousands of samples.

Their micro-flow system ran more than 2000 samples from human cells, tissues, and body fluids. Timing varied by less than 0.3 percent, and protein amounts by under 7.5 percent. Deep runs found over 9000 proteins in 16 hours. Tagging samples together lifted output to 11 proteomes in the same span. One column handled more than 7500 samples without clear loss. The authors argue the setup suits many kinds of protein research.
europmc-pmc6981831:
Rapa and co-authors review natural agents that may calm inflammation and oxidative stress in chronic kidney disease. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Kidney disease advances toward failure needing dialysis or transplant. Body-wide inflammation and oxidative stress drive many of its complications.

Those complications include malnutrition, artery hardening and calcification, heart failure, anaemia, and bone and mineral disorders. They also raise cardiovascular deaths. Beyond standard anti-inflammatory and antioxidant drugs, certain minerals, vitamins, and plant-derived compounds show promise. The authors survey the evidence for each. They caution that many trials were small with short follow-up. Longer studies, they argue, are needed before these agents can be recommended with confidence.
europmc-pmc7005631:
Silva and co-authors review short-chain fatty acids as messengers between gut and brain. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Endocrinology. Gut bacteria ferment fibre and resistant starch in the colon. Their main products are these small fatty acids. The gut microbes are now known to steer metabolic, immune, and hormone systems.

A wired gut-brain axis lets microbes influence brain chemistry and behaviour. The fatty acids are prime suspects for carrying those signals, tuning nerve, immune, and hormone routes at once. Exactly how they act on the brain is not fully worked out. The authors gather what is known, warn that most studies are in rodents, and sketch how brain disorder treatments might exploit this channel. Better maps of the pathway, they argue, could yield new drug targets for central nervous system disease.
europmc-pmc7025531:
Choudhari and co-authors review plant chemicals in cancer treatment for Frontiers in Pharmacology. Cancer remains a leading cause of death worldwide. Decades of synthetic drug development have not greatly lifted overall survival, so researchers keep looking to natural compounds. Plants supply many proven cancer drugs, including taxol relatives, vinca alkaloids, and podophyllotoxin relatives.

These phytochemicals act through several routes. They can boost antioxidant defences, neutralise carcinogens, slow cell division, trigger cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis, and adjust the immune system. The review describes the active compounds, their drug actions, and their molecular targets. It also maps recent trends and gaps in discovery work, arguing that plant chemistry still holds untapped leads for new cancer medicines.
europmc-pmc7048131:
Ma, Qin, and Li review the STAT3 signalling pathway in breast cancer for Cell Communication and Signaling. Breast cancer is the second leading cause of cancer death in women, and drug resistance limits the few treatments available. STAT3, a transcription factor, serves as an early tumour marker. When overactive and switched on constantly, it promotes malignancy.

Clinical and laboratory evidence ties active STAT3 to tumour growth, spread, and resistance to chemotherapy. New work has mapped regulators above STAT3 and target genes below it, filling in the pathway's wiring. Small molecule inhibitors that block STAT3 activation show promise as treatments. The review gathers these advances systematically, from pathway discovery to drug candidates. Its message is practical: a single overactive switch helps drive this cancer, and learning to turn it off could give resistant tumours a new line of attack.
europmc-pmc7098031:
Ye and co-authors review the animal origins of human coronaviruses, in the International Journal of Biological Sciences. Seven human coronaviruses are known. Most came from bats, often through an intermediate animal host. Two cause mild colds, while SARS, MERS, and SARS-CoV-2 can kill.

The review traces how each virus was found, and how each crossed into humans. It compares the seven viruses by evolution and genome recombination. It also sets out what a virus needs to switch hosts with success. The COVID-19 outbreak is read against that history. Readers learn why naming the animal hosts matters for stopping the next spillover before it starts.
europmc-pmc7143931:
Batiha and co-authors review quercetin, a plant flavonoid found in berries, apples, tea, cabbage, nuts, and onions, in Foods. Quercetin has traditionally been used against cancer and viral illness, and for allergic, metabolic, inflammatory, eye, heart, and joint disorders. The review covers its chemistry, how the body handles it, and its tested activities.

Lab and animal work shows action against bacteria, viruses, and parasites including Plasmodium, plus antioxidant, anti-cancer, and liver-protecting effects. It also blocks acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme tied to Alzheimer's disease. The compound gathers mainly in the lungs, liver, kidneys, and small intestine and leaves through urine, faeces, and breath. Safety and dosing evidence are part of the survey.
europmc-pmc7185831:
La Scola and co-authors test when COVID-19 patients stop being contagious. Their study appeared in the European Journal of Clinical Microbiology & Infectious Diseases. Hospitals needed a clear rule for releasing patients from isolation wards. The team compared PCR test values with growing live virus in cell culture. PCR can detect virus traces long after a patient is infectious.

Samples with high cycle threshold values failed to grow virus in culture. Above a Ct of about 33 to 34, patients seemed no longer contagious. The finding held with their own test system. Such patients could leave hospital care or strict confinement, they argue. The rule could free beds and staff during a surge. It also rests on an earlier study of a drug combination from the same group.
europmc-pmc7189231:
Li and co-authors introduce BEHRT, a deep learning model that reads electronic health records. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Most diagnoses happen only after symptoms become obvious. Earlier warning could allow earlier care and better planning. BEHRT adapts the transformer design, first built for language, to patient visit histories.

The model predicts the likelihood of 301 conditions at future visits. It learns from sequences of past diagnoses and treatments. The team tested it on three tasks with different time horizons. These covered the next visit, the next 6 months, and the next 12 months. BEHRT handled all of them in a single framework. The authors present it as a step toward earlier detection. Health systems could use such forecasts to target checkups.
europmc-pmc7226731:
Poitelon and co-authors review the fats that build myelin, the insulation wrapping nerve fibers. Their article appeared in Cells. Myelin lets nerve signals travel fast and supports neurons. It is unusually rich in lipids. Making a sheath demands heavy fat production plus uptake of fatty acids from outside the cell.

The review lays out the basic biology of myelin lipids. It then covers recent findings on how myelinating cells control fat metabolism. Different lipid species serve structure, signaling, and energy roles. Errors in this fat handling can disturb the whole nervous system. The authors aim to give future studies a firm base. Their overview connects cell biology to diseases where myelin breaks down.
europmc-pmc7239331:
Dehning and co-authors detect the moments when Germany's COVID-19 interventions began to bite. Their study appeared in Science. Short-term forecasts guide urgent containment choices. The challenge is spotting when growth truly changes. The team combined a standard epidemic model with Bayesian inference to track the growth rate over time.

Clear change points matched the dates of announced measures. School and store closures took effect on March 16. A contact ban followed on March 23. Growth fell from 30 percent to 12, then to 2 percent, as the first measures landed. Even 2 percent still meant the epidemic was growing. Only after the contact ban did spread tip into decay. The authors conclude the full package was necessary to stop exponential growth.
europmc-pmc7265231:
Denisenko and co-authors compare ways to prepare tissue for single-cell RNA studies. Their methods study appeared in Genome Biology. Sample handling can change which cells survive and which genes appear active. No full side-by-side test had been done. The team used adult mouse kidney tissue to fill that gap.

They compared warm digestion with cold digestion on ice. Cold work avoided a stress response seen at body temperature. Frozen storage lost many kidney lining cells. Methanol fixing kept cell mix better but leaked some RNA. Single-nucleus methods also missed some immune cells. The full dataset is released for others to reuse. Readers can pick a method with its biases in view.
europmc-pmc7285131:
D'Avolio and co-authors compare vitamin D levels in Swiss patients who tested positive and negative for SARS-CoV-2. Their short study appeared in Nutrients. Vitamin D had been suggested to lower infection risk, but direct measurements in tested patients were scarce. The team looked back at plasma levels of 25-hydroxyvitamin D in a tested cohort.

Patients with positive PCR tests had a median level of 11.1 ng/mL, compared with 24.6 ng/mL in negative patients, a significant gap. The difference held when patients over 70 years were examined separately. The authors present the finding as preliminary. They suggest supplementation might lower infection risk, and call for randomized trials and large population studies to test whether raising vitamin D actually helps.
europmc-pmc7292831:
Tang and co-authors review how liver cancer cells learn to resist sorafenib, a standard drug for advanced disease. Their review appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Sorafenib blocks several enzymes at once, promoting cancer cell death, choking tumor blood supply, and slowing growth. It is an effective first-line therapy for late-stage hepatocellular carcinoma, yet resistance keeps developing.

Recent studies point to four sources of resistance: epigenetic changes that reprogram genes, transport processes that move the drug, shifts in how cells die, and the tumor microenvironment around the cancer. The authors summarize the principles behind each route and outline strategies intended to delay or reverse resistance and improve outcomes for patients whose tumors no longer respond.
europmc-pmc7379131:
DeCordova and co-authors review glioblastoma in Frontiers in Immunology, the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults. Even with surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy, prognosis stays poor. The authors focus on two reasons: the tumor's extreme variety and its suppressive immune surroundings.

Tumors differ between patients and within a single mass, and their cells can shift identity. The local environment, rich in tumor-associated macrophages, blunts immune attack and feeds drug resistance. Late diagnosis and deep infiltration add to the difficulty. New genome and gene-activity profiling has sharpened the picture of this landscape. The review argues that better immunotherapy depends on understanding that environment in detail.
europmc-pmc7379631:
Almanza and co-authors review stress signaling in the endoplasmic reticulum in The FEBS Journal. This cell compartment folds roughly one-third of all cellular proteins, the first step of the secretory pathway. When folding demand overwhelms capacity, alarm pathways called the unfolded protein response switch on.

The response first tries to restore balance, expanding folding capacity and pausing production. If that fails, the same pathways trigger cell death. The review traces the field from the compartment's discovery to the latest work on how this signaling touches other organelles and shapes cell behavior. Clinical applications close the account. Protein folding, the authors show, is a balance point between health and disease in every cell.
europmc-pmc7402631:
Hsieh and co-authors design a stabilized coronavirus spike protein in Science. The spike is the vaccine target, but in its natural form it is metastable and hard to manufacture, flipping shape and giving low yields. The team tested 100 structure-guided designs to lock it in its prefusion shape.

They found 26 single changes that raised yield or stability, then combined the best. The winner, HexaPro, carries six proline substitutions and expresses about 10 times more protein than its parent. It survives heat stress, room temperature storage, and three freeze-thaw cycles. A 3.2 angstrom structure confirmed the locked shape. A sturdy, high-yield spike speeds vaccine making and antibody test production alike.
europmc-pmc7414031:
Greco and co-authors test the toxicity of synthetic antimicrobial peptides in Scientific Reports. Such peptides promise new antibiotics, but odd toxicity models slow their path to the clinic. The team studied a library of 24 peptides aimed at veterinary pathogens, in cells and in rats.

Red blood cell damage varied by species, worst for dog cells and mildest for cattle cells, with human cells in between. Against three human cell lines the peptides looked more stable still, and therapeutic indexes of 50 to 500 suggested real selectivity for bacteria over body cells. Three peptides dosed into rats at multiples of their working dose caused no systemic toxicity. The assays, the authors stress, do not line up neatly, which is itself the warning.
europmc-pmc7426331:
Houbraken and co-authors set out a fresh classification for Aspergillus, Penicillium, Talaromyces, and their kin. These fungi, in the order Eurotiales, matter for food, homes, health care, and industry. Older schemes rested on visible traits, which gene data have since challenged.

The team rebuilt family links with a nine-gene dataset. They accept four known families and add one new family, Penicillaginaceae. The order holds 28 genera in their scheme. For Aspergillus and Penicillium they update the ranks below genus: subgenera, sections, and series. A full list of accepted species in the order closes the work. Taxonomists gain one shared, gene-based frame for these fungi.
europmc-pmc7462931:
Koepsell reviews glucose transporters in the brain and their roles in health and disease. Neurons need a steady glucose supply from the blood. Transporters in capillaries and brain cells secure that supply.

The brain uses the GLUT1-6 and GLUT8 carriers plus the sodium-linked SGLT1. They move glucose across the blood-brain barrier to astrocytes and neurons. Their activity adapts to shifts in neuron work and glucose supply. The review sets out each carrier's traits and brain locations, drawn mostly from rodent work. It covers roles in energy supply, glucose sensing, feeding behavior, learning, and memory. It then turns to disease: GLUT1 deficiency, diabetes, Alzheimer's, stroke, and brain injury all involve these carriers.
europmc-pmc7466131:
Picca and co-authors review how mitochondrial faults, oxidative stress, and brain inflammation intertwine. Oxidative stress reflects a breach in a cell's antioxidant guard. Mitochondria both make reactive oxygen species and suffer from them.

Under stress, parts of mitochondria, including their DNA, can escape the organelle. Freed mitochondrial DNA can act as a danger signal. It binds receptors that spark innate immune inflammation. Such inflammation marks many brain disorders, so these signals may form a shared thread. The review sets the story in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's diseases and in Down syndrome. It explores weak spots in mitochondrial quality control. Those weak spots may yield new drug targets for neurodegeneration.
europmc-pmc7475031:
Minh, Hahn, and Lanfear give new methods to measure agreement among gene trees in phylogenomic data. Two scores do the work. The gene concordance factor shows how many decisive gene trees hold a given branch.

The site concordance factor is new here. It shows how many decisive DNA sites back a branch. Both scores give a full picture of disagreement that classic support values miss. The package handles uneven species coverage across gene trees, a common flaw in big data sets. It runs inside the free IQ-TREE software, with a tutorial for users. Rooted tree cases get their own treatment. The authors show how to read the scores on real data. The tools help teams judge which branches of an evolution tree are solid.
europmc-pmc7501731:
Remmerie and co-authors find a recruited macrophage group in fatty liver that differs from resident Kupffer cells. Fatty liver disease spans simple fat buildup to steatohepatitis. Liver macrophages were thought to drive much of the harm.

In diseased livers, Kupffer cells fell in number. Bone marrow recruits took their place in the tissue. The recruits split into two states: one near the calm resident type, one like lipid-linked macrophages of fat tissue. The lipid-linked group made osteopontin, a marker tied to scarring in patients. They sat in zones where Kupffer cells were scarce. The work shows the liver macrophage pool is far more mixed than once thought. Finer targeting, the authors say, is needed for fatty liver drugs.
europmc-pmc7510731:
Park and co-authors analyze contact tracing in South Korea during the early COVID-19 outbreak. The team studied reports from January 20 to March 27, 2020. Tracing shows where spread risk runs highest.

The data covered 59,073 contacts of 5,706 index patients in the national reports. Of 10,592 household contacts, 11.8% had COVID-19 in the tracing records. Of 48,481 nonhousehold contacts, 1.9% had COVID-19 in the same data set. Home exposure thus carried far more risk than outside contact. The authors credit protective measures and social distancing with cutting the odds of spread. Their numbers give tracers a clear priority order. Household rings need the fastest and closest follow-up in an outbreak.
europmc-pmc7528031:
Nguyen, Smith and Jain improve nucleic acid detection with the Cas12a enzyme. Cas12a systems can signal a target without lab copying steps. Their limit had been detection only near the picomolar range.

The team extended the guide RNA at either end. A 7-mer DNA extension worked across targets. It raised collateral cleavage up to 3.5-fold. It also improved how well targets were told apart. The system reached the femtomolar range without pre-amplification. With RT-LAMP, it was built into a paper test for SARS-CoV-2. That test gained up to 23-fold higher sensitivity in 40–60 min.
europmc-pmc7672931:
Kadry and co-authors give an overview of the blood-brain barrier and how to judge its health. The barrier controls what passes between blood and brain. Its tight seal keeps the brain's inner setting stable, which nerve cells need to work well.

The review lays out the cells and structures that form the barrier and their jobs. It explains how fluid stress helps keep the seal sound. It then links barrier breakdown to a range of brain diseases. The authors close with markers that can gauge barrier leak in the lab or in patients, with the pros and cons of each.
europmc-pmc7894131:
Voysey and co-authors report a pooled analysis of trials of the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine, also called AZD1222. The vaccine was approved for emergency use in the UK as two standard doses. The planned gap between doses ran from 4 to 12 weeks. The team combined four randomised trials to test dose timing and single-dose effects.

Across the trials, 17,178 people were included in the main analysis. Overall efficacy more than 14 days after the second dose was 66.7%. Results varied with the gap between doses. Longer gaps looked at least as good in the exploratory results. The authors note that a 3-month gap could help when supplies are scarce. More people can gain first-dose cover early. Protection after the second dose may also improve with the longer wait.
europmc-pmc7905231:
Shields and co-authors present a review of reactive oxygen species and lifespan. Ageing is the top risk factor for heart disease, brain degeneration, and cancer. A long-held theory blames damage from reactive oxygen species for much of ageing. The review tests that theory against two kinds of evidence.

Comparative studies measure such damage across species with different lifespans. Shorter-lived species tend to carry more damage, which fits the theory. Experiments go further by raising or lowering these species in one animal. Often, more of them shortens life and fewer extends it. Yet the review also finds clear cases that run the other way. Raising the species sometimes lengthened life. The authors conclude the link is complex. The evidence base also rests on a few short-lived species.
europmc-pmc7930231:
Misrani and co-authors present a review of mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress in Alzheimer's disease. Mitochondria make the energy that keeps cells alive. They change shape by splitting and merging to stay healthy. Damaged ones are cleared by a process called mitophagy. When these systems fail, the fallout can drive brain disease.

The review gathers the main forms of failure found in this disease. They include excess reactive oxygen species, faulty calcium handling, and loss of energy output. Defects in shape control, transport, and clearance add to the damage. Such faults are now seen as core steps in how the disease develops. The authors then review ways to restore mitochondrial health. Exercise, an antioxidant diet, and targeted drugs may slow the onset and pace of decline.
europmc-pmc8081831:
Carnicer-Lombarte and co-authors review the foreign body reaction and its toll on nerve implants. Any implanted material draws immune cells that try to destroy it. When they fail, scar tissue walls the device off. That wall dulls the link between electrode and nerve. Nerve prosthetics live or die by that link. They have to catch faint axon signals and spark small fiber groups.

The review explains how the reaction builds, step by step. It then surveys the three families of nerve interface. Cuff, penetrating, and regenerative designs each meet the reaction differently. Long-term function fades in all three as scarring grows. Smaller, softer devices may provoke less reaction. Drugs that calm the response offer another lever. Materials that dissolve after doing their job close the survey. Shrinking implants make the problem more urgent, not less.
europmc-pmc8156131:
Chen and Wang review how social media serves health purposes. Use grew fast, above all during the COVID-19 pandemic. Past reviews tended to cover one use at a time, such as campaigns or teaching.

The pair searched 12 databases for peer-reviewed studies from 2006 to 2020. They coded each study by year, field, country, and method. Their aim was to map all health uses found so far. The synthesis shows new uses that emerged in recent years. It also marks gaps where research is still thin. Each coded trait helps show how the field changed since the last broad review, in 2013.
europmc-pmc8193431:
Payne and co-authors measure how often MIS-C followed SARS-CoV-2 infection in United States youth. The syndrome is a rare, severe inflammatory state in children and teens. Their cohort study covered April to June 2020.

The study counted 248 people with MIS-C among those under 21 years. Incidence came to 316 cases per 1,000,000 infections. Rates ran higher in Black, Hispanic or Latino, and Asian or Pacific Islander youth. Younger people faced higher rates than older ones. The authors call for work on why rates differ by group and age. The study frames MIS-C as a rare outcome overall.
europmc-pmc8387231:
Salminen and co-authors give an expert consensus statement that defines postbiotics. The term was in wide use in papers and on products, but with no fixed meaning. A panel from the International Scientific Association for Probiotics and Prebiotics met in 2019 to settle the scope.

The panel defined a postbiotic as a preparation of inanimate microorganisms, or their parts, that gives a health benefit. Working products must hold inactivated cells or cell parts that add to the benefit. Metabolites may or may not be present. The statement also covers proof standards, safety, and the effects on science, industry, and regulators. Clear terms should aid future product work.
europmc-pmc8393631:
Soroka and co-authors ask whether LAMP, a DNA copying method from 1998, beats the better-known PCR. LAMP works at one steady temperature, so no cycling machine is needed. A dry block heater or simple incubator can run it.

The method can build up huge copy numbers in under an hour. It uses two to three primer pairs that check up to eight target spots, which makes it highly specific. Its main enzyme also removes the need for a DNA melting step. Results can come fast, at times by eye alone. The review weighs LAMP against PCR across fields. It highlights RT-LAMP as a rapid test for SARS-CoV-2.
europmc-pmc8620231:
Gabriel and co-authors introduce TSEBRA, a tool that picks the best gene predictions from the BRAKER annotation suite. BRAKER has two pipelines for marking protein-coding genes in new genomes. One uses RNA data, the other uses proteins from other species. Each alone leaves part of the evidence unused.

TSEBRA compares the two output sets with a rule set. It weighs support from RNA data and from related proteins for each transcript. Tests on genomes of 11 species showed higher accuracy than either pipeline alone. It also matched or beat a rival combiner tool. The tool is fast and easy to run. It helps genome teams use all their evidence at once.
europmc-pmc8675431:
Frangou and co-authors chart cortical thickness across the human lifespan in 17,075 healthy people aged 3 to 90 years. Brain thickness links to thought and behavior. Sound age curves need very large samples. Data came from the ENIGMA consortium, which pools scans across many sites.

For most brain regions, thickness peaked in childhood. It then fell with age, fast at first and more slowly after the third decade. A few regions broke this pattern, such as the entorhinal cortex. People differed most in temporal and frontal regions. Age explained up to 59 percent of the variance in thickness. The curves can serve as a norm for later studies of brain disease.
europmc-pmc8693031:
He and co-authors describe the traits of the Omicron variant of SARS-CoV-2 and ways to prevent its spread. The variant was first reported in South Africa in late November 2021. Cases rose fast after its appearance. The World Health Organization named it a variant of concern within days.

Omicron carries a high number of mutations. Fifteen sit in the spike protein's binding domain alone. It shares some changes with the alpha, beta, and gamma variants. These raised concern about spread, severity, and immune escape. The authors compare spike changes across all five variants of concern. They close with steps that may curb its spread.
europmc-pmc8786931:
Li and co-authors trace a large, well-documented outbreak of the SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant in mainland China. All 167 infections were linked back to one first case. Daily PCR tests on quarantined contacts gave a rare, close view of spread. The team compared Delta viral loads with those of the first epidemic wave.

When Delta cases first turned PCR-positive, viral loads ran about 1,000 times higher than early-wave cases. That hints at faster growth and greater infectiousness early on. Transmission usually passed through a tight bottleneck of one to three virus particles. A few within-host variants still seeded later cases. The study shows how small variant pools can shape an outbreak.
europmc-pmc8992231:
Liu and Rocklöv review how fast the Omicron variant spreads compared with Delta. They ran a rapid review of reproduction number studies. Two numbers frame spread. The basic number counts spread in a fully naive population. The effective number counts spread amid immunity and controls. Omicron's figures tower over Delta's on both counts.

The pooled estimates put Omicron's basic number at 8.2 on average across the studies reviewed. Its effective number averaged 3.6 in populations with some immunity in place. Against Delta, the effective number ran nearly four times higher, and the basic number about two and a half times higher. Omicron was first found in Botswana and South Africa in November 2021, and soon dominated worldwide. The review gives planners a compact spread estimate.
europmc-pmc9104731:
Ho and co-authors survey hydrogels and their uses in biomedicine. Hydrogels are networks of polymer chains that soak up large amounts of fluid. Their high water content and soft, porous form make them much like living tissue. Some types break down safely in the body, while others can be tuned by design.

The survey first covers structure, types, and ways to make hydrogels. It then turns to four main medical uses. Those uses are 3D cell culture, drug delivery, wound dressings, and tissue engineering. The authors show how traits like stiffness and decay rate can be set for each job. Readers get a full entry point to a fast-growing materials field.
europmc-pmc9252731:
Madeira and co-authors describe the search and sequence analysis tool services from EMBL-EBI in 2022. EBI Search gives full-text search across nearly 5 billion entries. The Job Dispatcher framework runs popular bioinformatics tools for the community. Both work through friendly web pages and through APIs.

The article reports recent improvements to both services. Updates were shaped by rising data demands during the COVID-19 pandemic. Tool catalogues span similarity search, alignment, and functional annotation. The services draw on major databases hosted at the institute. Free access helps researchers worldwide run core analyses. Readers get a current guide to infrastructure that underpins much daily bioinformatics work.
europmc-pmc9287331:
Zomer and co-authors release version 3 of the Global Aridity Index and Potential Evapotranspiration Database. The database gives high-resolution world maps of water demand and dryness. Values are monthly and yearly means for 1970 to 2000 at 30 arc-seconds detail. The math follows the FAO Penman-Monteith reference method.

Tests against weather station data gave strong matches, with r-squared values from 0.83 to 0.90. The new version tracks real data better than the one before. Earlier versions were downloaded over 47,000 times and cited in nearly 1,500 works. Uses span farming, water planning, genetics, and climate studies. Source code is released with the data. The set replaces all older versions for future work.
europmc-pmc9346631:
Dyall and co-authors gather recent advances on polyunsaturated fatty acids and the signals made from them. These fats sit in cell membranes and shape how membranes behave. They also serve as raw stock for a family of messengers called oxylipins. Enzymes or free radicals do the conversion.

Classic members include prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes. Newer classes cover omega-3 resolving mediators, elovanoids, and fatty esters of hydroxy fatty acids. The review explains how each class is built and what it does. Desaturase enzymes that make the parent fats get close attention. New detection tools are driving fast discovery in this field. The authors, all active researchers here, map where proof is firm and where it thins.
europmc-pmc9800531:
Du and Guo review recent progress on ferroptosis, the iron driven form of programmed cell death. The process hinges on iron buildup and fat oxidation damage. It differs from other death paths in cause and look. Many diseases carry its fingerprints in their course.

Work on the pathway has named several key control points. The guard enzyme GPX4 stands at the center of defense. A transport system that feeds cell antioxidants matters too. Drugs that trigger the death are called inducers here. Drugs that block it are classed as inhibitors. The review sorts both camps by their target path. Iron, fat, and antioxidant routes each get their own lists. Nanoparticles and gene tools join the compound lists. The authors discuss medical uses for both directions. Open questions for the young field close the review.
fort-lo-1931:
Things fall, move, and appear where they should not in Fort's third book, Lo, of 1931. Teleportation is his word and his theme: matter shifted by a force no law yet names. Poltergeists, falls from clear skies, and wild shifts of place fill the file.

Fort piles case on case from the news of the world, each with its date and source. His tone is drier and his aim surer than in the first books. Lo is the damned data at its strangest and most pure. Few books make the world feel so thin at the seams.
frankenstein-1831:
Mary Shelley took her famed novel in hand once more and made this new form in 1831. It is the text most readers have known since that year. She added a long new start, in which she tells how the tale came to her in 1816.

The frame of the tale is reworked, and Victor's fate bears a more dark and fixed cast. The being he made stands in a more grave light, and the blame shifts in tone. This is Frankenstein as Shelley at last chose to leave it to the world.
frus-1861-d131:
On 17 June 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton in a settled, watchful tone. The letter is document 131 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid June letters from Seward have a settled feel: the lines are set, the work is watch and ward. His note to Dayton keeps Paris inside the same firm frame as London. The two posts, read together, formed the Union's wall in Europe. London and Paris, held in one frame, left the South no great door into Europe. No great door left open meant no great hope left alive for the South in Europe.
frus-1861-d231:
Orders from Washington reached James Shepherd Pike in a State Department letter dated 16 May 1861. It stands as Document 231 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the opening months of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d31:
On 30 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Henry Sanford, his envoy in Belgium. The letter is document 31 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The Union defeat at Bull Run on 21 July shook faith at home and abroad. Seward now had to hold foreign courts steady while the army rebuilt. A letter to Brussels nine days after the battle belongs to that work of repair and resolve. After Bull Run, Seward's aim was to show a Union shaken but far from beaten. Resolve, repeated in plain words, was the coin Seward paid out all that autumn.
frus-1862-d131:
The home office spoke to Charles Francis Adams on 18 August 1862, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 131 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d231:
The second Stuart letter of 2 September 1862 stands as Document 231 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William Stuart, acting head of the British legation, sent both letters to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Two letters in a day from the legation suggest several live matters at once, each kept on its own sheet by custom. Early September 1862 gave the legation plenty to handle: invasion news, shaken markets, and fresh instructions to seek from London. Paired letters like these show formal business keeping its order in a disordered week. Cases under such notes were often small: one ship, one prisoner, one point of form.
frus-1862-d31:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 11 March 1862. It stands as Document 31 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d331:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 6 October 1862 in a letter printed as Document 331 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

By the time Dayton wrote, the Emancipation Proclamation's text was known in Paris and French opinion was stirring. Working-class sympathy for the Union grew harder for the emperor to ignore. Dayton's report that week fed Washington's sense that the proclamation was doing diplomatic work no envoy could have done alone. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war. Dayton's French was limited, and he leaned on his staff and on careful written notes.
frus-1862-d431:
On 16 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this reply to Gabriel García Tassara, the Spanish minister in Washington. It stands as Document 431 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Mid-July 1862 was a low point for Union arms, with McClellan driven back from Richmond. Foreign ministers in Washington watched for signs that the government might bend, and Seward's notes had to show no bend at all. His exchange with Tassara kept Spain at formal arm's length on the war while handling the standing business between the two countries. The letter is a sample of Seward's desk diplomacy in the war's hardest summer.
frus-1862-d531:
On 7 June 1862, the same day the Dutch minister's two notes were dated, Secretary of State William H. Seward answered Roest van Limburg. The reply is Document 531 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Same-day answers were Seward's specialty when a matter was warm, and the Dutch file in June 1862 was warm indeed. His reply kept the exchange moving without conceding the Union's reading of its belligerent rights at sea. The Netherlands, whose trade the blockade touched daily, pressed its points through Van Limburg with equal energy. Read in sequence from Document 527, the June letters form a compact case study in how wartime questions between friendly governments were actually worked through.
frus-1862-d631:
On 6 May 1862 Edward Joy Morris sent this report from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 631 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Morris's May report came from the far end of the Department's world in a season of Union advance. At the Ottoman court the American war was by then a settled topic: a great republic was fighting its rebels, and the powers watched. His dispatch kept the record of American business at the Porte complete for the spring. Read with the instructions Seward sent him, it shows a mature posting running itself, with Washington informed at intervals and local judgment trusted in between.
frus-1863p1-d131:
