On 26 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 131 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a dispatch often held what the first had no room for. Adams's pair of 26 March closed the legation's mail for a crowded week. This letter is its second half. With the Seward sheet of the same date set just before the pair in the volume, the cluster shows the sea mail at its busiest. Two pens worked one war, an ocean apart.
frus-1863p1-d231:
Writing from London on 10 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The dispatch is document 231 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d31:
On 16 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in London. The letter is document 31 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. Seward's January mail to the legation runs thick in this part of the volume.

The secretary wrote to keep Adams's hand strong in talks with Lord Russell. Each letter restated the Union's claims and fed the envoy the facts he needed from home. This one falls between Adams's reports of mid-January, a sign of how tight the loop had grown. It is a plain working sheet, and its worth is in the chain it holds together.
frus-1863p1-d331:
The American answer to London on 3 December 1862 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 331 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d431:
The letter printed as document 431 was written on 28 March 1863 by William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the spring of 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page.
frus-1863p1-d531:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote this official letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 23 May 1862. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d631:
Dated 16 October 1863, document 631 is a letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d131: Secretary Hull wrote to Minister Kirk in Cairo on November 16, 1943, six days before the Cairo Conference opened in Kirk's city. The letter is Document 131 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Washington-to-host messages in the final week tended to the practical, though this record names no subject. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series, among the papers of the president's voyage and arrival.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d231:
Paper C.C.S. 300/2, issued by the United States Chiefs of Staff aboard the Iowa on 18 November 1943, estimates the enemy situation in the Pacific and Far East for 1944. A long appendix carries the detail, with separate notes on what the Soviets and the Chinese might do.

The estimate expects Japan to stay on the strategic defensive through 1944, striking locally where needed. Tokyo would fight hardest to stop Allied air bases rising in China and to hold Burma, while watching the Soviet border with care. War with the Soviet Union is judged likely only if Japan became convinced that Moscow meant to attack her, or to hand Siberian air bases to the other Allies.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d31: One day after Stalin's reply, Roosevelt wrote to him again, on September 9, 1943. The letter is Document 31 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Back-and-forth at this speed shows the summit planning gathering pace as autumn began. The record gives sender, receiver, and date, and no subject line. Readers will find the message in the Foreign Relations volume, in the sequence that runs from Quebec toward Moscow, Cairo, and Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d331:
General Patrick Hurley sent President Roosevelt a second telegram from Tehran on 26 November 1943, following his wire of earlier that day about the Soviet invitation. He had since toured the offered quarters with General Connolly, Secret Service agent Rowley, and Soviet security officers.

The suite sits inside the Russian Embassy compound, in the building Reilly had inspected. It holds six rooms to the left of the entrance, a large reception room, bedrooms, and a dining room. A kitchen below serves the President's staff. It is steam heated, has a private entrance, and stands on the same floor as, and adjoining, the large conference room. Only bathtubs and toilets, removed earlier, need putting back. Hurley judges the quarters far better than the American legation for convenience, communications, and security, while repeating that he told the Russians the legation decision was definite.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d431: President Roosevelt wrote a short letter of welcome to President Ismet Inönü of Turkey from Cairo on 3 December 1943, as Inönü set out for the second Cairo Conference. The letter was carried to Adana by the President's son-in-law, Major John Boettiger. He rode aboard the plane sent to collect the Turkish party. The plane was in the command of Major Otis Bryan. Roosevelt hopes Inönü will have a smooth trip, and says he looks forward with great pleasure to seeing him on Saturday afternoon.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d531:
Lord Halifax, the British ambassador in Washington, wrote to President Roosevelt on December 24, 1943. A Christmas Eve letter from an ambassador to a president was unusual paper, crossing the line between formal business and personal regard. The State Department printed it in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Halifax, a former foreign secretary and viceroy of India, brought great weight to the Washington embassy. His access to Roosevelt was part of the alliance's daily machinery in the capital. For readers, the message shows the British mission working its most important relationship at the highest level, even on a holiday, as the conference season closed.
frus-1944-quebec-d131:
London's chiefs of staff cabled General Eisenhower on September 10, 1944, with an urgent request about Warsaw. The British ambassador in Moscow had reported the Soviet position. Moscow was willing to cooperate in supply drops if the aid followed a prearranged plan, and His Majesty's Government wanted no chance of helping the Poles to be missed.

The chiefs asked Eisenhower to consider mounting a supply-drop operation at the earliest possible date. British representatives in Moscow had been told of the Russian decision and asked to make the needed arrangements. Eisenhower was to inform General Deane, the American mission chief in Moscow, of his decision and his requirements from the Russians.
frus-1944-quebec-d231:
The secretaries of the Combined Chiefs drafted the implementing messages on September 12, 1944, as C.C.S. 618/4. Identical letters, adjusted for the recipient, were proposed for Generals Burrows and Deane, the British and American mission chiefs in Moscow. Each man was to propose the tripartite Military Committee to the Soviet General Staff at once.

The message to Deane stresses the limits: the committee would be purely consultative, unable to decide anything without reference home. It must not impinge on the European Advisory Commission's work. A cardinal point was that the Russian member be a senior General Staff officer. With the three armies approaching each other, Deane was told to act immediately so the committee could function soon.
frus-1944-quebec-d31:
Harry Hopkins wrote to Prime Minister Churchill on August 28, 1944, the first of three messages from him to Churchill bearing that date. The State Department printed them in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Three messages in a day from the President's aide suggest detailed work being finished: the Quebec Conference was a fortnight away, and its arrangements and agenda ran through Hopkins. He wrote as Roosevelt's agent, free to arrange what the President would later approve. For readers, the cluster shows a summit being built piece by piece in late August, in the alliance's most trusted staff channel.
frus-1945-50-intel-d131:
Russell, assistant secretary of state for administration, sent an instruction to Alling, the American minister in Tangier, on 3 January 1947. Instructions from the department direct a post's conduct. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Tangier appears in both volumes of this slice of history: a Potsdam question in 1945, and a post receiving department instructions in 1947. The paper belongs to the volume's State thread, where intelligence business touched ordinary diplomacy in small ports. Readers can take it as a sign of the system's settling. The secret work of the postwar world now ran through channels as plain as an administration chief's instruction to a minister in North Africa.
frus-1945-50-intel-d231:
The General Counsel of the Central Intelligence Agency (Houston) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 7 April 1948. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 231 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The young CIA was still defining its job, while the Council weighed how far secret action abroad should go.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d31:
Donald Russell, assistant secretary of state for administration, wrote to McCormack, the special assistant for research and intelligence, on 22 October 1945. Both men served in the State Department. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Russell ran the department's housekeeping: people, money, and space. McCormack's new intelligence office needed all three at once, having just absorbed the OSS analysts. An inside paper from the administration chief to the intelligence chief shows the unglamorous work of housing a new function. Readers often skip such papers, yet they decide whether bright plans live or die. This one shows the State Department's intelligence office being built from the inside.
frus-1945-50-intel-d331:
A memorandum dated 20 November 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Armstrong). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Lovett. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 331 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The old board and its group were gone, replaced that fall by the CIA under the new National Security Council.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d431:
On 6 January 1950 the National Security Council issued Intelligence Directive No. 12. The text is document 431 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Two directives on one day point to a full agenda at the start of 1950. The Council used the numbered series to keep every agency inside one frame. Read beside Directive No. 11, this order shows the steady, formal way the early Cold War state managed its secret work. Issued as a pair, the two January orders divided fresh duties between the same set of agencies. The pair shows the Council at its most brisk, settling two points in a single day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d131:
Writing from Warm Springs, Georgia, on 4 December 1944, President Roosevelt gave the State Department three points to keep in the linings of their hats. His short memorandum to Secretary Stettinius is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers the summary of British views sent on 29 November.

Germany, he says, should be let back industrially far enough to meet her own needs. But she should do no exporting for some time, until we see how things work out. Second, “we are against reparations.” Third, “we do want restitution of looted property of all kinds.” The one-page note cut across months of staff argument in the President's plainest style.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d231:
Stettinius told Harriman on 30 October 1944 to put the Soviet government straight on Iran. His secret cable, number 2566, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Soviet press articles and statements by Mr. Kavtaradze had shown Moscow's annoyance at Iran's freeze on oil talks.

Harriman is to say that Washington noticed the annoyance. He is also to lay out what the American embassy in Tehran was told to convey. The American firms chasing a concession in southern Iran were disappointed, but Washington expressed confidence in Iran's good faith. When talks resume, American firms expect treatment no worse than any other foreigner's. The policy, the cable begins to explain, rests on respect for the sovereign right of an independent nation.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d31: From Moscow on 26 December 1944, Harriman sent Roosevelt a report the day after Christmas. It is document 31 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences, published by the Department of State. His holiday-week reporting kept Washington current on Soviet attitudes at a moment when the president was weighing what could realistically be achieved at Yalta in February.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d331:
Dinner talk at Yalta on February 4, 1945, turned serious in its last half hour, and Bohlen's minutes preserve it. Most of the evening was general and personal. Stalin, Roosevelt, and Churchill stayed in very good humor. Then the talk drifted to the rights of small powers in the peace body planned for after the war.

Stalin made his view plain more than once. The three great powers had borne the brunt of the war. They had freed the small states from German rule. So, he argued, they should hold the right to keep the peace. No lesser state, he implied, could have an equal say. The minutes catch a core Yalta dispute surfacing over dinner.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d431:
Article by article, officials took apart the prisoner-of-war draft on February 9, 1945, and this memorandum records the examination. The preamble drew no comment. Neither did Article I. Then the Soviet negotiator, Novikov, began asking for changes in wording.

In Article II, one phrase should be replaced so each side would take the necessary steps to implement the agreement. Elsewhere, transfers should be effected as a rule by agreement, or only after notice to the competent authorities. For Article III, Novikov preferred the Soviet draft's text. The record is dry, clause by clause. It is also where the repatriation bargain took its final legal shape.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d131:
Acting Secretary Grew noted a British hope for early talks in a memorandum dated July 7, 1945. The memo is document 131 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. John Balfour of the British Embassy had called that morning about the coming meeting of heads of government in Berlin.

Balfour said his government very much hoped one or more Americans bound for Berlin might pass through London first. That way, the two sides could talk over matters coming up at the main meeting. He knew Washington would not want the Russians to think the two were ganging up on them, but thought lower-level experts could come quietly. Grew replied that feeling in the American group ran against such early talks, though he would look into it at once. Nothing in the record shows the visit happening.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d231:
Ambassador Winant handed the foreign ministers proposal to Anthony Eden in a letter dated July 8, 1945. The letter is document 231 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It transmits the draft the President planned to present to Churchill and Stalin early in their talks.

The same document was being shared in advance with the British and Soviet governments, Winant explains, in the belief that they might wish to think it over before the meeting. Harriman delivered the same paper to Molotov in Moscow the same day. The enclosed text matches the State Department's proposal for a Council of Foreign Ministers. Sharing the draft early was a deliberate American choice: the machinery question headed Truman's agenda, and he wanted no ally surprised by it.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d31:
Truman sent a second envoy in this telegram to Churchill of May 22, 1945. He was asking Joseph E. Davies to come to London ahead of the pending three-power conference. A number of matters needed exploring with Churchill, which Truman preferred not to handle by cable. Davies would be in London probably on the twenty-fifth.

He asked Churchill to see Davies at his convenience. The wire, sent by Navy channels, ran in parallel with the Hopkins mission to Moscow. Together the two journeys — Davies west-facing, Hopkins east-facing — prepared the ground for Potsdam by personal talk rather than paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d331:
Partition of Germany is the question a briefing book paper of June 29, 1945, answers with a clear no. Its recommendation: the United States should oppose splitting Germany into two or more separate states. Border changes and cessions, it says, are a different matter from partition itself.

The discussion traces how the idea rose and fell in Washington. Roosevelt at Tehran was ready to see five German states, but by the Crimea conference he had changed his mind. He then opposed taking up partition before the fighting ended and conditions could be studied. The paper carries that later, cooler judgment into the Potsdam briefing book.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d431:
Washington's concern over Clay's Berlin deals comes in General Marshall's top secret message of July 10, 1945. The interim commitment to provide food and coal for Berlin, outlined in Clay's message of July 9, causes concern, Marshall writes. The wish for three-power control and government of Berlin is appreciated, but the agreement must not prejudice America's basic principles in Germany.

He lists disturbing questions. The State Department advises, first, that this government cannot accept the Soviet position that Silesia has been turned over to Poland. The reply, Marshall notes, had been agreed by representatives of the State and War Departments, and the State Department would advise Murphy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d531:
Air communications with Moscow are discussed in a memorandum of conversation by Edward Page, first secretary of the Moscow embassy, dated June 29, 1945. Ambassador Harriman inquired whether there had been any developments in opening new routes to Moscow. Vyshinsky replied that he had been too busy with the Czechs, the Poles, and the Berlin conference to give the question any time.

Planes, though, were flying back and forth to Berlin, and communications were much better than previously. Events had overtaken themselves, Vyshinsky indicated, and the Moscow-Berlin service would be open to American passengers. Harriman expressed the hope that the United States-Soviet line could be opened shortly. Vyshinski said he favored the Berlin route and saw no reason it should not open once technical details were worked out.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d631:
Ambassador Wallace Murray reported from Tehran on June 19, 1945, on pulling U.S. troops out of Iran. His secret wire is document 631 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Washington had asked about speeding the withdrawal up.

Murray doubts a fast, full exit is possible for anyone. The British, he says, are even keener than the Americans to see foreign troops go, so they need no prodding. Yet British forces must guard the oil fields and the Abadan refinery in the southwest, both vital to the war on Japan. Some 1,500 U.S. men must likewise stay at Abadan airfield while war planes pass through. Murray adds a sly warning about Moscow. The Russians might pull all their troops out overnight and claim the credit for it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1031: Ambassador John Winant cabled the Secretary of State from London on July 24, 1945. Only an extract of the message is printed here. Winant reports that the European Advisory Commission met the night before to finish two outstanding documents. One was the agreement amending the zones of occupation in Germany. The British told the Americans they lacked full authority to accept the Soviet draft of the final paragraph. That paragraph belonged to the report covering the agreement. The extract ends there, with the wording still unsettled.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1131:
On 21 July 1945 the three heads of government approved this text at Potsdam. It stands in the volume beside the draft they had weighed. Approval turned working words into a summit decision, one the three powers were bound to honor.

Agreed texts of this kind went into the summit's official record. They were the points on which the talks had closed, at least for that week. Set beside the draft version, the approved words show which lines survived the leaders' review. The gap between draft and final text is where the bargaining lives. This entry preserves the finished side of that exchange.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1231:
Sato answered Tokyo on 21 July 1945, the same day as the minister's twin cables. The Moscow envoy's reports formed a steady answer to Togo's hopes: polite Soviet phrases, no firm word, no date for an envoy's hearing. Time favored Moscow, not Tokyo.

Sato read the delay rightly as a kind of answer. His cables grew blunter as the week wore on, urging Tokyo to face facts. This dispatch sits in that sequence. It is part of the hidden record at Potsdam. The Allied leaders read this enemy traffic each morning, while they set the terms Japan would soon receive.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1331:
Assistant Secretary Dunn wrote to the Secretary of State on 23 July 1945. Dunn was among the most seasoned career envoys on the American team. His notes carried staff judgment to the chief in the middle of the talks.

A message from Dunn at Potsdam joined two layers: the working staff and the man who bargained for the United States. It could fix a stand, report a talk, or ready the chief's next move. This one dates from the second week's start. It shows the professional core of the team at work, in the plain channel of a note to the secretary.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1431:
The Soviet delegation submitted another text on 29 July 1945, the third of that date in the volume's closing pages. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Three texts in a day from one delegation is a drafting offensive. As Potsdam wound down, the Soviet side worked to lock its gains into the conference's papers before the leaders left Germany. Readers can follow the effort across this cluster and into the protocol. The texts also show the limits of paper power. Some Soviet wording was taken, some was fought to a draw. The difference between the two is the summit's true result.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-131:
Cohen's notes continue with the Potsdam session of July 28, 1945. Benjamin Cohen recorded the talks as Attlee replaced Churchill at the British seat. His notes appear in the second Potsdam volume among the layered American records. Each set from Cohen adds a lawyer's check on the words exchanged.

Readers who compare Cohen with the formal minutes gain depth. He tends to catch qualifications and asides that summaries drop. Those small words later mattered in disputes over the settlement. The notes show the care with which the American side guarded its record, day after day, session after session.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-31:
Philip Mosely, a U.S. political adviser at Babelsberg, sent word to Ambassador Winant in London on July 20, 1945. The extract is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It concerns the agreement on additional requirements to be imposed on Germany.

Mosely reports that Vyshinsky told him the day before of Moscow's stance. The Soviet government had approved the agreement, save for its new title and new first paragraph. He expected those last points to be cleared shortly. A note adds color from a private Mosely letter of July 24. The title and preamble, he learned, had to be referred to Stalin himself before the Soviet signer could be instructed to sign. The full text of Mosely's message is printed later in the volume as document 1036.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d731:
The United States delegation put forward this proposal on July 30, 1945, two days before Potsdam closed. Document 731 belongs to the endgame. Late texts were drafted with the finish in view. Each line was weighed for what the other sides might still accept. The proposal joined the second Potsdam volume.

Endgame proposals repay study. They show what a side still hoped to win when time ran short. Readers can compare the text with the protocol signed on August 1. The distance between them maps the last concessions. The document catches the conference at its most practical: aims trimmed to the size of the possible.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d831:
A second Barnes letter from Bulgaria is dated July 31, 1945, as document 831. Two reports on the conference's last full day close his run in this volume. The representative in Sofia wrote to the Acting Secretary of State. This one joined the second Potsdam volume beside its pair.

Closing pairs of letters show a post tidying its account. Barnes left his record complete as the summit ended. Readers gain a double exposure of Bulgaria at the hinge. The document ends the Bulgaria thread of this run on a fitting note: a watcher still watching, as the lights of the conference went out.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d931:
American staff compiled this undated manuscript working paper of German asset figures during the Potsdam talks. It uses 1936 data. The tables compare the eastern zone, Berlin excluded, with the land east of the Oder-Neisse line. Sums are in billions of Reichsmarks, with shares of the Reich beside them.

Factory assets in the east came to 5.3 billion, near 29 percent of the Reich. Total assets were 20.1 billion in the east and 7.1 billion east of the Oder-Neisse. The paper also lists movable assets, livestock, and farm machinery. Population in the east was 24.6 million in 1939, about 35 percent of the Reich.
frus-1952-54v10-d131: Editorial Note 131 in the Iran volume covers talks between McGhee and Mosadeq in November 1951. They met on November 13 and twice on both November 15 and 17. McGhee floated a joint oil consortium and a World Bank trusteeship for Abadan. Mosadeq held out for a Persian Gulf price of $1.75 per barrel. McGhee warned that this price blocked any deal. President Truman's interim reply on aid also reached Mosadeq at the second November 15 meeting.
frus-1964-1968-south-central-america-mex:
Volume thirty-one of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1964 to 1968 covers South and Central America and Mexico in the Johnson years. The Office of the Historian publishes the series from declassified files. After the Cuban revolution, Washington's watchword in the region was counterinsurgency.

The papers record military aid, police training, and support for anti-communist governments across the continent. The Alliance for Progress, Kennedy's aid program, runs through them as it fades under Johnson. Mexico gets its own careful diplomacy, as a neighbor too large to pressure openly. The volume shows the Cold War's southern front in daily cables rather than crises.
frus-1989-92v31:
Volume XXXI of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1989-1992, is devoted to START I, from 1989 to 1991. A brief first chapter prints five documents from 1988. Seven chapters then proceed by half-years to August 1991. The papers follow the Bush team's review of arms policy and the slow restart of talks. Sea-launched and air-launched cruise missiles prove the hardest items. One late memo notes that on sea-launched missiles, range was the sole question left.

Attribution rules for future heavy bombers also stayed open late. The treaty was signed in July 1991, as the volume closes. The records show a deal built clause by clause.
gao-gaoreports-b-298831:
AllWorld Language Consultants, Inc. protested a Drug Enforcement Administration award to Conduit Language Specialists. The sealed-bid buy covered language services for the San Francisco field office. Tasks span monitoring, interpretation, translation, and transcription. GAO decided B-298831 on December 14, 2006.

One claim attacked the winner's very low prices. GAO set that claim aside. A low price goes to a firm's fitness, not bid form. The agency had found the firm fit, a call GAO rarely reviews. A second claim faulted overtime rate math. GAO found that slip a small flaw that could be waived. The award stood. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298931:
ViroMed Laboratories protested an Army call to set a buy aside for small firms. The contract covered HIV-1 testing and reporting services. The set-aside turned on hopes of two or more fit small-firm bids. GAO ruled in B-298931 on December 20, 2006.

The firm said the agency's market probe was too thin. It had not checked the small firms' claims of skill. GAO found that step was not owed here. No proof showed the small firms had misstated their skills. An officer may trust such claims absent a red flag. The probe met the fair-effort bar. The set-aside could stand. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299931:
GlassLock protested an Environmental Protection Agency task order to Commercial Window Shield. The order covered window retrofits that hold glass shards in a blast. The work spans 15 agency sites in the United States and Puerto Rico. GAO decided B-299931 and B-299931.2 on October 10, 2007.

The terms let firms cite past jobs from the past 5 years. The agency gave the winner strengths for jobs older than that span. It also marked those strengths under a plan head, not the past-work head. That double count clashed with the stated scheme. Past work had its own scoring home. Such drift in the review tainted the pick. GAO sustained the protests.
gao-gaoreports-b-310031:
FitNet Purchasing Alliance lost most of its protest. GAO ruled in B-310031 on September 21, 2007. The Veterans Affairs office ran a reverse auction for TV sets. It sought 170 hospital-grade sets and mounts for a Florida site. The office then killed the auction. It reposted the need for schedule firms alone. FitNet fought both acts.

GAO threw out part of the claim and denied the rest. FitNet was not next in line for the killed buy. That gap strips its right to fight the kill. The repost for schedule firms was a lawful path. Firms with no stake in a dead buy cannot shape the new one.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-131:
Loan Commitments, GAO-05-131 of February 14, 2005, digs into a quiet but vast part of bank lending. Banks held about $1.6 trillion in shared loans in 2003. Pledges to lend made up $1 trillion of that sum, about 64 percent. A pledge lets a firm draw cash later, on set terms. Critics ask if banks price those pledges too cheap.

GAO sets pledge prices next to loan prices. It looks at what trade data exist for pledges. It looks at swap deals banks use to shed pledge risk. It ends with how banks book pledges on their ledgers, and if fair value books would tell a truer tale.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-231:
Information Security, GAO-05-231 of May 13, 2005, flags new breeds of online attack that stalk federal systems. Old attack forms have merged into mixed, sharper threats. Spam floods mail. Fake notes, called phishing, trick staff into giving up secret data. Spyware tracks what a user does in the dark. Each craft grows more slick each year.

GAO weighs the risk these threats pose to federal facts. It asks agencies how high they rate the risk and what they do to blunt it. It lists joint steps by government and firms. It ends with the gaps that still leave the whole system open.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-331:
National Airspace System, GAO-05-331 of June 10, 2005, takes a fresh grade of a flight control upgrade that has slipped for over two decades. The Federal Aviation Administration's vast build sits on GAO's high-risk list since 1995. A new arm, the Air Traffic Organization, was made in February 2004 to run the work on feat-based lines. Hope rode on that shift.

GAO asks how the big buys track cost, time, and feat aims. It asks what steps cured old flaws, and what steps still lack. It asks how a tight federal purse will press the plan. Gains stand, the title grants; hard tests stand too.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-731:
Egypt's economic reform is at the center of GAO-05-731, a report dated July 11, 2005. Since 1992, a U.S. aid program has paid Egypt's government as it finished agreed reform steps. The aim was a freer, more market-based economy. GAO tracked the payments and the steps finished. It also weighed what limited the program's sway.

GAO found the program had paid about $1.8 billion since fiscal year 1992. Egypt finished 136 of 196 reform steps, about 70 percent, mostly in finance and trade. Some reforms cost Egypt more than the aid offset. Fear of unrest also slowed change. And repeated deadline extensions weakened the terms tied to the money. A new deal was signed in March 2005.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1031:
Watch list screening and its side effects fill GAO-06-1031, a report issued September 29, 2006. A joint center holds the merged list of known or suspected terrorists. Border and other agencies screen names against it. Name-only matching can flag the wrong person. Some names may sit on the list by mistake. GAO asked how many people are misidentified and how. It also mapped the fixes and redress paths open to them.

Headings state the findings. Misidentified people are likely a small share of all screened, but still a substantial number. They face delays and other harms. Most cases arise when a traveler's name resembles a listed name. Faulty or partial data causes others. Agencies annotate records and keep a cleared list to speed repeat travelers. Most redress queries come from misidentified people. GAO made no recommendations at this time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-231:
Dumping duties on Chinese goods and the method behind them are analyzed in GAO-06-231, dated January 10, 2006. U.S. firms hurt by unfair imports can seek antidumping duties. The Commerce Department treats China as a nonmarket economy. Its special method for such cases is widely thought to yield higher duties. If China earns market status, that method ends. GAO explained the method and compared duties on China with those on market economies. It also mapped when the method would stop and what that change would do.

The title states the likely effect: some Chinese firms would pay lower duties. Others would see little change, since the method bites unevenly. The report is the last in a series on fair trade with China. Commerce agreed with the findings. It called the report timely and helpful. The study gives Congress a clear view of a technical tool with large trade stakes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-31:
Computer security at the military's supply agency falls short in GAO-06-31, a report dated October 7, 2005. The Defense Logistics Agency moves food, fuel, medicine, clothing, and spare parts to the armed forces. Its systems carry the data that keep that flow moving. GAO was asked to judge whether the agency runs a sound security program. It reviewed ten systems in depth.

The agency has built parts of a program, GAO found. It has a central security team and a senior officer in charge. Other core pieces lag across the board. Risk checks were uneven, and staff with security duties lacked full training. Controls were not tested each year as required. Fix-it plans for known flaws stayed unfinished. The agency also lacked a sound process to approve systems for use. Blurry duties and faulty tracking data fed the gaps. Until fixed, the supply chain's data stays exposed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-331:
What peace in Haiti costs under two flags is compared in GAO-06-331, dated February 21, 2006. The UN fields about 85,000 staff in peacekeeping across 16 countries. The United States gives about $1 billion a year to support those missions. Doubts about UN accountability have sharpened interest in the comparison. GAO priced the actual UN mission in Haiti. It then priced a made-up U.S.-run version of the same job. Cost models from the defense and state departments built the U.S. figure.

The study tests which factors could swing the U.S. price most. It also lists the strengths each side brings to leading such work. Blue helmets draw troops from many nations at shared cost. A U.S. mission offers speed and heft at full American price. Lawmakers weighing burden-sharing get hard numbers here. The report avoids a verdict on who should lead. It prices the choice instead.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-431:
Park budgets rose or fell over five years, and units coped in varied ways. In report GAO-06-431 (March 31, 2006), GAO tracks National Park Service operations funding. Advocacy group reports had raised doubts about whether park funds were adequate. GAO traced funding trends for operations and visitor fees from fiscal years 2001 to 2005. It then looked closely at 12 high-visitation park units.

For those units, GAO showed funding trends and their effect on operations. It also reviewed recent management steps on fiscal performance. The service had taken steps to improve accountability at park units. Readers can compare system-wide trends with unit experience. The study ties money to daily park work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-831:
Blueprints for how agencies run and use technology fill GAO-06-831. The report is dated August 14, 2006. A sound enterprise architecture maps an agency's operations and systems, guiding each new investment. Without one, agencies build duplicate systems that do not work together. GAO rated departments against its management maturity framework. GAO also asked what separates agencies that use architecture well from those that do not.

GAO found the overall state of architecture management to be a work in progress. A few agencies had largely satisfied the framework's demands. Most had not. GAO's central lesson is in its title: leadership remains the key. Where top leaders treat architecture as a management tool, it shapes real choices. Elsewhere it stays a paper exercise. The report is a status check on a governmentwide reform.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1131:
Fees charged to air travelers from abroad are examined in GAO report GAO-07-1131, dated September 24, 2007. Arriving guests face checks for legal entry papers and banned goods, from drugs to farm pests. In 2003 the Homeland Security Department merged customs, immigration, and farm checks into one program.

Three fees tied to those checks stayed legally apart. Their take was about $1 billion in fiscal year 2006. GAO asked how the fees are set, gathered, and split. It weighed gains and hurdles of that path, for agencies and users. Key points need care, GAO said, whether or not the fees are merged.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-231:
Partnership insurance policies shield part of a buyer's savings if they later need Medicaid. GAO tested whether the programs save public money in GAO-07-231, issued May 11, 2007. Four states ran such programs: California, Connecticut, Indiana, and New York. GAO compared partnership policies with plain long-term care policies. It studied buyer incomes and ages. It modeled how buyers would have paid for care without the program.

Partnership buyers tended to buy richer coverage, GAO found. Their policies must carry inflation protection by rule. Premiums run higher because of those required benefits, not the asset shield itself. In two states, 55 percent of buyers over age 55 had household incomes of $5,000 a month or more. Such buyers could likely pay for care on their own. GAO concluded the programs are unlikely to yield Medicaid savings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-31:
Renovating the United Nations headquarters in New York will cost far more than first planned. GAO tracked the project in GAO-07-31, a report dated November 16, 2006. The 2005 estimate reached almost $1.75 billion. That is up about $560 million from the 2002 figure of $1.19 billion. Later start dates, design changes, and a new work approach drove the rise. The United States is host country and largest funder.

Planning follows sound construction practice, GAO found. Stakeholders help shape the design, and review teams check the work. Buying is the weak link. The UN manual lacks guidance for construction buying. Its contract review panel cannot keep pace with the workload. Vendors have no independent channel to protest awards. Member states still had not chosen how to pay. One cash option would charge the United States $302 million over 5 years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-331:
Half of disability cases that reach court bounce back to the agency for another look. GAO studied the remand cycle in GAO-07-331, a report dated April 5, 2007. Disability programs paid about $128 billion to 12.8 million people in fiscal year 2005. Court reviews of denied claims rose 20 percent over a decade. They grew from about 10,300 in 1995 to some 12,400 in 2005. GAO traced outcomes and the reasons cases return.

Remands were the most common court outcome, GAO found. They made up 50 percent of decisions. Their share rose 36 percent across the decade. After remand, 66 percent of claimants won benefits. Outcomes varied sharply by region in 2005. One circuit remanded 74 percent of cases while another remanded 35 percent. Judges often cite weak decision writing and misuse of evidence. The agency's data on remand reasons are spotty, GAO said. Two offices track them without coordinating.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-531:
Spending by special prosecutors is audited in GAO-07-531, a GAO financial audit dated March 30, 2007. The audit covers the six months ended September 30, 2006. It takes in one office of independent counsel and one office of special counsel. Both draw on a permanent, open-ended fund inside the Department of Justice. Law at 28 U.S.C. 596(c)(2) charges GAO with the audit.

The special counsel covered is Patrick J. Fitzgerald, whom the Justice Department let tap the same fund. Independent counsels must report their spending twice a year under the statute. GAO's job is to test those statements of expenditures. The volume is a narrow fiscal record: what was spent, under what authority, in half a year of work. Such audits form the public trail for probes that run outside the normal chain of command.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-631:
Keeping forces ready eats about 40 percent of the defense budget, and GAO-07-631, dated May 18, 2007, tracks where that money goes. Operation and maintenance funds pay for training, supply, gear upkeep, and base support. In fiscal year 2005 they took about 40 percent of all defense spending. More of the work now goes to contractors instead of troops or civil staff. Logistics, base services, tech support, and office help lead the shift.

A House panel told GAO to chart the trend. GAO read 10 years of budget and contract data. It built case studies of outsourced work at three bases. The report asks whether buying services fuels the cost growth or merely rides it. Views on the gains and risks of the shift close the study. GAO makes no recommendations here; the aim is a shared fact base for a fight about who should do the military's support work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-831:
Health checks for deploying troops are examined in GAO-07-831, dated June 22, 2007. Since the mid-1990s, GAO has faulted the Defense Department's tracking of troop health. A law at 10 U.S.C. 1074f orders a medical tracking system. It requires health exams before and after deployments abroad. The system includes mental health checks and blood samples. GAO asked whether the system exists as the law demands.

The department has a tracking system that meets the law's terms. Troops fill health questionnaires within 60 days before deployment. Providers review the forms and medical records for fitness. Blood draws and immunization checks form part of the process. A quality assurance program reviews how the checks are done. That program lacks a full oversight frame, GAO found. It needs reporting rules and outcome measures to prove it works. GAO urged the department to build that frame. The department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1031:
Iraq's oil wealth and public spending are tallied in GAO report GAO-08-1031, dated August 5, 2008. Iraq holds an estimated 115 billion barrels of crude oil, the third largest reserve in the world. Oil exports bring in over 90 percent of the Iraqi government's revenue. In June 2008, GAO had flagged low Iraqi spending in key sectors.

This report tracks Iraq's revenues and spending from 2005 through 2008. It also counts Iraq's deposits and budget surpluses through 2007. A further part totals U.S. spending on rebuilding Iraq since 2003. GAO made no recommendations. It did weigh what slows Iraq's pace of spending on its own needs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-31:
Grant takers who dodge taxes close the tax abuse series in GAO report GAO-08-31, dated November 16, 2007. Since February 2004, GAO has shown contractors and health providers taking federal money while owing taxes. This study turns to grant and direct aid recipients. It drew on the three largest payment systems, which moved over $460 billion in fiscal years 2005 and 2006.

Tens of thousands of recipients owed about $790 million in federal taxes as of September 30, 2006. GAO probed 20 cases of abuse in depth. Most recipients pay what they owe, it notes. It urged the budget office to weigh tax checks at the award stage.
hermes-unveiled-1831:
The man known as Cyliani wrote this alchemy account in 1831. It was printed the year after, and the hosted copy is an English version. Cyliani claims he made the Philosopher's Stone at last. He says the search took thirty-seven years and brought him loss and grief.

His preface warns the young away from the art's false roses and thorns. Later pages give his first method, on the azoth or philosopher's mercury. He speaks of two metallic natures and an astral spirit. Readers meet a rare first-hand tale of a life spent on the great secret.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-ben-eliez: Aaron ben Eliezer, called Saggi Nehor, a euphemism for the Blind, is the subject of this Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He was a liturgical poet who lived in Safed from the year 1545. His collection of poems and prayers was printed at Mantua in 1561 as Sefer ha-Miznefet, the Book of the Miter. The booklet treats chiefly the glories of Palestine, the entry says. Love of that land had drawn him from his home. Poems on the thirteen articles of the Jewish creed are also included.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abba-of-carthag: Abba of Carthage was a Palestinian amora who flourished at the end of the third century. His birthplace was Carthage itself. The entry is firm on one point of names. It is wrong, it says, to link his surname to Cartagena in Spain, or to a town in Armenia. He is named often in the Jerusalem Talmud. He also appears often in the haggadic traditions, the non-legal lore handed down with the legal teaching of his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abelman-ilia-so:
Ilia Solomonovich Abelman was a Russian astronomer, born at Dünaburg, now Dvinsk, in 1866. He died at Wilna on December 29, 1898. At the gymnasium of Riga he took the gold medal in 1887. He went on to Moscow University for astronomy and geodesy, then spent a year, 1892-93, at Berlin. He worked at the observatories of Pulkovo and St. Petersburg.

Still at school in 1887, Abelman published a book of algebra problems. His treatise on falling stars was taken up by Moscow as a text-book for young astronomers. A further work, on the motion of certain meteor streams, came out in 1898. It was issued by the Imperial Russian Astronomical Society, of which he was a member. He wrote for Russian and German journals as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abishur-father-: Abishur, glossed as "Father is a Wall," receives only a brief notice after the volume's index pages. He is identified as a Jerahmeelite, a son of Shammai. The sole source cited is First Chronicles ii. 28, 29. No acts, dates, wife, or children are given for him in the text provided. Readers get a name, a meaning, a father, and a tribal link, and nothing further about his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-achish-731: Achish was king of Gath in the days of David and Solomon. David fled to him twice while Saul hunted him. The first time David was known, so he played the madman and got away. The second time Achish treated him well, as a foe of Saul. Achish led the Philistine host that beat Israel at Gilboa. Saul and his sons died in that fight. Two runaway servants of Shimei later fled to Achish. Rabbinic tales add Goliath's brothers to his guard.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-victor-83: Victor Adler was an Austrian doctor, newsman, and labor chief. He was born at Prague on June 24, 1852. His work as a doctor brought him face to face with Vienna's poor. He studied their state and gave up his practice for social thought. In 1890 he fused Austria's split workmen into one strong party. Its chief aim became the vote for all men. On March 9, 1897, Vienna workmen voted for the first time. They won fourteen seats. Adler lost his own race. Since 1894 he has edited the chief labor paper of Vienna.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-ahai-iii-93:
Born in Lydda in southern Palestine, Aha III was a Palestinian amora of the fourth century who settled in Tiberias, where he, Huna II., and Judah bar Pazi formed a court of justice. A recognized authority on Halakah, he surpassed his elder namesakes in Haggadah and is quoted by haggadists more often than any of them.

On Abraham's attempt to sacrifice Isaac, Aha argued that the patriarch misunderstood the call: God asked for a living child on the table, not a dead one. The entry also records his epigram that privation leads the Jew back to God, and his praise for anyone who speaks a good word for Israel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-ii-ni:
Alexander II., Nikolaievich, was emperor of Russia. He was born at St. Petersburg on April 29, 1818. He was assassinated there on March 13, 1881. He came to the throne on March 2, 1855, before the Crimean war had ended. His great reform was the freeing of the serfs in 1861. He also eased censorship, remade the courts, and shortened army service.

Toward the Jews he moved against his father's harsh policy. He shut the cantonist schools that had seized Jewish boys. He opened high schools and universities to Jews. Laws of 1859 and 1861 let scholars, graduates, great merchants, and makers settle outside the Pale. Artisans won the same right in 1865. For the 2,500,000 Jews of the Pale itself, though, little changed. Russian Jews still called him their liberator, and they mourned him deeply when he was killed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ali-ibn-sahl-ib:
Ali ibn Sahl ibn Rabban al-Tabari was a physician in Irak. He worked about the middle of the ninth century. He was born in Taberistan. His father Sahl was known for work in the stars and in number. At Rai the young Razi studied medicine under him. He later served two califs at court.

Seven works are listed under his name. The first is a system of medicine in seven parts. Its title means the garden of wisdom. Other books treat food, drink, and health care. One book deals with charms and amulets. One deals with cupping as a cure. The entry names the old sources for his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-angyal-engel-da:
David Angyal was a Hungarian writer born on November 30, 1857. After study at the University of Budapest, he taught at a high school in that city. Heavy teaching duties did not stop his writing on history and letters.

His works include a study of the poet Berzsenyi in 1879 and a life of Imre Tokoly, dated 1657-1705, in 1882. His 1889 history of Hungary, running from Matthias II to the death of Ferdinand III, formed the sixth volume of a national history. He also turned Macaulay and Paul Janet into Hungarian, wrote essays for the press, and edited the poets Kolcsey and Kisfaludy. The entry ends by noting that Angyal has been baptized.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-apes-1631:
Apes enter the Bible in First Kings, chapter 10, verse 22, and its parallel in Second Chronicles. Ships of Tarshish brought them from Ophir along with gold, silver, ivory, and peacocks. The Hebrew word for ape, kof, is a loan from the Tamil kapi, the entry explains.

That Indian root has been used to place Ophir at the mouth of the Indus. Apes were never native to Palestine, though Assyrians took them as tribute. In rabbinic writing, apes look so like man that a special blessing was said on seeing one. The rabbis also called them a luxury, told of apes trained as servants, and read an ape in a dream as a bad sign.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-archer-archery-:
Archer and archery open with the bow as a weapon of war and the chase, known to the Hebrews from patriarchal times. Genesis ties the bow to Ishmael, Esau, and Jacob. Jonathan and Jehu were expert archers, the entry says, and the tribe of Benjamin was famed for its sons' skill with the bow.

After the battle of Gilboa, David urged archery practice in Judah, and the push took root. Some 250 years later Hosea could use the bow as the sign of Israel's military power. Assyrian monuments show the tactics: showers of arrows first, then a close charge with sword and spear. A psalm verse also hints at arrows tipped with burning matter for firing besieged towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arthur-legend-1:
King Arthur's cycle of stories reached Jewish readers in a Hebrew translation made in 1279. Its title means The Book of the Destruction of the Round Table. The translator's name cannot be learned, and only fragments survive, in a Vatican manuscript printed in 1885. They cover parts of the Life of Lancelot, the Birth of Arthur, and the Quest of the Grail.

In his preface the translator gave two motives: the closing sermon on repentance, and relief from his own low spirits. Italian words in the Hebrew point to an Italian source, now lost, itself a short form of the vast romance. The entry stresses the odd contrast: tales of bloodshed and loose love, so foreign to Jewish ideals, retold in Hebrew, with the Grail quest bound to the Christian mass.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asser-carel-203:
Carel Asser, a Dutch jurist, was born at Amsterdam on February 15, 1780. He was a son of Moses Salomon Asser. He studied law and language at the Athenaeum in Amsterdam and took his doctor's degree on July 3, 1799. He then practiced law in Amsterdam. He and his friend Jonas Daniel Meyer were the first Jews to become lawyers after the Batavian republic was set up.

Early fame came from one defense. A man of Dordrecht stood accused of blasphemy for doubting the divinity of Jesus and the Trinity. Asser and Meyer defended him so well that the chief attorney took notice. Jewish causes also held Asser. At sixteen he helped found the Felix Libertate society, aimed at freeing Dutch Jews, and on March 26, 1796, he signed a petition for their emancipation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-auerbach-solomo: Solomon Heymann Auerbach was a Hebrew scholar. He was born at Posen at the end of the eighteenth century and died there in 1836. He translated the book of Habakkuk into German, with notes to explain it. That version came out at Breslau in 1821. He also worked on the Bible translation led by Zunz. For that project he supplied the rendering of Ecclesiastes. He wrote a Hebrew commentary on Ecclesiastes as well, published at Breslau in 1837, the year after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azubib-nehorai-: Nehorai b. Saadia Azubib was rabbi at Algiers. He died in October 1785. He wrote several prayers for a yearly feast the community kept. The feast marked the beating back of O'Reilly's attack on Algiers in 1775. Some Arabic poems of his appear in a printed collection of praises of God, issued at Oran. He also wrote a short commentary on the hymn collection used in the rite of Algiers, printed at Leghorn. The entry praises him most for his unselfishness, for which he was famed in his city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bamoth-baal-the: Bamoth-Baal, "The Heights of Baal," was a high point in the land of Moab, named in Numbers xxii. 41. It was allotted to the Reubenites, as Joshua xiii. 17 records. The entry links it to the Bamoth of Numbers xxi. 19 and to Bethbamot in the Moabite Stone. Where it stood is argued: some put it on Mount 'Aṭṭârûs, while G. A. Smith favors Conder's view, one of the cromlechs above the Wady Dchîded, northeast of the Dead Sea. Eusebius' site on the Arnon is rejected.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barley-2531: Barley is a cereal often named in the Old Testament as a common food of Palestine. Second only to wheat in bread, it marked poverty and fed the poorer people. It is grown everywhere in Palestine, mainly as provender for horses and asses; in Europe and America, oats take its place. In the Jordan valley the seed is sown in autumn and harvest begins in April, running into August on the heights. The barley most grown in antiquity was the six-rowed kind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-basnage-jacob-c:
Jacob Basnage was a Protestant pastor born at Rouen, France, on Aug. 8, 1653. He led the church at Rouen from age twenty-three. After the Edict of Nantes was revoked, he moved to Holland in 1686 and later served at The Hague, dying there on Dec. 22, 1725.

Basnage wrote some twenty-five works on theology and the history of religion. Chief among them is a history of the Jews meant to carry Josephus forward to his own day. The long entry weighs that history's methods, its use of Jewish sources, and its critics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beeliada-baal-k: Beeliada was a son of David, named in the fourteenth chapter of First Chronicles. In Second Samuel and in an earlier chapter of Chronicles the same son is called Eliada. The entry explains the shift as a scribe's choice: the name Baal was hateful to the copyist, who swapped in El in its place. It points readers to a second entry for more cases where the name Baal was masked in the text in this same guarded way.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berdychev-polis:
Berdychev, in Polish Berdyczew, is a city in the government of Kiev, in Russia. It holds one of the largest Jewish communities in that land and is often called the Jerusalem of Volhynia. Jews were there by the sixteenth century, when the town lay under Polish rule.

Great fairs set in 1765 turned it into a trading center that drew Jews from all parts. Counts of its Jews rose from 1,220 in 1765 to 1,951 in 1789. About 1780 the famed Levi-Isaac made it his seat, and the town became a center of Ḥasidism in Volhynia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-betting-3231:
Betting is a mutual agreement on gain and loss. Two parties stake money on an uncertain event. The entry says it was unknown in Biblical times. Scripture never mentions it directly. Some Proverbs verses may hint at easy gain. The entry quotes them on wealth gotten by vanity.

One Talmudic tale tells of a real bet. Two men wagered 400 zuz on provoking Hillel. Hillel stayed patient and won the lesson for them. The entry then turns to law. Bettors were barred from giving evidence. Two reasons are given for that bar. One calls the winnings robbery. The other calls betting wasted, idle time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bischoffsheim-r: Raphael Nathan Bischoffsheim was a merchant and philanthropist. He was born at Bischofsheim-on-the-Tauber in 1773. He died at Mayence on January 22, 1814. He reached Mayence during the French Revolution. From small merchant he became an army purveyor. He presided over Mayence's Jewish community. An 1808 list counted him among its foremost Jews. Such men supplied notables for the Paris Sanhedrin. The entry rests on family and city records.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blumenstock-von:
Leo Blumenstock von Halban was an Austrian physician born at Cracow on March 11, 1838. He died there on Feb. 28, 1897. He studied in Cracow and Vienna and took his medical degree in 1862.

Blumenstock taught in the law faculty and then held the chair of forensic medicine at Cracow. He served as a medical expert at the court and was raised to the nobility in 1891. He wrote on gas poisoning, dynamite deaths, and loss of speech. From 1877 he edited a Polish medical weekly. He also sent many essays on his field to Polish journals in Cracow, Lemberg, and Warsaw over his long career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brandeis-moses-: Moses Brandeis, surnamed Harif, the Keen, was a German rabbi and Talmudic teacher. He was born about 1685 and died on June 24, 1761, in Mayence. His surname marks his fame as a sharp dialectician. He left no writings behind him. He studied at Prague and directed a school at Fürth. In 1717 he became chief rabbi at Jung-Bunzlau. In 1733 he took the rabbinate of Mayence. He also followed the strict rules of Isaac Luria as a cabalist.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-burg-meno-3831:
Meno Burg was a German military officer born in Berlin on Oct. 9, 1789. His father was poor, but a cousin with a government post took him as an apprentice. He became a field surveyor in 1807. When the Napoleonic wars came, the Guards refused him as a Jew. Prince August's help got him into the artillery instead.

Burg taught geometry at Danzig and then at Berlin's military school from 1817. His geometry textbook was often reprinted and translated. The king held back his captaincy and wished him to adopt Christianity first. Burg refused, argued his case, and won the promotion. He rose to major in 1847 and wrote his service memoir. He died in Berlin in 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-callenberg-joha: Johann Heinrich Callenberg taught theology and philology and pushed missions to convert Jews. Born of peasant parents at Molschleben on Jan. 12, 1694, he took a philology chair at Halle in 1735 and a theology chair in 1739. In 1728 he founded the Institutum Judaicum and attached a printing office to it. That press printed the Gospel and other Christian books in Judeo German for Jewish readers. He sent missionaries across Europe and aided converts. His early hope of converting Moslems failed when he tried it later. The institute lasted until 1791, past his death in 1760.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cardoso-elijah-: Elijah Aboab Cardoso was a giver and the founder of the Hamburg synagogue, who lived in that city in the first half of the seventeenth century. He came from a Spanish family of the name and was among the first Jewish settlers in Hamburg. In 1630 he founded the first Portuguese synagogue there. The act took nerve. The senate shrank from letting Jews build a synagogue, for fear the town's zealots would fix their eyes on the Jews. The entry gives no birth or death dates for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castro-adolf-de: Adolf de Castro was a Spanish historian, a member of the Academy of History at Madrid, who lived at Cadiz and died there in October 1898. He wrote the first short history of the Jews in Spain based on careful study. His Historia de los Judios en España appeared at Cadiz in 1847 and in English at Cambridge in 1851. Castro insisted that he wrote without passion, as a man neither Jewish nor of Jewish descent. Unlike Amador de los Rios, he condemned the Inquisition outright.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chile-4331:
Chile is a republic of South America, bounded by Peru, Bolivia, the Argentine Republic, and the Pacific Ocean. Soon after America was found, Jews, open and secret, settled across South America. They moved as Inquisition pressure shifted. Early in the sixteenth century, New Christians from Callao, in Peru, drifted to Santiago, in Chile.

Spies of the Holy Office soon tracked them down. Evidence was gathered from Buenos Aires, Mexico, and Old World cities. An accused Jew could be jailed in Chile, tortured into confession, and sent off for execution at Cartagena or Lima. The scholar Francisco Maldonado de Silva was jailed in Chile and burned at Lima on Jan. 23, 1639. The entry lists early victims by name and age. Several men named were jailed in Chile, lost their goods, and died at that same Lima burning in 1639.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coblenz-gerson-: Gerson ben Isaac Moses Coblenz was a French rabbi and author, born about 1717. He died at Metz in the first half of the eighteenth century, as the entry gives it. He studied under Jacob, author of Shebut Yaakob. He served as dayyan at Metz. His chief work, Kiryat Hanah, is a book of responsa finished at age twenty-five. His son Jacob published it at Metz in 1785. More rulings appear inside other rabbis' books. He also wrote notes on the Turim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohn-samuel-453: Samuel Cohn, a German political economist, was born at Bromberg in 1862. He died in Berlin on July 30, 1900. He studied philology and history at Berlin and took a doctorate there. Then he turned to economics. Journalism began with the Oldenburg Korrespondenz. From about 1889 he wrote often for Berlin papers. For years he served as secretary to Friedrich Goldschmidt. Late in life he edited the Oekonomist. His one book, on the finances of the German Reich, appeared in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-czarniecki-stef:
Stefan Czarniecki was a Polish general, born in 1599. He died at Sokolovka, Volhynia, on Feb. 12, 1664. He won fame in the wars against Sweden and Russia from 1656 to 1661. Unlike Wishnevietzki, the protector of the Jews in the Cossack uprising, Czarniecki dealt very harshly with them. Taken by the Tatars after the defeat at the Yellow Waters, he spent two years as a captive.

Freed, he fought the Cossacks again and helped beat them near Berestaczko. When Sweden invaded, Poland became a battleground of three powers. Jews got protection from none. Retreating before the Swedes, Czarniecki vented his rage on them. The entry lists his kills town by town: 200 in Kobylin, 300 in Lenczyc, 600 across four more towns. Hundreds of families in Cracow were wiped out in 1656.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-ben-abrah: David ben Abraham Shemariah was a cabalistic writer who lived at Salonica toward the end of the sixteenth century. He wrote "Torat Emet" (The True Law), a shortened version of the section on Genesis in the Zohar, with a commentary and glossary added. After finding a copy of the Zohar Ḥadash, printed at Salonica in 1597, he added material from some of its sections to the book. The finished work, with an appendix, was printed at Salonica in 1604.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-debts-of-decede:
Debts of decedents concerns what a dead person's creditors can claim from the estate he leaves. Under the old Talmudic rule, a dead man's goods and money could not be seized for his debts. Only his land, called the estate with responsibility, stood as security. His widow, too, claimed her marriage settlement from that fund.

Later ages changed the rule. As Jews became landless traders, the Geonim made goods and claims answerable for debts as well. Orphans were always held bound, in conscience, to pay their father's debts from what they received. Bond creditors could take back from buyers land the heirs had sold. The entry also treats appraisal and sale of infant heirs' lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-distaff-5231:
A distaff is the stick that held flax or wool ready for hand-spinning before the spinning-wheel. The spinner tucked it under the left arm or in the girdle. Fibers were drawn off and twisted by the right hand's thumb and finger. The finished thread was wound onto an oval reel.

In Israel, skill with the distaff counted as women's wisdom, and its cloth sold even abroad. Spinning women helped equip the sanctuary, as Exodus notes. The entry untangles two Hebrew terms in Proverbs xxxi. 19, where scholars swap the senses of distaff and spindle. It also cites Maimonides for a fuller account of the tools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dropsie-moses-a:
Moses Aaron Dropsie was an American lawyer born in Philadelphia on March 9, 1821. He began as a store-boy, then learned watchmaking. Law study under Benjamin Harris Brewster followed. He died at Philadelphia on July 8, 1905.

Admitted to the bar in 1851, Dropsie ran for mayor as a Whig in 1852 and opposed slavery. He promoted Philadelphia railways and chaired a bridge commission in 1870. Jewish education filled much of his life. He led Maimonides College, then Gratz College from its founding in 1893. Philadelphia Jewry knew him as a steady worker for schools and charities. He also published a work on Roman law of testaments in 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-edessa-urhai-54:
Edessa, the modern Urfa, is a city in Asiatic Turkey, in the vilayet of Aleppo. Jewish writings barely name it. Yet Jews surely lived there early. A pre-Christian ruler of the place was saved, tradition says, by a Jewess named Kutbi.

In the first century a Parthian house tied to Adiabene ruled Edessa. The apostle Addai lodged with a Jew named Tobias there. The Peshitta translation, with its Jewish leanings, was made in Edessa. Its old chronicle names at least two synagogues. One became a chapel in 412, and a mosque rose on a synagogue site in 825.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-b-dinai: Eleazar ben Dinai led Zealot bands in the years 35 to 60 C.E. His story opens with a border fight in Peraea. Jews there clashed with the pagans of Philadelphia over land lines. The procurator Fadus killed one Jewish leader and exiled two more. When Samaritans later killed Jewish pilgrims, Jews called Eleazar down from the hills. He struck back by wasting the district of Akrabatene. The procurator Felix caught him at last by a trick. Felix sent him in chains to Rome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-eleazar:
Eliezer ben Zadok was a tanna of the first century. In his youth he saw the Temple in its full glory. He later saw the Romans destroy it with his own eyes. In Jerusalem he ran a wine and oil trade with a partner. After the fall he lived at Acco. There he saw famed rich families sunk in ruin and want.

The entry follows him to Jabneh and beyond. His reports from Temple days were trusted on many points of law. Some rulings of the Sanhedrin rest on his word. His notes may have formed a lost book on mourning rites. He died far off at Ginzac in Media. His son learned of the death three years later. The entry then turns to his grandson of the same name. That second Eliezer argued law points with the later pupils of Akiba.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ergas-joseph-be:
Joseph ben Immanuel Ergas was an Italian rabbi and cabalist born in Leghorn in 1685. He died on May 19, 1730. Other rabbis cite him often in their responsa and legal works. His name is tied most closely to a fight over the teachings of Nehemiah Hayyun, whom he accused of Shabbethaian heresy.

Two of his books attack Hayyun directly, both printed at London in 1715. Shomer Emunim sets a philosopher and a cabalist in dialogue. Mebo Petahim opens the true Cabala and warns against a heretical kind. Dibre Yosef collects sixty-eight of his responsa. Minhat Yosef gathers ethical rules and sayings of ancient authors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-farrar-ferrar-a: Abraham Farrar was a Portuguese physician and poet born at Porto who died at Amsterdam in 1663. He practiced medicine at Lisbon, then moved to Amsterdam. In 1639 he became president of the Portuguese community there. He was nephew of Jacob Tirado, founder of Amsterdam's first Portuguese congregation. Manasseh ben Israel was his friend and dedicated a work to him. Farrar's own book, printed at Amsterdam in 1627, renders the 613 commandments in Portuguese verse. In it he calls himself the Portuguese exile.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fir-or-fir-tree:
Fir, or fir tree, is the usual old rendering of a Hebrew tree word. The Revised Version puts cypress in the margin in most places. Old versions vary a lot. They give cypress, pine, juniper, cedar, and almond tree. The entry argues from the flora of Syria. In most passages the tree grows high on Mount Lebanon, near the cedar.

That setting points to a true fir of the high zones. It can match the cedar in height and beauty. One passage in Hosea is an exception. There the tree bears fruit that can be eaten. That must be the stone pine, the entry says. Fir wood also makes fine spear shafts and sounding boards.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frauenschul-or-:
Frauenschul is that part of a synagogue which is set apart for women. It may be an added wing, as at Prague and at Worms. Or it may be a gallery, most often at the back of the building on the west side. The split of the sexes in worship is likely as old as synagogue services themselves. Yet old sources do not mention it. Talmudic reports tell of a women's gallery in the Temple at Jerusalem. From it the women could watch the rites, while a grating hid them from the men's view.

The rabbinical codes say nothing on the Frauenschul. One late authority ruled that a women's synagogue is not as holy as the men's part. Reform synagogues often seat men and women together on one floor. In America the family pew came in through Reform practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gaunse-gaunz-ga: Joachim Gaunse, a German mining expert born at Prague, turns up in English state papers under Elizabeth. He worked at Keswick in Cumberland from 1581 and stayed in England until late 1589. He brought a new method for making copper and for smelting copper and lead ores. In September 1589 at Bristol he spoke in Hebrew and declared himself a Jew. He was seized and sent to the privy council in London. No harsh action by the council is recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gerstle-lewis-6:
Lewis Gerstle, a Californian pioneer born in Ichenhausen, Bavaria, on December 17, 1824, died at San Francisco on November 19, 1902. He came to America in 1845 and began as a peddler at Louisville. Gold drew him west to San Francisco. He sold apples, mined at Placerville, and kept a small shop near Sacramento. Trade with partners later made him rich in stock work.

When the United States gained Alaska in 1867, Gerstle helped form the Alaska Commercial Company. Its seal contract of 1870 paid the state sums said to cover the whole Alaska purchase price. Gerstle led the firm from 1885 until his death. The company supplied the world with dyed sealskins.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goding-6731:
Göding, a Moravian town in Austria, held about 10,000 people in 1900, more than 1,000 of them Jews, and its community ranked among the province's oldest. Records of its burial society show old and new cemeteries already in 1682. The Thirty Years' war shrank the community so much that it long lacked its own rabbi.

Vienna exiles swelled the town in 1670, and synods met there in 1689 and 1716. In June 1774 Maria Theresa expelled all Göding Jews; Joseph II later readmitted thirteen families, who formed the core of a new community. The entry names notable rabbis, among them Samson Bacharach, and notes a rabbi was inducted again in 1899 after a gap of 126 years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gottschalk-loui:
Louis Moreau Gottschalk was an American pianist. He was born at New Orleans on May 8, 1829. He died at Rio de Janeiro on Dec. 18, 1869. Paris gave him his musical schooling from 1841 to 1846. At sixteen he had already written "Le Bananier" and "La Bamboula." Tours of France, Switzerland, and Spain followed from 1845 to 1852.

From 1853 he played across the United States and the Americas. The entry calls him the first American pianist to win world fame. His original flavor came from Spanish, Cuban, and Black folk song heard in boyhood. His orchestral works include two symphonies and two operas never performed. His piano pieces number about ninety.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-guidacerius-aga:
Agathius Guidacerius was an Italian Christian Hebraist. He was born at Rocca-Coragio, Calabria, in the late fifteenth century. He learned Hebrew from a Portuguese rabbi at Rome. He then taught Hebrew at the university there. In 1530 Francis I made him professor at the Collège de France. In Paris he expounded the Hebrew and Greek texts of Scripture.

His chief work was a Hebrew grammar drawn from Ḳimḥi. It appeared at Rome in 1514 and often at Paris. He wrote a Latin version of Ḳimḥi's grammar in 1540. He also wrote on Hebrew letters, vowels, and accents. His commentaries cover the Psalms, Canticles, and Ecclesiastes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haggai-7031:
Haggai was a Judean prophet of the early years after the exile, a fellow worker with Zechariah. His name means "festal" or "feast of Yah," and it shows up on Semitic inscriptions. Next to nothing is known of his life. From his own words some infer that he had seen the first Temple, which would make him very old in 520 B.C.
