Lu Zhou and nine co-authors present a 2023 paper on detecting the COVID-19 virus with light scattering instead of labels or probes. Their method uses surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy: molecules on a gold nanoparticle film scatter laser light in a fingerprint pattern, hugely amplified. Spectra were collected from four coronavirus types grown on the film. The signals were rich enough to detect the virus at very low doses.

A standard statistical method, principal component analysis, then pulled out the key bands that separate the viruses. It distinguished SARS-CoV-2 and its variant from the other coronaviruses in the set. The authors argue the pairing of the spectroscopy with the analysis could identify multiple viruses quickly, even new ones, without designing a specific probe for each. The work points toward fast, low-cost virus screening for future outbreaks.
pmc-10742131:
Marco Baralle, Maurizio Romano, and Christoph Englert ask whether changes in RNA splicing drive aging or merely follow it, in a twenty twenty-three review. Splicing is the editing step that cuts and joins gene messages, letting one gene make several protein forms. As bodies age, splicing patterns shift, which changes the mix of protein forms. Three kinds of splicing change stand out in old tissue.

These shifts can alter protein parts and can mark messages for destruction, changing what cells build. The levels of splicing factors also drift with age, and faults in splicing genes can speed aging diseases. The authors warn that telling cause from effect is hard. They lay out what proof a claim of cause would need and why the question matters for longer healthy life.
pmc-10742631:
Quillet and six co-authors map synaptic circuits of itch-related spinal neurons in mice, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Certain dorsal horn neurons carry a receptor tied to itch signaling. They were thought to relay itch to brain-bound projection neurons. Super-resolution imaging reveals their incoming connections in detail.

Inputs arrive sparsely from pain fibers and touch fibers alike. Several excitatory interneuron groups also connect onto them. Activating these cells switches on projection neurons beyond the superficial layer. Deep dorsal horn and lateral nucleus targets appear unexpectedly. The circuit is broader and more diverse than assumed.
pmc-10743631:
Nadja Abele and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-three analysis of heart tissue from anesthetized pigs. Chronic heart failure pairs high blood levels of stress hormones with weak heart mitochondria. The team asked whether those links appear at normal hormone levels in healthy animals.

They reused material from a controlled study of young pigs, some exposed to early weaning stress. Blood hormone and damage markers were measured during the procedure. After death, heart tissue was tested for mitochondrial breathing, receptor levels, and protein marks. Readers get a careful baseline picture of hormone and heart-energy relations without disease in the way.
pmc-10745931:
Diaz-Formoso and coauthors test staph germs from wild hake fish for drug resistance. Loose antibiotic use has spread drug-proof germs widely. Such germs in seafood pose a health risk to buyers. The team took germs from eight hakes in the northeast Atlantic.

They found 27 staph germs that lack one clotting trait. Six species were named, led by one common skin type. Film growth on surfaces was tested in lab trays. Drug tests showed which drugs still halt each germ. Gene checks hunted resistance and virulence traits. Fish may carry proof germs to the food chain.
pmc-10748431:
Jens Egeland and co-authors test white noise as an aid to attention in children in a 2023 study. A brain arousal model claims steady noise can lift a flagging arousal system and steady performance. The team used a standard continuous performance test, which tracks response speed and its variability over time, in sixty-five children from a psychiatric unit with high or lower ADHD symptoms.

Each child took the test with and without white noise. Noise cut overall response variability, helped most late in the test, and steadied responses at the slowest event rate, especially in the high-symptom group. That group also missed fewer targets under noise. Error counts overall did not change. The authors advise replication with other noise types and levels.
pmc-10753431:
Jana Stein and co-authors report a 2023 clinical trial of brief online therapy for Arabic-speaking people with posttraumatic stress disorder. Care given over the internet can help groups that get little support, yet it was not clear which parts of the care do the work. The trial took place with people across the Middle East and North Africa.

In all, 365 people were split among three groups. One group used exposure work, facing hard memories in a guided way. One group used methods that reshape harsh thoughts about the self and the world. The third group waited for care. The team tracked stress signs, mood, and quality of life over time.
pmc-10759631:
In Bangladesh, public farm advisors have struggled to run rice growing demonstrations well, so a private version pairs seed dealers with their farmer customers. Tanjina Parven led a team that assessed this new system. They interviewed thirty-three dealers and ninety-two customer farmers, and held group talks to round out the picture.

Farmers named higher profit, a bigger say in decisions, and sharper marketing skills as the top gains. Dealers stressed the help small farmers got and the rise in local rice output. The weak spot was slow delivery of seeds and supplies, traced to dealers misjudging what their farmers needed. The authors suggest watching the young system over time before spreading it country-wide.
pmc-10776831:
Dental X-rays and scans hold early signs of disease, but reading them takes expert time. The authors review how artificial intelligence is changing dental and jaw imaging. Their study follows standard rules for systematic reviews and gathers clinical research from 2009 to 2023 across major medical databases.

The collected studies apply deep learning to many tasks. These include estimating age, spotting lesions at tooth roots, outlining jaw structures, judging face and jaw deformities, and tracing the nerve canal in the lower jaw. Across tasks, the tools defined anatomy and found disease with high accuracy. The review concludes that AI speeds up reading, supports earlier detection, and can improve patient outcomes. The authors frame the future as teamwork between clinician skill and machine precision, rather than replacement of the dentist.
pmc-10795831:
Charles Danan and co-authors show that a fast-growing cell type in the gut lining depends on an RNA-editing enzyme to stay alive. These transit-amplifying cells renew the intestine but also take heavy damage from radiation and chemotherapy. The enzyme, METTL3, tags RNA with chemical marks that help turn messages into protein.

When the team removed the enzyme in mice, the cells died, the gut's folds shrank, and the animals wasted and died. Reading the tagged and active RNAs showed hundreds of messages made into protein less often, many tied to growth signals such as Kras. The team confirmed the link between the enzyme and Kras in living tissue. The findings tie RNA marks to gut health and repair.
pmc-10801231:
Matilde Contreras and co-authors describe a border health mission during COVID-19 in a paper reporting 2023 work. Where Brazil, Colombia, and Peru meet on the Amazon, remote river towns had little testing or vaccine access at the pandemic's height. In August 2021 a Fiocruz Amazonia team and partners mounted a wide intervention at the port of Tabatinga.

A boat served as floating lab and storehouse at the busy terminal. The mission monitored 891 people for the virus and its lineages, vaccinated 536, handed protective gear to over two thousand, and trained local lab and health staff, with supplies donated. Migrants, traders, soldiers, townspeople, and river villagers crossed paths at the port, making it a natural choke point for reaching the region.
pmc-10882631:
Surendra Sharma, Shailesh Choudhary, and Julia Vorobiov lead a team reproducing tick-bite meat allergy in mice engineered to lack the sugar at its center. Their study was published in two thousand twenty-three. The syndrome makes people allergic to red meat hours after eating it. Tick bites are the suspected sensitizer.

Mice lacking the alpha-gal sugar were bitten by two tick species, then fed pork. Lone star tick bites raised allergy-linked antibodies far more than gulf coast tick bites. Pork challenge dropped the lone-star group's body temperature, an allergy sign. Bite-site skin showed its own immune gene patterns. The model separates the two ticks' roles cleanly. It also gives researchers a living system for mechanism hunting. Why one tick sensitizes and the other barely does is the open question. Prevention ideas can now be tested before human studies.
pmc-10940331:
Lihua Yao and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three study predicting cognitive impairment with tablet tests and machine learning. Early detection matters for older adults' wellbeing. Two short tasks measure memory for sequences and mental flexibility.

Eighty-six patients took the tablet assessments. A statistical model first merged both tasks into one composite score. Several learning models then competed to flag impairment. A random forest model performed best across repeated testing rounds. The key lesson was that one fixed cutoff misleads. Flexible models using the full score pattern sorted patients more reliably.
pmc-11046631:
Elizabeth Nelmes and co-authors argue that sepsis trials shut out cancer patients unfairly in an opinion piece from two thousand twenty-three. About a fifth of sepsis cases occur in people with cancer. Yet such patients are often barred from the trials that guide sepsis care.

The authors report findings that cancer patients are under-represented, often with no clear reason given. They question whether results from the enrolled mix can be carried over to varied cancer groups. Their call is for wider inclusion, so the evidence base matches the patients who actually get sepsis. Closing that gap, they say, would sharpen sepsis care for a large share of cases.
pmc-11531931:
Jameson Mori, William Brown, Daniel Skinner, Peter Schlichting, Jan Novakofski, and Nohra Mateus-Pinilla wrote a 2024 paper on rating deer habitat in Illinois. White-tailed deer are common across the state, and managers need maps of where the land suits them. An older rating used satellite images from 1996 and worked only at county scale.

The team rebuilt the rating with land cover data from 2001 to 2021 and at much finer scales, down to small survey plots. They checked their scores against deer numbers using a statistical model that also weighed hunting and deer density. The updated maps performed well. Finer maps help the state set hunting rules and spot where deer may crowd farms or roads.
pmc-11534431:
Mengfei Liu and six co-authors build gene markers for a forest pest sawfly, in a 2024 paper. The sawfly damages pine forests across a wide northern range, and its subgroups are poorly sorted. Short repeating DNA stretches, called microsatellites, make handy markers for telling populations apart.

From the sawfly's genome the team developed fifty-six markers and tested them in two Chinese populations. The markers split into high, moderate, and low information levels. Many also worked in three related sawfly species, giving those fields free tools. Grouping analyses separated the two populations into distinct clusters, hinting at real geographic structure. The marker set equips future work on how this pest spreads and whether its named subspecies hold up.
pmc-11535031:
Shaobo Wu and co-authors investigate a little-known gene across cancers, then zoom in on kidney cancer, in a 2024 study. The gene, ZBED3, carries instructions for a protein with a zinc-finger domain. Mining public cancer databases, the team compared its activity in tumours and healthy tissue. In clear cell kidney cancer, the most common kidney malignancy, the gene's activity was markedly reduced, and lower still in advanced stages and grades.

Patients whose tumours kept more ZBED3 activity lived longer overall. Genes moving with it clustered around inflammation responses and DNA methylation. Immune cell infiltration patterns also shifted with its level. Lab experiments verified the database picture. The authors propose ZBED3 as a prognostic marker in kidney cancer, low levels warning of aggressive disease, and as a thread worth pulling in immunity research.
pmc-11538031:
Abdolreza Sheibani and colleagues test whether gallstones raise the risk of fatty liver. Their case-control study from twenty twenty-four runs at two hospitals in Ahvaz. Fatty liver and gallstones often appear in the same patients. Both share many metabolic risk factors too.

Three hundred patients split evenly between fatty liver cases and controls. Ultrasound defined who had fatty liver disease. Age and sex were similar across the two groups. Gallstones showed a significant link with fatty liver status. The authors argue stones mark higher liver risk, not just shared habits. Which condition comes first cannot be settled by this design. Screening one condition may justify checking the other.
pmc-11574031:
Jeffrey Zamora Goicoechea and co-authors gauge breathing symptoms in e-cigarette users who never took up smoking, the cleanest test of vaping's own harms. Most past studies are muddied because most vapers used to smoke. The VERITAS study surveyed adults in six world regions with no set smoking history and no regular use of other tobacco goods.

The vapers, 491 people who had vaped in the past week, were compared with 247 controls who never vaped regularly, using a standard symptom score. Symptoms were rare in both groups: over eight in ten said they rarely or never had any of the five symptoms asked about. Vapers scored a bit worse on average, but the gap fell well short of the mark set for clinical relevance. A one-off survey cannot prove long-term safety, and past trial smoking was more common in vapers.
pmc-11579931:
Xiangyang Pei led a team grading shale rock quality in southern China in a 2024 study. Deep sea shale in the Zigong block holds gas in thin layered bands called laminae. The type and pairing of those layers may decide how good the rock is as a reservoir. They imaged thin sections and mapped minerals and chemistry with several advanced tools.

Layer type and pairing clearly shaped porosity, permeability, and gas content. One three-part pairing stood out, with the most organic matter, brittle minerals, and pore space. The team calls it the sweet spot for shale gas work in these formations. The findings give a theoretical base for hunting and developing deep shale gas.
pmc-11584931:
Camillia Lui and co-authors broke apart lumped data to reveal suicide risk among Asian American, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander teenagers in California. Suicide is a leading cause of death for these youths, but grouping them hides big differences. The team used survey data from over half a million public high school students.

In the combined group, about seventeen and a half percent reported suicidal thoughts in the past year. Split into subgroups, the rate ran from about thirteen percent for Asian Indian students to over twenty-one percent for Filipino students. Teenagers with mixed ethnic or racial identity showed higher risk in every group. The authors say counting subgroups separately is essential to see who needs help.
pmc-11585931:
Jie Cheng and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on burnout and presenteeism among anesthesia nurses in China. Presenteeism means working while unwell, with lost output. The team surveyed 568 registered anesthesia nurses across Sichuan hospitals in mid-2024, using standard scales for burnout, psychological capital, and invisible absence.

Burnout ran high and tracked with more presenteeism. Psychological capital, a bundle of hope, confidence, and resilience, tracked with less of both. Model tests showed capital partly carried the link between burnout and presenteeism: burned-out nurses with stronger capital showed up impaired less often. The authors suggest building capital as a buffer for this workforce.
pmc-11590831:
Maria Melendo-Viu and colleagues published a cohort study in 2024. They studied inherited thick heart muscle disease in Spain. All patients carried truncating variants in one gene. The gene, MYBPC3, helps build heart muscle fibers. Such variants were once linked to mild disease. Patients and relatives were followed for years retrospectively. Heart thickness, pumping function, and events were recorded. Carriers with and without disease were compared. Average participants were middle-aged with few symptoms.

Heart thickening was modest in most carriers overall. Affected patients had thicker walls than relatives clearly. Only a minority of relatives developed the disease phenotype. Pumping function was generally preserved in the cohort. The picture supports a relatively favorable outlook here. Family screening still matters for early detection. Long follow-up helps refine risk for relatives.
pmc-11595731:
Sara Mantovani and co-authors report outcomes of a neck muscle flap used as a safety net in tracheal surgery in a 2024 paper. Five patients at two Italian centers between 2011 and 2023 needed complex repair of the windpipe. Cases included large tissue loss, wall death from spreading neck infection, and extra long abnormal connections between windpipe and food pipe. The flap was freed from the skull base and rotated on its lower stem onto the repair site.

Goals were a stable airway, a working digestive tract, and patient survival. Follow up used scopes and scans at set intervals over months. The authors detail how the muscle rebuilt missing wall in one case and was layered between sutures in others. Readers see a versatile salvage technique for catastrophic airway cases.
pmc-11596331:
Collins and four colleagues test how lab digestion changes the health compounds in processed sorghum grain in twenty twenty-four. Sorghum is rich in polyphenols, plant compounds that fight cell damage. Color rich types, black and red, may hold more than white types. The team ran the grains through a fake gut and a cell layer that mimics the gut wall.

Digestion doubled the share of compounds freed from one black type. Black types also led on damage fighting power. Twelve freed compounds that crossed the cell layer had not been reported in sorghum before. One compound surged in black types after digestion but was absent in others. Processing shaped the gains by type, they found.
pmc-11598031:
Haiyan Huang and her eight co-authors, publishing in 2024, test how the harsh soils of southwest China's karst country affect oat seedlings. The region's rocky desertification leaves soil rich in calcium, alkaline, and dry. The team exposed oat seeds to three stresses in the lab. They varied calcium salt levels, acidity from pH 3 to 9, and drought using a standard drying solution.

Each stress had a sweet spot and a breaking point. A pinch of calcium helped seeds sprout and roots grow, while heavy doses shut them down. Mild drought also boosted sprouting, but stronger drying blocked growth. Acidity itself barely changed sprouting, yet alkaline conditions dragged all growth measures down. The authors give concrete ranges for planting oats in these soils. They frame the results as a guide for growing oats and breeding tougher varieties in the region.
pmc-11600331:
Krishna Mishra, Zehua Wu, Christian Erker, Klaus Müllen, and Thomas Basché study how to make a near-infrared light emitter shine brighter, in a 2024 paper. Such emitters matter for imaging and quantum tools. Their glow is usually dimmed by energy lost as vibration. The team worked with a molecule called dibenzoterrylene. They swapped its hydrogen atoms for the heavier form, deuterium. Both bulk and single-molecule tests were run.

The swap lengthened the glow and raised its yield by up to sixty percent. That clear isotope effect fingers carbon-hydrogen vibration as a main loss path. Loss rates in different solvents followed a known energy gap rule. Temperature from near zero to room level barely changed the loss rate. The results point to a design rule for bright infrared emitters. Replacing light atoms with heavy ones can pay off. The work suits quantum light source builders.
pmc-11602431:
Risa Hirata and co-authors survey leadership among general physicians in Japan. They find snags in education and research. Their 2024 questionnaire study is aimed at members of a society for hospital general medicine.

Two hundred eighty-six physicians gave replies to the survey, which did not take their names. It was done in February 2024. General physicians must lead in clinical care, in education, and in research. Yet the set skills for each zone are set out in a poor way. The survey asked which types of leadership those who replied value most, across those zones. Results were joined with views from experts and with a review of past work. The team aims to set out the profile of leadership that general medicine calls for. Training programmes can then aim at skills that time on the job, on its own, may not build in a way that can be trusted.
pmc-11603331:
Li Li and Chenhao Zhong model and tame the shaking of rolls in a cold rolling mill, in a 2024 study. Vertical vibration of the work roll can mar steel strip and wear the mill. The shake grows from the nonlinear play between roll and metal.

Their model joins dynamic rolling force with nonlinear spring and damping terms. Time delay traits shaped stability in strong ways, and stiffer damping shrank the shake and its resonance band. A feedback controller that uses delay itself was tuned to crush large swings. Computer runs confirmed the plan. The work gives mill designers a base for predicting and curbing the shake.
pmc-11603631:
Yuanyuan Guan and eight co-authors published a 2024 study mapping the GRAS gene family in wheat and testing one member against powdery mildew. This fungal disease cuts wheat yield and quality worldwide, and GRAS proteins steer plant growth and stress responses. The team found 179 GRAS genes spread unevenly over seven chromosomes, sorted into twelve subfamilies. Gene duplication, mostly large segmental copies, explained the family's rapid growth.

Three quarters of the expressed genes answered to biological stresses. Focusing on one gene, TaeSCL6, the team showed it reacts to mildew infection. Wheat with that gene silenced, by two independent methods, caught the disease more easily. The authors conclude the gene defends wheat and offer the family map as breeding material for resistant cultivars.
pmc-11603831:
Merga Siyoum and co-authors measure how common treatment-resistant depression is at Ethiopia's main mental hospital in this 2024 study. The condition means depression that stays after standard drug courses. Its scale in Ethiopia was not well documented, which hampers planning of care.

The team surveyed 412 follow-up patients with major depression at the hospital in Addis Ababa in early 2021. About forty-two percent met the study's measure of resistant depression. The odds were more than twice as high in women as in men. Having psychosis alongside depression, having a physical illness as well, and having a family history of mental illness each raised the odds further. The authors urge routine screening for resistant cases and better diagnostic tools at the hospital. They also call for preventive steps aimed at the groups most at risk.
pmc-11604731:
Qian and seven co-authors review programmed cell death across biology and disease, in work from twenty twenty-four. Programmed cell death is a regulated, active process governed by specific genes and proteins. Multiple distinct forms have been identified in recent years, each with its own machinery.

Mechanisms, biological functions, disease links, and therapeutic targets are covered in the review. Understanding these pathways matters across many fields, from development to cancer. Each death form is also a potential drug lever: block it to save cells, trigger it to kill tumors. The review maps that landscape for researchers entering the area.
pmc-11605731:
Shu-Ching Chang and co-authors build a personal risk score for melanoma's return in a 2024 study. Early-stage melanoma usually ends well, yet up to thirty percent of patients later develop spread. The team derived a score from five clinical and tissue factors in over twenty-six hundred patients with clear sentinel nodes.

A Gompertz survival model fit the score best, beating standard rivals on fit tests. Its predictions tracked real outcomes closely at two, five, and ten years. Discrimination stayed strong for two decades of follow-up. Ten-year recurrence risk ran from under five percent in the lowest third of scores to about a third in the highest. The authors offer the tool for individualized counseling: a patient can see their own time-shaped risk, not a stage average. They present it as ready for guiding follow-up intensity.
pmc-11606031:
Michal Laron and co-authors compare views of hospital care at home in Israel in this 2024 paper. Hospital at Home gives acute hospital level care in a patient home instead of a ward. The model grew during the COVID-19 pandemic but stayed limited in Israel. The work draws on surveys made for the 2022 Dead Sea Health Policy Conference.

One survey covered 342 physicians and the other covered 424 members of the public aged 35 and older. Physicians rated home care more highly than the public did. More doctors than lay respondents judged its quality, safety, and communication as good as hospital care. The gap helps explain slow uptake.
pmc-11607931:
Eight surgeons ask whether body weight drives implant loosening after knee replacement in a paper from 2024. Aseptic loosening is a leading cause of late failure. The study reviewed three hundred fifty-four patients split evenly at a body mass index of thirty. Imaging, surgical details, and complications were compared over long follow-up. Only four patients developed loosening at all.

No clear difference in loosening or other complications appeared between the weight groups. Ages and implant types were similar across groups. The authors conclude weight alone does not decide loosening risk. They recommend a broader prevention approach covering patient and implant factors. Larger cohorts with longer follow-up would sharpen the answer.
pmc-11608231:
Atenasadat Hosseini and four colleagues build a cerium catalyst on halloysite clay for making tetrahydroquinolines, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The aza-Diels-Alder reaction is a key route to these bioactive compounds. An imine and an alkene cyclize in the catalyst's presence. Their catalyst anchors cerium ions on chemically functionalized halloysite.

The support was built stepwise: silane treatment, a triazine linker, then a chelating acid, then cerium loading. Analysis showed amorphous grains tens of nanometers across with sparse cerium content. Catalytic activity was tested on the target reaction. Reusability, a practical necessity for such catalysts, was also studied. The work adds a clay-based option to the catalyst toolbox. It targets efficient synthesis of a medicinally valued ring system.
pmc-11608331:
Sorting time series into classes, like recognizing activities or faults, keeps getting better with deep learning, but models grow heavy and hand-designing them is hit or miss. Peng Wang and three co-authors built a lightweight transformer framework in a 2024 paper that designs itself. Its parts split time and channel features apart to cut cost, use a fuzzy position code, and process locally with small convolutions.

An automated search method tunes the structure and prunes it, removing guesswork. On standard public collections of time series, the framework matched or beat heavier rivals while staying light. The authors pitch it for civil, industrial, and military uses.
pmc-11609131:
Anna Schlomann and co-authors adapt a mobile device proficiency questionnaire into German for use with older adults, in work published in 2024. The original questionnaire is a trusted measure of basic and advanced phone and tablet skills. A German version would let aging and technology research align across countries.

The team translated the scale with a controlled procedure and tested it in two samples of adults aged fifty to ninety-five. The German scale matched the original's structure and showed excellent consistency. Scores held steady over a two-year gap between test waves. As expected, scores rose with education and device use and fell with age, and women scored lower than men. The authors offer the tool for research in German-speaking countries.
pmc-11609731:
Ischemic priapism, a prolonged painful erection, is a rare emergency often blamed on antipsychotic drugs, and delay can cause lasting damage. The six authors report a 59-year-old man with schizophrenia who had been stable on long-acting risperidone injections. After a switch to paliperidone he developed ischemic priapism. The suspected mechanism is blockade of alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, though hard data are thin.

Once the priapism resolved, the team treated him with aripiprazole plus olanzapine. His psychiatric symptoms improved and the priapism did not return. The authors suggest switching to antipsychotics with lower alpha-1 affinity can treat schizophrenia without recurrence. They also note that metabolic enzyme differences and dose may play roles, and they call for more evidence to guide drug choice after such an event.
pmc-11611131:
Kyoko Noguchi and co-authors pilot a program to improve mouth health in older adults who receive nursing visits at home, in a 2024 feasibility study. Older patients needing long-term care in Japan often have poor oral health, which affects eating and general health. The pilot asked whether patients or family caregivers could deliver daily mouth care suited to each mouth.

Three visiting nursing stations took part, and 52 people enrolled, about three-quarters of those approached. Care ran at least once a day for four weeks. About eight in ten participants finished the final survey, and roughly two-thirds followed the plan as asked. Scores on a standard oral health checklist improved steadily across the month. The authors call the approach workable and call for a larger, stronger trial to prove its effect.
pmc-11614531:
Mathilde Grimée, Aimee R Taylor, and Michael T White modeled why the two main malaria parasites so often infect the same people, in a study published in 2024. In many regions both species circulate, and one may wake the other from dormancy. Simple chance would predict fewer double infections than surveys show.

The authors reviewed published rates and found the two parasites' spread rises and falls together, with double infections above the chance level. Their model adds one feature: people differ in how much mosquitoes bite them. That uneven exposure alone explained the pattern well. Simulations then tested two treatment ideas, finding a modest effect for fever-driven waking and a large one for treating one species' cases with a cure that also clears the other.
pmc-11621331:
Mas-Fontao and coauthors gauge kidney involvement in prediabetes across Europe in a large trial. Prediabetes raises risk for kidney harm before full diabetes starts. The team used data from a large trial called ePREDICE. The cohort held 967 people from seven states in Europe.

Kidney function was scored with a standard equation for all. Just over 9 percent had kidney abnormalities in all. Excess filtration was found in 20 people in the cohort. Protein in urine was found in 45 people in the cohort. Reduced function stage was found in 29 people. Age and height linked inversely to excess filtration.
pmc-11623931:
Broken bones heal because stem cells in the bone's outer membrane wake up and rebuild. Simon Perrin and co-authors map that awakening cell by cell. They built a single-nucleus atlas of the resting periosteum and of the early fracture site. Resting stem cells carry known stemness markers. After injury they first turn into a temporary fibrogenic cell type. Only then do they become bone or cartilage builders.

Distinct gene programs steer each fork, involving Notch, Wnt, and the body clock. The temporary cells also send out most of the signals in the fracture zone. The authors cast them as coordinators of early repair, not just raw material.
pmc-11624231:
Lindberg leads a large team studying repeat radiosurgery for pituitary tumors, in work from twenty twenty-four. Gamma Knife radiosurgery is well established for pituitary adenomas left after surgery or growing again. Some tumors grow even after a first radiosurgery, and repeat treatment value was unclear.

The population based cohort measured long term progression free survival after repeat treatment. Pituitary adenomas are benign but can harm vision and hormone balance as they grow. Proof that a second focused radiation session controls growth durably would spare many patients a return to open skull surgery, with its higher risks.
pmc-11624731:
Noa Gordon and eight co-authors published this cohort profile in 2024. It describes a national registry that tracked men with prostate cancer across Ireland. The registry was set up in 2015 to follow each man's path from diagnosis through treatment, so care could be improved.

From 2016 to 2020, the registry enrolled 6,816 newly diagnosed men at sixteen hospitals, both public and private. Staff recorded full clinical details, and 873 men also filled in surveys about their own outcomes. Early findings show that many cancers were caught by chance blood tests while still at an early stage. The team invites researchers worldwide to use the data. A next phase will add a quality registry and a store of tissue samples.
pmc-11626431:
Ruidong Zhou and seven co-authors present a 2024 lab method, written in Chinese, for testing shrimp for traces of farm chemicals. The food in question is the whiteleg shrimp, a widely farmed seafood. Shrimp extracts hold many fats and other matter that cloud test results, so clean-up is the hard step. The team built a new clean-up material by mixing carbon nanotubes with a seaweed-based gel.

With the new material and a fast filter column, extracts can be cleaned in one pass. A sensitive mass-based test then measures sixty-six farm chemicals at once. Spiked shrimp tests showed steady results and low detection limits across the full set. The authors call the method fast, cheap, and fit for routine food safety checks on farmed seafood.
pmc-11628931:
Rita Cordeiro and a large team of co-authors compared sample types for diagnosing mpox across 1,914 samples from 953 confirmed cases, in this 2024 study. Labs needed to know where the virus hides best and how long each site stays reliable. Lesion swabs came back positive in about ninety-one percent of cases, with rectal swabs close behind.

Throat swabs and urine lagged well behind, and their virus levels ran much lower. Lesion loads held steady for a month after symptoms began, while rectal and throat levels faded sooner. About five percent of patients were caught only by a throat swab despite negative lesions. The authors urge multisite testing, with lesion swabs as the anchor sample.
pmc-11631731:
Yingying Liu and six co-authors linked mothers' exercise in pregnancy to ADHD risk in preschoolers, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Moderate exercise in pregnancy is known to help children, but its tie to attention disorders was little studied. The web survey covered thousands of children aged three to six in southwest China.

Children whose mothers exercised under twenty minutes a day showed ADHD risk signs at about double the rate of children whose mothers exercised longer. Adjusted analysis kept the link strong. The pattern looked the same for boys and girls and across mothers' smoking, sleep, and anemia status. The authors urge moderate daily exercise in pregnancy, while calling for forward-looking studies to confirm the tie.
pmc-11632431:
Wei She, Yago Garitaonaindia, and Yun Lin review the newest progress in liquid biopsy for lung cancer, in this 2024 narrative review. A liquid biopsy reads tumor traces in blood instead of cutting tissue. The authors searched three databases for work from 2018 to mid 2024 on circulating tumor DNA, tumor cells, and related markers.

Recent gains sharpen both sensitivity and specificity of the tests. The review tours the marker zoo: tumor DNA and RNA, whole tumor cells, exosomes, small vesicles, metabolites, platelets educated by tumors, and plasma proteins. Each can aid early detection, prognosis, and personal treatment choices. Hurdles remain before routine use, from standardization to cost. The authors expect steady refinement to move liquid biopsy into everyday lung cancer care.
pmc-11634031:
Wang and coauthors find that blocking a decoy switch helps fish hearts heal. Heart growth drugs that boost a growth signal have failed in people. The team tried a new tack in zebrafish, which regrow heart tissue well. They blocked a decoy receptor that soaks up the signal.

Fish with the blocked switch healed cold-hurt hearts far better. New vessels grew fast, and heart wall spread wider. More heart cells woke and split to rebuild tissue. Scarring fell in those healed hearts as well. Blocking the growth signal erased all those gains. Gene scans showed vessel cells drove much of the gain.
pmc-11636531:
Sander Tabernee Heijtmeijer and ten co-authors test augmented reality guided surgery for placing cheek bone implants in human cadaver skulls. These implants are hard to place due to thin bone, poor sight lines, and long drill paths near key structures. The study came out in twenty twenty-four.

The guide links a trade navigation system to a headset that overlays the plan on the skull. Twenty implants were placed in five skulls after full upper jaw removal. Post scans were matched to the plan to read entry and exit drift and angle drift. Results were set against a past study that used printed guides for the same task.
pmc-11640231:
Da Luz Neto and co-authors test how well microscope findings on kidney biopsies can pin down lupus nephritis. A biopsy proof of this kidney disease can by itself establish a lupus diagnosis, yet no set of tissue features formally defines it. The study compared 731 biopsies from lupus patients and patients with look-alike kidney diseases.

Five features together flagged lupus kidney disease with high accuracy. They include a growth pattern in the kidney's filters, deposits under the lining, and a rich mix of antibody stains. The same features separated lupus from a close mimic, membranous nephropathy. The authors offer the five-feature set as a working diagnostic rule for Latin American practice.
pmc-11640431:
Chien-Hao Su and four colleagues measure liver inflammation risk in cancer patients taking everolimus, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The drug treats breast, kidney, and pancreatic neuroendocrine cancers. It can wake hepatitis B virus up again. Taiwanese records covered patients treated over more than a decade.

Three hundred seventy-seven patients met the entry criteria. The liver ill struck over a quarter of virus-positive patients. It also hit about a sixth of virus-negative ones. The virus woke again in about a ninth of unprotected virus-positive patients. Preventive treatment roughly halved that rate. Two virus-negative patients still got severe hepatitis from the woken virus. Positive surface antigen and one companion drug raised the risk. The authors urge screening and preventive antivirals in endemic regions.
pmc-11640531:
Nobutaka Nishimura and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on whether the time of day changes how well a glow-based test finds bladder tumors. The test feeds patients a compound that cancer cells turn into a glowing dye, which then marks tumors under special light. Glow strength varies between patients for unclear reasons. The team suspected the body's daily clock, which runs the dye's production line.

In two bladder cancer cell lines and in mouse grafts, dye buildup rose and fell on a daily rhythm. Two clock genes tracked that rhythm, and two enzymes on the production line cycled as well. In patients, tumor glow in surgery photos grew through the day. It peaked in operations run in the late afternoon slot. The team proposes timing the test to the clock, scheduling resections when the glow runs strongest, to miss fewer tumors.
pmc-11641031:
Iuliana Mihaela Deleanu and six co-authors published this study in 2024. It builds a germ-fighting film for food packaging from plant-based cellulose. Plain bacterial cellulose is strong and pure but does nothing against microbes, so the team loaded it with metal nanoparticles.

The particles, zinc oxide and silver, were made the green way, using turmeric extract instead of harsh chemicals. They were folded into a blend of two cellulose forms. A battery of instruments confirmed the particles sat inside the film and mapped its structure and heat behavior. The team then challenged the film with three microbes: two common bacteria and a yeast. Work of this kind aims at wraps that keep food fresher for longer without plastic. The study lays out the recipe and the checks behind it.
pmc-11642231:
Amauri Ernesto Gomes and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four study of self-compacting concrete mixed with steel fibres and recycled additions. The additions were rubber and marble or granite residue. No earlier work had combined all of them in one mix.

Fresh concrete was tested for flow and passing ability with standard funnels and rings. Hardened samples were checked for strength, stiffness, water uptake, and vibration damping. More rubber meant better energy absorption but weaker strength and flow. One blend with fibres and both residues stood out for damping. Such mixes could suit structures needing vibration control.
pmc-11644431:
Fomekong Rachel Merveille Fomekong, Baozhu Jia, Zhizun Xu, Bissih Fred, and Udo Frese review sensor fusion for underwater mapping robots in two thousand twenty-four. Underwater craft must map and locate themselves at once, a task called SLAM, yet the sea dims sight, shifts fast, and blocks GPS signals.

The review sorts the senses a craft can blend: motion units, speed logs, cameras, sonar, and laser ranging. Fusion recipes, from Kalman and particle filters to graph methods, are weighed for accuracy, cost, and toughness. Newer tools, quantum sensors and AI-tuned filters, get a look as well. Case studies show real trade-offs. The authors close with future needs: taming drift, noise, and the sea's surprises.
pmc-11644531:
Kanat Beknazarov and colleagues study how shungite rock from Kazakhstan affects the physical and mechanical properties of nitrile rubber composites. Their 2024 study tests the carbon-rich mineral as a partial or full replacement for carbon black filler.

Shungite ore and its floated concentrate both contain carbon plus various metal oxides. Flotation raised carbon content more than threefold while cutting silica content threefold. Replacing carbon black with shungite lowered the rubber compound's viscosity by up to about twenty-nine percent. Safe processing time and curing time both lengthened by roughly a third. Carbon content of the filler barely influenced these processing measures. Property changes at low replacement levels are detailed further in the study.
pmc-11644931:
Shaoxin Wang and seven colleagues built a torsion pendulum sensitive enough to test space gravitational-wave sensors on the ground. Space detectors need test masses floating nearly perfectly freely, and stray forces must be understood before launch. Their pendulum uses a commercial autocollimator as its optical readout. The paper details the operating principle, the structure, and laboratory background-noise measurements.

Sensitivity reached one hundred-billionth of a newton-meter per root hertz across the millihertz band where space detectors listen. That qualifies the apparatus to verify inertial sensor components before they fly. Ground testing is where space missions quietly succeed or fail: catching a noisy subsystem costs weeks here, but the mission in orbit. Construction lessons from this pendulum feed directly into the next generation of test rigs for gravitational-wave payloads.
pmc-11646431:
Lei Liu and nine co-authors review twenty years of work on a class of diabetes drug candidates that keep stalling at the liver, in this 2024 review. These compounds switch on the FFAR1 receptor to coax insulin out. Several reached large trials, yet none has won approval, mostly because they injured the liver.

The review traces the harm to the molecules' greasy acid heads, which spawn toxic byproducts. Newer designs shrink the molecule, cut the grease, and borrow shapes from natural products. One candidate built that way looks liver-safe so far and sits in mid-stage trials. The authors also survey hopes beyond diabetes, in fatty liver and stroke, and point to AI-aided design as the way forward.
pmc-11648731:
Naseralallah and three co-authors reviewed in twenty twenty-five how drug experts on the care team help patients around surgery. Such experts check drugs, teach staff, and shape rules for safe use. The team searched large health banks for trials of their work in this phase of care.

They kept nineteen studies with more than seven thousand patients in all. Most work mixed drug care with teaching and rule-making. Pain care got better, and clots, gut stress sores, and sick feels all fell. Gains for long-term ills like high blood pressure were less clear. Most proof was weak, so the team calls for stronger trials.
pmc-11649631:
Shiri Shinan-Altman leads a team on couples and endometriosis. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses deep talks with couples. The disease hits about one in ten women of childbearing age.

Diagnosis can lag years behind first signs, causing strain. Each partner was talked to alone for this study. Talks were read both as one voice and as a pair. Three themes rose, from life in doubt's shadow. Coping at diagnosis could be joint or solo in the pairs. Life after diagnosis swung between hardship and growth.  Ten couples took part in the deep talks held.
pmc-11649831:
Jawad Abdulla and eight colleagues published a study in two thousand twenty-four on hearing processing after stroke. Stroke often damages the auditory pathway, causing problems from sound detection to meaning. The recovery window between three and twelve months was the focus.

Forty patients underwent brain scans, cognitive screening, hearing tests, and a staged battery of central auditory tasks. Damage involving the primary auditory cortex tracked with worse early sound perception scores. A severity index counting affected auditory brain areas correlated negatively with early perception performance. The authors say lesion mapping predicts who struggles most. They argue auditory testing belongs in stroke rehabilitation planning.
pmc-11651131:
Loredana Stavar-Matei and co-authors review how the COVID-19 pandemic changed pneumococcal ear infections, drug resistance, and vaccination in children. Their 2024 review centers on a bacterium that lives quietly in children's noses yet can trigger invasive disease. Ear infection is among its most common harms in the youngest children.

The authors gather open evidence on invasive pneumococcal disease in under-fives during and after the pandemic. Rates and resistance depend on vaccine status, local strain patterns, season, co-infections, and social conditions, all of which the pandemic shuffled at once. Lockdowns cut many childhood infections while disrupting vaccine schedules. Sorting those opposing effects guides catch-up immunization and antibiotic choices.
pmc-11653831:
Alethea Desrosiers and co-authors published a study in 2024 on tailoring a youth-focused mental health intervention for schools in Sierra Leone, using an implementation blueprint methodology. Interventions that work in high-income countries can fail in low- and middle-income settings if they clash with local needs and resources. The study set out to map what would support or hinder implementation, and to build a plan.

The researchers interviewed two Ministry of Education officials and thirty school staff, including teachers and principals. Rapid qualitative analysis identified the barriers: buy-in from staff, parents, and students; teacher motivation; time in the school day; limited funding; and enthusiasm fading over time. The group reconvened to rank the barriers by importance and by how changeable they were. Strategies addressing the top barriers were selected for the blueprint. The study examines whether the blueprint methodology is feasible in a setting.
pmc-11654331:
He Zhu, Jiahui Lei, Fan Gao, Yingjie Guo, and Limin Zhao shared a review in twenty twenty-four. It is about a two-drug inhaler for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The pair is umeclidinium and vilanterol. The pair opens the airways and improves lung function. But how it stacks up next to rival one-drug and two-drug options was not clear. The team pooled the trial data to find out.

They pooled seventeen randomized trials. The trials covered nearly thirty-two thousand patients in all. Two-drug therapy pairs the two drug classes. It gives additive airway opening. The pair studied here raised lung capacity scores. It eased breathlessness scores too. It cut how much patients felt their symptoms, next to the other options. The team weighed triple therapy with a steroid added as well. The synthesis gives clinicians hard numbers to compare for a crowded shelf of inhalers.
pmc-11655231:
Faith Bernadette Descallar and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on how commercial infant formulas behave in a simulated baby stomach. Formula composition varies widely, and digestion quirks affect what nutrients a baby actually gets. The team ran stage-one formulas through a dynamic lab model of the infant stomach, tracking structure, stability, and protein breakdown.

Casein-heavy formulas clumped strongly in acid, trapping fat droplets in curds that lingered and slowed both protein digestion and fat emptying. Whey-heavy formulas stayed looser, digested faster, and emptied quickly, though added thickeners made them clump fat instead. The findings help explain why babies handle formulas differently and guide gentler designs.
pmc-11655731:
Toni Ivicic and colleagues published a case series in 2024. They studied ultrasound signs of lung blood clots. Pulmonary embolism is notoriously hard to diagnose quickly. Symptoms range from none to sudden death. Heart ultrasound usually checks heart size and function. A flow pattern in the outflow tract may help more. Early systolic notching appears in many risky cases. Three emergency patients with that pattern are shown. None had prior heart or lung disease known. Their initial risk scores looked low beforehand.

Heart scans showed the notching pattern first in each case. CT scans then found large central clots. The clots blocked the main lung arteries. Ultrasound was the only early clue in some. The sign could speed up confirmatory scanning greatly. Selected patients may benefit most from this check. Wider validation is still needed before routine use.
pmc-11655831:
Emmanuelle Baillet and co-authors ask whether early craving patterns predict long-term addiction outcomes in a 2024 study. Craving that shifts hour by hour is known to foreshadow drug use in the short term. The team tracked craving many times a day during the first two weeks of outpatient treatment in Bordeaux, France, then followed patients for five years or more.

Thirty-nine patients took part. Those still using their main substance at follow-up had shown a slower fall in craving during those first two weeks. Their craving also carried over less from one moment to the next, suggesting jumpier reactions to cues. Average craving level alone did not predict outcome. The authors say slow early relief from craving may signal resistance to treatment and flag patients who need adjusted care.
pmc-11655931:
Pei Zhang and Qingzhao Chu hunt for new treatment targets in breast cancer in this twenty twenty-four paper. When two genes fuse by mistake, they can build mixed proteins. Those mixed proteins may also give the immune system fresh targets, since their joined parts look foreign to the body.

The pair used computing tools to find fusion genes in breast tumors and judge which ones track with patient outcomes. They then built the mixed proteins on screen and picked out bits that the immune system might spot. Thousands of candidate bits covered most patients, and a small set was confirmed in real tumor samples. The library could feed future immune treatments.
pmc-11656231:
Samal Kaumbekova and co-authors published this 2024 study on what gold nanoparticles do to a common blood protein. As medical uses of nanoparticles grow, so does the need to know how they reshape the proteins they meet, since a bent protein may stop working or seed disease. The team paired lab tests with computer simulations on bovine serum albumin.

Light-based tests showed the protein losing its neat secondary structure when gold particles and table salt acted together. A dye test found the particles also suppressed the growth of flat beta sheets in buffer. Simulations traced the first grip between particle and protein, and compared particles of five, three, and one nanometer. Salt, the team conclude, is no bystander in these meetings.
pmc-11656431:
Ping Yang and nine colleagues pooled clinical trial data on liver toxicity from antibody-drug conjugates used in breast cancer. These targeted drugs deliver chemotherapy straight to cancer cells, but the liver still takes damage. The systematic review searched three databases through March twenty twenty-three. Liver enzyme elevations were the main measure. Incidence was combined across trials with meta-analysis, and drugs were compared against each other.

Overall rates of liver injury were high. Sacituzumab govitecan produced the highest rate of one enzyme's elevation, about twenty-five percent. Trastuzumab deruxtecan led for a second enzyme, at about thirty-two percent. Grades of severity were separated in the analysis. The twenty twenty-four ranking helps oncologists anticipate which conjugate needs the closest liver monitoring in breast cancer patients.
pmc-11656831:
Alireza Shariati and a team of co-authors reviewed mRNA cancer vaccines from lab to bedside. Their review, from twenty twenty-four, deals with shots that teach the immune system to hunt cancer cells. Trial reads so far show the shots are safe and borne well. They can be mass made fast, and the immune lift hits both the main tumor and its spreads. Extra immune switch codes can ride in the same mRNA to boost the punch.

Snags stand in the way: the mRNA breaks down fast, immune cells take up too little, and the body fights the carrier. The team walks the fixes in play. Readers get a full bench to bedside map of a new cancer shot era.
pmc-11657531:
Andrew Evans and co-authors test, in 2024, what happens when a stress-related brain signal is blocked in mice bred to develop Alzheimer's-like disease. Norepinephrine steers attention, arousal, and brain inflammation, and earlier drug work hinted it shapes the disease process. The team blocked the signal three ways.

They silenced the brainstem hub that supplies the signal, gave a common blocking drug, and deleted its receptors only from microglia, the brain's immune cells. First, cleared whole brains were imaged in three dimensions to map where plaques, reactive microglia, and signal loss overlap. The design lets each blocking route be judged against inflammation and pathology readouts.
pmc-11657831:
Ji, Yang, and Niu profile bone marrow fluid in relapsed leukaemia in twenty twenty-four. Acute myeloid leukaemia often returns after treatment. The team searched marrow supernatant for proteins and metabolites tied to relapse. Genetic traits of the cancer were analysed alongside the chemistry.

Samples came from seven relapsed and thirty-three non relapsed patients. Near one thousand proteins and near five thousand metabolites were identified. Clustering found groups tied to three high risk gene mutations. Fifty-seven proteins and one hundred ninety metabolites linked closely to relapse. Lipid metabolism stood out in the marrow environment of the disease. The authors say these signatures could guide prognosis and further study.
pmc-11658231:
Jiali Yao and co-authors present a 2024 study of daily habits and blood sugar spikes after meals in adults without diabetes. What mix of food, movement, and sleep best tames those spikes in real life was not clear. The team tracked Asian adults in Singapore over nine free living days.

Phones logged meals, wrist bands logged movement, and skin sensors logged sugar around the clock. Thousands of meals entered the study. Carb rich and deep fried foods raised spike size, while protein rich foods lowered it. Refined grains showed the strongest rise of all. Movement after a meal cut spikes a lot, above all at mid to strong pace. Longer sleep also helped. Spikes ran lowest in the morning.
pmc-11659231:
Fangfang Liu and four co-authors link a mother's contact with pesticides around conception to birth defects in her child, in a 2024 journal article. The study draws on a large survey in Shaanxi Province in northwest China. It covers births from 2010 to 2013.

The survey held 29,204 women, and 562 of their babies had a birth defect. Defects were far more common in the group with pesticide contact than in the group without it. After the team weighed age, food, and other factors, contact still more than doubled the risk of defects overall. The risk of heart defects in the child ran about three times as high. The authors urge care with farm chemicals for women who may conceive.
pmc-11661731:
Shengmin Mei, Jie Xiang, Li Wang, Yuan Xu, and Zhiwei Li published this study in 2024. It asks whether livers from brain-dead donors whose hearts had stopped and been restarted make risky transplants. Surgeons have debated such organs for years, and nobody had measured how the arrest's length matters.

The team mined a United States registry covering two decades and over 115,000 liver recipients. After matching similar patients, about seven thousand pairs remained. Organs from arrest donors did at least as well: slightly shorter hospital stays and slightly better graft survival at one, five, and ten years. Early graft failure did rise with longer arrest times. Arrests under thirty minutes had the lowest failure rate of all, even beating donors with no arrest. The authors suggest such livers should not be refused on history alone.
pmc-11662931:
Lindsey Pale and five co-authors screened the genome for genes that guard DNA gaps left by a cancer drug. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with cisplatin, a platinum drug that stays a mainstay for most cancers. How it kills is still part dim. Fresh work shows gaps of single strand DNA pile up after the drug restarts copying past its lesions. That pile may set how keen a tumor is to the drug, most in BRCA weak lines.

Genome wide knockout screens flagged a pair, HELQ and RAD52, as the axis that runs gap repair. Too much of the gap maker enzyme fills gaps with no extra drug keen found in their tests. Readers get a fresh lever of drug response.
pmc-11667731:
Marc Villabona and four co-authors tuned light-switched compounds that swing in acidity, in a paper published in 2024. Such switches let light steer chemical and biological steps from a distance. Their builds pair a weak acid part with a two-form switch. Light flips the switch, which joins or cuts the link between the acid part and the pulling groups, and the acid strength swings with it.

The team varied the structure of the build to widen that swing. Their best builds beat the swings that earlier work had shown. The paper maps which structural traits pay off, so later builds can start from strength. Light-set acidity could steer drug action, sensors, and smart gels in time. The work is a design guide as much as a result.
pmc-11668731:
Caroline Maretz and four co-authors published a 2024 review of infectious keratitis, a sight-threatening infection of the cornea, in western New York. They gathered ten years of cases at the University of Rochester, 935 in all, and tracked patient traits, care, and outcomes. The study focused on treatment failure, defined as healing that took over two weeks or needed surgery, and on who got cultures or surgery.

Older age, a prior corneal transplant, severe vision loss at arrival, and large ulcers all predicted failure. Fungal and protozoan infections also failed more often. Patients living far away arrived with worse ulcers and needed surgery more. Black patients received corneal cultures less often than White patients. The authors offer the regional picture as a guide for spotting risky cases early.
pmc-11671931:
Ida Arentz Taraldsen and co-authors test a machine that doses oxygen automatically against nurses doing it by hand, in this 2024 trial paper. Heart patients often need oxygen kept inside a tight saturation band. Both too little and too much can harm.

Sixty cardiac patients were randomized for twenty-four hours of care. The automatic group spent a median eighty-seven percent of the time in range. Manual care managed about sixty-one percent. Time spent below range also shrank with the device. The authors conclude automation holds oxygen steadier than intermittent checks allow. The authors conclude automation holds oxygen steadier than intermittent checks allow, with less staff effort per patient.
pmc-11672831:
Myeong Uk Kuk and co-authors find that two drugs together can roll back cell aging better than either alone. Aging cells drown in reactive oxygen species, corrosive molecules that damage their parts. The team screened pairs of senomorphic drugs, compounds known to trim those species, and one pair stood out: blockers of the BRAF and p38 MAPK pathways.

Together, the two cut reactive oxygen far more than the sum of their single effects. Mitochondria recovered, and the visible marks of senescence eased. Gene reading pointed to a single key player, a metal-binding gene called MT2A, which the pair switched on. Forcing that gene on by itself copied the pair's benefits. The authors say the work opens a route to anti-aging combinations, and even to single-gene tricks that mimic them.
pmc-11673131:
A team of researchers compares how hearing loss types affect children's language in a paper from 2024. Hearing loss in childhood can slow syntax, meaning use, and social communication. The study tested one hundred forty children aged six to twelve. They were grouped by loss type, from one-sided conductive to two-sided mixed loss, plus a control group with normal hearing. A standard language battery measured each child's skills.

All language domains differed across groups, with severe or two-sided loss scoring lowest. Loss type was the strongest predictor of total language score. Age at diagnosis and device fitting also mattered, and years of therapy helped somewhat. The authors stress early, thorough hearing and language support.
pmc-11674831:
Christodoulos Chatzigrigoriadis and co-authors report, in a 2024 case study, a rare soft tissue tumor found as a groin lump in a man treated for urinary stones. The tumor type, called deep angiomyxoma, is benign but creeps into nearby tissue and often grows large. It is far more common in women and is often mistaken for a hernia or other groin lumps in men.

The patient, an older man, came in with blood in his urine from stones and a silent groin mass. A body scan confirmed the mass, and it was removed surgically. The authors stress scans and biopsy before surgery, since this tumor returns often and needs clear margins and long follow-up.
pmc-11674931:
Om Roy, Yashar Moshfeghi, Agustin Ibanez, Francisco Lopera, Mario Parra, and Keith Smith present a method to read fast-changing brain links from EEG despite heavy noise. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Brain links computed over short windows are easily swamped by static and false matches.

Their method, called FAST, first averages stable long-term links across a whole group for a pair of memory tasks. That average becomes a filter for each person's fleeting links. In simulations the method separated true differences where standard approaches failed. Applied to Alzheimer's patients, it tied a classic brain wave link pattern to working memory deficits. The tool may help memory clinics read short brain signals with more trust.
pmc-11675031:
Rosaria Ferrara and co-authors present a 2024 study on what nurses know about autism. Autistic people often face barriers because others around them know little about the condition. Nurses and nursing students work closely with patients, so their knowledge matters for good care.

Sixty-six nurses in a master's program filled in a questionnaire. It covered four areas: general facts, symptoms, screening and diagnosis, and treatment. General knowledge scores were good, and most knew autism is a developmental condition present from birth. The authors also tested links between scores and personal traits such as age and background. Studies like this help schools spot the gaps that training should fill first.
pmc-11675131:
Timur Hakan Barak and four co-authors test a horsetail plant extract for guard against diabetic kidney harm. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Plants of this genus serve as food and folk care for kidney ills and diabetes. The kind studied is a folk remedy in Türkiye for kidney trouble.

The extract is rich in flavonoids and phenolic acids, curbs cell stress, and blocks enzymes tied to diabetes. In cell tests it lifts guard proteins tied to both ills. They also run a mock digestion first: the active load falls, yet stays high enough to back the old folk use. The plant looks fit as a functional food for this guard role.
pmc-11675231:
Shasha Zhai and co-authors sequence, in a 2024 paper, the full mitochondrial genome of a fringe tree, an ornamental species native to North China. The tree sampled was ancient, over five hundred years old. Mitochondrial DNA, inherited apart from the main genome, carries clues to the species' evolution and biology that can guide its protection.

The genome forms a single loop of about 658 thousand bases, with a guanine-cytosine share near forty-five percent. The team catalogued thirty-seven protein-coding genes, twenty transfer RNA genes, and three ribosomal RNA genes, plus many repeats and fragments strayed in from the chloroplast genome. Family trees built from the protein genes place a close cousin species as the tree's nearest relative. The authors deposit the result as the first full mitochondrial record for this species, for use in breeding and conservation work.
pmc-11675631:
Ryosuke Takata, Atsushi Masumori, and Takashi Ikegami explore in this 2024 study whether AI agents can grow distinct personalities just by talking. Past work gave each agent a fixed character and memory from the start. Here, agents based on large language models begin alike and chat in a group simulation. The question is whether differences appear on their own.

The agents traded natural language messages and formed loose communities. To keep chats going, they invented hashtags and even false claims. Their word choices grew more varied over time, and their moods shifted with each exchange. Personalities seemed to emerge and change as groups formed. The authors say this setup offers a new way to study how collective behavior arises in artificial groups.
pmc-11676431:
Victor Lu and co-authors (2024) mapped sports-related neck injuries in American children over a decade. Using a national injury surveillance system, they counted emergency visits for patients aged six to eighteen from 2014 to 2023. The weighted total came to about 361,000 visits, with no clear rise or fall across the years. Boys made up three fifths of cases. Strains were the most common diagnosis, followed by pain and bruising. Fractures were rare.

Most children, about 95 percent, were treated and sent home. The study identified what predicted needing higher-level care instead. Older age, being male, injury to another body part, and any diagnosis other than a strain all raised the odds. Football drove the most visits overall, while cheerleading led for girls. The authors say these patterns can sharpen both prevention programs and emergency triage rules for young athletes.
pmc-11676831:
Di Hu and co-authors test whether an amino acid salt can make a rectal drug gentler in this 2024 paper. Sodium aescinate is used on skin to cut inflammation and swelling. Its strong irritation bars use on damaged skin and mucous membranes. The team paired it with arginine hydrochloride in a gel.

Computer docking first checked how the two compounds interact. Gels were then made at several mix ratios and tested for acidity, stability, and spread. Animal tests measured irritation of the rectal lining and anti hemorrhoid effects. A mix ratio of one to six worked best. It cut irritation sharply while keeping the drug action. Safety tests for acute toxicity and skin sensitivity were also run on the chosen gel.
pmc-11678831:
Giannotta, Ruggiero, and Trabacca tie kids' brain ills to body clock faults in this twenty twenty-four review. Clock slips show in head pain, fits, and mind ills of the young. Sleep woes, mood swings, and dull wit track those slips with care.

Inside, three search banks gave the team near ninety works for the pool. Sleep gland and stress gland flows ran off-beat in most ills they read. Clock gene shifts tied to fit counts and fit clocks in one ill. Sleep pills, light care, and act drills each eased clock drift in trials. The team backs clock-fit care as part of ward plans for kids.
pmc-11678931:
Heat slows the legs of top-flight footballers, in plain counts. Vladimir Pavlinovic, Ryland Morgans, and Toni Modric read every Champions League match of one season in 2024, one hundred twenty-five games tracked by camera. Games were binned by the air's heat at kickoff, from near frost to warm. The catalog adds a fourth author the head byline lacks.

In the warm bin, teams ran less ground in whole than in the cool bins. Fast running and hard bursts fell most, against every cooler bin. Even flat-out sprints shrank against one cool bin. The drops held across thirty-two teams, so shape and squad do not explain them. The team urge heat plans in fixture lists and in-match cooling for the warm months.
pmc-11679131:
Metal exposure is widespread, but its link to osteoporosis in the general population is thinly documented. Jianing Liu and Kai Wang mined the United States NHANES survey from 1999 to 2020, covering 15,923 participants with urine measures of nine metals. Bone status came from dual-energy X-ray scans. They combined weighted quantile sum regression with clustering to weigh each metal's role and to split people into high and low exposure groups.

Cadmium stood out as a clear risk factor, with an odds ratio of 1.19 and two thirds of the mixture weight. Lead mattered most for 30 to 49 year olds and Mexican American participants, and antimony for Black participants. The high-exposure cluster had 1.74 times the osteoporosis odds and higher cumulative mortality. The authors conclude urinary metals track both osteoporosis risk and prognosis.
pmc-11679431:
Zhirui Zhao and co-authors present a 2024 study of a smart control method for a soft elbow exoskeleton used in rehab. Air driven muscles power the device, which helps patients bend and stretch the elbow. Classic control leaves high contact torque and shaky accuracy when loads shift.

Their method blends fuzzy logic that tunes resistance on the fly with a step back design for the control law. A repeat learning loop and an adaptive layer sharpen position accuracy under shifting loads. Tests in simulation and in a live elbow task beat two rival methods. Tracking error fell by about a fifth against a standard method. Contact torque at rest fell by near half. The authors see use in other soft robots.
pmc-11679531:
Marta Siewert and co-authors published this clinical study in 2024. It compares ways of washing out the jaw joint, a treatment for painful jaw problems. The wash can be done with one needle or two, and doctors sometimes add a healing substance into the joint at the same visit.

Ninety-six patients took part, half with worn joint surfaces and half with a slipped disc inside the joint. Care was repeated monthly for six months. All groups had less pain and could open their mouths wider. The one-needle method matched the two-needle method on pain and did better on mouth opening. Patients with a slipped disc gained more opening than those with worn surfaces. Added substances cut pain further, and one of them helped opening most.
pmc-11679831:
Ping Li and six co-authors work out what one cutter gene does in the wheat-blight fungus. Their study, from two thousand twenty-four, knocks the gene out and puts it back.

The cutter class at stake helps plants grow, and helps germs fell their hosts. The blight germ is the chief cause of the wheat ill. But its cutters' roles were dim. One gene bore the class marks: a kept core form and a tag that sends it out of the cell. The team named it for its class. Out-and-back strains were built. Their growth, spread, and host harm were read twixt the wild and the changed.
pmc-11680031:
Levente Víg and a team of co-authors built a brain implant that releases compounds on a flash of light in a 2024 paper. The device starts as a soft electrode sheet that records brain activity. Into its surface they set upconverting nanoparticles, crystals that turn near-infrared light into visible light inside tissue.

That visible light triggers chemical uncaging, freeing small amounts of a model dye right at the implant. The electrodes still record the brain's response at the same time. The paper works through the hard parts: coating the particles, fixing them to the silicone, and proving they stay put in dish and animal tests. The authors show the implant's electrical function survives the upgrade.
pmc-11680231:
Hosameldeen Mohamed Husien and co-authors review molecular tools in farm animal diversity and breeding. Chip tests read hundreds of thousands of DNA markers. They can find single-letter variants, genes of interest, marks of past selection, and the DNA regions tied to traits farmers care about.

These data power genomic selection. A reference group of animals, with both DNA and trait records, is used to learn each marker's effect. Any young animal's breeding worth can then be estimated from DNA alone. The gains are largest for traits that are sex-limited, weakly inherited, or measured late in life, and faster turnover cuts the gap between generations. The review traces the tools from older markers to high-density chips and sequencing. It weighs what they have done for farm stock: faster genetic gain with less guesswork, and a clearer record of diversity.
pmc-11683731:
Hamilton and coauthors map yak head tissue to guide humane bolt stunning. Yaks give meat, fiber, and transport in many lands. Yak meat sales grow in the United States as a lean choice. Bolt stunning is approved for cattle before slaughter.

No peer-checked guide for yak bolt sites existed before this work. The team used ten cadaver heads from young male yaks. Source yaks were aged two to four years. They located the thalamus, a brain part key for feeling. Tissue depth at the best bolt site was gauged. Their guide aims for fast, humane stunning in practice.
pmc-11685331:
Toshihiko Matsuo, Yoshitaka Iwamoto, Hironori Okamoto, and Daisuke Iguchi report an unusual infection case, in a paper published in 2024. Their patient was a seventy-four-year-old woman. Her heart valve infection appears to have started in her sinus and eye socket. Half a year before falling ill, scans for a stroke showed a tangle of abnormal veins behind her right eye. No sinus trouble was noted then.

She arrived with two days of fatigue and appetite loss. Her right eye bulged, and inflammation markers were very high, but she had no fever. Scans now showed sinus infection and a mass where the vein tangle sat. A blood germ known for deep infections grew in culture. Brain scans showed small stroke spots, fitting valve infection spread. A long course of penicillin cured her, and the bulge receded.
pmc-11686531:
Dominik Spuehler and colleagues ran a cadaver study in 2024 after a puzzling hip case. A patient had a failed hip replacement removed for infection. No new joint could be fitted, so the hip stayed without one. That salvage surgery is called a Girdlestone procedure. The patient later showed partial paralysis of the thigh muscle. The team asked how the surgery shifts anatomy near the femoral nerve. They dissected the nerve in eight cadaver pelvis halves.

The team then performed the surgery on the specimens. They loaded the leg and recorded how the thigh bone moved. The bone shifted up, back, and sideways, and it rotated outward. Those shifts pulled on the outer branch of the femoral nerve. Entry points of nerve branches into muscles moved by varied amounts. The authors link that stress to poor function after surgery. They urge care for the nerve during this salvage operation.
pmc-11688331:
Village chickens in South Africa are a valued farm resource: they ease poverty and supply protein. But climate change and demand for high-performing exotic breeds put these locally adapted birds at risk. The four authors genotyped 244 village chickens from districts in Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal, plus conservation and reference flocks, with a 60K chip. They assessed risk status, signs of adaptation, and where the birds would suit the environment.

Effective population sizes in village flocks ranged from 18 to 53 twelve generations back. Genetic analysis split the birds into five clusters, with some breeds apart from village stock. The team found 386 outlier markers tied to ten environmental variables. Niche modeling showed some village birds fit only a narrow home area, while others from one village fit a broad range, with elevation and a cold-month measure as key drivers. The results can guide conservation and breeding choices.
pmc-11689331:
Jeremy Lim-Soh and co-authors chart how social support changes over time for family caregivers of older adults. Support is known to shape caregiver burden and depression, yet few studies treat support itself as something that rises or falls. The team followed 278 Singaporean caregivers of adults aged 75 and older who needed help with daily living, interviewing them up to four times over two years.

Using group-based trajectory modeling, the team found five distinct paths of perceived support. Three paths were stable and covered 91 percent of caregivers. Two paths declined, covering the remaining 9 percent. Psychological resilience went together with higher support only along the stable paths. The authors say most caregivers hold steady support, but a minority lose it. They call for work on why that decline happens and for programs aimed at the caregivers most at risk of isolation.
pmc-11690631:
