Frances Yang, Maria Roche-Dean, and Kristine Williams shrink a caregiver well-being survey into a shorter, sound measure, in a research paper from 2024. Long surveys tire respondents, yet well-being has many facets. The team worked with a national caregiving study's seventeen well-being questions.

Using answers from 2,376 caregivers, they tested the questions' structure two ways. Twelve questions formed a strong short scale with three facets. One facet covers positive mood, one covers isolation, and one covers inner distress. The short form keeps high reliability while cutting burden. Survey teams can now gauge caregiver well-being with fewer questions and still trust the scores.
pmc-11691531:
Lacey DiFranco and four co-authors shared a poster in 2024 on an online training course that prepares older adult volunteers to lead music activity programs for people living with dementia. Music interventions are strongly supported as a way to treat dementia symptoms. The program described uses older volunteers as session leaders, addressing both staff shortages in residential care and the need for engaging social activities.

The team developed two prototype versions of the course. They tested them with twenty-five older volunteers and twenty-five long-term care staff across seven focus groups. Both groups requested training modules on responding to challenging behaviors, on communication barriers, and on the facts of dementia. They liked the self-paced format and interactive online tools. Some were hesitant about technology-based training, and many wanted additional printed materials. The findings now shape the full course.
pmc-11692231:
Namhee Kim and four co-authors published a review and meta-analysis in 2024 on exercise performed with music for frail older adults. Earlier research suggested that music could add to the benefits of exercise, but the full picture across physical and emotional health had not been brought together.

The reviewers searched seven databases and kept seventeen studies, most of them randomized controlled trials. Pooling the results showed that exercise with music reduced frailty and depression. It also improved results on a timed walking test and increased handgrip strength. The authors conclude that, by helping both body and mood, exercise with music could improve quality of life and reduce the burden of frailty. They describe it as a strong option for older adults who live at home in the community.
pmc-11692431:
Ana Clara Costa Pinaffi da Langley and co-authors run a pilot study of time-restricted eating in healthy older adults, in work published in 2024. Eating within a daily window is a gentler alternative to strict calorie cuts and has shown heart and metabolic benefits. Its effect on brain blood flow in older adults was unknown.

Six women completed six months of a daily fourteen-hour fast. The team measured how well brain vessels respond to mental tasks, using near-infrared light sensors, and profiled blood metabolites. Vessel responses in the front of the brain rose clearly after the programme. Levels of several metabolites tied to vascular health and anti-inflammatory action also rose. The sample was tiny, so the authors frame the work as a pilot. Larger trials would be needed to confirm the brain benefit.
pmc-11693031:
Mineko Wada and Kazuya Takeda interview Japanese older adults about living through the government's push toward a digital society. Their study came out in 2024. The national slogan promises that no one will be left behind, but older users' own views were little known.

Eighteen community-dwelling adults described both gains and grievances. They disliked the dehumanization of services, feared surveillance through digitized personal data, and worried about scams and fraud. Help with digital problems was hard to reach when they needed it. Against that, they valued wider social connection and entertainment. The authors urge planners to fund immediate, human support for digital adaptation, since literacy gaps, not resistance, drive most of the negative views.
pmc-11693131:
Lingming Chen and colleagues compared the social lives and mental health of older Chinese Americans and White Americans in 2024. Research on healthy aging among Asian Americans is rare, leaving gaps in what services assume. The study enrolled over five hundred community-dwelling adults aged sixty-five to ninety-five in Massachusetts, about a fifth of them Chinese. Participants completed a lifestyle questionnaire covering social activity and support.

Mental health was measured with standard scales for depressive symptoms, anxiety, perceived stress, and resilience. Regression models adjusted for age, gender, self-rated health, activity, pain, and living alone to isolate ethnic differences. The comparison matters because social connection protects mental health in old age, and immigrant elders may maintain it differently. Findings like these can guide culturally aware outreach instead of one-size programs.
pmc-11696431:
Emiliano Isaías Alanís-Manzano and four co-authors simulate how water wraps around rare earth ions. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, runs moving-atom models at room heat. Five ions from the lanthanide group are tested, from light to heavy. The first shell of water around each ion is hard to pin down, yet it shapes how the ions act in solution.

The team places up to twenty-seven water molecules around each ion in the model. A modern calculation method gives a good mix of accuracy and speed. It matches known ion-to-water distances very closely. The shells prove restless, with waters swapping in and out fast. Preferred shell sizes differ by ion, as bulk data suggest.
pmc-11697331:
Kurumi Mori, Takaichi Watanabe, and Tsutomu Ono published a 2024 study of a way to make plant-based particles that are not round. Off-round particles have a large surface for their size, which suits drug delivery, catalyst work, and absorption tasks. Old ways to make them have limits. The method of the team uses a chip with flows, a microfluidic device, where droplets shrink in a bath.

One number rules the story: the race between spread within the droplet and the shrinkage of the droplet. When the shrinkage wins, a stiff layer forms at the face of the droplet. That layer then buckles as the droplet fades, and off-round shapes come out: bowls and double dips. The team varied the flow mix and the bath composition to steer the number. Films of the droplets caught the birth of the layer and the bending in the act.
pmc-11704431:
Varshney and co-authors review 172 patients treated for meningioma, the most common primary brain tumor. The study covers patients seen at a medical university hospital in India from 2010 to 2019. The team looked at symptoms, scan findings, and outcomes after treatment. They tracked function, complications, deaths, and how long patients stayed free of recurrence.

Most patients were in their forties or fifties at presentation. The average tumor measured about 36 millimeters across. About three quarters of tumors sat away from the skull base. Tumors came back in 11 patients, on average about 55 months after surgery. Most patients kept good function, the authors report.
pmc-11706531: Yuichiro Yokoyama and co-authors report surgery on a heart tumor that burst through the heart wall in this 2024 case. A man of sixty-one arrived with fluid crushing the heart. The cause was a rare cancer invading the right atrial wall. The tumor had spread across the free wall of that chamber. Surgeons removed it while a bypass machine ran his circulation. They rebuilt the wall with patches from his own tissue and cattle tissue. Wall rupture from this cancer is rare; the paper reviews earlier cases.
pmc-11706731:
Young-Min Han and seven co-authors published an animal study in twenty twenty-four on Hongjam, a steamed, freeze-dried silkworm powder, against liver cancer in mice. Liver cancer usually grows out of chronic injury and inflammation and still has a grim outlook. The team tested whether the traditional food could protect the liver and slow tumors.

Mice received two cancer-causing chemicals over seventeen weeks, with Hongjam mixed into food at three doses. Treated mice developed fewer and smaller tumors with milder tissue damage. Blood markers of liver injury fell, notably bilirubin. Tumor tissue showed lower proliferation signals and more of a cell-death protein. The powder acted on both sides: less growth, more cancer cell suicide.
pmc-11709531:
Marcos Schaan Profes and three co-authors describe a 2025 lab study on tau, a protein that builds up in Alzheimer disease and related illnesses. The team built a cell system that uses light to switch tau clumping on and off. The system uses a light-sensitive protein called CRY2 joined to tau, which lets the team control when and where clumps form.

Cells grown in dishes formed stable tau clumps after light exposure, and the clumps carried marks seen in Alzheimer disease. Tests confirmed large tau clusters, and live imaging showed that different forms of tau clumped at different speeds. The authors argue the tool can speed the search for drugs that slow tau clumping.
pmc-11709631:
Jeffrey Motter and co-authors ask, in 2025, the reverse of the usual dementia question: if older adults score intact on simple tests, how safe are they really? The team used a large aging study cohort of six hundred forty-seven people without dementia. Each person took a smell test and a short memory test, and most also had a brain scan for amyloid.

Over about eleven years, roughly ninety-five percent never developed dementia. Those intact on both simple tests stayed dementia-free in over ninety-eight percent of cases. The authors compare that reassurance with the scan's accuracy and with combinations, aiming at cheap first-line screening.
pmc-11710531:
Zikun Yang and co-authors describe a 2025 study of gene activity in brains from people of three ethnic groups with Alzheimer disease. Gene control helps shape how the disease starts and grows, yet most past work used one group. The team built a shared gene activity record to compare groups.

They read gene activity in tissue from more than five hundred donor brains across six brain banks. They then checked their findings in a second large study and in single cell data. Some known genes shifted in all groups, while heat shock genes stood out most. Two genes led in the Hispanic group alone. The authors stress that broad samples change what studies find.
pmc-11712131:
Patra Blekou and co-authors describe a guided park walk program for people with dementia in a 2025 report from Greece. Greece counts about 160,000 people living with dementia and far more family carers. Lockdown years cut social contact and mood for many of them. Alzheimer Athens and a large cultural center in Athens built the walk to respond.

Once a month, two health workers lead a ninety-minute tour through the Stavros Niarchos Park. Walkers explore the garden's trees, shrubs, and scented Greek plants, then view an art display. The walk ends with paired tasks that use what the tour covered. About twenty-five people join each walk, and more than three hundred have taken part since January 2023.
pmc-11712431:
Mahnaz Shekari and co-authors test how blood and spinal fluid markers match tau scans in a 2025 study of early Alzheimer's disease. Fluid tests are cheap and easy, but their link to tau tangles in the earliest stage was not well mapped. The team studied ninety-nine adults with no symptoms from the ALFA+ cohort in Spain.

Each person had two kinds of PET scan, MRI, thinking tests, and fluid samples. Only nine people showed tau in the earliest brain regions. Fluid tau markers rose with scan tau in those regions, with one marker, ptau217, tracking best in both spinal fluid and plasma. Two people broke the expected spread order. The authors say fluid tests can help flag who needs a tau scan in prevention work.
pmc-11712731:
Jack Lei Yang and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on sex gaps in Alzheimer's disease. The gaps tie to tau protein and to how the memory hub links with the rest of the brain. Women get the disease more often and often fare worse on tests. Earlier work hinted that these links differ by sex and by tau load.

The team scanned twenty patients and twenty healthy adults from a large data bank. People with higher tau in their blood showed unlike link patterns around the memory hub. Among patients with high tau, men and women differed as well. The authors say care may need to be tuned by sex, not just by stage of illness.
pmc-11713331:
Erin Beck and co-authors report results for an AI platform that recruits patients for an Alzheimer's drug trial, in this 2025 paper. Trials for early disease need proof of amyloid in the brain by PET scan, and many hopeful patients fail that step. Better picking before the scan could save time and money.

The platform searches health records in a large data network and matches patients to trial rules. In an ongoing early-stage trial, patients it sent passed the amyloid scan at a rate of sixty-four percent. Other sources reached only twenty-three percent. The authors say sharper matching also cut trial costs by trimming failed scans.
pmc-11713931:
Rashmita Chatterjee and Zahra Moussavi study motion sickness from virtual reality games in people with Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. Virtual worlds can help patients train safe travel skills in a life like setting. The catch is cybersickness, with head pain, nausea, and a lost sense of place.

Their game, Barn Ruins Navigation, was built to cut sickness. It keeps the view narrow, slows turns, uses a simple stick, and runs on a laptop screen rather than a head set. Thirty adults played it: ten young adults, ten healthy older adults, and ten people with mild to mid disease. All filled in a sickness survey after play. The team compared scores to see if patients felt worse than the other groups.
pmc-11714131:
Anat Marmor and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on cognitive reserve in Alzheimer's disease. Reserve is the idea that a well-built mind can hide brain damage for a time, so two people with the same damage may show unlike symptoms.

The team looked back at records for more than six hundred patients over age sixty-five at a memory clinic. They used years of schooling as the mark of reserve. Across the whole group, schooling did not track the age at diagnosis. Within the better-schooled group, though, more schooling did mean a later diagnosis. In both groups, more schooling went with faster decline once the disease showed. The authors say the reserve effect is not a straight line. Care and testing plans should fit each group's pattern, they argue.
pmc-11714331:
Sapir Golan and thirteen co-authors link belly fat stores to thinking scores and brain size in midlife adults at high risk of Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. Body mass alone hides where fat sits. The team split fat into liver, pancreas, deep belly, and under skin stores.

The study held 204 healthy adults, mean age near sixty, whose parents had the disease. Belly scans measured each fat store, and tests scored thinking and brain size. More liver fat went with less gray matter overall. In men only, more pancreas fat went with weaker thinking and memory scores. Deep and surface belly fat both linked to smaller frontal areas in both sexes. The authors say fat place, not just amount, matters.
pmc-11714831:
Ingryd Mayara Nascimento Martins-Pais and co-authors examine a 2025 study of exercise and thinking skills in older adults in Brazil. Their data came from a long study of aging that included more than nine thousand adults aged fifty or more. Tests covered memory, sense of date and time, and naming words. People also reported how much moderate and hard exercise they did each week.

After some records were set aside, just under eight thousand people remained in the study. Those who did at least the advised amount of moderate exercise scored better on thinking tests overall. Doing far more than that amount was also linked to better scores. Hard exercise, by contrast, showed no clear link to test scores in this group. The authors note that moderate weekly activity may help protect the aging brain.
pmc-11715131:
Amy Packer and co-authors asked whether the caps on the ends of chromosomes help explain who gains from exercise. The caps, called telomeres, wear down as cells age and split. The parent trial tested weight training in folk whose thought loss stems from small vessel harm in the brain. This side study read cap length in blood cells across the trial year.

Ninety-one adults aged fifty-five and up with mild thought loss took part. Half trained with weights twice a week, and half did balance and tone work. Cap length was read at the start, at six months, and at the year's end. The lab reads proved steady when the same sample was run twice. The team will now set cap length and its change next to gains in thought and brain scans.
pmc-11715631:
Ashleigh S Vella and a large group of co-authors report worldwide rates of new dementia cases for the COSMIC collaboration in 2025. COSMIC joins cohort studies of memory from many countries into one shared pool. The team set out to give fair incidence rates by age and sex for rich and poor countries alike. Past global rates leaned too heavily on high-income countries, where diagnostic methods also differ.

The pool drew on 36 member studies in 28 countries on six continents. Rates rose steeply with age in all countries, for men and women. In most countries the sexes matched at younger ages, while older women often had higher rates than older men. The team reads the gaps between countries as real, not just a quirk of diagnostic methods. Work continues to add more studies and to align rates where no group diagnosis was made.
pmc-11715931:
Bao Hoang and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on spotting mild cognitive impairment from talk and face cues. Mild impairment is an early stage on the way to dementia, and catching it early helps both care and trials.

The team used more than three thousand recorded chats with sixty-nine older adults from an online social trial. They pulled features from word choice, sentence build, and reply length. They also read seven basic emotions from face images. A key snag is that each person's style swamps the disease signal. Their fix, called subject harmonization, strips out person-specific patterns. With that fix on the language data, detection improved. Mixing the emotion data in needed more care. The authors say such low-cost digital signs could aid early screening.
pmc-11716231:
Paola Filigrana and co-authors trace how money and schooling across a lifetime shape later thinking skills, in a 2025 paper on Hispanic and Latino adults. Hardship early in life has been linked to memory problems in old age. The team wanted to know whether position in childhood, midlife, or both predicted how fast cognition changed. Their data came from a large community study of Latinos in the United States.

The study followed 6,351 adults aged forty-five to seventy-four, with a second round of testing about seven years later. Childhood position came from parents' schooling, while midlife position combined schooling, income, job, and assets. People who moved up in life were compared with those who stayed low or stayed high. Higher midlife standing was tied to a slower drop in test scores over the follow-up years.
pmc-11721431:
Stef Jacobs and co-authors review how experimental evolution can reveal drug resistance in disease-causing fungi. Their 2024 paper notes that resistance insights guide strategy, yet fungi remain understudied next to bacteria. Growing fungal populations under drug pressure in the lab lets researchers watch resistance emerge rather than infer it afterward.

The review stresses the method's range: lab setups can mirror both clinic and environment, the two arenas where resistance forms. The authors also argue for adding evolutionary modeling to sharpen what the experiments mean. Lessons from bacteriology and fresh work in mycology anchor the case. A wider use of these methods could help medicine stay ahead of resistant fungal infections, a growing threat to patients with weak immunity.
pmc-11723531:
Samad Raza and co-authors report twenty years of results for a rare heart valve repair, in a study whose head dates to 2024. The tricuspid valve sits on the right side of the heart, and bad leaks there are hard to fix. Their hospital used donor valve tissue to replace part of the valve rather than all of it.

Fourteen patients took part, from a newborn to a man or woman in their seventies. Most had birth defects of the valve, and the rest had valve infection. After a median follow-up of seventeen years, most lived free of severe leaks. Few needed a second operation. The results support the partial approach as a lasting option.
pmc-11726831:
Florian Neukart, Reuben Brasher, and Eike Marx propose the quantum memory matrix as a unified answer to the black hole information paradox, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The paradox pits quantum unitarity against Hawking radiation that seems to erase information. Their hypothesis makes space-time itself a quantum information reservoir.

Quantum imprints at the Planck scale would store state details directly in the fabric of space-time. A quantized model with clear encoding and retrieval rules is built out. The combined math keeps unitarity intact. Contrasts with holography, complementarity, and loop gravity are drawn. Observable hints, like slight deviations in Hawking heat, close the case.
pmc-11728231:
Ana Gil-Villalba and colleagues published a medical study in 2024 on laser treatment for vulvar lichen sclerosus. The condition is a long-lasting inflammation of the genital skin. It mainly affects women after menopause and can scar and cause pain. Strong steroid creams are the standard treatment, but some cases resist them.

The study followed seventy-five women whose disease had resisted standard care. Each received four sessions of fractional carbon dioxide laser treatment. Most women completed the full course. Itching, pain, and painful intercourse all dropped clearly afterward. Quality of life and sexual function scores improved as well. The authors present the laser as a short-term option for stubborn cases.
pmc-11737431:
Sunga and five co-authors report surgical management of three heart problems at once, in work from twenty twenty-four. The rare mix holds a thickened heart muscle disease with outflow blockage, a flail mitral valve leaking severely, and severe lung hypertension of both types.

Lung hypertension alone predicts higher death in this muscle disease when managed with drugs, and often rules out surgery. The case details how the surgical team planned and carried out treatment despite that risk. Reports like this give other centers a reference when the same triple threat appears and no guideline covers the combination.
pmc-11740031:
Wang, Yang, Gao, Xu, and Gao test blood inflammatory ratios as predictors of hospital death in severe COPD flare with respiratory failure, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Flare plus respiratory failure sharply raises mortality in COPD. Simple blood ratios may flag high-risk patients early on admission. Data come from the MIMIC four intensive care database.

Over twelve hundred patients yield a hospital mortality near six percent. Neutrophil and nutrition indices show nonlinear links to mortality with clear inflection points. A glucose ratio also predicts higher mortality after adjustment. Three other indices show no significant association in this cohort. Neutrophil ratio edges out rivals on predictive accuracy, though all are moderate.
pmc-11745031:
Maria Chiara Bazzini and ten co-authors present a 2024 study of how young children plan a reach and grasp task. In a planned act, the end goal shapes each step before it, like notes in a tune. The team asked whether this chain-like planning looks the same in autistic children and their siblings.

Three groups of preschool children took part: autistic children, their non-autistic siblings, and other young children. Each child reached for an object and placed it in boxes of two widths. Typical children changed both reach and place times to fit the box. Both other groups changed mainly the last step, which hints that early signs may run in families.
pmc-11751631:
Andre C Faubert and Shang Wang present a free viewer for huge time-lapse microscope image sets, in a paper the head dates to 2024. Three-dimensional imaging over time is basic to biology research. Such data can reach terabytes in size. Most viewers cannot mix volumes with different voxel counts, data types, and imaging modes in one timeline. Their tool, Open Chrono-Morph Viewer, fills that gap.

The viewer uses a simple interface for quick inspection. Volumes are stored as separate files in a common format, easing tool chains. Movable clipping surfaces let users slice into shapes fast. A scriptable animation feature supports repeatable, publication-grade visuals. The code is pure Python built on common libraries. That choice invites community contributions. Versions run on the three main desktop systems. Tutorials and a converter plugin come with the release.
pmc-11771831:
Almadani and co-authors survey emergency doctors in Saudi Arabia on barriers to urgent care for children. Many emergency rooms lack child-sized tools and staff trained for young patients. Those gaps put children at real risk during emergencies.

The survey ran from March 2023 to January 2024 and drew 197 of 214 doctors, a 92 point 1 percent response rate. Junior residents made up 40.1 percent of those who replied. The top barriers were finding the right drug dose, at 20.8 percent, and dealing with parents, at 19.8 percent. Doctors also rated their confidence in child care. Fewer than half of the doctors felt sure of their child care skills.
pmc-11780331:
Yamakawa and co-authors hunt gene spots for potato flesh tint and starch sap marks. Kids of multi-set crops take more than one gene set in birth. That spread blocks spot hunts for farm marks in such crops. It also blocks DNA mark breed work for those marks in fields. A past way, QTL-seq, reads whole gene sets to find such spots. That way pulls lone-copy marks in full for the spot hunt.

Here, twin-copy spots get hunted by bent set picks in the way. Marks are flesh tint and starch sap load in spud tubers. The F1 kids came from a cross of Touya and Benimaru spuds. One Touya spot for gold flesh sat on gene lane 3 in the hunt. A beta part gene sits near that spot in the lane set. One Benimaru spot for low starch sap sat on lane 2.
pmc-11782131:
Wong and co-authors test whether ear-based nerve stimulation is feasible for minority patients with nerve pain in this 2025 study. Peripheral neuropathy, often from chemotherapy or diabetes, lacks good non-drug options. Stimulating the vagus nerve through the ear is a promising candidate.

The project paired a survey with a small sham-controlled pilot trial at the University of Miami. Sixty-two survey respondents, 78 percent of them Black or Hispanic/Latino, reported heavy symptoms. Fully 82 percent expressed interest in the stimulation approach. Recruitment used culturally sensitive methods to include groups often missed by research. The pilot then checked feasibility, acceptability, and early effects in Black and Hispanic/Latino patients directly.
pmc-11782231:
Microscopic worms that attack plant roots cost farmers dearly, and the chemical poisons used on them face growing bans. In this 2024 review, Prabhakaran Vasantha-Srinivasan and co-authors survey a living alternative: bacteria of the Bacillus genus. These common soil bacteria attack root-knot and cyst nematodes on several fronts at once.

They seep compounds that kill the worms, chew through their outer skin, and switch on the plant's own defenses from inside. Beyond killing pests, the bacteria enrich soil life and help nutrients cycle, which chemical treatments do not. The authors propose folding Bacillus products into integrated pest plans rather than swapping one silver bullet for another. The goal is harvests protected with the soil left healthier.
pmc-11805031:
Manish Shrigiriwar and co-authors published a research paper in 2024 on how oral health shapes quality of life for prisoners in a central jail in India's Vidarbha region. Prisoners are a neglected group for dental care. The team examined 440 male inmates and gave them a fourteen-item survey on the daily impact of mouth problems.

Average impact scores sat in the middle of the scale. Of the seven life areas asked about, psychological discomfort scored worst, while limits on daily function scored least. Tooth decay counts were taken alongside the survey. The authors say the findings can guide dental programs inside prisons, where check-ups also raise awareness of mouth care.
pmc-11810931:
Yang and a large team develop a rapid test for three calf diarrhoea viruses in twenty twenty-five. Viral calf diarrhoea causes high illness and death rates in cattle worldwide. Symptoms of the three viruses overlap, so lab tests must tell them apart. The team built a one step multiplex PCR test for that purpose.

Primers and probes target a distinct gene region in each virus. The test detects as few as twenty-four copies per millilitre for each pathogen. Repeat runs varied by less than one point five percent. Eighty faecal samples from Shanghai farms checked against standard methods agreed well. One virus, bovine kobuvirus, was the most common find. All three viruses were reported in the region for the first time.
pmc-11888731:
Khansa Taha Ababneh and three co-authors report a case from twenty twenty-four. Their patient was a young man with sore gums, heavy tartar, and teeth he did not like. He also used a drug for acne at the time.

Care began with deep cleaning so the team could see the mouth well. Tests showed wide gum disease, loose roots, bad bite, and some bone loss. The team taught home care, cleaned the roots, and set a long plan. At a later check, plaque and bleeding had fallen a lot. The case shows why early gum care helps later tooth work.
pmc-11892431:
Su-Been Yang and a team of co-authors improve an enzyme used to build drug-like nucleosides, in two thousand twenty-four. The enzyme swaps bases between building blocks and is handy for making nucleoside analogs. It works well on natural targets but poorly on a fluorinated one used for therapeutic strands.

Starting from a known improved mutant, the team ran two rounds of random mutation and screening. Two new mutants showed higher activity on the fluorinated target. A combined mutant beat the wild type by a wide margin, above all at higher heat. Tests pinned down which change aided heat stability and which aided binding and speed. The authors offer the mutants as efficient catalysts.
pmc-11931331:
Badri Rijal and eight co-authors review five years of spinal disorders at Nepal's National Trauma Center. Their observational study was published in twenty twenty-four. Spinal injuries disable heavily and cluster in poorer countries, where data are scarce.

Of nearly twenty-one thousand patients, about one in ten had a spinal injury. The typical patient was forty-three years old, and two-thirds were men. Falls caused nearly six in ten cases, ahead of road crashes. The median stay ran twelve days. The profile points prevention squarely at falls from height, a known hazard in Nepali building and farm work, and sizes the burden for planners.
pmc-11959131:
Nine cancer experts from Latin America, led by Anelisa Coutinho, set out shared guidance in 2024 for treating a hard form of colon and rectal cancer. The cancer has spread and carries a mutation called BRAF-V600E. Targeted drugs can help these patients, yet testing and treatment vary widely across the region.

Convened by the Americas Health Foundation, the panel reviewed how the mutation is tested, how cases are diagnosed, and what care patients receive. They call for local guidelines, team-based tumor boards, and routine gene testing of tumors. The group also gives advice on first treatments, later treatments, and surgery after diagnosis, aiming to close gaps in care across Latin America.
pmc-12021531:
Donghoon Kang and five co-authors study two cell markers in stomach cancer in this two thousand twenty-three paper. The markers, ABCG2 and CD133, are linked to cancer stem cells. In many tumors, high levels of such markers go with worse outcomes. Whether that holds for stomach cancer was unclear. The team measured both markers in tumor samples from four hundred fifty-nine patients.

All patients had surgery to remove their stomach tumors. The team stained the samples and scored marker levels by strength. They then compared levels with how patients fared after surgery. The goal was to learn whether these markers can flag high-risk patients. Such flags could guide closer follow-up or added therapy. The paper adds data to a mixed field on stem cell markers and prognosis.
pmc-12052431:
Jasmine Veitch, Jeff Bowman, Dawson Ketchen, and Albrecht Schulte-Hostedde study how three skin parasites share North American red squirrels. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Parasite links, host traits, and site facts can all shape who meets whom on a host. One mite and two flea kinds were taped on these squirrels.

Once host and site facts were weighed, pair links read as chance. Yet the mite split its ties by flea kind, one down and one up, and those ties hung on time trends. The team reads time of year, not germ war, as the driver here. Heat, rain, and damp tests are urged next.
pmc-12097431:
Tin Zar Tun, Kaung Myat Thwin, Sachiko Takehara, and Hiroshi Ogawa measure a mouth exercise skill in older Japanese dental patients, in a 2024 study. The skill is repeating syllables like pa, ta, and ka as fast as possible. It reflects tongue and lip function. The team tested one hundred twenty-seven outpatients aged sixty-five and over. They also measured tongue pressure, chewing skill, and swallowing.

Interviews covered social ties, mood, and thinking ability. Average repeat rates sat near six per second. Two syllables slowed with age, as did tongue pressure. One syllable's rate tied to remaining teeth. Another tied to tongue pressure, chewing, and swallowing trouble. Social engagement and sex also showed links in early analysis. The authors say this quick test reflects wider oral health. Adding it to routine dental checks deserves study. Keeping the mouth strong supports eating and quality of life.
pmc-12312731:
Lingxue Tang and Tong Wang present a study of a gene risk model for lung adenocarcinoma, a common and varied lung cancer. The head of the text dates the work to 2024. Fatty acid metabolism has emerged as a key driver of this cancer's growth, so its genes may hold forecast value.

The team mined a cancer atlas for fat metabolism genes whose activity splits by outcome. A shrink method picked a set of genes for a risk score. Patients with low scores lived longer than those with high scores. High risk tumors carried more mutations and looked more apt to gain from immune therapy. A second data set backed the model's accuracy. The authors name the score genes as possible care targets.
pmc-12599531:
Andrea Rodil, Jan Deska, and Martin Prechtl wrote a tutorial in 2025 on formaldehyde as a one-carbon building block for a fossil-free future. Formaldehyde and stand-in chemicals for it sit at the centre of many reaction networks, in both factories and living cells. The tutorial introduces researchers and students to that chemistry and its wider promise.

Uses covered include storing renewable energy in liquid hydrogen carriers, making renewable fuels, capturing and reusing carbon, and upgrading biomass. Related small molecules such as methane, methanol, and formic acid enter the discussion too. New catalytic strategies for using this abundant block are the practical core for readers planning greener synthesis.
pmc-12660931:
Hongxin Cheng and co-authors show that pulsed electromagnetic fields slow artery plaque growth in mice, in a 2025 study. Plaque buildup underlies most heart and brain vessel disease. Standard drugs and stents carry side effects or limits. The fields are noninvasive and calm inflammation. The team used mice bred to develop plaques. Some lacked a key inflammation switch gene. Human vessel cells and patient blood samples joined the work.

Inflammatory cell death, called pyroptosis, marked disease progress. The fields suppressed the inflammasome that drives it. Plaque formation shrank and progression slowed. Blood protein scans showed the same death signals raised in patients. Membrane proteins changed most clearly. The mechanism runs through membrane tension. Fields tune a tension-sensing channel, easing cell power failure. Less death of vessel lining cells followed. The authors offer a new physical route against plaque disease.
pmc-12679731:
Gaia Marcolli and co-authors test whether fluid from human dental stem cells helps wounds heal in leeches, in this 2025 paper. Slow-healing wounds plague aging populations, and stem cell fluids have shown repair potential. The medicinal leech offers a clean living model with well-mapped healing biology.

Leeches were cut surgically and treated with either the stem cell fluid or a plain control. Tissue was checked at two days, three days, and one week. Shape, staining, and gene tests tracked new vessel growth and repair. The study asks whether the human fluid speeds the leech's own regeneration, a hint for wound therapies.
pmc-12685731:
Kowalewska and co-authors trace how high blood lipids harm brain blood vessels, from cells to whole animals. Lipid problems weaken how small arteries widen, in part by changing ion channels. The team focused on one potassium channel, Kir2.1, in the brain's vessels.

Tests moved from single cells to isolated arteries to live mice imaged by MRI. Two mouse models with lipid problems showed a sharp drop in channel activity in vessel lining cells. Removing cholesterol from cell membranes restored that activity. Flow-driven widening also fell in brain arteries, matching the cell-level defect.
pmc-12686531:
Md Ashraful Haque and nine co-authors published this engineering paper in 2025. It presents a small antenna built for future 6G wireless links, which will use very high terahertz waves. The design has two elements, a graphene patch, and a four-leaf slot shape cut into it.

The antenna is tuned to a center frequency in the terahertz band and works across a wide span of nearby frequencies. In tests it showed strong gain, high output, and very little signal leaking between its two ports. The authors also built a simple circuit model that matched their full simulations. Machine learning methods helped them search design settings faster and fine-tune the result. They suggest the antenna could serve fast data links, medical imaging, and fine sensing tasks.
pmc-12687531:
Barrios and colleagues show in twenty twenty-five that removing eraser enzymes for one histone mark rewires stress genes in fission yeast. Histone marks tag the spools DNA wraps on, guiding which genes switch on. Two erasers strip one such mark, and cells missing either eraser resist oxidative stress because their stress genes run hotter, even at rest.

The two erasers work in different gene zones: one at start sites within an activating complex, the other along gene bodies. Both losses raise related marks and loosen chromatin before stress hits. One loss still needs a partner complex for resistance, while the other does not. The authors map how mark crosstalk times gene activation.
pmc-12689631:
Fast and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a genome editing method that selects edited cells without marker genes. Editors usually add drug resistance or glow markers to find edited cells. Those markers can disturb cells and fail for single-letter edits. Their method, SNIPE, selects by the DNA sequence itself. It enriches precisely edited cells about sevenfold on median. The team validated it across forty-two edits in varied cell types and species.

They used it to restore ancestral gene letters seen in Neandertals and Denisovans. Modern humans carry changed versions at those sites. The method also killed cultured tumor cells with abnormal genotypes. It repaired a disease-causing mutation carried on one gene copy. Marker-free selection widens what precision editing can attempt, the authors argue.
pmc-12695931:
Felix Schreyer leads a team on moving the EU from net zero to zero fossil. Their study from twenty twenty-five uses an integrated assessment model. The EU climate goal needs a strong cut in fossil fuel use.

If a full phase out is doable or wise was unclear. In the cheapest net zero path, fossil use falls a lot by mid century. Renewables, direct electrification, hydrogen, and biofuels fill most gaps. Hard oil and gas uses persist in chem, flight, and shipping. Swapping them for e-fuels raises cut costs a lot. Extra effort is the core tale.
pmc-12696131:
Praful Nandankar and colleagues build a wireless car charger that thinks, in this engineering study from twenty twenty-five. Plug-free charging for electric cars usually wastes energy when coil alignment or load shifts. Their system links the coils to the internet of things, sensing heat, current, and voltage in real time and adjusting power on the fly.

A small controller chats over a standard messaging protocol, and users can retune coil settings remotely. The team then ran a designed set of trials, varying coil gap, input voltage, and load, and fitted a response surface model to find the sweet spot. Predictions matched measurements within a few percent. At its best the charger hit about ninety-three percent efficiency, beat a fixed design by seven percent, and ran far cooler. Response lag was a tenth of a second. The authors pitch it as a stepping stone to smart-grid charging.
pmc-12698531:
Michael Kamal and co-authors review how cell aging, called senescence, undermines the repair of aging skeletal muscle, in a paper from 2025. Muscle heals through resident stem cells called satellite cells. With age those cells dwindle in number and vigor, and muscle mass and strength fall with them.

Senescent cells have stopped dividing for good and leak a mix of signals that harm their neighbors. The review gathers evidence that such cells blunt the stem cells' work in old muscle. It also covers efforts to clear senescent cells with targeted drugs and so restore repair. The authors weigh what is proven, what is likely, and what a therapy would need to show before use in people.
pmc-12698631:
Arkers Kwan Ching Wong and co-authors ask Hong Kong health workers what it takes to keep telemedicine for diabetes going in this 2025 study. Diabetes is common and costly to manage over years. Video and phone visits could ease routine follow-up in primary care. Real-world use, though, has been uneven and often dropped. The team interviewed staff in a hybrid program at public clinics. Twenty-one professionals shared their experience of running it.

They named what helps, what blocks, and what resources lasting use needs. Front-line views differ from planners' hopes in telling ways. Sustaining a service, not launching it, is the study's focus. The work is qualitative, built on staff interviews. Its lessons apply to other chronic care by video. Hong Kong's public primary care is the setting throughout.
pmc-12698931:
Yongqi An and six co-authors coat vascular stents with platelet membrane, armor borrowed from the blood's own clotting cells. A stent surface must do two opposite things: refuse clots while inviting the vessel lining to grow over it. Membrane coatings worked on nanoparticles but fell apart on full-size devices under flow.

Their fix cross-links the membrane with a green tea compound, epigallocatechin gallate, anchoring vesicles into a stable, uniform layer on many substrates. The coating survived deformation and a month of rinsing with its structure intact. Key membrane proteins, including the don't-eat-me signal CD47 and integrins, stayed functional. In rabbits, coated stents showed much less acute clotting.
pmc-12699831:
Jing Tong and co-authors studied immune cell surfaces in tuberculosis patients in a 2025 paper. Natural killer cells are front-line immune cells that help fight the TB germ. Their surface holds signal parts that can switch them up or down, and TB may shift that balance.

The team compared blood cells from healthy people, people with quiet latent TB, and people with active lung TB. A broad flow test read many surface parts on each killer cell, with and without a dose of TB germ parts. The maps show how active disease reshapes the cell surface. Such shifts could point to new care that frees the cells to fight harder.
pmc-12703131:
Jie Jin, Yan Hu, and Ling Yan Du pool studies to find what forecasts poor outcomes in infections by a drug-proof hospital germ, in a meta-analysis from 2025. The germ resists carbapenem antibiotics, leaving few treatments and high death rates. Knowing who fares worst helps doctors triage care.

Fourteen studies covering 2,250 patients met the bar. Heart disease, kidney injury, shock, pneumonia, and blood cancers each raised the odds of bad outcomes. Kidney injury and shock more than doubled or tripled the risk. Study quality was graded with a standard scale. The authors offer the list as a bedside risk guide for a feared infection.
pmc-12704231:
Teng Wang and nine co-authors present a 2025 study of a gene copy change in multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells. Extra copies of a segment on chromosome 17 are common in this disease. A loss of the same segment is a known bad sign, but the meaning of a gain was murky.

The team reviewed 125 patients treated at one center from 2015 to 2024. A lab test read each patient's chromosome profile. Patients with the gain fared far better than those with the loss: longer time before growth returned, longer before the next treatment, and longer survival. The authors float the gain as a favorable sign.
pmc-12704431:
Luis Suarez Carreon and co-authors present a 2025 case report on a rare stomach cancer. Squamous cell cancer that starts in the stomach makes up under half a percent of stomach tumors. Strict tissue and stain checks are needed to rule out look-alike cancers. The patient is a 30-year-old woman with long anemia and repeated upper gut bleeding. Scans showed a large growth pushing into the pancreas tail and spleen.

Surgeons removed the whole stomach plus parts of pancreas, spleen, and colon. The work began with keyhole surgery and shifted as needed. The tumor's origin stayed indeterminate after checks. Case reports like this guide the next team that meets this rare tumor. They show that wide removal can be done and how the diagnosis is nailed down. Young age makes the case stand out, since stomach cancer usually strikes far older patients.
pmc-12704931:
Arnoldo Brasil Muniz and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five cross-sectional study of sleep apnea risk in socially vulnerable Brazilian children. Blocked nighttime breathing harms growth, learning, and oral health. Its links to mouth-related quality of life in poor communities were untested.

Four hundred schoolchildren aged three to ten took part. Parents completed sleep and oral-health questionnaires while a calibrated examiner recorded decay and bite problems. Statistical models linked apnea risk scores with clinical findings and daily-life impacts. The study maps an under-recognized burden where dental and sleep care rarely meet.
pmc-12708631:
Laurent Monino and seven co-authors compare two ways to build a bypass in the stomach, tested in pigs. Their 2025 study uses an endoscope with ultrasound to join the stomach to the bowel. The join treats a blocked stomach outlet. A metal stent holds the new channel open, though stents can land in the wrong place.

One method feeds the stent over a guide wire; the other works wirelessly in a simpler way. Eleven joins were made in ten living pigs, then followed for twelve weeks. The wireless method scored far better on ease and needed fewer attempts. It also had fewer forced stent mishaps, though the gap was not firm. A rescue move, placing a second stent inside the first, mostly worked.
pmc-12709031:
Yoon and co-authors report real-world results for a targeted leukemia drug in this 2025 multicenter study. Adults whose B-cell leukemia returns or resists treatment face poor odds. Inotuzumab ozogamicin delivers a toxin straight to leukemia cells.

The prospective study followed 100 patients, a quarter with the Philadelphia-positive subtype. Many had relapsed after transplant or after another modern therapy. After one cycle, 60 percent reached complete remission or remission with partial blood recovery. The best response rate after two cycles was 67 percent, and 63.1 percent cleared measurable residual disease. Thirty-nine responders went on to transplant. The authors also catalog the drug's side effects in everyday practice.
pmc-12709131:
Weibing Yang and nine co-authors shared a study in twenty twenty-five. They measured the true dose of the killer molecule in photodynamic therapy. The punch of the therapy comes from singlet oxygen. Its faint glow can be detected in a direct way. A multispectral luminescence method captures that glow. But to turn glow into dose, the field lacked a standard.

The team worked in a laboratory phantom. A drug formulation was excited by laser at several concentrations. A specialized spectrometer recorded the emission. They benchmarked the luminescence readings against a known method. That method is model-based dosimetry. It computes reacted oxygen from first principles. If the two agree, the direct measurement is certified. The authors aim to give therapists a dose gauge they can trust. The treatment is dosed by recipe for now.
pmc-12710231:
Lajos Szentgyorgyi, Salman Pervaiz Butt, and Bhuvaneswari Krishnamoorthy trace the history of ECMO, the machine that oxygenates blood outside the body. Their review was published in twenty twenty-five. The therapy grew out of heart bypass work in the mid twentieth century.

Standalone ECMO arrived in the nineteen seventies. Since then, better circuits, oxygenators, and pumps made it safer and more effective. Its uses spread from lung failure to heart failure and as a bridge to transplant. Recent work shrinks the kit, cuts cost, and makes it portable enough for use beyond big intensive care units. The authors frame ECMO as a lifeline for the worst heart and lung failure, and chart where development heads next.
pmc-12712231:
Julia Olson and co-authors watch how elk trade feeding time against watching for two different predators, in this 2025 paper. Mexican wolves and mountain lions both hunt elk in the Arizona and New Mexico border country. The team observed elk across seasons and hours, scoring feeding, hard vigilance, and multitasking. Risk maps for each predator came from habitat models and movement data.

Elk fed less where either predator's risk ran high. Under wolf risk they watched harder and multitasked more, and herds bedded down less. Individuals seemed to repay lost feeding with extra feeding bouts later, at rest's expense. The wish to multitask hinged on how short-term and long-term wolf risk combined. The authors urge predator studies to count these hidden costs.
pmc-12714231:
Margaret Morash and others put out a cell biology study in 2025 on gut hormone cells in zebrafish. Enteroendocrine cells are rare cells in the gut lining. They release peptide hormones that help run the digesting of food. The team set out to name the subtypes of these cells and the hormones each one makes.

Using single-cell gene data, the team found starter cells and six subtypes. The subtypes looked the same in young and adult fish. Mass testing then found mature hormones from most hormone genes. The team also built reporter fish to trace cell lines. Oddly, taking out one key starter type cut only some subtypes. Another cell type fed another set, hinting at own paths of growth.
pmc-12716031: Shira Levy and seven co-authors report in a 2025 paper how common certain gut bacteria are in infants. The bacteria carry genes to make colibactin, a compound that can damage DNA, and early exposure was thought to leave mutations that raise colon cancer risk later. Checking infants during the first two years of life, the team found these bacteria in more than half of them. That very high rate suggests carriage is likely normal in early gut development, and more work is needed to learn when it can cause harm.
pmc-12717231:
Six authors present a trial from two thousand twenty-five testing a multinutrient supplement in healthy vegans. Vegan diets can run low on certain vitamins, and the study checked status for vitamins A, B2, B12, and K, plus folate and choline. The trial was randomized, double-blind, and placebo-controlled.

Seventy-two vegan adults in Germany, aged nineteen to fifty-seven, took the supplement or a placebo for four months. Blood markers and diet records were taken at the start and the end. After adjustment for starting values, age, and sex, the groups showed no significant differences in how most of the vitamin markers changed.
pmc-12717531:
Hui Zheng and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a gene that may predict how brain tumors behave. Gliomas are cancers of the brain's support tissue, and their course varies widely. The claudin family of genes helps seal cell sheets, and its role in gliomas was unclear. The team focused on one member, CLDN22.

They mined a large public cancer atlas with many kinds of molecular data. Tumors were grouped into subtypes, and machine learning tools picked out the features that matter most. Immune profiling checked how the gene relates to the cells around the tumor. The authors argue this gene marks both outlook and likely response to immune therapy. Such markers could help doctors sort patients for trials.
pmc-12720431:
Laura Nübler and a large team set out a trial protocol for raising health insurance renewals in Ghana. Their protocol from twenty twenty-five targets the national scheme in Kumasi. Most Ghanaians register, but many let annual coverage lapse. Forgetfulness is a leading reason for those gaps.

A huge member pool will be randomised into study arms. One group gets phone reminders about renewal deadlines. Another gets automatic renewal arranged for them. A comparison group follows the usual process. Mobile renewal already simplified payment steps years ago. Behavioural nudges may close the remaining follow-through gap. Results could guide insurance design across similar schemes.
pmc-12720631:
Acute kidney injury is a frequent and serious complication after lung transplantation. It worsens both recovery and survival. Chongyang Ye and co-authors review what is known about predicting, preventing, and managing this problem. They explain the mechanisms that damage the kidneys around the time of transplant, including low blood flow and drug toxicity. They also list the risk factors that make injury more likely, such as prior kidney weakness and events during the operation.

The review surveys the prediction models researchers have built to flag high risk patients early. It then turns to prevention: careful fluid and blood pressure management, watching drug doses, and close monitoring after surgery. For patients who do develop injury, the authors describe current management steps. They stress that early recognition and fast intervention improve outcomes, and they call for more research to refine both prediction and care.
pmc-12721131:
Chen and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a review of tiny materials that boost T-cell therapy for bladder cancer. Bladder cancer returns often, and standard surgery and drugs give weak long-term results. T cells can hunt and kill tumor cells, but tumors suppress them and wear them out. Nanomaterials can deliver antigens and immune drugs straight to the tumor site. They can also reshape the tumor surroundings to help T cells work.

The review covers T-cell types, their roles near tumors, and how exhaustion develops. Strategies include sparking tumor cell death that alerts immunity. Others reprogram metabolism or release signals slowly for lasting activation. The authors look ahead to artificial intelligence designs and personalized care. Safety and tumor diversity remain key hurdles for clinical use.
pmc-12722231:
Qingkun Jiang and four co-authors trace how tongue cancer cells weaken the immune cells sent to kill them. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Tumors that resist the drug cisplatin tend to end badly, and natural killer cells are part of the body's defense against them.

The team found that resistant cancer cells shed tiny packets loaded with a long RNA called SNHG26. Killer cells take in the packets and the RNA. Inside, it triggers the loss of a key factor and blocks a growth signal, while also freeing a second pathway. The result is killer cells that grow less, wake up less, and kill less. Removing the RNA reversed the effect in lab and animal tests.
pmc-12726831:
Natasha Ironside and a large team of co-authors predict dangerous brain bleed growth from the first scan in this 2025 study. After a spontaneous brain hemorrhage, the clot often expands, and expansion foretells death and disability. Subtle shape clues on the opening scan may warn of growth, but eyes miss them.

A math method that treats images as piles of mass to be moved extracted those clues automatically. Big size, uneven density, ragged shape, and rim density all marked future growth. A model blending those traits with clinical data beat clinician checklists and other learning methods on fresh patients. The authors prize the method's readability: each feature has a physical meaning doctors can inspect.
pmc-12727431:
Ruiyun Chen, Qian Ju, Liming Feng, and Lin Zhang review, in twenty twenty-five, a cell death pathway as a drug target in stomach cancer. The pathway, ferroptosis, kills cells via iron-driven damage to fats in cell membranes. Its disruption can drive stomach cancer growth, spread, and drug resistance. The review first sets out how ferroptosis works. It then sums up how triggering it can resensitize cancer cells to chemotherapy and immune therapy.

Plant extracts and traditional medicines can trigger ferroptosis via key pathways, the authors note. New nanoparticles can carry drugs that trigger it while slowing cancer growth, including stem-like cancer cells. Other named drugs are covered too. The review ends with prospects for clinic use.
pmc-12728231:
George Muratoreanu and co-authors (2025) mapped where soil erosion threatens the Bistrița River basin in Romania. They related erosion to twelve environmental and human variables. Three learning algorithms competed: support vector machines, nearest neighbors, and random forests. Thousands of data sets trained, validated, and tested the models. The random forest performed best, and its map split the basin into five risk classes. The team then asked what changes by 2050 under different forest futures.

If logging continues and rain falls slightly, risk grows. Restoring the forests of 2001 reverses the trend. Heavy planting in the worst-hit sub-Carpathian zone, over fifty thousand hectares, would move very-high-risk land down a class. The price tag, about 775 million euros, may block that plan. Smaller plantings still helped in the model: each added block of forest cut erosion steadily. The authors offer the maps and scenarios to local authorities planning land care.
pmc-12729231:
Isabela Cristina Santos Freire de Paula and co-authors pool world data on deaths among babies born too early, in a review paper from 2025. Preterm birth is the leading cause of death in the first month of life. The risk climbs steeply the earlier a baby is born.

The team gathered 47 cohort studies from many databases and combined their results. Across all preterm births, about 8 of every 100 babies died in the first 28 days. The rate was 40 percent for the earliest group, born before 28 weeks, and 15 percent for the next group. For babies born at 32 to 37 weeks, the rate was close to zero. The authors note wide gaps between studies and urge care in reading the pooled figures.
pmc-12729531:
Leilei Zeng and co-authors hunt genes behind the fast growth of the giant grouper, a prized farmed fish, in work from 2025. The species is the largest and fastest growing of its kind, and a favored father in hybrid breeding. Why it grows so fast was unclear.

The team bred a self-crossed hybrid stock whose young split sharply by growth speed. Comparing the fastest and slowest groups by gene and RNA checks flagged a region on chromosome two. That region held twenty-three candidate genes and five telling DNA variants. Three genes stood out, tied to cell growth, early development, and energy use. Their activity patterns backed the link to fast growth.
pmc-12732731:
Ribeiro and co-authors ask older adults how a physical activity program shaped their health and quality of life. Activity programs are a key tool for healthy aging. Yet joining one depends on personal views and social background. Fourteen older adults, 11 of them women with a mean age of 68, joined two focus groups. All took part in a supervised program in southern Brazil. Talks were sorted into themes by structured analysis.

Themes covered health and aging, engagement with activity, and views on health promotion plans. Participants also named barriers to reaching such programs. Their accounts show what keeps older adults coming back. Program designers can use the lessons to widen access.
pmc-12733331:
Seong-Hee Ko and a team of co-authors review tiny proteins in this twenty twenty-five paper. These microproteins are built from short stretches of code once thought to make nothing. New tools that track protein building and weigh cell contents have shown that many of them do real work in the body.

Some help cells burn fat and make energy; others help move calcium in muscle or link key cell parts. A few shift their activity when food is scarce or rich, which hints they could serve as markers of diet and health. The review sums up what is known and where these small proteins may matter for treating disease.
pmc-12733731:
Jang Woo Ha and co-authors test rapamycin on immune cells from vasculitis patients in a 2025 paper. The diseases studied, GPA and MPA, involve harmful inflammation of blood vessels. The team asked whether rapamycin shifts helper T cells toward or away from key types.

They cultured stored blood cells from 20 patients, half men and half women, with and without rapamycin. After three days of stimulation, they measured cell types by flow cytometry. Rapamycin changed the shift toward TH1 cells, the interferon-making type. The drop was clear in cells from patients with active disease, but not in inactive cases.
pmc-12733831:
Marta Olszewska, Krzysztof Schwermer, and Krzysztof Pawlaczyk review newborn screening for Fabry disease, in a 2025 paper. The disease is a genetic storage disorder: a missing enzyme lets a fatty substance build up and harm organs. Symptoms vary widely and are easy to miss, so diagnosis often comes late. Screening newborns could catch cases early, but it is not yet standard anywhere.

Over twenty pilot programs worldwide suggest the disease is more common than once thought. Many finds are gene variants whose harm is unknown, which clouds what to do next. The review weighs screening methods, real rates, and the ethics and costs involved. The authors close with design advice so screening improves health without needless worry or waste.
pmc-12733931:
Guofeng Xing and seven colleagues profile the genetics of childhood heart muscle disease in China, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. Pediatric cardiomyopathies come in several forms with different causes. Genetic testing can reveal the culprit and guide family screening.

The cohort held fifty-five patients treated at Beijing Anzhen Hospital between two thousand twenty-one and two thousand twenty-four. Dilated and hypertrophic forms dominated, with smaller numbers of arrhythmogenic and restrictive cases. Whole-exome sequencing found clearly pathogenic variants in about a fifth of patients. Two genes, MYH7 and MYBPC3, appeared most often. Detection rates varied by subtype, highest in hypertrophic disease. The authors chart the phenotype spectrum alongside the genetic findings.
pmc-12734231:
Dario Collia and co-authors study how healthy children's hearts deform during exercise, in a paper from 2025. The heart reshapes its chambers to raise output during effort. The same reshaping, pushed too far, underlies heart failure. Child data can show the healthy pattern in its pure form.

Three-dimensional ultrasound tracked the heart at rest, during exercise, at peak effort, and twice in recovery. Two lenses were used: how the heart muscle strains, and how blood flows inside the chambers. Flow measures included swirl patterns and the forces that move blood. Results were read against a reference group of healthy children. The early findings may help separate normal adaptation from the first signs of disease.
pmc-12734731:
Lu Xu and co-authors published this study in 2025. It builds a glass coating that is both water-hating and nearly invisible. Two sizes of silica particles are stacked with care, then treated with fluorine to lower surface energy. The mixed-scale texture traps air and flattens light scatter at once. Coated glass passed over ninety-five percent of light, with haze under one percent. Water beaded at a steep angle and slid off at a whisper of tilt.

The film also cut reflections by about five percent against bare glass. Dirt rinsed away in the self-cleaning manner such surfaces promise. Toughness tests were broad: deep cold, damp heat, and long outdoor exposure all left it working. The authors aim the coating at lenses, optics, and solar panels, where clarity and cleanliness pay rent every day.
pmc-12735331:
Mohammed Al-Salihi and co-authors pool trials comparing keyhole surgery with drug care alone for bleeding inside the upper brain, in work from twenty twenty-five. Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage kills and disables at high rates. Minimally invasive drainage promises gentler clot removal, but its edge over medicine was unsettled.

Thirteen studies, mostly randomized, covered about twenty-nine hundred patients. Surgery raised the chance of good functional recovery and cut thirty day deaths. The gain concentrated in one technique, guided needle drainage with clot dissolving drugs, and in treatment within a day. Deep clots showed mixed effects. Severe side events ran lower with surgery, while rebleeding and intensive care time did not differ clearly.
pmc-12735931:
Manuela Cassotta and colleagues systematically reviewed in two thousand twenty-five whether yerba mate, the South American tea plant, could help rheumatoid arthritis. This joint disease is driven by lasting inflammation and oxidative stress. Mate contains plant compounds, including chlorogenic acids and rutin, known to calm inflammation and oxidation in other settings.

Their search gathered human, lab, and animal studies on mate preparations and its isolated compounds. Infusions and extracts pointed to reduced inflammation signals, though study designs varied widely and bias checks were applied carefully. Rheumatology readers get an honest evidence map: interesting signals, clear gaps, and no basis yet for treatment claims.
pmc-12739131:
Atiqah Hazan, Amalia Saperi, Nurfatihah Zulkifli, and four colleagues turn a food bacterium into a vaccine platform in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Existing COVID-19 vaccines cut deaths but do not reliably stop spread, so mucosal vaccines are wanted. The team engineered Bacillus subtilis, a safe Gram-positive bacterium, to display the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein on its spores as they formed, then dosed Balb/c mice with the altered spores.

Two weeks after the second dose, mice showed raised spike-specific IgM, IgG, and secretory IgA, the antibody class that guards mucosal surfaces. CD4 and CD8 T cell responses rose, and restimulation with spike peptides raised both inflammatory signals, interferon gamma, interleukin-2, and tumor necrosis factor, and the calming interleukin-10. Serum from dosed mice neutralized the virus. The authors present spore display as a promising, stable platform for mucosal vaccines against SARS-CoV-2 and possibly other lung pathogens.
pmc-12743031:
Anja Ernst and Jonas Haslbeck present latent class vector autoregressive models for time series in psychology, in a methods paper from 2025. Daily measures let researchers track within-person dynamics, such as mood shifts. People differ in those dynamics, and the standard multilevel model treats the differences as a smooth spread of values.

The latent class form treats differences as kinds, sorting people into discrete clusters with their own dynamics. The paper gives an accessible entry to the model. A simulation tests how well it can be estimated in applied-like settings. A new software package makes fitting easy. A full tutorial on emotion dynamics walks through fitting and reading results.
pmc-12747331:
Chaihong Zhang and Lihong Chen wrote a study, published in twenty twenty-five, about a plant compound called 6-methoxyflavone. The compound kills HeLa cells, a line of cervical cancer cells, by ferroptosis. That is a form of cell death driven by iron and by damage to the fats in cell walls.

The team checked for this death in several ways, among them electron microscopy and tests of key cell chemicals such as glutathione. Wider tests of proteins and small molecules then pointed to one target, SLC1A5. That protein moves amino acids into the cell. Docking tests and gene loss tests backed its role in the death. Shutting a gate that feeds the cell may thus set off iron-driven death, a route drug makers can test in other cancers.
pmc-12747431:
Harooni and five colleagues design new compounds to switch on an immune sensor in twenty twenty-five. The sensor, TLR7, spots virus like patterns and fires immune alarms. Few drugs on the market target it, so fresh leads are prized. Computer feature models screened databases for fits, and docking ranked the hits.

One ring scaffold stood out as the lead shape. Two series of variants were designed, docked, and made by green routes. Safe compounds were tested on immune cells for alarm signals. One variant drove the strongest rise in three key signals. Docking scores matched the lab ranking well, the team notes.
pmc-12748531:
Ahmed Nahari and co-authors survey nurse well-being in 2025 across Saudi Arabia. Nurses face heavy loads and stress at the bedside, yet little was known about how nurses in this country feel and what shapes their state. The team set out to measure well-being and find its key drivers.

They gathered answers from five hundred fifty nurses in many settings. Close to three in four nurses scored at risk of poor well-being, and frontline nurses fared worst. School level, work site, region, and job satisfaction all linked to the scores. Long experience slightly lowered risk, while critical care work raised it sharply. The authors urge steps to guard nurse health and cut burnout.
pmc-12748931:
Hongli Sam Goh and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-five survey on why nursing home staff in Singapore consider leaving. Turnover in long-term care strains morale and patient outcomes. The study weighed personal traits, work environment, and job satisfaction together.

Over one hundred fifty staff at two nursing homes answered standard questionnaires. Overall intention to leave sat at a moderate level. Women, mid-career staff, and nursing aides showed the strongest intentions. Satisfaction with manager support and staffing levels mattered most. Care home leaders get concrete levers for keeping experienced staff in place.
pmc-12749431:
Kotaro Shobayashi and co-authors build, in a 2025 study, a microneedle patch that delivers a precise dose of a COVID-19 vaccine. Patches promise vaccination without deep needles or cold storage chains. Their design adds guide pillars that place the vaccine load exactly, using a recombinant vaccinia virus carrying the coronavirus spike gene as the payload.

Each patch held a high, verified dose of live virus. In mice, the patch raised strong spike-specific antibodies, including neutralizing ones. When the mice were later exposed to the virus, every patched animal survived and held its weight, while control groups fared badly. The authors present the platform as a stable, low-invasive route for vaccination that could be spread widely, including far from central clinics.
pmc-12749831:
Pranata and a large team present a study from twenty twenty-five on reusing a bone drug for Crohn's disease, guided by genomics. Crohn's is a chronic gut inflammation with no cure. The team gather over a thousand disease-linked gene variants from a catalog. Expansion by linked variants grows the set hugely. Fourteen annotation layers narrow it to forty-five high-confidence risk genes. Drug interaction databases are screened against those genes. A bone drug tops the list through one gene's pathway.

That gene peaks in the gut segment Crohn's hits hardest. Network maps tie it to mast cells in the gut lining. Blocking its signal could calm local inflammation with less body-wide harm. Lab and clinical tests are still needed.
pmc-12752831:
Rebecca Saunders and Lipi Buch published a veterinary case report in 2025 about a seriously ill spaniel. The six-year-old dog had suffered collapsing episodes for two months. It also ate poorly, tired easily, and looked lethargic. Scans showed a severely enlarged, weak heart.

Blood work pointed to an underactive thyroid gland. A heart monitor recorded the dog during a collapse at discharge. The dog stopped breathing, and resuscitation restored it quickly. The monitor showed a steady rhythm, ruling out a rhythm cause. Treatment combined heart medicines with thyroid hormone replacement. Doses were tuned at later rechecks. The case shows thyroid crisis can mimic primary heart disease, yet prove reversible.
pmc-12753931:
Chirag Chandnani, Shlok Kulkarni, Geraldine Amali, and Rohini Selvaraj map land use around Pune, India, from satellite images with a new neural network, in a twenty twenty-five study. Fast, unplanned city growth there has fed floods and landslides. Good land maps guide planning. Their network swaps the usual neuron switch for wavy, repeating ones, letting one neuron draw several decision edges.

On Landsat-8 images, the wavy model reached about ninety-six percent test accuracy. It beat standard networks on precision and recall as well. The authors say the design generalizes better on mixed land types. The work supports tighter land planning for fast-growing cities.
pmc-12754631:
Shihao Song and seventeen co-authors uncover a new quorum-sensing circuit in a lung pathogen. Their 2025 paper studies Pseudomonas aeruginosa and a fatty signal it releases. The signal, cis-2-decenoic acid, was known to scatter biofilms. How it steers the cell's genes stayed unclear.

The signal binds FadD1, an enzyme that normally handles fatty acids. Bound FadD1 grips gene switches more tightly, turning many genes up or down. The enzyme thus moonlights as a global regulator. It also acts on a cousin signal from another species, sharpening competition. A metabolic enzyme evolved into a signal reader, the team shows. That twist rewrites how this pathogen coordinates its virulence.
pmc-12754931:
Harun Aslan and Gülsüm Şeyma Koca, publishing in 2025, study how foreign university students in Turkey handle health worries online. Students abroad face language barriers and an unfamiliar health system, so many turn to the internet. There, anxious searching can feed a loop. Poor views of one's own health drive more searching, which raises health anxiety. That anxiety can in turn erode the ability to judge online health information well. The authors surveyed 352 such students at one university.

Their analysis found that how students view their health predicted how well they could use online health information, with anxious searching and health anxiety carrying much of that effect in a chain. Students with negative views of their health searched more, worried more, and judged sources worse. The authors call for digital health programs shaped to these students' cultures to cut through misinformation.
pmc-12755731:
Kasthuri Sivalogan and co-authors check whether giving pregnant women clean cookstoves made their babies grow longer, in a 2025 study. Smoke from biomass cooking is tied to stunted growth. A four-country trial gave gas stoves and fuel to half of 3,195 pregnant women in Guatemala, Peru, India, and Rwanda. Babies were measured at birth and at three-month intervals to one year.

Growth fell into three tracks: high, medium, and low length for age, covering about 13, 54, and 33 percent of babies. The split between tracks did not differ between stove and control groups. Cleaner cooking alone, the authors conclude, did not bend infant growth in this trial, even though the smoke burden fell.
pmc-12755831:
Daouda Libanio and co-authors give, in twenty twenty-five, the first full description of local Muscovy ducks in Benin, West Africa. The duck is a key poultry bird for rural life in Benin. No prior study had documented its traits there. The team assessed four hundred six adult ducks from ninety-three small farms across three ecological zones in the south. They recorded both quality traits, such as feather color, and measured traits, such as body size and weight. Males were larger than females across most measures.

White feathers dominated, with black and ash also common. A rare blue eye color was reported for the first time. Beaks were mostly pink and skin mostly white. Traits varied by color type and by zone, which shows rich diversity for breeding.
pmc-12756331:
TRPV1 is a channel protein best known for sensing heat and chili peppers, but it sits in the heart, where its everyday job is unclear. Nolwenn Tessier and co-authors mapped the published literature on TRPV1 in heart science. They found clusters on injury, blood vessels, and nerve control, but nothing on baseline function in animals lacking the channel. They examined male mice with the gene deleted, testing the living heart, isolated cells, and fine cell structure.

By nearly every measure the knockout hearts were normal: pumping, electrical signals, calcium handling, and energy producing mitochondria all matched ordinary mice. Calcium signals shifted without practical effect. Only under the microscope did differences appear: muscle units sat slightly longer, and cell nuclei changed shape. The authors conclude TRPV1 is not needed for the heart's normal work at rest, and its roles likely show only under stress or injury.
pmc-12756431:
Hongjuan Wang and co-authors mapped the gene response of a medicinal plant to lab-made drought, in a 2025 study. The plant, Blumea laciniata, is a documented herb in Chinese medicine with uses against infection. Knowing how it copes with dry spells can guide how it is grown as the climate shifts.

Drought was faked with a polymer at two strengths, and leaf samples came at five points over seven days. The stronger dose hurt leaves more, causing yellowing, curling, and death spots.
