Protective chemistry rose as the stress wore on. Gene reads showed a broad reshaping of activity, and a network method grouped the genes that move together under stress.
pmc-12768631:
Marcus Borin and a team of co-authors report a study coded OP74, published in twenty twenty-five. They compare fast drug approvals in the United States with choices made in Brazil. In the United States, a fast path lets some drugs for grave illness reach patients early. It rests on stand-in measures of benefit, with full trials to follow.

The team took data on drugs on that fast path from the Food and Drug Administration. They then set those outcomes next to Brazilian choices on the same drugs. Gaps between the two can affect patient safety and public care. Readers see where the two systems agree, where they part, and why that matters after a drug reaches the market.
pmc-12771131:
Likun Peng and six co-authors pool the trial evidence on vitamin A and vitamin D3 supplements for child growth in poorer countries, in this 2025 review. Both vitamins are vital for growing bodies, yet past trials disagree on whether giving them as supplements makes children taller or heavier. The team combined randomized trials in children up to age fourteen.

Twelve trials covering 6,340 children met the rules. Vitamin D3 alone did not improve height or thinness scores, though it slightly raised a weight for age score. Vitamin A alone showed no clear effect on any growth measure. Giving both vitamins together modestly improved weight for age in children under five, but results varied a lot between studies. The authors call the likely benefit small and unsettled.
pmc-12772931: Ozcan Ozeke, Dursun Aras, and Serkan Topaloglu published a short cardiology paper in twenty twenty-five on a pacing clue seen during ventricular tachycardia. When pacing stops the racing rhythm without capturing the whole heart, the authors argue, the pacing site likely sits inside the critical re-entrant circuit. The sign holds even when concealed entrainment cannot be demonstrated there. It usually appears by chance, but they note it can also be provoked deliberately with a single extrastimulus, helping locate tissue for ablation.
pmc-12781531:
I-Ji Jeong and co-authors study complete pathological response after arterial chemoembolization in liver cancer patients who later received transplants in a 2025 paper. Killing all viable tumor before transplant is linked to better outcomes. The team ask which patients with that response still face recurrence.

Records covered more than two thousand transplant patients over fifteen years. About two hundred fifty achieved complete response, after roughly two treatment sessions on average. Recurrence stayed low for years and survival stayed high. Larger or multiple non viable tumors independently raised recurrence risk and lowered survival, defining a higher risk subgroup.
pmc-12784931:
Gianluca Vanni and co-authors ask whether reconstruction complications delay cancer therapy after mastectomy in a 2025 study. Implant reconstruction comes in two placements: above the chest muscle, the newer pre-pectoral way, or beneath it. The above-muscle route skips muscle cutting and may ease pain and recovery. Worry persists that its complications could push back follow-up treatment.

The Rome team reviewed six hundred twenty-two patients over ten years. Overall complication rates were much the same for both placements. Slow wound healing was more common above the muscle; bleeding was more common below it. Surgery ran shorter with the newer route. In adjusted models, skin-reducing mastectomy, smoking, and diabetes predicted delayed therapy. The reconstruction technique itself did not. The authors conclude complications did not shift the start of added treatment in this series.
pmc-12785131:
Kine Bergum Hjellegjerde and colleagues explore blood clotting in dogs with steroid-responsive meningitis-arteritis using viscoelastic monitoring. Their 2025 prospective study recruits patients from four United Kingdom referral hospitals.

The disease is a systemic immune-mediated inflammation that occasionally causes spontaneous bleeding inside or outside the nervous system. Twenty dogs were tested with a bedside coagulation monitor between twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-five. One dog showed an over-clotting result, and two showed excessive clot breakdown patterns. No dog had clinical signs of vascular complications during the study. The authors suggest further work on the clot-breakdown system and vessel lining in affected dogs.
pmc-12787131:
Shigehisa Tamaki and co-authors test a waveform method for tracking a rare bleeding disorder in patients on a new antibody drug, in a 2025 study. In this disorder, the immune system attacks factor VIII, a protein blood needs to clot. The drug emicizumab treats it well, but it distorts the standard clotting tests doctors rely on. The team used clot waveform analysis, which reads the shape of the clotting curve.

Across three cases, one waveform variant tracked the factor VIII activity left in the blood. The team also found that common test reagents differ in how sensitive they are to the disorder. The drug stopped major bleeding in the cases studied. Antibody levels against factor VIII could still be measured during treatment with the waveform method. The authors offer it as a practical monitoring tool.
pmc-12787631:
Álvaro Cortés, María Carmen Pérez-Rubio, and Álvaro Hernández improve the sound pulses behind indoor ultrasound positioning, in a 2025 paper. Satellites fail indoors, so systems locate people and goods with ultrasound instead. Commercial speakers offer narrow bandwidth, and moving targets warp the echoes, both capping accuracy.

The authors propose a filter-based way to shape the emitted pulse and compress its echo on arrival. Pulse compression sharpens timing, which is what position rests on. Their method aims to stretch coverage beyond the few square meters of earlier systems while resisting the Doppler warp from motion. Centimeter-level indoor fixes support hospitals, warehouses, and assistive tools that must track assets in real time.
pmc-12788031:
Shengchao Cui led a large team building a self-cleaning road coating in a 2025 paper. The coating blends three light-active materials in a layered structure that keeps excited charges apart longer and narrows the energy gap, so it harvests more visible light. Sprayed on asphalt test plates, it attacks vehicle exhaust gases directly. They measured gas cleanup plus road traits like hardness, grip, and freeze-thaw wear.

Under an hour of natural light, cleanup reached about half for nitrogen oxides and around a fifth for hydrocarbons and carbon monoxide. Repeat tests held nearly the same levels. All road performance measures met national standards, the team reports.
pmc-12794031:
Hanyue Xing, Xu Ma, Fanqiang Meng, and Zhanjiang Li map how fatigue reshapes the links among sleeplessness, anxiety, and depression, in a 2025 study. The three conditions feed each other in both directions. Fatigue is a known bridge symptom between them. Whether it also moderates their ties was unexplored. The team studied five hundred forty-four patients with chronic insomnia. Standard scales measured sleep, anxiety, depression, and fatigue. A moderated network method estimated the web.

Symptoms linked to each other in both directions, confirming the tangle. Fatigue changed the strength of several key ties. It moderated links between broken sleep and thinking problems. It also moderated links tying body anxiety to daytime trouble. Three symptoms sat at the network's center. Mental anxiety was one. Insomnia's hit to quality of life was another. The authors suggest treating fatigue may loosen the whole knot. Targeted trials could test that idea.
pmc-12800231:
Shaobo Yang and colleagues offer a two thousand twenty-five analysis of the E2F gene family across many cancers. E2F proteins control how cells read their DNA and can drive tumour growth. Few earlier studies had examined them across cancer types at once.

Using several public databases, the team compared E2F levels in normal and tumour tissue. They linked expression to survival, stage, mutations, drug response, and immune features. Lab checks focused on one member, E2F5, with gene readout and cell experiments. The results frame E2F genes as possible combined markers for judging and managing cancers.
pmc-12801831:
Filiz Kaya, Esra Özayar, and Ayça Özcan lead a team comparing two sedation recipes for elderly patients undergoing a bile duct endoscopy, watching what each does to thinking afterward. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The procedure is increasingly done in older adults. Sedation choices may cloud or spare the aging brain.

Nearly two hundred inpatients received propofol alone or propofol plus dexmedetomidine. Mental state exams ran before the procedure and twice after. Baseline scores matched between the groups. The combination group improved significantly at both later checks. Pre-frail patients gained the most from the pairing. The authors read this as a cognitive edge for adding the second drug. Frailty screening helped predict who benefits. Anesthesia for the elderly gains a practical data point.
pmc-12802231:
Hana Hanzlikova leads a team on flu, weather, and death in the Czech Republic. Their study from twenty twenty-five spans near four decades. Flu peaks in winter and adds to winter deaths there.

The team modeled extra deaths in a set of flu waves. Weather was checked from weeks before to weeks after each peak. Waves were grouped by death toll and by main virus type. Tests also sought which weather marks link to wave starts. Links of weather, flu, and health stay complex, they note. The long span adds weight to the finds.
pmc-12804931:
Chengsheng Zhan and three co-authors automate magnetic map making for navigation. Their 2025 paper improves geomagnetic maps used indoors and out. Such maps guide devices where satellite signals fail. Their accuracy hinges on kriging, a method that needs a well-fit variance model.

Fitting that model by hand leans on expert judgment and varies by person. The team's neural network reads samples and infers the model settings itself. An encoder-decoder design with an attention block sharpens the guesses. Maps built this way came out smoother and truer than standard kriging. The workflow also runs with less manual fuss. Better magnetic maps mean steadier navigation in signal dead zones.
pmc-12809931:
Ceylan Ertuğrul and Burak Apaydin counted why children receive cone-beam scans at one dental hospital, in a study published in 2025. The scans give fine 3D views of the jaw, but dose fears run high for children. Records from 2018 to 2025 held 266 scans of children aged five to fourteen. That was about two in a hundred of the clinic's young patients.

Most scans examined the upper jaw, and the front teeth zone led for both sexes. Surgery drove more than eight in ten scans; brace work drove the rest. Stuck teeth topped the cause list, then cyst-like growths, extra teeth, and midline extras. The widest view size was the most used. The authors say scans in children stay rare and surgery led.
pmc-12812631:
Zhenxing Feng and co-authors build a CT based model to spot noninfectious flare ups of COPD in this paper, published in 2025. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease flare ups without infection are hard to identify. No reliable blood marker exists for them. Misreading the cause can lead to wrong treatment.

Records covered 352 patients at Tianjin Chest Hospital from 2019 to 2023. Of those, 181 had noninfectious flare ups and 171 were stable. Whole lung scans were split into three habitat zones by clustering. Texture features from each zone were combined with clinical factors in prediction models. Patients were split into training and test groups. The habitat approach aims to read flare risk from lung patterns invisible to the eye.
pmc-12815731:
Mengjue Li and colleagues present a 2025 animal study on sunflower, known in science as Helianthus annuus, and its effect on heart attacks in mice with clogged arteries. Heart attacks most often start when fatty plaque in an artery breaks open. The team asked whether adding sunflower to the diet could limit the harm that follows.

Mice bred to lack a key fat-clearing protein were split into four groups. Some ate a high-fat diet, and one group got that diet plus sunflower powder. After the team tied off a heart artery, the sunflower group showed less heart damage and scarring. Blood and heart tissue also held lower levels of proteins that drive swelling and stress. The results point to sunflower as a possible aid worth more study.
pmc-12816231:
Shivaprakash and co-authors review spit protein signs for spotting early childhood tooth decay, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Four databases yielded eleven studies that fit the rules. Bias checks used a set quality tool.

Only three studies scored low risk across all domains, and the rest were mixed or weak. Still, pooled signs point to real promise in spit tests. Named candidates span mucins, amylase, and small protein bits. The authors urge stronger trials before firm claims. Spit checks could help stop new holes early in small children. Readers get a hopeful but honest read of a painless test path.
pmc-12817731:
Nigerian husbands rarely attend antenatal visits, and Ilerioluwa Taiwo Adeniyi and co-authors asked expectant mothers what they make of that absence. Twelve women at a teaching hospital joined focus groups. Their picture was mixed: partners were scarce at clinic appointments and almost never present in labor rooms.

Yet the same men often shopped for delivery supplies and arranged transport. The mothers wanted more: a husband's presence in labor, they said, would ease their workload fears and give emotional ballast. Barriers included the men's work schedules, their discomfort, cultural and religious expectations, and some mothers' own mixed feelings. The authors urge programs that invite men in deliberately.
pmc-12819431:
Zi Qin Ng and Jih Huei Tan describe a keyhole surgery for right-sided bowel cancer in an eighty-eight-year-old patient. The operation removed half the colon along with its full fatty sheet and the central vessels that feed it. The report focuses on an added step: clearing lymph nodes below the stomach outlet. That step is debated and not done as a rule.

Here it was chosen because the patient had warning signs of node spread, a high marker level and blocking symptoms. The article walks through the key steps, stressing careful tying of vessels and fine dissection to avoid bleeding and leaks of lymph fluid. It shows how the extended clearance can be done safely.
pmc-12819831:
Si-Jie Li and three co-authors read the design values of nursing homes from their own chosen photos, in a 2025 journal article. Homes post photos on care portals to show what they stand for. Those picks reveal what each home prizes in its built space, from light and green to calm halls.

The team gathered 3,578 photos from 389 homes. A large vision language model turned each photo into a structured audit text. Text tools then grouped like audits and refined a shared statement set. A sorting method built on meaning likeness found four belief types that cover most of the spread. The authors offer the types as a guide for designers who want health aims, not taste alone, to rule home design.
pmc-12820031:
Organic light-emitting diodes dim their own future: the brighter they run, the faster they die. Binyu Wang and co-authors dodge that trade-off with texture. They built the diode layers on a substrate carved with tiny corrugations, packing more glowing area into the same panel footprint. Each square centimeter of panel then works less hard for the same brightness.

The corrugated devices spread their layers evenly, gaining up to forty percent more area. At equal panel brightness they lasted 2.7 times longer than flat controls. They also extracted up to forty percent more of their light. The trick worked for both major diode chemistries. The authors offer it as a route to durable OLED lighting.
pmc-12820331:
Ng and a team including Tse study ankle muscle traits in stroke survivors in twenty twenty-five. Stroke changes muscles in ways that affect movement, walking, and balance. The team measured strength and stiffness of two ankle muscles. They compared sixty-five chronic stroke survivors with thirty-one healthy older adults.

Strength of the two ankle muscle groups tracked together in survivors. Stronger ankle muscles linked to better motor control and some aspects of stability. They also linked, in a negative direction, to timed mobility and walking tests as scored. Stiffness of both muscles linked negatively to postural stability measures. Ankle strength differed clearly between survivors and healthy controls. The authors map how muscle properties relate to recovery outcomes.
pmc-12821831:
Sara Mahomed, Thomas Hanscheid, and Yara Almeida lead a team showing that the red blood cells feeding malaria parasite cultures are a hidden source of irreproducibility. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Growing the deadliest malaria parasite in the lab underpins drug and vaccine work worldwide. Yet papers rarely say whose blood the parasites grew in.

An AI-assisted review of nearly a thousand studies found most omitted donor origin and blood group. Fewer still named the anticoagulant used. In their own experiments, parasite growth varied more than sixfold across donors. The donor effect stayed stable when retested years later. Slow-growth donors had lower hemoglobin and more anemia history. The authors urge journals to demand blood sourcing details. A methods footnote, they show, can be an experimental variable.
pmc-12824331:
Daneshgar, Bagherzadeh, Sojdeh, and Rabiee tune pore design in a titanium framework material in twenty twenty-five. The material, MIL-125, is a porous crystal with uses in medicine. Controlling its pore size in a green way is still a challenge. The team used synthesis time as a simple lever for that control.

By varying only how long the reaction ran, they made variants with distinct shapes and pore traits. Tests of surface area, crystal structure, and form backed the analysis. Math fitting functions helped model how the pores developed. The twenty-four hour sample had the highest surface area and pore volume. It suits slow, sustained drug release. Shorter runs gave frameworks better fit for other therapy uses. The authors frame this as a sustainable pore size concept.
pmc-12827131:
Alshehri and seven co-authors identify compounds in kola nut seeds and test their anticancer potential computationally, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Kola nut is a traditional African stimulant and medicine with long use. Seed extracts are profiled by gas chromatography and mass spectrometry first. Selected compounds are then docked against a cancer-linked enzyme, PI3K alpha.

Seventy-eight compounds span alkaloids, flavonoids, fatty acids, and carbohydrate classes. Fifteen bioactive compounds enter the docking shortlist for testing. Five of them bind the target enzyme with favorable energies. Small stimulant compounds like caffeine bind weakly by comparison here. The seed's chemicals look like promising scaffolds for future drug development.
pmc-12827331:
Yan Pan and co-authors make high-grade filter membranes in seconds in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The membranes are covalent organic frameworks, lattices with orderly pores. Growing them large and well-ordered usually takes long trial and error.

Their method grows the lattice at the face of a special emulsion. Starting pieces line up inside a liquid network, so building and ordering happen at once in tight space. Water by-products get trapped fast, which speeds the reaction. A scraping process yielded a sheet about half a meter by a meter. The membrane let water through fast and removed salt from protein mixes at ninety-eight percent, beating shop benchmarks.
pmc-12828031:
Conor Treacy and co-authors built a three-color light-based sensor to test whether two proteins meet and pull on each other inside living cells. The proteins, RIAM and vinculin, sit in focal adhesions, the spots where a cell grips its surface. Their method passes energy between three glowing tags in a chain, read out by timing single photons, so meetings and forces can be mapped in space and time.

The team checked the sensor with purified proteins, light spectra, structural models, and electron microscopy. In mouse cells lacking vinculin, the sensor showed RIAM binding to one end of vinculin at the grip spots. Force-sensing versions read an average pull of about three piconewtons per adhesion, matching vinculin's known role in sensing force.
pmc-12831431:
Daniel Ariza-Suarez leads a team that seeks root rot strength in peas. Their study from twenty twenty-five uses a wide set of pea types. Root rot comes from soil germs that act as a group.

The team used gene marks from a large pea panel. They found a new gene zone tied to rot strength. Two genes in that zone look like good leads for control. A full gene guess model caught much of the trait spread. Plant height and shoot weight did not mark health well. Breed work could use these finds.
pmc-12833031:
Dengue fever can reach the eye, and one rare effect is a small dead zone in the center of vision. Salil Mehta reports a 33-year-old man with confirmed dengue. Five days into the illness, with fever, rash, and gum bleeding as his platelets fell, he noticed a blind spot and mild blur in his right eye. Scans showed the bright band in the inner retina that defines paracentral acute middle maculopathy.

Mehta suspects the dengue virus starved a deep layer of retinal blood vessels, either through local inflammation or thickened blood. The man was treated with oral steroids that tapered weekly, and within two days his sight improved and the retinal lesions shrank. The report urges doctors to treat a new central blind spot during dengue as a warning sign worth imaging at once.
pmc-12835931:
Rheumatoid arthritis makes pregnancy riskier, but the size of each risk is still being pinned down. Samar Al Emadi and co-authors follow 101 pregnant women with the disease and 226 healthy controls at a Qatar hospital in this 2025 study.

Women with arthritis miscarried far more often, delivered early more often, and needed caesarean sections at twice the control rate. Their babies were about three times as likely to be born underweight. Disease stayed active in roughly a quarter to a third of patients late in pregnancy. The authors urge specialized prenatal care with close tracking of disease activity and treatment.
pmc-12839031:
Qiong Ge and co-authors tested augmented reality teaching for music emotion skills in a 2025 study. Music students often listen without deep emotional engagement. The team compared AR-guided imagery against self-generated imagery while students appreciated Chinese pipa music.

Eighty-one students took part in three groups of 27: AR instruction, visual imagery alone, and no instruction. Brain scanners recorded teacher and student activity at the same time, watching for their brains to fall into sync. Both teaching methods improved students' ability to tell emotional tones in music apart, compared with no instruction. The study links a teaching technology to shared brain activity during lessons.
pmc-12842631:
Sibusiso Buthelezi and Jules Tapamo improve learned image compression in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Neural codecs based on autoencoders rely on entropy models, priors over the compressed form, usually built from small networks. Those local priors miss complex global links in the latent space, wasting bits. Full transformer priors capture global structure but cost too much computing for high-resolution images. The authors split the difference with a hybrid design.

Their framework couples a standard autoencoder with a patch-based Swin transformer hyperprior in layers. Shifted window attention models local and global context well, and a smooth quantization module lets the rate-distortion goal train end to end. A better model of the latents yields more compact codes. On the Kodak, JPEG AI, and CLIC datasets, the hybrid beat methods using simpler entropy models on rate-distortion results and visual quality at lower bitrates.
pmc-12843831:
Alessandra Signorile and six co-authors make alumina surfaces love water for weeks with laser texturing. Their 2025 paper carves micro-patterns into ceramic plates with femtosecond pulses. Wetting control matters for implants and prostheses that meet body fluids. Most treatments fade within days, though.

Triangular grooves of varied depth were cut into the plates. Water contact angles were tracked daily for over forty days. Deeper grooves held their hydrophilic pull longest. Without a stabilizing bake, the deepest patterns stayed super-wettable the whole test. A bake after cutting changed the balance in the other samples. Groove depth, it turns out, is a dial for lasting wetness.
pmc-12844031:
Jiayi Xun and co-authors review ways to boost nitrogen removal in membrane bioreactors, in an overview from two thousand twenty-five. Nitrogen pollution feeds algae blooms and foul, dark water bodies. Membrane bioreactors pair biological treatment with fine filtering and look strong for the job.

The review explains the removal mechanisms and their traits in depth. Key settings that sway efficiency, from oxygen to sludge age, get close analysis. Boosted process designs built around the reactor are summed up. Membrane fouling, the system's main headache, gets its own counter-strategy section. Future research directions close the piece.
pmc-12844331:
Munseong Bae, Eunbi Jang, Chanik Kang, and Haejun Chung present an optics design study from 2025. They design a flat lens for heat imaging, the kind used in cheap sensors for homes and small devices. Normal lenses for this task are bulky or costly and see only a narrow view.

Their lens was shaped by a computer method that works back from the wanted image. It spreads light over a tiny four-by-four heat sensor and sees a view about one hundred degrees wide. Tests showed a much wider view than a standard lens while staying small, cheap, and low in power use.  Uses named in the study include room occupancy counts, smart buildings, and fire watch outdoors.
pmc-12845831:
Ketzarly Gallardo Durán and colleagues report a rare bleed that surfaced months after gallbladder surgery, in this case report from twenty twenty-five. The bleed is hemobilia: blood leaking into the bile ducts through an abnormal link with a liver artery. It is uncommon but can kill.

Their patient, a woman in her twenties, had her gallbladder removed in the autumn of twenty twenty-three, seemingly without trouble. By the next February she was vomiting blood in repeated bouts. A camera exam showed blood coming from the bile duct. Scans found a ballooned weak spot, a pseudoaneurysm, on the right liver artery, with dilated ducts and air where none should be. She crashed into shock and needed intensive care and transfusions. A stent placed through the vessels sealed the leak, the treatment of choice. The lesson: think of this link when bleeding follows gallbladder work, even late.
pmc-12847831:
Przemysław Śleszyński and Mariusz Kowalski share a data set of Polish general election results in a 2025 paper. The set covers every general election from 1990 to 2024. Results are given for two levels of districts: 41 for the lower house and 94 for the upper house of parliament.

Pulling this together was hard because Poland redrew its district borders many times, which breaks simple comparisons across years. The authors rebuilt the results inside one fixed set of units and sorted more than three hundred election committees into five broad political options. They attach a digital map of the districts, so users can join the tables to the map and chart change over time.
pmc-12847931:
Lei Zhang and nine colleagues published a virus study in two thousand twenty-five on bird flu adapting to mammals. The H5N1 virus spilled into United States dairy cows in two thousand twenty-four, raising pandemic fears. The team hunted for changes in one viral gene segment, PB2, that help it thrive in mammals.

They pinpointed a change called M631L that arose as the virus moved from birds into cattle. In mice it made the virus about as harmful as a long-known danger change. Several other new and known changes also appeared. All worked by helping the virus use a host protein from cows and humans more effectively. The authors urge tighter watch on farm and wild hosts.
pmc-12851431:
Justin Mathew and co-authors test whether strict blood transfusion rules after spine surgery leave patients worse off. During the pandemic blood shortage, hospitals transfused only when haemoglobin fell below seven and a half grams per decilitre. The team compared 51 deformity surgery patients under that rigid rule with 43 treated later under looser thresholds. The groups matched in age, sex mix, blood loss, and operating time.

The lowest haemoglobin after surgery was about the same in both groups, about nine against nine point three, and the rigid rule did not lengthen hospital stay. Across all 94 patients, stay was predicted by how low haemoglobin fell. Patients bottoming out below seven and a half stayed eight point two days on average, against three point six days for those staying above nine and a half. The authors call for work on why low counts and long stays travel together.
pmc-12853831:
Xu and six co-authors rank biomarkers and drug targets in gastric cancer trials, in work from twenty twenty-five. Gastric cancer is a leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Trial activity is intense, but which targets recur most often, and are safest, needed a map.

A trial database was mined for global and Chinese gastric cancer trials. Five drugs and their linked biomarkers and targets were investigated in depth. Target safety was judged with normal tissue gene data from a public atlas, joined with cancer data. Prioritized targets can focus future trial design on the most tested and tolerable options.
pmc-12854931:
Sumit Banerjee leads a team with a shoulder case of synovial chondromatosis. Their case from twenty twenty-five deals with a young adult male. The disorder is a rare benign joint ill with loose bodies.

Shoulder cases are uncommon and can mimic other joint ills. He had chronic pain and stiff movement sans prior trauma. Scans showed many calcified bodies inside the joint space. Keyhole surgery removed the bodies and part of the lining. About twenty fragments were taken out in the surgery. He regained full pain free movement in months.
pmc-12860031:
Siqun Xiao, Die Qiu, Wen Zhang, and Shunv Cai run a dose-finding study for pain control during a liver tumor procedure in a 2025 paper. The procedure burns tumors through the skin with heat. Tumors near the liver's surface hurt more during burning, so the team asked how much of the pain drug alfentanil each group needs.

Sixty patients were split by how close the tumor sat to the liver capsule. Doses rose or fell step by step based on the prior patient's response, a method called up-and-down allocation. The dose that worked for half the patients was clearly higher for surface tumors. The authors say teams should plan stronger pain control for those cases.
pmc-12864631:
Masood Badri and co-authors chart mental health gaps across social groups in Abu Dhabi, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Data came from a quality of life survey with over one hundred thousand respondents, narrowed to about sixty-five thousand adults. Feelings such as sadness, anxiety, loneliness, and poor focus were compared across groups.

Young adults aged fifteen to twenty-nine reported the highest emotional stress. Women and non-Emiratis showed more negative indicators than their counterparts. Non-heads of household and private-sector workers also carried heavier distress. The authors frame the gaps as built into social roles and work structures. Targeted, inclusive policy is their prescription.
pmc-12890531:
Ananth Aditya Jupudi and co-authors used deep gene sequencing to find immune cell patterns tied to Sjögren's disease, in a study published in 2025. In this disease, immune cells gather in the saliva glands and damage them, causing dry mouth. The team focused on the receptor codes that let these cells pick their targets.

They sequenced receptors from blood cells of patients and healthy controls, plus gland cells from the same patients. Some expanded gland cells shared receptor codes with blood cells, and patient blood showed a narrower, more private set of codes than healthy blood. The shared codes grew more common as saliva flow fell. The team also found two protein targets that these cells attack, which could guide future treatments.
pmc-12970531:
Sebastián Tenorio and co-authors build a rule-based tool that sorts anemia in dialysis patients, in work from 2025. Anemia is a common harm of kidney disease and drives illness, death, and cost. Right sorting guides iron and hormone drug use. The team fed lab data from eight hundred eighty-three adults on dialysis in 2023 into rules drawn from three guideline sets.

The tool sorted most patients into working iron shortage, with lack of total iron next. A quarter showed signs of a severe gland overdrive. One in ten mixed both flags, which hints at drug resistance. The authors back the tool for steady, proof-based care.
pmc-12983331:
Jinhua Yang and co-authors map where large language models are used in mental health in this review, published in 2025. Chatbots and text models are being tried for screening, support, and therapy aids. The field is moving fast, and its safe limits are unclear. The team searched eleven databases and kept twenty-nine studies for close review.

Most work aims at high-volume screening and help for clinicians. Specialized smaller models often beat general ones on accuracy for common disorders. Training data leans heavily on social media text. Weak spots include poor fit for non-Western cultures and trouble tracking a patient's history over time. The authors urge stronger ethics rules and deeper clinical grounding.
pmc-13086531: Mohammad Rasel, Abdullah Al-Jubair, Sudipta Banik, and Afsana Mimi report a thirteen-year-old child in Bangladesh simultaneously infected with typhoid fever and hepatitis A. Both infections are endemic in the region and attack overlapping organ systems. Together they produced a prolonged fever with jaundice, a presentation that can mislead clinicians toward a single diagnosis. The case reminds practitioners in endemic settings to test for coinfection when fever and jaundice persist, since each disease needs its own management.
pmc-13087131:
Clarimma Sessa and six co-authors analyze the very stones of the Great Pyramid's inner chambers to guide their conservation, working inside the ScanPyramids mission. The King's and Queen's chambers weather differently because their stones differ, granite against limestone. Salt blooms on the surfaces are the visible symptom.

In the Queen's chamber, halite drives the white efflorescence on the limestone. In the King's chamber, granite minerals are altering to clay, which feeds salt growth on the upper blocks. The team reports the first in-place X-ray fluorescence imaging of Aswan granite, mapping elements without touching the surface. A chemometric shortcut using spot readings is proposed for telling mineral phases apart. Everything aims at prevention rather than repair.
pmc-13128431:
Jianyong Wei and eight colleagues mined CT scan textures of carotid plaque and its surrounding fat to predict repeat strokes on the same side. After a first stroke from carotid narrowing, recurrence risk varies widely between patients. The study looked back at patients scanned between 2016 and 2024 and followed them with MRI for recurrence. Software on its own segmented plaque and fat, extracting hundreds of radiomic features.

Three models competed: clinical factors alone, radiomics alone, and both combined, across five learning algorithms. The best was chosen by skill in telling cases apart, and cross-checked again and again. Fat around the artery carries a swelling signal that plain stenosis percentages miss. A model that can be read matters in the clinic, since prevention decisions like surgery need justification. The 2026 work pushes stroke prediction from a single narrowing measurement toward tissue characterization.
pmc-13128631:
Lina Stagneth and co-authors set out in 2026 a study plan on holding attention in older hospital patients. Keeping focus matters for walking, driving, and conversation, and it fades with age and brain disease. The SENSE-AGE study will look for brain-wave markers of that fading.

The plan enrolls 120 geriatric patients. Each will do attention tasks and rest while a 32-channel cap records brain activity. The team will also test thinking skills and ask about fatigue, sleep, and quality of life. Fifty patients will repeat the tests after two to three weeks of standard geriatric treatment. The hope is an objective marker for early detection and better targeting of care.
pmc-13133331:
Mohamed Rami Mahmoud and three co-authors built a new way to grade satellite reads of an invasive weed. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, deals with water hyacinth in Lake Tana, Ethiopia. This lake feeds the Blue Nile, and the weed chokes its surface. Field surveys are too sparse to grade the reads by ground truth. Their frame grades them by how well they track weather and water drivers, a known stand in path.

They ran eleven years of reads from three satellite lines through eleven methods. Two Sentinel based marks scored best on their coherence scale. Readers who watch lakes get a way to trust space reads when boots on the ground are few.
pmc-13134931:
Ibtisam Haidar and eight co-authors measure how often diabetes patients in Morocco skip their medicines, in a 2025 study. Missing doses of type 2 diabetes drugs leads to poor blood sugar control and more complications. The study ran in the endocrinology department of a university hospital in Casablanca. Three hundred twenty-nine adult patients took part, and their adherence was scored with a standard eight-item scale.

Just over half of the patients showed low adherence. The team used statistical models to link poor adherence with social, clinical, treatment, and behavior factors. Naming the strongest drivers helps clinics target support where it counts, such as simpler dosing or cost relief. The findings give Moroccan health planners local numbers instead of guesses borrowed from other countries.
pmc-13136931: Farnaz Araghi and colleagues report a pigmented skin cancer near the anus that mimicked melanoma. Their case report from twenty twenty-six stresses early checks of lasting lesions. Pigmented basal cell carcinoma is rare in the anal area. Its dark look can fool clinicians into expecting melanoma instead. Tissue study and immune staining settled the true diagnosis in this case. The authors urge prompt surgical care once the diagnosis is clear. Mild symptoms and embarrassment should not delay examination of such lesions, they argue.
pmc-13146931:
Jagat Pal Yadav tested whether blocking an inflammation switch in the brain can limit stroke damage. The switch, called the NLRP3 inflammasome, drives swelling and cell death after a stroke blocks blood flow. Yadav used a rat model of stroke to test a drug that targets it. The drug, MCC950, is known to block this pathway with precision.

Forty-eight rats had a brain artery blocked for a short time. Half got the drug when flow returned and again a day later, and half got a dummy shot. Treated rats had brain damage about a third smaller than controls. Their movement and nerve scores were better at one and three days. Levels of the switch and its partner proteins fell sharply, and the blood-brain barrier held up better. No side effects appeared.
pmc-13149631:
Paola Alberti and co-authors review whether a blood protein can warn which cancer patients will suffer nerve damage from chemotherapy. The side effect affects about 70 percent of patients on certain drugs, and roughly 30 percent keep chronic symptoms that erode daily life. The candidate marker, serum neurofilament light chain, rises when nerve fibres are injured. The review grew out of an expert workshop that weighed the evidence and the gaps.

Eleven studies found that rises in the marker after two or three chemotherapy doses tracked how severe the nerve damage later became. Yet marker levels varied widely between studies, as did the drugs, doses, and measures used, so the experts judged it not ready for routine care. The authors lay out the validation steps still needed and the barriers to bringing any such marker into clinics.
pmc-13152931:
Poor sleep is easy to overlook when cancer is advanced, yet it shadows everything else. Shauna Munir, Eva Jones, Faith Precious Omeokwe, and Andrew Neil Davies scope the literature on insomnia in palliative care. Four databases were searched from the start, plus hand searching. Studies needed a validated sleep tool or an objective measure. Sixteen studies qualified.

Disturbed sleep traveled with fatigue, drowsiness, anxiety, and depression. Quality of life suffered, and survival ran shorter. The authors call insomnia an orphan symptom in this setting. They urge teams to screen every palliative patient for it. When found, it deserves full assessment and treatment like any other symptom.
pmc-13155431:
Flore Vancompernolle Vromman and five colleagues test an explainable AI tool that predicts well-being from lifestyle data, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. Well-being drives public health, yet it rests on many shifting factors. Their first study built a simple, regularized model from a small set of lifestyle and setting factors. The second study tested how different kinds of explanation shaped user satisfaction with the tool's feedback.

More than twelve hundred people took part in the final sample. Any explanation beat none. Visual and interactive explanations scored highest, with text and number formats close behind. The authors argue that clear explanations build the trust such tools need to help people reflect on their lives.
pmc-13157631:
Steffani Simone and co-authors published a 2026 case report on a rare injury: bleeding inside the gallbladder after a blow to the belly, with the gallbladder wall intact and the liver unharmed. Gallbladder injury from blunt trauma is uncommon, and bleeding into it without a tear is rarer still. The patient was a fifty-five-year-old man with upper belly pain after chest and abdominal trauma.

A first scan showed a swollen gallbladder holding dense fluid. A second scan with contrast dye caught dye leaking into the gallbladder, proof of active bleeding. Since the man was stable, doctors first managed him without surgery. Later scans showed the gallbladder fully filled with dense material and its wall slightly thickened. That change led to removal of the gallbladder by keyhole surgery. The authors stress how repeated scans with contrast can reveal this hidden injury.
pmc-13164731:
Michał Musiał and co-authors soak a natural zeolite mineral with paraffin wax and find the mix stores more heat than the wax alone explains. Their study appeared in 2026. Phase change materials bank heat by melting and release it by freezing. Loading wax into porous clinoptilolite kept it from leaking when liquid. Measured melting and freezing enthalpies beat the values expected from wax content alone, by about fourteen percent at half wax and forty-four percent at forty percent wax.

The team also found the loading level where leakage stays at zero, and confirmed the two parts do not react chemically. The authors credit the mineral's pores with organizing the wax into a more favorable structure, a cheap upgrade for building heat storage.
pmc-13165531:
Perlinski, Faltynski, and Swietlicka set two AI ways to spot falls on heat shots. One way, GCN, reads bone maps as web forms for its picks. One way, YOLO, hunts forms in each shot frame on sight. Heat shots let the pair work in dark rooms with no lamp. The GCN form tops 99 percent on its sort scores. It reads both flat and deep bone maps in the runs.

YOLOv8 gets timed for live spot work on heat frames. Each way has clear strong points in the head-to-head runs. YOLO pins where a form sits in the frame fast. GCN reads how the form moves through the fall path. A mixed frame pairs both skills for field use next. Old-age care and ward watch stand as the use case.
pmc-13167331:
Fei Le and co-authors review immunotherapy for head and neck cancer in a 2026 paper. This cancer ranks seventh worldwide, and tumors driven by HPV respond better to immune drugs than those driven by carcinogens. The review centers on PD-1 and PD-L1 blockade.

Landmark trials made two checkpoint drugs standard for recurrent or spread disease, adding months of survival over older regimens. Combinations with chemotherapy, radiation, or other antibodies push results further. A recent trial of surgery-time immunotherapy doubled event-free survival. The review also covers immune side effects and what comes beyond checkpoint blockade.
pmc-13167631:
Jarno Hakkers and four co-authors test added bone reconstruction in implant infection surgery in a 2026 trial. Peri-implantitis destroys bone around dental implants and can loosen them. Whether rebuilding the defect during surgery beats cleaning alone was untested for deep-walled defects.

Fifty-two patients were randomly split between standard surgery and surgery plus reconstruction with their own bone, a graft, and a membrane. Probing depth and bone level on scans were the main measures after one year. Bleeding around the implant and full disease resolution were also tracked. Statistical models handled repeated measures within patients. The trial focuses on defects with three or four remaining walls, where grafts stay contained. Results guide dentists choosing how aggressive implant salvage surgery should be.
pmc-13172431:
Minsuk Yang led a team hunting for gene-signal patterns in childhood asthma in a 2026 study. Asthma varies a lot between children, and so does response to treatment. Tiny gene regulators called microRNAs may mark distinct forms of the illness. The team profiled these regulators in hundreds of children from a long-running program.

Grouping by those profiles gave three clusters, each with its own signal pattern and pathway themes. Basic traits looked alike across clusters, but lung response to a steroid drug differed. Two clusters fared better after treatment than the third. Blood cell counts further shaped the picture inside clusters. The work hints these patterns could guide care.
pmc-13177031:
Dimitry S Davydow and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six Danish registry study linking air pollution to Lewy body and Parkinson-related dementias. Fine particles and nitrogen dioxide were the exposures of interest. Evidence for these specific dementias was limited before.

Nationwide records identified cases diagnosed over two decades. Each case was matched with ten controls by age, sex, and time. Average pollution exposure over the prior ten years was estimated per person. Statistical models adjusted step by step for social and economic factors. The study adds registry-scale evidence to the air and brain health debate.
pmc-13179731:
Christopher Russell and co-authors ask whether antibiotics can stop early when a sick child tests positive for a virus in work dated two thousand twenty-six. The children all have tracheostomies, neck tubes that aid breathing, and were in hospital with suspected bacterial infection of the airway. A fast viral test that comes back positive hints the germ may not be bacterial.

Six children's hospitals pooled over five hundred stays from two thousand twenty-one to two thousand twenty-four. The team linked early stopping to stay length, later intensive care moves, death, and return stays within thirty days, using models that balance background traits. The aim is to trim drug use without harm, a live question in children's wards.
pmc-13181131: Julian Keil and co-authors show that a moving pattern of light spots can raise fast brain rhythms in mice, in a 2026 study. Flicker therapy usually floods the whole view at once, yet the eye and brain filter out fast rates. Their staged flicker steps across space in sequence, which slips past that filter. In the mouse visual cortex, power rose in the band from one hundred to one hundred ninety cycles per second. The authors propose staged input as a fresh way to lift fast rhythms.
pmc-13186231:
Raquel Amado and co-authors published this 2026 real-world study on treating dark circles under the eyes. The injected product is a gel of polynucleotides, DNA fragments purified from trout, sold under the name PN HPT. It adds volume at once and is said to rebuild the tissue under the skin over time.

The open study followed 61 adults treated at clinics in several countries, each with three injections spaced a few weeks apart. Photos taken one and three months after the last session were compared with the starting images for color and pigment changes. Both the treating specialists and the patients judged the results. Studies like this test how a cosmetic treatment performs outside strict trials.
pmc-13191231:
Mei-he Long and co-authors present a 2026 study of a feed additive pair, benzoic acid plus cinnamon essential oil, against necrotic enteritis in broiler chickens. The gut disease, driven by a Clostridium bacterium, costs poultry producers heavily, and antibiotic limits keep tightening. The team tested whether the blend protects growth and gut health under challenge.

Three hundred day-old broilers were split into five groups with six replicates each. Controls ate the plain diet, challenged birds were infected, and three groups got low, medium, or high doses of the blend. Growth, antioxidant measures, immune markers, and gut condition were compared, to find a dose that shields birds without drugs.
pmc-13193931:
Emma Hilby and Molly McCue study how behavior predicts assistance dog careers in a paper from 2026. Assistance dogs take varied jobs, from alerting partners to medical changes to fetching items on request. A poor career fit can stress the dog and waste training. The team analyzed records from six organizations in the United States and Canada, covering hundreds of placed dogs and more released from training.

Standard behavior checklists were compared across career types. Dogs slow to settle were more likely to become response dogs. Strong handler-dog teamwork also raised those odds, as did being male. Alert dogs tended to be more excitable and body sensitive. Facility dogs showed a distinct profile of their own.
pmc-13196531:
Zhiyong Rao and six co-authors feed broiler chickens an enzyme that breaks down a feed toxin and track the gains, in a 2026 journal article. The toxin, aflatoxin B1, spoils feed across the trade and harms the liver. The enzyme, CotA, is a fresh oxidase that can disarm it.

The trial split 432 day old chicks into four groups: plain feed, toxin feed, enzyme feed, and both. Toxin birds weighed about a tenth less at day forty-two and wasted more feed. Their breast meat also lost more water in storage and cooking. Enzyme birds kept near normal weight and meat quality, and their liver cells stayed sound. Tests tied the guard to less toxin left in the liver and a block on iron linked cell death.
pmc-13196631:
Dirk van Lier and colleagues report a 2026 safety study of Procizumab in animals. Procizumab is an antibody drug that blocks DPP3, an enzyme released in shock that breaks down signals controlling blood vessel tone. Before human use, the team had to check harm in rodents and primates.

Mice and monkeys got the drug by vein on four days at several dose levels. Blood tests showed fast, dose-linked peaks and quick clearing. The drug cut DPP3 activity at once, as planned. No deaths or organ damage were tied to the drug. Some blood enzyme rises in monkeys reversed on their own. The clean results supported a first safety trial in humans.
pmc-13196931:
Tao Luo, Qingpeng Huang, and Jingyan Mai published a 2026 study of young farmers in Guangdong Province, China. More young people are entering agriculture there. Their skills shape rural development directly. The study drew on interviews and questionnaires. Twenty-one cities supplied the data.

Careers were traced in three stages. Entering, settling, and growing a farm business differ. Skills fell into three levels as well. Technical skills form the base. General abilities and core literacy sit above. Each level needs its own training style. Results can guide talent programs and rural policy. Supporting young farmers means matching training to career stage.
pmc-13197431:
Jesse Koster and colleagues offer a 2026 theory review on crises and social cohesion, the bonds that hold a society together. Crises can unite people or split them, and the path is rarely clear in advance. The authors use interdependence theory, which weighs how much people rely on each other and on the state.

They compare four crisis types: natural hazards, pandemics, economic slumps, and wars. Each type reshapes reliance, fairness of burdens, and whether interests clash or align in its own way. Effects also unfold on distinct time scales. The authors close with lessons to help societies brace for strain, such as watching who bears costs and who can act together.
pmc-13197831:
A team of co-authors presents a study dated two thousand twenty-six on whether blocking a growth switch could treat osteoporosis. The switch, called mTOR, controls cell growth, and animal work suggests blocking it protects bone. Whether that holds in people was unclear.

The authors used Mendelian randomization, a method that treats inherited gene variants as a natural experiment. They asked whether lifelong, genetically higher activity of the switch tracks with lower bone density. Variants near the gene served as the instruments. Data came from large genome studies and gene-expression maps, and several forms of the analysis were combined to test the idea.
pmc-13198131: Juan Mundisugih and Rajiv Mahajan present a 2026 heart case built around a rhythm tracing. An eighty-three-year-old patient came in with palpitations, and repeated tracings showed a fast, narrow-pattern heartbeat that shifted in regularity and shape. Such mixed patterns can hide the cause if read too quickly. The authors show how tracking shape changes across repeated tracings reveals the mechanism at work. Their lesson is that close reading beats quick pattern matching for complex rhythm cases, and a diagnosis then points treatment at the right target.
pmc-13200531:
Faiza Sarwar and colleagues present a 2026 case report on glittering eye particles that mimicked pus. Asteroid hyalosis is a harmless buildup of sparkling particles in the eye's gel. Rarely, a slipped lens lets them drift forward and fake a pus layer, a pattern called pseudohypopyon.

Their patient was a 67-year-old man with sudden painful vision loss in his left eye. His lens had shifted forward, and eye pressure spiked far above the healthy eye. Lamp exam showed the false pus layer in the front chamber. Gel scans confirmed the sparkling deposits behind the lens. Old trauma and weak lens supports set the stage. Spotting this mimic early can spare wrong treatment and save sight.
pmc-13203231:
Zhen Li and co-authors report experiments from two thousand twenty-six on how partners in a joint task remember each other's goals. Working together is more than moving in sync: partners treat the task as something they do as a pair. That shared stance might make a partner's target stick in attention and memory.

Pairs searched for items from different categories, and a trial counted only when both partners answered right. A surprise test later showed people recognized their partner's target items better than distractors, for both living and object stimuli. Attention to partner items also rose in one experiment. In a third, the memory edge survived three days and helped pairs work faster after targets switched. The authors say cognition organizes itself around the shared goal.
pmc-13205031:
Valentin Ivanov and three colleagues report using a fluorescent dye alone to stage breast cancer spread, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Sentinel node biopsy guides axillary treatment decisions. Standard mapping needs radioisotopes, blue dye, or both, each with drawbacks.

Indocyanine green fluorescence was the sole tracer for 260 consecutive patients at one Bulgarian hospital. Surgery took place during two thousand twenty-four and twenty twenty-five. The team measured mapping success, node counts, metastasis detection, and short-term outcomes. Fluorescence-only staging would simplify logistics and avoid radiation handling. Retrospective single-center data cannot settle the question alone. The cohort adds real-world numbers to a growing comparison with conventional tracers.
pmc-13206031:
Albina Kaumenova and a large team of co-authors published this dairy study in 2026. It tackles a plain waste problem: cheese making leaves behind whey, a thin liquid rich in protein. The team mixed milk and whey in ten set blends, with whey shares from low to high, and checked what each blend held.

They used light-based scans and lab tests to map fat, protein, and amino acids in each mix. A scoring method then weighed food value, balance, and wise use of a by-product in one index. Mid-range blends beat the extremes, and the mix with thirty percent whey scored best of all. The work shows food plants a clear way to pick blend ratios that waste less whey and keep drinks rich in protein.
pmc-13208031:
Kexin Qu and eight colleagues published a kidney cancer study in two thousand twenty-six on a water-channel protein called AQP9. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma spreads early, and spread drives its poor outcomes. The team asked what AQP9 does in this cancer and whether it can be blocked.

AQP9 was higher in tumours than in healthy tissue and marked worse survival. Removing it slowed growth, movement, and invasion in cells, while adding it sped those traits through a signalling pathway. Computer screening flagged the antibiotic tedizolid as a binder of AQP9. The drug reversed the protein's effects in cells and in mouse tumours. The authors propose AQP9 as both a warning marker and a drug target.
pmc-13208931:
Cosmina-Theodora Vulpescu and co-authors published a review in 2026 on fatty liver and artery disease in diabetes. Fatty liver tied to metabolism is common in type 2 diabetes. Whether it drives artery hardening on its own is disputed, with studies split by method and group.

The review followed standard rules and searched three databases for studies from the past decade. Most kept studies looked at one point in time; only one followed patients forward. Fatty liver tied to more plaque growth in neck arteries, even in lean patients. Links to wall thickness measures clashed across studies. Liver scarring tied to vessel aging more strongly than fat alone. The authors call for uniform, forward-looking studies to settle the question.
pmc-13209631:
Chenguang Wang and a team of co-authors set a three arm plan to judge a factory change for a biosimilar drug. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, deals with CMAB007, a China cleared copy of omalizumab. After clearance, its process was tuned: media was honed and one clean step swapped. Yield rose five fold with the same host cell line. Such shifts demand strict proof that quality and care acts hold.

The team set new make, old make, and the origin drug side by side. Key quality traits were tiered by risk, each tier with its own pass marks. Deep lab reads checked shape and build. Readers in drug making get a tiered bridge for post clearance change.
pmc-13210131:
Luana dos Anjos and co-authors review guanidine compounds against neglected tropical diseases in a 2026 article. These diseases, caused by protozoan parasites, burden low and middle income countries heavily. Guanidine groups carry a strong positive charge and bond readily, making them attractive building blocks for drug design.

The review sums up a decade of work on compounds active against Chagas disease, sleeping sickness, leishmaniasis, and several other infections. Studies cover synthetic, natural, and repurposed drugs. The group appears to tune activity by changing charge, bonding, and physical traits, acting on enzymes, DNA, and parasite membranes.
pmc-13212831:
Amber Nehan Kashif and co-authors model in 2026 how wasted energy arises in a flowing nanofluid that also carries swimming microbes. The fluid passes a stretching vertical sheet inside a porous material, under sunlight-like radiation and mixed convection.

Their equations include drag effects beyond the classic porous-flow law, plus delayed heat and mass transfer rather than instant responses. Solved semi-analytically, the model shows how each factor shifts speed, temperature, concentration, and disorder production. Raising one fluid parameter slowed the flow, while a particle-drift factor lifted temperature and concentration. Disorder fell with some factors and rose with others. Results may guide solar collectors and medical devices using such fluids.
pmc-13213131:
Linda Carolina Henao-Rodríguez and colleagues study in 2026 why some Colombian homes save water when their towns have plenty of it but the water is not safe to drink. Past work on saving dealt with dry areas, not with places where dirt in the water drives the choice.

They used a 2024 survey of 4,246 homes in 13 towns with high risk scores for bad water. With two kinds of models, they asked which social and home traits predict saving steps, from cheap ones to costly ones. They also gauged how much the mere sense that water is dirty pushes homes to save. Schooling and wealth stood out among the traits that mattered in the early results.
pmc-13213331:
Yuri Narusawa and a large team describe in 2026 an ovarian cancer whose two components looked deceptively mild under the microscope. Carcinosarcomas mix gland-like cancer with fleshy sarcoma tissue and usually appear high grade, making this case hard to classify.

The patient, a woman in her forties with endometriosis, had tumours in both ovaries removed along with her womb. Most of one tumour resembled a benign fetal muscle growth, with only a small patch of clear cell cancer. A year later the sarcoma part spread to her lungs, and she died twenty-nine months after surgery despite chemotherapy. Gene sequencing found shared mutations in both parts, proving a single origin.
pmc-13214431:
Knees that cave inward on landing raise injury risk for young women athletes. Nizami Chalabiyev and co-authors asked whether muscle tone and stiffness, not just activation, explain the pattern. Thirty-six volleyball players aged twelve to eighteen split evenly by a one-leg squat test. A handheld device measured tone, elasticity, and stiffness of leg muscles. Sensors timed and sized muscle firing during spike landings.

The inward group showed higher tone and stiffness ratios between paired muscles. Two key muscles fired weaker and later in that group. Yet no single measure predicted the landing angle in the final model. The authors argue that tissue properties deserve a place beside activation in screening. Ratios between muscle pairs may matter more than any one muscle.
pmc-13214831:
Orna Levran and co-authors compare gene marks between two paths out of opioid addiction in a 2026 paper. One group stays on methadone, a daily drug that blocks cravings. The other group has stayed clean for over ten years with no such drug. Chemical marks on DNA, which tune gene activity, may differ between the two paths.

Blood DNA from 114 people on methadone and 136 people long abstinent was read on a chip that scans the whole genome. A total of 135 mark sites differed at a strict level of proof. The sites map to 157 genes, many of them long non-coding genes. The pattern may hint at how each route reshapes the body's gene settings.
pmc-13215631:
Sakshi Setia and co-authors published a 2026 evaluation of a storytelling chatbot rolled out in Brazilian schools to build teenagers' skills in supporting peers' mental health. The chatbot, named Cadê o Kauê?, struggled during its first school implementation phase.

The team interviewed project members in Brazil and the United Kingdom and mapped their accounts onto the NASSS framework, which sorts implementation problems into technology, organization, and wider system domains. Weak internet access, uneven school infrastructure, and varying teacher readiness stood out. The authors recommend offline options, more teacher training, and whole-school engagement so the tool fits Brazil's shifting social and political context.
pmc-13216131:
Mutinta Malawo Matungu and co-authors present a 2026 review of lead pollution in soils around African mining areas. Lead does not break down in the environment, and it reaches people through dust and through crops grown in contaminated ground.

Following PRISMA guidelines, the team gathered 92 peer-reviewed articles published between 2000 and 2024. Soil lead levels in West and Southern Africa exceeded permitted limits, while monitoring was patchy in the north and east. Lead accumulated in food crops, with children facing the sharpest health risks. Plant-based cleanup helped, especially with biochar added, but results varied with local conditions. The authors call for cheaper local methods and a unified monitoring framework across the continent.
pmc-13216531:
Alia A. Othman and Dina A. Elmanakhly present a 2026 algorithms paper on planning flight paths for drones that carry mobile edge computing servers. Battery limits make every metre and hover count, so the route itself becomes an energy problem to optimize.

Their algorithm, FGODE, mates a fungal growth optimizer with differential evolution, mixing wide exploration with local refinement. Supporting tricks include a greedy rule for ordering stop points, opposition-based learning for elite candidates, and Gaussian mutation to escape stalls. In benchmark experiments the hybrid beat several established optimization algorithms on energy-related measures. The authors present it as a practical planner for drone-assisted computing services that must serve ground devices without draining the aircraft.
pmc-13217431:
Ying Zhu and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study asking whether years of anti-VEGF eye injections, the standard rescue for wet age-related macular degeneration, quietly damage the retina's own blood vessels. Imaging that maps those vessels in fine detail made the question testable.

The study followed 164 eyes from 107 patients for an average of 34 months; injected eyes received about thirteen injections. Baseline vessel measures matched between injected and non-injected eyes. Over follow-up, nearly every vascular metric changed identically in both groups. Only the foveal avascular zone grew marginally more in injected eyes, and no vessel change tracked with vision change. The authors conclude that repeated injections leave retinal vasculature essentially unharmed.
pmc-13218131:
Billy Vinette and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for a realist review of continuing education for oncology nurses. Nurses are central to high-quality cancer care, yet their uptake of evidence-based practices stays inconsistent even though continuing education is widely used to promote it. A realist review asks a different question: how, why, for whom, and in which settings does education actually change practice?

The review will follow established realist synthesis standards and use the Theoretical Domains Framework to organize possible mechanisms of change. The team has drafted 33 initial programme theories, built from the framework, earlier reviews, expert input, and consultation with oncology nurses and managers. Systematic searches across five databases, covering English and French literature from high-income countries, will test and refine those theories. Findings will be shared through open-access publications and conferences, with nursing associations involved to keep the conclusions clinically useful.
pmc-13220831:
Yingyuan Yu and a large dermatology team build genetic prediction models for therapy response in psoriasis in a 2026 study. Narrow-band ultraviolet B phototherapy is effective, cheap, and safe for psoriasis, yet patients vary in how they clear and who suffers side effects, and clinicians have had no way to forecast. Two hundred fifty-two patients received twelve weeks while they collected data and blood for scanning.

The scan flagged variant markers in genes as tied to early improvement at four weeks, to reaching the seventy-five percent milestone by week twelve, and to adverse events. Variants near a potassium gene and in two genes marked the side-effect risk. Prediction models from these signals discriminated responders with accuracy between 0.80 and 0.85. The authors note the threshold used, which was looser than the strictest standard, stating that external cohorts must validate the models before a clinic should act on them.
pmc-13222031:
Xu Li and colleagues rank acupuncture combinations paired with core stability training aimed at chronic nonspecific low back pain, in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Thirty-two randomized trials with 2,726 patients were pooled from eight databases searched through March 2025. Pain and disability scores were the main outcomes, with safety tracked where reported.

Combinations generally outperformed single interventions. Moxibustion plus training on unstable surfaces ranked highest for pain relief, though the supporting evidence was limited. Reported side effects were usually mild and uncommon, but safety reporting was patchy across trials. The authors present the ranking as guidance for clinicians and policy makers, with clear warnings about evidence gaps.
pmc-13222631:
Anastasios Chatzichidiroglou and co-authors report superior mesenteric artery syndrome in a 17-year-old boy, in a 2026 case report. The syndrome squeezes the duodenum between two major arteries, blocking food passage. He had endured two years of nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, early fullness, and growing abdominal swelling before a recent sharp worsening.

CT imaging finally showed the artery angle narrowed to about ten degrees, with the stomach and upper duodenum hugely dilated. A nasal tube drained the stomach and nutrition support followed, easing the acute crisis without surgery. Six months on, weight gain remained poor, underlining that clearing the blockage is not curing the condition.
pmc-13223031: Miaowei Wang and Dae-Keun Jeong report a case of ultrashort wave therapy for a pus-filled ear cartilage infection that followed surgery for chronic ear disease, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Care for this ill is long and complex when drugs and surgery stand alone. The case adds physiotherapy of this wave kind to surgery and antimicrobial care. The mix lifts the effect of care and shortens the time to heal. The authors urge wider use of such a team approach.
pmc-13223231:

A 60-year-old man under observation for chronic lymphocytic leukemia developed painful purple skin lesions and leg ulcers that would not heal. pmc-13224031:

Microfracture surgery pokes small holes in bone to spark cartilage repair, but the new tissue is usually the weaker fibrous kind. The team traced why that happens and tested a gel designed to steer repair toward the glassy, durable kind.

pmc-13231631:
Ben Hood and colleagues examine in 2026 how patient and public involvement really works inside United Kingdom clinical research. Forty interviews covered lay contributors, trial sponsors, involvement leads, and ethics committee members.

Stronger infrastructure, earlier involvement, and better proof of impact are proposed so contributors shape research rather than decorate it.
pmc-13233631:
Luana dos Santos Souza and colleagues published a 2026 randomized trial report on filling worn tooth necks, lesions not caused by decay. The trial tested ethanol-wet bonding, where pure ethanol prepares the dentin before glue is applied, against standard water-wet bonding, across four adhesive combinations. One hundred forty-eight lesions were filled with the same composite material and reviewed over six years.

Survival was highest for the standard water-wet group, followed by two ethanol groups using water-friendly adhesives. The ethanol group paired with a water-repelling bonding resin failed far more often, with under half surviving. The authors conclude the technique's success depends heavily on adhesive chemistry.
pmc-13234031:
Marcelo Boareto and colleagues published a 2026 modeling study of a drug approach to jet lag and other circadian disorders. The brain's master clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus, is held in sync partly by vasopressin signaling. Blocking its V1a receptor with the drug balovaptan sped up how fast mice resynchronized their activity rhythms after the light schedule jumped six hours, mimicking a long flight east.

It also predicts bigger phase shifts for individuals with longer internal days, pointing to a way to personalize future trial design.
pmc-13234431:
Linda Andersson and colleagues studied in 2026 whether body weight relates to hip dysplasia grades in young adult dogs in Sweden. Hip dysplasia is a common joint disorder that can shorten a dog's healthy life. Screening results and weights came from the Swedish Kennel Club for more than one hundred thousand dogs across many breeds. Records covered the years 2007 through 2016.

Strength of the link differed by breed, showing that genetics and size shape the effect. The authors suggest keeping weight lower may help protect against severe hip disease. Screening programs could use the finding when advising breeders and owners about growth and feeding.
pmc-13235031:
Shima Asghari and co-authors review stem cells from dental pulp as a source for rebuilding teeth and gum tissue, in work from twenty twenty-six. These cells can copy themselves and turn into several tissue types. Studies from twenty ten to twenty twenty-five span dishes, animals, and early human trials.

Animal work rebuilt pulp, dentin, ligament, cement, and jaw bone. Human trials found the cells safe and saw better pulp life and gum measures. Small samples and mixed methods temper the claims. Standard protocols are the next need.
pmc-13235231:
George F. Pavis and co-authors trialled in 2026 a coffee cherry extract in trained cyclists to test effects on performance and recovery fuel. The extract concentrates caffeine and plant polyphenols from the whole coffee fruit, usually discarded during processing. pmc-13236631:
Wongelawit Zerihun and colleagues report a heart attack case in a man with alpha-gal syndrome. Their case report from twenty twenty-six links a tick-related food allergy to heart disease. The syndrome causes allergic reactions to red meat after lone star tick bites. Newer evidence ties it to faster artery clogging as well.

Stent treatment opened the blocked artery successfully. His only notable history was the alpha-gal syndrome itself. The authors warn that this allergy may carry real heart risks.
pmc-13236731:
Levy and colleagues describe seven years of running a cardiovascular tissue bank inside an Israeli hospital. Frozen human heart valves and vessel tissues, called homografts, are vital for repairing hearts, above all in children, where man-made options are limited. Sheba Medical Center built a bank meeting good manufacturing practice rules inside the public health system.

The paper shares how the bank was run from 2018 to 2025 and what it delivered in care. Tissue banking is logistics as much as medicine: donors, testing, storage, and rapid supply to theatres. Their account gives other hospitals a working model for a service patients never see but often depend on.
pmc-13237531:
Ya-Lan Chiu and co-authors built and tested a virtual reality system in 2026 for measuring neck sensorimotor control, the sense of where the head is and how it moves. Thirty healthy adults took five VR tests covering neck range of motion, position sense, head-tilt response, a figure-of-eight movement task, and postural sway. Everyone repeated the tests a week later, and VR scores were checked against laboratory motion capture and clinical tools.

Scores repeated well, with reliability statistics mostly in the good to excellent range. VR measures also matched the reference methods closely across the tasks. The authors present the headset system as a standardized, user-friendly alternative to the complex rigs clinics usually need. Neck pain care is the intended first application.
pmc-13239131:
Andrew A. Davinack simulated repeated gene flooding in 2026, testing a proposed invasion-control tactic where inbred individuals are released again and again to swamp a resident population's genes. Earlier work had shown resident alleles can collapse under sustained influx, but the governing dynamics were unclear. Davinack varied migration intensity in forward-time population genetic simulations with density regulation.
