The threshold held up across changes in mating structure and in how worse-off the migrants were, pointing to sheer influx as the dominant driver. The results warn managers that gene flooding may do nothing until it suddenly does a great deal.
pmc-13239331:
Sami Ur Rehman and colleagues report a 2026 intensive care case involving a young woman who took a deliberate overdose of three prescription medicines. The drugs were amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant, plus perindopril and amlodipine, which lower blood pressure and slow the heart.

On arrival her blood pressure was dangerously low, her heart raced, and blood tests showed severe acid build-up. Clinicians gave fluids, strong drugs to support circulation, and sodium bicarbonate for the antidepressant poisoning. After advice from a poisons service they added high-dose insulin with sugar, a treatment aimed at the calcium channel blocker. The report shows how combined overdoses need several treatments running at once.
pmc-13239431:
Stephenson and colleagues map every registry that tracks people with Klinefelter syndrome. The condition, where males carry an extra X chromosome, affects health across the lifespan, yet organised data on patients is scattered. Their scoping review hunts through many sources for registries that collect such data, and records what each one actually gathers.

A key question is whether any registry exists for this syndrome alone. Registries drive research on rare conditions by pooling patients no single clinic could study. The map shows where data sit, what is missing, and how a future dedicated registry should be built, which is the authors' stated purpose for the work.
pmc-13239931:
Umaimah Batool Mirza and co-authors describe a double hepatitis infection in a teenager in a 2026 case report. Hepatitis A and hepatitis E both spread through contaminated water and food, and together they can produce unusual presentations that complicate diagnosis in regions where sanitation is poor.

A previously healthy 14-year-old girl developed nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite, then sudden jaundice with dark urine but no fever or pain. Blood tests confirmed fresh infection with both viruses, and ultrasound showed a swollen-looking liver pattern nicknamed starry sky. Fluids and symptom relief alone brought steady recovery, and she remained well at a two-week check with normal tests.
pmc-13240131:
Saachi Bhattessa, Tirth Dave, and Priti Modi present a case linking fibromyalgia with past Epstein-Barr virus infection in a 2026 report. Fibromyalgia causes widespread pain, fatigue, and thinking problems without objective test findings, which makes diagnosis contentious and slow when other conditions overlap.

The authors use their patient to argue that testing for past Epstein-Barr infection can add useful context. People with fibromyalgia often carry raised antibody levels against the virus, suggesting the immune response after infection may feed into symptoms. Such testing cannot diagnose the condition on its own, they stress, but it can reduce uncertainty while clinicians work through the standard criteria and rule out other causes.
pmc-13240731:
Rabia Idrees and co-authors present a 2026 laboratory study of lead harm in developing chick embryos. Lead is a toxic heavy metal that can disturb growth before birth. The team tested whether vitamins B6 and B12 together could reduce that harm.

Lead exposure produced head, eye, beak, spine, and limb defects, along with higher embryo deaths. Embryos receiving both lead and the vitamin pair fared better than those given lead alone. The results suggest the two vitamins can soften lead-driven developmental damage, a finding with possible relevance for polluted environments.
pmc-13242031:
Yi Cai and a large team present a 2026 study of a light-activated molecule shaped to attack tumor DNA directly. In a mouse breast cancer model after surgery, one treatment during the operation prevented local regrowth, built immune memory, and slowed distant tumors and lung spread. pmc-13242131:

Users detailed their chosen modalities, monthly spending, and distress levels. Most German CAM sits outside insurance reimbursement.

Blood cancer patients spent the most, near two hundred thirty euros. More modalities meant proportionally higher monthly bills, feeding financial toxicity risk.
pmc-13242831:

pmc-13245531:
Camila A Picchio and colleagues review care models for hepatitis B and C across Europe in a 2026 Series paper. An estimated 29 million people in the WHO European region live with chronic infection. Deaths from viral hepatitis now pass those from HIV and tuberculosis combined.

Point-of-care tests and services based where patients already are show clear gains. Big gaps remain: many infections stay unfound, and at-risk groups face unfair access. The authors say 2030 goals need faster case finding and broader care.
pmc-13245931:
Chirag Bariya and co-authors build and pilot a digital skills framework for India's frontline health workers in this 2026 study. pmc-13248031:

The pooled trials, few and short with small crossover designs, showed short-term improvements in selected measures such as cardiac output and ejection fraction. pmc-13248531:

The applicant sought three additional processes, bringing the total to six.

The highest estimate was about half a milligram per kilogram of body weight each day in European populations. Judged against the earlier safety work, the panel found no concern under the revised conditions of use.
pmc-13249631:

pmc-13249731:

pmc-13250231:

pmc-13250631:

pmc-13251731:

pmc-13252731:

pmc-13253431:

pmc-13254231:

pmc-13254931:

pmc-13255031:

pmc-13255231:

pmc-13255531:

pmc-13256231:

pmc-13256431:

pmc-13257131:

pmc-13257531:

pmc-13257631:

pmc-13257731:

pmc-13258031:

The authors say the light method may help surgeons place entry points more safely in such eyes.
pmc-13259031:

Chattering fell clearly against a standard terminal sliding controller.
pmc-13259431:

pmc-13260031:

pmc-13260131:

The team tracked key molecules for cell energy and redox balance, meaning the balance of oxidation and reduction reactions, including NAD-related compounds and ATP, the cell's main energy currency.

Exposure rapidly oxidized those molecules and drained total NAD content over time, while the cells stayed alive. Treated cells partly lost ATP and could not raise lactate production when their breathing chain was blocked. Blocking certain enzymes called PARPs lessened the NAD and ATP losses and preserved that backup energy response. After the stress ended, cells given a NAD precursor restored their levels and function.
pmc-13260431:
Mengyao Ma and co-authors fed in 2026 adult beagle dogs a supplement of postbiotics made from Bifidobacterium animalis for 42 days. Postbiotics are non-living bacterial products that may benefit health without the storage problems of live probiotics. Dogs received a plain diet or one of two supplement doses.

Growth and routine blood measures did not change, yet several health markers improved. Antibody levels rose, while inflammatory signals such as tumor necrosis factor fell in both dose groups. Defense enzymes against oxidative damage climbed, and bone formation markers rose at the higher dose. Coat quality improved, with smoother hair cuticles and richer amino acid content. Stool chemistry and gut bacteria also shifted toward a friendlier mix, with more helpful species and fewer potential pathogens.
pmc-13260831:
Eric Kenji Lee and eleven colleagues present PhysMAP, a framework that names neuron types from electrical recordings in living animals. To record many neurons at once is routine, but knowing which cell type each one is remains hard. PhysMAP borrows from multi-omics analysis: it weighs several recording features together to build clear representations. Applied to seven data sets, those representations matched genetically defined cell types better than any single feature set.

That match let the framework label cell types even without ground truth in new recordings. Labels could also transfer from marked data sets to unmarked ones. Inferred types showed traits consistent with their supposed identities. The method even exposes batch effects that skew typing. For systems neuroscience, sound cell typing unlocks circuit level reading of behavior experiments.
pmc-13261431:
Jianlong Wang and colleagues tested in 2026 two additives for water-based drilling mud used in a troublesome Pakistani shale. Drilling mud must carry cuttings and limit fluid loss, yet the Ranikot shale swells and sheds sand when wet. Their mix paired a zinc oxide and carbon nanotube composite with a natural biopolymer, tuned through thirteen designed experiments.

Raising the composite dose cut fluid loss volume from 26 milliliters to about a quarter of that amount. Shale swelling likewise plunged from over seventeen percent to under six percent at the top dose. The composite's long fibers thread into tiny pores and bridge them shut, blocking water entry. The biopolymer added little, and too much of it tangled and clumped, undoing the even spread. Statistical checks confirmed the composite drove both gains.
pmc-13261631:
Rui Wang and colleagues assessed in 2026 whether gene sequencing of patient samples helps diagnose invasive fungal infections in intensive care. Many such infections strike patients without the classic risk factors, and standard tests miss fungi often. Their review covered 106 adults treated between mid-2022 and early 2025, split by immune status.

Two thirds of the patients had working immune systems, though many carried other illnesses. Sequencing found most of the 81 pathogens identified overall and excelled at rare fungi and mixed infections where standard tests fell short. Its results changed care for seventy-five patients, about seven in ten. Fluid washed from the lungs gave the most useful samples, while blood gave the least. The authors back sequencing as a strong add-on, with specimen choice shaping the benefit.
pmc-13263331:
Shunyu Xiang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a smart gel that fights bacterial wilt, a destructive tomato disease. The disease is caused by the bacterium Ralstonia solanacearum and is hard to catch early. The team's hydrogel, a water-holding jelly, has two linked networks that respond to acidity.

When soil turns acidic, as it does in diseased fields, the first network loosens and releases an antibiotic plus zinc. The second network then falls apart, adding an amino acid and more zinc. One root application protected plants for up to fourteen days. In field trials, control lasted up to thirty days and largely preserved the tomato yield.
pmc-13263431:
Jieqiong Chen and seven co-authors test a brain scanning method for newborn injury in a 2026 paper. Oxygen-starved brain injury in newborns lacks objective early markers. The standard spectroscopy method is weak at sensing short-lived chemicals that matter early. Their study used newborn rats with the injury modeled on one side of the brain, confirmed by tissue staining. Both the standard method and a full-intensity alternative were run on a strong animal scanner.

They compared chemical levels between the injured and healthy sides in two brain regions, plus scan quality measures for each method. As the title reports, the new method detected raised taurine and creatine in the injured brain.
pmc-13263731:
Paisit Kosum and colleagues describe a fatty heart tumor hiding in a spot never before reported: the right atrial appendage. Cardiac lipomas are benign and usually silent, found by accident. Their 2026 case began when a sixty-year-old woman arrived with a pulmonary embolism and scans caught a small moving mass.

Magnetic resonance imaging confirmed the lump was fat, consistent with lipoma. It had not caused her embolism, but its mobility in a slow-flow pocket raised fears of blockage and clots. Surgeons removed it through a minimally invasive operation, adjusting cannula plans around the appendage. Tissue examination proved the benign diagnosis.
pmc-13263931:
Lei Li and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on mouth bacteria as noninvasive markers for esophageal cancer, cancer of the food pipe. Early detection matters, yet the standard test, endoscopy, is invasive and costly. The team sequenced bacteria from tongue-coating samples of 440 people: patients with the cancer, healthy controls, and patients after radiotherapy.

Cancer patients carried a more diverse oral community, with more Veillonella, Streptococcus, and Actinomyces and less Porphyromonas and Rothia. A six-marker classifier separated patients from controls with about ninety-four to ninety-five percent accuracy. Radiotherapy shrank diversity, and a separate marker set predicted which patients would progress within six months with about ninety-nine percent accuracy.
pmc-13264031:
Soon Yi and co-authors present a 2026 modeling study on predicting how long therapeutic messenger RNA lasts in solution. RNA breaks down mainly by hydrolysis, a chemical reaction with water, and structure can shield vulnerable sites. Broad measures such as overall folding energy miss local weak points along the molecule, so predictions have stayed imprecise.

The authors show that fine-scale pairing odds for each position add information beyond global measures. Combining local and global features gave a compact four-feature model named STRAND. It cut prediction error by more than half compared with earlier machine learning approaches and held up across different transcripts. Designers gain a simple, interpretable tool for choosing more stable RNA sequences.
pmc-13264431:
Nelson M H Teo and co-authors wrote a 2026 case report and literature review on cystic squamous cell carcinoma, a skin cancer that grows as a cyst rather than a solid lump. Its mild look often delays care. The paper aims to clear up how this form shows itself and how it should be handled.

Their patient was a 55-year-old man with a scalp lump that had no clear bad signs. He wanted it removed because it bothered him. A first cut-out showed the cystic cancer under the microscope, so a wider cut followed, and he healed well. The authors note that case reports are rising, and they urge wide removal and scans once lab tests confirm this cancer.
pmc-13264531:
Mei Zhang and a large team report a 2026 trial of a glucose sensor worn for 15 days by adults with diabetes in China. The device tracks sugar levels all day without finger pricks. The team checked its accuracy and safety at many sites, on both the upper arm and the belly.

Seventy-four people took part, each wearing four sensors. Readings on the arm differed from lab values by 8.44 percent on average, and on the belly by 8.91 percent. Agreement within set limits topped 94 percent at both sites. On standard error grids, almost all readings fell in the safe zones. The authors say the system stayed accurate and safe across the full wear period.
pmc-13264731:
Shutong Shao and colleagues develop a nomogram to predict serious pancreatic leakage after major pancreatic surgery in a 2026 study. Over one thousand patients having pancreatic head removal were split into training and validation groups. Variable selection and regression identified five independent predictors: soft gland texture, narrow duct, higher body weight index, longer operation and absence of diabetes. Inflammatory blood markers, though examined for association, did not survive into the final prediction tool built for bedside use.

About eighteen percent developed the clinically relevant leak. The visual score discriminated far better than two existing fistula risk scores in both groups. Surgeons can estimate risk before and during surgery to plan drainage, monitoring and feeding strategies. External validation in other centers is still needed before general adoption.
pmc-13264831:
Mario Andrea Latorre and co-authors wrote a 2026 study on inflammatory bowel disease unclassified, the label used when gut inflammation cannot be sorted as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. Doctors did not know how often that label sticks over time. Using records from a large Leeds hospital unit, the team followed such patients to 2025.

The group held 153 patients, with a mean age of 46.6 and mean illness length of 13.1 years. Their drug patterns sat between the two named diseases: more use of one gut drug and more biologic use than colitis, but less than Crohn's. Steroid use and health care use ran higher than in both named diseases. At the end, 88.2 percent still carried the unclassified label. The authors call it a lasting form in its own right.
pmc-13264931:
Abi Woodward and colleagues map research on social prescribing for minority ethnic groups in the United Kingdom, in a 2026 scoping review. Social prescribing connects patients with community support instead of medicine alone. Minority groups face unequal access to many services. How well these programmes reach them was unclear.

Seventeen papers met the inclusion rules. Common offers included advice, arts and culture, nature activities, and exercise. Cultural fit, strong community links, and link worker support helped people engage. Language problems, low awareness, logistics, and stigma held people back. Reporting of ethnicity was often patchy. The authors call for clearer reporting and more culturally tailored designs.
pmc-13265231:
Luqiao Li and colleagues look for markers that predict immunotherapy benefit in advanced melanoma in China, in a 2026 study. Single-drug immunotherapy helps only a limited share of Chinese patients. Records covered 62 patients treated at one Nanjing hospital from 2019 to 2022. Tumour gene testing and blood measures were collected.

More than five spread sites, liver or bone spread, and certain blood patterns linked to shorter time without progression. Combined chemotherapy improved survival. Common gene changes included NRAS and CDKN2A. One mutation, in KMT2A, independently predicted shorter benefit. The findings help sort patients into risk groups.
pmc-13265431:
Maira Inderyas and colleagues scan long COVID brains with an ultra-strong magnet during a mental conflict task, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Nineteen patients, twelve recovered controls, and fifteen never-infected controls performed the Stroop test inside a 7-tesla scanner, which reads blood-oxygen signals with unusual fineness.

Against the recovered group, long COVID patients showed weaker activation in two hub regions: the anterior cingulate, a conflict monitor, and the precuneus, a self-and-memory hub. In the precuneus, weaker signal tracked with higher pain scores and longer illness. Patients were also slower on the task than the never-infected group, though direct brain contrasts with that group were not significant. The authors read the pattern as disturbed cognitive control circuitry, plausibly from blood flow and inflammation problems, giving the fog of long COVID a measurable address.
pmc-13266131:
Jason P Murphy and the team identify required competencies for expert infection nurses in Sweden, in a 2026 consensus study. Infection threats and drug resistance are growing system challenges. Formal evidence on essential skills for these nurses was lacking. Thirty-one academic and medical experts completed three rating rounds.

Agreement, set at three-quarters, was reached on sixty-two of seventy-four proposed skills. Agreed areas spanned microbiology knowledge, medical judgement, prevention, collaboration, and leading during extreme events. Person-centred care and mentoring also featured. Cross-culture care, green goals, and ethics items missed agreement. Those gaps are flagged for future work.
pmc-13266231:
Lijun Pan and co-authors review in 2026 why meat and meat products develop unpleasant off-flavors, and how producers can limit them. They name the main chemical culprits, including aldehydes, ketones, sulfides, and amines that produce fishy, stale, or strong animal odors. Examples range from boar taint in pork to the sharp smell of mutton.

Formation routes covered include lipid oxidation, protein breakdown, microbial action, and the build-up of compounds from feed or the environment. Control options span physical, chemical, and biological methods, plus combined approaches used during breeding, processing, and storage. Food scientists and processors get a single map linking odor chemistry to practical quality control.
pmc-13267231:
Adrian Treves, Sedona Chinn, and Miha Krofel wrote a 2026 paper about research findings that will not die. Science does not correct itself on its own, they argue, and wrong results can keep being cited with approval. They add a new label, vampire articles, next to the known idea of zombie articles, which are retracted papers that keep being cited.

A vampire article must meet two tests: its result cannot be reproduced, and it is still cited with approval in policy, papers, or private messages. The authors sort repeat attempts into four types and suggest how many failed repeats should trigger action. Two cases, on shooting coyotes from the air and on predicted overfishing, show the harm. They urge sharper retraction rules.
pmc-13267531:
Mario Romeo and colleagues present a 2026 case report on treating a bowel cancer spread in the liver. Their patient was a 52-year-old woman whose rectal cancer had been treated with drugs, radiation, and surgery. One liver spot, about 17 millimeters wide, sat near a large vein and bile ducts in a liver full of cysts, making standard imaging unclear.

A contrast ultrasound scan showed rim brightening and fast washout, signs of living tumor. Surgery and heat-based burning were judged poor fits for the spot's position. Doctors instead used electric pulses, a method that kills cells without heat, guided by ultrasound. The scan right after showed full coverage. Six months later, scans showed no leftover or returning disease in the liver.
pmc-13267731:
Yucui Ding and colleagues report a 2026 study of a nano-sized drug carrier built to overwhelm breast cancer cells with calcium. Drug resistance and spread limit chemotherapy for breast cancer. The carrier wraps a plant compound, oridonin, in a manganese-based mineral sheet inside a fat shell aimed at tumors. Once inside a cell, it sets off a self-feeding loop of stress.

Stress in the cell's protein workshop forces calcium into its power plants, which then fail and burst out damaging oxygen chemicals. Manganese adds more of those chemicals and wakes an immune alarm pathway. Immune cells inside the tumor shifted to an attacking mode, and killer T cells moved in. In mice, the carrier strongly shrank tumors with no clear whole-body harm.
pmc-13267831:
Ji-Seong Jeong and colleagues present a 2026 rat study of silica nanoparticles breathed in during pregnancy. These tiny particles are among the most made nanomaterials, used in industry, medicines, and consumer goods. The nose and lungs are a main entry route, yet pregnancy risks were little studied. Pregnant rats received the particles through the nose daily in mid-to-late pregnancy, at four dose levels including none.

Treated mothers showed mild inflammation and healing changes in the breathing passages. No mothers died, and no general poisoning appeared. Checks of the litters and unborn young found no harm to development at any dose. The authors say the particles hurt only the surfaces they touched under these conditions. They still urge more studies, since particle types and exposure patterns vary widely.
pmc-13268231:
Mehmet Beler and Yusuf Bilal Çelenk present a 2026 study of insomnia in people aged 80 and over. This oldest group grows fast yet is rarely studied for sleep. The team enrolled 419 patients at a Turkish city hospital's advanced age unit in late 2025, using a standard insomnia severity questionnaire; a score of eight or more counted as insomnia.

About 38 percent had insomnia. It was more common in women and in those with low income. Past falls, high blood pressure, diabetes, and taking many medicines all linked to insomnia. Severity rose with the number of chronic diseases and the number of drugs taken. The authors argue insomnia at this age is not normal aging but a treatable problem, and that routine sleep checks belong in care of the very old.
pmc-13268631:
Xingyu Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 machine learning study predicting lab test orders in emergency departments. Lab testing guides emergency care, but overuse wastes money and time. The team analyzed 13,115 adult emergency visits from a 2021 national US survey. They built models from structured record data, from free-text complaint notes converted by a language model, from both together, and from an averaged ensemble.

The combined model predicted test ordering best, clearly beating either data type alone. The ensemble also did well but did not top the combined model. Older age, ambulance arrival, abnormal vital signs, and chronic illness predicted testing; injury visits predicted less testing. The authors say joining structured and text data could power decision support that trims unnecessary tests without missing needed ones.
pmc-13269031:
Celina Wojciechowska and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on death risk after removing heart device leads. They tested two simple scores, first built to judge stroke risk, as tools to predict death after the procedure. The scores add points for age, sex, and common health problems.

The study followed 3,822 patients treated between 2006 and 2023 at busy centers. Patients scoring three or more died more often at 30 days, one year, and three years. That cut point caught 80.6 percent of later deaths, with 62.3 percent exactness for survivors. Each extra point on the newer score raised death risk by 11.7 percent overall.
pmc-13270031:
Long Jing and co-authors published a case report and literature review in 2026 about a 50-year-old woman treated for a brain aneurysm, a bulge in a brain artery. She had a stent-assisted coiling procedure through blood vessels, which went smoothly. The next day she developed continuous seizures, a medical emergency called status epilepticus.

A brain scan showed mild swelling on the right side, pointing to brain injury from the imaging dye used in the procedure. Prompt seizure drugs and supportive care followed. She recovered fully, with no lasting deficits. The authors summarize how this dye reaction presents when seizures dominate, to help clinicians spot and treat it early.
pmc-13271331:
Shuang Liu is lead author of a 2026 journal article on FTL008.16, a bispecific antibody designed to switch on T cells only inside tumours. Drugs that activate the 4-1BB receptor on T cells can fight cancer but have been limited by liver damage. This antibody also binds 5T4, a protein found on tumour cells, so activation needs both targets.

In cell tests, the antibody boosted T cell growth, signal release, and tumour killing only when 5T4 was present. In two mouse tumour models it beat a standard 4-1BB antibody, fully clearing tumours in one model. In monkeys, even a high dose caused no rise in liver enzymes, suggesting a safer profile.
pmc-13271431:
Ticiana De Francesco is lead author of a 2026 multicentre study comparing two tiny drainage devices for glaucoma, the Xen63 gel stent and the Preserflo microshunt. Both lower eye pressure by draining fluid. Both were implanted alone, with a drug to limit scarring, in this study looking back at past cases.

At twelve months, complete success was about sixty-two percent for Xen63 and about seventy-four percent for Preserflo. Complete success meant pressure controlled without glaucoma medicines under strict rules. That gap was not statistically clear. Complications were more frequent with Xen63, at about sixty-two percent against about twenty-nine percent. Reoperations were also more common, at about seventeen percent against four percent. Pressure reduction and medicine burden were otherwise comparable.
pmc-13271931:
Rui Tang and coauthors pool in 2026 animal studies on ginseng extract as a supplement for weakened bones. Ginseng is widely used in traditional practice, and its active compounds may protect bone. The team wanted firm numbers on whether the extract improves bone strength in osteoporosis models.

Across 28 controlled animal studies, the extract raised bone mineral density and improved the inner spongy bone structure. Treated bones also bore higher loads before bending, and blood markers of bone building rose. Benefits looked stronger in female and naturally aged animals at moderate doses. The authors note that animal success still needs testing in people.
pmc-13272231:
Riccardo Maria Borgo is lead author of a 2026 cross-sectional study linking retinal damage to cognition in multiple sclerosis. In that disease, immune attacks on nerves cause brain shrinkage and disabling thinking problems. Eye scans called OCT measure retinal layer thickness quickly and cheaply. They offer a possible window on brain degeneration.

One hundred people with multiple sclerosis had thinking tests, brain MRI scans, and retinal scans of several layers. Thinner retinal layers tracked with smaller brain volumes and lower cognitive performance. One layer, the ganglion cell layer, showed the strongest links, especially with processing speed and executive function, and was the only retinal predictor left in statistical models. Patients with impaired cognition had thinner ganglion and nerve fibre layers.
pmc-13272331:
Jialei Chen and coauthors track in 2026 how age reshapes blood immune measures and gut microbes in adult broiler chickens. Gut microbes steer immunity, but most poultry studies stop at young birds. Yellow-feathered broilers aged one to four years gave blood and fecal samples for immune assays and microbial sequencing.

One blood protein peaked at one year, while antibody IgG climbed steadily with age. Overall microbe community structure did not separate cleanly by age, though spread within groups did. A few microbe-immune correlations appeared, including one gut genus rising alongside IgG. The authors label those links exploratory pending confirmation.
pmc-13272731:
Kendra Rodeghiero leads a 2026 longitudinal study of bacteria in the lower airways of pigs, comparing animals with and without lung lesions. The lesions matched infection with Mycoplasma hyopneumoniae, a common swine pathogen. Samples of airway mucus and lung tissue were taken from nursery through slaughter.

Pigs without lesions showed richer and more diverse bacterial communities during finishing, while pigs with lesions had lower diversity and less change over time. Only 18 bacterial variants appeared in all phases in both groups. Two candidate marker types were flagged for each group, but the authors treat those links as preliminary and specific to this data set, needing further checks.
pmc-13273231:
Ritam Das wrote a 2026 article on improving phage therapy with antidefense proteins taken from the environment. Phages are viruses that kill bacteria, and doctors used them against infection long before antibiotics spread. Rising drug resistance has revived interest in this old approach.

The opening sections trace the history from the first observations of phages in the early twentieth century through early treatments for dysentery and cholera. Use faded once mass produced antibiotics arrived, though work continued in parts of Europe. Das frames the modern problem as bacteria defending themselves against phages, much as they resist drugs. The article's stated aim is to show how antidefense proteins found in nature could help therapeutic phages break through those defenses.
pmc-13273631:
Khan and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on cutaneous leishmaniasis in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. This skin disease is spread by sand fly bites. The study links hospital records with a household survey. It asks where cases cluster and which habits raise risk.

The team counted 5,123 confirmed patients at 17 district hospitals during 2020. They also surveyed 576 households about schooling, family size, knowledge, and spray use. Big families, low schooling, and poor knowledge were tied to more cases. Spray use was tied to lower risk. The authors tested new sticky traps for sand flies. Most flies were caught 30 to 121 centimeters above the ground. That height detail can guide where teams place traps and spray.
pmc-13273831:
Alcohol harms the liver partly from the gut: a leaky intestine lets bacterial products reach the liver and stir inflammation. Xianda Wang and co-authors trace one leak pathway in mice, centered on an enzyme called MLCK that loosens the seals between gut lining cells. Deleting the enzyme, either everywhere or only in the gut lining, changed the course of alcohol-driven liver disease.

Without the enzyme, liver injury markers fell by about half. A version of the enzyme stuck in the on position sped the disease instead. The team shows a fat-based signal switching the enzyme on through calcium, which opens the seals. Immune cells in the gut then grabbed more material and primed inflammatory helper cells. Blocking this pathway, they argue, could become a treatment strategy.
pmc-13274131:
Siyao Liu and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a fat-handling protein that helps an aggressive breast cancer grow. HER2-positive breast cancer spreads readily, and disordered fat use inside tumors may fuel it. The protein STARD10 moves lipids within cells, but its role in this cancer was unclear.

STARD10 levels were higher in HER2-positive tumors and marked a poorer outlook for patients. In two lab cell lines, extra STARD10 sped growth, movement, and invasion, and fat droplets built up. In mice it sped tumor growth and spread to the lungs. The effect ran through a signaling chain named cAMP, PKA, and CREB1, which the authors propose as a drug target.
pmc-13274831:
Ahadul Hassan Bhuiyan Konok and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on adverse birth outcomes across Bangladesh. Using the national Demographic and Health Survey, the team analyzed pregnancy outcomes for 10,254 ever-married women. They counted four problems: stillbirth, early birth, low birth weight, and death in the first month of life.

Low birth weight was commonest at 14.3 percent of pregnancies, followed by early birth at 8.9 percent, with stillbirth and newborn death each at 1.3 percent. The authors report about one in seven births involved at least one problem. Twin births, household wealth, place of delivery, and the mother's wish for the child recurred as linked factors. They recommend equity-focused maternal care and stronger women's decision-making power.
pmc-13275531:
Yves Moreira Ribeiro and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how the natural estrogen estrone, a pollutant in farm runoff and sewage, harms fish reproduction. Zebrafish were exposed for forty-nine days to three estrone levels found in real surface waters, from twenty to two thousand nanograms per liter. The team then examined ovaries, hormone levels, and spawning success.

Exposure reshaped the ovary: more immature egg cells and withered follicles, more inflammation, and fewer support cells. A related hormone and a growth factor signal rose at the lower doses, while a nitrogen stress marker climbed at the higher ones. Egg production fell in every exposed group, and fertilization rates dropped significantly at the two higher doses, even at common environmental levels.
pmc-13275631:
Luis Parmenio Suescún-Bolívar and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on tiny plastic bits in water and the germs they may carry. The team studied recycled PET, the plastic used in drink bottles, cut into microplastics. They asked how Escherichia coli, a common gut bacterium, sticks to and changes on these plastic surfaces.

The team checked the plastic with light-based tests and microscopes before and after contact with the bacteria. The tests found nine clear chemical bands for PET, and neither cleaning nor bacteria changed the plastic much. Microscope views showed bacteria clinging to the surfaces and forming biofilms, thin layers of living cells. Colonies also fermented lactose, a milk sugar, less well. The authors propose their setup as a model for tracking how plastics move microbes in water.
pmc-13276231:
Wang Yi and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a better endoscopic fix for bleeding-prone veins in the stomach. Gastric varices are swollen veins caused by liver cirrhosis, and their bleeding can be deadly. Standard banding treatment often grips the vein incompletely, so rebleeding is common.

At one Chinese hospital, ninety-nine patients had either standard banding or banding assisted by a metal clip. The clip method cleared the veins in a single session for about seven in ten patients, versus about half with standard care. Early rebleeding hit none of the clip group but about one in eleven of the standard group. Death rates and side effects were similar. The authors caution that the rebleeding benefit is exploratory and want larger, forward-looking trials to confirm it.
pmc-13276431:
Sunyan Hong and colleagues present a 2026 vision system for spotting defective green coffee beans automatically. Hand sorting is slow, tiring, and inconsistent, yet bean quality drives prices worldwide. Their system builds on the YOLOv10 detection model and targets fast factory use.

Three design changes cut computing load while sharpening fine detail and wider context. The dataset covered seven defect types graded to speciality coffee standards. Five-fold testing gave detection scores above ninety-eight percent for precision and recall, with answers in about two milliseconds. The model was also smaller and faster than a newer baseline, which suits sorting lines with limited hardware.
pmc-13276531:
Mariana Arino and co-authors present a 2026 case report on a rare, poorly understood degeneration of the cornea's edge. Peripheral nodulocystic corneal degeneration forms clear blister-like nodules around the cornea's rim. Only one similar case had been reported before, leaving its course and treatment undefined.

Their patient was a fifty-two-year-old woman with joint aches throughout her body and a past history of LASIK eye surgery in both eyes. She reported worsening dryness and discomfort in the left eye. Examination found multiple blister-like nodules in both eyes, mostly along the upper and outer edges. Scans showed cyst-like spaces under the surface layer and mild loss of the cornea's inner cells. She declined surgery, and symptoms eased with anti-inflammatory and lubricant eye drops plus a pressure-lowering drop. The authors discuss how degeneration, body-wide inflammation, and prior surgery may interact.
pmc-13277231:
Islam El-Malky leads a 2026 hospital study of brain bleeding in older patients, from a stroke care unit. The bleeding, called spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage, starts inside the brain without an injury. The team compared 71 patients aged seventy or older with younger patients among 238 cases, tracking recovery and death.

Older patients more often had high blood pressure, worse stroke scores, and lower alertness scores on arrival. They also more often showed signs of a vessel disease linked to aging. Their one-month death rate was higher and their three-month function was worse. Higher alertness and lower stroke severity scores predicted a better outcome. Age alone was not the whole story, the patterns suggest.
pmc-13277631:
Yuanxia Wang and co-authors compare two bacterial strains for fermenting mulberry juice in a 2026 food study. Mulberries are rich in vitamins and protective plant compounds but spoil very quickly. Fermentation with lactic acid bacteria can extend use and add function.

The plantarum batch kept the strongest antioxidant activity and richer flavour mix. Sugars from the fermented juice also showed enzyme effects relevant to blood sugar control.
pmc-13278331:

Metal sensitivity is a growing concern in joint replacement, and earlier work suggested lower quality of life with these implants. The team reviewed 6,954 knee replacements from 2019 to 2022 in a Mayo Clinic database.

Only 320 operations used hypoallergenic implants; the rest used standard ones. Readmission within thirty days was about two point two percent in the hypoallergenic group versus about zero point seven percent with standard implants. No link appeared with body weight, illness burden, heart disease, diabetes, alcohol, smoking, or medical complications. Extra vigilance for this group is the authors' practical advice.
pmc-13278831:

Built on a secure university platform, the chatbot writes SQL code, runs it, and returns both code and results, keeping protected health information inside approved systems.

Clinicians posed thirty questions, and outputs were compared with a data scientist's code. The chatbot read the intent of about seventy-three percent of prompts correctly. Its generated code and final outputs were each accurate in roughly fifty-three to sixty-three percent of cases. Errors clustered around group comparisons, ambiguous variables, and open-ended exploration.
pmc-13279031:

For the newer direct anticoagulants, the three chatbots scored broadly alike. The results suggest patients can get reasonable plain-language answers from these tools, but expert checking still matters for high-risk therapy.
pmc-13279331:

pmc-13279531:

pmc-13279631:

The main outcome mixed death, transplant, and dangerous heart rhythms.

pmc-13280031:

pmc-13280531:

pmc-13280831:

pmc-13280931:

pmc-13281231:

pmc-13281431:

pmc-13281631:

pmc-13281931:

pmc-13282131:

pmc-13282531:

pmc-13282731:

pmc-13283031:

pmc-13283431:

pmc-13284831:

pmc-13285631:

pmc-13285831:

pmc-13285931:

pmc-13286231:

pmc-13287031:

pmc-13287331:

pmc-13287431:

pmc-13287531:

pmc-13287731:

pmc-13289131:

pmc-13289331:

pmc-13289731:

pmc-13289931:

pmc-13290331:

pmc-13290531:

pmc-13290931:

pmc-13291331:

pmc-13291731:

pmc-13291831:

pmc-13291931:

pmc-13292331:

pmc-13292431:

pmc-13292531:

All Gram-negative samples formed visible strings, while Gram-positive ones formed none, matching stain results fully in this set. Gene checks on some samples backed the sorting.
pmc-13293631:
Andreu Vilaseca and co-authors describe, in a 2026 study, rare cases where Ma/Ma2 autoimmunity hits only peripheral nerves, sparing the brain. This immune condition usually strikes the central nervous system and often pairs with cancer.

Within cohorts totaling 212 patients with Ma/Ma2 syndromes, just 7 had peripheral-only illness, with a median age of 68 years, an age the authors give. Illness forms included sensory neuron damage and mixed root and nerve patterns. Cancer was found in 6 of the 7 patients. After about two years of follow-up, symptoms improved or held steady in three patients and worsened in four.
pmc-13293731:
Xiaoting Xiao and co-authors find, in a 2026 study, that a standard blood-thinning drug at clinical doses boosts a cancer-killing virus in bladder cancer cells. Doctors feared heparin drugs might block the virus, since they mimic a surface sugar the virus uses to attach.

High doses did block infection, yet doses matching patient blood levels instead helped the virus attach through surface sugar proteins and kill more tumor cells. The boost only worked in cells with weak interferon defenses. In animals, clinical-level dosing strengthened tumor control without added toxicity. A routine drug may thus aid, not hinder, virus therapy.
pmc-13293831:
Osman Akay presents a 2026 scoping review with bibliometric mapping on sharenting, the habit of parents posting about their children online. Drawing on Web of Science and Scopus, the review gathers work from media studies, child development, law, health, and communication to see how disclosure connects with privacy, autonomy, and digital identity.

Altogether 252 English articles and reviews from 1992 to 2025 met the criteria. Output stayed low for years, then grew after 2016 and rose sharply from 2019. Recurring ideas include consent, boundary control between parent and child, and how a lasting online presence forms before a child can choose it.
pmc-13294631:
Yutaka Okagawa and colleagues report a 2026 multicentre study from Japan on stopping certain blood-thinning drugs before polyp removal. Guidelines allow a one-day pause for antiplatelet drugs other than aspirin and P2Y12 blockers, but supporting evidence is weak. The team asked whether pausing lowered delayed bleeding after colon procedures.

Records covered 506 patients who had hot snare polypectomy or mucosal resection while on one such drug alone. After matching, 192 pairs were compared, and delayed bleeding occurred in 1.0 percent of each group. One clotting event followed a pause and none followed continuation, leading the authors to question routine stopping and call for prospective trials.
pmc-13294931:
Lola Aubry and colleagues describe a young woman with two rare conditions together in a 2026 case report. Isaacs syndrome overexcites peripheral nerves, causing twitching, cramps, sweating, and bladder and bowel problems. Polyarteritis nodosa inflames medium blood vessels across the body, and the pairing had not been reported before.

The student first arrived with severe lower back pain, then lost weight and developed skin lesions and gut vessel inflammation on scans. Treatment with intravenous cyclophosphamide plus corticosteroids brought full clinical remission. The case widens the list of illnesses that can underlie Isaacs syndrome and may guide doctors facing similar mixed pictures.
pmc-13295031:
Haruto Ishikawa and Yasuhisa Mizutani bring two ancient light-sensing proteins back to life in the lab, in a 2026 study. Microbial rhodopsins are membrane proteins with seven spirals that pump ions or sense light. Rebuilding their ancestors tests how those jobs evolved, yet standard methods trim the floppy loops outside the membrane, since gaps in the sequence lineup make them unsure.

The pair's method guides the lineup with protein structure and infers the gaps outright. Their rebuilt ancestors stayed compact, with no phantom stretches, and folding software shaped them with trust, loops and all. Both proteins were made in bacteria and bound their light-catching pigment. Under light, the schizorhodopsin ancestor pumped protons in a cell test, while the heliorhodopsin ancestor did not, matching its living kin.
pmc-13295531:
Dora Bjedov and colleagues review earthworm immune cells and body fluid in a 2026 article. Cells floating in the worm's body cavity, called coelomocytes, eat invaders, wall off foreign matter, and attack tumour cells in tests. The surrounding fluid carries its own defensive molecules, from pore-forming lysenin to germ-killing peptides.

These cells react sensitively to heavy metals, pesticides, tiny plastics, and engineered particles, changing survival, energy state, and eating activity. Such responses make them handy living gauges for polluted soils. The authors also note drug and farm promise in the fluid's ingredients, while classification and signalling gaps still need closing.
pmc-13295931:
Aqeeb Ur Rehman and colleagues describe a 2026 registry protocol for severe kidney failure needing dialysis across Latin America. The region carries a heavy burden yet lacks its own outcome data, which leaves practice and policy inconsistent between hospitals.

The LATAM-AKID study will enrol critically ill adults with the most severe kidney injury in hospitals across ten countries, using one shared database. Care details will be gathered through the first week, with outcomes checked at discharge and ninety days, led by deaths in hospital. Planned analyses compare dialysis types, illness severity and country income levels.
pmc-13296331:
Victoria Sherwood and co-authors survey ten years of change in how new antibodies are found, in a 2026 review. Antibodies are proteins the immune system makes to bind one target. New tools let teams study huge numbers of single B cells, the cells that make antibodies, and link each one's gene code to what it binds. Tiny fluid devices screen the cells at high speed, and gene reading recovers both chains of each antibody at once.

Work has shifted from simple binding tests toward tests of what an antibody can do. Computer methods, from machine learning to shape models, feed results back into the next round of lab work. Lab and computer steps thus refine each batch of candidates together. The authors say such loops promise faster, more hands-off routes to antibodies for tests and treatments.
pmc-13296631:
Sukjoo Cho, Katherine Shelmidine and Jason T. Yustein review, in 2026, why osteosarcoma, the main bone cancer of teenagers, varies so wildly within and between tumours. Treatment has barely changed in forty years, and this patchwork biology is blamed for stalled progress.

Causes span unstable genomes, broken tumour suppressors, extra copies of growth genes, inherited risks and a varied tumour neighbourhood, plus shape-shifting cells and chemical tags. Answers proposed include marker-guided risk sorting, better lab models and combined drugs hitting growth, immunity and metabolism. Maintenance therapy ideas are also weighed.
pmc-13296831:
Hervé Tshikomba Mbuyamba and colleagues present, in 2026, a rare surgical emergency in a forty-seven-year-old woman: a gallstone that escaped through a channel into the bowel and blocked it. She arrived after a week of cramping pain, four days without stool, vomiting and a swelling belly.

Gallstone blockage causes only a small share of bowel obstructions yet kills a notable fraction of patients, partly because signs are vague and diagnosis drags. The case review covers classic scan clues and the debated surgical options. The authors stress thorough checking when obstruction has no clear cause.
pmc-13297131:
Linzhu Fang and colleagues identify a wheat switch gene that boosts the waxy coating on leaves in a 2026 plant study. That cuticular wax shields the crop from drought and other stresses. Turning down the switch gene, called TaMYB46, left plants with less wax and leakier leaf coatings.

A second gene, encoding an enzyme that activates fatty building blocks, proved central to making the wax. The switch protein was found sitting on that gene's control region and turning it on. Silencing either gene cut wax accumulation in the experiments. The pair forms a tidy regulatory module that breeders might exploit for hardier wheat.
pmc-13297931:
Ioana Maria Marinescu leads a large team reporting a 2026 antibacterial hydrogel platform for soft tissue and wound care. Polyacrylamide gels are biocompatible yet lack germ-killing action and can be weak in strength. Their design adds cellulose nanofibers carrying silver nanoparticles, with the fibers also helping form and stabilize those particles.

Analysis found two particle populations that may give both quick bacterial contact and a longer release of silver ions. Adding more hybrid material changed swelling, stiffness, and surface wetting in tunable ways. Colony counting confirmed germ-killing activity in the higher-silver formulations against several pathogenic strains. The team positions the material as an adaptable candidate needing further development.
pmc-13298231:
Yu Zhang and a team report clinical features and prognosis for growth hormone-secreting pituitary tumours, in a 2026 retrospective study. These tumours cause acromegaly and serious complications, and surgery is the main treatment. Their analysis covered 344 patients, searching for factors tied to hormone non-remission or recurrence after removal.

Recurrence itself, high hormone levels before surgery, and higher Knosp grades, which grade tumour invasion toward nearby vessels, emerged as key risk factors. The team also built prediction models for non-remission and recurrence risk. They propose the results can sharpen patient stratification and follow-up planning, though the study rests on past records from clinical care.
pmc-13299231:
Why do health staff in South Africa pick their jobs, and why do they quit them? Modupe Busisiwe Makwarela and her team put both asks to the field in a 2026 talk-based study. They spoke with ten staff from the fields of drugs, food care, mind care, and ward care, in state, paid, and school posts, till the tales ran dry.

Kind hearts, kin sway, past life, pay and job safety, and school marks all shaped first picks, as did the lack of a guide. Shifts took many forms: deep skill in one field, a switch of field, a full exit from health work, or side work past health. Staff, shop-floor, and red-tape strains drove the moves. The team call for rule change that serves those who stay as well as those who train next.
pmc-13299931:
Seung-Woo Baek and others frame bladder cancer drug resistance as a staged molecular evolution rather than simple mutation selection, in a 2026 review. A gemcitabine-resistant cell model supplies the time course. Early adjustment quiets cell-cycle and sugar-burning routines while raising epigenetic give and rewiring energy use toward mitochondria and lipids.

Later, resistance hardens through matrix reshaping, growth and stress signalling, and immune-metabolic exchanges inside the tumour surroundings. Mapping a resistance score onto patient tumours suggested similar patterns occur in patients. The authors argue treatment should strike the passing adaptive states before resistance settles, opening a timed window for treatment.
pmc-13300031:
Yoshihito MATSUZAKI and colleagues treat a stroke caused by a torn middle cerebral artery with clot removal as the first move, in a 2026 case report with literature review. Such dissection is a rare stroke cause with no settled management. Their young adult patient arrived with headache, vomiting, weakness on one side, and language loss.

Combined stent-retriever and suction thrombectomy fully reopened the vessel, and balloon widening then fixed the remaining narrowing without a permanent stent. Later vessel-wall imaging confirmed the tear. He recovered well with no further damage over six months. Careful device choice and long imaging follow-up are stressed.
pmc-13300531:
P Mahajan and co-authors review four years of left bundle branch pacing at one center in a 2026 retrospective analysis. The physiologic pacing method has spread quickly, but long-term safety and durability data remain thin. The team gathered 271 patients implanted between January 2019 and November 2023 who had complete electrocardiogram, device, and ultrasound follow-up, all with confirmed selective capture of the bundle at implant.

Average procedure time was seventy-five minutes. Among patients who began with left bundle branch block, the paced QRS width trended narrower over four years without reaching statistical significance, and pumping function likewise held steady rather than improving. Thresholds stayed acceptable, with only two patients above two volts at four years and no lead revisions needed. One in five patients showed a persistent right bundle pattern at four years. The authors call the technique reliable and low in complications over the long term.
pmc-13300631:
D Parfianowicz and colleagues compare ultrasound-guided venous access with fluoroscopy-guided access for implanting cardiac electronic devices in a 2026 retrospective study. Ultrasound may skip radiation at the puncture step, yet hard outcome data are limited. The review covered 514 implants at a large center during 2023, with 297 patients in the ultrasound group and 217 in the fluoroscopy group, compared with models that adjust for other factors.

After accounting for the number of leads placed, neither procedure time nor total radiation exposure differed in any clear way between approaches. Complications were nearly absent, with none in the ultrasound group and a single collapsed lung in the fluoroscopy group. The authors conclude ultrasound access is safe and sound, while noting a puzzle: sparing radiation at access did not shrink the overall dose, which comes mostly from later steps.
pmc-13300831:
Blood thinners face a stiff test in cardiac amyloidosis, where clots and bleeding both threaten. Hussein Abdul Nabi and colleagues compared warfarin with newer direct oral anticoagulants in a 2026 multicenter review of 422 Mayo Clinic patients who had both amyloidosis and atrial fibrillation. Median follow-up ran 4.3 years.

Twenty-one patients suffered a thromboembolic event. Yearly rates came out low and close, at 0.83 percent on warfarin and 0.67 percent on the newer drugs, a gap without statistical weight. Major bleeding touched 9.9 percent of patients overall, again without a clear winner. Pauses in therapy longer than five days raised clot risk, the sharpest warning in the data.
pmc-13301031:
Two lichens new to science emerge from Anhui Province in a 2026 taxonomic study by Yi-Shan Feng and colleagues. The crustose genus Lecidella gains Lecidella biformis and Lecidella versicolor, named from combined evidence of form, chemistry, and DNA phylogeny. Both species grow in the southeastern Dabie Mountains.

Together with L. albida, the pair forms a well-supported branch marked by tiny fruiting bodies under half a millimeter and the compound atranorin. Biformis shows two-toned discs and an extra chemical, while versicolor shifts from yellow youth to nut-brown maturity. Full descriptions, photographs, and a key to all Chinese Lecidella species round out the account.
pmc-13301431:
Wojciech Ł. Grześkowiak and Martyna Wienke test sheep wool grease as a green wood preservative in a 2026 materials study. Scots pine samples were coated with four lanolin emulsions, some fortified with boric acid, then challenged with water behavior measurements and decay fungi, molds, and microfungi. The question was whether the wax could push water off the surface and starve the organisms that rot timber.

Treated wood turned water repellent: droplet contact angles climbed from about fifty-eight degrees untreated to between eighty-five and one hundred five degrees, on par with paraffin and carnauba wax coatings. Decay slowed, with mass loss cut by up to roughly thirty percentage points against the brown rot fungus, though gains against the second test fungus were small. Boric acid strengthened fungal resistance while trimming the water repellency slightly. The authors position lanolin emulsions as a sustainable alternative to conventional hydrophobic treatments.
pmc-13301531:
A trainee's ultrasound hand steadies with practice, María Teresa García-Martínez and colleagues show in a 2026 learning-curve study of plantar fascia measurement. Eighty-four adults, half with plantar fasciopathy and half pain-free, were scanned twice each by an expert sonographer and a supervised student. Agreement and drift over time were the points of interest.

Across the whole span, the two examiners' thickness readings matched at group level. Sliced by period, though, real gaps appeared in the first two months, November to December 2024, then faded from view. Agreement crept upward descriptively as the student logged supervised scans. The authors frame the pattern as exploratory evidence for structured training and oversight in ultrasound teaching.
pmc-13302231:
N Augustin and co-authors track, in a 2026 study, how pacing thresholds evolve after implantation of a leadless pacemaker in the heart's upper chamber. The atrial device, approved in Germany in 2024, pairs with a ventricular unit to form a fully leadless two-chamber system. Thresholds at implant looked high even when positioning seemed perfect.

Fourteen patients implanted between August 2024 and October 2025 were compared with fifty recipients of the matching ventricular device. Atrial thresholds started significantly higher than ventricular ones, then fell markedly and settled at low, stable levels over six months. Ventricular thresholds barely changed. The authors blame swelling at the contact point, proportionally larger in the small upper chamber, and call for work on the mechanism.
pmc-13302331:
Giuseppe Neri and a large team review, in a 2026 review, how safely invasive procedures can be done while adults are supported by ECMO. The machine oxygenates blood outside the body. These very ill patients often need surgery or bedside procedures, yet the blood thinning ECMO requires raises both bleeding and clotting dangers.

Forty-six studies met the criteria, grouped into six procedure families from airway work to major abdominal and chest surgery. Airway and scope procedures generally succeeded in chosen patients, though registry data showed bleeding in about a quarter of tracheal cases. Emergency chest and abdominal operations carried the heaviest burden of bleeding, transfusion, and death. The authors urge procedure-specific planning with blood-thinning management matched to each patient.
pmc-13302531:
Fungicides are learning to aim, Xiyu Wu and colleagues survey in a 2026 review of targeted discovery against crop fungi. Resistance and tighter environmental rules are squeezing the old broad-spectrum chemistry, so researchers increasingly design compounds around chosen weak points. The review sorts the new strategies into three families and weighs each for selectivity, durability, and the risk of fresh resistance.

One family attacks processes the fungus cannot live or infect without. A second disarms virulence, blunting the tricks pathogens use to slip past plant defenses. A third recruits the plant itself, switching on or redirecting its immunity. Repurposed drugs, structural biology, and AI-assisted design speed the search, the authors note.
pmc-13303331:
Sarah Jane Harrison and colleagues review, in a 2026 paper, the case for starting long-acting injectable antipsychotics early in schizophrenia rather than reserving them for crisis. Injections every few weeks keep drug levels steady and remove daily pill burden, yet clinicians often wait until repeated relapses prove pills are failing. The first five years after diagnosis are framed as the critical window.

Evidence gathered here links early injection use to fewer relapses, better daily functioning, and lower overall care costs. Barriers include negative views among clinicians, patients, and families, plus thin guideline support and limited education. The authors propose teaching programmes and guideline updates to normalise early use. Gaps in direct evidence for first-episode patients are acknowledged plainly.
pmc-13303431:
Nicolo' Monti and colleagues report a 2026 cohort study of growth problems in children adopted across borders. The group studied 1,955 children seen at a large children's center in Italy between 2015 and 2025, most aged one to nine years.

Growth was judged with World Health Organization standards for stunting, underweight, and thinness. About one child in eight showed stunting or underweight, and thinness was less common. Anemia, age one to four years, Asian origin, and fetal alcohol spectrum disorder raised the risk of poor growth. The results point to early screening and nutrition support soon after adoption.
pmc-13303931:
Po-Sung Chen and colleagues craft light, strong titanium alloys in a 2026 materials study. Swapping niobium for zirconium in a medium-entropy mix lowers weight while keeping the toughness that transport and energy uses demand.

Four mixes with rising titanium shares were cast and checked. All held a single crystal structure, and more titanium traded some strength for slightly better stretch. Rolling plus fast heating then lifted performance a great deal. One mid mix heated at the lowest tested level paired very high yield strength with good stretch and low density, marking it as a strong candidate for light parts.
pmc-13304631:
Tao Liu, Clementina Manera, and Francesca Gado argue, in a 2026 review, that natural product research works best when discovery, mechanism, and supply advance together. Plant and microbial molecules like paclitaxel and artemisinin occupy chemical ground that synthetic libraries rarely reach, yet the useful ones hide as trace ingredients in messy mixtures. Older isolate-and-test pipelines kept rediscovering known compounds.

Modern campaigns instead map extracts by mass spectrometry and molecular networking, spotting known scaffolds before any bench work. Genome mining predicts what silent pathways could produce, while protein-target methods read a compound's targets inside living cells early enough to guide priorities. Organoids grown from patient tissue test relevance in realistic settings. Finally, engineered microbes ferment scarce products at scale, turning a rare extract into a supply that factories can make.
pmc-13304831:
Madeline R. Bolding and co-authors build a lab method for raising antibodies against membrane fats rather than proteins in a 2026 study. Fats change little between germ strains, so they may offer broad targets that protein hunting misses.

Tiny lipid discs carrying bacterial surface fat served as bait in phage and yeast display screens. Rival and subtraction steps cut sticky false binders, and winners were sharpened for stronger signals. The same setup then fished out antibody fragments that bind discs made from plague germ membrane fat, with some selectivity over control discs. More work must pin down exact targets.
pmc-13305331:
Ragini Gopagoni and colleagues describe a 2026 case of lung scarring in a man with celiac disease, paired with a review of lung problems in that condition. Gut illness from gluten can reach many organs, yet lung links remain rarely reported.

The 55-year-old had well-controlled celiac disease before breathlessness and cough grew. Scans were unclear, so surgical biopsy confirmed the usual interstitial pneumonia pattern of scarring. Immune blood tests stayed negative and no other cause surfaced. Despite diet lapses being addressed and a scarring drug, disease advanced to lung transplant. The link stays unproven and needs study.
pmc-13305431:
Juan Song and co-authors study how added microbes reshape root chemistry in the sweetgum tree Liquidambar formosana in a 2026 experiment. Roots leak compounds that feed soil life, and the two-way exchange may steer tree growth itself.

A bacterium, a root fungus, and both together were added to young trees. Combined dosing lifted growth most and eased stress chemistry in roots. Chemical profiling showed broad shifts in amino acids, acids, and sugars, with one sugar falling in both roots and leaks, hinting at lower stress demand. Richer carbon leaks may strengthen helpful microbe partnerships.
pmc-13305631:
Hui Lu and co-authors offer a 2026 plain language summary of a survey on treatment preferences in hemophilia care. People with the bleeding condition and caregivers of affected children in the United States and United Kingdom weighed made-up treatment options online.

Choices varied benefits, risks, and delivery style, from vein injections to newer under-skin shots. Adults and caregivers mostly agreed on what mattered. Taking treatment less often ranked highest of all features. Respondents would accept somewhat higher risk or lower benefit in exchange for fewer doses, a trade-off that drug makers and clinics should weigh when planning care.
pmc-13306231:
Higor Antonio-Domingues studied pollen from Madagascar members of the plant genus Vernonia in a 2026 survey. Light and electron microscopes documented 37 of 44 known island taxa, a broad sweep for a group famous for tangled classification.

Measured traits split the pollen into two types, a split backed by statistical pattern analysis in the reported results. A pore structure never before recorded for the genus also appeared during the survey. Further joint studies across Africa and Madagascar will test whether these pollen marks stay useful for naming species and tracing family history.
pmc-13306431:
Kexin Guo proposed a self-taught system for reading machine health from many sensor streams in a 2026 study. Noise, timing mismatch between streams and hand-made labels have limited earlier tools, especially under extreme faults.

Environmental, device, network, behaviour and log signals are treated as one state view, learned through masked time modelling and contrastive training without manual labels. Error scores of 0.0167, 0.0856 and 0.1291 on three standard measures beat rivals including LSTM and Transformer models in reported tests. The authors present the features as stable, transferable and readable for later tasks.
pmc-13306731:
Maria Breygina compared flower chemistry in two tobacco lines with differing seed output in a 2026 study. Fortune plants grow longer flowers, larger fruits and more seeds than Samsun, and stigma fluids guide pollen growth in both lines.

Samsun stigma fluid carried higher overall oxidative power and possibly more nitric oxide in spectrometer checks. Fortune held more of a protective enzyme in stigma tissue and more abscisic acid in its fluid in reported measures. Young style growth checks added enzyme activity patterns, linking redox balance to pollination success. The gap in fluid traits may help explain why one line sets far more seed.
pmc-13307431:
Yanhui Tian and co-authors examine in 2026 how a ring shaped carbon fibre part hardens, pairing computer models with strain sensors built into the part. They first measured how the LD-2184 resin cures, its stiffness when fully hard, and how much it expands with heat.

Rings were wound wet with fibre, and tiny fibre sensors tracked pull along the axis during curing. The model joined heat flow, cure chemistry, and shape change in one frame. Measured and modelled strain differed by 7.15 percent in the final check, which backs the model. Left over stress came mostly from resin shrinkage and from cooling under mould restraint.
pmc-13307631:
Betsy Armenta-Leyva and colleagues pool 145 studies in 2026 on detecting viral genetic material from samples dried onto commercial filter papers. They promise cheap collection, transport, and storage for human and animal testing. Thirty-nine paper types appeared, led by cellulose brands such as Whatman and FTA products.

Detection success varied widely, from under half to nearly all expected positives depending on paper type. Virus target mattered too, with rates spanning a broad middle range. Storage temperature, drying time, and humidity could shift recovery, yet many studies reported those conditions poorly. Polyester and glass fibre papers appeared less often in the literature. The authors call for head-to-head designs that compare papers across conditions honestly. Without such rigour, they warn, field programmes may trust a paper beyond its proven limits.
pmc-13308631:
Raphiel J Murden and co-authors develop in 2026 a probability based take on JIVE, a method that splits shared and solo patterns across data sets taken from the same people. Their version, ProJIVE, learns both parts at once through an expectation step that seeks the best fit for the full model.

Joint fitting can beat step wise rivals on accuracy, since each part is shaped with the other in view from the start. Tried on brain shape and thinking scores in Alzheimer disease, the joint scores tied to dear lab markers of the illness. Code is shared in public, so other teams can test the method on gene, scan, and chemistry data sets.
pmc-13308731:
Xiaona Liu and Wei Zhao review in 2026 nano sized tools that aim to retrain the immune system in allergic rhinitis, a long term nose ill that burdens many lands. Shots that teach tolerance are the sole care that can change the course, yet they take years and vary a lot by person.

Tiny carriers such as polymer bits, fat bubbles, and cell shed packets can ferry allergens to the right cells with tight release control. Nano vaccines and nano sized binders add fresh ways to calm the skewed response at its root. Smart systems that sense local cues may lift both gain and safety at once. Human proof still trails the lab work by a wide margin.
pmc-13309131:
Helena M Swinkels, Mary A Georgilas, and Steven Keeler argue in 2026 that town pool closures in Canada cut a core health tool, not a mere luxury for towns. Pools are often first on the block when budgets pinch, yet swim cover has not kept pace with growth, and many pools near the end of their working life.

Swimming loads most muscle groups, spares joints, cools people in heat waves, and teaches a skill that guards against drowning in lakes and seas. A fresh federal fund of 30 billion dollars for town builds gives a chance to fix and grow the pool stock. The authors urge that pools rank high when that cash is shared.
pmc-13309431:
Dan Adler and colleagues argue in a 2026 theory article that science splits into law-finding work and history-tracing work for a basic reason. Laws work when each event can be treated as separate, with past events leaving the rules unchanged. Evolution breaks that habit, since each step changes the next step.

A simple formal model shows how objects that merely persist longer can build population-level change without genes or copying. Placed beside law-based science, the model yields a four-part map of kinds of inquiry. The authors claim that history-based fields need their own building style of explanation. The piece speaks to readers who study how evolution should be explained.
pmc-13310631:
Mélina Côté and colleagues rebuild in 2026 the full nutrient makeup of packaged foods from their labels and ingredient lists, filling a gap in food data banks that mostly cover generic items. The data covered 5,371 packaged products sold in Québec across 17 categories. A language algorithm matched each ingredient to its closest entry in the national nutrient file.

A maths model then solved for ingredient shares that match the declared label values. Over half the ingredients matched their data bank matches with high closeness scores. Median error stayed under twenty percent for energy and the ten label nutrients, within the leeway rule-makers accept for labels. Six food categories did strongly, while three categories gave poor figures on several nutrients. Complete profiles for packaged foods would sharpen dietary studies, since such products supply nearly half the energy in many countries.
pmc-13310931:
Qi Wang and a large team offer a practical lab test for nerve disease antibodies in a 2026 study. Live cell tests best detect antibodies tied to optic and spinal cord attacks, yet they are costly and hard to standardize. Fixed cell tests are easier but miss more cases, so a cleaning step for blood samples was built.

A lysate product soaks up interfering matter before the fixed test. In blind tests with 818 people in two cohorts, the cleaned fixed test matched or beat the live test for both antibody types, with near perfect accuracy on controls. Wider labs could adopt the method for routine diagnosis.
pmc-13311331:
Horace Cheuk Wai Choi and co-authors model the costs and gains of widening HPV vaccination in Hong Kong in a 2026 analysis. Since 2019 the city has offered two doses to schoolgirls aged 10 to 12.

The model weighs the current girls-only plan against vaccinating boys too, in one or two doses, over a 100-year span. Two doses for both sexes cost too much per health gain at the stated prices. One dose for both sexes came out cost-saving or good value in all runs, if boys' uptake passed half and one dose guarded for 30 years. The results guide a cheaper path to wider cover.
pmc-13311631:
Jiayu Zhang and colleagues detail a 2026 interview study on involving awake intensive care patients in shared decisions about their care. Staff views on the practice were gathered at one accredited hospital in Hangzhou, China.

Sixteen ICU doctors and nurses, aged 23 to 45, were interviewed between September and November 2024. Three themes emerged. Staff saw patients as often not ready, with shifting capacity, raw emotions, and limited grasp of choices. Doctors acted more as advisors, nurses felt sidelined, and team talk was patchy. Involvement could protect or burden patients. Clearer roles and structure are urged.
pmc-13311831:
S Knaga and co-authors present a 2026 study on dosing broiler chicks before hatching. Chicks got a prebiotic or a fatty acid donor in the egg, and gut microbes were read at six weeks of age.

On day twelve of incubation, 1068 fertile Ross 308 eggs were split into four groups. The groups were untouched, salt-water, galactooligosaccharide, and sodium butyrate. Gut contents from the small intestine and cecum were gene-sequenced at day 42. The prebiotic raised microbe variety and favored Lactobacillus and kin. The butyrate reshaped communities more sharply, cutting Lactobacillus and lifting other groups. Early dosing, it seems, steers the gut for weeks.
pmc-13311931:
Maxime Pichon and co-authors report a 2026 comparison of gut microbiome testing offered by French medical biology laboratories. Interest in self-testing is rising. Yet the scientific validity and clinical meaning of commercial kits remain in question. Acting as an ordinary patient would, the researchers chose five laboratories through standard internet searches in June 2024. They sent each one portions of a single pooled stool sample from a fictitious healthy 40-year-old man.

Even at the kit stage, the laboratories differed widely. Contents ranged from collection instructions and questionnaires gathering basic personal or clinical details to promotional material with no biomedical purpose. The team set out to compare packaging safety, data handling, and final reports as well. They treated the exercise as a national-scale check on standardization. Their findings already show a market with little common structure, which complicates any advice patients might draw from results.
pmc-13312031:
Ronja Hugg, Marc Stegger, and Bo Söderquist report a 2026 study on whether long-term dalbavancin treatment breeds resistant staphylococci in patients. Dalbavancin is a long-acting antibiotic used for prosthetic joint and other implant infections, and laboratory work had warned that low drug levels can select resistant strains. The team sampled nose and perineum swabs from 19 patients treated for at least twelve weeks and from 25 control patients awaiting elective joint surgery.

Cultures grew on plates containing graded dalbavancin doses, and resistance was checked against standard breakpoints. Four of the 19 treated patients carried resistant Staphylococcus epidermidis, with minimum inhibitory concentrations from 0.38 to 0.75 in the reported units, while no control sample yielded resistant staphylococci, a statistically significant contrast. The authors conclude that resistance genuinely emerges during prolonged treatment in the body, a caution for reusing the drug when infections recur.
pmc-13312131:
Wenyu Tang and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, how the severity of tooth-root lesions relates to thickening of the sinus lining in people with severe gum disease. Both advanced periodontitis and apical periodontitis can swell the membrane of the nearby maxillary sinus, a detail that matters when planning surgery or implants.

The team analyzed cone-beam scans from 330 patients with stage III or IV periodontitis plus apical disease in upper back teeth. Sinus lining thickening appeared in both stages, spread across both sides, and rose modestly but significantly with lesion grade. Thickening was strongest at the upper first molar, which sits closest to the sinus floor. The authors offer the findings as support for careful preoperative checks of the sinus before dental work in this area.
pmc-13312531:
Yunfeng Zheng and co-authors report a 2026 study of copper-molybdenum nanozymes designed to clear infected burn wounds.
