Once body weight was accounted for, males matched females in resistance, which suggests males could serve in field monitoring.
pmc-13393231:
Ghaffar Kiani reviews fifteen years of Iranian work on genetically modified rice. The crop is pressed by drought, salty soils, and pests in a country that leans heavily on it for food security. A national research programme has moved from gene discovery to field trials, and Kiani maps that path through a systematic search and thematic reading of the literature. Insect-resistant Bt lines headline the results.

Field data show the engineered lines holding stable inserted genes, stacking several traits, yielding more, and needing less pesticide with a smaller environmental footprint. Yet planting remains blocked by a biosafety framework that does not function and by public scepticism. Contrasting Bangladesh, where modified crops reached farms, Kiani argues science alone cannot close the gap. Working regulation is one missing piece. Public engagement that frames home-grown modified rice as a sustainability tool is the other.
pmc-13393331:
Herrera-Luna and colleagues developed a light-driven method in 2026 to make aryl boronate esters, building blocks prized for assembling new molecules and medicines. Their recipe uses visible light alone, with no light-absorbing catalyst and no metal, and runs inside a gel open to the air. The starting materials are common aryl halides, ring compounds carrying a halogen atom that is easy to swap.

The gel gave the fragile reaction a stable setting. The method worked across halides bearing many other groups, such as alcohols, amines, and esters, in some cases giving the product in full yield. Light-absorption tests and magnetic resonance experiments showed the partners first join in a ground-state complex held by hydrogen bonds, weak links between molecules, and computer models backed that picture. The authors present the route as a greener way to a key class of reagents.
pmc-13393931:
Qingqing Zhang and others pilot village-doctor care with cash perks and video links for old rural adults with sugar illness in a 2026 chance-assigned trial. Rural sugar care lags for want of funds, spotty sugar checks, and scarce doctor advice.

Six Baima Township village clinics were split by chance into plain care or joined care with cash perks plus video help. Among 215 finishers, the joined-care group cut its long-term sugar mark more over three months than plain care did. The pilot backs scaling doctor-led, perk-backed video care to lift rural sugar control.
pmc-13395431:
Johannes Malm and colleagues pilot, in 2026, daily tracking of dementia behaviour symptoms in Swedish nursing homes. Such symptoms swing by day and setting, yet notes are often rare. Staff at four units logged symptoms each shift for eight residents over ninety days. A digital form held both a standard scale and personal items.

Nearly twenty-two thousand entries were logged in all. Staff kept up the routine on about three quarters of shifts, though rates varied by resident and worker. Each entry grew faster with practice, halving in time by the last month. Symptom counts swung widely within one person across days. Staff found the routine easy to fit in.
pmc-13396031:
Colin R. Tosh and co-authors used a computer model to test whether trees planted in fields shield crops when bad weather strikes early in the season. Their 2026 study simulated one hundred years at Wakelyns, a farm in southeastern England known for alley cropping with rows of trees.

The Hi-sAFe model grew winter wheat and peas under two climate paths, a middle course and a very high emissions course, from 2001 to 2100. Yields were checked for steadiness and for losses in years with harsh early weather. The results support the view that the shelter, shade, and water effects of trees can soften climate shocks at the growth stages when young crops are most at risk.
pmc-13396331:
Wei Li and co-authors compared two look-alike forms of early lung cancer that both appear as solid masses on scans, in a 2026 study. Mucinous adenocarcinoma, which makes mucus, may behave differently from the common non-mucinous kind, and telling them apart early could shape care.

The review covered 579 patients with stage I disease, averaging about 60 years old. Clinical features, scan traits, gene changes, and relapse patterns were set side by side for the two groups, and survival curves were compared with standard methods. Models then tested which factors predicted relapse or death, giving surgeons a clearer picture of whether the mucus-making type needs different handling.
pmc-13396431:
Xin Li and co-authors combined genetics with lab checks to hunt for blood chemicals that cause, rather than merely accompany, the foot deformity called hallux valgus, better known as a bunion. Their 2026 study used Mendelian randomization, a method that treats inherited variants as a natural experiment.

Screening 1,400 serum metabolites flagged two tied to lower bunion risk: the amino acid cysteine and a bile-related compound. No reverse effect of the deformity on their levels appeared. Following cysteine, the team predicted 548 genes it may act on and found 47 shared with bunion-linked genes. Those shared genes clustered in known signaling pathways, giving drug hunters concrete targets.
pmc-13396631:
Zhao and co-authors enable, in 2026, high-voltage lithium metal batteries with ether electrolytes by adding a trace of lithium borohydride, 0.05 molar, to create dihydrogen bonds. Ethers suit lithium metal but normally decompose above 4.0 volts. The borohydride's hydridic hydrogen bonds to the solvent's slightly positive hydrogens. That weakens lithium-solvent binding, speeds lithium shedding its solvent shell at the anode, and shields the solvent's weak sites at the cathode from oxidation.

The modified electrolyte stayed oxidatively stable to 5.54 volts while keeping ionic conductivity above 16 millisiemens per centimeter at 30 degrees Celsius. Lithium cells against NCM811 cathodes retained 87 percent capacity over 400 cycles, while the conventional ether electrolyte collapsed to 5.6 percent retention under the same cycling. Full cells with thin lithium and loaded cathodes ran stably over 100 cycles at a 4.5-volt cutoff. The authors present dihydrogen bonding as a simple, synthesis-free route to high-voltage ether electrolytes.
pmc-13396731:
Leong and team map, in 2026, the absorption landscape of far-red Photosystem II, the machinery some cyanobacteria rebuild to harvest light beyond the visible range. In far-red mode, swapped subunits install chlorophylls, types f and d, that catch longer wavelengths. For the complex from Chroococcidiopsis thermalis and a Calothrix species, they combined cryo-electron microscopy, sequence checks, and charge analysis to assign each pigment its site and wavelength.

The C. thermalis structure revealed a subunit found only in far-red mode, PsbH2-prime, forming part of a chlorophyll f site, and the analyses assigned four chlorophyll f sites. Calothrix lacks the subunit and carries two of the four chlorophyll f sites found in its relative. Assigning wavelengths to red-shifted chlorophyll gives modelers the tools to simulate energy transfer through the far-red complex. The authors highlight shared features that let these microbes survive where white light barely reaches.
pmc-13397331:
Madhusudan Channappa and co-authors tested whether a plant protein drink taken before a sugar load blunts the blood sugar spike that follows, in a 2026 crossover study. Fourteen people with already-compromised blood glucose control took part.

Each volunteer received the Nutrilite All Plant Protein as a preload before a standard 75-gram glucose drink. It was served in 250 milliliters of spiced buttermilk. Each volunteer also had a control session without it, in a fixed order. Because every participant served as their own comparison, the design isolates the preload's acute effect despite the small group. A protein that softens post-meal spikes could earn a place in dietary care for early diabetes.
pmc-13397531:
Neel Vishwanath and fellow authors revisit whether men bleed more than women after facelift surgery under modern care. Their 2026 study matches male and female patients of one senior surgeon from January 2014 to January 2024. Men were long thought riskier because of thicker skin, richer blood supply and habits such as drinking or smoking.

Each man was paired with a woman of similar age, body size, smoking and health profile, and all shared one strict routine to prevent blood collections. That routine used set cutting methods, careful sealing of vessels and local tranexamic acid where noted. If rates now match, the old sex gap may reflect outdated care rather than the patients themselves.
pmc-13397631:
Xavier Perafita and others offer a poverty-normalized spatial Bayesian model beyond the Gini index in a 2026 study. The Gini index is widely used for income inequality, but it compares poorly across areas with different socioeconomic builds and wobbles in small populations.

Adding the poverty rate as an offset within Bayesian spatial modeling sharpened precision and comparability of small-area estimates. On income data for 8,043 Spanish municipalities in 2022, the normalized index bared inequality patterns the stock index missed. Researchers gain a fairer map of territorial inequality for small areas and for funding choices.
pmc-13397731:
Eng-Kean Yeong and co-authors test whether stem cells from the placenta can lift early survival after severe burns when basic care falls short. Their 2026 animal study responds to settings where fluids and warmth, the twin pillars of burn care, may arrive late or in short supply. The cells are known to calm inflammation, which drives much of the early danger.

Sixty male rats received standard full-thickness burns over 40 percent of the body, then were split into six groups mixing fluid dose, warming method and cell treatment by vein. Survival was tracked for 14 days, with blood levels of three inflammation markers also measured. Design lets the team judge whether cells help on top of, or in place of, ideal support.
pmc-13398131:
Quanxing Yao and colleagues craft a transistor that thinks and changes colour at once, copying how chameleons shift skin tone. Their 2026 study pairs a plastic semiconductor, P3HT, with an ion gel so voltage-driven ions tune both electric flow and colour. Robots and embodied machines need sensing, processing and feedback in one loop, and a device that shows its state could serve all three.

Ion entry creates charge carriers that reset the plastic's energy levels, flipping its light absorption in step with its conductance. The colour swing is strong and reversible, echoing a synapse's graded response in the same motion. Such dual behaviour could let robot skins sense, compute and signal without separate display hardware bolted on.
pmc-13398531:
Nick Patterson and co-authors read ancient genomes from a Himalayan cave to date a meeting of peoples. Their 2026 study sequences ten individuals from Old Lady Spider Cave in Ladakh, 4,000 metres up, buried about 1,500 years ago. South Asia's past is hard to reconstruct because ancient DNA from the region is scarce.

The ten genomes look alike and carry a rare blend: roughly half ancestry like today's North Indians and half like ancient Tibetans. Measuring the length of inherited blocks dates the mixing to at least 50 generations before these people lived, around 2,800 years ago. A high crossroads of trade routes, Ladakh kept that blended heritage while surrounding populations shifted.
pmc-13399331:
Mohamed Mowafy and colleagues built a flat, circuit-board style power combiner able to handle kilowatt pulses for L-band radar, reporting in 2026. Solid-state radar transmitters gang several amplifier modules together to reach high peak power. The Gysel design suits this job because its isolation resistors bolt to ground, giving heat a direct escape path. It has usually been built in bulky waveguide form.

The team's four-way planar version, etched on RO4003C substrate, reached a 3 kilowatt peak output. Their optimization adjusted line impedances and lengths while accounting for current flow, heat dissipation, and manufacturing tolerances. The prototype covered 1.2 to 1.4 gigahertz with input return loss better than 15 decibels and isolation above 25 decibels. Bench results matched simulations closely, which the authors offer as proof that planar construction can serve kilowatt-class radar.
pmc-13399631:
Wen-Cheng Shi and colleagues compared two forms of bupivacaine for a chest-wall nerve block in older patients having keyhole lung surgery, in a 2026 randomized trial. Liposomal bupivacaine packages the same drug in tiny fat bubbles that release it over up to three days. The team tested whether it eases pain and opioid use after video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery.

A total of 116 older patients were allocated to standard or liposomal bupivacaine, with the block placed before anesthesia began. Pain scores matched at most time points but ran significantly lower in the liposomal group at 24 and 36 hours after surgery. That group scored higher on the QoR-15 recovery questionnaire at 24 hours, pressed the pump fewer times, and used less sufentanil between 24 and 72 hours. Rates of side effects and postoperative delirium did not differ. The authors say the long-acting form buys a real, if time-limited, advantage for this age group.
pmc-13399931:
Angelo A. Mattos and colleagues review how a disturbed gut microbiome helps drive acute-on-chronic liver failure, the catastrophic flare of cirrhosis that fills hospital wards, in this 2026 article. Drawing on clinical studies and meta-analyses, the authors put gut bacteria escaping into the body at the center of the story.

Their account runs from imbalance to catastrophe: cirrhosis skews gut microbes, the skewed community inflames the intestinal wall, and the leaky barrier lets bacterial products flood the portal blood. That flood ignites the inflammation that tips a compensated patient into organ failure. Because dysbiosis sits upstream of the cascade, the review tours microbiome-directed treatments as candidate therapies, from probiotics and rifaximin to fecal transplants. The authors present such treatment as a plausible way to change the disease's course rather than a proven one.
pmc-13400131:
Soh Yamamoto and colleagues report three adolescents whose chronically low platelets unexpectedly surged after taking the influenza drug oseltamivir, in a 2026 case series from Japan. Across four influenza episodes, every one treated with oseltamivir, platelet counts climbed sharply about a week and a half after the antiviral started.

The median count rose from 9.1 to 26.7 in units of ten thousand per microliter, peaking at a median of 11.5 days after oseltamivir began. One girl's count overshot to 93.1 in the same units before settling. Two episodes forced the team to cut or pause eltrombopag to avoid excessive clotting risk, and counts drifted back to baseline over a median of 57 days. No thrombosis, major bleeding, or other harm occurred. They advise planned monitoring when children with chronic ITP on eltrombopag receive oseltamivir.
pmc-13400531:
Fan Yang and colleagues review, in 2026, how the stiffness and softness of lipid nanocarriers shape their fate in the body. These tiny fat-based packages, including liposomes and lipid nanoparticles, ferry drugs to targets. Yet their behavior at the boundary with cells and tissues varies widely, slowing clinical use.

Mechanics, the authors argue, is a key hidden variable. The review gathers measured mechanical traits for three carrier types, the structural features that set them and the ways stiffness affects uptake, travel and delivery. It also covers tools for measuring mechanics and engineering tricks to tune them. Building a shared database, they say, would let designers craft carriers by mechanical design rather than trial and error.
pmc-13400631:
David Bescoby and co-authors release, in 2026, a global dataset mapping the exact boundaries of coastal World Heritage Sites. The Glo-CoH dataset digitizes 1,250 individual sites that sit along coasts below 20 meters elevation, spanning cultural, natural and mixed listings and a vast total area. Boundaries were drawn from site plans and satellite imagery. A validation exercise on a sample found over nine in ten digitized sites reached top accuracy grades. The free dataset is aimed at researchers and planners judging climate exposure.
pmc-13400731:
Yan-Bo Li and colleagues report, in 2026, a reaction that swaps a single boron atom for a carbon atom inside a ring molecule while keeping everything else in place. Such single-atom skeletal editing lets chemists isolate the effect of one atom change, a prized tool in drug design. Methods for it in aromatic systems are rare.

Their process converts ring compounds called benzazaborines into quinolines, using glyoxylic acid as the carbon source. The group originally attached to boron is caught and reattached to the product, making this a true single-atom swap rather than a rebuild. The reaction tolerated many functional groups and worked on late-stage derivatives of natural products and drugs. Detailed mechanism studies accompany the method.
pmc-13400831:
You-Fan Peng and colleagues ask, in 2026, whether eating more cholesterol raises the odds of prediabetes, the borderline blood sugar state that precedes diabetes. Many nutrients have been tied to prediabetes risk, but dietary cholesterol itself was unexamined. Data came from a United States national health and nutrition survey spanning 2011 to 2016.

Based on day-long dietary recalls, people with prediabetes reported higher cholesterol intake than those with normal blood sugar. Intake also tracked modestly with fasting glucose and long-term sugar markers across all participants. After adjustment, higher cholesterol intake was independently linked to prediabetes, with odds roughly a quarter higher. The authors suggest limiting dietary cholesterol may help prevention, while noting survey data cannot prove cause.
pmc-13400931:
Faranak Behnaz and colleagues run, in 2026, a randomized trial comparing two sedation drugs during stereotactic brain biopsy, a needle procedure done through a fixed head frame. Dexmedetomidine calms patients while easing blood pressure and stress responses. Remifentanil is a very short-acting opioid. The trial weighed sedation depth, vital signs, pain and recovery.

One hundred forty patients were assigned to one drug or the other under single-blind conditions. The remifentanil group reached deeper sedation scores. The dexmedetomidine group kept higher heart rate and blood pressure readings during surgery. Afterward, that group reported less pain and needed significantly less morphine in recovery. The authors present a trade-off: deeper sedation with one drug, better pain control with the other.
pmc-13401131:
Sonia Baumard and co-authors use, in 2026, a case of typhoid fever with a dangerous immune overreaction syndrome to ask how that syndrome should be treated when typhoid triggers it. The syndrome, called HLH, is a life-threatening state where immune cells stay switched on. Guidance exists for tuberculosis-triggered cases, but not for typhoid.

Their illustrative case involved an eighteen-year-old French man of Senegalese ancestry. Alongside it, the authors reviewed past published typhoid-linked cases. They asked two questions. Is specific immune treatment always required on top of antibiotics? And if so, should steroids or intravenous immunoglobulins be preferred? Standard scoring helps diagnosis, while steroids, immunoglobulins and chemotherapy drugs remain the main first-line options in general practice.
pmc-13401531:
Jingchen Jia and co-authors ran a 2026 split-mouth randomized trial on laser treatment for pain after orthodontic tooth movement, comparing pulsed Nd:YAG laser settings against a continuous-wave laser. Soreness after braces are fitted or adjusted hurts the patient experience and compliance.

Ninety-six first-time fixed-appliance patients were assigned to four groups of 24: pulsed laser at low, medium, or high frequency, namely 10, 15, or 20 hertz, or a continuous-wave semiconductor laser. Within each patient, one randomly chosen side of the mouth received active treatment while the other side got a sham procedure, making every participant their own control. A digital pressure algometer measured pressure pain thresholds. The team aimed to find the best frequency and firm evidence for pulsed laser pain relief in orthodontics.
pmc-13401631:
Julia Stalder wrote a 2026 patient perspective piece on ductal carcinoma in situ, the so-called stage zero breast cancer, drawing on her own diagnosis. The condition is non-invasive, yet standard care brings surgery, radiation, and hormone therapy, a mismatch she calls a distressing paradox.

Research increasingly suggests many DCIS cases would never progress to invasive disease if left alone, but clinicians cannot yet predict reliably which ones will. Stalder examines how inconsistent language between providers, uneven risk communication, and a shortage of balanced educational material shape the choices patients face, especially without access to specialist centres. Her recommendations target transparency, shared decision-making, and patient-centred support, with continued research and better risk stratification tools.
pmc-13402231:

The health financing resolution, adopted on May 24, 2025, responds to an expected 40 percent cut in external health aid and rising out-of-pocket costs for patients. The authors recommend health diplomacy, stronger regional cooperation, shared digital systems, and local drug manufacturing to convert the Assembly's commitments into fair outcomes on the ground.
pmc-13402831:
Hao-Yu Lan and colleagues shrink monolayer semiconductor ribbons to a few dozen nanometers wide and find the transistors get better, not worse. pmc-13403031:

Modern mortality still runs 40 to 60 percent when drainage lags.

Their patient was diagnosed from laboratory findings and clinical examination. He recovered on an appropriate medical approach alone, against the usual insistence on operative drainage by routes from thoracotomy to thoracoscopy. The authors do not dismiss surgery. They use the success to argue recognition speed and immediate broad antibiotics decide survival first. Drainage strategy, they note, remains contested territory. The case adds a data point for carefully chosen nonsurgical management.
pmc-13403731:
Yongfeng Liu and colleagues found a greener way in 2026 to cook up glowing crystal dots for light amplifiers. The dots, made of a lead halide crystal, shine brightly yet lose much light to waste paths. Their recipe uses lecithin, a natural fat-like coat, plus a simple solvent.

One batch yielded over 10 grams of dots, with room to scale up further. The coat calmed surface flaws and slowed clumping during growth. Dots kept shining under air, heat, strong light, and harsh solvents. Light output reached about 95 percent efficiency in their tests. Amplifier thresholds fell to levels the team calls record-low for plain dot films.
pmc-13404931:
Jordan L Hickman and team mapped how direct electrical stimulation of the neocortex engages neurons in three dimensions. Higher amplitude raised the density but not the reach of directly responsive neurons, with fewer than 5 percent switched on directly. Mice weakly sensed single pulses, with no gain from amplitude. The work argues that patterning, not spike count, governs impact.
pmc-13406631:
Kazushige Migita and colleagues describe gallbladder surgery in a man kept alive by an implanted heart pump, in a 2026 case report. The man in his fifties had carried a HeartMate II pump for six years while waiting for a donor heart. Fever and upper belly pain signalled an inflamed gallbladder with stones.

Blood thinners, pump hardware and the risks of inflating the belly for keyhole surgery all complicated action. Doctors first drained the gallbladder through the liver to cool the infection. Delay carried its own danger, since infection could seed the pump and end transplant hopes. The case shows the staged reasoning such patients demand, in a field with thin formal evidence.
pmc-13406731:
Małgorzata Chojak and Marta Czechowska-Bieluga use brain wave markers to guide support for children from alcohol-affected families, in a 2026 study. Such children grow up with chronic stress that can disturb attention and body tension. Resting brain recordings offer an objective window beside teacher and parent reports.

The theta-to-beta ratio separated the groups most strongly among all markers tested. Frontal alpha asymmetry, another popular marker, lost significance after correction for multiple comparisons. Children from affected families showed weaker attention regulation and higher physiological arousal in the reported profile. The authors rank markers into a hierarchy so schools and social services can match interventions to each child's measured needs.
pmc-13407831:
Chenqi Liao, Danyang Sun, and Xiong Wang review, in 2026, delivering Alzheimer's medicines up the nose to reach the brain. Many candidate drugs never reach useful levels in the brain. They also cause body-wide side effects. The nose offers smell-nerve and trigeminal routes into the head. These partly bypass the blood-brain barrier, especially when drugs ride in engineered nanocarriers.

Platforms range from lipid particles and polymer nanoparticles to gels and delivery devices. Design dials include particle size, surface charge, mucus interaction, and targeting decorations. Translation stalls on species differences in nasal anatomy, tiny dose volumes, device variability, thin human data, and manufacturing and safety hurdles, which the authors catalogue frankly.
pmc-13407931:
Jacob Rosenberg and Kristoffer Andresen ask, in 2026, who will still know how to repair groin hernias the open way in Denmark. By 2025 only 19 percent of one-sided repairs were open, and open work was thinly spread. Of forty departments still doing it, eighteen performed fewer than twenty a year and only four exceeded a hundred. Reoperation rates after open repair have climbed across successive five-year periods while keyhole rates held steady. Maintaining universal open competence through ordinary training no longer looks realistic, so the authors suggest centralising open surgery and leaning into keyhole training.
pmc-13408131:
Raviteja Sista and team built standard Reporting and Data Systems for laparoscopic cholecystectomy, the gold-standard gallbladder removal op. Their 2026 work takes on scattered, free-form pre-, intra-, and post-op data across centers, which hampers filing, retrieval, and quality comparison. Reporting systems already make radiology uniform, but surgical data lacked a like standard.

One hundred surgeons of varied skill reviewed the system, with 73 percent agreeing it logs apt data well and 77 percent favoring regular use. The center-neutral proforma aims to make surgical data uniform for better care management, pending uptake and outcome studies.
pmc-13408431:
Seyedeh Zahra Miri and co-authors test in 2026 whether gum from the wild almond kin Amygdalus scoparia can fight the germs behind tooth decay. Both lab strains and strains taken from patients were used. Against a patient strain of the main decay germ, the extract's zone beat the zone from chlorhexidine. The mouthwash drug still won on raw strength per dose. Patient strains resisted more than lab strains throughout. The team presents the gum as a hopeful natural option, not a finished swap.
pmc-13409031:

pmc-13410431:

pmc-13411431:

Adapted models beat their baselines, which supports the simulator as a training tool.
pmc-13411931:

The researchers trapped voles at 58 sites across a contact zone between two host lineages.

One reassortant, carrying a swapped middle segment that codes for the surface glycoprotein, dominated most of the zone. pmc-13412131:

Too much or too little gain raises risks for mother and child, and the team scored diets from food questionnaires against weight change and vitamin and mineral intake.

pmc-13412331:

Donation during redeployment processing could add more, and the authors dismiss harvesting blood from the dead as unsound.
pmc-13413731:
Desirée Victoria-Montesinos and co-authors review in 2026 how exercise and food complicate life with type 1 diabetes even when an automated insulin system runs the show. Dual-hormone pumps, activity sensors, and metabolite-guided tuning are flagged as promising but unproven in daily life.
pmc-13414831:

pmc-13415031:

Interviews surfaced five themes, including fear built on memories of past allergic reactions.
pmc-13415331:

pmc-13415431:

pmc-13415531:

pmc-13415831:

pmc-13418131:
Nora A AbdelMotlb and colleagues compare benzoic acid with salicylic acid as growth regulators for Swiss chard, in a 2026 field study over two seasons. pmc-13418431:

pmc-13418831:

pmc-13419031:

pmc-13422831:

pmc-13422931:

pmc-13423031:

pmc-13423831:

pmc-13424531:

pmc-13424731:

pmc-13424831:

pmc-13425031:

pmc-13425631:

pmc-13425831:

pmc-13425931:

pmc-13426231:

pmc-13427131:

pmc-13427431:

pmc-13429131:

pmc-13429631:

pmc-13430431:

pmc-13430731:

pmc-13431031:

pmc-13431131:

pmc-13431231:

pmc-13431331:

pmc-13431431:

pmc-13432531:

pmc-13432831:

pmc-13433331:

pmc-13433931:

pmc-13434031:
