Ventricular fibrillation with no structural cause explains a slice of cardiac arrest survivors, and stray early beats are often the trigger. In this patient those beats arose where a false cord, a fibrous band, anchored from the tricuspid valve ring to the right ventricular wall.

The authors reason that muscle fibers inside the band either fire spontaneously or grow excitable where mechanical tugging strains the attachment. Because sedatives easily silence right-sided trigger beats during procedures, they used pace mapping, stimulating candidate spots to mimic the guilty beat's signature. Imaging from inside the heart guided the ablation before, during, and after. Freeing the trigger and treating the surrounding substrate, they report, can deliver lasting freedom from arrhythmia.
pmc-13493831:
Cui, Li, and Wang present AdaptiveFrequencyNet, a forecasting model for long runs of time-stamped data such as electricity use or weather. Long-range forecasts are hard because patterns repeat at several scales at once. Older methods split the data into fixed frequency bands that cannot adapt. Their 2026 design learns its own split using adjustable filters, then blends information across scales with attention, the technique that lets a model weigh which parts of the data matter most.

Tested on six standard benchmarks against nine rival models, the new network posted competitive errors while keeping a moderate size. Results varied by dataset: it matched the leading transformer model on one electricity series, while rivals edged it on a weather benchmark. The authors are candid that rankings depend on the dataset and forecast horizon. Their claim is narrower than a clean sweep: learnable decomposition holds its own without rigid frequency splits.
pmc-13494031:
Cillis, Lanorte, and Nolè use satellite images to watch for vegetation stress across two river basins in Basilicata, southern Italy, over seven years. Healthy plants reflect light in a pattern captured by the NDVI index, and places where growth deviates sharply from the norm can signal drought damage, land abandonment, or degradation. Their 2026 study ran a technique called selective principal component analysis over Sentinel-2 records from 2017 to 2023 to pull real change out of ordinary seasonal swings.

Forests mostly improved, with around three fifths of forest area showing significant, mainly positive anomalies over six-month windows. Grasslands told the opposite story: nearly seven tenths of their area showed significant anomalies, and most of those were negative, pointing to declining growth. Shrublands barely changed and proved the most stable cover type. The authors offer the method as a low-cost early-warning framework for land managers under a shifting climate.
pmc-13494531:
Elio Adib and others reply to commentary on radiation therapy after neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy for locally advanced lung cancer in patients who did not reach surgery. In 2026, the letter thanks the commentators and agrees that caution is vital before look-back plans enter routine practice. Surgery was abandoned for very different reasons across patients.

Those whose surgery was aborted for contraindications such as advance or spread fared worse than those blocked by an acute medical event. The groups cannot fairly be compared with patients who underwent resection. Pneumonitis risk from immune priming must also be weighed case by case. The authors urge deliberate upfront selection and multidisciplinary planning, with larger randomized trials still needed before radiation becomes a standard rescue path.
pmc-13495431:
Tüfekçi and co-authors test a six-week sprint program built around direction changes in young basketball players in this 2026 trial. Basketball demands repeated sprints, jumps, and sharp cuts. Twenty male under-19 players were split evenly into training and control groups.

The training group added change-of-direction repeated sprints three times a week to normal practice. Tests before and after covered the countermovement jump, squat jump, 30-meter sprint, and a T-test of agility. The training group improved significantly on all four measures within itself. Against controls, the jump gains were clearly better, while sprint and agility edges did not reach significance. Coaches gain most, it seems, in explosive power.
pmc-13498931:
Saif Syed and five co-authors reviewed how socioeconomic disadvantage affects oral health in older adults, in a systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2026. Oral disease is common in later life, but evidence on income and social position was scattered across studies using different measures. The team searched three major databases and kept 68 studies of people aged 75 and older.

Across the pooled studies, disadvantaged older adults kept fewer healthy teeth and were more likely to have lost all their teeth. They had more tooth decay, attended the dentist less regularly, and scored worse on oral health related quality of life. For gum disease, dry mouth, and oral function, the pattern was similar but too limited for a pooled estimate. The tooth gap was widest, which the authors read as disadvantage building up over a lifetime. They urge planners to weigh socioeconomic factors in dental care for older adults.
pmc-13499031:
Tang and a team in China tested in 2026 a new drug tactic against retinoblastoma, an eye cancer of young children. Extra copies of the MYCN gene drive the worst cases, yet MYCN has long been hard to drug. Their compound, HLB-0532259, is a PROTAC, a molecule built to tag a target protein for disposal. They tried it on two cell lines and on tumors in mouse eyes.

The compound broke down MYCN in a dose linked way, and one cell line proved more prone to it than the other. Gene and protein scans showed a fast switch on of the p53 to p21 path, a brake that halts cell growth. DNA repair genes fell, damage built up, and cells slid into senescence, a state where growth stops. In mice, shots into the eye shrank tumor load and cut cells still marked for growth.
pmc-13499331:
Lei Huang and colleagues survey in 2026 whether mental resilience softens the link between bad academic events and anxiety among clinical medicine postgraduates in China. These trainees work under heavy pressure, and setbacks such as failed exams or criticism are common. A total of 1,182 postgraduates at one large medical school answered an anonymous online survey using an eight-item setback checklist, a standard anxiety scale, and a ten-item resilience scale.

Students who reported setbacks had far higher odds of probable anxiety disorder, and low resilience alone also raised the odds sharply. Statistical interaction tests showed the two risks amplified each other, since the setback link was much stronger among low-resilience students than among high-resilience peers. The authors suggest that screening for resilience and building coping support could help training programmes protect students after academic blows.
pmc-13499731:
Poddar, an obesity medicine specialist, and Nadglowski, a patient advocate, hold a clinical dialogue about obesity and liver disease for a 2026 journal podcast article. About a billion people worldwide live with obesity, yet the usual body mass index label misses where fat sits, and belly fat drives the worst metabolic harm. The conversation centres on what good, respectful obesity care looks like in practice, and on waist-based measures that capture risk better.

Liver health anchors the discussion, since three quarters of people with obesity have metabolic fatty liver disease. A substantial minority progress within a decade or so to its inflamed, scarring form. Both conditions usually cause no symptoms, so they stay undiagnosed without deliberate screening. Drawing on Nadglowski's lived experience, the pair argue for routine complication checks, including liver assessment, inside holistic obesity care rather than weight lectures alone.
pmc-13499931:
Deepak K Saini and colleagues evaluate in 2026 keyhole screw fixation for burst fractures of the thoracolumbar spine in patients without nerve injury. Open surgery stabilises such fractures well yet strips back muscles and adds surgical harm, so screws placed through small skin punctures aim for equal stability with less tissue damage. Their prospective study treated 46 consecutive adults aged 18 to 50 at a tertiary public hospital over eighteen months, using standard X-ray guidance in the operating room.

Falls from height caused most injuries, and the second lumbar vertebra was the commonest level affected. Operating time averaged under two hours with modest blood loss in the reported figures, hospital stays ran short, and pain scores fell within days. Spine alignment and vertebral height both improved significantly, and most screws sat perfectly placed on post-surgery scans, with no infections, implant failures, or revisions in early follow-up.
pmc-13500531:
Sunil Lavadiya and colleagues design in 2026 a layered solar absorber that harvests sunlight across a wide band while barely caring about the sun's angle. Most absorbers work narrowly and fade in ultraviolet and near-infrared light, so the team stacked iron, silica glass, an advanced carbon material called MXene, and iron again in a repeating patterned structure. Computer simulations with the finite element method tuned the shape, materials, and layer thicknesses for peak performance.

Uptake exceeded ninety percent across three separate wavelength bands in the tuned design, according to the simulations. The design held for both light polarisations across approach angles from straight-on to steeply tilted, a wide-angle strength prized for real rooftops and collectors. Machine learning models were trained to predict absorption behaviour and agreed with the simulations. Head-to-head checks with published designs favoured the new stack for photothermal energy harvesting.
pmc-13500731:
圣莉 程 and others survey nurses on acceptance of AI systems that dynamically assess venous thromboembolism risk in hospital patients. In 2026, the study collects valid surveys from 2,323 nurses at tertiary hospitals in Anhui Province between April and June 2025. It uses latent profile analysis to find distinct acceptance groups and logistic regression to explain them. Nurse acceptance directly shapes whether smart nursing tools work in practice.

Three profiles emerged: low acceptance with concern and resistance at about seventeen percent, medium acceptance with cautious waiting at about fifty-one percent, and high acceptance with active embrace at about thirty-three percent. Professional attitude, night shift frequency, years of service, and prevention knowledge predicted group membership. Managers should target support and training by profile rather than one uniform rollout.
pmc-13500831:
Mahdee Jodayree leads a four-author team with a 2026 framework for predicting which students risk failing, without pooling their records in one place. Schools increasingly want early-warning models, yet centralizing sensitive student data raises privacy and ownership concerns. Their system, called FL-AtRisk-DP-PBT, trains a shared logistic regression model across schools using federated averaging, so records stay local. Client-side differential privacy adds noise for protection, and a proof-before-train protocol logs each school's part so the process can be audited.

The team tested three setups on a main cohort of 14,003 students split into ten simulated schools, plus two public education datasets. The central model reached 99.14 percent accuracy, while the private federated version reached 98.00 percent, a small cost for the added protections. On the two public datasets the private version scored about 93 to 94 percent accuracy. Feature patterns stayed similar across setups, keeping the model interpretable.
pmc-13501631:
Jie Zhou leads a fifteen-author team reporting a 2026 nanomedicine study of eyedrops for uveitis, a sight-threatening inflammation inside the eye. Biologic drugs each block one target and need injections into the eye, which carry risks when repeated. Screening identified two disease drivers, VEGF and tumour necrosis factor alpha. The team engineered one bispecific antibody, V5-3, that blocks both at once, then packaged it with a dithiolane molecule into nanoparticles that cross the eye's surface after topical dosing.

Compared with the free antibody, the nanoparticle drops entered cells better, curbed microglial growth and movement, and cut inflammatory cytokine release. In cell and animal models the dual targeting combined anti-inflammatory and anti-vessel-growth effects, easing symptoms and tissue damage in the retina. Toxicity was negligible across the models tested. The authors present the drops as a noninvasive candidate for a disease where delivery is the bottleneck.
pmc-13501831:
Lili Xie leads a six-author team presenting a 2026 review of questionnaires that measure quality of life in multiple myeloma, judged by the COSMIN standards for measurement quality. Twenty-six studies covering fourteen patient-reported instruments qualified. The myeloma-specific module EORTC QLQ-MY20 was evaluated most often, followed by instruments such as MyPOS, HM-PRO, and FACT-MM. Evidence clustered on internal consistency, structural validity, and construct testing, while measurement error, criterion validity, and cross-cultural validity were rarely examined.

No instrument earned uniformly high-quality evidence across all the properties that matter. The EORTC QLQ-MY20 and MyPOS carried the broadest supportive evidence and look like the most defensible choices for myeloma-specific use. Even they lack strong content validity work and long-term measurement studies. The authors urge future research to involve patients in validating what the forms ask, and to test responsiveness when health changes.
pmc-13503031:
Summo and colleagues launch SynFlow, a web tool that turns genome rearrangement maps from figures into displays researchers can explore live. Structural variants, the inversions, swaps, and insertions or deletions that reshape genomes, are usually plotted as fixed images by the SyRI detection software. Their 2026 article presents a browser app that loads SyRI output and rebuilds those plots as interactive views, shareable by link.

Users can filter events in real time, reorder genomes, and zoom into rearrangements, including the translocations that static plots handle worst. The site offers three doors in. Users can browse ready made datasets such as banana and grapevine genomes. They can upload their SyRI results. Or they can run the built in workflow that detects variants and displays them in one pass. The team shows the tool matching published synteny figures while adding the exploration those figures cannot offer. Source code is public on GitHub.
pmc-13503431:
Yan and Zhong mine twenty years of American adverse event reports to profile palivizumab, the antibody given to fragile infants to prevent severe RSV lung infection. Trial data cover narrow populations. The 2026 study extracted over fourteen thousand reports naming the drug as the prime suspect from the FDA database covering 2004 to 2024. It then ran four statistical methods to find reactions reported more often than chance would suggest.

Most reports concerned infants under two years, and hospitalisation was the commonest serious outcome, recorded in about three fifths of cases. Three body-system categories lit up as statistical signals, two of them new: infections and infestations beyond RSV, and congenital or genetic disorders. The authors stress that reporting patterns are not proof of causation, especially in babies already gravely ill, but argue the novel signals deserve targeted follow-up in registries.
pmc-13503931:
Roxana González-Stegmaier leads a team profiling gut microbes in Chilean patients with and without colon growths, in a 2026 study. Colon cancer often grows out of such growths, called adenomas. Gut microbes are thought to help steer that path, yet local baseline data were missing.

Gene reads from stool samples showed a shifted mix in patients with growths. One broad germ group rose while another fell, against healthy peers. A sulfur-using genus that makes a gas linked to DNA harm was more common in the growth group. The authors treat the work as a first map for their population. They say microbe profiles may one day aid early checks for colon disease.
pmc-13504831:
Junfeng Wang and others present THC-Net, a focus-based deep learning model predicting chromatin spaces from histone modifications. In 2026, the model joins transformer self-attention, Hyena long-sequence model, and convolutional local feature extraction to classify active A spaces and repressive B spaces without costly Hi-C tests. Three-dimensional genome architecture governs cell fate and disease.

Across six cell lines, cross-cell-type testing reached an average area under the receiver operating curve of 93.1 percent, outperforming other methods. Feature analysis showed high redundancy among the six histone inputs, with the model relying mainly on strong active enhancer and promoter signals to define A spaces. Team gain a versatile tool for precise space prediction.
pmc-13505031:
Yuzer and Ozasir ask an endodontic question: how dry should a root canal be before sealing it, especially when redoing a failed treatment? Moisture left in dentine can weaken the seal, and retreatment dentine behaves differently from virgin dentine. Their 2026 laboratory study prepared 192 extracted human premolars and dried canals four ways, from paper points to ethanol rinses. It sealed them with either an epoxy resin or a newer calcium silicate sealer, then measured how hard each seal resisted being pushed out.

Bond strength rose toward the root tip in nearly every group, and retreated teeth bonded far more strongly than first-time teeth at the tip, more than doubling the average push-out strength there. Ethanol drying won in several tip conditions, while the two sealers performed indistinguishably at every level. The authors say drying protocol and treatment history matter more than sealer brand here.
pmc-13506331:
Simon Whitburn and others estimate heat-ray forcing of long-lived halogen gases straight from orbiter readings. In 2026, the study joins fifteen years, 2008 to 2022, of color-split heat glow from the Heat Air Sounding Wave-mixer on Metop orbiters with ground and space level readings. Heat-ray rate had earlier been estimated only at second hand through models.

Clear-sky on-the-spot heat-ray rates are found for CFC-11, CFC-12, sulfur six-fluoride gas, HCFC-22, and HFC-134a. Checks mostly confirm model guesses, with the largest gaps for CFC-11 and sulfur six-fluoride gas, estimated twenty-seven percent lower yet within doubt bounds. The work grounds climate impact guesses for ozone-eating and swap-in gases in direct watching.
pmc-13506631:
Takuma Makino and colleagues present 2026 real-world outcomes for surgery in advanced head and neck cancer, before immune drugs around surgery came into use. Their single-center review covers 233 patients who had curative surgery for locally advanced squamous cell cancer. The team tracked event-free survival, overall survival, and whether return disease could still be treated.

One-year event-free survival reached about two thirds of patients, while overall survival was near nine in ten. Disease returned in about one third of patients, and salvage surgery linked to better survival after return. Heavy node spread and invasion into veins or nerves marked worse outlooks. The data give a baseline for judging newer combined care.
pmc-13507131:
Yonghui Wang leads a 2026 team that reports the first clear ground radar sighting of natural electron Bernstein waves in Earth's ionosphere, the charged upper air layer. These faint waves travel across the magnetic field and show a ladder of tones at multiples of the electron spin rate. The Sanya radar in China caught the pattern with wide-band, high-detail scans.

Seven clear harmonic lines matched theory, helped by energetic photoelectrons and a beam aimed nearly across the magnetic field, which limits signal loss. Tone spacing acts as a ruler for electron density and sideways electron temperature, values hard to get by standard radar in that geometry. The method opens a new window on plasma states.
pmc-13507231:
Ruixiang Liu and others test how mental load affects neural speech tracking in healthy adults. In 2026, the electroencephalography study studies twenty-nine people listening to continuous speech with or without concurrent mental arithmetic, using time response functions, neural network decoding, and phase-coupling links tests. Everyday listening often competes with memory and focus demands.

Higher load reduced recoverable speech-envelope information, lowering delta-band prediction rightness and decoding performance, though theta-band encoding did not differ clearly. Delta responses shrank in amplitude without shifting peak latency, while delta coupling became more clustered and small-world-like. Mental load thus weakens neural speech representations and alters frontotemporal coupling, even without degraded speech or competing talkers.
pmc-13508231:
Jagdeep Singh leads a nine-author team studying how long-term fertilizer and cattle manure use changes phosphorus and carbon stored in soil clumps, in 2026 work. Soil is made of aggregates, clusters that hold nutrients and carbon in different ways. The long-term trial compared several rates of mineral phosphorus, manure alone, and mixes of both. It ran in soils that started with high or medium test phosphorus. Wheat yield and soil measures were tracked.

Readily available organic phosphorus rose with fertilizer up to a middle rate, above all in large aggregates. Mixing manure with that middle fertilizer rate lifted organic phosphorus well beyond manure alone in both soil types. Carbon stored in aggregates also climbed, most sharply in the medium-phosphorus soil. Mixed treatments gave the highest wheat yields in both soils. The work shows starting soil phosphorus and clump size steer how nutrients and carbon build up.
pmc-13509331:
Julia Leipner and five co-authors compare how finger joints move during sport climbing in younger and older adults, in a 2026 study. Nine younger climbers near age 34 and eleven older climbers near age 56 climbed a set boulder problem using four grip types, from the tight crimp to the relaxed open hand. Motion cameras tracked the joints, special holds measured force, and ultrasound checked for bony growths linked to joint wear.

Older climbers bent the middle finger joint far less in tight grips, while both groups moved alike in the open-hand grip. Bony growths were rare in younger climbers yet common in older ones, and greater growth went with less bending. Older climbers also used lower forces in set grips while keeping full grip strength, a pattern the authors read as a protective way of moving.
pmc-13510031:
Lehmann and colleagues published a 2026 study on dental implants that pipe light into jawbone. Bacteria films on implant edges can trigger bone-losing gum disease there. Light-activated killing, called photodynamic inactivation, offers a gentler add-on treatment. Ceramic zirconia implants can themselves carry the light to the bone edge.

Computer simulations, built from CT scans, tracked the light spread in jawbone. Light passed the implant edge at strengths above the killing threshold set. Changing implant shape and light placement steered where the dose landed. Pig and human jaw tissue behaved alike in the optical measures. The path toward patient trials looks open, the authors conclude. Design tweaks could target uneven film patches case by case. The implant itself acts as the light guide in the concept.
pmc-13511631:
Giuseppa Luisa Sanfilippo and six co-authors test whether gene variants in a family of antiviral signals shape T cell responses after COVID-19 vaccination, in a 2026 preliminary study. Fifty vaccinated people gave cells that were challenged with virus spike pieces in the lab, and the team measured three immune signals inside two T cell classes. Each person was typed for variants in two related interferon lambda genes.

One variant form in the fourth family member went with higher production of the growth signal IL-2 in killer T cells, while the alternate form went with a lower response. No clear effects appeared in helper T cells or for the other two signals measured. The authors suggest that typing this gene could one day help tailor vaccination plans, while stressing the small group and early stage of the work.
pmc-13513031:
Lanmei Wei, Minting Liang, Xi Zeng, Wancheng Liu, and Zhengwei Wu build a nanoemulsion of mint essential oil for greener control of two corn pests, in 2026 work. Mint oil evaporates fast, mixes poorly with water, and breaks down, while chemical sprays breed resistance and pollute. Tiny droplets stabilized by a tuned surfactant blend solved the handling problems: one surfactant pairing at a set ratio gave small particles that stayed stable through dilution and spinning tests.

At a mid-range concentration, the preparation stopped fall armyworm eggs from hatching completely. The same strength killed every corn aphid tested, both young and adult. The authors present the composite as a fresh route to green corn protection. It can cut chemical residues and slow resistance build-up, supporting more sustainable farming where both pests pressure yields.
pmc-13513831:
Hadidi and colleagues studied whether community leisure activities improve well-being and belonging for Iranian immigrant women in Ottawa, Canada, in 2026 research on newcomer health. The women, aged 30 to 55 and Farsi-speaking, joined three activities run with PAND Settlement Services. The three were a classical Persian dance workshop, a guided tour of the National Gallery of Canada, and a group walk along the Rideau Canal.

Evidence came from 32 post-activity evaluation surveys, the researcher's field notes, and two follow-up feedback sessions. Participants rated all three activities positively for enjoyment, accessibility, and social contact, describing them as a break from routine and a chance to meet women sharing their language and migration experience. Continued attendance, though, depended on time pressure, caregiving duties, weather, transportation, and cost. Hadidi argues leisure should be funded as a real part of settlement support, not an optional extra.
pmc-13514531:
Stamatios Katsimperis, Lazaros Tzelves, Patrick Juliebø-Jones, and Andreas Skolarikos survey, in a 2026 review, blood-borne microRNAs as markers for testicular germ cell tumours. These cancers are highly curable, yet doctors still lean on three older blood markers that miss many cases and rise for unrelated reasons. Tiny RNA fragments shed by tumours, above all one called miR-371a-3p, promise a sharper liquid biopsy across diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment choices.

The assembled results show miR-371a-3p identifying viable tumours of most types with accuracy beyond the classic markers, falling fast when treatment works, and climbing again at relapse. Its blind spot is teratoma, a tumour type it cannot detect, which matters when scans leave masses behind after chemotherapy. Katsimperis and colleagues see a near-clinic tool that needs standard methods and prospective trials before it guides routine decisions.
pmc-13514731:
Kang-Il Kim and six co-authors ask when an intravenous dose of stem cells best helps a broken bone heal, in a 2026 rat study. Mesenchymal stem cells given through a vein can boost fracture repair, yet earlier work had not settled whether immediate or delayed delivery works better. Forty-nine rats with thigh-bone fractures were assigned to receive donor bone-marrow stem cells right away, after one day, or after seven days, with a small untreated control group.

At six weeks, the seven-day group showed significantly more new bone formation than both earlier groups and the controls, alongside higher tissue repair grades. Growth signals tied to blood vessel growth and bone building, including VEGF and BMP-2, also ran higher in that group. Kim's team proposes that waiting a week, as early inflammation settles, gives the cells their best working conditions.
pmc-13515331:
Chen introduces a 2026 special issue of collected papers on microorganisms in agriculture, surveying how microbes can promote plant growth, fight disease, and clean polluted soil. The eleven papers apply genome sequencing and other multi-omics tools to microbes that cycle nutrients, protect crops, and break down contaminants. The editorial frames these studies against soil degradation, heavy metal buildup, and climate stress on the root zone.

Among the highlighted work, one study reported the first complete genome of Glutamicibacter endophyticus and showed the strain lifting wheat germination under salt stress from 37.5 percent to ninety-five percent, while another found a fungus, Purpureocillium lilacinum, that suppressed the root pathogen Rhizoctonia solani by eighty-six percent in laboratory assays. Other papers covered compost extracts with nitrogen-fixing bacteria on soybean and integrated fertilization on arugula. Chen presents the collection as a map of where agricultural microbiology is heading.
pmc-13515831:
Mingnan Zhuang, Yufei Li, Zhengqi Qiu, and Xueqin Zhang pool trial evidence on breaking up long sitting spells, in a 2026 three-level meta-analysis. Sitting for hours harms blood sugar control, and short activity breaks are widely advised, yet their instant effects in healthy people were unquantified. The team gathered randomised crossover trials from five databases through March 2026, ending with twenty-three independent groups of volunteers.

Breaks produced small but real drops in blood glucose and insulin compared with unbroken sitting. Blood fats, measured as triglycerides, did not budge reliably. Two further measures stayed inconclusive. No break style, intensity, or timing proved superior to the rest. The authors rate the certainty of evidence low across the board. Zhuang's team calls interrupting sitting a low-burden habit worth adopting while better trials are run, rather than a proven clinical prescription.
pmc-13516031:
Kelly Zúñiga-Vera and five colleagues hunt viruses in Ecuadorian shallots in a 2026 study. Shallot is an emerging crop in Ecuador, and viral infections cut yield and quality while detection and cures lag. The team screened market shallots from Quito suppliers with RT-PCR tests for the five commonest shallot viruses, from shallot latent virus to iris yellow spot virus.

Two viruses turned up. Shallot latent virus appeared quietly, while iris yellow spot virus, which causes severe symptoms, was found in Ecuadorian shallots for the first time. The team then grew plants from shoot tips, a standard cleaning trick. The regenerated plants came out fully free of the iris virus, though the latent virus persisted through the process. Zúñiga-Vera's team offers shoot-tip culture as a partial cleaning method that can already lift planting stock quality.
pmc-13516331:
Alabbas and Alqahtani reported a 2026 drug discovery study hunting new blockers of HER2, a growth signal protein that drives some breast cancers. Tumours with too much HER2 grow, spread, and resist therapy more readily. The pair combined machine learning screening with physics based simulation to search chemical libraries.

Four fingerprint based models were trained on ten thousand checked compounds from the ChEMBL database, and the Random Forest model performed best. Alabbas screened a large library with it, then docked the top hits into the HER2 binding pocket and ran two hundred nanosecond simulations of their stability. Three compounds beat the reference blocker on binding and interaction quality. Lead-2 stayed most stable in simulation, while Lead-1 showed the most favourable binding energy.
pmc-13516431:
Nicolò Salvi and Mariangela Morlando review circular RNAs in neurons in a 2026 article. These loop-shaped RNA molecules, closed into rings, resist breakdown and pile up in the nervous system. Neurons park them in specific districts: the branching dendrites, the long axon, and the synapses where signals cross. Such precise placement implies active transport, and the review focuses on the machinery that might haul them there.

Protein-and-RNA parcels riding the cell's transport system are the leading candidate mechanism. Where the loops land may tune synaptic strength and the local switching of genes, shaping learning-related change. When RNA transport goes wrong, neurons suffer, and the authors trace links to developmental and degenerative disorders. Salvi and Morlando frame transport control as the missing middle between a loop's birth and its job at the synapse.
pmc-13518231:
Alexander Berne and co-authors read Mars's tides to find a warm layer under its southern highlands in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Mars's off-center orbit and tilted axis make the Sun's pull flex the planet with the seasons. That flex stirs the gravity field in ways that betray the deep interior.

Tracking data from three orbiters showed one gravity component swinging up to three times past forecasts for a uniform planet. The mismatch fits a mantle whose stiffness varies by over twenty percent in a north-south pattern matching the crust split at the surface. The team infers a pocket two to four hundred degrees warmer under the south, held for billions of years by thick crust or slow convection.
pmc-13518831:
Mohamed B Jalloh and colleagues mapped why heart and vessel care falls short in Sierra Leone, where deaths from such disease keep rising. Published in 2026, the scoping review screened 498 records from 2000 through early 2025 and kept 40 sources, sorting findings against the World Health Organization building blocks of a health system. The lens was fair access to care for all, not just care in big city hospitals.

Clinics built for infectious disease left heart care thin, with readiness near 41 percent for HIV services but under 17 percent for heart care. City life raised the odds of high blood pressure and diabetes, yet primary care still leaned toward rural maternal health. Costly care, drug shortages, and scarce stroke scans pushed people away from formal clinics. The authors urge shared tasks among health workers, pooled drug buying, guarded heart-care budgets, and better digital tools to close these gaps.
pmc-13519031:
Zhifan Huang and four colleagues present CURE in 2026, a method for making a trained graph neural network forget chosen nodes, edges, or features, as privacy law increasingly demands. Graph data complicate forgetting because influence spreads to neighbors through message passing. Earlier methods traded away too much accuracy or left traces behind.

CURE first selects the nodes most entangled with the deletion targets, judging both structure and meaning. A contrastive step then pulls the forgotten nodes' representations away from their relatives in embedding space, erasing their imprint. A PageRank-based guard keeps predictions steady for everyone else. Across experiments, CURE balanced utility, speed, and completeness of forgetting better than baselines, with stronger privacy protection.
pmc-13520231:
Shao-kun Sun, Tong Shen, Zi-jian Zhou, and Qin Zhou follow 109,018 older adults in Kunshan, China in 2026 to test whether a combined healthy lifestyle score predicts cancer risk. Western evidence is plentiful, while Chinese senior data were scarce. The score summed five habits measured at enrollment: smoking, alcohol, diet, body mass index, and physical activity.

Over a mean follow-up of 7.34 years, 2,115 new cancers appeared. Risk fell in a clear dose-response as scores rose. Scoring a perfect 5 versus 0 to 2 cut the hazard to 0.37 overall, and protection looked stronger past age 70 than in the sixties. Diet and exercise were the strongest single contributors after mutual adjustment.
pmc-13521231:
Yunxiang Zhu leads a large team in 2026 on predicting Salmonella Enteritidis growth on chicken meat washed with slightly acidic electrolyzed water, a gentle chlorine sanitizer. Older growth equations showed a steady bias under changing temperatures, which limited precise food-safety planning.

The team bolted a machine learning corrector onto a classic growth curve and used explanation tools to see where the old model went wrong. The hybrid fit the data far better, cutting prediction error by about forty percent. The bias traced to three simplifications in the classic curve. Scenario tests suggested a mid-strength sanitizer dose lowers peak bacterial counts notably across storage temperatures. The authors offer the framework for optimizing sanitizer use in poultry plants.
pmc-13521731:
Anna Resende, Lucy Campbell, Catarina Vinagre, and Alice Rogers test how muddy water and warming hit a small shore fish, in work from 2026. Coasts face heat and silt together as the climate shifts. Heat changes appetite and oxygen supply, while silt can blur or sharpen a fish's view of prey.

The common triplefin struck at prey more slowly in cloudy water, a sign it hunts by sight and loses ground in silt. Routine and burst swimming held steady across all tanks, though. Oxygen use during a fast heat ramp was logged to link heat limits with performance. The fish copes with motion demands but pays in feeding. The study warns that clear-water hunters suffer as shores silt up.
pmc-13522131:
Xue Li and five co-authors present a 2026 study of HPV types in cervical infections in Chongqing, China. Cervical cancer is a heavy burden in the southwest of the country. Local data on which virus types dominate, and how they tie to the vaginal environment, have been thin.

Over six years, the team tested more than twenty four thousand women aged eighteen to eighty. Each woman got virus typing for 23 subtypes, a cell test, and a check of the vaginal microbe balance. About 21.7 percent of women carried the virus. One type, HPV52, stood out as the most common in infections and in early lesions, the authors report.
pmc-13522531:
Ran and colleagues modelled a 2026 scenario in which global shipping switches its energy to hydrogen. Ships burn fuel equal to about two hundred million tons of oil each year and foul coastal air. Hydrogen could cut carbon emissions, but its health and money benefits had not been counted.

Linking emission, air quality, and health models, Ran estimated the switch could avert roughly 129,500 early deaths each year worldwide. Three quarters of the gain came from lower ozone and one quarter from fewer fine particles in the air. Southern Asia gained most on ozone, while Eastern Asia gained most on particles. The avoided deaths were valued near 306 billion dollars yearly, led by India, Japan, and the United States.
pmc-13522931:
A large team of co-authors reports a trial dated two thousand twenty-six on a plant extract and weight loss. The extract comes from the leaves of Moringa oleifera, a plant used as a new food resource in China. The team asked whether it helps people with simple obesity lose weight, and how.

Thirty-five people took either the extract or a placebo for ninety days, without knowing which they got. Both groups also got diet and lifestyle advice. Body measures were taken monthly, and stool and blood samples were tested for gut microbes and body chemistry. The extract group lost more on a key weight index while keeping more muscle.
pmc-13523231:
Eunice Y Lee and colleagues add dietary information to genetic risk prediction in Native Hawaiian adults in a 2026 study. Genetic scores alone explain limited variation in body mass and diabetes and often transfer poorly across ancestries. Data came from more than fourteen thousand cohort members, with genetic data in a subset, and dietary scores were learned by machine learning from hundreds of food variables.

Scores built across ancestries predicted both traits better than single-ancestry scores. The best dietary score explained as much body mass variation as the genetic score did. Combining the two significantly outperformed either alone for body mass and gave a smaller gain for diabetes. The dietary score also tracked several chronic diseases, partly through inflammation and blood fats, supporting combined genetic and dietary models.
pmc-13523331:
Junyu Wang leads a randomized trial of school flag football in Shanghai in a 2026 study of children aged nine to eleven. One hundred forty-seven children were assigned to twice-weekly hour-long flag football sessions for ten weeks or to usual physical education. Fitness was measured before and after with a shuttle run, a jump rope test, and a short sprint, with heart rate monitored in a subsample.

Post-program data were available for most children. The football group improved more on jump rope performance and sprint time than controls. No clear group differences appeared for shuttle run performance or estimated aerobic capacity. Subgroup patterns varied by sex and starting weight, with normal-weight boys gaining most on endurance measures. The authors suggest differentiated progression to spread benefits more evenly across children.
pmc-13523431:
Luis Delgado-Flores and colleagues report a 2026 multicenter comparison of two reverse shoulder replacement designs used after acute fractures near the top of the upper arm bone. Four centers took part, two using implants that shift the joint center inward and two using designs that shift it outward. The patients all had complex fractures and were followed for at least two years after surgery.

The group included 122 patients, and shoulder function was scored with the Constant score at two years. Average scores were nearly identical between the two designs, and complication rates were similar. Healing of the greater tuberosity, a bony prominence where tendons attach, mattered most. It healed in about two thirds of patients, and those patients scored clearly higher. Regression analysis left tuberosity healing as the only independent predictor of a better result.
pmc-13523531:
Lei Tian and colleagues report 2026 maize experiments linking blocked pollination to early aging of the plant and disturbed storage reserves. When grain demand falls, maize ages faster, yet the molecular chain was unclear. The team used an inbred line known for early aging after grain removal.

Plants grown without pollination were compared with normally pollinated plants, with grain sampled from 6 to 24 days after silking. Blocked pollination triggered early senescence, and the sharpest gene activity divergence appeared between 14 and 18 days. Pathways for starch, sucrose, and trehalose handling were disrupted. Network analysis found five gene modules tied to energy, photosynthesis, and stress, plus twenty hub genes as candidate regulators. The work connects reduced grain demand with coordinated metabolic change.
pmc-13523731:
Shang-Yi Lin and five colleagues analyze fluconazole tolerance in Candida albicans bloodstream isolates from Taiwan, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Tolerance is an emerging phenotype in these infections, distinct from outright resistance. Its links to genetic lineages and virulence traits were unclear. The team typed isolates from three hospitals in southern Taiwan.

One hundred seventy-nine isolates were profiled for tolerance, biofilm biomass, and enzyme activity. Genetic typing found one hundred sixty-nine unique sequence types across fourteen clades. High tolerance was spread broadly across diverse lineages. One clade stood out with higher tolerance and biofilm formation. Statistical analysis tied high tolerance to that clade and to protease activity, not biofilm biomass. Tolerance, the authors show, is a lineage-spanning trait with specific hotspots.
pmc-13524831:
K Taylor Wild and Nancy B Spinner argued for faster genetic diagnosis of inborn errors of metabolism in newborns. Published in 2026, the commentary responds to a study that used exome sequencing to solve three methylmalonic acidemia cases and four CBS deficiency cases in Pakistan, a country without population-wide newborn screening. Such disorders can bring severe disability, yet many are treatable if caught early.

The catch is timing: diagnoses in that study arrived at ages one to fourteen, too late to prevent much harm. Early treatment can cut metabolic crises and deaths in one disorder and prevent intellectual disability entirely in the other. The authors note pilot sequencing programs in several countries and argue that genome sequencing, now possible within hours to days, should join biochemical screening. Readers get an urgency case for catching treatable disorders before symptoms lock in.
pmc-13525031:
Huong Giang Nguyen and a large team set a shared base curve for low-press waste gas catch on a stock sieve. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. The work ran as a world lab ring test led by the US NIST on its grade test stock. Eighteen labs sent in twenty-one data sets of gas catch at room heat.

A shared curve with a trust span was drawn from the pool. The stock read as fit to grow to a full base stock, the first sieve form of its kind at NIST in bead shape. Side files hold the full sets.
pmc-13525931:
Florian Scheichel and co-authors study how a rare brain lymphoma reacts to steroid drugs, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. This tumor often shrinks on steroids, but the range of responses was not mapped. Scans from two patient groups were read after a week of steroid care.

Most tumors shrank, with a median shrink of about forty percent. A smaller share grew despite the drugs. Shrinkage did not track with dose, though a blood marker hinted at a link. Patients whose tumors shrank lived far longer on median than those whose tumors grew. Response may thus flag outlook, the authors say.
pmc-13526731:
Yao Yao and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a four-gene prognostic signature for oral squamous cell carcinoma drawn from two newly described cell-death pathways, disulfidptosis and cuproptosis. Genes from these pathways might carry outcome information, yet no validated combined signature existed for this mouth cancer. Public expression cohorts supplied discovery, training, and validation data.

The signature combines CDKN2A, FLNA, GLS, and TLN1, and its risk score predicted survival independently of six clinical factors. A combined clinical-genomic model beat either part alone, reaching a five-year accuracy measure of 0.805 in area terms. The signature validated significantly in two external cohorts, with a matching trend in a third. Single-cell data placed one gene mainly in malignant cells and two in fibroblasts, hinting at tumor-stroma crosstalk, and laboratory assays confirmed all four genes were raised in cancer cell lines.
pmc-13527131:
Zhong and colleagues introduce Unify in 2026, a machine learning method that compares single-cell gene data across species. Comparing cell atlases between species is hard because genes diverge over evolution and lab batches differ. Unify builds shared cell profiles called macrogenes, which group genes by function rather than by one-to-one matching.

The method blends gene activity data with embeddings, meaning numeric summaries, from protein and general language models. It removed batch effects while keeping real biological signals in species separated by over 700 million years of evolution. Unify also predicted how mouse cells respond to perturbations better across species and rebuilt more accurate cell-type family trees. The authors present it as a tool for evolutionary biology and cross-species genomics.
pmc-13527531:
Zhaowei Tong and eight colleagues test whether the liver drug ursodeoxycholic acid can blunt COVID-19 by lowering the ACE2 entry receptor. The drug inhibits a receptor that controls ACE2 levels. In their study, 142 patients received standard antivirals, and eighty-nine also took the bile acid drug for ten days.

ACE2 levels in blood and its gene expression in blood cells fell faster in the treated group. In cell culture the drug reduced ACE2 and blocked infection by a pseudovirus carrying a recent spike variant. Twenty-one inflammatory cytokines were significantly lower with treatment, consistent with calming the cytokine storm. The authors report improved clinical outcomes and propose the drug as an adjunct antiviral strategy.
pmc-13528031:
Parham Dastjerdi and eleven colleagues compare three treatments for a leaking mitral valve caused by heart failure in a 2026 meta-analysis. The options are a catheter clip procedure, surgical valve repair, and medicines alone. The team searched four databases for survival curves. They rebuilt patient-level data from sixteen studies holding 4,570 patients.

Clip patients were older and sicker than surgery patients at the start. Both procedures cut death risk versus medicines alone over up to five years. Surgery cut it the most. The clip carried higher risks of renewed leaking, reoperation, and late death than surgery. Still, clip patients had fewer hospital stays and fewer major events than the medicine group. The authors call the clip a strong option for high-risk patients, with surgery more durable.
pmc-13530231:
Andrea R Zammit and co-authors connect stable personality traits to molecular subtypes of Alzheimer dementia in a 2026 brain study. Traits such as worry proneness, loneliness, and sense of purpose predict dementia risk, but the biology underneath stayed obscure. Tissue data came from 822 donors in two long-running aging studies.

A molecular timeline and three dementia subtypes, first built from many data layers, held up in two fresh samples. Standard pathology, brain shape, and genetic risk set all subtypes apart from healthy brains yet failed to separate subtypes from each other. Traits still split the subtypes, suggesting personality-linked pathways act through metabolism.
pmc-13531531:
Peter Hanlon and co-authors argue in a 2026 primary care essay that naming the degree of frailty improves care for older people. Frailty means weakened resistance to shocks such as infection or a fall, plus slower recovery afterward. Clinicians often spot it by eye, so the authors ask what formal grading adds.

Severity changes prognosis and care needs sharply, so a mild score and a severe score should trigger different plans. Population tools can flag high-risk groups, while a nine-point bedside scale grades individuals during ordinary visits. Grading lets teams anticipate crises, plan ahead, and match support to what patients value.
pmc-13531831:
Bolin Chen and colleagues target in 2026 a protein that blocks cell cleanup and worsens scarring after chemical burns to the eye surface. Alkali burns trigger a growth pathway that overproduces scar material and clouds the cornea. A mouse burn model tracked the blocker protein LRPPRC over time and tested silencing it.

Burned corneas swelled, grew new vessels, and showed rising blocker levels by day 14. Gene silencing or inhibitor eye drops eased swelling and vessel growth, revived cleanup proteins, and quieted the scarring pathway. Human corneal cells in dishes responded the same way, supporting drop development.
pmc-13531931:
Obed Akwaa Harrison and colleagues measure in 2026 how much folate Accra mothers actually get from green leafy vegetables. Surveys covered 388 pregnant and nursing mothers in one Accra district, while lab tests measured folate in the leafy vegetables eaten locally, fresh and after brief steaming. Folate shortfalls drive birth defects in Ghana.

Intake ran low in both frequency and amount. Kontomire leaves led the menu, while three other greens were almost never eaten. Fresh leaves held rich folate levels, yet steaming destroyed anywhere from a small share to over three quarters depending on the vegetable.
pmc-13534531:
Nora S Siefert and colleagues characterise in 2026 the mammalian RAVE complex, a helper that assembles proton pumps on lysosomes and related compartments. These pumps acidify cell compartments so enzymes can break down waste, and yeast assembly was known while mammal control was not. Systematic tests mapped when and where the complex acts.

Under normal conditions the complex broadly supports pump assembly and acid levels. When a key nutrient sensor switches off, the complex moves to lysosomes and is required for a surge in breakdown activity. Loss of the complex left faulty lysosomes piling up inside cells.
pmc-13534731:
Huijie Zhou and colleagues report in 2026 that blocking XPO1, a cell export protein, weakens DNA repair and boosts radiation effect in extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma. The rare, aggressive lymphoma often resists radiation when disease returns. Tumour samples showed high XPO1 levels tied to worse survival.

Removing one copy of the gene impaired faithful repair, and the drug KPT-330 copied that defect and paired well with radiation. The drug traps a growth factor inside the nucleus, lowering repair genes. Two heavily treated patients responded to combined care with manageable side effects.
pmc-13536131:
Rasmita Shrestha and Aditya Shakya survey protective gear use among tea workers in Ilam district, Nepal, in a research paper from 2026. Tea processing exposes workers to many hazards, and gear only helps when worn fully. The team interviewed 269 workers face to face.

Most workers, about eighty-three percent, used at least one piece of gear. Only thirteen percent wore the complete set. The kind of work shaped use, and workers given a full free set by employers used gear far more. The authors urge employers to supply complete sets at no cost and to enforce their use, since partial gear leaves workers exposed.
pmc-13538331:
Jinrong He and seven colleagues wrote a review in twenty twenty-six that appraises how well trials of physical activity for people with neurodevelopmental disorders report harms. Guidelines more and more back exercise programs for this group. Yet trials often watch for and report harms in patchy ways, so the safety record stays thin.

The team searched five databases in November twenty twenty-five and ran three more rounds of snowball searching. Only trials with random assignment of physical activity programs counted. In all, three hundred nine trials, with 13,228 participants, were taken in. None of them fully met the CONSORT-Harms rules for watching and reporting harms. Most of those that did report harm spoke of sore muscles, mild pain, or unease. If harms stay out of sight while gains are plain, doctors and families cannot weigh the true balance of a program.
pmc-13539431:
Ng Boon Hau and eight co-authors trace a woman's vena cava compression to breast filler that had wandered, in a 2026 case report. Injectable fillers are sold as gentle alternatives to implants, but delayed migration is increasingly reported. The woman, in her fifties, developed facial puffiness and swollen chest veins. Scans elsewhere had found enlarged chest lymph nodes squeezing the superior vena cava, the great vein draining the head and arms.

A surgical biopsy showed chronic inflammation, and careful history-taking finally surfaced her earlier hyaluronic acid breast fillers. Later scans showed the nodes growing, with features suggesting migrated filler. The case warns that cosmetic history belongs in the workup of unexplained chest compression.
pmc-13539931:
Wenjiao Xu leads a 2026 study comparing how often a rare fetal heart position, mirror-image dextrocardia, appeared before and after China lifted COVID-19 controls in December 2022. In this condition the heart points right, mirrored from its usual place.

Ultrasound records from three Xi'an hospitals covered matching four-month windows in 2019, 2022, and 2023, backed by an online survey of pregnant women nationwide. A single case appeared in the 2022 window, while twenty-one cases appeared in early 2023 among a similar number of scans. The authors report this sharp rise and frame it as a signal needing careful follow-up rather than proof of cause.
pmc-13540831:
Guogang Xin and six colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a five-question scale that quickly gauges how school students feel about artificial intelligence. Schools adopting AI tools need a short, trustworthy attitude measure that fits large surveys.

Two samples of Chinese middle and high school students, totalling well over fourteen hundred respondents, completed the new AIAT-5 scale. Internal consistency was strong, and factor analyses supported a single underlying dimension with high loadings for every item. Attitudes correlated positively with knowledge of generative AI, curiosity, life satisfaction, and, notably, internet addiction scores. The authors present the scale as a practical instrument for tracking student views as classroom AI spreads.
pmc-13540931:
Hiroshi Ito and four colleagues survey, in a 2026 study, how medical representatives in Japan experience rude or unprofessional behaviour from doctors they visit for work. Communication between doctors and industry representatives shapes care quality, yet this relationship had rarely been studied from the representatives' side.

Ninety-eight representatives answered a web survey. Nearly nine in ten reported some problematic behaviour, most commonly doctors refusing to respond to work matters at all. Sexual harassment was reported by about fourteen percent, oftener by younger representatives and women. Long waits of over an hour before meetings touched nearly four in ten, especially the younger and less experienced.
pmc-13541231:
Nisha Arya and co-authors study how to bring diabetic eye care into two rural clinics in New York. Diabetic eye disease is the top cause of blindness in United States adults. Fewer than half of rural patients get the yearly screens that could save sight. The clinics tried remote image reads and pop-up eye clinics inside primary care.

Records for 885 adults with diabetes sorted patients by care path taken. Those seen on site were the most socially strained of the groups. Pop-up visits were kept at a rate near fifty-eight percent of bookings. Remote images came back readable in over ninety percent of cases. Patients called both paths a handy one-stop shop, and staff named workflow and booking snags.
pmc-13541831:
Meixner, Leo, and Sperlich argue that the VO2max number, the ceiling of oxygen use, tells only half an endurance athlete's story. The other half is glycolytic power: how fast muscles can flood the blood with lactate during maximal effort. Their 2026 study tested fifty cyclists with a ramp test for VO2max. On another day, a fifteen-second all-out sprint's blood samples yielded each rider's peak lactate accumulation rate, and the team measured endurance thresholds.

Holding VO2max constant statistically, riders with faster lactate accumulation hit their metabolic thresholds at lower power, with moderate-to-strong negative correlations across several thresholds. Adding the sprint measure to prediction models explained more of the threshold variation than VO2max and sex alone, while sprint work added little. The authors propose sprint lactate profiling as a complement to VO2max for setting training zones.
pmc-13542131:
Mohammad Rostami and Afsaneh Fatemi present, in a 2026 study, a faster object-detection system for spotting surface flaws on aluminium profiles during manufacture. Low contrast, glare, and stretched thin defects defeat standard detectors that read only the ordinary image.

Their design feeds a YOLOv8 detector three views of the same surface: the plain image, a wavelet view that exposes frequency patterns, and a filter view that stresses edges and texture direction. An attention module weighs the three streams for each defect type. On a public benchmark the system scored highest among rivals on both strict and lenient accuracy measures while running above one hundred frames per second, fast enough for production lines.
pmc-13542331:
Jiyeon Kang and Yujin Jeong chart how quality of life returns after intensive care in this 2026 study. Survivors often live with lasting limits, yet their paths differ widely. The team followed patients from nineteen intensive care units in four South Korean hospitals for two years after discharge.

A standard five-part health questionnaire was repeated over the follow-up for 609 survivors. Statistical grouping found three paths. About fifty-eight percent held steady near the national norm. About thirty-two percent stayed below par, with mobility and pain problems still present at two years. Ten percent stayed profoundly low across most areas of life. Older age, less schooling, and delirium during the stay raised the odds of the middle path. Multiple chronic illnesses and discharge to a care facility marked the lowest path. The authors advise follow-up care shaped to each survivor's likely path.
pmc-13543431:
Zhijing Zhang and co-authors published a 2026 study mapping T-cell exhaustion in colorectal cancer, where worn-out immune cells help tumours resist immunotherapy. Merging single-cell and bulk gene-expression data, the team traced how killer T cells slide along a spectrum of exhaustion inside tumours. Network analysis and ten machine-learning methods narrowed the signal to core genes, which were assembled into a risk score and checked in independent patient groups and in real tumour specimens.

The resulting score rests on five genes: KLF3, LMNA, SLC2A3, ARL4C, and TIMP1. High scores predicted poorer survival and a more immunosuppressive tumour neighbourhood. Laboratory staining confirmed the genes were expressed as predicted and sat alongside killer T cells in patient tissue. A five-gene readout of exhaustion could help clinicians sort colorectal patients by likely immunotherapy benefit and design combinations aimed at reviving tired T cells.
pmc-13543531:
In 2026, Dongsheng Ni and colleagues published a study asking whether PCSK9 inhibitors, powerful cholesterol-lowering drugs, carry any risk to thinking and memory. Worry persists because cholesterol matters to the brain and earlier evidence conflicted. The team triangulated three sources. One was reports in the United States adverse-event database. Another was Mendelian randomisation using genetic data from British and Finnish biobanks. The third was experiments in Alzheimer's-model mice given gene knockout or drug inhibition of PCSK9.

The reporting analysis found no raised signal for cognitive problems with these drugs, and a below-unity signal for Alzheimer's reports specifically, unlike statins, which did show signals. Genetic analysis found no causal link between mimicked PCSK9 inhibition and Alzheimer's risk. Treated mice cut their harmful cholesterol by over half with no loss of cognition, neuron integrity, or rise in brain plaques. Three independent methods converge on neurocognitive safety.
pmc-13543631:
Aron Kiros Bipsue, Hussen Mekonnen Asfaw, and Nete Tewfik Yusuf published a 2026 survey of delays in diagnosing and treating childhood cancer at Tikur Anbessa hospital in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Parents of 244 children, average age just over six, were interviewed about the road to care, and records were reviewed. Delays were split into family-side delay, over thirty days before seeking care, and health-system delay after reaching it.

Patient delay affected fifty-two percent of children, and system delay hit seventy-three percent. Children aged five to nine waited longer than toddlers, and rural families waited more than urban ones. Visiting a traditional healer first multiplied delay odds nearly eightfold. Inside the system, lacking insurance and the family's first contact point predicted hold-ups strongly. Fixing childhood cancer outcomes in Ethiopia, the authors argue, starts with shortening a journey that currently fails at both ends.
pmc-13544631:
Qi Wu and co-authors present FlexBIP, a flexible framework for predicting interactions between biomolecules, in a 2026 paper. Such predictions underpin cell biology and drug discovery, yet most tools handle one task or one data type, which limits their reach. Their design splits a molecule's own features from the web of connections it sits in, then fuses the two adaptively.

Node traits, link properties, and extra graph information can all enter as available. The same frame covers same-type and mixed-type interactions, plus yes-no, multi-class, and numeric predictions. Tests across fifteen benchmark datasets spanning eight task types are reported as strong.
pmc-13545631:
Jia-Wei Song and co-authors described in 2026 the care of a baby whose small intestine was blocked before birth by a thin membrane, a condition called type I membranous jejunal atresia. A 27-year-old woman was referred at about 26 weeks of pregnancy after scans suggested a fetal bowel obstruction. The team confirmed the finding with standard ultrasound and dynamic scanning rather than advanced three-dimensional imaging.

Genetic testing was done to rule out chromosome problems, even though such blockages usually follow a blood vessel accident in the womb rather than a genetic cause. Excess amniotic fluid in the case came from the blockage itself, which stopped fluid from passing through the gut. The report walks through imaging, surgery after birth, and the shared workflow meant to standardize care for similar babies.
pmc-13546531:
Ye Chen and colleagues searched in 2026 for molecular markers that track how far adenocarcinoma of the esophagogastric junction has advanced, since judging stage before treatment is difficult. Mining a public cancer database for genes that differ between tumor and normal tissue, they narrowed the field and verified two candidates, ASPN and LBH, in patient samples with staining tests.

ASPN ran high in tumors and rose further with stage, while LBH ran low and fell further as tumors advanced. A prediction chart combining both markers with sex, tumor size, and differentiation separated early from advanced disease with excellent accuracy. The authors present the chart as support for earlier, more personal treatment decisions.
pmc-13548331:
Lei Hou, Xiao-Hua Zhou, Fuzhong Xue, and Hao Chen introduce a two thousand twenty-six method for fairer causal inference from genetic data. Most large genetic studies draw heavily on European populations. Findings may not carry over to other ancestries.

Their framework, called TL-HDMR, transfers knowledge from data-rich groups to understudied ones. Two screening steps pick helpful source data and remove faulty genetic instruments. Simulations showed better accuracy than rival methods. Applied to stroke, the method surfaced metabolic signals across several ancestries. Readers interested in health equity get a concrete statistical tool for high-dimensional biology.
pmc-13548531:
Jian Wei and colleagues compare six antibiotics mixed into acrylic bone cement for fighting Gram-negative infections around joint implants, in a 2026 laboratory and animal study. Surgeons use such cement to hold implants and deliver medicine locally, yet no shared guidance exists on which drug to choose. Each antibiotic was loaded at high dose into cement samples for release, strength, and bacteria-killing tests over twenty-eight days.

Adding any drug weakened the cement somewhat, though most mixes stayed above the accepted strength threshold. Tobramycin released the most drug overall, while meropenem killed bacteria most strongly in the dish. Meropenem cement then went into rats with infected joint implants, where treated animals carried far fewer bacteria in surrounding tissues than controls. The authors frame the results as a starting point for cement selection in Gram-negative infections.
pmc-13550131:
Titze and three colleagues install a synthetic carbon path into a soil bacterium to eat ethylene glycol in twenty twenty-six. The feedstock can come from carbon dioxide or plastic waste. The path, called SAGA, runs poorly in the usual lab bacterium for energy reasons. The new host burns the feed with enzymes that do not run backward.

Gene cuts cleared rival paths and freed the needed helper pool. Carbon tracing counted how much product truly flowed through SAGA. Its share rose step by step with each fix. Slow glucose feeding lifted the total share further. Product yield fell at the leanest feed, a trade off to solve.
pmc-13550431:
Sura Abdulateef Al-Shammari and colleagues stack several learning machines into one heart disease predictor, in a 2026 study using a classic multi-site dataset. Single models often plateau on health records. The pipeline therefore runs a support vector machine and a convolutional network side by side. Together they extract two different kinds of features. One reflects class confidence, and the other captures layered local patterns. The merged features feed a neural network whose settings are tuned by a grey wolf optimization algorithm that mimics pack hunting.

Fourteen patient variables from the Cleveland, Hungarian, Swiss, and Long Beach collections supplied the tests. Accuracies ranged from about eighty-eight percent on the hardest set to ninety-six percent on the Swiss set, with statistical tests confirming gains over baselines. The authors argue heterogeneous feature fusion plus nature-inspired tuning sharpens early heart disease prediction.
pmc-13551531:
Elif Erbay and Çağdaş Erkan Akyürek published this 2026 study on forecasting ambulance demand and planning station capacity in Ankara, the capital of Türkiye. Minutes saved before hospital arrival can decide survival, so services must match ambulances to future demand. The authors worked from 943,412 cases handled by 139 ambulance stations, focusing forecasts on seven districts, and tested five forecasting methods from classical statistics to deep learning.

Yearly call totals crept upward across the period analysed. The ARIMA and neural-network autoregressive models forecast best, judged on standard error measures, with ARIMA especially reliable for short horizons. Forecasts then fed Monte Carlo simulations, which model uncertainty in call volumes and travel times, to find how many ambulances each station needs to hit response-time targets. The authors argue that pairing demand forecasts with simulation-based capacity planning improves both the speed and the reach of prehospital emergency care.
pmc-13553331:
Weiyang Xu and six co-authors published a 2026 trial of a sirolimus gel for children with superficial microcystic lymphatic malformations, vessel growths that form small blisters on the skin. Thirty patients aged 2 to 15 used a 0.2 percent gel twice daily for twelve weeks at one center. Doctors graded response from photos, exams, and symptom scores.

Every child improved somewhat, and 29 of 30 met the response bar. Pain scores fell clearly in those who had pain. In ten children with measurable growths, the largest diameter shrank from about 3.2 to 1.9 centimeters. Side effects stayed mild and local, and blood levels of the drug stayed very low. The authors call the gel effective and safe over the short term, with longer follow-up still needed.
pmc-13553631:
Haixiang Zhang and four colleagues review proof that germs can set off diseases in which the body attacks itself. Their 2026 review weighs population studies, clinic reports, and animal work side by side. Nine diseases receive close attention, among them lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome. Certain bacteria and viruses recur as suspects, including a common gut bacterium and the virus behind glandular fever.

Germs may fool the immune system by looking like body tissue, or by stirring it up as bystanders get hurt. In people primed by their genes, such hits can start lasting self-attack. Gaps still break the chain from that proof to useful care. The review maps what is known for work on early warning and targeted steps to block disease.
pmc-13554131:
Kunyi Huang and colleagues tested whether a green tea compound can protect the brain in obesity, publishing the study in 2026. Obesity is tied to shrinkage of the hippocampus, a memory centre, and to insulin resistance, both of which feed cognitive decline. An early clue came from UK Biobank adults with obesity, where higher green tea intake trended with larger hippocampal volume.

The team then gave mice on a high-fat diet a human-achievable dose of epigallocatechin-3-gallate, the main green tea catechin. Treated mice lost weight, showed calmer inflammation, better insulin sensitivity, less hippocampal shrinkage, and smaller memory deficits. The compound restored synaptic structure by quieting an inflammatory pathway, repairing insulin signalling, and switching on cellular clean-up, motivating dietary trials in people.
pmc-13554231:
Junyi Zhan leads an eleven-author team building a learning model to flag rebleeding risk after treatment for burst veins in the food pipe in a 2026 study. Such bleeding strikes people with scarred livers, and bleeding again within a year can kill. The team trained on 373 past patients and checked the model on 119 later ones. A pruning step picked eight key signs from the clinical data.

Eight learning methods raced, and a boosted-tree model won clearly. It ranked risk with high accuracy in both the training group and the fresh check group. The team placed the model on a web page for bedside use. Doctors can enter a patient's signs and get a personal one-year risk estimate to guide follow-up care.
pmc-13554531:
Diana Alfonso Vergel and co-authors present a study dated 2026 on kidney function in transgender people on hormone therapy. Doctors estimate kidney filtering rate from blood tests, but the formulas depend on sex. How that rate truly changes over time on hormones has not been fully mapped.

The team followed 166 patients treated at a hospital in Bogotá, Colombia, for up to thirty-six months. The group held ninety-four women and seventy-two men. For trans women, the rate held steady, and estrogen use linked to a higher rate. For trans men, the rate fell slowly month by month under both formula versions. Age affected the rate in both groups, as it does in the general population.
pmc-13555931:
Eustes Kigongo and four colleagues review world efforts to lift participation in screening for breast, cervical, and bowel cancers in a 2026 scoping study. Uptake stays uneven despite screening's power to catch cancer early. One hundred ten studies from 2016 to 2025 were sorted with two standard frameworks, one for barriers and supports, one for real-world performance. Ten kinds of intervention emerged.

Education, reminders, self-sampling, outreach, peer counselling, and media campaigns all featured. Combined packages of several tactics showed the greatest impact overall. Most trials, though, ran in tightly controlled settings, limiting how well results carry to daily practice. Gaps in cultural fit stood out plainly. The authors call for practical, culturally tuned, multi-part studies with longer follow-up.
pmc-13556031:
Ning Yang and Shui Jin built in 2026 a diagnostic model for colorectal adenomatous polyps, growths in the bowel that can turn cancerous if missed. Catching them early lowers cancer risk, so the pair looked for blood markers that might flag them without a scope. Their retrospective study compared 220 polyp patients treated at an Anhui hospital in 2023 with 220 healthy people examined the same year.

The groups differed in sex, age, body mass index, cholesterol and fat measures, and a panel of inflammation ratios drawn from routine blood counts. Stepwise analysis singled out sex, age, cholesterol, triglycerides, and one inflammation ratio as the useful signals. Combined into a model, these ordinary measures offered fair accuracy for spotting polyps. The authors present the model as an aid to early clinical identification, not a replacement for endoscopy.
pmc-13556231:
Shane McFarlin and eight colleagues published this 2026 study identifying the transferrin receptor, the cell's iron gate, as a co-receptor that parvovirus B19 uses to enter the blood precursors it infects. The virus causes aplastic crises and fetal hydrops, yet no antivirals or vaccines exist, because its entry route was unclear. Using a proximity-labelling enzyme, the team tagged host proteins during entry. They then tested candidates by gene knockdown and binding assays.

Transferrin receptor 1 stood out. Knocking it down in virus-permissive cells reduced viral entry and replication, and binding between the viral protein and the receptor's domain was confirmed. Blocking that contact, with an antibody against the receptor's tip or with the iron carrier ferritin, cut viral binding, entry and replication in lab-grown blood precursors. Mutating the binding regions abolished receptor binding. The authors establish the receptor as an entry partner and an antiviral target.
pmc-13558331:
Dan Cogălniceanu and colleagues map research on removing introduced fish from mountain lakes. Their systematic review from twenty twenty-six covers standing waters in mountains. Alien fish damage fragile mountain ecosystems built without them. Removal practice is far less studied than introduction harm.

Thirty-five publications met the review criteria for analysis. Most studies came from North America and targeted salmonid fish. Physical removal methods dominated the published attempts. Chemical methods formed the second largest group. Success varied with method, species, and lake character. No single approach worked everywhere, the authors conclude. Prevention and fast early action remain the safest strategy overall.
pmc-13558531:
Jiafeng Liang and nine colleagues asked in 2026 whether adding radiotherapy to immunotherapy improves results in advanced non-small cell lung cancer. Immune drugs are now a first treatment mainstay, yet resistance arrives for most patients, and radiation is known to stir immune responses. Their retrospective study covered 141 patients with stage IV disease at Hangzhou Cancer Hospital who received immunotherapy or chemoimmunotherapy, with or without radiation.

Patients who also received radiation went about twice as long before progression and lived considerably longer in the comparison. Benefit concentrated in non-squamous tumours and in patients who had not already cycled through immunotherapy once. Radiation given alongside or just after immune treatment helped more than radiation aimed only at symptoms. Severe lung inflammation after chest radiation stayed uncommon. The authors support testing the combination prospectively.
pmc-13558631:
Muhan Yu and thirteen colleagues reviewed in 2026 what happens when patients with metastatic breast cancer receive a second course of the cell-cycle drugs known as CDK4/6 inhibitors. These pills, paired with hormone therapy, are standard first treatment for hormone-sensitive, HER2-negative disease, yet progression and side effects force changes, and retreatment value was unproven. Records from two institutions covered 78 patients treated between 2018 and 2025 in three switching patterns.

Switching from one drug, abemaciclib, to another, palbociclib, gave the longest median time before treatment failed. Nearly two thirds of that group stayed on the second drug longer than on the first. Patients whose first course ended over side effects fared better than those whose cancer had progressed, while spread to internal organs predicted a poor retrial. The authors back selective retreatment and call for prospective trials.
pmc-13560231:
Flaminia Riggio and three colleagues review how extracellular vesicles from skeletal muscle carry signals to motor neurons, for better and worse.
