Their 2026 article synthesizes work on these tiny lipid-wrapped parcels, which ferry proteins, RNAs, and metabolites between cells. Muscle-derived vesicles help maintain the neuromuscular partnership in health.

In motor neuron diseases such as spinal muscular atrophy and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the same channel can turn pathogenic. Vesicles may deliver misfolded proteins and faulty RNAs that push neurons toward degeneration. The review weighs evidence for vesicles as couriers of disease spread along the muscle-nerve axis. It also evaluates their promise as diagnostic biomarkers readable from body fluids, and as therapeutic vectors that might one day deliver corrective cargo. The authors call for deeper mapping of vesicle contents in health and disease.
pmc-13562331:
K. Jinno and three colleagues report a 2026 prospective study on judging, before surgery, how hard a robot-assisted rectal operation will be. Working with 158 patients, the team split the operation into two stages, one for freeing the colon and one for freeing the rectum. Each stage received an anatomy-based difficulty grade from one to three. The authors then searched routine pre-surgery information for factors that could predict those grades.

For the colon stage, body mass index, sex, lung disease, and age gave a fair forecast. For the rectal stage, body mass index, sex, and prior combined chemotherapy and radiation gave a stronger one. The group turned the final formulas into a ready-to-use calculator. Surgeons could use such scores to expect trouble early and adjust their plan for each patient.
pmc-13562431:
Yuya Hamanaka and co-authors show how giant jumping genes reshaped a fungus tamed for food making in Japan, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. The fungus brews sake and ferments miso and soy sauce. Its wild kin makes toxins, so the tame form split off long ago. The jumping elements, called Starships, carry extra genes as cargo.

Cargo gains and losses during taming likely helped make food output safe and stable. Even strains with the same Starship class held unlike cargo mixes, tied to their food uses. The picture credits the elements with fast change under human selection. Readers see a hidden engine behind a kitchen workhorse.
pmc-13562531:
Yong Li and four colleagues build a lean vision network that helps robot boats spot small floating rubbish on water. Uncrewed surface vessels collect drifting waste, yet waves, glare, and shore shadows confuse ordinary detectors, and floating items are often tiny in the frame. The 2026 design, named SEBR-YOLOv8n, reworks a compact detector with a two-way weighted feature pyramid that boosts small targets. A transformer-based decoder and a refined box-matching loss sharpen the results further. The whole model holds only five million parameters.

On a standard floating-waste image set, the network reached detection scores of about 91 and 50 percent, beating its base model by roughly six and four points. A second dataset confirmed the gain, and images with synthetic extra samples scored higher still. The authors argue the design gives cleanup vessels sharp eyes without heavy computing hardware.
pmc-13562631:
Chuanzhong Liu and four colleagues study the minority of ovarian cancer patients whose main blood marker stays normal, and build a tool to predict their survival. Most epithelial ovarian cancers raise the marker CA125, so guidance built on typical cases may mislead them. The 2026 team pulled 13,068 patients from the United States SEER registry and added 138 patients from their own hospital as a check. Patients with normal levels tended to live longer.

A survival model drawn as a nomogram chart weighed what mattered most for the normal-marker group. Age counted, as did how far the cancer had spread, the tumour's tissue type, and whether lymph nodes were removed. Each factor adds points toward a personal survival estimate. The authors offer the chart as a counselling aid for a group that marker-based monitoring serves poorly, since their disease can progress without tripping the usual alarm.
pmc-13563731:
Ihab A. Naser and two colleagues ask whether belly fat in heart attack patients comes with higher levels of a molecule that chokes a protective vessel enzyme. The molecule, ADMA, blocks the enzyme that makes nitric oxide, the vessel wall's relaxing signal. Their 2026 cross-sectional study enrolled 120 patients with confirmed heart attacks, aged 30 to 65, at four government hospitals in the Gaza Strip during 2023. Waist size, body mass, blood fats, ADMA, and homocysteine were all measured, and 53.3 percent of patients met the waist cutoff for central obesity.

The centrally obese group carried clearly more ADMA, by 35.1 nanograms per millilitre, and more homocysteine, by 7.7 units, alongside worse cholesterol patterns. In the full regression, waist circumference was the only independent predictor of ADMA levels. The authors label the work exploratory: a single snapshot cannot prove that belly fat raises the molecule, so they call for studies that follow patients forward in time.
pmc-13565431:
Ruben Cuadros-Cuya, Victor Vergara-Rubín, and Ignacio Jauralde-Garcia swap fishmeal for fly larvae meal in pacu feed, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. They fed 320 young pacu for sixty days, swapping in zero, thirty, sixty, or one hundred percent of the fishmeal. First they measured how well the fish digest the full-fat larvae meal.

Digestion rates were high for protein, fat, and energy. Fish on the thirty percent swap grew as well as the control group. Higher swaps cut growth and feed use and thinned the gut wall. The team caps safe swap at thirty percent.
pmc-13567631:
Zhang, Liu, and Xie let AI propose formulas for how porous solids weaken in this study from twenty twenty-six. Porosity counts missing material but says nothing about broken load paths. The team simulated over ten thousand bonded-particle specimens across five defect families. Human investigators fixed the rules: allowed inputs, physical priors, and a strict size cap.

Language models suggested descriptor ideas, which the authors curated into a measurement bench. Simple fitted formulas with six descriptors beat a three-dimensional neural network on the test bench. On fresh specimens the formulas predicted stiffness decay better than strength decay. The authors float a two-stage failure idea from that gap. All evidence is numerical, pending lab validation.
pmc-13568231:
Thanh-Diane Nguyen, Donatien Grolaux, and Jean Vanderdonckt shape a shared gesture vocabulary for smart rings that control home devices. A ring can steer Internet of Things (IoT) gear with a flick, yet no one knew which gestures users link to which commands. A shared set must also suit a whole household, not one hand. Their 2026 framework, Oringano, builds that set from user input, step by step.

Thirty users coined gestures for 15 home actions, from selections and moves to media playback. Concrete actions drew strong agreement, while abstract ones split widely. Shared gestures beat personal ones on agreement by a wide margin, though users took longer to coin them. A phone app for managing the sets scored 4.5 of 5 for ease of use. The team ends with design rules for ring gesture sets a household can share.
pmc-13571331:
Yuta Kitagata and colleagues present, in a 2026 case series, a CT imaging method with radial cross-sections for planning repair of a leaking tricuspid valve. The valve's complex shape makes surgery hard to plan. Four patients with severe leakage had scans rebuilt into slices radiating around the septal leaflet, the anchor point of the method, using standard workstations.

The radial views mapped gaps where leaflets fail to meet, spots of prolapse, and how far leaflets are tethered down, amounting to a virtual rehearsal of the operation. All four repairs followed the scan plan and sharply reduced leakage. The team presents the method as a reproducible roadmap that any center with CT can adopt.
pmc-13571431:
Lab protocols that other teams can copy are the quiet backbone of drug research. Beatrice Masotti and co-authors publish one for measuring a Parkinson's-linked enzyme at work. The enzyme, LRRK2, tags a partner protein called Rab10, and that tag is a trusted readout of its activity. Their method counts tagged Rab10 spots inside cultured brain support cells with automated imaging. Steps cover cell growth, staining, image capture, and software analysis.

The protocol runs on a named high-content imaging system with its partner software. It adapts to other cells that make the enzyme. A scalable, shared method lets labs compare results on candidate drugs evenly. The authors frame it as a platform for studying the enzyme in health and disease.
pmc-13572331:
Carolin T. Lehner and colleagues tracked type 1 diabetes incidence in Bavarian children and adolescents from 2012 to 2021, publishing the claims-based study in 2026. Bavaria lacked a diabetes registry, leaving a gap in longitudinal monitoring for Germany's largest state. The team analysed routine insurance claims covering two million young people, identifying 5,762 new cases and comparing pre-pandemic years with 2020 and 2021.

Incidence rose on average 3.7 percent yearly in girls and 5.0 percent in boys, steepest in boys aged 0 to 4 and girls aged 15 to 19. Interrupted time-series analysis showed no clear pandemic jump for either sex, though one model hinted at a level rise for girls. The authors stress continued surveillance as incidence climbs.
pmc-13572431:
Abdelkadir Muzey Mohammed, with four colleagues, presents a 2026 model study of HIV spread tied to rape during the Tigray war in northern Ethiopia. The war ran from 2020 to 2022 and brought mass sexual violence, broken clinics, and lost health staff. Hard numbers on new infections from that violence have been scarce.

The team built a risk equation that links war intensity to rape rates, attacker counts, injury severity, and drops in preventive drug use and care. Data came from national statistics, UNAIDS, the World Health Organization, and past studies. The model gave a median of 122 new infections from mass rape, a median rise in incidence of 13.8 percent. The rise in overall prevalence was tiny, near 0.002 percent. The authors urge rape prevention, fast access to preventive drugs, and mobile clinics.
pmc-13573431:
Øivind Skeidsvoll Solvang, with three colleagues, presents a 2026 design study for a health record framework built around information flow, not apps. Patients with many conditions cross clinics and hospitals on winding paths, and their records scatter. Teams then miss parallel treatments and make weaker, less safe calls.

The team joined a scoping review with a deep read of 14 patient records from northern Norway that span 1954 to 2024. A 19-year sample journey, checked by clinicians, exposed repeat failures in how information moves. The design answers with layers that split user screens, path logic, and secure storage. Tokens that carry codes and pointers grant read-only virtual access to source records, with consent and audit built in. A test hospital stay showed timely alerts and governed access.
pmc-13575131:
Saleh Asnaashari, Sadegh Yousefi, and Maria P Nikolova use machine learning to predict density in 3D-printed metal parts in a 2026 study. The printing method, laser powder bed fusion, melts metal powder layer by layer. Part density depends on laser power, scan speed, and hatch spacing in tangled ways.

The team trained six models on 287 published measurements, ranging from a neighbour-based method to neural networks tuned four different ways. A committee system then blended the six predictions into one. The blended approach captured the link between settings and density well on standard accuracy measures. The authors caution that the mixed sources of the data, plus a few outlying values, add uncertainty to the forecasts.
pmc-13575631:
Xianxian Li and six co-authors pool trials on whether hard blood pressure lowering after a brain bleed curbs swelling around the clot. Their systematic review and meta-analysis was published in twenty twenty-six. That swelling marks secondary brain injury, but whether pressure control shrinks it was uncertain.

The team searched three databases to early twenty twenty-six for studies comparing intensive with standard lowering in spontaneous bleeds. Six studies fed the narrative part and four the pooled math, covering about two thousand patients in total. Bias was judged with a standard tool. The pooled estimate addresses swelling growth in the first day. The answer matters because pressure is one of the few levers doctors can pull in the first hours.
pmc-13576331:
Shaoyu Han and four colleagues test virtual reality training for a chest drainage procedure in a 2026 randomised trial with medical interns. Thoracentesis, drawing fluid from around the lung with a needle, is hard to practise on real patients safely. Twenty interns were split evenly between VR simulation plus theory and mannequin practice plus the same theory, over four weeks.

Scores were marked on a 300-point checklist covering steps before, during, and after the procedure. The VR group lagged at week two, a sign of early adjustment to the headset. By weeks three and four it pulled clearly ahead. At the end, 80 percent of the VR group reached the excellent band against 10 percent of controls. No adverse events occurred. The authors call the method a useful extra, while noting the tiny sample makes results preliminary.
pmc-13576631:
Katelyn Elizabeth Golden and co-authors present a case report, published in 2026, on a rare cancer of the nose and sinuses. The cancer is defined by a joining of two genes, named DEK and AFF2, and it can look harmless under the microscope while still acting in an aggressive way. The report describes one patient whose tumor had spread into the skull and the eye socket.

The patient was a woman aged sixty-seven whose tumor grew fast and invaded nearby tissue. Its cells looked bland and even resembled a benign growth, which made the case hard to read. RNA testing found the gene fusion and settled the diagnosis. Tests also showed a marker linked to immune therapy and few other changes. The authors stress that gene testing is key to naming this rare cancer correctly.
pmc-13577331:
Katherine Young and co-authors analyze a trial subgroup of patients with severe lung infection treated by a drug blend, in a study from 2026. The blend joins imipenem with relebactam, which shields it from bacterial defenses. The patients had hospital-acquired or ventilator-linked pneumonia, some caused by germs that resist imipenem alone.

Among 215 treated patients, 18 had germs that resisted imipenem but yielded to the blend. Their death rate at day 28 was 22.2 percent, close to the 18.8 percent for patients with imipenem-sensitive germs. Lab work on the isolates tracked the genes behind resistance. New resistance to the blend arose during care in only three patients. The authors read the blend as a sound option for these hard infections.
pmc-13578231:
Kyu Kwan Park and co-authors report a 2026 lab test of a laser driven ultrasound tool aimed at blood clots inside vessels. Clots can block flow and trigger strokes, yet judging a clot's size and breaking it up in a narrow spot remain hard tasks. Their setup uses a photoacoustic lens, which turns laser light into focused sound waves.

The longer lens reached deeper than earlier versions while keeping a tight focal spot. Listening to echoes with a water based sensor let the team tell clots apart by thickness down to a tenth of a millimeter in vessel-like models. Raising the laser energy widened the breaks the tool made, and computer models backed the way the sound pattern shifted with thickness.
pmc-13578331:
Chunxiang Xue and Zheng Gao build a 2026 vision system that watches football clips and calls fouls to back up referees. Fine calls hinge on small details of contact that human officials can miss at full speed. Their system reads three streams at once: how players look, how they move, and how their body joints track through the play.

A focus step zooms in on the key contact moment inside long clips. A calibration step then scales the stated confidence so the odds mean what they say. On more than twelve thousand pro match clips the system sorted five foul types with strong accuracy. Its calls also matched FIFA trained referees closely, and answers came fast enough to sit beside live video review gear.
pmc-13578731:
Rehana Rauf and colleagues fuse two deep learning designs to sort gut diseases from endoscope images, in a 2026 study. Gut cancers rank high among cancer deaths, yet early spotting saves lives, and single AI models often falter on new data or miss either fine detail or wide context. Their system pairs a layered pattern network with a patch based transformer that reads long range links.

Features from both models were merged by weight, then a tree growth search pruned the extras. The lean set fed standard classifiers. On two public image sets of four and eight thousand pictures across eight disease classes, accuracy neared ninety nine percent, with matching scores for catching cases and avoiding false calls. The authors offer the blend as a steadier second reader for scope exams.
pmc-13581431:
Liubov Govta and co-authors trace how a wheat resistance gene switches on defense programs against stripe rust. Their 2026 paper studies a fungal disease that constrains wheat output worldwide. The resistance gene came from wild emmer wheat and encodes a tandem kinase, a double-headed signaling protein.

The team compared resistant and near-identical susceptible lines over a week of infection. They combined tissue study, reactive oxygen measures, gene activity sequencing, and network analysis. The resistant line limited fungal growth and raised reactive oxygen. Thousands of genes changed activity, in waves: early signals tied to cell death at invasion sites, then later wall strengthening and defense chemistry. The timeline shows resistance as a staged program, not a single switch, which helps breeders judge durability.
pmc-13582031:
María Jiménez-Buedo questions two famous games used to measure generosity in a paper from 2026. In the ultimatum game, one player splits money and the other can reject the split. In the dictator game, the splitter decides alone. Many researchers treat results from these games as thermometers for fairness or altruism across cultures.

Jiménez-Buedo argues the traits these games claim to measure are loosely defined and shift between studies. That looseness breaks the claim that the games measure one stable thing. She traces both conceptual and practical problems behind the measurement view. Her verdict is that the games suit open exploration better than precise measurement. The paper urges care in how results are reported.
pmc-13582131:
Sultan Alhabdan and co-authors measure e-cigarette use among Scots with chronic lung disease, in a 2026 study. The disease, a long term blockage of air flow, is strongly tied to smoking. Vaping is promoted in Britain as a harm cutting step, but use among these patients was little described.

Survey data from 2018 to 2022 covered close to nine hundred adults with the diagnosis. About twelve percent now vaped. Use ran higher among current and former smokers than among those who never smoked. Younger age and poorer areas also tracked with use. Among smokers, women and younger adults vaped more. The results can shape quit support for this group.
pmc-13582331:
Yu Wang and Changqiang Si ask how grand heritage becomes a beloved character brand, using Mount Tai in China as the test case. Their study appeared in 2026. Sites want mascot-like figures, in the mold of famous regional characters, that carry culture into media and merchandise. The team built a scoring model to rank the mountain's cultural symbols, then surveyed audiences on how the chosen figures landed emotionally.

Person-like expression and emotional comfort in the designs strongly raised audience resonance. That resonance, in turn, strengthened cultural identity and the wish to buy and share. Grand narratives presented plainly did little. The authors say heritage travels when it is shrunk to a face people can feel for, a lesson for cultural tourism everywhere.
pmc-13583231:
Zhang and coauthors find a splicing factor that drives liver cancer growth. Faulty gene splicing is a hallmark of liver cancer. Which splicing factors drive cancer programs stayed largely unmapped. One factor, called RBM25, was high in liver tumors.

High levels tracked with poor patient outlook in the data. Cutting the factor slowed cancer in lab and mouse models. Patient-derived mini tumors also grew less without it. The factor steers splicing of a partner gene to a cancer form. That form then steadies a growth driver called YAP. The chain names new drug targets in liver cancer.
pmc-13583531:
Alon and Levkovich review how patients use generative AI tools to find health information in twenty twenty-six. Unlike web search, these tools give answers in a chat like form. That change can affect how users judge trust, check facts, and decide to see a clinician. The authors mapped the early research on this shift.

The review included twenty-seven studies from twenty twenty-two onward. People used the tools to judge symptoms, learn about conditions, and find care. Ease, clarity, and a personal feel helped use, as did comfort in asking. Lack of trust was the top barrier, mainly when sources were missing or hard to check. Privacy worries and weak prompting skills also held some users back.
pmc-13585331:
Raphael Lotan and colleagues compare two scan types for a neck condition in a 2026 study. Cervical myelopathy arises when a narrowed neck canal squeezes the spinal cord. MRI shows cord damage best, while CT shows bone best. Which one measures the narrowing more truly was still debated.

The team studied twenty patients who had both scans before surgery to widen the canal. At every neck level, CT reported larger canal and cord-sac areas than MRI. The two sets of measures agreed moderately to strongly for the canal itself. One CT measure, a small canal area low in the neck, tracked closely with signs of cord damage on MRI. The authors say CT gives the sharper picture of bony narrowing. Using both scans together, they argue, gives the fullest view before surgery.
pmc-13585831:
Stephan Seifert explains a data method for reading complex chemical measurements in this 2026 paper. Instruments such as mass spectrometers produce hundreds of readings per sample, and sorting samples is only half the job: knowing which readings drive the sorting matters just as much. His focus is a method called Surrogate Minimal Depth, built on random forest, a model that grows many decision trees.

Random forests hide stand-in variables inside their trees, and this method uses those stand-ins to judge not only each reading's weight but also how readings sway one another. That joint sway is framed as a supervised correlation score, tuned by the sorting task itself. Worked examples on several kinds of analytical data show how the method picks variables and maps their links for a clearer read of messy datasets.
pmc-13586031:
Vitória Karolina Brandão Souza and a large team test a safer cousin of the heart drug digoxin against brain inflammation. The new compound, called BD-8, comes from the same plant steroid family but was built to spare healthy cells. In their 2026 study, they checked it in lab-grown brain and immune cells, then in animals given a bacterial toxin that sparks brain inflammation and slows movement.

BD-8 harmed cultured cells only at doses far above those that hurt cells with plain digoxin. In the animals, it kept movement near normal, cut a marker of fat damage in two brain regions, and tuned the brain's own antioxidant enzymes. It also lowered the inflammatory signal IL-6 without touching a growth factor for neurons. Blood markers for heart, liver, and kidney stayed steady, which supports its safety case.
pmc-13586831:
Sakone Sunantaraporn and co-authors screen cave sand flies in northern Thailand for germs they may carry, in work from twenty twenty-six. Sand flies spread several germs of concern for people and animals. Caves shelter the flies and large bat groups, which can host many microbes.

The team caught more than six hundred flies in three caves in Chiang Rai and pooled them for gene tests. Screens covered viruses, blood parasites, and bacteria. Hits included a rhabdovirus and parasites that cause leishmaniasis and related diseases. Two pools held a blood parasite genus called Hepatocystis, a first find in Thai cave sand flies. No Bartonella was found. The work maps germ range in cave systems.
pmc-13587031:
Yi Li and four co-authors review measures of insulin resistance used to judge fatty liver disease tied to metabolic trouble, in a paper from twenty twenty-six. The disease, now the world's most common chronic liver condition, has insulin resistance at its core. Clinicians use a range of blood-based scores and indices to gauge it without invasive tests.

The review sums up how far each indicator has gotten in clinical assessment, and where each falls short in practice. The authors look ahead to sharper non-invasive markers, models that fuse several layers of biological data, and care tailored to the individual patient. Their aim is better management of the disease and better outcomes for patients.
pmc-13587131:
Minghui Yu and four colleagues review how gut microbes differ across three locations in colorectal cancer. Their twenty twenty-six review compares microbes found in feces, on the gut lining, and inside tumors themselves. Studies often mix these sample types, which the authors say produces inconsistent findings. A sample's location shapes what its microbes can reveal.

Each niche has its own makeup and formation mechanisms, and the niches influence one another. The authors propose a model of seed banks, colonizers, and specialized populations to describe the hierarchy among them. Sorting samples by location could make findings more reproducible. That in turn would help microbes serve early detection, prognosis, and treatment decisions in colorectal cancer care.
pmc-13588531:
Tianfang Shao and six co-authors test prediction models for drug resistance in tuberculosis across countries in a 2026 study. Fluoroquinolone antibiotics anchor the modern short treatment for drug resistant TB, so knowing resistance early shapes the regimen. Where fast lab tests are missing, models using patient traits could fill the gap, but most were built inside one country.

The data held over five thousand patients from eight countries, about a third of them fluoroquinolone resistant. The team compared three strategies: one pooled model, country specific models, and models trained on some countries and tested on held out ones. Three algorithm families were tried. The cross country checks show how far such predictions travel geographically.
pmc-13588631:
Mengjiao Liu and four co-authors link how easy an AI practice system feels to how deep nursing students engage, in a 2026 journal article. The path runs through two mind states: stray load, the wasted effort a clunky tool adds, and flow, the lost in it feel of good work.

The team surveyed 2,016 nursing students online, with help from teachers at sixteen colleges who passed the link on. Set scales fed a path model with re sampling checks. Easy use went with low stray load and high engagement. Low load went with more flow, and flow with more engagement, so the chain held in order. The load to flow link ran stronger in students less at home with tech. Since all was read at once, cause stays open.
pmc-13588831:
Subin Na and two colleagues ask what makes mental health workers good at helping clients recover. This kind of care prizes client autonomy, hope, and community life over symptom control alone. Their 2026 survey drew anonymous answers from 188 practitioners in United States organizations serving adults with serious mental illness. A model then tested how cultural humility, recovery attitudes, and hands-on recovery skills fit together.

Cultural humility, meaning steady self-reflection and fair partnership with clients, went hand in hand with warmer recovery attitudes, which in turn tracked stronger hands-on skills. Attitudes carried a bit over half of humility's total effect, and the pattern held across age, background, and job lines. The authors urge clinics and team leads to build this humility first, calling it the root of good recovery practice.
pmc-13589731:
Phanthipha Laosam and co-authors review healing peptides drawn from slaughterhouse blood. Blood proteins are a vast, cheap stream that meat plants mostly waste. Cutting them with enzymes frees short chains with real biological effects. Reported actions span antioxidant, calming, and blood-pressure and blood-sugar control.

The review links each peptide's shape to what it does in the body. Species of origin shift the activity in ways past work left scattered. Proline and water-shy building blocks help peptides survive digestion intact. Bleaching the red pigment widens food uses for the source protein. The authors frame blood peptides as a green ingredient class for future foods.
pmc-13591131:
Zhiling Lu and colleagues published a 2026 review of a long non-coding RNA in human cancer. Such RNAs regulate genes without making proteins. This one sits opposite a growth-related gene. Evidence links it to many tumor types. It often helps cancers grow and spread.

The RNA soaks up smaller regulatory RNAs. That frees their target genes to act. Key signaling pathways shift as a result. Effects include faster division, invasion, and drug resistance. In one lung cancer type it suppresses tumors instead. Its levels track patient outcomes closely. A marker with two faces needs careful, cancer-specific reading.
pmc-13591331:
Stomach cancer kills many people worldwide, and tumors that resist treatment often rewire how they use energy. Xiangyang Wang and co-authors review how that metabolic rewiring shapes the immune landscape inside the tumor. Cancer cells, support cells, and immune cells compete for the same fuels.

The tumor burns sugar fast and floods its surroundings with lactate, while starving immune cells of key nutrients. Killer T cells weaken in that hostile mix. Suppressor cells, by contrast, thrive there. Four waste and signal pathways feed into the same immune checkpoints, forming a self-reinforcing circuit of suppression. The review surveys drugs that block sugar use, amino acid breakdown, or these waste signals, often paired with immunotherapy. The authors stress that a treatment helping one cell type may hurt another, so mapping metabolism in place matters.
pmc-13591731:
Jiahao Lv and five colleagues test, in 2026, whether aerobic exercise can ease muscle wasting in mice carrying tumors. Cancer cachexia, the wasting syndrome, thins muscle through swelling, metabolic upset, and tissue breakdown. Mice with colon tumors were split into rest and treadmill groups, with healthy controls beside them. After four weeks the team weighed a calf muscle and read its gene activity in bulk.

Tumor mice lost muscle weight and showed jumbled fibers. Exercised tumor mice regained weight and trended toward healthier tissue structure. Gene patterns tied to swelling and protein breakdown, raised by the tumor, partly reversed with exercise. A gene called S100a8 stood out as a hub candidate, though Lv and the team say its role needs proof.
pmc-13592331:
Yaying Zhan and ten co-authors study hormone dips during fertility treatment and their link to pregnancy, in a paper published in twenty twenty-six. In IVF cycles, the hormone estradiol is pushed high to grow eggs. A dip before the trigger shot is common, but whether it hurts outcomes was poorly understood.

The team reviewed over eleven hundred patients treated at one center across two years. Hormones were measured at the start and at trigger day, and any dip between checks was scored as a percentage fall. Patients were grouped by whether they conceived and whether they had a live birth. The link between dip size and outcome bent rather than running straight, the title notes. The records give clinics a base for judging when a dip should change plans.
pmc-13593131:
Qi An, Yuxuan Tao, Peiguo Wang, and Zhongqiu Wang report a rare nasal cancer that replied more than once to joined care. Their case report, from twenty twenty-six, deals with NUT carcinoma. This cancer is scarce and fierce, and proof to guide care is thin. The patient was a forty year old woman sent on after a nasal mass was cut out. Her course then took in eye pain, head pain, loss of sight, and spread to spine and chest.

Tests backed the NUT call, with a high growth index. Care joined radiation with other modes in rounds. The tumor shrank back more than once on that path. Readers learn how a rare midline cancer can run and how repeat multi mode care can hold it for spans.
pmc-13594531:
Chen and ten co-authors identify a group of stress-hormone neurons that drives fear to spread beyond the place where it was learned. Such fear generalization is a core feature of post-traumatic stress and related disorders. The neurons sit in a small brain region called the dorsal bed nucleus of the stria terminalis.

Strong shock training made mice freeze in both the training room and a similar room. The neurons fired around the start of freezing in both settings. Silencing them reduced generalized freezing, while activating them increased it. Blocking their hormone receptor in the same region also cut freezing. The authors name this circuit as a key driver of generalized fear.
pmc-13594631:
Mattia Pravato and colleagues published a 2026 study of egg-laying hens in tiered housing. Four hundred fifty hens lived in two pens. Video recorded their behavior across three months. January, March, and June brought different indoor climates. Observers scored behavior every fifteen minutes.

Ground pecking dropped in January cold. Preening and scratching rose instead. Dust bathing and piling peaked in March. Perching on tiers was commonest in cold months. Resting patterns shifted modestly with season. Overall, hens used the tiers sensibly. Daily rhythms stayed consistent across climates. Housing design should protect this natural repertoire year-round.
pmc-13594931:
Jaejun Lee and colleagues combined an ultrasound stiffness measure of the liver with a simple blood-based score. The pairing was meant to forecast when chronic liver disease will tip into decompensation. That failure stage is marked by fluid buildup and bleeding. Their two-center study followed 2,759 patients who had shear wave elastography between 2019 and 2025.

Stiffness alone predicted trouble well, with readings above a chosen threshold marking clearly higher risk. The blood score, built from albumin and bilirubin, added independent information rather than duplicating the scan. A blended formula the authors call SALBI beat both parents and a standard severity score in training and test groups. A simple three-tier grouping also separated patients sharply. Their risks of decompensation differed more than sixteen-fold. The authors propose the combined score as a practical clinic tool for deciding who needs closest watching.
pmc-13597831:
Amparo Guemes leads a team that compares thin film nerve cuffs. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with peripheral nerve recording. Shop bought rubber cuffs are the standard tool for this.

Thin film cuffs bend well, shrink small, and flex their layout. Both cuff types were placed side by side on rat nerves. Signals came from pain muscle tests and ankle moves. Noise ratios did not differ in a clear way. Thin films more often tagged signals as inbound ones. They look like a real rival to shop cuffs.  Both were tested under sleep drugs in rats.
pmc-13598231:
York and co-authors report the first clean isolation of a hard-to-study bacterial enzyme, in this 2026 paper. The enzyme, called BchE, helps build bacteriochlorophyll, the pigment some bacteria use to harvest light. It performs a six-step oxidation that closes a ring in the pigment, without oxygen.

Earlier work showed the enzyme needs vitamin B12, another helper molecule, and a strong reducing agent, but it fell apart outside cells. The team found a way to purify it in active form and study its spectra. With the pure enzyme in hand, they rebuilt its reaction in a test tube and watched the pigment product form.
pmc-13598631:
Yovita Hartantri and co-authors published this case report in 2026. It tells of a 64-year-old man with undiagnosed diabetes who arrived with fading consciousness and spreading dead tissue across the back of his head and around one eye. He was in septic shock with kidney injury and heart rhythm problems. The first diagnosis was necrotizing fasciitis, a bacterial flesh-eating infection, backed by an early fungal smear that came back negative.

Antibiotics and surgical removal of dead tissue followed. Wound cultures then grew a drug-resistant bacterium, which seemed to confirm the bacterial story. Only later did tissue culture reveal the true cause: mucormycosis, an aggressive fungal infection. The antifungal drug started late, and the man died on the twelfth day. The authors urge doctors to suspect the fungus early in diabetics with fast-spreading dead tissue, and to biopsy deeply rather than trust one negative smear.
pmc-13598931:
Haixia Cui and co-authors propose a simpler way to deliver lattice radiation therapy. The technique peppers a tumor with high-dose spheres. Low-dose valleys separate the spheres. The pattern exploits the contrast between them. Standard planning uses heavy optimization that is slow and can blur the intended peaks and valleys, so the team tested arranging the spheres in a non-flat, three-dimensional pattern with dynamic conformal arcs.

Water phantom experiments compared several sphere geometries, and a one-centimeter sphere spaced four centimeters apart balanced dose contrast against valley sparing best, with all plans keeping complexity low. The same recipe was then applied to two patients with gastrointestinal stromal tumors to check organ sparing and planning time. The authors conclude the geometric approach is feasible and far simpler than inverse optimization, preserving the peak-to-valley structure that makes lattice therapy attractive for bulky tumors.
pmc-13599531:
Padmaja Nagabhyru leads a seven-author team profiling the chemical arsenal of a fungus living inside a forest grass, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Epichloë fungi inhabit grasses and manufacture alkaloids that deter grazing animals. Wild populations are rarely surveyed comprehensively.

The grass was bearded shorthair, a woodland species in Kentucky; its partner fungus passes through seeds. High-resolution mass spectrometry methods were refined to detect and quantify the alkaloids quickly. Six grass populations were profiled. Chemotypes carried two or three alkaloids from a known set. Such chemistry varies between populations, shaping which insects and herbivores the grass resists. Understanding natural variation informs both ecology and forage breeding, where protective fungi are deliberately introduced.
pmc-13601831:
Ziyi Zhu and Shumin Li report in 2026 a blood study of an immune signal in asthma. Asthma involves tangled networks of immune messengers, and OX40 ligand helps switch on the Th2 arm, the arm most tied to allergic airway inflammation. Whether blood levels of this molecule track with the wider activation pattern was unclear. The pair measured it alongside many immune factors in 82 asthma patients and 40 healthy controls.

Multiplex testing captured Th2, Th17, inflammatory, and calming mediators, plus chemokines and total IgE, while breathing tests measured lung function. Correlation and regression analyses searched for factors tied independently to OX40 ligand levels. Framing the molecule as a biochemical regulator, the authors place it inside the network rather than treating it as a lone marker. Their analysis shows how a single co-stimulatory signal relates to the broader immune activation profile driving asthma symptoms.
pmc-13603431:
Bingfeng Zheng and co-authors review materials that deliver nutrients and active compounds to the right place in farm animals, in a paper from 2026. In feed, many useful compounds break down during processing, storage, or passage through the gut. That waste lowers the value animals get from their feed.

Carriers such as nanoparticles, microcapsules, and gels can shield a compound and release it at the right site and pace. The review lists how each carrier type is made, from gel setting and spray drying to fiber spinning. It also covers how the products are checked, from size measures to imaging in live animals. Uses in poultry, pigs, and cattle are reviewed, with stress on gut health and immune support.
pmc-13604731:
Richárd Tóth and co-authors survey why women in Hungary do or do not attend cervical cancer screening, in a 2026 study. Screening catches the disease early, yet attendance depends on more than access and awareness. The team asked about past care experiences and how doctors talk with patients about the test.

The survey gathered 5,196 women through a patient charity campaign, social media, and paper forms in communities, between late 2023 and late 2024. About 60 percent had been screened within the past year, while 3.5 percent had never gone. Attendance peaked among women aged 25 to 54 and fell off at younger and older ages. Talking about screening with family and friends went with more recent attendance. The authors argue that good experiences and clear talk from physicians help keep women coming back.
pmc-13604931:
Bhupendra Singh Rawat leads a twelve-author team reporting in 2026 an iron-based route to healing the inflamed bowel. These bowel diseases involve disturbed gut microbes and disordered iron handling. The hormone hepcidin promotes healing partly by blocking ferroportin, the channel cells use to export iron. Which cells' channel matters was unknown. Profiling mouse and human colon tissue, the team found the working channel concentrated in resident immune cell groups.

In mice, a rare colon-resident macrophage type carried especially high levels of it. Delivering hepcidin to the colon hit the macrophage channel without upsetting whole-body iron balance. That targeted strike reshaped the gut microbiome and sped recovery after gut injury. The authors' model holds that problem bacteria depend on macrophage-supplied iron, and cutting that supply lets the gut lining heal. They present colon-targeted channel blockade as a treatment window worth developing.
pmc-13606031:
Dany Millones-Liza and five colleagues published a consumer study in two thousand twenty-six on Andean grains among young Peruvians. Grains like quinoa and tarwi are nutritious local heritage foods. Yet young adults eat them only now and then, and the reasons were not well mapped.

Over one thousand consumers answered a structured survey. Quinoa led by far, eaten by about eight in ten; tarwi trailed under one in ten. Most buying and eating was occasional, usually raw grain from local markets for home cooking. Health value and naturalness drove purchases most, with cultural identity a secondary pull. Price, not knowing how to cook the grains, and lack of time were the top barriers.
pmc-13606431:
Achraf Ammar and colleagues published a survey study in 2026 on social participation across Mediterranean countries. Joining in social life is an important part of health. Its links with daily habits and mental state were rarely studied together. The data came from the multinational MEDIET4ALL survey.

Over four thousand adults in ten countries answered the survey. A short questionnaire measured their social participation. The team then tested many possible correlates at once. These included diet, movement, sleep, psychology, and technology use. Layered statistical models separated stronger links from weaker ones. Extra checks looked at differences by sex and region. The study aims to show which everyday factors travel with an active social life.
pmc-13607331:
Zayana Ali and five colleagues review how gene-activity reading at scale has changed bone study. Bone constantly remodels through teamwork among stem cells, bone builders, bone eaters, and immune cells; older methods could not capture that complexity. Their review walks through four tool generations, from bulk RNA sequencing, which averages whole tissue, to single-cell sequencing. Spatial methods keep location, and multi-omics designs layer several data types at once.

Each method carries flaws: bulk blends signals, single-cell loses spatial context, and computing is heavy. Spatial and multi-omics approaches add position, epigenetic, protein, and metabolite data. The authors see the payoff in sharper biomarkers, new drug targets, and more personal bone treatment.
pmc-13609331:
Anja Milosavljević and co-authors published this 2026 study of a virus that attacks sugar beet in Serbia. The virus causes rhizomania, a root disease that cuts yields worldwide. Over three years, the team sampled 72 fields across 31 places in the main beet-growing regions.

The virus turned up in about a quarter of the samples, many from beet bred to resist it. Gene reading sorted the Serbian strains into five variants of a key protein, all within the European A-type family, close to Italian strains. One field held a variant known for breaking the main resistance gene. The team also found a fifth RNA segment, of the J type, in Serbia for the first time, a find with real weight for breeders.
pmc-13609531:
Maulet Meruyert and four colleagues bake protective metal coatings in a vacuum to see how their internal phases rearrange. At 800 degrees, diffusion switched on and new nickel-aluminum and chromium phases formed. By 900 degrees the coating had homogenized further while keeping β-NiAl central, and roughness bottomed out. At 1000 degrees, chromium and nickel oxides appeared and the coating mingled with its iron-bearing base. The 1100-degree treatment brought the deepest change: alumina and spinel oxides formed, and a mixed transition zone with small voids appeared. The authors map these thresholds so engineers can pick temperatures that stabilize the coating.
pmc-13610531:
Dai Shi and co-authors review, in 2026, imaging tracers that target the immune cells living inside tumors. Macrophages inside tumors offer a workaround: they are plentiful in nearly all tumors and carry distinctive surface targets. Trials of immune treatments aimed at these cells make measuring their targets without biopsy a pressing need. The review sums up the candidate targets and the tracers built to image them. Better imaging could guide both diagnosis and immune therapy choices.
pmc-13611931:
Wenzhuo Ran, Xiaozhou He, and Deng Luo use broad viral sequencing to map co-infections in children with RSV in work dated two thousand twenty-six. RSV is a top cause of chest infection in young children. Standard tests check a short list of viruses, so other viruses in the same child can be missed.

Nine more human respiratory viruses showed up across the group, some outside routine test panels. Most samples held at least three viruses, and one held seven. What those extra finds mean for illness is still unclear, and the authors call for forward-looking studies.
pmc-13612931:
Akihiro Matsumoto and co-authors test carbon electrodes in light-powered retinal implants in work dated two thousand twenty-six. Such implants aim to restore sight by sparking the retina with tiny solar cells. The team built silicon arrays with forty and two hundred micrometer pixels, each a small solar junction.

Fresh carbon, baked from a precursor, served as the electrode, a first for this field. Single pixels gave up to half a volt under near-infrared light despite the harsh baking step. On mouse retina tissue, light pulses from the implant raised nerve firing clearly, at strengths matching natural white light replies. A channel blocker then silenced the signals, proving they were biological. Pig retina tests with pillar-shaped carbon electrodes also fired nerves.
pmc-13614131:
Disnel Ferrera-Carracedo leads a team reporting in 2026 on light-emitting materials built around copper iodide clusters wrapped in crown-shaped host molecules. Tuning such phosphors is hard, since their glow depends on the snugness of the surroundings.

The team paired the cluster with a ring molecule called 18-crown-6 and three ammonium partners of growing size and water-repelling character. With the cluster kept the same while the frame changes, the work gives materials designers a knob they can turn to tune colour and brightness.
pmc-13615031:
Arnav Barve and colleagues review in 2026 fractures of the transverse processes, the small wing-like bones sticking out from each vertebra, in professional athletes. These breaks are usually classed as minor and stable, yet for a pro athlete they can wreck training and force hard choices about when to play again. Even a stable break can hide other injuries, so full scans matter, and CT imaging stays central despite newer MRI tricks. The review lays out treatment, rehab steps, and return-to-play thinking in one place. Team doctors get a grounded path from diagnosis to a safe comeback.
pmc-13615731:
Drozdzewska, Burde, Müller, Merle, and Gehlen test in twenty twenty-six a cell-growth enzyme as a blood and body-fluid marker for horse lymphoma. The enzyme's blood level had given mixed results for this cancer, and fluid from body cavities was untested. Both measures ran higher in lymphoma horses, and each separated the groups fairly well at set cut-offs. Fluid levels exceeded blood levels overall, yet the two did not track each other, so they carry different information. The authors say both aid diagnosis but neither suffices alone. Samples came from routine workups at referral hospitals.
pmc-13616131:

Four months later, firm nodules grew on both sides of the scar. A wider second surgery with on-the-spot margin checks cleared it, and staged repair followed. pmc-13616531:
Giuseppe Barberis Barcia, Inés Toranzo-Nieto, Verónica González-Calle, and seven colleagues report, published in 2026, a heart disease hiding inside a family screening. One scan hint suggested an infiltrative disease rather than inherited muscle growth. A bone scan found no trace of the amyloid type. Blood protein tests, though, showed a skewed light-chain ratio.

That clue led to a heart tissue biopsy, which proved AL amyloidosis. In this disease, a plasma cell clone makes protein that folds wrong and clogs organs. Heart involvement drives the outlook, and early finds are rare. The man started a four-drug regimen. The authors stress two habits: use every imaging tool, and always screen blood proteins when heart walls thicken without a cause.
pmc-13616831:

Of those, 1,199 cases built the score, which combines a physiology score and an operation severity score through standard modelling. The rest served to validate it against rival systems. A tailored, current score could help surgeons counsel families honestly and aim scarce intensive care at the patients most likely to crash after surgery.
pmc-13617131:
Joanie Theriault, Anick Sauvageau, Catherine Briand, and Johana Monthuy-Blanc describe building a college course with the people it serves. Their twenty twenty-six article comes from Quebec's first Recovery College, where courses support mental health recovery. The course at hand concerns eating attitudes and behaviors.

The build ran in three phases: joint production with trainers who have lived experience, a validation round with a mixed-expert group, then a trial run with four learner groups over a year. Sessions, journals, and interviews were analyzed. Blending lived, clinical, and theory knowledge took set practices: open debate, clear roles, and shared tools. The process improved both the course and the trainers' own skills.
pmc-13618331:
Manoj Kumar and three colleagues build a germanium-oxygen dimer that opens routes to rare germanium compounds, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Heavier cousins of carbonyl compounds are hard to pin down. Their double bonds to oxygen are unstable. A brace-like ligand holds the germanium atoms steady here.

Adding a strong acid partner let the team trap a germanium version of phosgene. It is the first such compound steadied this way. Stripping chloride from the dimer gave a family of charged rings instead. Their cores form a flat square of germanium and oxygen atoms. Tests and math show the bonds are single and lopsided, not double. The brace ligand's strong giving power makes these species reachable. New germanium chemistry follows from the platform.
pmc-13618931:
Marcela C. Tozzo and seven colleagues test whether merely looking at pictures of shoulder movements unsettles the autonomic nervous system of people with chronic shoulder pain. The team tracked heart rate variability, blood pressure variability, baroreflex sensitivity, pressure pain thresholds, and self-rated pain before, during, and after.

Some interaction effects appeared in baroreflex effectiveness, while other variability measures did not separate the groups, and self-rated resting pain did not change. The authors read the pattern as evidence that even imagined or observed movement engages the emotional machinery that shapes pain perception in chronic shoulder pain.
pmc-13619431:
Hussain Almohammed and co-authors pool past trials to compare two clot-busting drugs for stroke, in a review from two thousand twenty-six. One drug is tenecteplase and the other is alteplase, the long-used standard. The team searched five large databases for trials and ward studies in adults with blocked-vessel stroke.

Twenty-four studies with more than twenty thousand patients were pooled. The newer drug gave a slightly better chance of full recovery at three months and a faster start to care. Deaths were lower in ward studies but not in strict trials alone. No clear safety gap was found. Readers get a balanced view that still calls for more strict trials.
pmc-13619631:
Oliver Vij and four colleagues analyzed exam questions from an online dentistry question bank to learn what makes a question sort strong students from weak ones. Their dataset held nearly forty-five thousand first attempts by seventy-six consenting students. Careful analysis focused on 691 dental materials questions, each answered by at least thirty students.

Questions of middle difficulty separated students best, matching a curved pattern rather than a straight line. Questions whose wrong answers attracted real choices also discriminated better, measured both by count of working distractors and by how evenly choices spread. Yet repeated split checks showed single-question scores jumping around a lot. The authors advise teachers to treat item statistics as an early warning that prompts review, not as a final verdict on a question.
pmc-13621131:
Li Li and Yuchao Hao review a weight-loss drug's second life in a 2026 paper. It also improves blood sugar control and heart risk factors. Its gut side effects, though predictable, often erode patient adherence.
